# Palbase — full documentation

> Palbase — the backend for apps. Every project has auth, storage, realtime,
> flags, notifications, secrets, analytics, AI and purchases, called from web
> apps with the publishable key (`palbase/web`), from iOS (Swift) and Android
> (Kotlin) with the native SDKs, and from servers with the secret key
> (`palbase/server`). Your own backend runs on a machine built from a GitHub
> branch on every push, beside a Postgres database of its own. Backends are
> `palbase/backend`: `@Controller` classes whose methods are routes,
> `@Injectable` services that arrive by constructor, a `@Module` that lists what
> exists, `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule)` in `src/main.ts`, and the schema
> declared with Palgres in `src/db/public.ts`. A push to the branch is the
> deploy; the CLI (`npx palbase`) does the rest — client apps, the purchase
> catalog, environments, tokens.



<!-- ===== getting-started/introduction ===== -->

# Introduction

Palbase is a backend platform in two halves. **Every project has a set of modules** — auth, storage, realtime, flags, notify, secrets and analytics — that an app uses with no backend of its own, the way it would use Firebase: sign users in, keep their files, push them messages, read flags, count events. And when a project needs code of its own, it runs on **machines** built from a GitHub branch on every push, beside **Postgres databases** of its own — with a TypeScript framework, `palbase/backend`, that is made for exactly that.

You can use either half without the other. Most projects start with the modules from an app, and add a backend when a rule has to live somewhere an app cannot change it.

## A taste

An app signs a user up with the project's publishable key:

```ts
// app/signup.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const palbase = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

const { user } = await palbase.auth.signUp({ email: "ada@example.com", password: "a passphrase of fifteen+" });
console.log(user.id);
```

A server — any server — sends that user an email with the secret key:

```ts
// server/welcome.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

await palbase.notify.sendEmail({ body: { to: "ada@example.com", subject: "Welcome", text: "Glad you are here." } });
```

And a backend of your own is a class whose methods are routes, served on a machine:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Database, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  // Every route needs a signed-in user unless it says otherwise; @User() is them.
  @Post("")
  async create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Promise<{ id: string }> {
    const [row] = await Database.$query<{ id: string }>("insert into notes (owner, title) values ($1, $2) returning id", [user.id, body.title]);
    return row;
  }
}
```

Push it to its branch, and the machine builds it and rolls it out beside the version that serves. The [Quickstart](/docs/getting-started/quickstart) does all three, end to end.

## What every project has

| Module | What it does | From an app (publishable key) | From a server (secret key) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **auth** | Users, sessions, passwords, passkeys, second factors, magic links, phone codes, social sign-in, test users | [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth) | [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication), [Test Users](/docs/backend/test-users) |
| **storage** | Buckets and files, public reads, signed URLs, image renditions | [Uploads](/docs/web/uploads) — through a URL a server signed | [Storage](/docs/backend/storage), [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads) |
| **realtime** | Channels over one socket: broadcasts, shared state, presence; a backend's gateways | [Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime), [Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways) | [Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime), [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways), [Channels](/docs/backend/channels) |
| **flags** | Feature flags and remote config, per-user values | [Web Flags](/docs/web/flags) | [Flags](/docs/backend/flags) |
| **notify** | Email, push, SMS and WhatsApp; templates, topics, preferences | a user's devices, preferences and topics | [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications) |
| **secrets** | The project's secrets, versioned, in two sets | — | [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets) |
| **analytics** | Events, identifies, page views; summaries, funnels and retention | [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) | [Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview), [Reading Analytics](/docs/analytics/reading) |
| **ai** | The platform's models: answers, tools, agents, and chats with the members a backend names | Through a backend's gateway: a chat's members join it ([Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways#chat-gateways)) | [AI](/docs/backend/ai) |

Each module answers at the project's address, under a path of its own (`/auth/…`, `/storage/…`, `/flags/…`), and each has a contract — the OpenAPI document the SDK's clients are generated from. The SDKs are a convenience over those paths, not a requirement: anything that speaks HTTPS can call them.

And for code of your own:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Machines** | Your program, built from a repository's branch and directory on every push; sizes that sleep and sizes that never do; logs, builds and rollback — [Machines](/docs/machines/overview) |
| **Databases** | Postgres 18 with pgvector and PostGIS, backups and point-in-time restore, a read-only SQL console in Studio — [Databases](/docs/machines/databases) |
| **`palbase/backend`** | Controllers, services and modules in TypeScript, secure by default, with the project's modules and its database built in — [Backend SDK](/docs/backend/overview) |

## The surfaces

| Surface | What it is | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| `palbase/web` | The client for web and JavaScript apps: `createClient` with the publishable key — auth, the session, the realtime socket | [Web SDK](/docs/web/overview) |
| `palbase/server` | The client for servers: `createServer` with a secret key — every module's server calls, and the receiver for the project's webhooks | [Server SDK](/docs/server/overview) |
| `palbase/backend` | The framework a machine runs: `PalbaseFactory`, `@Module`, `@Controller`, and `Palbase`, `Database` and `Log` | [Backend SDK](/docs/backend/overview) |
| `palgres` | The database half of the framework: the schema in TypeScript, typed queries, and migrations that run beside the version that serves | [Schema](/docs/backend/schema), [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations) |
| Studio | Organizations, projects and environments; every module's screens; machines, databases, keys and secrets | [Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations) |

Palbase has SDKs in TypeScript (`palbase/web`, `palbase/server`, `palbase/backend`), Swift and Kotlin. An iOS app takes the Swift SDK, `palbase-swift` with Swift Package Manager ([iOS SDK](/docs/ios/overview)), and an Android app the Kotlin one, `studio.palbase:palbase` and an artifact per module ([Android SDK](/docs/android/overview)). An app on another platform, such as a game engine, calls the modules over HTTPS with the publishable key in the `apikey` header and the user's access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`, the same requests the SDKs make.

The TypeScript SDKs are one npm package, `palbase`, whose parts are its subpaths — the CLI comes with it (`npx palbase`) — and `palgres`, which `palbase/backend` brings: `npm install palbase` (or `bun add palbase`). They ship compiled, under the Palbase SDK License ([Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure)).

## Organizations, projects and environments

An **organization** is a team, a **project** is an app in it, and an **environment** is the thing that runs: each one a project of the platform's own, with **nothing shared** with another environment — its own address, its own keys, its own users and files, its own machines and databases. A staging copy of production is a second environment, with its machines built from another branch. Everyone in the organization reaches its projects at their role, owner, admin or member: members, invitations, roles and the audit log are in [Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations).

A project's **first environment** has the slug `main`. Every environment answers at one address, named by its **ref**:

```text
https://<ref>.palbase.studio
```

The ref is on the environment's **Settings**, and it never changes. A machine of the environment answers under the app domain — `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio` for the one named `backend` — and a database at `<name>-<ref>.db.palbase.studio`.

## The keys

An environment has **publishable keys** — each [registered app](/docs/apps/overview)'s own, the one the environment was made with, and any you make — and **any number of secret keys**, on **Settings › API keys**:

| Key | Looks like | Role | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Publishable | `pb_<ref>_c…` | `anon` | In apps: a browser bundle, a mobile app. What it reaches is what an app may do, and the signed-in user's token decides whose data. |
| Secret | `pb_<ref>_s…` | `service_role` | On servers only: a machine's secrets, a server's environment. It opens the whole project — every user, every file, every secret. |

The ref is in the key, so a key names its project. A secret key is made with a name (**Create secret key**), **shown once**, and revoked on its own (**Revoke**) — give each server its own, and a leaked one is replaced without touching the others. `createClient` refuses a secret key, and `createServer` refuses to run in a browser.

Every request to the project carries one of them in the `apikey` header; a request with none is `401 missing_api_key`, and a key of another project is the same as none (`401 invalid_api_key`). A user's access token, when one is sent, must be one this project issued (`401 invalid_token` otherwise). Past the project's requests-per-second limit, a request is `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After: 1`; past its requests for the period, under a quota that refuses, `429 quota_exceeded` with `Retry-After` until the next period.

> **Note:** The project's address answers a browser on any site. A browser app calls it directly, with the publishable key and the signed-in user's token, as [Web SDK](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser) explains. Your own machine's backend answers cross-origin requests itself, for the origins it names.

## How code reaches a machine

One way: **a push to the machine's branch.**

1. [Connect GitHub](/docs/machines/github) — install **Palbase Cloud** on the account that owns the repository, and connect it to the environment.
2. Open a machine on a repository, a branch and a directory of it (**Backend › Machines › New machine**).
3. Push. A push that changes the machine's directory is built — its `Dockerfile`, or what Railpack detects — and rolled out beside the version that serves; it takes traffic once it answers its health check.

There is no deploy command and no tool to install. A release whose machine migrates a database runs the migration itself, beside the version that serves; a release that does not come up never takes a request; and any build that succeeded can be returned to ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds)).

# Quickstart

In this guide you create a Palbase project in Studio, sign a user up and in from a web app, write a small backend with `palbase/backend`, put it on a machine by pushing it to GitHub, and call it from the web app as the signed-in user. Nothing here is run from a command line of Palbase's — the project is Studio's, the deploy is `git push`.

## Before you start

| You need | Why |
|---|---|
| **A Studio account** | where the project lives — Palbase is opening step by step: [request access](/signup) |
| **A GitHub repository** you can push to | a machine is built from a branch of it |
| **Bun 1.4** — [bun.sh](https://bun.sh) | the backend runs on Bun, and `bun install` writes the lockfile its build installs from |
| **Node.js 22** | the web app (Next.js) |

> **Note:** The SDK is one npm package, `palbase` — `palbase/web` for the app, `palbase/backend` for the backend (it brings `palbase/server` and `palgres`), and the CLI (`npx palbase`): `npm install palbase` (or `bun add palbase`).

## 1. Create a project

In Studio, **Projects › Create project**: a **Project name**, its **First environment**, and the **Organization** it belongs to (asked only when you have more than one). The first environment's slug is always `main`.

Open the environment. Everything in this guide is that environment's — it is a project of its own, with its own address, keys, users, machines and databases:

- its **address**, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio` — the ref is on **Settings**;
- its **publishable key**, `pb_<ref>_c…`, on **Settings › API keys** — the key apps ship.

## 2. Sign a user up from a web app

Start a Next.js app and give it the web SDK:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "palbase": "^0.10.0",
    "next": "^16.3.4",
    "react": "^19.2.7",
    "react-dom": "^19.2.7"
  }
}
```

and three settings, in `.env.local`:

```text
NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL=https://<ref>.palbase.studio
NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pb_<ref>_c…
NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL=https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio
```

**A browser calls the project's address directly.** The address answers a page on any site, so nothing stands between the app and the project ([Web SDK](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser) says what it answers, and why the browser is the one to call it). Next.js needs no setting for the SDK: the package is compiled JavaScript.

The client is made once, in the browser, with the project's address:

```ts
// lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient, type PalbaseClient } from "palbase/web";

let client: PalbaseClient | undefined;

/** The project's client: its publishable key, and the signed-in user's session. */
export function palbase(): PalbaseClient {
  client ??= createClient({
    url: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL!,
    publishableKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY!,
  });
  return client;
}
```

And a page that signs up, signs in, and — after step 6 — calls the backend:

```tsx
// app/page.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { PalbaseError } from "palbase/web";
import { palbase } from "../lib/palbase";

export default function Home() {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
  const [password, setPassword] = useState("");
  const [said, setSaid] = useState("");

  async function attempt(work: () => Promise<string>) {
    try {
      setSaid(await work());
    } catch (e) {
      setSaid(e instanceof PalbaseError ? `${e.status} ${e.code}: ${e.message}` : String(e));
    }
  }

  const signUp = () =>
    attempt(async () => {
      const { user } = await palbase().auth.signUp({ email, password });
      const session = await palbase().auth.currentSession();
      return session ? `signed up and in as ${user.id}` : `signed up as ${user.id}: verify the address, then sign in`;
    });

  const signIn = () =>
    attempt(async () => {
      const result = await palbase().auth.signIn(email, password);
      return result.user ? `signed in as ${result.user.id}` : "this account asks for a second factor";
    });

  const callBackend = () =>
    attempt(async () => {
      const session = await palbase().auth.currentSession();
      if (!session) return "sign in first";
      const res = await fetch(`${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL}/me`, {
        headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${session.accessToken}` },
      });
      return `${res.status} ${await res.text()}`;
    });

  return (
    <main>
      <input value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} placeholder="email" />
      <input value={password} onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)} placeholder="password (15+ characters)" type="password" />
      <button onClick={() => void signUp()}>Sign up</button>
      <button onClick={() => void signIn()}>Sign in</button>
      <button onClick={() => void callBackend()}>Call the backend</button>
      <p>{said}</p>
    </main>
  );
}
```

Run it (`npm run dev`), sign up, and the user is in **Auth › Users** in Studio. A password of a single factor is 15 characters at least. A project that asks for a verified email answers the sign-up without a session; the verification is [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth)'s to explain.

You have used one module — auth — with no backend at all. Storage, realtime, flags, notify and analytics are the same: every project has them, the publishable key reaches what an app may do, and the secret key reaches the rest ([Introduction](/docs/getting-started/introduction)).

## 3. Write the backend

A backend is its own directory — its own repository here — that a machine builds:

```text
notes-backend/
├── Dockerfile
├── .env.example
├── package.json
├── bun.lock
├── tsconfig.json
└── src/
    ├── main.ts
    ├── app.module.ts
    ├── me.controller.ts
    └── modules/notes/
        ├── dto.ts
        ├── notes.controller.ts
        ├── notes.module.ts
        └── notes.service.ts
```

```json
{
  "name": "notes-backend",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": { "start": "bun run src/main.ts" },
  "dependencies": {
    "palbase": "^0.10.0"
  }
}
```

The decorators read the types TypeScript emits, so `tsconfig.json` turns both on:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}
```

The schemas of a domain sit in its `dto.ts` — each one a value for `@Body` and a type of the same name:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/dto.ts
import { z } from "palbase/backend";

export const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
export type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

export const Note = z.object({ id: z.string(), owner: z.string(), title: z.string(), created_at: z.string() });
export type Note = z.infer<typeof Note>;
```

The service holds the logic. This one keeps notes in the machine's memory — enough to see the whole path work; [step 8](#8-where-next) gives it a database:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFound } from "palbase/backend";
import type { CreateNote, Note } from "./dto";

// In this process only: a machine that sleeps, or a second copy, does not have them.
@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  private readonly notes = new Map<string, Note>();

  list(owner: string): Note[] {
    return [...this.notes.values()].filter((n) => n.owner === owner);
  }

  create(owner: string, input: CreateNote): Note {
    const note: Note = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner, title: input.title, created_at: new Date().toISOString() };
    this.notes.set(note.id, note);
    return note;
  }

  get(owner: string, id: string): Note {
    const note = this.notes.get(id);
    if (!note || note.owner !== owner) throw new NotFound(`no note ${id}`);
    return note;
  }
}
```

The controller is HTTP only — and every route needs a signed-in user unless it says otherwise:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { CreateNote, type Note } from "./dto";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  constructor(private readonly notes: NotesService) {}

  @Get("")
  list(@User() user: UserT): Note[] {
    return this.notes.list(user.id);
  }

  @Post("", { rateLimit: { max: 30, window: 60 } })
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    return this.notes.create(user.id, body);
  }

  @Get("/{id}")
  read(@Param("id") id: string, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    return this.notes.get(user.id, id);
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Module({ controllers: [NotesController], providers: [NotesService] })
export class NotesModule {}
```

`/me` answers who the caller is:

```ts
// src/me.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/me")
export class MeController {
  @Get("")
  me(@User() user: UserT): { id: string; email: string | null; emailVerified: boolean } {
    return { id: user.id, email: user.email, emailVerified: user.emailVerified };
  }
}
```

The root module lists what exists, and `main.ts` serves it. The browser calls the backend from the web app's origin, so the backend names that origin (CORS is the backend's own to answer):

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { MeController } from "./me.controller";
import { NotesModule } from "./modules/notes/notes.module";

@Module({ imports: [NotesModule], controllers: [MeController] })
export class AppModule {}
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

// Serves on $PORT. The project's address, id and secret key come from the
// environment: the machine is started with them.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, {
  cors: { origins: (process.env.WEB_ORIGINS ?? "http://localhost:3000").split(",") },
});
```

How the machine runs it:

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun:1.4.2-alpine@sha256:d888c0ae6c86d7866ff10c5aafdd9077b36aee6455b33dd270fb93c0dd5cef6f
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json bun.lock ./
RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile --production
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
USER bun
CMD ["bun", "run", "src/main.ts"]
```

And what it needs before it can start — the build reads this file, and waits rather than roll out an app that would not:

```text
PALBASE_URL=
PALBASE_PROJECT_ID=
PALBASE_SECRET_KEY=
```

Run `bun install` once to write `bun.lock`, and commit everything.

## 4. Give it the secret key

The machine is started with `PALBASE_URL` and `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID` by the platform. `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` is yours to give — the backend uses it to reach the project's modules and to check its callers' sessions.

1. **Settings › API keys › Secret keys**: a **Key name** (`notes backend`), **Create secret key**. It is shown **once** — copy it now.
2. **Environment › Variables**, **Add secret**: the name `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, the key as its value.

The secret is in the environment's **production** set. A machine starts with the set it names, which you choose in the next step.

## 5. Connect GitHub and open the machine

**Backend › Machines › New machine**:

1. **Connect GitHub** — GitHub asks where to install **Palbase Cloud**; choose the repository, and connect it to this project by writing its ref when Palbase asks. Back in Studio, **Refresh** ([Connecting GitHub](/docs/machines/github)).
2. **Repository**: `you/notes-backend`; **Branch**: `main`; **Directory**: empty (the repository's root).
3. **Name**: `backend` — the machine of that name answers at `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio`. **Size**: `shared-256`. **Port**: `8080`.
4. **Create machine**.

The branch's head is built at once. Its build stops at **Waiting for variables**, `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` missing: the machine starts with no secrets yet. Open it, **Edit settings**, **Secrets: Production secrets**, **Save settings** — and the waiting build rolls out by itself. `.env.example` is what caught it ([Builds](/docs/machines/builds#envexample-what-the-program-must-be-given)).

## 6. Push

From now on, a push is the deploy:

```bash
git commit -am "Notes: read one by id"
git push origin main
```

The commit gets a **Palbase Cloud** check on GitHub — *Building*, then *Rolled out* — and the machine page lists the build with its log. The new version starts beside the old one and takes traffic once it answers its health check; a version that does not come up never takes a request.

## 7. Call it

Without a token, the backend refuses — in the envelope every refusal comes in:

```bash
curl -i https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio/me
# HTTP/2 401
# {"error":"unauthorized","error_description":"This route needs a signed-in user","status":401,"request_id":"req_…"}
```

From the web app, signed in, **Call the backend** answers `200` with the user's id and email: the browser sent the session's access token, and the backend checked it against the project. Notes work the same way — `POST /notes` with `{"title": "…"}` and the same header.

What the backend writes is on its machine page under **Logs**, and `Log` from `palbase/backend` puts the request's id on every line ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds#logs)). Every request to the environment's address, whichever module answers it, is on Studio's **Logs** page ([Logs](/docs/getting-started/logs)).

## 8. Where next

- **A database.** **Database › Databases › New database**, then give it to the machine with **Run migrations** on. Declare the table in `src/db/public.ts`, pass it to `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { db: { schemas: [schema] } })`, and the next push migrates it before the new version serves: [Databases](/docs/machines/databases), [Database](/docs/backend/database), [Schema](/docs/backend/schema).
- **Who sees what.** Row-level security in the schema keeps each user's rows theirs, whatever a route forgets: [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security).
- **The other modules** from the backend — files, email, flags, realtime — are `Palbase.storage`, `Palbase.notify`, `Palbase.flags`, `Palbase.realtime`: [Storage](/docs/backend/storage), [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications).
- **More environments.** A staging environment is another environment of the project, with machines built from another branch.

# Organizations

Studio has three levels. An **organization** is a team: its people and their roles, its access tokens and its audit log. A **project** is an app, in one organization. An **environment** is what runs: each one a Palbase project of its own, with its own address, keys, users, files, machines and databases, and nothing shared with another.

```text
Organization      its members and their roles, access tokens, the audit log
└── Project       an app
    └── Environment   main, staging, a developer's own: address, keys,
                      users, files, flags, machines, databases
```

Everyone in an organization reaches every project and environment of it, at their role in the organization. There is no role per project or per environment.

## Organizations

Before your first project, Studio asks you to create your organization, and you are its **owner**. Any account makes more:

```sh
palbase orgs:create "Acme"
palbase orgs:list                 # your organizations and your role in each
```

An organization's **Projects** page lists its projects, and an admin renames it under **General**.

## Projects and environments

An admin creates a project, in Studio (**New project**) or from the CLI; it opens with its first environment:

```sh
palbase projects:create shop --org acme            # its first environment, main, and its keys
palbase envs:create staging -P shop                # a second environment
palbase envs:create staging -P shop --from main    # opened with main's module settings
```

- **The first environment's slug is `main`**, whatever it is called on screen: it is the project's production one, and a CLI change to it asks for confirmation.
- **Another environment's slug** starts with a letter and continues with up to 38 letters, digits or hyphens; `local` is not one. An environment's name on screen can change; its slug never does.
- **`--from`** opens the new environment with another's module settings: secrets by name, not by value. With `--with-cloud` its machines and databases are declared alike too, built from the same branches, with no data.

Each environment has its own address and keys ([Introduction](/docs/getting-started/introduction#the-keys)), and its own usage ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)).

An admin deletes an environment under its **Settings › Danger zone**, or with `palbase envs:delete <slug>`; deleting a project, under its **Settings › Delete project** or with `palbase projects:delete <project>`, deletes every environment of it. An environment's users, files, flags, keys and secrets go with it, and its machines and databases are deleted too.

## Members and invitations

An organization's **Members** page lists its people, each with their role and when they joined; its admins also see the invitations still open.

An admin invites someone by email, as an **admin** or a **member** (member unless said), with **Add member** or from the CLI:

```sh
palbase orgs:members:invite ada@example.com --role admin --org acme
palbase orgs:members:list --org acme
palbase orgs:members:remove ada@example.com --org acme   # a member, or an invitation still open
```

- **Accepting.** The invited person signs in to Studio with the email the invitation names, and accepts it there. The email must be verified: an account whose address is not is refused (`403 email_not_verified`). An invitation does not expire; it waits until it is taken or withdrawn.
- **Inviting again** keeps the invitation, with the new role and the new inviter.
- **The mail.** An invitation is mailed from Palbase when the inviter's own email is verified. An address gets one invitation mail a day from an organization and five a day from all of them together; past that the invitation still waits for it in Studio, unmailed.
- **How many.** An inviter makes 20 invitations an hour and 100 a day, and an organization 20 an hour, however many admins it has (`429` with `Retry-After`).

A member leaves an organization with `palbase orgs:members:remove` and their own email. An admin takes away a member or an admin; only an owner takes away an owner. The organization's last owner stays: make another owner first (`409 last_owner`).

A person who leaves, or is taken away, takes with them what they held at the organization's environments: the CLI's keys they were given, and the access tokens they made.

- **Owners hear of every new role.** When someone — or an access token — is given a role in one of the organization's environments, or a higher one, each owner is mailed: who, which role, which environments, when. An owner whose own owner role is taken is mailed too. The same person and role is mailed to an owner once a day for an environment, the environments it came in named in one mail. The mail comes from Palbase's platform itself, not from Studio, to the address the owner signs in with: if you did not expect it, take the person away under **Members** and write to security@pallasite.net.

## Roles

| | Member | Admin | Owner |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Open every project and environment, and read its screens: users, files, flags, logs, usage, machines and their builds | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| See which secrets there are and their versions, and the API keys by their last characters | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Read with a module's questions that change nothing: a funnel, a retention table, the database's read-only SQL console, a machine's `GET` from **Try it** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Change anything in an environment: settings, users, flags, files, templates, machines, databases, secrets | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Read a secret's value, a task's payload, a coupon's one-time codes | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Make and revoke API keys; take a CLI key (`palbase env:pull`, `palbase run`); mint environment tokens | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Create, rename and delete projects and environments | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Invite and take away members and admins; withdraw invitations; rename the organization | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Manage access tokens; read the audit log | | ✓ | ✓ |
| Make or unmake an owner; take away an owner | | | ✓ |

A member's change to an environment is refused with `403 console_role_required`, and the refusal is kept in the audit log. In Studio, an owner changes a member's role from the **Members** list.

A role is read on every request: a member made less than an admin keeps none of the CLI keys they had at the organization's environments, and the admin tokens they made stop working at once. An access token acts at its role, member or admin and never owner, and no more than its maker's role now ([Access Tokens](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens)).

## Your Studio account

**Account security**, in the account menu at the top right, is your own account's:

- **Two-factor authentication**: a second step when you sign in, with an authenticator app or by SMS, and **recovery codes** for when you have neither. They are shown once: keep them where you keep passwords.
- **Passkeys**: sign in with this device's fingerprint, face or screen lock, or a security key, instead of a password. Add one, rename it, or remove it.
- **Connected accounts**: sign in with Google or GitHub, when Studio offers them. The last way you sign in cannot be removed: add a password or a passkey first.

A change to how you sign in needs a sign-in from the last five minutes; an older one is asked to sign in again first. Turning off a second factor asks for your current password.

The CLI signs in as you, and holds a session of yours ([CLI](/docs/cli/overview#signing-in)).

## The audit log

An organization's **Audit log** says who changed what at its environments, newest first: the change, the environment, who made it — a member by their email, an access token or an environment token by its name — the method and path, and the status it was answered. It holds every change made through Studio, the CLI and tokens; a change refused for its role; and every read of a secret's value. The path is kept without its query and the body not at all, since what was sent can hold a secret. Plain reads are not kept.

Its admins read it in Studio, or from the CLI:

```sh
palbase orgs:audit --org acme --limit 100
```

A module keeps a change made through Studio as Studio's: the audit log is where whose it was is kept. See [`palbase orgs:audit`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-orgsaudit).

## Related

- [Access Tokens](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) — for CI and agents, at a role of the organization
- [Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits) — what each environment uses
- [CLI](/docs/cli/overview) — signing in, and choosing an environment
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#orgs) — `orgs`, `projects` and `envs`

# Architecture

A Palbase backend is a plain TypeScript repository, and **one declaration says what exists, who owns it and what it may reach**: a `@Module` lists a domain's classes — its `controllers`, its `providers`, what it `exports` and whose exports it `imports` — and a class that no module lists is **refused at boot**, by name. The root module is the one `src/main.ts` hands to `PalbaseFactory.create`; every other module is reached from it through `imports`.

Dependencies arrive through the **constructor**, and the container supplies them: a dependency is named by its parameter's **type** and by nothing else. There is no `@Inject`, no `useFactory`, no `forwardRef` and no token registry. What the platform gives every handler — the project's modules, the request's database, the log — is **imported**, never injected: `Palbase`, `Database` and `Log` from `palbase/backend`.

This page answers one question: **what shape does the code take?** It is the shape of Palbase's own examples and of Studio's backend; [Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure) lists the files, and [Modules & Dependency Injection](/docs/backend/modules) the full declaration surface.

## The layers

| Layer | What it does | What it never does |
|---|---|---|
| `src/main.ts` | Boots the app: `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, config)` — the database's schemas, CORS, the routes' default auth and limit | holds routes or logic |
| `src/app.module.ts` | The root: `imports` every domain's module | owns a domain's classes |
| `src/modules/<domain>/<domain>.module.ts` | The declaration: which classes the domain owns, and which of them another domain may reach | holds logic · lists a class another module owns |
| `src/modules/<domain>/<name>.controller.ts` | HTTP only: validates input through a schema, picks the caller, turns the service's answer into the response. Listed in `controllers` | imports `Database` · holds business rules · keeps per-request state on the instance |
| `src/modules/<domain>/<name>.service.ts` | The decisions: which rows, whose, in what order; the calls to the project's modules. `@Injectable()`, listed in `providers` | knows about HTTP (no request, no response) · builds its own dependencies |
| `src/modules/<domain>/dto.ts` | Schemas — each a **value** for `@Body` and a same-named **type** | holds logic |
| `src/db/public.ts` | **Is** the database: tables, columns, indexes, [row-level security](/docs/backend/row-level-security) | produces migration files — there are none |

In one line: **controllers thin, services thick, schemas quiet, `db/` the single truth — and the module is the registration.**

A domain is a **folder** with a module in it, and adding one is adding a folder and naming its module in the root's `imports`. The file suffixes (`.controller.ts`, `.service.ts`) are a convention that helps a reader and decides nothing: what decides is the list a class appears in and the decorator it carries.

The rule that carries the most weight is the narrowest: **a controller does not import `Database`.** When a route starts reaching for a table, the logic has moved into the layer that is hardest to test, and the layer that was meant to hold it becomes decoration.

## Where does this go

| The need | Its home |
|---|---|
| Validate input | a schema in the module's `dto.ts`, passed to `@Body(Schema)` / `@QueryParams(Schema)` |
| Enforce ownership | a row-level-security policy in `src/db/public.ts` **and** the service's `where` — the policy is the backstop, not a reason to stop writing the filter |
| A business rule, a calculation, an ordering | the service |
| Answer with an HTTP status | `throw new NotFound(…)` (or `Forbidden`, `Conflict`, `PalError`) — from the service or the controller; no response object is needed |
| Call another domain | name its class in your constructor — its module `exports` it, and yours `imports` that module |
| Send an email, sign a file URL, read a secret | `Palbase.notify`, `Palbase.storage`, `Palbase.secrets` — in the service |
| Work at start-up or shutdown | an `onStart()` / `onShutdown()` method on a provider — awaited in dependency order |
| Work on a schedule | a [cron](/docs/backend/cron) — not a timer: a machine that sleeps runs none |
| Work done once, now or later | a [task](/docs/backend/tasks) on the machine's queue — not a cron that looks in a table every minute |
| Register a new class | add it to a module's `providers` (or `controllers`) — nothing else registers anything |
| A setting | an environment variable of the machine; a secret is a project secret the machine starts with |

## One vertical, end to end

A `notes` domain, in the order you would build it.

### 1. The database

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, index, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

// Each user's notes, theirs alone: row-level security says so, whatever a route forgets.
const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: text(),
    title: text(),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("notes_own").for("all").to("authenticated").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
  ],
  indexes: (p) => [index("notes_owner_created").on(p.col("owner"), p.col("created_at"))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```

One file per schema, each with a default export. There are no migration files: a release migrates the database to this declaration beside the version that serves ([Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations)). The request runs as its caller — `authenticated`, with the token's claims — so `auth.uid()` is the signed-in user, and the policy holds for every query of the request.

> **Note:** `ownedByUser()` is the column type made for `owner`: when the user is deleted, their rows go. The platform tells the app through the project's webhook (`user.deleted`), so an app whose schema has an `ownedByUser()` or `userRef()` column does not boot without `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, the secret of the project's webhook endpoint — and an endpoint cannot be made from Studio. A project without one keeps its owner column a `text()` with a policy, as here. See [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks).

### 2. The schemas

```ts
// src/modules/notes/dto.ts
import { z } from "palbase/backend";

export const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
export type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

export const ListNotes = z.object({ limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20) });
export type ListNotes = z.infer<typeof ListNotes>;

export const Note = z.object({ id: z.string(), title: z.string(), created_at: z.string() });
export type Note = z.infer<typeof Note>;
```

Each schema is exported twice under one name: the **value** a decorator validates with, and the **type** a signature reads. Any Standard Schema works — zod, valibot, arktype; `z` is re-exported from `palbase/backend` so the app and the framework agree on one zod.

### 3. The service

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Database, Injectable, Log, NotFound } from "palbase/backend";
import type { CreateNote, Note } from "./dto";

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  async list(owner: string, limit: number): Promise<Note[]> {
    // RLS already narrows this to the caller's rows; the filter says what the route means.
    return Database.public.notes.findMany({
      where: { owner },
      select: ["id", "title", "created_at"],
      orderBy: { column: "created_at", direction: "desc" },
      limit,
    });
  }

  async create(owner: string, input: CreateNote): Promise<Note> {
    const note = await Database.public.notes.insert({ owner, title: input.title });
    Log.info("note created", { note: note.id });
    return { id: note.id, title: note.title, created_at: note.created_at };
  }

  async remove(owner: string, id: string): Promise<void> {
    const gone = await Database.public.notes.deleteMany({ where: { id, owner } });
    if (gone === 0) throw new NotFound(`no note ${id}`);
  }
}
```

`Database` is **the request's own transaction**: it is opened by the first query, committed when the handler returns — before the answer goes — and rolled back when it throws. A service the handler calls shares it, so a route's writes land together or not at all. It is reached inside a request (a handler, a service it calls, an `@On` handler), never at import time or from a timer.

`Database.public.notes` is typed by the declaration file Palgres writes from `src/db/public.ts` ([Database](/docs/backend/database)): a column that does not exist, or a value of the wrong type, is a compile error. Raw SQL is `Database.$query(sql, params)`.

### 4. The controller

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Delete, Get, Param, Post, QueryParams, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { CreateNote, ListNotes, type Note } from "./dto";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  // The container supplies this. Nothing here constructs or imports an instance.
  constructor(private readonly notes: NotesService) {}

  @Get("")
  list(@QueryParams(ListNotes) query: ListNotes, @User() user: UserT): Promise<Note[]> {
    return this.notes.list(user.id, query.limit);
  }

  @Post("", { rateLimit: { max: 30, window: 60 } })
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Promise<Note> {
    return this.notes.create(user.id, body);
  }

  @Delete("/{id}")
  remove(@Param("id") id: string, @User() user: UserT): Promise<void> {
    return this.notes.remove(user.id, id);
  }
}
```

Every route needs a signed-in user unless it, its controller or the app's config says otherwise (`{ auth: false }`); `@User()` is that user. A body that fails its schema is a `400` naming the fields, a caller over the route's limit a `429`, a thrown `NotFound` a `404` — all in the platform's one envelope ([Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors)). A handler that returns nothing answers `204`; anything else is JSON.

### 5. The module

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Module({
  controllers: [NotesController], // its entry points
  providers: [NotesService], //      the classes it owns
  exports: [], //                    which of them another module may reach
  imports: [], //                    whose exports this module may reach
})
export class NotesModule {}
```

That list **is** the registration, and the only place ownership is decided. `exports` stays empty until another domain needs one of these classes; until a name appears there, nothing outside the module can reach it. Imports are not transitive: a module reaches the exports of the modules it imports, and of no others.

### 6. The root and the boot

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesModule } from "./modules/notes/notes.module";

@Module({ imports: [NotesModule] })
export class AppModule {}
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";
import schema from "./db/public";

// Serves on $PORT with its database; run by a release with PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE,
// it migrates the database to this schema and exits.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { db: { schemas: [schema] } });
```

At boot the container reads every module, refuses what is wrong — a class no module lists, a dependency from a module that is not imported or a class it does not export, a cycle — naming the path that led to it, builds every class once, runs their `onStart()` and serves. The project's address, id and secret key come from the machine's environment.

## Never write this

These are the shapes a code assistant reaches for by default. Every one is wrong here:

- **Express-style handlers** — `app.get(...)`, `(req, res) => …`. A route is a **method on a class**.
- **A `ctx` object or middleware** — there is no context to thread and no pipeline to mount; auth, validation, limits and the error envelope are the framework's.
- **A class no module lists** — refused at boot, by name.
- **`@Inject`, `useFactory`, `forwardRef`** — a dependency is named by its constructor parameter's type and nothing else.
- **An `interface` as a dependency** — it has no runtime existence. Use a class, or an `abstract class` with one listed subclass: the container gives the one owned subclass for it, and refuses by name when there are none or two.
- **NestJS lifecycle names** — `onModuleInit`, `onApplicationBootstrap`, `onModuleDestroy` … are refused at boot. The hooks are `onStart()` and `onShutdown()`.
- **A hand-wired singleton** — `export const notes = new NotesService()`. Mark it `@Injectable()`, list it, and let the container build it once.
- **I/O in a constructor** — it runs while the app comes up, synchronously. Start-up work goes in `onStart()`, which is awaited before the first request.
- **A timer for scheduled work** — a machine that sleeps runs no timer, and three copies run three. Use a [cron](/docs/backend/cron), or a [task](/docs/backend/tasks) for work done once.
- **State in the instance that must outlive a request** — a machine may run several copies, and sleeps; what must be shared goes in the database.
- **A migration file** — there are none. The schema file is the declaration.
- **`try { … } catch { return 500 }`** — throw the error class and let the framework build the envelope; swallowing it turns a `404` into a `500`.
- **Hand-built responses** — no `new Response(...)`, no `JSON.stringify`. Return the value; return nothing for `204`.
- **A secret in the repository** — the secret key and every credential are project secrets the machine starts with; `.env.example` names them, never their values.

## Adding a feature

1. `src/db/public.ts` — declare the table and its policies.
2. `src/modules/<domain>/dto.ts` — the schemas, each a value and a type.
3. `src/modules/<domain>/<name>.service.ts` — the logic; `@Injectable()`, its dependencies as constructor parameters.
4. `src/modules/<domain>/<name>.controller.ts` — the routes; the service in the constructor, never `Database`.
5. `src/modules/<domain>/<domain>.module.ts` — list them; name the module in the root's `imports`.
6. Regenerate the tables' declaration file, if the schema changed ([Database](/docs/backend/database)).
7. Push. The release migrates the database beside the version that serves, then rolls the new version out.

## Give this to your agent

For the full reference — every decorator, every module call, every schema builder — point your coding assistant at **`/llms.txt`**, the index of these docs, or **`/llms-backend.txt`**, the slice for writing a backend: getting started, the backend SDK, the server SDK and machines, in one file. Assistants fetch those when you name them; they do not go looking.

# Project Structure

A Palbase backend is a directory a [machine](/docs/machines/overview) builds: a TypeScript app that Bun runs as it is, a `Dockerfile` that says how, and a `.env.example` that names what it must be given. Nothing in it is generated by a tool of Palbase's, and nothing is read by its location but the file `src/main.ts` starts with — what exists is what the modules list.

This page walks that directory file by file. The layout is the one Palbase's own examples and Studio's backend use.

## The layout

```text
notes-backend/                       ← the machine's directory (its `path`)
├── Dockerfile                       how the machine builds and runs it
├── .env.example                     the variables it must be given
├── package.json                     its dependencies — `palbase` among them
├── bun.lock                         what `bun install --frozen-lockfile` installs
├── tsconfig.json                    decorators on, with their emitted types
└── src/
    ├── main.ts                      PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, config)
    ├── app.module.ts                the root module: imports every domain
    ├── db/
    │   └── public.ts                the `public` schema: tables, indexes, policies
    └── modules/
        ├── notes/
        │   ├── dto.ts               schemas: each a value and a type
        │   ├── notes.controller.ts  routes
        │   ├── notes.service.ts     logic
        │   └── notes.module.ts      what the domain owns, and exports
        └── core/
            ├── core.module.ts
            └── health.controller.ts
```

Two rules decide everything else:

- **A class exists when a module lists it.** A `@Controller`, an `@Injectable()` or an `@On` handler that no module lists stops the boot, naming it. A folder grants nothing.
- **A domain is a folder with a module in it**, named in the root module's `imports` (or in the imports of a module the root imports).

## `src/main.ts`

The process starts here, and it is short:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";
import schema from "./db/public";

await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, {
  db: { schemas: [schema] },
  cors: { origins: ["https://app.example.com"] },
});
```

`PalbaseFactory.create` builds every class, runs their `onStart()` and serves — on `$PORT`, which the machine sets. Everything in its config is the backend's own, with a default:

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `palbase` | from the environment | The project: `url` (`PALBASE_URL`), `projectId` (`PALBASE_PROJECT_ID`), `secretKey` (`PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`), `webhookSecret` (`PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) |
| `auth` | a signed-in user | Every route's auth unless the route or its controller says otherwise |
| `rateLimit` | 300 a minute per caller | Every route's limit unless it says otherwise; `false` for none |
| `bodyLimit` | 1 MiB | The largest request body |
| `cors` | off | The origins browsers may call from: `{ origins: [...] }` or `"*"` |
| `db` | none | The app's database: its `schemas`, and its address unless `PALBASE_DB_URL` says |
| `openapi` | `true` | Serve the app's contract to the platform, which Studio's backend screens read |
| `port`, `host` | `$PORT` (else 8080), `0.0.0.0` | Where it listens |
| `boot` | 5 attempts, 1 s doubling | A start whose `onStart()` fails is tried again from scratch |

A value missing or malformed stops the boot before any request is served, naming both ways to give it. What cannot heal by waiting — a missing setting, a DI mistake — stops at once; a database not up yet is waited for. See [Backend SDK](/docs/backend/overview).

## `src/app.module.ts`

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { CoreModule } from "./modules/core/core.module";

// One import per domain: NotesModule joins this list beside CoreModule.
@Module({ imports: [CoreModule] })
export class AppModule {}
```

The root owns nothing of its own here; it is the list of domains. A small app may list a controller or two in it directly.

## `src/modules/<domain>/`

One folder per domain, and in it the four files of [Architecture](/docs/getting-started/architecture): the module, the controller, the service and the `dto.ts`. A domain that needs another's class names it in a constructor, and its module imports the module that exports it:

```ts
// src/modules/core/health.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/health", { auth: false })
export class HealthController {
  @Get("")
  health(): { ok: true } {
    return { ok: true };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/core/core.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { HealthController } from "./health.controller";

@Module({ controllers: [HealthController] })
export class CoreModule {}
```

A route's path is its own: `/health` above is the app's, at the machine's address. Two first segments are not yours — `webhooks`, where the platform delivers the app's events and each `@Webhook` class takes a third party's ([Webhooks](/docs/backend/webhooks)), and `_palbase`, the platform's own way in — and a controller mounted under either is refused.

## `src/db/`

One file per Postgres schema, each with a **default export**, `defineSchema("<name>", { tables })`: `public.ts` for `public`, `billing.ts` for a `billing` schema. `src/main.ts` hands them to `db.schemas`.

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: text(),
    title: text(),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```
 A release migrates the database to them beside the version that serves; there are no migration files ([Schema](/docs/backend/schema), [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations)).

`Database.public.<table>` is typed by a declaration file written from those schemas with Palgres' `makeEnvDts` — commit it beside them, and write it again when a schema changes ([Database](/docs/backend/database)).

An app with no database has no `src/db/`, and no `db` in its config.

## `package.json`

```json
{
  "name": "notes-backend",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": { "start": "bun run src/main.ts" },
  "dependencies": {
    "palbase": "^0.10.0"
  }
}
```

The SDK is one npm package, `palbase`: `npm install palbase` (or `bun add palbase`). A backend imports the framework from `palbase/backend`, which brings what it is built on — `palbase/server` (the project's modules, as `Palbase`) and `palgres` (the database) — and `reflect-metadata`, which the framework loads itself. The package ships compiled JavaScript with its type declarations; Bun runs the app's own TypeScript as it is. `z` from `palbase/backend` is the zod the framework is built with: import it from there, and the app and the framework agree on one. `palbase init` writes this `package.json`.

## `tsconfig.json`

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}
```

`experimentalDecorators` and `emitDecoratorMetadata` are what make constructor injection work: the container reads each constructor's parameter **types** from the metadata TypeScript emits. Bun reads them from this file. A runner that does not emit the metadata — esbuild, and the tools built on it — leaves the container nothing to read, and the boot stops naming the class and the cure. `noEmit` is right: nothing is compiled ahead of time, and `tsc --noEmit` is the type check.

## `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun:1.4.2-alpine@sha256:d888c0ae6c86d7866ff10c5aafdd9077b36aee6455b33dd270fb93c0dd5cef6f
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json bun.lock ./
RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile --production
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
USER bun
CMD ["bun", "run", "src/main.ts"]
```

The machine builds the directory's `Dockerfile` when it has one; without one, Railpack detects what the directory is and plans the image ([Builds](/docs/machines/builds)). A backend ships its own, for two reasons: the decorators need `tsconfig.json` beside the sources, and `bun run src/main.ts` is exactly how the app is meant to start. Pin the base image by digest, so a rebuild of the same commit builds the same image.

The process listens on `$PORT` and stops cleanly on `SIGTERM`: it finishes the requests in flight (20 seconds at most), runs `onShutdown()`, and exits — which is what a rollout asks of the version it replaces.

## `.env.example`

```text
# The names this backend reads. The machine is started with them;
# their values are never in the repository.
PALBASE_URL=
PALBASE_PROJECT_ID=
PALBASE_SECRET_KEY=
```

A build reads it as the list of variables the program needs, and does not roll out until the machine has every one — its own environment, its secret set, or what the platform gives it. It names variables, never their values: commit it, and keep the values in the project's secrets ([Builds](/docs/machines/builds)).

## What the process is given

On a machine, the program finds these in its environment:

| Variable | Set by | |
|---|---|---|
| `PORT` | the platform | The port to listen on |
| `PALBASE_URL` | the platform | `https://<ref>.palbase.studio` |
| `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID` | the platform | The project's id — the `project_id` its access tokens carry |
| `PALBASE_REPLICAS` | the platform | How many copies of the machine run |
| `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET` | the platform | The key the platform signs its calls to the machine with |
| `PALBASE_DB_URL`, `PALBASE_DB_CONNECTIONS` | the platform, given a database | Its address as the app login, and one copy's share of its connections |
| `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` | the platform | The machine's own secret key of the project (`machine: <name>` among its API keys): `Palbase.*` calls, and checking callers' sessions |
| `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | the platform | The secret the project's events reach the machine signed with, at the endpoint the platform keeps for it |

And what it answers the platform, at paths the internet never reaches: `GET /_palbase/health` — `200` while it serves, `503` while it stops, the machine's health check. Its contract is written by its build (run with `PALBASE_CONTRACT_OUT`, the app writes it and exits), not asked of it while it serves.

## Running it on your own machine

The same directory runs anywhere Bun does:

```bash
PALBASE_URL=https://<ref>.palbase.studio \
PALBASE_PROJECT_ID=<project id> \
PALBASE_SECRET_KEY=pb_<ref>_s… \
PORT=8080 bun run src/main.ts
```

It is a client of the project like any other: the secret key reaches the project's modules, and a caller's token is checked against the project. Studio does not show the project's id, which a machine is given; it is the `project_id` claim of any access token the project issues — the one your web app's session holds. Off a machine there is no `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`, so the contract is not served. An app with a database also needs `PALBASE_DB_URL`, a database whose schema it can bind to; a release migrates the database before the version that reads it starts — locally, run the app once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start` and the owner's address in `PALBASE_DB_OWNER_URL` ([Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations)).

## In a repository of several apps

A backend need not be a repository of its own. In a monorepo it is one directory of it — the machine's `path` — and an app that imports a sibling package is built with the repository's root as its `context`, its `Dockerfile` copying from there ([Connecting GitHub](/docs/machines/github#one-repository-several-machines)). A push builds the machines whose directory it changed, and no other.

- [Architecture](/docs/getting-started/architecture) — what goes in each file, and why
- [Quickstart](/docs/getting-started/quickstart) — this layout, end to end
- [Modules & Dependency Injection](/docs/backend/modules) — the four lists, and what the boot refuses
