# Access Tokens

An **access token** lets a CI job or an agent act on an organization without a person signing in. It is set as the `PALBASE_TOKEN` secret of the job, and works the way a fine-grained personal token on GitHub or an access token on Vercel does, at the level of the organization.

Admins and owners manage tokens in Studio, under **Organization › Access tokens** (`/organizations/{id}/tokens`). Open the organization switcher at the top left and choose **Access tokens**, or choose it in an organization's left menu, or from **Access** in any of its environments. Members do not see them.

## Creating one

**Create token** asks for:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Name | What the token is for, up to 100 characters on one line: `GitHub Actions` |
| Role | **Member** or **Admin**. Never owner |
| Expires after | 7, 30, 90 (the default), 180 or 365 days, or a number of days from 1 to 365 |

The token starts with `pbo_`. Studio shows it **once**, when it is created. Store it as your CI's `PALBASE_TOKEN` secret; you will not see it again. Afterwards the list shows only its last four characters, as `pbo_…a1b2`, with who made it, when it was made, when it expires and when it was last used.

If the answer to creating one is lost, Studio does not send the request again: it asks you to check the list. A token that was made but whose value was lost is deleted and made again.

## What a token can do

- It acts on the organization's projects and environments with its role: member or admin, never owner.
- An admin token opens projects and environments, registers a project's apps and sets them in each environment, and adds an environment's webhook endpoints — what a program that opens a project for each product does with no one signed in, as a Firebase service account adds an app.
- An admin token can get a CLI key. That key lives at most one day and appears in the environment's API keys as `CLI — token <name> (<host>)`.
- An admin token links a GitHub installation that another environment of the organization linked to an environment, with no GitHub sign-in: `POST /v1/environments/{ref}/github/installations` with `{ "installation_id": 123, "from": "<the other environment's ref>" }`. The environment reaches the repositories the GitHub user who linked it there can push to, and repositories created later that they can push to. With `"repositories": ["owner/name", …]` (the CLI's `github:connect --from <env> --repo owner/name`) it reaches those alone, and never one created later: what a program that opens a project for each product gives each product, so that one product's environment builds nothing of another's.
- An admin token mints [environment tokens](#environment-tokens).

## What a token cannot do

- It cannot do what only a person can: manage the organization, its members, roles and invitations, or tokens; create or revoke an environment's API keys; or reach Palbase's own environment.
- It never has more than its creator's **current** role. If the creator becomes a member, their admin tokens stop working at once. If the creator leaves the organization or is deleted, their tokens go with them.

## Deleting one

Deleting a token makes its next request fail, and the CLI keys it got are revoked. Deleting does not undo what the token did: the deploys it made and the settings it changed stay.

The webhook endpoints a token made stay too, and keep receiving events: an endpoint's secret signs what is delivered to it and opens nothing of the platform, so it belongs to its environment, as with Stripe's and GitHub's webhooks. Each endpoint names who made it in **Settings › Webhooks**, and when you delete a token Studio lists the endpoints it made, by address and environment, before you confirm (`GET /v1/orgs/{id}/tokens/{token}/webhooks`). Remove them in their environment if you no longer want them. API keys, which do open the platform, are made by a person only.

An expired token is marked **Expired** in the list and no longer works; delete it to tidy the list.

## Environment tokens

An **environment token** is for a program that works in **one** environment — an AI agent building one product — for a few hours, the way a GitHub App's installation token is for one installation. It starts with `pbe_`, and it is set as that program's `PALBASE_TOKEN`.

It is minted with `POST /v1/environments/{ref}/tokens`, by an admin of the organization (signed in, or with an admin access token) or with the environment's own **secret key** in the `apikey` header and no one signed in:

```json
{ "expires_in_minutes": 60, "name": "agent" }
```

Studio shows it **once**. It lives 60 minutes unless you ask otherwise, 240 at most, and never longer than the access token or key that minted it.

### What it can do

In its environment it does what the role of whoever minted it does there, as their own CLI would: an admin's token reads and changes the environment's machines, databases, users, flags, apps and webhooks, and sets its secrets. A token minted with the secret key acts as an admin. The role is read on every request, so a token never holds more than its minter holds now. Its changes appear in the organization's audit log under its name.

Outside its environment it does nothing. Another environment of the project answers `404`. The project itself and the organization answer `403 token_out_of_scope`, and so does anything that changes the project (its name, its apps, its environments). When it reads its project, it sees only its own environment.

**A full token of the admin role, or one minted with the secret key, is, in what it can reach, an admin of its environment.** It deploys machines, and the code it deploys runs with a secret key of the environment (`PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, which the platform gives every machine) and reads the environment's secrets. What that code takes, it keeps after the token has ended. So:

- give a full token only to an agent you would trust as an admin of that environment;
- for narrow work, mint a token with [`scopes`](#narrowing-it): no scope deploys anything;
- the closed list below closes the routes that make or show a credential in their own answer, not what deployed code can do.

### What no environment token can do

These routes are closed to every environment token: each one makes an identity, or makes or shows a credential that would outlive the token, in its own answer. Everything else is open at the minter's role, deploying code included (see above).

They answer `403 token_out_of_scope` (or `person_only`), whoever minted the token, in Studio and at the environment's modules alike:

- mint a token: an environment token, or an organization's access token;
- create, revoke or list API keys, or take a CLI key;
- change the organization's members, roles or invitations;
- delete the environment or the project;
- link a GitHub installation from another environment;
- sign in as one of the environment's users, or make a password reset for one;
- set a user's password or email: create or import users, change a user's email (test users are its to make);
- create an OAuth client or a service account, rotate one's key, or change where an OAuth client's codes go;
- define a role, or give or take one from a user; make, change or remove an auth hook, whose claims go into every user's token, an app's role among them;
- create a database, or make new passwords for one: both answers show its passwords;
- read a secret's value, a task's payload (it may carry a token) or a coupon's one-time codes. Setting a secret is allowed;
- set or remove a sign-in provider's client secret, or change which apps' sign-ins with it the environment takes (its client ids);
- bring or remove a message provider (where the project's mail and texts are sent, and with whose credentials);
- override or remove a template that carries a sign-in or reset credential — a reset or magic-sign-in link, a verification or invitation link, a one-time code — on email, SMS or WhatsApp. The app's own notification templates stay open, so an agent still brands them.

The last three close the roundabout ways to a user's own credential: a sign-in provider's client of one's own, a message provider aimed at a server of one's own, or a reset template that tucks the link into one it fetches, would catch a sign-in the way signing in as the user would.

The sender's own settings stay open — a token sets the project's `from` address and reply-to (`/notify/settings`), and the site and redirect URLs a new product signs in against (`/admin/auth-settings`). These change where a link points, but no credential leaves unless the user follows the link themselves.

Each module refuses these itself, on the route it matched, so writing the path another way does not get past this list: an escape, a dot segment, other letter case or a slash at the end all name the same thing.

A link the token signs does not outlive it either. A signed download or upload URL, a package's upload link, a link to hand over an Apple or Stripe key, a signed bundle's download link and the link that connects GitHub all end no later than the token. The answer's `expires_at` says when.

Test users, and the sign-ins made for them, are open: they are test fixtures, and `auth:test-users` is for them.

### Narrowing it

`scopes` narrows a token to what they name, and nothing else is reached, a read as much as a change:

```json
{ "scopes": ["machines:read", "machines:logs", "auth:test-users"], "expires_in_minutes": 60, "name": "agent" }
```

| Scope | What it reaches |
|---|---|
| `machines:read` | The environment's machines, their builds, crons and queues (not a task's payload), contracts, metrics and pull requests' previews |
| `machines:logs` | A machine's logs and its builds' logs |
| `machines:previews` | A machine's pull request preview opened again (`palbase machines:previews:open`): what a push to the pull request would build anyway — never a commit the token's holder chooses |
| `apps:sync` | What `palbase apps:sync` reads: the project's apps as they are in this environment, their client settings, the machines' contracts |
| `auth:test-users` | The environment's test users: made with their sign-ins, listed, deleted, their kept mail and texts read (`palbase auth:test-users:messages`), a sign-up address made (`palbase auth:test-users:address`). Not other users |
| `support` | A question to Palbase's support line (`palbase support:ask`, `POST /ai/support-questions`): an agent asks Palbase what it cannot find out, not the person it works for |

### When it stops working

It stops working when it expires, when it is revoked (`DELETE /v1/environments/{ref}/tokens/{id}`, by an admin, by a token of an admin's role, or by a narrowed token itself), and when what minted it no longer holds: the admin is no longer an admin, the access token is deleted, or the secret key is revoked (within a minute). `GET /v1/environments/{ref}/tokens` lists the live ones by their last four characters.



<!-- ===== getting-started/billing ===== -->

# Billing

Each environment is billed on its own, by the calendar month (UTC): it has its own plan and its own free quota, as a project of its own. What it owes is charged to a **payment account** — an organization's cards and billing details — which pays for every organization linked to it: its own, and others its owners or admins link to it. Nothing is paid ahead. Each environment is on one of two plans:

- **Free**: charged nothing. Every item has a free quota each month, and past it the environment is slowed or stopped ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits#what-a-free-project-gets)); its machines and databases are of the free sizes. Every environment starts on Free. Until the organization is paid for by a payment account that has paid a charge, a person opens at most 2 projects of 2 environments each — one deleted counts until the month is out, so deleting and opening again brings no new month of free quotas — and a Free project is opened by a person, not an organization's access token.
- **Pay as you go**: an owner or an admin moves the environment there, while a payment account with a card pays for its organization — never on its own. What it uses past its own free quota is priced and owed to that account as it is used; it may open every size of machine and database. There is no monthly fee.

When an environment's month reaches its limit, only it falls back to the free quotas; the organization's other environments go on. The prices, the free quotas and the terms are on the [billing terms](https://palbase.studio/legal/billing) page.

## Opening a payment account

An owner or admin opens it in Studio, on the organization's **Billing** page, by accepting the terms for the organization (Studio records who, when, and which version), then saves a card on Stripe's page (**Billing › Payment › Add card**), which asks for the billing address and, for a business, its VAT number. Nothing is charged. A prepaid card is refused. The organization is then paid for by its own account.

## Linking organizations to a payment account

One payment account pays for many organizations: an organization that opens an organization for each of its customers pays for all of them from one account, and bills each customer from the account's monthly report. On an organization's **Billing › Paid by**, an owner or an admin of it who also manages a payment account (an owner or an admin of the organization it is) links it to that account, or stops it being paid for. Stopped, its environments on Pay as you go go Free; what they owed until then stays the account's.

A linked organization's people see their own environments, plans and usage, never the account's cards or invoices. The account's **Billing › Paid organizations** lists every organization it pays for.

## How a payment account is charged

- **At the month's end**: on the first day of each month (UTC), what the environments it pays for owe of the month before is charged in one Stripe invoice, a line for each environment (past 250, one for each organization).
- **At its threshold**: during a month, as soon as what they owe and is not charged yet comes to the account's threshold, it is charged at once: **25 USD**, or **50 USD** once the account has paid every charge without fail for 3 months. The threshold grows no more.
- A charge of less than 0.50 USD waits for the next one. Tax is added on top as the billing address requires; a VAT-registered business in the EU is invoiced under the reverse charge. Stripe emails each invoice; **Billing › Invoices** lists them, an unpaid one with its page to pay it on.

The charge is taken from the default card; when it declines, the account's other cards are tried in turn.

## When a charge is not paid

A declined charge is tried again every day, and the account's owners and admins are emailed each time, with the day its environments go Free. If it is still unpaid **7 days** after it was first declined — or as soon as what the account owes, unpaid and not yet charged, comes to **twice its threshold** — the environments on Pay as you go it pays for are held to the free quotas: their machines and databases of a paid size stop (`402 machine_not_paid` while it lasts), Palbase's AI models past their month's free dollar are refused (`402 ai_payment_required`; a project's own provider key goes on), and their data is kept. Saving a card, or paying the invoice on its page, brings them back at once.

A payment disputed with the card's bank holds them at once, and the disputed card is taken off the account; a card saved again lets them go.

Credit loaded ahead under the earlier terms is carried to the account's balance at Stripe and applied to its next invoices: nothing of it is lost.

## Cards and billing details

**Billing › Payment** lists the account's cards. **Add card** saves one on Stripe's page — nothing is charged — and makes it the default unless you say otherwise; any other card can be made the default or removed. The default card is removed only when it is the last one; charges then wait for a card.

**Edit billing details** sets the name, address and tax number (a VAT number in the EU) the next invoices are made out to. The address is checked for tax at once: one that cannot be placed is refused, and nothing changes.

## What is charged

**Usage** shows the month: each environment's plan and what it used, and to an owner or an admin what that came to before its free quota (gross), what it was charged past it and what it owes. Any member reads what was used; the amounts are an owner's or an admin's. **Download CSV** gives it item by item.

A payment account's **Monthly report** gives the month of every organization it pays for — each environment, what it owes — and its CSV each item of each environment: what an organization that pays for its customers' organizations bills them by.

Palbase AI's models, on Palbase's own provider keys, are their provider's price and 10%, and each month brings each environment $1.00 of them free. A project may have a monthly AI budget of its own ([AI](/docs/backend/ai#what-it-costs)). A call under the project's own provider key is the provider's to bill. Requests, push notifications, and email, SMS and WhatsApp sent through the project's own provider are not charged.

## Each environment's own

For each environment, an owner or an admin can, on **Billing › Environments › Manage** or from the API:

- move it to **Pay as you go**, or back to **Free**: charged nothing more and held to the free quotas;
- set a **monthly limit**: at it, the environment falls back to the free quotas until the month ends, while the others go on;
- **freeze** it: its requests are refused (`403 project_frozen`), its machines and databases stop, its data is kept, and only what it stores is charged. Unfreezing brings it back.

## Emails and webhooks

A payment account's owners and admins are emailed when a charge is declined (each day it is tried again) and when the environments it pays for are held; an environment's organization's, when its month reaches its limit. What happens at once to several environments comes in one email, naming each.

Each environment's own webhooks are told the same as it happens, as `billing.payment_failed`, `billing.held` and `billing.limit_reached` ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks#the-events)) — an organization that runs its customers' apps tells them from there. They carry nothing of the account's — no amount, no card's decline, not why it is held — but, for a declined charge, the day the environment goes Free (`free_on`).

## From the terminal

The CLI does what the Billing page does, as you or with an admin's [access token](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) in CI — save opening the payment account and saving a card on Stripe's page, which are a person's:

```bash
palbase billing                                   # who pays, the account's standing, each environment's plan, month and limit
palbase billing:env shop/staging                  # an environment's own: its plan, limit and month
palbase billing:env shop/staging --plan pay_as_you_go --limit 25
palbase billing:env shop/staging --plan free      # --frozen yes|no
palbase billing:invoices                          # the account's charges' invoices
palbase billing:charges --period 2026-10 --csv    # the month's charges by environment and item, as the page downloads them
```

The environment is `project/environment` or its ref, else the one chosen for the directory; the organization is `--org`'s, else that environment's. Amounts are in US dollars, to the cent. A member reads the plans; the money is an owner's or an admin's.

## The API

What Studio's Billing page does, an admin's [access token](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) does too — save opening the payment account and saving a card on Stripe's page, which are a person's. The calls are on Studio's API, under the organization:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing` | Who pays for it, its own payment account and how it stands, and each environment's plan, month and limit |
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/environments/{ref}` | An environment's own: its plan, limit and month |
| `PATCH /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/environments/{ref}` | Its `plan` (`free`, `pay_as_you_go`), `frozen`, `monthly_limit_micros` (`null`: none) |
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/cards` | The cards, the default first |
| `PUT /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/cards/{card}/default` | Makes a card the default |
| `DELETE /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/cards/{card}` | Removes a card; the default only when it is the last |
| `GET` / `PUT /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/customer` | The name, `address` and `tax_id` (`{ "type": "eu_vat", "value": "…" }`, or `null`) the invoices are made out to |
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/charges?period=2026-10` | The month's charges, by environment and item: units, gross and charged, and what each owes |
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/charges.csv?period=2026-10` | The same, as CSV |
| `GET /v1/orgs/{id}/billing/invoices` | The account's charges' invoices |

Amounts are in micro-dollars (1,000,000 is $1), in whole cents. A member reads the plans and what was used; amounts and money are an admin's.

## Related

- [Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits) — what is metered, and what a free environment gets
- [Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations) — roles, and who is emailed
- [Access Tokens](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) — an admin token for the API

# Usage & Limits

Every environment's use is metered by the calendar month (UTC): what its modules did, what its machines and databases ran, and what it sent. Studio shows it on the project's **Settings › Usage**, environment by environment.

An environment is held to limits of three kinds, and each one says so in its answer:

- **Rates**, per second: a call over one is refused for that second (`429` with `Retry-After: 1`).
- **Limits on the month**: a limit set on one of the environment's metrics refuses that use, or only counts it, until the month ends.
- **What a free project gets**: its traffic is slowed past 5 GB, its chat messages past a million a month or 1 GiB kept, and a free database sleeps past its 400 hours. None of them stops the project or loses its data.

## Where usage is shown

**Project › Settings › Usage** shows one environment at a time (choose it at the top when the project has more than one) over the last 3, 6 or 12 months:

- this month's API requests, monthly active users, stored data and machine hours, each beside its months;
- **Limits**: each limit set on the environment, with what this month has used against it, and **Blocked** once a limit that refuses is reached;
- a chart per month of requests, active users, notifications sent by channel, stored data, download traffic, realtime messages, analytics events, machine hours, machine internet traffic, response traffic and database hours by size;
- **Every metered item**: every metric the environment used, this month and the month before.

Every member of the organization reads it ([Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations#roles)). The organization's owners are also mailed when a free project has sent 80% of its month's traffic and when it has sent all of it, and when a free database has been awake 80% of its hours and all of them.

## What is metered

| Metric | What counts |
|---|---|
| `requests` | **API requests**: each request to the environment's address that a module answers. Not among them: the cache's calls, the stores' reports to purchases (`/purchases/webhooks/…`), and the files the platform moves for a module's own work, such as an AI workspace's |
| `auth.mau` | **Monthly active users**: the users who signed in or kept a session alive in the month |
| `notify.email`, `notify.push`, `notify.sms`, `notify.whatsapp` | **Email**, **Push**, **SMS** and **WhatsApp** sent: an email through any sender (those through Palbase's shared sender are also `notify.email.shared`), a push delivered to a user on any of their devices, a text or a verification code, a WhatsApp message |
| `notify.sms.shared` | **Verification codes through Palbase's Twilio**, in nano-dollars at Twilio's price: each code's text at the dearest price Twilio lists for its country (which carrier a number is on is not known before it is texted), and $0.05 for each code approved. An environment with no SMS provider and no verification service of its own sends its codes (phone sign-in, SMS second factor, `/notify/verifications`) this way, from a Twilio Verify service of its own: its texts say the code is from the project when the environment has paid rights, from Palbase otherwise. Billed at Twilio's price and 10%, its first $4 of a month free; a free environment past them sends no more until the month ends (`429 quota_exceeded`) |
| `storage.bytes` | **Stored data**: the objects and their renditions, the month's largest |
| `storage.egress` | **Download traffic**: what storage sent, a part of response traffic |
| `storage.operations` | The requests storage served |
| `storage.transforms` | **Image transformations**: a picture made over from an original (resized, cropped, re-encoded); one answered from what was made before is not one |
| `cache.bytes`, `cache.egress` | **Cache memory**, the month's largest, and **Cache reads**, a part of response traffic ([Cache](/docs/backend/cache)) |
| `realtime.messages` | **Realtime messages**: each one delivered — a broadcast to ten subscribers is ten |
| `realtime.connections` | Realtime connections open at once, the month's largest |
| `messaging.messages` | **Chat messages**: each message the project's people, or its server, sent in its conversations; one sent again with the same client id is one |
| `messaging.bytes` | **Chat message storage**: what the project's messages weigh where they are kept — each one's sealed text and 768 bytes for its row and indexes — the month's largest |
| `calls.bytes` | **Call data**: what the media server sent the people, and the agents, of the project's calls — their sound, picture and data from the others, voice and video alike ([Calls](/docs/calls/overview#what-it-costs)) |
| `flags.reads` | The flag reads clients made, answered in full or not modified |
| `analytics.events` | **Analytics events**: captures, identifies, aliases, screens and page views (setting a person's properties is not counted) |
| `analytics.perf`, `analytics.traces`, `analytics.console` | Performance samples kept, request traces taken, console records kept ([Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview)) |
| `machines.seconds` | **Machine hours**: how long the machines were awake, each copy counted; `machines.seconds.<size>` the same by size |
| `machines.egress` | **Machine internet traffic**: what the machines sent to the internet |
| `edge.egress` | **Response traffic**: what the environment's answers sent its clients, its modules' and its machines' alike |
| `machines.builds.seconds` | **Build hours** |
| `machines.images.bytes`, `machines.logs.bytes` | **Machine images** kept, the month's largest, and **Machine logs** kept |
| `databases.seconds.<size>` | **Database hours**: how long the databases of each size were awake |
| `databases.bytes`, `databases.backups` | What the databases hold, and what their backups hold, the month's largest |
| `databases.traffic` | What the databases read from and wrote to their disks |
| `databases.egress` | **Database client traffic**: what the databases sent clients that connect to them over their own addresses (`psql`, a backend on your computer) |
| `ai.tokens.<provider>.<model>.<kind>` | **AI tokens** with Palbase's provider keys, by model and kind: `input`, `image_input`, `output`, `cache_read`, `cache_write`. A model used with the project's own provider key is the provider's to count |
| `ai.images.<provider>.<model>` | **AI images** made, by model |
| `ai.machines.seconds`, `ai.voice.seconds`, `ai.web_search.calls` | **AI workspace hours**, **AI voice hours** and **AI web searches** |

A metric that is "the month's largest" is a level, not a sum: what the environment held at its most during the month.

## Rates

| What | How much | Past it |
|---|---|---|
| The environment's requests | 200 a second, unless Palbase set another | `429 rate_limited`, `Retry-After: 1` |
| What apps send to analytics | 1,000 events, samples, traces and records a second, counted apart from the requests | `429 rate_limited` |
| The cache's calls | As many a second as the requests, counted apart from them; 8 MiB read and 2 MiB written a second | `429 rate_limited` |
| Your backend's own routes | What each route's `rateLimit` says ([Controllers & Routing](/docs/backend/controllers)) | `429 too_many_requests` |

Realtime has rates of its own, which a project may lower ([Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime)), and so do sign-ins and the messages a project sends. The SDKs send a refused call again on their own, waiting what `Retry-After` asks, when it is a read or a write that cannot be done twice ([Server SDK](/docs/server/overview#retries)).

## Limits on the month

A limit on the month names one metric of one environment and how much of it the month may use, and is one of two kinds: one that **refuses** past it, and one that only **counts**. Palbase sets them; the **Limits** panel lists those set on the environment. A month's use starts again at 00:00 UTC on its first day.

When a limit that refuses is reached, that use is refused until the month ends, and the refusal's `Retry-After` is the seconds until then:

| Limit on | What is refused |
|---|---|
| API requests | Every request to the environment's address but those not counted (above): `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Monthly active users | New sign-ups: `403 signups_closed`. Sign-ins go on: the people already counted keep their accounts |
| Email, push, SMS or WhatsApp | Sending on that channel: `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Stored data | Writing to storage: `429 quota_exceeded`. Reads go on |
| Realtime messages or connections | A new socket: `429 quota_exceeded`, with `Retry-After: 3600` (an hour, not the month's end); and a server's broadcast: `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Flag reads | Reading the flags: `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Chat messages, or what they weigh | Sending a message, a person's or the server's: `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Voice or video call time | Starting a call of that kind: `429 quota_exceeded`. Calls going on go on to their end |
| Analytics events, samples, traces or console records | Sending that kind: `429 quota_exceeded` |
| Machine hours | The machines: they are stopped, dedicated sizes too, and a request to one, a new machine, a cron or a task is `429 quota_exceeded` |

A limit that counts refuses nothing: the use goes on and is metered.

## What a free project gets

An environment is free while it is on the Free plan — every environment starts on it — while the payment account that pays for it is held for a charge unpaid, and while its month is at its monthly limit ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)). Each environment's limit is its own: one at its limit holds no other.

- **Sizes.** Its machines are of the `shared-256` size, the one free machine size, and it has one database at most, of the `free` size: a project holds one database of a free size at a time ([Databases](/docs/machines/databases#sizes)). Every other size is paid for: opening a machine or a database of one, or moving one to it, is `403 size_not_available`. `palbase machines:sizes` and `palbase databases:sizes` list the sizes and which of them the environment may open now ([Machines](/docs/machines/overview#sizes)).
- **Traffic.** It sends 5 GB a month at full speed: its machines' internet traffic and its response traffic together. Past it, until the month ends, its machines' traffic and answers and the files its storage hands out go at about 256 kbit/s; nothing is stopped, and the API's other answers are not slowed. A slowed project's downloads are paced, and one more than it may have under way at once is `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After`. A file the CDN answers from its own copy never reaches the project, and is neither counted nor slowed ([The CDN](/docs/backend/storage#the-cdn)). See [Reaching the internet](/docs/machines/overview#reaching-the-internet).
- **Chat messages.** 1 million messages a month, and 1 GiB of them kept. Past either, until the month ends, the project's messages go at about one a second, all its people and its server together: a send waits its turn, 10 seconds at the most, and one whose turn is further off is `429 slowed` with `Retry-After` — the SDKs keep it in their outbox and send it again. No message is lost, and reading, syncing and everything else go on at full speed. What is kept counts at its month's largest, so a project that keeps more than 1 GiB is slowed again early each month: remove old messages, or set the project's retention ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#the-projects-settings)), to stay under it.
- **Calls.** 25 GB of call data a month. Past it, until the month ends, no call starts (`429 quota_exceeded`); calls going on go on to their end ([Calls](/docs/calls/overview#what-it-costs)).
- **A free database** is awake 400 hours a month at most. Past them it sleeps until the month ends, refusing connections, with its data kept; from then its next connection wakes it.
- **AI.** $1.00 of Palbase's models a month, at the provider's price and 10%. Past it, until the month ends, a call to them is `402 ai_payment_required`; a call under the project's own provider key goes on ([AI](/docs/backend/ai#what-it-costs)).

An environment on Pay as you go is never slowed for its traffic, and its machines and databases may be of any size; a database of the `free` size keeps its 400 hours whoever holds it. What it uses past its own free quotas is charged to the payment account that pays for its organization ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)).

## Each module's own limits

| Module | Limits |
|---|---|
| Storage | 5 GiB an object unless the bucket says less; a signed URL lives 7 days at most ([Storage](/docs/backend/storage)) |
| Cache | 25 MiB of entries, the ones nearest their end dropped to make room; 512 KiB a value ([Cache](/docs/backend/cache)) |
| Tasks | 100,000 tasks not yet done, or 256 MiB of what they carry ([Tasks](/docs/backend/tasks)) |
| Machines | 5 machines, 1 to 5 copies each, 50 builds a day, logs kept 7 days ([Machines](/docs/machines/overview#limits)) |
| Databases | 3 a project, one of them of a free size at a time; a database full to its size's storage turns read-only ([Databases](/docs/machines/databases#sizes)) |
| Analytics | Events kept 90 days unless changed, 365 at most ([Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview#how-long-it-is-kept)) |
| Calls | 100 people a call, agents included; a person starts 10 calls a minute, and 60 an hour unless the project says otherwise; ended calls kept 400 days ([Calls](/docs/calls/overview#the-projects-settings)) |

# Logs

Studio's **Logs** page lists what happened in an environment, newest first, one category at a time:

| Category | A line is | Its source | Its level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Requests** | A request to the environment's address, whichever module it went to, as the platform's edge answered it — refused ones too | The module: `auth`, `storage`, `realtime`, `flags`, `notify`, `analytics`, `secrets`, `machines` (databases included), `stores`, or `other` for a path no module answers | Info below 400, warn a 4xx, error a 5xx or no answer at all |
| **Auth** | An event of auth's audit trail: a sign-in, a sign-up, a password or session change | The event, such as `auth.login.success` | Warn a failure |
| **Notifications** | An email, SMS, WhatsApp message or push sent, and what became of it | The channel | Error one that did not arrive (failed, bounced, rejected, expired) |
| **Machines** | What a machine wrote, its migration runs included ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds#logs)) | The machine | The level the line says of itself |
| **Builds** | A build of a machine's commit | The machine | Error a failed build, warn a cancelled one |

Each category is narrowed by text, by source and by level, over the last 15 minutes up to the last 7 days. **Live** reads again every 5 seconds; **Paused** holds the list still while you read it. A line opens whole, each of its fields with a copy button. The address of the page carries the category and the filters, so a view can be shared.

## Request lines

A request line holds what the edge knows of the request, and nothing it carried:

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `ts` | When the request arrived |
| `module` | The module it went to |
| `method`, `path` | The path **without its query**: a signed URL's signature and a token travel in the query, so it is never kept. Past 2,048 bytes it is cut |
| `status` | What the client was answered; `0` when it got no answer |
| `duration_ms` | Until the last byte of the answer was sent |
| `client_ip`, `user_agent` | Who asked: the client's address as the edge saw it, and its user agent (its first 512 bytes) |
| `request_id` | The `X-Request-Id` the client was answered with — the one to quote when asking about a request |
| `flags` | Present when the request ended short of a module's answer: `UAEX` the key or rate check refused it, `NR` no module answers its path, `UF` or `UH` the module could not be reached, `UT` it did not answer in time, `DC` the client went away |

Not its headers, not its body. A line is kept **7 days** and deleted within a day after; only the project it was made for reads it. Anyone can send a project requests, and a refused one is a line too: under a flood, each of the platform's edges keeps about 1 MiB of a project's lines a second and drops the rest, so a flood to one project does not cost the others their lines.

From a server, `GET /analytics/requests` with the project's secret key answers the same lines, newest first:

| Query | |
|---|---|
| `window_seconds` | How far back, 1 to 604,800 (a week); an hour when left out |
| `module` | One module's requests only |
| `level` | `info`, `warn`, `error`, one or more, comma-separated |
| `q` | Text found in the path or the user agent, or a request id or a client address, exactly |
| `limit` | How many lines at most, 1 to 500 (100 by default) |
| `cursor` | The `next_cursor` of the page before; absent on the last page |

```ts
// scripts/errors.ts
type RequestLine = { ts: string; module: string; method: string; path: string; status: number; request_id: string };

const res = await fetch(`${process.env.PALBASE_URL}/analytics/requests?window_seconds=600&level=error`, {
  headers: { apikey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! },
});
const { requests } = (await res.json()) as { requests: RequestLine[]; next_cursor?: string };

for (const r of requests) console.log(r.ts, r.status, r.module, r.method, r.path, r.request_id);
```

A secret key never goes in a browser: a call that carries one from a web page is refused (`401 secret_key_in_browser`).

# CLI

`palbase` is the command line for your organizations, projects and environments. It comes in the same npm package as the SDKs: `npx palbase <command>` runs it with nothing installed, and in a project that depends on `palbase` it runs the version installed there.

A machine is deployed by a push to its branch, which builds and rolls it out ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds)); `palbase machines:deploy` builds the branch's head again, for a push GitHub did not deliver. The CLI does what a push does not — registering client apps and writing their settings, the purchase catalog, an environment's auth, storage, flags and notification settings, tokens for CI and agents, a database's dumps and restores. It is also how a script, a CI job or an AI agent works with Palbase. Every command is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference).

## Signing in

```sh
npx palbase login
```

`login` shows a one-time code and opens Studio, where you approve it while signed in. On a computer with no browser — a server, a container, an agent's sandbox — `palbase login --no-browser` prints the address to open on any device. The CLI then holds a session of yours: Studio lists it beside your other sessions, and ending it there signs the CLI out. `palbase logout` ends it from the terminal, and `palbase whoami` prints who the CLI acts as.

## Choosing an environment

Most commands act on one environment of one project. `palbase use` chooses it for the directory you are in:

```sh
palbase use shop/main          # the project "shop", its environment "main"
palbase use acme/shop/staging  # when two organizations have a project named "shop"
palbase status                 # who you are there, its machines and databases
```

The choice is kept on this computer, not in the repository, so two checkouts of the same project can each act on their own environment. Commands run in that directory, or one under it, act on it. `-P <project>` and `-E <env>` choose for a single command instead:

```sh
palbase flags:list -P shop -E staging
```

A change to a production environment asks for confirmation; `--yes` gives it in a script. `--non-interactive` makes a command refuse anything that would ask, and `--json` prints the answer as JSON for a program to read. These are the [global flags](/docs/cli/reference#global-flags) every command takes.

## Projects, environments and keys

```sh
palbase projects:create shop                 # a project with its first environment, main; its keys are printed
palbase envs:create staging --from main      # another environment of the project chosen here
palbase keys:create --kind publishable --label web
palbase open auth                            # the environment's Auth section in Studio
```

`palbase projects:list` and `palbase envs:list` list what you can reach. A new key's value is printed once; `palbase keys:list` lists the environment's keys without their values, and `palbase keys:revoke <key-id>` refuses whatever holds one from its next request.

Two environments of a project drift apart as settings change in one and not the other. `palbase config:diff --from staging --to main` shows how their module settings differ — auth, storage, flags, notifications, realtime, analytics — and `palbase config:copy --from staging --to main` makes the second equal to the first; secrets are not copied, only named. `palbase types:pull` writes the environment's secret, flag, bucket and role names into `palbase/palbase-env.d.ts`, so `Secrets.get`, `Flags` and `Storage.buckets` accept those names and no others.

## Running a backend on your computer

`palbase init` starts a backend on `palbase/backend` in the current directory: a health route, its module, its tests and a Dockerfile; `--db` adds a schema with its routes and their test ([Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure)). Nothing that already exists is written over.

The backend needs the environment's address and a key to run. Two commands give it them:

- `palbase env:pull` writes them into `.env.local`, between markers it owns; the rest of the file stays as it is. The key is yours, lasts 30 days, and is revoked by `palbase logout`. No secret's value is written: the app reads the project's secrets when it starts.
- `palbase run -- bun dev` runs a command with them in its environment and writes nothing to disk.

`palbase test` runs the backend's tests the way the platform runs them before a build takes traffic: test users are made for the run, their tokens are handed to the command, and they are deleted when it ends ([Testing](/docs/backend/testing)).

```sh
palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url http://localhost:8080 -- bun test ./tests
```

## In CI

A CI job signs in with an organization's access token instead of a person: set it as the job's `PALBASE_TOKEN` secret, and the CLI acts with it at its role — member or admin — on every project of the organization.

```sh
palbase tokens:create github-actions --role admin --days 90
```

The value is printed once. Tokens are listed with `palbase tokens:list` (never their values) and revoked with `palbase tokens:revoke <name>`; [Access Tokens](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) says what a token may and may not do. In CI, `palbase apps:sync --check` exits 1 when the app's committed settings and clients are not what the project gives now.

## For an AI agent

An agent that works on one environment gets an environment token rather than an organization's: it does what your role does in that environment alone, for a few hours, and never makes or shows a standing credential, changes people or roles, or deletes a project or an environment.

```sh
palbase env:tokens:create --minutes 120 --name coding-agent
palbase env:tokens:create --scope machines:read,machines:logs   # only read machines and their logs
```

Give the agent the value as `PALBASE_TOKEN`. `--scope` narrows it to `machines:read`, `machines:logs`, `apps:sync`, `auth:test-users` or `support`. `palbase env:tokens:list` lists the live ones and `palbase env:tokens:revoke <id>` ends one at its next request. The docs an agent reads are at `/llms.txt`, with every page in one file at `/llms-full.txt`.

## Searching the docs

`palbase docs:search` finds what these docs say about what you need — by its meaning, in your own words; ask in English, the docs' language — and prints the sections that answer it, each with its address and its text:

```sh
palbase docs:search "<what you need>"
palbase docs:search "<what you need>" --limit 3 --json
```

Say what you need as a question of your own — what you are trying to do, not the words of a heading — and the search finds the sections that mean it.

It needs no sign-in, and a page changed here is found by what it says now within minutes. A caller searches 10 times in ten seconds, 30 a minute and 300 an hour: a sign-in or `PALBASE_TOKEN`, sent when there is one, as itself, and a search with neither by its address. When many search at once, a search waits its turn for a few seconds, or is told to search again in a moment. `--json` prints what the search answered — what an agent reads.

## Asking Palbase's support line

What the docs do not answer — a command or call that fails with nothing to act on, a page that is wrong or missing, something Palbase seems not to do — goes to Palbase's support line:

```sh
palbase support:ask "machines:deploy fails with build_failed and the log ends at npm ci — what is wrong?"
```

The answer comes from these docs and from what the environment shows you: its machines, their last builds and the end of a failed build's log, read with your own sign-in or token and sent with the question. When the answer is that Palbase lacks something, the CLI prints a case number: Palbase has it, and you are told by email when Palbase closes it. An answer that finds nothing lacking is printed alone, with no case number. Keys, tokens and passwords in a question are masked before anyone reads it. Palbase keeps every question with its answer — masked, without what the environment showed or who asked — to see what it is asked most and make these docs better there; a project's questions go when the project is deleted. An agent asks with an environment token that has the `support` scope. A person asks 30 questions an hour, a project 60.

## What the commands cover

| Group | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`orgs`](/docs/cli/reference#orgs), [`projects`](/docs/cli/reference#projects), [`envs`](/docs/cli/reference#envs) | Organizations and their members, projects, environments ([Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations)) |
| [`tokens`](/docs/cli/reference#tokens), [`keys`](/docs/cli/reference#keys), [`env`](/docs/cli/reference#env) | Access tokens, an environment's API keys, environment tokens and `.env.local` |
| [`apps`](/docs/cli/reference#apps) | The apps that call the project, and the settings and backend clients written into their repositories ([Client Apps](/docs/apps/overview)) |
| [`auth`](/docs/cli/reference#auth) | Sign-in providers, settings, roles, hooks, users, the audit trail ([Auth](/docs/auth/overview)) |
| [`storage`](/docs/cli/reference#storage), [`flags`](/docs/cli/reference#flags), [`notify`](/docs/cli/reference#notify), [`realtime`](/docs/cli/reference#realtime), [`analytics`](/docs/cli/reference#analytics), [`secrets`](/docs/cli/reference#secrets), [`webhooks`](/docs/cli/reference#webhooks) | Each module's settings and data |
| [`purchases`](/docs/cli/reference#purchases) | The catalog, paywalls, the stores' connections and customers ([Purchases](/docs/purchases/overview)) |
| [`stores`](/docs/cli/reference#stores) | Builds, testers and review on TestFlight and Google Play ([App Distribution](/docs/distribution/overview)) |
| [`github`](/docs/cli/reference#github), [`machines`](/docs/cli/reference#machines) | Connecting GitHub, machines, their builds, logs, crons and tasks ([Machines](/docs/machines/overview)) |
| [`databases`](/docs/cli/reference#databases), [`db`](/docs/cli/reference#db) | Databases, their backups, connection addresses, `psql`, dumps and schema plans ([Databases](/docs/machines/databases)) |
| [`config`](/docs/cli/reference#config), [`types`](/docs/cli/reference#types) | Comparing and copying module settings between environments, and the environment's names as TypeScript types |
| [`docs`](/docs/cli/reference#docs) | Searching these docs by meaning ([Searching the docs](#searching-the-docs)) |
| [`support`](/docs/cli/reference#support) | A question to Palbase's support line ([Asking Palbase's support line](#asking-palbases-support-line)) |

# CLI reference

Every command of `palbase` 0.33.0 — the CLI in the `palbase` npm package — as its own help prints it. Run it with `npx palbase <command>`, or `palbase <command>` once the package is installed; `palbase help <command>` prints the same in a terminal. Signing in, choosing an environment and using a token in CI are in [the CLI overview](/docs/cli/overview).

419 commands in 35 groups.

## Global flags

Every command takes these.

```text
  -P, --project <project>  the project (name or id; org/project when the name is in two organizations)
  -E, --env <env>          the project's environment (slug or ref)
      --json               print the answer as JSON
      --non-interactive    never ask: refuse what would need a question
  -y, --yes                confirm a change to a production environment without asking
      --debug              print each request the command sends
  -h, --help               show help
```

## General

### `palbase login`

Sign in with your Studio account

```sh
palbase login
```

Shows a one-time code and opens Studio, where you approve it while signed in there.
The CLI then holds a session of yours: Studio lists it with your others, and ending it there signs the CLI out.
On a machine with no browser (a server, an agent), open the address it prints on any device.

```text
      --no-browser  print the address instead of opening a browser
```

### `palbase logout`

Sign out: the session is ended at Palbase and forgotten on this computer

```sh
palbase logout
```

### `palbase whoami`

The account the CLI acts as, and the environment chosen for this directory

```sh
palbase whoami
```

### `palbase use`

Choose the environment this directory acts on (kept on this computer)

```sh
palbase use [<project>[/<env>] | <org>/<project>/<env>] [--clear]
```

Commands run in this directory, or a directory under it, then act on that environment unless -P/-E say otherwise.
Nothing is written into the project: two checkouts of it can each act on their own environment.
With no argument and a person at the terminal, it lists your environments to pick from.

```text
      --clear  forget the choice made for this directory
```

### `palbase status`

The environment this directory acts on: who you are there, its machines and databases

```sh
palbase status
```

### `palbase open`

Open the environment in Studio (its overview, or a section: auth, storage, flags, …)

```sh
palbase open [section]
```

### `palbase init`

Start a backend on palbase/backend here (or in `<dir>`): a health route, its module, its tests, a Dockerfile; --db adds a schema, its routes and their test

```sh
palbase init [dir] [--db] [--print]
```

Nothing already there is written over: a file init would write that exists stops it, naming the file.
--db's table is typed in palbase/palbase-env.d.ts by the block palbase db:types writes of the schema: run db:types again when you change it.
--print writes nothing: it prints the files as JSON ({ name, db, version, files: { `<path>`: `<text>` } }), for a program that seeds a repository with this release's starter (bunx `palbase@<version>` init --print `<name>` --db).
Then: bun install, palbase use `<project>/<environment>`, palbase env:pull, bun dev.
Its tests: bun test (here, no app); palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url http://localhost:8080 -- bun test ./tests (against the app you started, as test users made for the run — with an environment's token, against the deployed machine: --base-url `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio`); on the platform, palbase machines:update `<name>` --test-command "bun test ./tests" --test-users alice,bob runs them against each new build before it takes traffic.

```text
      --db     with a database: a schema file (a table each user reads alone) and its routes
      --print  print the files as JSON, write nothing ([dir] names the package)
```

### `palbase strings`

Keep the app's translations (palbase/strings/) with its code: each t("…") a sentence, every language's file with it

```sh
palbase strings [--source <language>] [--add <language>] [--translate] [--prune]
```

Reads every t("…") the backend's source calls — imported from palbase/backend, or from a module of the app that re-exports it — in the app's directory (the nearest one up with a package.json). A sentence new in the code is added to each language's file, empty: t() answers it in the source language until it is translated. A translation is kept.
A sentence the code no longer calls is kept and listed; --prune takes it out of every file. A call it could not follow (a t from a module it does not read, a linked directory) is said, where.
palbase/strings/_meta.json names the source language (the one the sentences are written in); each other language is `palbase/strings/<language>.json`, "sentence": "translation". Edit them as any file of the app.
--translate has the environment's ai module translate what is empty (the project's AI use, as any other: its cost is in the AI usage; production's asks first). A translation is used as it is written; correct it in the file.
A table in the earlier format (version 2) is written in this one.

```text
      --source <language>  the language the sentences are written in, for a table not made yet (tr, en, pt-BR)
      --add <language>     a language to translate into: its file is made (may be given more than once)
      --translate          translate what is empty, with the environment's ai module (-P/-E, or palbase use)
      --prune              take the sentences the code no longer calls out of every file
```

### `palbase run`

Run a command with the environment's address and your own key in its environment, nothing written to disk

```sh
palbase run [--secrets development|production] -- <command> [args…]
```

palbase run -- bun dev, palbase run -- npm test: the app reads the project's secrets at boot (PALBASE_SECRETS).

```text
      --secrets <set>  the project's secrets the app reads at boot: development (default) or production
```

### `palbase test`

Run the backend's tests as the platform does before a build goes out: test users made for the run and deleted after, `PALBASE_TEST_*` in the command's environment

```sh
palbase test [--machine <name>] [--users <names>] [--base-url <url>] [--secrets development|production] [-- <command> [args…]]
```

palbase test --machine backend --base-url http://localhost:8080: the machine's own test command and test users, as the platform runs them before each build of it rolls out.
palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url http://localhost:8080 -- bun test: api.signInAs("alice") acts as a test user made for this run.
The command gets what palbase run gives it, and PALBASE_TEST_AUTH_URL (the environment's address), PALBASE_TEST_IDENTITIES (the run's test users, each with its token) and, with --base-url, PALBASE_TEST_BASE_URL (where the app under test answers; without it HTTP tests skip themselves).
The test users are deleted when the command ends, however it ends — Ctrl-C too: the command is stopped, they are deleted, and palbase test ends as the signal would have.
With an environment's token (PALBASE_TOKEN, scope auth:test-users) the test users are made and deleted with the token, and no key is made: the command gets no PALBASE_SECRET_KEY, so test the app where it is deployed — palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio` -- bun test ./tests (the machine named backend; `https://<name>-<ref>.app.palbase.studio` for another, as machines:list shows).

```text
      --machine <name>  a machine whose test command (when no command is given) and test users (when --users is not) are run
      --users <names>   the test users to make for the run, comma-separated
      --base-url <url>  where the app under test answers (http://localhost:8080)
      --secrets <set>   the project's secrets the app reads at boot: development (default) or production
```

### `palbase billing`

Who pays for an organization, how its payment account stands, and each environment's plan, month and limit

```sh
palbase billing [--org <org>]
```

A member reads the plans, what was used and who pays; the money (amounts, the card) is an owner's or an admin's.

```text
      --org <org>  the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
```

### `palbase journeys`

The environment's journeys: each one's key, name, status, way in, and when it was published

```sh
palbase journeys [--status draft|live|stopped]
```

```text
      --status <status>  draft, live or stopped alone
```

## `env`

### `palbase env:pull`

Write what the backend needs to run here into .env.local: the environment's address and your own key — no secret's value

```sh
palbase env:pull [--file <path>] [--secrets development|production]
```

The app reads the project's secrets at boot (PALBASE_SECRETS); their names are listed as comments: set one in the file to override it.
The key is yours (CLI — you (this computer)), good for 30 days, made again by env:pull and run; palbase logout revokes it.
Only the block between the palbase markers is written; the rest of the file stays as it is.

```text
      --file <path>    the file (default .env.local)
      --secrets <set>  the project's secrets the app reads at boot: development (default) or production
```

### `palbase env:tokens:list`

The environment's live tokens, by their hint (never their values)

```sh
palbase env:tokens:list
```

### `palbase env:tokens:create`

Mint a token of the environment for a program (an AI agent): your role in this environment alone, a few hours; shown this once

```sh
palbase env:tokens:create [--scope <scope>[,<scope>]] [--minutes <n>] [--name <name>]
```

It does in this environment what your role does — as your own CLI would — but never makes or shows a standing credential (a key, a token), changes people or roles, or deletes a project or an environment; nothing beyond this environment.
--scope narrows it to: machines:read, machines:logs, machines:previews, apps:sync, auth:test-users, support — machines:read reads the machines, their builds, crons, queues and pull requests' previews; machines:logs their logs; machines:previews opens a pull request's preview again (machines:previews:open: what a push to it would build anyway); apps:sync what palbase apps:sync reads; auth:test-users makes and deletes test users; support asks Palbase's support line (palbase support:ask).
Give it to the program as PALBASE_TOKEN: the CLI acts in this environment alone with it. It ends after --minutes (default 60, at most 240), and with what minted it.

```text
      --scope <scope>  narrow it to: machines:read, machines:logs, machines:previews, apps:sync, auth:test-users, support (comma-separated, or given again); none: your role
      --minutes <n>    how long it lives (default 60, at most 240)
      --name <name>    what it is for, as the environment lists it
```

### `palbase env:tokens:revoke`

Revoke an environment's token (by its id; with PALBASE_TOKEN an environment's token, `self` revokes it): refused from its next request on

```sh
palbase env:tokens:revoke <id|self>
```

## `types`

### `palbase types:pull`

Write the environment's secret, flag, bucket and role names into palbase/palbase-env.d.ts as types: Secrets.get, Flags and Storage.buckets take them and no other

```sh
palbase types:pull [--file <path>]
```

The names of the production secrets — what the machines start with, and so what Secrets.get reads there; development's are a developer's — leaving out what the platform sets itself (PALBASE_SECRET_KEY …), every flag, each bucket with its renditions (`Storage.buckets.<name>.getPublicUrl(path`, { variant })) and every role — never a value.
Only the block between the palbase:stack markers is written; the rest of the file stays as it is. Run it again when a name is added or taken away.

```text
      --file <path>  the file (default palbase/palbase-env.d.ts)
```

### `palbase tokens:create`

Make an access token of an organization for CI or an agent; its value is shown this once

Give it to the CI as the secret PALBASE_TOKEN: the CLI acts with it in place of a sign-in. It reaches its organization's projects and environments at its role, and nothing of its people or tokens.
It ends after --days (default 90, at most 365), and goes when it is revoked or when the one who made it leaves the organization.

## `account`

### `palbase account:tokens:list`

Your account tokens (for a program that opens organizations): name, how many organizations they reach, when they end and were last used — never their values


### `palbase account:tokens:create`

Make an account token for a program that opens organizations; its value is shown this once

```sh
palbase account:tokens:create <name> [--days <n>]
```

Give it to the program as its secret (PALBASE_TOKEN, or palbase/cloud's token): it opens organizations — you their owner, the token their admin — and builds projects and environments there.
It reaches only the organizations it opened, never your others; it makes no token or key and changes no one's place. It ends after --days (default 90, at most 365), when it is revoked, and, in an organization, when you leave it.

```text
      --days <n>  how many days it is good for (default 90)
```

## `billing`

### `palbase billing:charges`

A month's charges, by environment and item — used, at the price table, charged past each one's free quota — as a table or as CSV

```sh
palbase billing:charges [--period <YYYY-MM>] [--csv] [--org <org>]
```

--csv prints the CSV Studio downloads.

```text
      --org <org>         the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
      --period <YYYY-MM>  the month (this one by default)
      --csv               print it as CSV
```

### `palbase billing:invoices`

The invoices of an organization's payment account — each month's charge, and each charge at its threshold: Stripe makes one of each, and emails it

```sh
palbase billing:invoices [--org <org>]
```

```text
      --org <org>  the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
```

### `palbase billing:env`

An environment's place in the bill — its plan, frozen, its month's limit — read, or changed

```sh
palbase billing:env [<project/env | ref>] [--plan free|pay_as_you_go] [--limit <usd>|none] [--frozen yes|no] [-y]
```

With no flag it shows the environment: its plan, limit and month.
Pay as you go: what it uses past its free quota is owed to the payment account that pays for its organization (palbase billing:payer), charged at the month's end and as it comes to the account's threshold. An environment is moved to it only while its organization is paid for by an account with a card.
At its limit it is Free until the month ends; the organization's other environments go on.
Frozen, its requests are refused and its machines and databases stopped, its data kept; only what it stores is charged. Freezing asks first; -y does not.

```text
      --plan <free|pay_as_you_go>  Free (charged nothing, held to the free quotas) or Pay as you go (what it uses past its free quota is charged)
      --limit <usd|none>           at most this much a month; none for no limit
      --frozen <yes|no>            frozen: its requests refused, its machines and databases stopped, its data kept
```

### `palbase billing:payer`

Link an organization to the payment account that pays for it — an organization of yours whose account it is — or to none

```sh
palbase billing:payer <account org | none> [--org <org>]
```

One payment account pays for many organizations: it is charged for what each one's environments on Pay as you go owe, in one invoice a month (palbase billing:report).
An admin of the organization who also manages the account (an owner or an admin of its organization) links it — or their account token. With none, its environments on Pay as you go go Free; what they owed so far stays the account's.

```text
      --org <org>  the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
```

### `palbase billing:paid`

The organizations an organization's payment account pays for — its managers'

```sh
palbase billing:paid [--org <org>]
```

```text
      --org <org>  the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
```

### `palbase billing:report`

A payment account's month: each organization it paid for, each environment, what it owes — as a table or as CSV (item by item)

```sh
palbase billing:report [--period <YYYY-MM>] [--csv] [--org <org>]
```

What an organization that pays for its own customers' organizations bills them by: --csv gives each item of each environment, and what the account is charged for it (owed).

```text
      --org <org>         the organization (name or id; the one of the environment chosen here, or your only one)
      --period <YYYY-MM>  the month (this one by default)
      --csv               print it as CSV
```

## `auth`

### `palbase auth:settings:get`

The environment's auth settings: passwords, email confirmation, sessions, tokens, passkeys, risk

```sh
palbase auth:settings:get
```

### `palbase auth:settings:set`

Change auth settings: key=value, a value read as JSON when it is JSON (12, true, ["https://…"])

```sh
palbase auth:settings:set <key=value>…
```

Text needs no quotes (site_url=https://shop.example); quote text that reads as JSON: from_name='"123"'.
The change is made on the revision read: one made beside it in the meantime (Studio, another terminal) is refused, not overwritten.
palbase auth:settings:get lists the keys.

### `palbase auth:providers:list`

The sign-in methods: email, phone and the social providers, whether each is on, their clients and stored secrets (by name)

```sh
palbase auth:providers:list
```

### `palbase auth:providers:set`

Turn a sign-in provider on or off and set it up: its client, its secret (from stdin), phone codes

```sh
palbase auth:providers:set <provider> [--enable|--disable] [setting=value…] [--client-id <id>] [--secret-stdin] …
```

email is always on. phone: --enable/--disable, and its code settings as setting=value (allow_signups, otp_ttl_seconds, otp_max_attempts, sender, sms_second_factor).
google, apple, github, microsoft: --client-id sets the browser client --client names (default web), made when the provider has none of that name.
--secret-stdin reads the client's secret from stdin (Apple: the .p8 signing key, with --team-id and --key-id) and keeps it under --credential (default: the provider's name). It is never taken from the command line and never printed.
--clients-file replaces the provider's clients with the file's {"browser_clients": […], "native_clients": […]} (native apps, several clients).

```text
      --enable               turn it on
      --disable              turn it off
      --client <key>         the browser client --client-id, --return-uri and the secret go to (default web)
      --client-id <id>       the provider's id of your app (Google web client id, Apple services id, Microsoft application id, GitHub client id)
      --return-uri <url>     where your app is sent back after sign-in (repeat it; replaces the list)
      --application <key>    the application the client is for (default app)
      --variant <name>       the build variant the client is for (default release)
      --directory <tenant>   microsoft: a tenant id, organizations, consumers or common (default common)
      --secret-stdin         read the client's secret (Apple: the .p8 key) from stdin
      --credential <key>     the name the secret is kept under (default: the provider's)
      --team-id <id>         apple: your team's id, with --secret-stdin
      --key-id <id>          apple: the signing key's id, with --secret-stdin
      --clients-file <path>  replace the provider's clients with the file's (JSON)
```

### `palbase auth:providers:disable`

Turn a sign-in provider off (phone, google, apple, github, microsoft); its clients and secrets stay

```sh
palbase auth:providers:disable <provider>
```

### `palbase auth:providers:secret:delete`

Delete a sign-in provider's stored secret by its name; one a client still uses is refused

```sh
palbase auth:providers:secret:delete <name>
```

### `palbase auth:hooks:list`

### `palbase auth:hooks:create`

Register a blocking hook; its signing secret is printed this once

```sh

```

```text
      --event <event>              before.user.create, before.login, before.token.issue, … (the module lists them)
      --url <url>                  the https endpoint auth calls and waits for
      --failure-mode <deny|allow>  what auth does when the hook does not answer in time (default deny)
      --timeout <ms>               how long auth waits, 100–5000 ms (default 5000)
      --disable                    register it turned off
```

### `palbase auth:hooks:update`

```sh

```

```text
      --event <event>              before.user.create, before.login, before.token.issue, … (the module lists them)
      --url <url>                  the https endpoint auth calls and waits for
      --failure-mode <deny|allow>  what auth does when the hook does not answer in time (default deny)
      --timeout <ms>               how long auth waits, 100–5000 ms (default 5000)
      --enable                     turn it on
      --disable                    turn it off
```

### `palbase auth:hooks:delete`

### `palbase auth:oauth-clients:list`

The OAuth clients of the environment's OpenID provider (apps that sign in with your users' accounts)


### `palbase auth:oauth-clients:create`

Register an OAuth client; a confidential client's secret is printed this once

```sh
palbase auth:oauth-clients:create <name> [--public] [--redirect-uri <url>…] [--grant <type>…] [--scope <scope>…] [--client-id <id>]
```

```text
      --public              a public client (a CLI, a mobile app): it has no secret
      --redirect-uri <url>  where it may send the browser back (repeat it)
      --grant <type>        authorization_code (default), refresh_token, client_credentials, urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code
      --scope <scope>       what it may ask for (default openid, profile, email)
      --client-id <id>      a client_id to use as it is (default: a random one)
```

### `palbase auth:oauth-clients:delete`

Delete an OAuth client (by its id or its client_id)

```sh
palbase auth:oauth-clients:delete <id|client-id>
```

### `palbase auth:import`

Bring users over with what they sign in with: ids, addresses, password hashes, providers, second factors, passkeys, open sessions

```sh
palbase auth:import <file|folder> [--pepper-stdin]
```

A folder holds import bodies, one a file (users-0001.json…, each without its pepper); a file holds one such body, JSON lines (a user each) or one JSON array.
Password and recovery-code hashes keep the source's pepper: give it on stdin with --pepper-stdin — never on the command line.
Users go 1000 a call. One refused does not stop the others; a user whose id or address the project has is refused, never overwritten.

```text
      --pepper-stdin  read the source's pepper from stdin
```

### `palbase auth:test-users:list`

The environment's test users (made with its secret key; their tokens say test: true)

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:list
```

### `palbase auth:test-users:create`

Make test users for a suite, of the kind a sign-in asks for: their passwords (and a second factor's key), and with --token an access token each, shown this once; --template has the backend write the data a screen needs for each

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:create [--count <n>] [--token] [--email <address>] [--password <pw> | --passwordless] [--phone <e164> [--otp <code>]] [--email-otp <code>] [--unverified] [--mfa totp|sms|email] [--template <name> [--machine <name>]]
```

A test user signs in as any user does; its tokens say test: true, so a backend can tell them apart. --token gives each an access token at once, for a test that calls the backend as that user.
Its mail and texts are kept for it, read with palbase auth:test-users:messages `<id>` — a sign-in link, a verification or second factor's code: a made address (…@test.invalid) is mailed nothing and a phone texted nothing, while --email with an address of yours gets its mail too.
Of the kind a sign-in asks for: --passwordless (a link, a code or a passkey alone), --unverified (its verification is tested), --phone with its fixed code (--otp, made when left out), --email-otp (a fixed code its email accepts: a reviewer reads no inbox), --mfa (a second factor from the start; totp answers its key once).
--template `<name>` has the backend write the data of its @TestUserTemplate({ name }) for each user — its seed for one account, in its own code (palbase/backend), run on the machine --machine names or the environment's only one, for test users alone. Each user is answered with the rows written, by table, or why its template was not (no_template, not_a_test_user, template_failed, template_timeout, machine_unavailable): the user is made all the same, and the command then ends with 1. At most 10 users at once with a template.
palbase auth:test-users:template writes another template for a user made with one; palbase auth:test-users:delete has the template undone before the user is deleted.

```text
      --count <n>             how many (default 1, at most 100; 10 with --template)
      --token                 an access token for each, too
      --email <address>       its address — one of yours gets its mail too (default: a made …@test.invalid)
      --password <pw>         its password (default: a made one)
      --passwordless          no password: it signs in by a link, a code or a passkey
      --phone <e164>          a verified phone, texted nothing
      --otp <code>            the phone's fixed code, six digits (default: a made one)
      --email-otp <code>      a fixed code its email accepts, six digits
      --unverified            its email unverified
      --mfa <totp|sms|email>  a second factor from the start
      --template <name>       a @TestUserTemplate of the backend's: its data written for each user
      --machine <name>        the machine whose backend has the template (default: the environment's only one)
```

### `palbase auth:test-users:messages`

A test user's mail and texts of the last 7 days, the 50 newest first: to whom, the code and the link each carried

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:messages <user-id> [--channel email|sms]
```

What a flow sent the user — a sign-in link, a verification or second factor's code, the project's own mail — is kept for it: a test reads the code or link here. --json answers each whole: its subject, text, HTML and the variables its template had.
A user who is no test user is refused (not_a_test_user): no one else's mail is kept.

```text
      --channel <email|sms>  only this channel's
```

### `palbase auth:test-users:address`

An address for an app's sign-up to be tested with: the account a sign-up with it opens is a test user, its mail kept for palbase auth:test-users:messages

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:address
```

The address (signup-…@test.invalid) is typed into the app's sign-up form: the account it opens is a test user — its tokens say test: true, it is not counted as an active user, its verification mail is kept, never sent. Used once.
It holds a place of the environment's test-user cap until it is used, or lapses a day after it was made. A sign-up with any other address opens an ordinary user.

### `palbase auth:test-users:template`

Have the backend write a @TestUserTemplate's data for a test user made with a template — the same one again answers what it wrote then

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:template <user-id> <template> [--machine <name>]
```

The user is one auth:test-users:create --template made on that machine: a test user is the machine's that made it. Asked again for a template it wrote, the platform answers what it wrote then, and the backend is not called.

```text
      --machine <name>  the machine whose backend has the template (default: the environment's only one)
```

### `palbase auth:test-users:delete`

Delete a test user — one made with a template has the backend undo it first

```sh
palbase auth:test-users:delete <user-id> [--machine <name>]
```

A test user made with --template is deleted through the machine that made it: the backend's undo of each template runs first — a template with none leaves its data to user.deleted (what ownedByUser() owns goes with the user) — and an undo that fails keeps the user, for the delete to be asked again. Any other test user is deleted at once.
Without --machine the environment's machines are asked which made the user; a token that does not list the machines deletes it at once, its templates left to user.deleted.

```text
      --machine <name>  the machine that made the user with a template (default: whichever did)
```
