
It answers once its DNS points at the platform and says it is this environment's (the TXT record): both are printed.
At an apex (example.com) its www is added too, and one redirects to the other, as Vercel does: the apex to www.example.com unless --primary apex; --only adds the domain alone.
An apex takes an A record at the platform's address, which any DNS host has; a subdomain a CNAME. A domain is one environment's until it is removed there.

```text
      --site <name>             the site (default: web)
      --primary <www|apex>      at an apex: the address visitors end up at, the other redirecting to it (default: www)
      --only                    add the domain alone: no www, no redirect
      --redirect-status <code>  the redirect's status: 301, 302, 307 or 308 (default: 308)
```

### `palbase hosting:domains:redirect`

Send a domain's visitors to another domain of the site's — the same path and query there — or, with --none, have it answer itself

```sh
palbase hosting:domains:redirect <host> (--to <host> [--status 301|302|307|308] | --none) [--site <name>]
```

It holds at once. A domain redirects to one that answers itself, and one others redirect to answers itself.

```text
      --site <name>    the site (default: web)
      --to <host>      another domain of the site's
      --status <code>  301, 302, 307 or 308 (default: 308)
      --none           redirect nowhere: the domain answers itself
```

### `palbase hosting:domains:remove`

Stop a site answering at a domain: at once, and another environment may add it

```sh
palbase hosting:domains:remove <host> [--site <name>]
```

```text
      --site <name>  the site (default: web)
```

## `databases`

### `palbase databases:sizes`

The database sizes, and which of them this environment may open now

```sh
palbase databases:sizes
```

### `palbase databases:list`

The environment's databases: size, state, how full

```sh
palbase databases:list
```

### `palbase databases:get`

A database in full, with how to connect to it

```sh
palbase databases:get <name>
```

### `palbase databases:create`

Open a database; its passwords are kept on this computer (the platform shows them once)

```sh
palbase databases:create [name] [--size <size>] [--allow <ip/cidr,…>] [--backup-days <n>] [--show-passwords]
```

```text
      --size <size>      its size (palbase databases:sizes lists what is open)
      --allow <list>     who may connect, as addresses or CIDRs, comma-separated (default: anyone with the password)
      --backup-days <n>  how many days of backups to keep, 1 to 35
      --show-passwords   print the passwords too (they are kept on this computer either way)
```

### `palbase databases:update`

Change a database's size, who may connect to it, or how long its backups are kept

```sh
palbase databases:update <name> [--size <size>] [--allow <list>|""] [--backup-days <n>] [--wait]
```

A new size is taken at once and the database moves to it serving on (palbase databases:sizes lists them): its sessions on the direct port end once, when its primary moves, and new logins wait a few seconds then.

```text
      --size <size>      the size to move it to
      --allow <list>     who may connect (comma-separated addresses or CIDRs); "" for anyone with the password
      --backup-days <n>  how many days of backups to keep, 1 to 35
      --wait             with --size: follow the move until it serves at the new size
```

### `palbase databases:password:reset`

Make a database role's password new; it is kept on this computer, the old one stops working

```sh
palbase databases:password:reset <name> --role owner|app [--show-password]
```

The app role's new password reaches the machines given the database as they roll out with it; they keep serving.

```text
      --role <role>    owner (migrations, the console) or app (what the machines use)
      --show-password  print it too
```

### `palbase databases:restore`

Bring a database back to a moment of its backups

```sh
palbase databases:restore <name> --to <time>
```

```text
      --to <time>  the moment, as an RFC 3339 time (2026-10-08T12:00:00Z)
```

### `palbase databases:delete`

Delete a database (the platform keeps it 7 days to take back)

```sh
palbase databases:delete <name>
```

### `palbase databases:undelete`

Take back a database deleted in the last 7 days

```sh
palbase databases:undelete <name>
```

### `palbase databases:purge`

Delete a deleted database for good, now

```sh
palbase databases:purge <name>
```

## `db`

### `palbase db:url`

A database's connection address, for any tool (Prisma, Drizzle, pg_dump, a GUI)

```sh
palbase db:url [name] [--role owner|app] [--pooled] [--with-password]
```

Without --with-password the address holds no password: give the tool PGPASSWORD, or pass --with-password and keep the line out of your history.
The address asks for a checked certificate (sslmode=verify-full). Node drivers check it against the system's roots by themselves; psql, pg_dump and other libpq tools do only with PGSSLROOTCERT=system (Postgres 16+). The address does not say so itself: a driver that sends what it does not know to the server (postgres.js) would be refused.

```text
      --role <role>    owner (migrations, dumps) or app (what the machines use); default owner
      --pooled         the pooled port (PgBouncer, transaction mode): for an app's many short connections
      --with-password  put the password in the address
```

### `palbase db:shell`

Psql on a database (it wakes if asleep); -c runs one statement and ends

```sh
palbase db:shell [name] [--role owner|app] [--command <sql>]
```

```text
      --role <role>    owner (migrations, dumps) or app (what the machines use); default owner
  -c, --command <sql>  run this and end
```

### `palbase db:dump`

A copy of a database (pg_dump's custom format), as its owner

```sh
palbase db:dump [name] [--file <path>] [--schema-only]
```

```text
      --file <path>  where to write it (default <database>-<time>.dump)
      --schema-only  its structure, not its data
```

### `palbase db:restore`

Load a dump into a database, as its owner: a custom-format dump (pg_restore) or a .sql file (psql)

```sh
palbase db:restore <file> [--db <name>] [--clean]
```

A database Palbase did not make is taken over by its first release: its tables stay as they are (palbase db:pull writes their schema files).

```text
      --db <name>  the database (default: the environment's only one)
      --clean      drop what the dump makes before making it again
```

### `palbase db:copy`

Copy a database's data from one environment of the project to another

```sh
palbase db:copy --from <env> --to <env> [--db <name>] [--to-db <name>]
```

The target is overwritten with the source: what it held of the same tables goes (pg_restore --clean).
An encrypted field (.encrypted(), palbase/server's fields) is copied as •••, sealed with the target's keys: one environment's values never land readable in another.

```text
      --from <env>    the environment copied from (slug)
      --to <env>      the environment copied into (slug)
      --db <name>     the source's database (default: its only one)
      --to-db <name>  the target's database (default: the same name)
```

### `palbase db:plan`

What a start of the app's schema would do to a database, and what it would refuse — nothing is changed

```sh
palbase db:plan [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>] [--check]
```

--check ends with 1 when the schema would be refused: run it in CI before a push to production (-E main).

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
      --check               end with 1 when the plan has refusals
```

### `palbase db:status`

A database's Palgres ledger: the version serving, and the migration open and who opened it

```sh
palbase db:status [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>]
```

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
```

### `palbase db:push`

Try the app's schema on a database: your own one at once, the environment's beside the version serving

```sh
palbase db:push [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>] [--reset]
```

On a database of your own (--url) the migration is started and completed at once; a refused one can --reset (its data goes, the schema is made anew).
On the environment's database it is only started: the release serving goes on with its version, your backend with yours; the next release completes it, or takes its place.
One migration is open at a time: yours is replaced by your next push; another developer's or a release's is said, and yours waits.
Production's schema changes with its releases alone: db:push refuses it (db:plan -E main shows what a release would do).

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
      --reset               with --url: make the schema anew, its data gone
```

### `palbase db:migrate`

A migration step by hand: start, complete or rollback — for a database whose app runs elsewhere, or to finish one

```sh
palbase db:migrate <start|complete|rollback> [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>]
```

An app that is not one of the environment's machines: start, release the app, then complete once the old one is gone (pgroll's way).

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
```

### `palbase db:pull`

Write the schema files (`db/*.ts`) of what a database holds: to take a database over

```sh
palbase db:pull [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>] [--dir <dir>]
```

Its first release then takes the database over: the tables stay as they are, nothing is copied.

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
      --dir <dir>           where db/ is written (default: here)
```

### `palbase db:seed`

Run db/seed.ts against a database that is not production

```sh
palbase db:seed [--url <postgres-url> | --db <name>] [--file <path>]
```

```text
      --url <postgres-url>  a database of your own (a local Postgres 18): the schema goes in it at once
      --db <name>           the environment's database (default: its only one)
      --entry <file>        the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
      --file <path>         the seed script (default db/seed.ts)
```

### `palbase db:types`

Write the app's tables into palbase/palbase-env.d.ts as types — rows, inserts, unique keys and relations both ways (with, has) — from its schema files

```sh
palbase db:types [--entry <file>] [--file <path>]
```

`Database.public.<table>` and `Database.<schema>.<table>` are typed from them with no import and no generic — the relations of a foreign key to another file's table too, which a schema's own type (TablesOf) cannot see: an app that declares Tables with TablesOf leaves that out once it has these. palbase init --db writes the block of its starter schema; run db:types again when a schema changes.
No database is asked: the app is started in its types mode, which reads its schema files and writes nothing else. Only the block between the palbase:env markers is written; run it again when a schema changes.

```text
      --entry <file>  the app's entry, what it is started with (default src/main.ts)
      --file <path>   the file (default palbase/palbase-env.d.ts)
```



<!-- ===== backend/overview ===== -->

# Overview

`palbase/backend` is the framework you write a Palbase backend in. You write plain TypeScript: class controllers whose methods are routes, `@Injectable()` services that hold the logic, schemas that validate what comes in, and a `@Module` per domain that says which of those classes exist. One call in `src/main.ts`, `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule)`, builds them and serves them over HTTP. Your repository is built into a [machine](/docs/machines/overview) on every push to its branch, and the machine runs that file. There is no deploy command and no router file, and nothing reads a directory by its name. The modules and the decorators are the whole contract between your source and the framework.

## Quick example

Four files make a working backend: the entry point, the root module, and one domain.

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

// Serves on $PORT (8080 unless the machine says). The project's address, id
// and secret key come from the environment: on a machine the platform sets
// PALBASE_URL, PALBASE_PROJECT_ID and the machine's own PALBASE_SECRET_KEY.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule);
```

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesModule } from "./modules/notes/notes.module";

@Module({ imports: [NotesModule] })
export class AppModule {}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Module({ controllers: [NotesController], providers: [NotesService] })
export class NotesModule {}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesService, type Note } from "./notes.service";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  constructor(private readonly notes: NotesService) {}

  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    return this.notes.create(user.id, body.title);
  }

  @Get("/{id}")
  read(@Param("id") id: string, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    return this.notes.get(user.id, id);
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Injectable, Log, NotFound } from "palbase/backend";

export interface Note {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

// Kept in memory to keep the example small; a real app keeps them in its
// database (see Database).
@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  private readonly notes = new Map<string, Note>();

  create(owner: string, title: string): Note {
    const note: Note = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner, title };
    this.notes.set(note.id, note);
    Log.info("note created", { id: note.id });
    return note;
  }

  get(owner: string, id: string): Note {
    const note = this.notes.get(id);
    if (!note || note.owner !== owner) throw new NotFound(`no note ${id}`);
    return note;
  }
}
```

That serves `POST /notes` and `GET /notes/{id}`, both for signed-in users only, because every route needs a user unless it says otherwise. A client calls them at the machine's address, `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio/notes`, with the user's access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls).

## The mental model

| Concept | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Module** | A class decorated with `@Module({ imports, controllers, providers, exports })`. It decides ownership: a `@Controller` or `@Injectable()` class no module lists stops the boot by name. The root module (`AppModule` above) is the one `PalbaseFactory.create` is given, and every other module is reached through `imports`. |
| **Controller** | A class decorated with `@Controller(basePath)`. Each method decorated with `@Get`, `@Post`, `@Put`, `@Patch`, `@Delete` or `@Query` is one route. |
| **Service** | An `@Injectable()` class listed in its module's `providers`. It holds the business logic, so controllers stay thin. |
| **Dependency injection** | A class names what it needs as constructor parameters, and the container supplies them by **type**. There is no `@Inject` and no token registry. |
| **Schema** | Any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) (zod, valibot, arktype) given to `@Body`, `@QueryParams` or `@Headers`. `z` is re-exported from `palbase/backend`. |
| **Answer** | What the method returns is the response: `200` with its JSON, or `204` when it returns `undefined` or `null`. |
| **Errors** | Throw `NotFound`, `Conflict`, `Forbidden`, … or a `PalError` of your own. Every refusal is sent in one envelope. |
| **Webhook** | A `@Webhook` class listed in `providers`: a third party's signed deliveries (Stripe, GitHub, Slack, …) at `POST /webhooks/<name>`, each handed to the `@On` of its event. See [Webhooks](/docs/backend/webhooks). |
| **Gateway** | A `@Gateway(pattern)` class listed in `providers`: a realtime channel of the app, with who may join, its typed events, and its members' messages, each answered with an ack. Apps join it through their generated client. See [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways). |

## What a handler imports

A handler or a service reaches three things by import. Nothing is injected for them, and there is no `ctx` parameter to pass around.

| Import | What it is | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| `Palbase` | The project's modules, called with the app's secret key: `Palbase.auth`, `Palbase.storage`, `Palbase.notify`, `Palbase.secrets`, `Palbase.flags`, `Palbase.analytics`, `Palbase.realtime`, `Palbase.machines`. It is the `palbase/server` client, made for you, with two more: `Palbase.ai`, the project's models, agents and chats, and `Palbase.gateways`, the app's gateways. | [Server SDK](/docs/server/overview), [AI](/docs/backend/ai), [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways) |
| `Database` | The request's own transaction against the app's Postgres: `Database.public.<table>`, `$query`, `$transaction`, `$atomic`, `$asService()`. Committed when the handler returns, rolled back when it throws. | [Database](/docs/backend/database) |
| `Log` | Structured logging: one JSON line per call, carrying the request's id. | [Logging](#logging) |

`Palbase` is bound when the app is served. Reaching it before `PalbaseFactory.create` has run throws `Palbase.<module> is reached before the app is served`. `Database` is the request's, so it is reached inside a request: from a handler, a service a handler calls, or an `@On` handler. Reaching it at import time, from a timer or from `onStart()` throws and names where it was reached.

Per-request values come from parameter decorators instead: `@User()`, `@OptionalUser()`, `@Body()`, `@QueryParams()`, `@Param()`, `@Headers()`, `@Req()`, `@RequestId()` and `@Client()`. See [Request Validation](/docs/backend/validation) and [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication).

## `PalbaseFactory.create(root, config?)`

The bootstrap takes the root module (or an array of them) and the backend's own settings. Each setting has one place: the app's defaults are here, a route's own auth and limit are on its decorator, and a module's settings (auth providers, storage buckets, notify senders) stay in that module, in Studio.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `palbase` | from the environment | `{ url, projectId, secretKey, webhookSecret }`: the project this backend belongs to. Each value is read from `PALBASE_URL`, `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` and `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` unless given here. |
| `auth` | `true` | Every route's auth unless its controller or the route says otherwise. See [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication). |
| `rateLimit` | `{ max: 300, window: 60 }` | Every route's limit per caller, unless the route says otherwise. `false` for none. |
| `bodyLimit` | 1 MiB | Bytes a request body may be. A larger one is `413 payload_too_large`. |
| `cors` | off | `{ origins: ["https://app.example.com"], maxAge? }`, or `origins: "*"`. A backend that browsers call from another origin names them here. |
| `db` | none | `{ schemas: [schema] }`: the app's database. See [Database](/docs/backend/database). |
| `port`, `host` | `$PORT` or 8080, `0.0.0.0` | Where it listens. `port: 0` takes a free one (tests). |
| `boot` | `{ attempts: 5, backoffMs: 1000 }` | How often a failed `onStart()` is tried again. |
| `exitOnFatal` | `true` | Exit 1 on an uncaught error. A test turns it off. |
| `env` | `process.env` | Where the `PALBASE_*` values are read from. |

A value that is missing or malformed stops the boot before any request is served, naming each problem and both ways to give it:

```text
[palbase] the app cannot start:
  - palbase.secretKey / PALBASE_SECRET_KEY is the project secret key (pb_<ref>_s…), kept in the project's Secrets
```

On a machine, the platform sets `PORT`, `PALBASE_URL` (the project's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`), `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `PALBASE_REPLICAS`, `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`, the machine's own `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` and its `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, plus `PALBASE_DB_URL` and `PALBASE_DB_CONNECTIONS` when the machine is given a database. Nothing is set by hand. The machine's key is a secret key of the project, listed under **Settings › API keys** as `machine: <name>`: revoked, it is replaced and the machine rolls out with the new one, and it goes with the machine. See [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets) and [Machines](/docs/machines/overview).

## What one request goes through

Every request takes the same path. Each step answers in the [error envelope](/docs/backend/errors) when it refuses:

1. **The route.** No route for the method and path: `404 not_found`.
2. **The caller.** A bearer token is verified against the project's keys. A route that needs a user and has none answers `401`. When tokens cannot be checked right now, the answer is `503 auth_unavailable` with `Retry-After`.
3. **A verified email**, when the route asks for one: `403 email_not_verified`.
4. **The route's rate limit**, spent before the body is read: `429 too_many_requests` with `Retry-After`.
5. **The body's size**: `413 payload_too_large`.
6. **The parameters**, against their schemas: `400 bad_request`, naming the fields.
7. **The handler**, inside the request's database transaction when the app has a database.
8. **The answer**: `204` for `undefined` or `null`, `200` with JSON otherwise.

Two first path segments are the platform's and never your controllers': `_palbase` (the app's health at `GET /_palbase/health`, and the platform's signed calls: its [crons](/docs/backend/cron) and [tasks](/docs/backend/tasks), an upload's steps, a [gateway](/docs/backend/gateways)'s, an agent's [tools](/docs/backend/ai#tools)) and `webhooks` (the platform delivers [events](/docs/backend/hooks) to `POST /webhooks/palbase`, and a [`@Webhook`](/docs/backend/webhooks) class takes a third party's at `POST /webhooks/<name>`). A `@Controller` mounted under either is refused when it is declared.

## Lifecycle

- **Boot.** Every class is built once, dependencies first. Then each one's `onStart()` runs, in that order. A boot that fails in `onStart()` (a database not up yet) is tried again from scratch after 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds. If it still fails, the process exits 1 and the machine starts it again. What waiting cannot fix, such as a missing setting or a [DI mistake](/docs/backend/modules), stops at once.
- **Serving.** `GET /_palbase/health` answers `200 {"ok":true}` while the app serves. It is the machine's health check by default.
- **Stopping.** On `SIGTERM` the app stops taking connections and gives the requests in flight up to 20 seconds. Then it runs every `onShutdown()`, in reverse order. Health answers `503` meanwhile. A machine's sandbox sends `SIGTERM` more than once, milliseconds apart: the app stops once, and a later signal changes nothing.
- **A crash.** An uncaught error or an unhandled rejection is logged. The requests in flight get a few seconds, and the process exits 1 for the machine to start it again, rather than run half-alive.
- **A migration run.** Started with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE`, the same image migrates its database and exits without serving anything. See [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

## Setup

A backend is an ordinary TypeScript project. The examples run on [Bun](https://bun.sh), which runs TypeScript and its decorator metadata as written, and whose SQL client the database uses by default. `tsconfig.json` needs two settings for the container to read constructor types:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2023",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "noEmit": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}
```

Without `emitDecoratorMetadata`, a class with constructor parameters stops the boot with `metadata missing`. A build that strips types without emitting metadata (esbuild) does the same; tsc, Bun and SWC emit it. How the repository is laid out and built is in [Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure).

## Logging

`Log` writes one JSON line per call: `time`, `level`, `msg`, the request's `request_id` when there is a request, and the fields you pass. An `Error` among them is written with its name, message and stack. `debug` and `info` go to stdout, `warn` and `error` to stderr. What a machine writes is in Studio's machine page and in its logs API. See [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds).

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.audit.ts
import { Injectable, Log } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class NotesAudit {
  record(noteId: string, payload: unknown, err: unknown): void {
    Log.info("note created", { noteId });
    Log.warn("rate approaching limit");
    Log.error("import failed", { error: err });
    Log.debug("raw payload", { payload });
  }
}
```

```text
{"time":"2026-10-08T09:12:44.012Z","level":"info","msg":"note created","request_id":"req_6f1c…","noteId":"3b0e…"}
```

The framework logs its own lines the same way, prefixed `[palbase]`: the routes it serves at boot, a handler's unhandled error (with the route), a module that did not answer.

## The rules checklist

1. **A class exists because a module lists it.** `@Controller` classes go in `controllers`, `@Injectable()` services and `@On` handler classes go in `providers`. A declared class no module lists stops the boot with `unowned class`. Export every class by name: modules import them as `import { X } from "./x"`.
2. **The root module is the one you pass.** `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule)` reaches every other module through `imports`, and imports are not transitive.
3. **Providers are `@Injectable()`.** A class in `providers` without it (and without an `@On` method) stops the boot with `undeclared provider`.
4. **Constructor parameters are classes.** An `interface`, a union or a primitive has no class to build, so it stops the boot with `unresolvable dependency`. Use a class or an `abstract class`.
5. **`onStart()` and `onShutdown()` are the lifecycle.** NestJS's `onModuleInit` and the rest are refused by name, so they are never silently ignored.
6. **Every route needs a signed-in user unless it says `auth: false`.** `@User()` on a route that does not need one stops the boot: use `@OptionalUser()`.
7. **Schemas are Standard Schema values.** Import `z` from `palbase/backend` and pass the schema itself: `@Body(CreateNote)`.
8. **Return the value, or nothing.** A handler's return is its `200` JSON; `undefined` or `null` is `204`. There is no response object to write to.
9. **Throw to refuse.** `throw new NotFound("…")` from a controller or a service. Anything that is not an `HttpError` is a `500`, logged with its stack.
10. **`experimentalDecorators` and `emitDecoratorMetadata`** in `tsconfig.json`.

# Modules & Dependency Injection

One `@Module` declaration says **what exists, who owns it, and what it may reach**. It is the only place ownership is decided. A `@Controller` or `@Injectable()` class that no module lists does not exist, and the app refuses to start rather than serve without it. Being in a particular folder grants nothing.

A dependency is named by its constructor parameter's **type**, and by nothing else. There is no `@Inject`, no `useFactory`, no `forwardRef` and no token registry.

## The four lists

A module is named after its **domain** and lives with it: `src/modules/notes/` holds the module, the controller, the service and the schemas that belong to notes.

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Module({
  controllers: [NotesController],
  providers: [NotesService],
  exports: [NotesService], // the class another module may reach
  imports: [],             // whose exports THIS module may reach
})
export class NotesModule {}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFound } from "palbase/backend";

export interface Note {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  private readonly notes = new Map<string, Note>();

  get(id: string): Note {
    const note = this.notes.get(id);
    if (!note) throw new NotFound(`no note ${id}`);
    return note;
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesService, type Note } from "./notes.service";

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  // The container supplies this. Nothing here constructs or imports an instance.
  constructor(private readonly notes: NotesService) {}

  @Get("/{id}")
  get(@Param("id") id: string): Note {
    return this.notes.get(id);
  }
}
```

Four lists answer four different questions, and nothing else answers them:

| List | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| `providers` | which classes does this module **own** (`@Injectable()` services, classes with [`@On`](/docs/backend/hooks) handlers, and [`@Webhook`](/docs/backend/webhooks) classes) |
| `controllers` | which `@Controller` classes it owns |
| `exports` | which of its own providers **another** module may reach |
| `imports` | whose exports **this** module may reach |

Every list is optional and empty by default. A module with nothing but `imports` is how the root module gathers the domains:

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesModule } from "./modules/notes/notes.module";

@Module({ imports: [NotesModule] })
export class AppModule {}
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule);
```

`PalbaseFactory.create` takes the root module, or an array of them. Every module the app has is reached from there through `imports`. A module nothing imports is not part of the app.

## A class no module lists does not exist

`@Controller`, `@Injectable()` and `@On` record the class they decorate when its file is imported. When the app is built, every recorded class must be owned by exactly one module the root reaches. Otherwise the app stops before it serves anything, and the error names the class:

```text
DiError:
Kind:  unowned class
Path:  PricingService
At:    PricingService
PricingService is declared but no module lists it: it would never be built

Potential solutions:
  - list it in a module's controllers or providers
  - or delete it
```

Every container error is a `DiError` with a `kind`, the path that led to it, and what to do. They are all raised at boot, before the first request, and none is retried: waiting does not fix a wiring mistake.

| `kind` | What it means |
|---|---|
| `unowned class` | A declared class no module lists, or a dependency nobody owns |
| `duplicate ownership` | Two modules list the same class, or an abstract dependency has more than one owned subclass |
| `undeclared provider` | A class in `providers` that is not `@Injectable()` (nor has an `@On` method), or a class in `controllers` that is not a `@Controller` |
| `unknown export` | A module exports a class it does not own |
| `unknown import` | Something in `imports` is not a `@Module`, or a module imports itself |
| `missing import` | A class needs another module's class, and its module does not import that module |
| `private dependency` | The other module owns the class but does not export it |
| `unresolvable dependency` | A constructor parameter typed as an interface, a union or a primitive |
| `metadata missing` | A class takes constructor parameters but no types were emitted |
| `dependency cycle` | `A → B → A` |
| `nest lifecycle name` | A class has `onModuleInit` or another NestJS hook, which would never be called |

## `exports` and `imports`: the boundary

A module reaches another module's class when **both** sides say so: the owner exports it, and the module that needs it imports the owner directly.

```ts
// src/modules/billing/billing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class BillingService {
  planOf(userId: string): "free" | "pro" {
    return userId.startsWith("usr_") ? "free" : "pro";
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/billing/billing.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { BillingService } from "./billing.service";

@Module({ providers: [BillingService], exports: [BillingService] })
export class BillingModule {}
```

```ts
// src/modules/reports/reports.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { BillingService } from "../billing/billing.service";

@Controller("/reports")
export class ReportsController {
  constructor(private readonly billing: BillingService) {}

  @Get("/plan")
  plan(@User() user: UserT): { plan: "free" | "pro" } {
    return { plan: this.billing.planOf(user.id) };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/reports/reports.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { BillingModule } from "../billing/billing.module";
import { ReportsController } from "./reports.controller";

@Module({ imports: [BillingModule], controllers: [ReportsController] })
export class ReportsModule {}
```

Leave `BillingModule` out of `imports` and the boot stops with `missing import`, naming both modules. Leave `BillingService` out of `exports` and it stops with `private dependency`. **Imports are not transitive.** If `ReportsModule` imports `BillingModule` and `BillingModule` imports `AccountsModule`, `ReportsModule` still cannot reach `AccountsModule`'s classes without importing it itself.

## Dependency injection: the constructor is the seam

Every owned class is built **once**, dependencies first, and every class that names it gets the same instance. A class names what it needs as constructor parameters; the container reads their types from the metadata TypeScript emits (`design:paramtypes`) and passes the instances in. Controllers take services this way, and services take other services.

```ts
// src/modules/notes/clock.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class Clock {
  now(): Date {
    return new Date();
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/reminders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";
import { Clock } from "./clock";

@Injectable()
export class RemindersService {
  constructor(private readonly clock: Clock) {}

  isDue(at: Date): boolean {
    return at.getTime() <= this.clock.now().getTime();
  }
}
```

### What the container cannot inject

A parameter's type must be a **class**: something that exists at run time. An `interface`, a type alias, a union, `string` or `number` erases to `Object` (or nothing) in the emitted metadata, and the boot stops with `unresolvable dependency`, naming the class and the parameter. Configuration that is a value (a URL, a limit) is read where it is used, from `process.env`. It is not injected.

## The abstraction is the type, the implementation is the provider

To depend on an abstraction, make it an `abstract class` and list a subclass in `providers`. A parameter typed as the abstract class gets the **one** owned subclass:

```ts
// src/modules/mail/mailer.ts
import { Injectable, Log } from "palbase/backend";

export abstract class Mailer {
  abstract send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void>;
}

@Injectable()
export class LogMailer extends Mailer {
  async send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void> {
    Log.info("mail", { to, subject });
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/mail/welcome.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";
import { Mailer } from "./mailer";

@Injectable()
export class WelcomeService {
  constructor(private readonly mailer: Mailer) {}

  welcome(email: string): Promise<void> {
    return this.mailer.send(email, "Welcome");
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/mail/mail.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { LogMailer } from "./mailer";
import { WelcomeService } from "./welcome.service";

@Module({ providers: [LogMailer, WelcomeService] })
export class MailModule {}
```

Two owned subclasses of `Mailer` make the choice ambiguous, and the boot stops with `duplicate ownership`. Ask for the subclass itself where you mean one. In a test, the same seam lets you pass any `Mailer` to `new WelcomeService(...)` directly. See [Testing](/docs/backend/testing).

## Why there is no `@Inject`, `useFactory` or `forwardRef`

Each of them answers a question the constructor already answers. `@Inject(TOKEN)` names a dependency by a token instead of a type, so the type and the token can disagree. `useFactory` builds an instance outside the container, where its dependencies are not checked. `forwardRef` exists to make a cycle work, and a cycle is a design problem: the boot names it (`A -> B -> A`) and the fix is a third class both depend on.

## `onStart()` and `onShutdown()`

A constructor is pure wiring: synchronous, no I/O, because the container runs it at boot. Startup work is a method on the class:

```ts
// src/modules/catalog/catalog.service.ts
import { Injectable, Log, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class CatalogService {
  private bucketReady = false;

  // Awaited before the first request, in construction order.
  async onStart(): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.storage.putBucket({ path: { bucket: "catalog" }, body: { public: true } });
    this.bucketReady = true;
  }

  // Run on SIGTERM, after the requests in flight have finished, in reverse order.
  async onShutdown(): Promise<void> {
    Log.info("catalog stopping", { bucketReady: this.bucketReady });
  }

  ready(): boolean {
    return this.bucketReady;
  }
}
```

- `onStart()` runs once per class, in construction order: a class's dependencies have started before it does. `Palbase` is bound by then. `Database` is not, because it is a request's.
- When one throws, the classes already started are shut down and the whole boot is tried again from scratch, waiting 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds (`boot: { attempts, backoffMs }` in `PalbaseFactory.create`). Every attempt builds new instances. After the last attempt the error is logged and the process exits, and the machine starts it again.
- `onShutdown()` runs in reverse construction order, and every one is tried even when one throws.

NestJS's names (`onModuleInit`, `onApplicationBootstrap`, `onModuleDestroy`, `beforeApplicationShutdown`, `onApplicationShutdown`) are refused at boot with `nest lifecycle name`. They would never be called here, so a class that relied on them would fail silently.

## `emitDecoratorMetadata` is what makes injection work

The container reads constructor types from the metadata TypeScript emits with `"experimentalDecorators": true` and `"emitDecoratorMetadata": true`. Bun, tsc and SWC emit it. esbuild does not. Without it, a class with constructor parameters stops the boot with `metadata missing`:

```text
DiError:
Kind:  metadata missing
Path:  ReportsController
At:    ReportsController
ReportsController takes 1 constructor parameter(s) but no types were emitted
```

Every class with a constructor parameter must carry a decorator (`@Injectable()`, `@Controller`), because TypeScript emits the parameter types only for a decorated class.

> **Note:** A class is recorded once its file is imported, process-wide. Two copies of `palbase/backend` in one app share the record, so a class declared through either is seen. A test that builds only part of the app must pass modules that own every declared class its imports bring in.

## A domain is a folder

`src/modules/<domain>/` is a convention, not a rule the framework reads: nothing scans a directory. A domain's module, controllers, services and schemas sit together because they change together, and the module is what makes them exist. The one other place the layout matters is the schema: the database's tables are declared in `src/db/` and given to `PalbaseFactory.create(…, { db: { schemas } })`. See [Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure) and [Schema](/docs/backend/schema).

- [Overview](/docs/backend/overview): the authoring model in one page

- [Testing](/docs/backend/testing): constructing a class with your own dependencies

# Controllers & Routing

Routes are declared in code, not in a router. A controller is a class decorated with `@Controller(basePath)`, and each route is a method decorated with `@Get`, `@Post`, `@Put`, `@Patch`, `@Delete` or `@Query`. The file lives with the domain that owns it (`src/modules/todos/todos.controller.ts`), and it is served because its module's `controllers` list names the class. There is no central router to register with. A `@Controller` class no module lists stops the boot, by name. See [Modules & Dependency Injection](/docs/backend/modules).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/todos/dto.ts
import { z } from "palbase/backend";

export const CreateTodo = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
export type CreateTodo = z.infer<typeof CreateTodo>;

export interface Todo {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
  done: boolean;
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/todos/todos.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFound } from "palbase/backend";
import type { CreateTodo, Todo } from "./dto";

@Injectable()
export class TodosService {
  private readonly todos = new Map<string, Todo>();

  list(owner: string): Todo[] {
    return [...this.todos.values()].filter((t) => t.owner === owner);
  }

  create(owner: string, input: CreateTodo): Todo {
    const todo: Todo = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner, title: input.title, done: false };
    this.todos.set(todo.id, todo);
    return todo;
  }

  get(id: string): Todo {
    const todo = this.todos.get(id);
    if (!todo) throw new NotFound(`no todo ${id}`);
    return todo;
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/todos/todos.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { CreateTodo, type Todo } from "./dto";
import { TodosService } from "./todos.service";

@Controller("/todos")
export class TodosController {
  // The container supplies this. Nothing here constructs or imports an instance.
  constructor(private readonly todos: TodosService) {}

  @Get("")
  list(@User() user: UserT): Todo[] {
    return this.todos.list(user.id);
  }

  @Post("", { rateLimit: { max: 10, window: 60 } })
  create(@Body(CreateTodo) body: CreateTodo, @User() user: UserT): Todo {
    return this.todos.create(user.id, body);
  }

  @Get("/{id}", { auth: false })
  get(@Param("id") id: string): Todo {
    return this.todos.get(id);
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/todos/todos.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { TodosController } from "./todos.controller";
import { TodosService } from "./todos.service";

@Module({ controllers: [TodosController], providers: [TodosService] })
export class TodosModule {}
```

That serves three routes:

| Method | Verb | Full path | Auth | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `list` | GET | `/todos` | a signed-in user (the default) | 300 a minute (the default) |
| `create` | POST | `/todos` | a signed-in user | 10 a minute |
| `get` | GET | `/todos/{id}` | anyone | 300 a minute |

At boot the app logs them: `[palbase] serving 3 route(s) on :8080`, with the list. Studio's **Backend › Endpoints** screen shows the same table, read from the app's own contract.

## `@Controller(basePath, options?)`

- `basePath` is where every route of the class is served (`"/todos"`). It must be a string.
- `options.auth` sets the controller-wide auth, which a route's own `auth` overrides. It is `true`, `false`, or `{ required?, verifiedEmail? }`. See [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication).

Controllers are built **once**, at boot, and that one instance serves every request. A field is fine for wiring (the services the constructor took), but never store per-request state in one: concurrent requests share it. Per-request data comes from the parameter decorators.

A `@Controller` class with no routes stops the boot (`@Controller X has no routes`): a controller with nothing to serve is a mistake.

> **Note:** Export the class by name (`export class TodosController`). Its module takes it with `import { TodosController } from "./todos.controller"`, and curly braces cannot see a default export.

## Method decorators

Six decorators declare a route. Each takes `(path, options?)`:

| Decorator | HTTP method | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `@Get` | GET | its body is never read |
| `@Post` | POST | |
| `@Put` | PUT | |
| `@Patch` | PATCH | |
| `@Delete` | DELETE | |
| `@Query` | QUERY | a safe, idempotent read that carries a body |

The options are `RouteOptions`, and the type is exported:

```ts
// src/modules/todos/route-options.ts
import type { RouteOptions } from "palbase/backend";

// What a method decorator's second argument accepts.
export const strict: RouteOptions = {
  // true, false, or { required?, verifiedEmail? }
  auth: { required: true, verifiedEmail: true },
  // this route's own limit per caller, window in SECONDS; false for none
  rateLimit: { max: 10, window: 60 },
};
```

That is all a route option says: who may call it and how often. Input comes from the parameter decorators ([Request Validation](/docs/backend/validation)), and the response is whatever the method returns ([Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors)).

The path argument must be a string. `@Get({ … })` throws when the class is declared, because the query string is read with `@QueryParams(schema)`, not with the path.

### `@Query`: reads with a body

`@Query(path, options?)` serves the route on the HTTP `QUERY` method. It is **safe and idempotent like GET, but carries a request body like POST**. Use it for reads whose input is too structured for a query string, such as search, nested filters or batch lookups:

```ts
// src/modules/todos/search.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Query, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

export const SearchTodos = z.object({
  titleContains: z.string().max(100).optional(),
  ids: z.array(z.string()).max(100).default([]),
});
export type SearchTodos = z.infer<typeof SearchTodos>;

@Controller("/todos")
export class SearchController {
  @Query("/search")
  search(@Body(SearchTodos) body: SearchTodos, @User() user: UserT): { owner: string; asked: SearchTodos } {
    return { owner: user.id, asked: body };
  }
}
```

A QUERY route's input rides in the **body**, read with `@Body`. Don't confuse the `@Query` *method* decorator with the `@QueryParams` *parameter* decorator (query-string input).

Choosing a verb for a read:

- **GET**: no input, or input that fits a few query-string values (`@QueryParams`).
- **QUERY**: a read whose input is a structured object.
- **POST**: the request changes state.

### Paths

A route's full path is `basePath + path`, split on `/` with empty segments dropped. So `@Controller("/todos")` with `@Get("")`, `@Get("/")` or `@Get("//")` is served at `/todos`.

A `{name}` segment is a path parameter, read by name with `@Param("name")`. `:name` means the same:

```ts
// src/modules/comments/comments.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/todos")
export class CommentsController {
  @Get("/{id}/comments/{commentId}", { auth: false })
  getComment(@Param("id") id: string, @Param("commentId") commentId: string): { todo: string; comment: string } {
    return { todo: id, comment: commentId };
  }
}
```

- Matching is a walk over segments with an **exact segment count**: `/todos/{id}` never matches `/todos/a/b`. Literal segments compare exactly, case included.
- The **first** route in declaration order whose method and segments match wins. One declared later that can never be reached is listed in the app's contract under `x-palbase-unreachable`, with the route that answers instead.
- A parameter's value is one segment, percent-decoded, always a string. A segment that is not valid percent-encoding is `400 bad_request`.
- `@Param("x")` naming no `{x}` in the route's path stops the boot.

### Paths that are the platform's

A machine's address is yours: your routes are served from its root, and nothing of the platform's modules (`/auth`, `/storage`, …) lives there. Two first segments are the platform's own:

- `_palbase`: the app's health (`GET /_palbase/health`) and the platform's signed calls (its crons and tasks, an upload's steps, a gateway's, an agent's tools), which the platform makes from inside. A request from outside to a `_palbase` path never reaches the app.
- `webhooks`: the platform delivers [events](/docs/backend/hooks) to `POST /webhooks/palbase`, and each [`@Webhook`](/docs/backend/webhooks) class takes a third party's at `POST /webhooks/<name>`.

`@Controller` throws when it is declared if its base path's first segment is either one, and the app does not start with a route whose full path begins with one, so the mistake is a boot error, not a route that is never called.

## Parameters your app makes: `@Resolve`

Most routes of an app with teams, workspaces or stores start the same way: find what the path names and check that the caller may touch it. Write that once, as a provider, and take its result as a parameter:

```ts
// src/modules/teams/current-team.ts
import { Forbidden, Injectable, NotFound, Resolve, type ParamResolver, type ResolveContext } from "palbase/backend";

export type TeamRole = "member" | "owner";
export interface CurrentTeamT {
  id: string;
  role: TeamRole;
}

@Injectable()
export class TeamOfRequest implements ParamResolver<CurrentTeamT, TeamRole | undefined> {
  // A real app reads the membership from its database here (Database.public.team_members.findUnique).
  private readonly members = new Map<string, TeamRole>([["team_1:user_1", "owner"]]);

  resolve({ params, user }: ResolveContext, atLeast: TeamRole | undefined): CurrentTeamT {
    const role = user ? this.members.get(`${params.teamId}:${user.id}`) : undefined;
    // A team the caller is not in is one that does not exist: a different answer would let anyone count them.
    if (!role) throw new NotFound("no such team");
    if (atLeast === "owner" && role !== "owner") throw new Forbidden("owners only");
    return { id: params.teamId, role };
  }
}

/** The team the path names, the caller's role in it checked. */
export const CurrentTeam = (atLeast?: TeamRole) => Resolve(TeamOfRequest, atLeast);
```

```ts
// src/modules/teams/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Delete, Get, Param, Post, z } from "palbase/backend";
import { CurrentTeam, type CurrentTeamT } from "./current-team";

const NewNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1) });

@Controller("/teams/{teamId}/notes")
export class NotesController {
  @Get("")
  list(@CurrentTeam() team: CurrentTeamT) {
    return { team: team.id, notes: [] };
  }

  @Post("")
  create(@CurrentTeam() team: CurrentTeamT, @Body(NewNote) body: z.infer<typeof NewNote>) {
    return { team: team.id, title: body.title };
  }

  @Delete("/{id}")
  remove(@CurrentTeam("owner") team: CurrentTeamT, @Param("id") id: string) {
    return { removed: id, from: team.id };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/teams/teams.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { TeamOfRequest } from "./current-team";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";

@Module({ controllers: [NotesController], providers: [TeamOfRequest] })
export class TeamsModule {}
```

- **A provider.** The resolver is an `@Injectable()` its module lists, and it takes its dependencies by constructor. The controller's module reaches it as it would a constructor's dependency: listed by the same module, or exported by one it imports. A resolver it cannot reach stops the boot, naming the route and the class.
- **What it is given.** `ResolveContext` has the path's parameters (decoded), the signed-in user (`null` on a route that needs none and was called by nobody), the request's headers and its id. The second argument is what the decorator was given: here, the role the route needs.
- **Before the body.** Resolvers run before every other parameter. A caller with no right to the team hears your `404` or `403`, not a `400` about a body they should never have been asked for.
- **In the request's transaction.** The resolver uses the request's `Database`, as the handler does: a write it made goes back with the handler's if the handler throws. A resolver that only read, before a handler that waits on something else, has its connection given back during the wait like any read of the request ([A handler that waits on something else](/docs/backend/database#a-handler-that-waits-on-something-else)).
- **Not in the contract.** The app's OpenAPI document shows the path's parameters, never the resolver.

A guard (`@UseGuards` and `@Roles` in other frameworks) answers only yes or no. The resolver answers with what it found, so the handler does not look it up a second time.

## Rate limiting

Every route has a limit: 300 requests a minute **per caller** unless `PalbaseFactory.create(…, { rateLimit })` or the route says otherwise. `rateLimit: { max, window }` allows at most `max` requests per `window` **seconds**. `rateLimit: false` turns it off for one route, and `rateLimit: false` in the bootstrap turns it off for every route that does not set its own.

A list of windows holds a caller to each of them — a burst, a minute and an hour: `rateLimit: [{ max: 10, window: 10 }, { max: 30, window: 60 }, { max: 300, window: 3600 }]`. A request over any of them is refused and told to wait the longest of their waits, and it is not counted in the windows that had room: a caller told to wait out a burst has not spent its hour on the requests it was refused.

```ts
// src/modules/todos/import.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

export const ImportTodos = z.object({ titles: z.array(z.string().max(200)).max(1000) });
export type ImportTodos = z.infer<typeof ImportTodos>;

@Controller("/todos")
export class ImportController {
  @Post("/import", { rateLimit: { max: 5, window: 60 } })
  importTodos(@Body(ImportTodos) body: ImportTodos, @User() user: UserT): { owner: string; imported: number } {
    return { owner: user.id, imported: body.titles.length };
  }
}
```

Over the limit, the route answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header in seconds and this body:

```json
{
  "error": "too_many_requests",
  "error_description": "Rate limit exceeded for this endpoint",
  "status": 429,
  "request_id": "req_6f1c…",
  "data": { "retryAfter": 42 }
}
```

How the limit counts, because it decides what the limit protects:

- **The caller** is the signed-in user (by the token's user id), or else the client's address. On a machine that address is the last `X-Forwarded-For` entry, the one the platform's edge appended; every entry before it is whatever the client sent. An IPv6 address counts by its /64.
- **The limit is spent before the body is read.** A caller over the limit is not read for, whatever it sends.
- **The window is fixed and kept in the process's memory**, per route and caller, for up to 100,000 keys; the key used longest ago goes first. A machine running several copies counts in each copy, so the limit holds per copy. A restart forgets every window.

There are no `X-RateLimit-*` headers: a refusal carries `Retry-After`, and a request that passed carries nothing.

> **Note:** This is your route's own limit. The project as a whole also has a requests-per-second ceiling at the platform's edge, which answers `429` above it.

To refuse inside your own logic (a per-resource cooldown, say), throw `new TooManyRequests({ retryAfter })`. It is sent the same way, with its `Retry-After`. See [Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors).

## CORS

A backend that browsers call from another origin names those origins in the bootstrap. Off unless given:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, {
  cors: { origins: ["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:3000"], maxAge: 600 },
});
```

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";

@Module({})
export class AppModule {}
```

- A preflight (`OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method`) from a named origin is answered `204`. One from any other origin is `403`, and its real request gets no CORS headers.
- Answers to a named origin carry `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and expose `Retry-After` and `X-Request-Id` to the page.
- Origins are `https://host[:port]`, with `http://` only for `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, and no path. Anything else stops the boot. `origins: "*"` allows any origin.
- The credential is the bearer token in `Authorization`, never a cookie, so there is no credentials mode to set.

## What a handler returns

The method's return is the answer. An object or an array is `200` with its JSON, and `undefined` or `null` is `204` with no body. A `Promise` is awaited first. A refusal is a throw ([Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors)).

When the answer needs its own status, headers or body, return a `Response`. It is sent as it was built, with the request's `X-Request-Id` and CORS' headers added:

```ts
// src/modules/files/files.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, Post } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/files")
export class FilesController {
  // 201 with where the new one is.
  @Post("")
  create() {
    return Response.json({ id: "f_1" }, { status: 201, headers: { location: "/files/f_1" } });
  }

  // Any status, with its headers: here a 412 and the version the client must send.
  @Get("/{id}/stale")
  stale(@Param("id") id: string) {
    return Response.json({ error: "precondition_failed", id }, { status: 412, headers: { etag: '"v7"' } });
  }

  // Not JSON: a CSV, downloaded as a file.
  @Get("/report.csv")
  report() {
    return new Response("id,name\n1,Ada\n", { headers: { "content-type": "text/csv; charset=utf-8", "content-disposition": 'attachment; filename="report.csv"' } });
  }

  // A stream, sent as it is made: one JSON line at a time.
  @Get("/feed")
  feed() {
    const encoder = new TextEncoder();
    const body = new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
      start(controller) {
        for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(`${JSON.stringify({ line: i })}\n`));
        controller.close();
      },
    });
    return new Response(body, { headers: { "content-type": "application/x-ndjson" } });
  }
}
```

The request's transaction ends when the handler returns, before the answer goes. A streamed body is read after that, so read what it needs from `Database` first. A returned `Response` is an answer, whatever its status: what the handler wrote commits. Only a throw rolls it back.

A `fetch()` answer can be returned as it is: its body is already decoded, so its `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` are not passed on, and neither is a connection's own header (`Connection`, `Transfer-Encoding`, …).

## Keep controllers thin

A controller reads the request (its parameters, the user, what [`@Resolve`](#parameters-your-app-makes-resolve) found) and hands it to a service. The logic and the database work belong in an `@Injectable()` service the controller takes in its constructor, which can be tested on its own and shared across controllers. See [Modules & Dependency Injection](/docs/backend/modules) and [Testing](/docs/backend/testing).

- [Request Validation](/docs/backend/validation): `@Body`, `@QueryParams`, `@Param`, `@Headers`
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication): route and controller `auth`
- [Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors): the answer and the envelope
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls): calling these routes from a browser

# Request Validation

A handler never reads raw input. Each part of the request it uses arrives through a **parameter decorator**, and every decorator that takes a schema validates before the handler runs. `@Body`, `@QueryParams` and `@Headers` take any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev): zod (re-exported as `z` from `palbase/backend`), valibot, arktype or another library that implements it. A request that fails one is answered `400` with the fields that failed, and the handler is never called.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/todos/dto.ts
import { z } from "palbase/backend";

export const CreateTodo = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(1).max(200),
  dueAt: z.iso.datetime().optional(),
  tags: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(10).default([]),
});
export type CreateTodo = z.infer<typeof CreateTodo>;

// The query string arrives as strings: coerce what is a number.
export const ListTodos = z.object({
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
  done: z.enum(["true", "false"]).optional(),
});
export type ListTodos = z.infer<typeof ListTodos>;
```

```ts
// src/modules/todos/todos.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, QueryParams, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { CreateTodo, ListTodos } from "./dto";

@Controller("/todos")
export class TodosController {
  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateTodo) body: CreateTodo, @User() user: UserT): { owner: string; todo: CreateTodo } {
    // body.tags is [] when the client sent none: the schema's output is what arrives.
    return { owner: user.id, todo: body };
  }

  @Get("")
  list(@QueryParams(ListTodos) query: ListTodos): { limit: number; done: string | null } {
    return { limit: query.limit, done: query.done ?? null };
  }

  @Get("/{id}")
  get(@Param("id") id: string): { id: string } {
    return { id };
  }
}
```

The handler gets the schema's **output**: defaults filled in, coercions and transforms applied. That is why the parameter's type is `z.infer<typeof Schema>`, written once beside the schema as a same-named type.

## The parameter decorators

| Decorator | What it reads | Validated |
|---|---|---|
| `@Body(schema)` | The JSON body | always (a schema is required) |
| `@QueryParams(schema)` | The query string, as an object of strings | always (a schema is required) |
| `@Headers(schema?)` | The request's headers, names lower-cased | when given a schema |
| `@Param("name")` | One path segment, `{name}` in the route's path | no: always a string |
| `@User()` / `@OptionalUser()` | The signed-in user | see [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication) |
| `@Req()` | The `Request` itself | no |
| `@RequestId()` | The request's id (`@TraceId()` is the same) | no |
| `@Client()` | `{ sdkVersion, appVersion, platform, osVersion }`, from the client's headers | no |

A schema passed to `@Body`, `@QueryParams` or `@Headers` must be a Standard Schema value, the object itself. Anything else (a type, a plain object, `undefined`) throws when the class is declared: `@Body(schema): schema is a Standard Schema (a zod, valibot or arktype schema)`.

### `@Body`

The body is read whole, up to the body limit (1 MiB unless `PalbaseFactory.create(…, { bodyLimit })` says otherwise). Past it, the answer is `413 payload_too_large`, before the schema sees anything. The body is parsed as JSON **whatever its `Content-Type`**. An empty body, or one that is not JSON, reaches the schema as `{}`, so the caller hears a validation error that names what was missing.

A `GET` never reads its body: a `@Body` on a GET route validates `{}`. Use `@QueryParams` for a GET, or a [`@Query`](/docs/backend/controllers) route when the input is structured.

There is no multipart and no file upload in a request body: a body is JSON. To take a file, the backend grants a [signed upload URL](/docs/backend/direct-uploads) and the client sends the bytes straight to storage.

### `@QueryParams`

The query string becomes an object of **strings**, `?limit=20&done=true` as `{ limit: "20", done: "true" }`. A key given twice keeps its last value. Coerce what is a number or a boolean in the schema (`z.coerce.number()`), and keep the schema an object of scalars.

### `@Headers`

Without a schema, `@Headers()` hands over every header as an object of strings, names lower-cased. With one, the object is validated and the schema's output arrives. A header schema should let other headers through (zod's objects strip unknown keys, so the handler simply gets the ones you named):

```ts
// src/modules/sync/sync.controller.ts
import { Controller, Headers, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const SyncHeaders = z.object({ "x-device-id": z.string().min(8).max(64) });
type SyncHeaders = z.infer<typeof SyncHeaders>;

@Controller("/sync")
export class SyncController {
  @Post("")
  sync(@Headers(SyncHeaders) headers: SyncHeaders, @User() user: UserT): { device: string; user: string } {
    return { device: headers["x-device-id"], user: user.id };
  }
}
```

### `@Param`

`@Param("id")` is the segment `{id}` of the route's path, percent-decoded, always a string. It takes no schema. Check its shape in the service (or with `schema.parse(id)`) when it must be a UUID or a number. A `@Param` that names no segment of its route stops the boot.

### `@Req`, `@RequestId` and `@Client`

`@Req()` is the web `Request`. For a route with a body, the body has already been read by the time the handler runs, so read it through `@Body`. `@RequestId()` is the request's id: the `X-Request-Id` the caller sent when it is 8 to 128 characters of `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ : -`, otherwise one made for it (`req_…`). It is in every answer's `X-Request-Id` header, in the error envelope and in every `Log` line of the request. `@Client()` reads what a client says of itself: `x-palbase-sdk-version`, `x-palbase-client-version`, `x-platform` and `x-os-version`, each `null` when absent.

```ts
// src/modules/support/support.controller.ts
import { Client, Controller, Get, RequestId, type ClientInfo } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/support", { auth: false })
export class SupportController {
  @Get("/whoami")
  whoami(@RequestId() requestId: string, @Client() client: ClientInfo): { requestId: string; platform: string | null } {
    return { requestId, platform: client.platform };
  }
}
```

## Where schemas live

Schemas are ordinary values. Put a domain's in its own `dto.ts` beside its controller, each exported as a value and a same-named type, so the controller reads `@Body(CreateTodo) body: CreateTodo`. Nothing discovers the file: it is an ordinary import. A schema two domains share belongs to the module that owns the concept, or to a small shared file both import.

Import `z` from `palbase/backend` rather than installing zod yourself. The framework re-exports the zod it is built with, so your schemas and the framework agree on one version.

## What a validation failure looks like

A failed schema answers `400 bad_request` in the [error envelope](/docs/backend/errors), with each failed field in `data.fields`:

```json
{
  "error": "bad_request",
  "error_description": "Request body failed validation",
  "status": 400,
  "request_id": "req_6f1c…",
  "data": {
    "fields": [
      { "field": "title", "message": "Too small: expected string to have >=1 characters" },
      { "field": "tags.3", "message": "Too big: expected string to have <=30 characters" }
    ]
  }
}
```

- `error_description` says which part failed: `Request body failed validation`, `Query parameters failed validation` or `Request headers failed validation`.
- `field` is the issue's path, dotted (`tags.3`). It is `""` for the value as a whole.
- `message` is the schema library's own message.
- At most 20 fields are listed. When there were more, `data.more` says how many: a body of a million bad items is not answered with a million lines.

A `BadRequest` you throw yourself has the same shape: `throw new BadRequest({ fields: [{ field: "name", message: "…" }] })`. A client handles both the same way.

## The body is data, never structure

Everything a request sent is marked as **data** where it enters: the body (as `JSON.parse` made it), the query, the headers and the user's metadata. The database takes values from data, but never a filter's operators, its branches, a `select`, an `orderBy` or a column name. `{ token: body.token }` cannot become `{ token: { neq: null } }` because the client sent an object there; the query refuses it with a `400` naming the field.

What a schema builds is the route's own: `z.object({ title: z.string() })` makes a new object, and its `title` is a value. What a schema lets through untouched (`z.unknown()`, `z.any()`, a passthrough's extra keys) stays the request's, and stays marked. Declare the shape of whatever you filter by. See [Database](/docs/backend/database).

## The answer is not validated

A schema validates what comes in. What the handler returns is sent as it is, so return the fields you mean to: build the answer from the row rather than returning the row, when the row holds more than the caller should see.

## What Studio shows

Each schema is also written into the app's contract as JSON Schema, for libraries that implement the Standard JSON Schema converter (zod does). Studio's **Backend › Endpoints** screen shows each route's body, query and header schemas from there. A schema whose library has no converter is described as any value. It is still validated.

## Related

- [Controllers & Routing](/docs/backend/controllers): the routes these decorators sit on
- [Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors): the envelope a `400` arrives in
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication): `@User` and `@OptionalUser`
- [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads): files, which never ride in a request body
