# Schema

Your database schema lives in your repository, in TypeScript, one file per Postgres schema: `src/db/public.ts` declares `public`, `src/db/billing.ts` declares `billing`. Each file default-exports a `defineSchema("<name>", { tables })` call naming its tables, columns, foreign keys, [Row-Level Security policies](/docs/backend/row-level-security), constraints, indexes and extensions. The DSL is Palgres', re-exported by `palbase/backend`, and it is the only description of the schema you write. There are no migration files: every release of your machine migrates its database to what these files declare, beside the version still serving — see [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import {
  boolean, defineSchema, defineTable, enumType, index, integer, jsonb,
  ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid,
} from "palbase/backend";

export const lists = defineTable("lists", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    title: text(),
  },
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("lists_own").for("all").to("authenticated")
      .using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))
      .withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
  ],
});

export const todos = defineTable("todos", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    list_id: uuid().references(() => lists.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    title: text(),
    status: enumType("todo_status", ["open", "done", "archived"]).default("open"),
    priority: integer().default(0),
    done: boolean().default(false),
    meta: jsonb().nullable(),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
  // `policies` and `indexes` are CALLBACKS: `p` carries this table's own column
  // names, so `p.col("ownr")` is a compile error, not a refusal from Postgres.
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("todos_own").for("all").to("authenticated")
      .using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))
      .withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
  ],
  indexes: (p) => [index("todos_owner_created").on(p.col("owner"), p.col("created_at"))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [lists, todos] });
```

The app hands its schemas to the framework in `src/main.ts`. That is how they are found — no directory is scanned:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";
import schema from "./db/public";

// Serves on $PORT with its database. Run by a release with PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE,
// the same image migrates the database to this schema and exits.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { db: { schemas: [schema] } });
```

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";

@Module({ imports: [] })
export class AppModule {}
```

Five things to notice:

- **A table is a value that knows its own name.** `defineTable("todos", …)` returns a binding, and `defineSchema` reads the name off it. That is what lets `todos` point at `lists`: one place writes each name, so a reference never resolves against a table whose identity is not set yet.
- **`defineSchema` takes an array** of those bindings, and its first argument is the schema's own name.
- **The file `export default`s the `defineSchema(...)` call.** `main.ts` imports that value; Palgres' type generator reads the same value.
- **Columns are `NOT NULL` by default**; `.nullable()` opts in to `NULL`.
- **RLS is on by default**, and declaring `policies` forces it on. A table with RLS and no policy denies everything — the most common reason a fresh backend's first `GET` returns `[]`. Read [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security) before your first release.

## One file per schema

```text
src/db/
  public.ts     → defineSchema("public", …)
  billing.ts    → defineSchema("billing", …)
```

Every schema the app declares is in the `schemas` list it gives `PalbaseFactory.create`, and its tables are reached as `Database.<schema>.<table>` — `Database.public.todos`, `Database.billing.invoices`. A foreign key into another schema imports the table binding and points at it:

```ts
// src/db/billing.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, numeric, uuid } from "palbase/backend";
import { lists } from "./public";

const invoices = defineTable("invoices", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    list_id: uuid().references(() => lists.id),
    amount: numeric({ precision: 12, scale: 2 }),
  },
  rls: false,
});

export default defineSchema("billing", { tables: [invoices] });
```

Export the tables another file references (`export const lists = defineTable(…)`). The written foreign key names its target with its schema — `billing.invoices.list_id` points at `public.lists`, never at a same-named table the `search_path` happens to find. A reference into a table no `defineSchema` has claimed is refused with both names, so declare the referenced schema's file and import it.

## `defineTable`

`defineTable(name, input)`. Only `columns` is required.

| Field | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `columns` | `{ [name]: ColumnBuilder }` | **required** — the table's columns |
| `rls` | `boolean` | defaults to `true`; `false` is the explicit opt-out for a public table |
| `policies` | `(p) => PolicyBuilder[]` | RLS policies; a non-empty list forces `rls` on |
| `primaryKey` | `string[]` | composite primary key, in order |
| `unique` | `{ name, columns }[]` | named multi-column `UNIQUE` constraints |
| `checks` | `{ name, expr }[]` or `(c) => CheckDef[]` | `CHECK` — raw SQL, or the typed `check(name, c.col("total").gt(0))` |
| `indexes` | `(c) => IndexBuilder[]` | `index("name").on(c.col("x"))`, partial, expression, unique, covering |
| `foreignKeys` | `(c) => ForeignKeyBuilder[]` | multi-column `FOREIGN KEY` |
| `raw` | `raw(name, sql)[]` | what the typed fields cannot say — another index method, an `EXCLUDE` |
| `ignored` | `boolean` | "this release no longer reads this table" — the first half of dropping it |

Every callback field is a callback for the same reason: the argument carries this table's own column names as a literal union, so a misspelt column is a compile error on the line you wrote it, not an error from Postgres in the middle of a release.

The returned value **is its columns**: `todos.id` is the `id` column builder, which is what makes `references(() => todos.id)` an ordinary expression your editor completes. The table's own metadata hangs off a symbol, so a column may be called `name`, `columns` or `rls` without shadowing anything. Each table gets its own copy of the column builders it is given, so a shared spread (`...audit`) of columns in two tables is two sets of columns.

## `defineSchema`

`defineSchema(name, input)`.

| Field | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `tables` | `TableHandle[]` | **required** — the `defineTable` bindings, in any order |
| `extensions` | `string[]` | Postgres extensions the migration creates — see [Postgres extensions](#postgres-extensions) |
| `raw` | `raw(name, up, { drop })[]` | schema-level units: views, functions, triggers over several tables |

`defineSchema` is where every pending reference is resolved: the `() => lists.id` callbacks run here, once every binding exists. Two tables of one name in one schema are refused, and so are two raw units of one name.

## Column types

All factories are imported from `palbase/backend`. The third column is the type `palbase-env.d.ts` gives the value on `Database.public.*` (see [Where the types come from](/docs/backend/database)).

| Factory | Postgres type | Row type |
|---|---|---|
| `uuid()` | `uuid` | `string` |
| `text()` | `text` | `string` |
| `integer()` | `integer` | `number` |
| `bigint()` | `bigint` | `string` |
| `numeric()` / `numeric({ precision, scale })` | `numeric` / `numeric(p,s)` | `string` |
| `boolean()` | `boolean` | `boolean` |
| `timestamp()` | `timestamp with time zone` | `string` |
| `date()` | `date` | `string` (`"YYYY-MM-DD"`) |
| `jsonb()` | `jsonb` | `Json` |
| `enumType(name, values)` | a Postgres enum type named `name` | the union of the values |
| `sqlType("inet")` | the Postgres type, as Postgres spells it | `string` — `number` for `smallint`, `real`, `double precision` |

A `.nullable()` column's row type becomes `T | null`. `.array()` makes any scalar an array — `text().array()` is `text[]`, surfaced as `string[]`, filtered with `contains` and `overlaps`; the only default an array takes is the empty one, `.default([])`.

`bigint()` and `numeric()` surface as **`string`**: a JavaScript number cannot hold a 64-bit integer past 2^53 or an arbitrary-precision decimal without rounding. Keep money in them and parse with `BigInt(row.amount)` or a decimal library — or declare `.asNumber()` on a column whose values you know fit in a JS number, and it surfaces as `number`. `date()` is a calendar day, not an instant: a JS `Date` would pick a time zone for it.

`sqlType()` is the escape hatch for a type the DSL does not offer — `inet`, `interval`, `citext`, `character varying(20)`, `vector(1536)`. Spell it as Postgres does (`character varying(20)`, not `varchar(20)`); a type the DSL has is refused by name (`sqlType("text")` asks for `text()`), so each type has one spelling.

### jsonb

A `jsonb()` column takes a plain object or array on insert and update — do not `JSON.stringify` it — and reads back as the value. `jsonb<T>()` takes a payload type, but **the type does not reach `palbase-env.d.ts`**: the generated file types every `jsonb` column as `Json`. Narrow it where you read it, with a schema you already have: `TagList.parse(row.tags)`.

### Enums

`enumType(name, values)` makes a real Postgres enum type, and the TypeScript side is the narrow union of the values:

```ts
import { defineTable, enumType, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const tickets = defineTable("tickets", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    // row type: "open" | "pending" | "closed"
    status: enumType("ticket_status", ["open", "pending", "closed"]).default("open"),
    tags: enumType("ticket_tag", ["bug", "billing", "other"]).array().default([]),
  },
});
```

The first argument is the Postgres type's name, not the column's. Adding a value is an ordinary migration; removing one is refused (Postgres cannot drop an enum value) — see [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

## Chain methods

Every builder method returns a builder, so modifiers chain.

| Method | Effect |
|---|---|
| `.primaryKey()` | `PRIMARY KEY` |
| `.notNull()` / `.nullable()` | `NOT NULL` (the default) / allow `NULL` |
| `.default(value)` | a literal `DEFAULT` |
| `.defaultRandom()` | `uuid()` — `DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` |
| `.defaultNow()` | `timestamp()` — `DEFAULT now()`; `date()` — `CURRENT_DATE` |
| `.defaultSql(expr)` | a default the database computes, written as SQL |
| `.dbAssigned()` | a trigger or rule writes the value: optional on insert, no `DEFAULT` in the DDL |
| `.unique()` | single-column `UNIQUE` |
| `.array()` | an array of this type |
| `.identity()` | `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` on `integer()`/`bigint()` — off every insert and update; `{ always: false }` is `BY DEFAULT` |
| `.generated(expr, { stored? })` | `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr)` — virtual by default (Postgres 18), `stored: true` on disk |
| `.references(() => t.col, opts?)` | a foreign key — see [Foreign keys](#foreign-keys) |
| `.selfReferences("column", opts?)` | a foreign key onto this same table |
| `.onDelete(action)` | `ON DELETE` of a foreign-key column |
| `.asNumber()` / `.asDecimal()` | surface a `numeric`/`bigint` column as `number`, or say `string` explicitly |
| `.renamedFrom(previous)` | this column used to be called `previous` |
| `.fillWith(sql)` | how to fill a `NOT NULL` column for rows that do not supply it — see [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations) |
| `.ignored()` | this release no longer reads or writes the column — the first half of dropping it |

## Foreign keys

The target is a **callback**: `references(() => lists.id)`, not `references(lists.id)`. It runs inside `defineSchema`, where every binding exists, which is what makes a cycle expressible.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `onDelete` | `"cascade"`, `"set null"`, `"set default"`, `"restrict"` or `"no action"` (the default) |
| `onUpdate` | the same actions, on a change of the referenced key |
| `as` | the forward relation's name — `list_id` gives `list` by default |
| `reverseAs` | the reverse relation's name on the parent — this table's name by default |
| `index` | `false` leaves the column without the index Palgres makes for a foreign key |

Postgres does not index a foreign key's column by itself, and every join through it and every `ON DELETE CASCADE` pays for that. Palgres makes `<table>_<column>_idx` for each one unless you say `index: false` — which is right only when the column is updated often enough that an index on it would cost more than it saves.

### Pointing at this same table

A parent pointer — category trees, replies, org charts — takes the column's name and no callback:

```ts
import { defineTable, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const categories = defineTable("categories", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    name: text(),
    parent_id: uuid().nullable().selfReferences("id"),
  },
  rls: false,
});
```

### Two tables that point at each other

A cycle needs an explicit return type on **one** side, and one is enough:

```ts
import { type AnyColumn, defineTable, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const members = defineTable("members", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    // the annotated side — without it TypeScript chases its own tail (TS7022)
    primary_team_id: uuid().nullable().references((): AnyColumn => teams.id),
  },
});

export const teams = defineTable("teams", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    lead_id: uuid().nullable().references(() => members.id),
  },
});
```

### Two foreign keys to the same table

Every foreign key gives two relation names, which [`with` and `has`](/docs/backend/database) read: the forward one on the child (`billing_address_id` → `billing_address`) and the reverse one on the parent (by default the child table's name). Two keys from one table onto one parent collide on the reverse side, so name at least one:

```ts
import { defineTable, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const addresses = defineTable("addresses", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), line1: text() },
});

export const orders = defineTable("orders", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    billing_address_id: uuid().references(() => addresses.id, { reverseAs: "billed_orders" }),
    shipping_address_id: uuid().references(() => addresses.id, { reverseAs: "shipped_orders" }),
  },
});
```

A collision is refused when the schema is built, naming both columns and the option that fixes that direction.

### Composite foreign keys

A key of more than one column is declared on the table, with its own name:

```ts
import { defineTable, foreignKey, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const projects = defineTable("projects", {
  columns: { org_id: uuid(), id: uuid().defaultRandom(), name: text() },
  primaryKey: ["org_id", "id"],
});

export const tasks = defineTable("tasks", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), org_id: uuid(), project_id: uuid() },
  // A task's project must be of the same organization — a per-column key cannot say so.
  foreignKeys: (c) => [
    foreignKey("tasks_project_fkey").on(c.col("org_id"), c.col("project_id")).references(projects, "org_id", "id").onDelete("cascade"),
  ],
});
```

## Rows that belong to a user

Your users are the project's [auth](/docs/web/auth) users, and they live in the platform, not in your database — so a column holding a user's id is plain `text`, with no foreign key. Two factories declare one, and say what happens to the row when that user is deleted:

| Factory | Means | When the user is deleted |
|---|---|---|
| `ownedByUser()` | this row **belongs to** the user — `text`, `NOT NULL` | the row is deleted |
| `userRef({ onDelete })` | this row **points at** a user — `created_by`, `edited_by` | `"cascade"`: deleted; `"set null"`: the column is set to `NULL` (declare it `.nullable()`) |

```ts
import { defineTable, ownedByUser, text, userRef, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    edited_by: userRef({ onDelete: "set null" }).nullable(),
    body: text(),
  },
});
```

**At most one `ownedByUser()` per table**: which column's user takes the row with them must not depend on the order the columns are declared in.

Deleting what a schema keeps of a user is the framework's job, not yours: when the platform delivers `user.deleted`, `palbase/backend` deletes the user's owned rows and nulls the `set null` references, in one transaction as the service role. That needs the delivery to arrive, so **an app whose schema declares either factory refuses to start without `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`** — on a machine the platform gives it, and keeps the machine's `/webhooks/palbase` endpoint for `user.deleted`. See [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks) for what that endpoint takes.

> **Note:** A plain `text()` column holding a user's id is not one the framework knows to clear: nothing deletes what it keeps when the user goes, and that erasure is yours to do.

## What is optional on insert

A column is optional on insert when the database can fill it: `.nullable()`, any default (`.default()`, `.defaultRandom()`, `.defaultNow()`, `.defaultSql()`), or `.dbAssigned()`. An `.identity()` (always) or `.generated()` column is on the row and off the insert entirely. Everything else is required. For `todos` above, `Database.public.todos.insert(…)` takes `list_id`, `owner` and `title`, and may take `id`, `status`, `priority`, `done`, `meta` and `created_at`.

## Constraints and indexes

```ts
import { check, defineTable, index, integer, numeric, raw, sqlType, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const products = defineTable("products", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    sku: text(),
    email: text().nullable(),
    price: numeric({ precision: 12, scale: 2 }),
    stock: integer().default(0),
    embedding: sqlType("vector(3)").nullable(),
    deleted_at: timestamp().nullable(),
  },
  rls: false,
  unique: [{ name: "products_sku_key", columns: ["sku"] }],
  checks: (c) => [check("products_price_positive", c.col("price").gt(0)), check("products_stock_not_negative", c.col("stock").gte(0))],
  indexes: (c) => [
    // partial: only the live rows
    index("products_live").on(c.col("sku")).where(c.col("deleted_at").isNull()),
    // partial UNIQUE: NULLs free, non-NULLs unique
    index("products_email_unique").unique().onExpression("lower(email)").where(c.col("email").isNull(true)),
    // covering, newest first
    index("products_stock").on(c.col("stock")).desc().include(["price"]),
  ],
  // What the typed fields cannot say: another index method, an operator class.
  raw: [raw("products_embedding", "CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS products_embedding ON public.products USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)")],
});
```

- **`unique`** renders a `UNIQUE` constraint and cannot carry a condition, because Postgres has no partial unique constraint. `index(name).unique().where(…)` is the declarative way to say "NULLs are free, non-NULLs are unique".
- **`checks`** comes in two forms: the typed callback above, whose column names are checked as you type, or `[{ name, expr }]` with the SQL written out. The typed form refuses a subquery or `auth.uid()` — a `CHECK` cannot hold either.
- **`indexes`** — `.on(...cols)` (order kept), `.onExpression(sql)`, `.where(pred)` in the same expression language as policies, `.unique()`, `.include(cols)`, `.asc()`/`.desc()`, `.nulls("first" | "last")`. A migration builds each one `CONCURRENTLY`, so a write never waits for it. An index whose definition changes under the same name is built beside the old one, which the version still serving reads through, and takes its name when the release completes.
- **`raw`** on a table runs its SQL as it is, as the tables' owner. A raw index is known by its name too, so a changed body under the same name is refused: give it a new name.

### Schema-level raw units

What belongs to no single table — a view, a function, a trigger over several tables — is a unit of the schema, and unlike a table's raw entry it has a teardown the migration runs:

```ts
import { boolean, defineSchema, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, raw, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const tasks = defineTable("tasks", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), owner: ownedByUser(), title: text(), done: boolean().default(false) },
  policies: (p) => [policy("tasks_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", {
  tables: [tasks],
  raw: [
    raw(
      "open_tasks",
      "CREATE VIEW public.open_tasks WITH (security_invoker = true) AS SELECT id, owner, title FROM public.tasks WHERE NOT done",
      { drop: "DROP VIEW public.open_tasks" },
    ),
  ],
});
```

A new unit runs its `up`; a unit whose `up` changed runs its previous `drop`, then the new `up`; a unit removed from the declaration runs its `drop`. A view must be `security_invoker = true`, so the reader's policies apply through it. A view, a trigger or a rule with no `drop` is refused — a rollback could not take it back. `{ before: true }` makes a unit before the tables: a domain, a type or a function a column's default calls.

## Postgres extensions

```ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, sqlType, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const places = defineTable("places", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    name: text(),
    at: sqlType("geography(Point,4326)"),
    embedding: sqlType("vector(1536)").nullable(),
  },
  rls: false,
});

export const geo = defineSchema("public", { tables: [places], extensions: ["postgis", "vector"] });
```

The migration runs `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS` for each, as the database's owner, who is not a superuser — so an extension must be one the owner may create. A Palbase database is Postgres 18 and makes these trusted beside Postgres' own trusted extensions (`pg_trgm`, `citext`, `pgcrypto`, `unaccent` and the rest of contrib's trusted set): `vector` (pgvector), `postgis`, `postgis_topology`, `postgis_raster` and `pg_stat_statements`. A typed column of an extension's type is an `sqlType()`; an index of its method is a `raw` entry. Extensions are only ever added.

## Row-Level Security in the schema

RLS is declared beside the columns, in each table's `policies`, and it is on for every table that does not say `rls: false`. The builder, the roles a policy names, membership policies and the service role are on [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security).

## From a declaration to a database

Edit `src/db/public.ts`, commit and push to the machine's branch. The machine builds your image, and before the new version serves, the platform runs that image once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start`: it migrates the database to the schema the image carries, while the version before keeps serving. Once nothing of the old version is left, it runs `complete`. You run nothing yourself, and a change that cannot run under both versions is refused before anything changes. How each kind of change goes — and which take two releases — is [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

## Related

- [Database](/docs/backend/database) — the typed `Database.public.*` surface these declarations type, and `palbase-env.d.ts`
- [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security) — policies, roles, and `$asService()`
- [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations) — how a release migrates, `renamedFrom`, `fillWith`, `ignored`, and what is refused
- [Databases](/docs/machines/databases) — giving a machine a database, and its migrations
- [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks) — `user.deleted`, and the webhook secret an app that keeps users' ids needs

# Row-Level Security

Row-Level Security (RLS) makes **Postgres** decide who may see and write which rows. The rule lives beside the table, declared in TypeScript in your [schema](/docs/backend/schema), instead of being scattered across handlers where one forgotten `WHERE owner = …` leaks somebody's data. Two facts decide whether your first release works: **RLS is on by default**, and **a table with RLS and no policies denies everything** — a table you have not thought about returns nothing, rather than every row to every caller. If your routes answer `[]` and `null` on data you know is there, that default is the first thing to check.

> **Warning:** This is the first release's silent failure. Declare `todos` with columns and no `policies`, push it, and the `POST` fails while the `GET` returns an empty array — no error names RLS, because nothing went wrong: the database was asked for rows and answered honestly that there are none this caller may see. The rule is one line, `rls = policies.length > 0 || table.rls !== false`, and it is fail-closed on purpose: an empty result is the cost of not thinking about a table, and a leak is the other one.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { boolean, defineSchema, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const todos = defineTable("todos", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    // The user this row belongs to: text, NOT NULL, deleted with the user.
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    title: text(),
    done: boolean().default(false),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
  // A CALLBACK: `p` carries this table's own column names, so a misspelt column
  // is a compile error rather than a refusal from Postgres mid-release.
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("todos_own")
      .for("all")
      .to("authenticated")
      .using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))
      .withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
  ],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [todos] });
```

```ts
// src/modules/todos/todos.service.ts
import { Database, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";
import type { Tables } from "palbase/backend/env";

type Todo = Tables["todos"]["row"];

@Injectable()
export class TodosService {
  // No owner filter anywhere: the policy is the filter.
  list(): Promise<Todo[]> {
    return Database.public.todos.findMany({ orderBy: { column: "created_at", direction: "desc" } });
  }

  // The policy's WITH CHECK refuses a row whose owner is not the caller.
  add(owner: string, title: string): Promise<Todo> {
    return Database.public.todos.insert({ owner, title });
  }
}
```

The service never says whose rows it wants. Postgres reads the caller off the transaction and applies `owner = auth.uid()` to every statement — the typed tables, `$query`, a `$transaction` plan — so a route that forgets a filter cannot read past it.

## How the caller reaches the database

Every request is one transaction, and it begins by binding the caller:

```sql
SELECT set_config('role', 'authenticated', true),
       set_config('request.jwt.claims', '{"sub":"…","role":"authenticated",…}', true)
       -- and the version's search_path and application_name
```

Both settings are transaction-local, so nothing carries over to the next request on a pooled connection. The claims are the verified access token's, and `auth.uid()` reads `sub` out of them. Everything on the default `Database` surface runs inside that transaction; there is no opt-in step and nothing to forget. Going past it takes the explicit [`$asService()`](#asservice-past-rls).

## The roles a policy names

Three Postgres roles exist, and what the request is decides which one it runs as:

| Role | Who runs as it | Policies |
|---|---|---|
| `authenticated` | a request with a valid access token — `auth.uid()` is the user's id | apply |
| `anon` | a request with no token (a route with `auth: false`), with no claims — `auth.uid()` is `NULL` | apply |
| `service_role` | `Database.$asService()`, and every request of an app that says `db: { requests: "service" }` | never apply — it has `BYPASSRLS` |

`.to()` defaults to `"authenticated"`, so a policy you write without one does nothing for an anonymous caller. A table that anonymous callers read needs a policy that names `anon`:

```ts
import { boolean, defineTable, policy, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const posts = defineTable("posts", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), title: text(), published: boolean().default(false) },
  policies: (p) => [policy("posts_read_published").for("select").to("anon", "authenticated").using(p.col("published").eq(true))],
});
```

`.to()` with no arguments is `PUBLIC` — every role. The machine connects as the database's app login, which may become `anon`, `authenticated` or `service_role` and nothing else; it cannot bypass RLS on its own. The owner — the role migrations run as — owns the tables, and the app never connects as it.

> **Note:** These roles are the database's, not the API keys'. The project's publishable key and secret key choose what a call to the [modules](/docs/getting-started/introduction) may do. A call to your machine's backend is decided by the user's access token, and inside it the only switch to the service role is the `$asService()` you write.

## Enabling RLS on a table

| You declare | Result |
|---|---|
| neither `rls` nor `policies` | **RLS on, deny-all** — the default |
| a non-empty `policies` | **RLS on**, whatever `rls` says — a policy on a table without RLS would be inert |
| `rls: false`, no policies | RLS off: every role reads and writes every row. An explicit opt-out for a public table |

A write a `WITH CHECK` refuses, or a statement on a table the caller's role has no grant on, throws an `HttpError` carrying Postgres' SQLSTATE `42501` in its `sqlstate`, and the request's transaction rolls back. Left to reach the client it answers as PostgREST does: `403 permission_denied` to a signed-in caller, `401 permission_denied` to an anonymous one, for whom signing in may be what is missing. The answer names nothing of the schema — the policy, the table and the row stay in the log. On the service role — `$asService()`, or every request of an app that says `db: { requests: "service" }` — nobody's rights were judged: a `42501` there is the app's own grants, and passes through as Postgres' error, a `500 internal_error`. When the client should know why, check what the caller may write before writing it and say so with your own `Forbidden` and code.

## The `policy()` builder

`policy(name)` starts a builder whose methods chain; the name is unique per table.

| Method | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `.for(command)` | `"all"` | `"select"`, `"insert"`, `"update"`, `"delete"` or `"all"` |
| `.to(...roles)` | `"authenticated"` | `"anon"`, `"authenticated"`, `"service_role"`; no arguments is `PUBLIC` |
| `.using(expr)` | none | `USING (…)` — which existing rows a command may see or touch |
| `.withCheck(expr)` | none | `WITH CHECK (…)` — which written rows are allowed |
| `.memberOf(table, fk, opts?)` | — | the membership subquery below; it **is** the `using`, so it refuses to combine with one |
| `.as(mode)` | `"permissive"` | `"restrictive"` ANDs the policy on top of the permissive ones |
| `.withoutIndexes()` | — | the columns it reads get no index of their own from it |

`using` and `withCheck` take the typed expression — built from the callback's `p` — or a raw SQL string for what the expressions cannot say. Prefer the typed form: `p.col(…)` is checked against this table's columns as you write it, a string only by Postgres when the policy is created.

| Expression | SQL |
|---|---|
| `p.col("owner")` | this table's column |
| `p.auth.uid()` | `(select auth.uid())` — evaluated once per statement, not per row |
| `.eq(x)`, `.neq(x)`, `.gt(x)`, `.gte(x)`, `.lt(x)`, `.lte(x)` | comparisons; `x` is another expression or a plain value |
| `.isNull()` / `.isNull(true)` | `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` |
| `.and(…)`, `.or(…)`, `.not()`, `p.and(…)`, `p.or(…)`, `p.not(…)` | combinations |
| `p.lit(v)` | a value, said explicitly |
| `p.existsIn(table, (row) => …)` | a correlated `EXISTS` subquery into another table |

A plain value on the right of `.eq()` is a literal, never a column: `.eq("owner")` compares with the string `"owner"`. A column is always `p.col("owner")`.

Every column a policy reads gets an index unless one already leads with it (`<table>_<column>_idx`), because it is read on every query of the table. `.withoutIndexes()` opts a policy out of that.

### Per-command policies

Split the policies when reads and writes have different rules — anyone signed in reads, only the owner changes:

```ts
import { boolean, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    body: text(),
    pinned: boolean().default(false),
  },
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("notes_read").for("select").using("true"),
    policy("notes_insert_own").for("insert").withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
    policy("notes_update_own").for("update").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
    policy("notes_delete_own").for("delete").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())),
  ],
});
```

Permissive policies for the same command **OR** together — a row is visible if any of them allows it. Use `.as("restrictive")` for a condition that must **also** hold whatever else is declared, such as a tenant guard.

## Membership: the pattern that does not recurse

Anything shared — a channel, a project, an organisation — has the same shape: a **membership table** joining users to the thing, and a policy on the thing asking whether the caller is in it. Written by hand the two policies point at each other, and Postgres refuses the pair when it is queried:

```text
ERROR: infinite recursion detected in policy for relation "channel_members"
```

The way out is to make it asymmetric. The membership table is protected by the caller's identity **alone** — it never looks at the thing it points to — and every other table asks it:

```ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, policy, text, userRef, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const channels = defineTable("channels", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), name: text() },
  // 2. The thing asks the membership table; memberOf() writes the subquery.
  policies: () => [policy("channels_member_read").for("select").memberOf("channel_members", "channel_id")],
});

export const channel_members = defineTable("channel_members", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    channel_id: uuid().references(() => channels.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    user_id: userRef({ onDelete: "cascade" }),
  },
  // 1. The membership table names auth.uid() and nothing else, so evaluating
  //    it never reaches another policy.
  policies: (p) => [policy("members_own").for("select").using(p.col("user_id").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export const messages = defineTable("messages", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    channel_id: uuid().references(() => channels.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
    author: userRef({ onDelete: "set null" }).nullable(),
    body: text(),
  },
  // 3. Anything hanging off the thing asks the membership table too, typed:
  //    `m` is channel_members' columns, `p` this table's.
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("messages_member_read")
      .for("select")
      .using(p.existsIn(channel_members, (m) => m.col("channel_id").eq(p.col("channel_id")).and(m.col("user_id").eq(p.auth.uid())))),
    policy("messages_member_write")
      .for("insert")
      .withCheck(
        p.col("author").eq(p.auth.uid()).and(
          p.existsIn(channel_members, (m) => m.col("channel_id").eq(p.col("channel_id")).and(m.col("user_id").eq(p.auth.uid()))),
        ),
      ),
  ],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [channels, channel_members, messages] });
```

`memberOf(membershipTable, foreignKey)` compiles to:

```sql
"id" IN (SELECT "channel_id" FROM "channel_members" WHERE "user_id" = (select auth.uid()))
```

`{ column }` is the column of this table the subquery matches (`id` by default — pass the foreign key's name on a child table), and `{ userColumn }` the membership table's user column when it is not `user_id`. `p.existsIn` is the typed form of the same idea: the subquery's columns come from the membership table's own declaration, so a misspelt one is a compile error too.

> **Note:** A policy `.for("select")` decides only what is visible. Writes need their own — `.for("insert")` with a `withCheck`, as `messages` has — or `.for("all")` when one condition governs both.

## RLS guards reads, not foreign-key checks

A `SELECT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` only ever reaches rows the caller may see. A **foreign-key check is not filtered**: when a row's foreign key points at a parent, Postgres validates that the parent exists whoever owns it. Without a policy that says otherwise, a caller can attach a child row to a parent it cannot read. Nothing leaks — it still cannot read the parent — but say what you mean, in the child's `withCheck`:

```ts
import { defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const orders = defineTable("orders", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), owner: ownedByUser(), note: text().nullable() },
  policies: (p) => [policy("orders_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export const order_items = defineTable("order_items", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), order_id: uuid().references(() => orders.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }), sku: text() },
  // Readable and writable only under an order the caller owns.
  policies: (p) => [
    policy("order_items_via_order")
      .for("all")
      .using(p.existsIn(orders, (o) => o.col("id").eq(p.col("order_id")).and(o.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))))
      .withCheck(p.existsIn(orders, (o) => o.col("id").eq(p.col("order_id")).and(o.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())))),
  ],
});
```

The `existsIn` runs as the caller, so the `orders` it sees are already the caller's own — the subquery asks the question the foreign-key check does not.

## `$asService()`: past RLS

Some code legitimately reaches across users — an admin route, a cleanup, a count over everyone. `Database.$asService()` returns the same typed surface running as `service_role`, which bypasses RLS:

```ts
import { Database } from "palbase/backend";

// The default: only the caller's own rows.
const mine = await Database.public.todos.findMany();

// The service role: every user's rows. Explicit, and greppable in review.
const all = await Database.$asService().public.todos.findMany();
```

- **It is a second transaction, on a second connection**, opened by its first use — the role is bound once, when a transaction begins. The two commit as two, the caller's first.
- **It keeps the caller's claims**, so `auth.uid()` still resolves in a trigger or a default inside it. It changes what may be touched, not who is asking.
- **It does not nest**: the surface it returns has no `$asService()` of its own.
- **Inside `$asService().$atomic(cb)`, use the handle `cb` is given** — the shared `Database` is refused there, so a helper written against the caller's RLS cannot quietly read everyone's rows.

Inside it your own code is the only authorisation left, so check the caller's right first and call it at the point of use. An app whose every table is the service role's — an operator's tool deciding in its routes who sees what — says so once, `db: { schemas, requests: "service" }`, and every request runs as `service_role`.

## Changing a policy

Edit `policies` in the schema file, commit and push to the machine's branch. The release's migration step changes the policy in place. Postgres keeps one set of policies per table, so a changed policy holds for **both** versions from `start` on — the version still serving is held to it too. A policy that reads a column (or another table) the same release renames is refused: rename in one release, change the policy in the next. See [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

## Related

- [Schema](/docs/backend/schema) — `defineTable`, `ownedByUser()`, and where policies sit
- [Database](/docs/backend/database) — the request's transaction, `$query`, and `$asService()`
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication) — who the caller is, and routes with `auth: false`
- [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations) — how a release applies a policy change

# Field Encryption

A column marked `.encrypted()` is sealed by your app before it is written and opened when it is read, with the project's own field keys. The database, its backups and a dump of it hold ciphertext; your code reads and writes the plain value, as with any other column. It is on every plan, at no cost.

It protects a field from whoever reaches the database without the app: a leaked dump or backup, a stolen database password, a read-only SQL injection. It does not protect it from your app itself — the app holds the keys while it runs.

## Quick example

```ts
// db/public.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, text, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

export const patients = defineTable("patients", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    name: text(),
    // Found by equality, and kept unique: { lookup: true } keeps a keyed hash beside it.
    national_id: text().encrypted({ lookup: true }).unique(),
    // Read and written whole, never searched.
    notes: text().encrypted().nullable(),
  },
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [patients] });
```

```ts
// src/modules/patients/patients.service.ts
import { Database, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class PatientsService {
  async admit(name: string, nationalId: string) {
    return Database.public.patients.insert({ name, national_id: nationalId, notes: "allergy: penicillin" });
  }

  async byNationalId(nationalId: string) {
    return Database.public.patients.findUnique({ where: { national_id: nationalId } });
  }
}
```

What the database holds:

```text
 name |                       national_id                       |       national_id_lookup
------+---------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------
 Ayşe | pbe1.k1.MzMzMzMzMzMzMzMztbNidvqiRRyDjN1Zkdx-38ei7bu3V…   | pbl1.cypF9YEDilHu_qYJy15Snch…
```

## What an encrypted column is asked

The database holds the column's ciphertext, not its value, so it can compare nothing there. An encrypted column takes text; what a query may ask of it is fixed by its type:

| | `.encrypted()` | `.encrypted({ lookup: true })` |
|---|---|---|
| Read and write the value | yes | yes |
| `isNull`, `null` | yes | yes |
| Equality: `{ col: v }`, `in`, `neq`, `findUnique` | — | yes, through the lookup |
| `.unique()`, `onConflict` | — | yes, kept on the lookup |
| `orderBy`, `gt`/`lt`, `contains`/`startsWith`, `search`, `min`/`max`, `groupBy`, an index | — | — |

What is refused is a compile error in a typed query, and an error naming the column when the query is built otherwise. The lookup is a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA256) of the value, kept in `<column>_lookup`, which your code never names; equal values have equal lookups, so a lookup tells which rows hold the same value — keep it off a column whose few possible values that would give away.

An encrypted column is not a default, a primary key, a foreign key, a generated column or a search column, and has no codec: `defineTable` refuses each, naming the column.

## Keys

Each environment has its own field keys, kept by the platform's secrets module and derived from the environment's data key, which the platform's key-encryption key (Azure Key Vault) wraps. Your app reads them with its secret key when it starts and every minute after; a schema without an encrypted column never reads them. The secrets audit trail (`palbase secrets:audit`) has each app key's first read in the hour, and every download by a developer.

A value is bound to its column — `table.column`, or `schema.table.column` outside public: moved to another column, or into another environment, it does not open, and a value changed in the database is refused when read, as is a plain value where an encrypted one belongs.

## Encrypting a column that holds rows

Add `.encrypted()` to the column and deploy. The release migrates beside the version that serves, as every [schema change](/docs/backend/migrations) does:

- While both versions run, the column keeps the form the old version reads — plain — and the new version reads either form.
- Once the old version is gone, the release seals every row, in batches, and from then on a plain value in the column is refused.

Taking `.encrypted()` off goes the same way the other way round. An encrypted column, or its table, is not renamed while it holds rows: its values are bound to its name.

## Rotating the keys

```bash
palbase fields:rotate
```

The new key comes into force five minutes later — every running app has fetched it by then. New values are sealed with it from then on, and a `palbase/backend` app seals the older values again with it in the background. The older keys go on opening what they sealed. An owner or an admin rotates; `palbase fields:list` shows the keys and which is in force.

## In Studio

The database's **Tables** screen shows an encrypted value masked. An owner or an admin of the organization opens one with **Show**: the secrets module opens it — the keys never reach Studio — and records who opened which column in the audit trail. A member sees the mask alone.

## Copying, dumping and leaving

- `palbase db:copy --from production --to staging` copies every encrypted value as `•••`, sealed with the target's keys: one environment's values never land readable in another.
- A dump (`palbase db:dump`) holds ciphertext. The environment's owner downloads the keys that open it — `palbase fields:keys --out keys.json` writes them into a file readable by its owner alone, and the download is in the audit trail. Keep the file as you keep the database's password.

## Without palbase/backend

A server with another way to its database — NestJS with TypeORM or Prisma, plain SQL — seals and opens a column itself with `palbase/server`, in the same format: a column one app writes, the other reads.

```ts
// src/patients/fields.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

/** Awaited at startup: after it, the calls below are synchronous. */
export const fieldsLoaded = palbase.fields.load();

/** What an INSERT writes: the sealed value, and the lookup it is found by. */
export function sealNationalId(value: string) {
  return {
    national_id: palbase.fields.encrypt("patients.national_id", value),
    national_id_lookup: palbase.fields.lookup("patients.national_id", value),
  };
}

export const nationalIdLookup = (value: string) => palbase.fields.lookup("patients.national_id", value);
export const openNationalId = (sealed: string) => palbase.fields.decrypt("patients.national_id", sealed);
```

```ts
// src/patients/patients.repository.ts
import { nationalIdLookup, openNationalId, sealNationalId } from "./fields";

/** Your Postgres client (pg's Pool, postgres.js), down to the one call used here. */
export interface Db {
  query(text: string, values: unknown[]): Promise<{ rows: { national_id: string }[] }>;
}

export async function admit(db: Db, id: string, name: string, nationalId: string): Promise<void> {
  const sealed = sealNationalId(nationalId);
  await db.query("INSERT INTO patients (id, name, national_id, national_id_lookup) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)", [id, name, sealed.national_id, sealed.national_id_lookup]);
}

export async function nationalIdOf(db: Db, wanted: string): Promise<string | undefined> {
  const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT national_id FROM patients WHERE national_id_lookup = $1", [nationalIdLookup(wanted)]);
  return rows[0] && openNationalId(rows[0].national_id);
}
```

The first argument is the column's address. A TypeORM column transformer is the same two calls:

<!-- fragment: a property shown out of its TypeORM entity -->

```ts
@Column({ transformer: { to: (v: string) => palbase.fields.encrypt("patients.national_id", v), from: (v: string) => palbase.fields.decrypt("patients.national_id", v) } })
national_id!: string;
```

`palbase.fields` needs Node's crypto: Node, Bun or Deno.

## Tests

`palbase/server/testing`'s `testFields()` gives keys of no project, held in the test's process. Pass them where the project's would go — `createRequestDatabase(sql, identity, { schemas, fields })` from `palbase/backend/engine`, or palgres' `createDatabase({ …, fields })` — for a test that runs an encrypted schema against a database of its own:

```ts
// test/fields.test.ts
import { expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { testFields } from "palbase/server/testing";

it("opens what it seals, at the same column alone", async () => {
  const fields = await testFields();
  const sealed = fields.encrypt("patients.national_id", "10000000146");
  expect(sealed.startsWith("pbe1.")).toBe(true);
  expect(fields.decrypt("patients.national_id", sealed)).toBe("10000000146");
  expect(() => fields.decrypt("patients.phone", sealed)).toThrow();
});
```

`palbase/backend/test`'s in-memory database keeps an encrypted column as a plain one, and does not refuse what the engine refuses on it.



<!-- ===== backend/request-encryption ===== -->

# Encrypted Requests

A field your route marks `encrypted()` is sealed by the app before the request leaves the device, and a field your route answers with `encrypt()` is opened by the app when the answer arrives. Your handler and the app's code see the value; everything between them — the network, the edge, a proxy, the logs, a debugging proxy, the browser's network panel — sees ciphertext. It is on every plan, at no cost.

It protects a field from whatever sits between the app and your code. It does not protect it from the device that typed it, nor from your backend, which opens it. To keep it sealed in the database too, store it in an [encrypted column](/docs/backend/encryption).

## Quick example

The backend: `tc` (a national ID) is encrypted in the request and in the answer.

```ts
// server/src/patients/patients.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, encrypt, encrypted, Get, NotFound, Param, Post, z, type Encrypted } from "palbase/backend";

const CreatePatient = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1).max(200),
  // Sealed by the app; opened before validation, so the handler and the schema see the value.
  tc: encrypted(z.string().regex(/^\d{11}$/)),
});
type CreatePatient = z.infer<typeof CreatePatient>;

interface Patient {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  tc: string;
}

@Controller("/patients")
export class PatientsController {
  private readonly patients = new Map<string, Patient>();

  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreatePatient) body: CreatePatient): { id: string; name: string; tc: Encrypted<string> } {
    const patient = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name: body.name, tc: body.tc };
    this.patients.set(patient.id, patient);
    // Sealed with the request's own key: only the app that asked opens it.
    return { id: patient.id, name: patient.name, tc: encrypt(patient.tc) };
  }

  @Get("/:id")
  get(@Param("id") id: string): { id: string; name: string; tc: Encrypted<string> } {
    const patient = this.patients.get(id);
    if (!patient) throw new NotFound("no such patient");
    return { id: patient.id, name: patient.name, tc: encrypt(patient.tc) };
  }
}
```

Once it is deployed, `palbase apps:sync` writes the app's client with the fields marked, and the app's calls are what they would be without them:

<!-- fragment: the app's module is the one palbase apps:sync writes for your project -->
```ts
// src/patients.ts
import { pb } from "../palbase/clinic-web";

const patient = await pb.backend.patients.create({ name: "Ada", tc: "10000000146" });
console.log(patient.tc); // "10000000146"
```

What went over the wire:

```text
POST /patients
Palbase-Encryption: 1.t1.gZlVWWADouVFMPA7e26mzk8OCPWBYEEnrr9VqRsqSgA.z-X3bStZx8D0K24F90qhbcbUTIIHDxZYWwnMIeFjZWcMqHk5nHmy7ZYKGyb8Idvo
{"name":"Ada","tc":"pbt1.fCnMiPfNbStaAugZD5anhbAszYy170oluQ_30omSb7lSOGzhJACqpVg"}

200
{"id":"a71f381e-b849-4ccd-9e0d-224a1fc80f2c","name":"Ada","tc":"pbt1.yrbQ_0Qhe_p0R7HXOgHgkXJKaeniFL8N9Jd1xNmZ50C_ckFf5tCPF7o"}
```

Each request has a key of its own, sealed to the project's key in use and bound to the project, the method, the route and its path's values; each field is bound to its place. A value moved to another field, a request replayed against another route or another record, does not open, and the backend answers 400.

## Marking a field

**In a request**, `encrypted(schema)` marks a field of the body or of the query, wherever it sits in the body: a nested object's field, every item of an array (`items: z.array(z.object({ tc: encrypted(z.string()) }))`), an optional field. A query's field is one of the query's own names. A path parameter or a header is not marked: it is part of the address the request is routed by.

**In an answer**, the handler returns the value through `encrypt(value)`, typed `Encrypted<T>`. The build reads the route's return type and writes the mark into the contract, as it writes every other answer's type: `{ tc: Encrypted<string> }` is a `string` the app opens. An answer the route declares as a named schema holds no mark — the build refuses it, naming the route — and a streamed answer and an upload carry no encrypted field.

A request that comes without its key to a route that marks its request is refused before the handler runs. A route that marks only its answer runs its handler and is then refused, since the answer cannot be sealed: keep such a route free of side effects, or mark a field of its request too.

## In the apps

The web, iOS and Android clients `palbase apps:sync` writes seal and open the marked fields themselves. The first call that carries one fetches the project's list of keys with the app's publishable key, and checks that the project signed it with the signing key `apps:sync` wrote into the app, and that it answers this call's fresh nonce: a list that does not verify is not sealed to, and the call fails with `encryption_keys_unverified` before anything is sent. A marked field that comes back plain fails with `field_not_encrypted`.

The [iOS](/docs/ios/debug-console) and [Android](/docs/android/debug-console) debug consoles record a backend call as it went: an encrypted field is shown sealed, and **Reveal** beside it shows its value. Nothing is recorded while the console is off.

## Keys

Each project has its own keys, and apps seal to the newest. An owner or an admin of the organization lists and rotates them:

```bash
palbase transit:list                      # the keys, the one in use, who made and retired each
palbase transit:rotate                    # a new key, in use at once; the older ones still open what is sealed to them
palbase transit:rotate --retire-previous  # a new key, and every older one refused from now on
palbase transit:retire t1                 # refuse one older key
```

A key thought exposed is rotated with `--retire-previous`. A request sealed to a retired key is refused at once, before it reaches your backend (which also refuses it on its own once it next fetches the keys, within a minute), and an app that sealed to it is told so: it fetches the list again and sends the call once more, sealed to the new key — the user sees nothing. An app fetches the list again every hour in any case. The secrets audit trail (`palbase secrets:audit`) has every rotation and retirement.

## Errors

A request the format refuses is answered `400`, with its code in `error`:

| Code | When | `data` |
|---|---|---|
| `encryption_required` | A marked field came plain, or the request has no `Palbase-Encryption` header. | `field`, `current` |
| `encryption_unopenable` | The request's key or a field does not open: changed, moved from another field, sealed for another project, route or record. | `field` |
| `encryption_key_retired` | The request is sealed to a key the project retired. The app's client fetches the list again and sends once more. | `current` |
| `encryption_key_unknown` | The request is sealed to a key the project has not made. The same. | `current` |

## Trying a route

curl and Postman send the field plain, and are refused. `palbase machines:call` calls a route as the app does — its marked fields sealed to the key in use, its answer's opened — and prints the answer:

```bash
palbase machines:call backend POST /patients --data '{"name":"Ada","tc":"10000000146"}'
```

Studio's **Try it** on a machine's endpoint seals and opens them the same way.

## Without palbase/backend

A server built another way — NestJS, Express, Hono, a route handler — opens a request and seals its answer with `palbase/server`'s `transit`, in the same format. Its contract marks the fields `x-palbase-encrypted: true`; served by its app (a machine made with `--openapi-path`), it is what `palbase apps:sync` writes the apps' clients from.

```ts
// src/transit.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

export const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

/** Awaited at startup: the project's keys, fetched again every minute and when a request names one not held. */
export const transitLoaded = palbase.transit.load();
```

```ts
// src/patients.ts
import { TransitRefusal } from "palbase/server";
import { palbase } from "./transit";

const patients = new Map<string, { id: string; name: string; tc: string }>();

/** POST /patients and GET /patients/{id}, as a fetch handler (Hono, Bun.serve, a route handler) takes them. */
export async function handle(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const key = request.headers.get("palbase-encryption");
  const id = new URL(request.url).pathname.split("/")[2];
  try {
    if (request.method === "POST") {
      // The route as the contract writes it: a key sealed for another route does not open here.
      const req = await palbase.transit.request({ header: key, method: "POST", path: "/patients" });
      const input = (await req.open(await request.json(), "/body", ["/body/tc"])) as { name: string; tc: string };
      const patient = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), name: input.name, tc: input.tc };
      patients.set(patient.id, patient);
      return Response.json(await req.seal(patient, ["/response/tc"]));
    }
    // A path's values are part of what the key is sealed for, in order.
    const req = await palbase.transit.request({ header: key, method: "GET", path: "/patients/{id}", params: [id ?? ""] });
    const patient = patients.get(id ?? "");
    if (!patient) return Response.json({ error: "not_found" }, { status: 404 });
    return Response.json(await req.seal(patient, ["/response/tc"]));
  } catch (e) {
    // Answered as palbase/backend answers it, so the apps' clients know a retired key when they meet one.
    if (e instanceof TransitRefusal) return Response.json({ error: e.code, error_description: e.message, data: e.data }, { status: e.status });
    throw e;
  }
}
```

In a NestJS controller the same calls go in its methods: the header through `@Headers("palbase-encryption")`, `open()` on the `@Body()`, the answer returned through `seal()`, and an exception filter that answers a `TransitRefusal` as above.



<!-- ===== backend/migrations ===== -->

# Schema changes

There are no migration files. Your [schema files](/docs/backend/schema) are the declaration, and every release of your machine migrates its database to what they say — **beside the version still serving**, so no request waits for a migration and no request of the old version meets a table it cannot read. You change `src/db/public.ts`, commit and push. You run nothing yourself: the platform runs your new image once to **start** the migration, rolls the new version out next to the old one while both read and write the same tables, and runs it again to **complete** once the old one is gone. A change that both versions cannot run through is refused before anything changes, and the version serving keeps serving.

## The workflow at a glance

```bash
# 1. Edit the declaration: add a column, rename one, tighten one.
#    src/db/public.ts
# 2. Regenerate the types, so Database.public.* matches what you wrote.
bun run scripts/palbase-env.ts
# 3. Commit and push to the machine's branch. That push is the release.
git commit -am "notes: pinned, and title is called subject"
git push
```

The machine builds the commit, and because it is given its database with **migrations on** (Studio: the machine's *Database* setting, "runs its migrations"), the release goes:

1. **start** — the new image runs once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start` and the database owner's address. Everything the new version needs is added next to what the running version uses. The new version is not rolled out until start succeeds.
2. **rollout** — the new version comes up beside the old one. Both read and write the same tables.
3. **complete** — once the new version has served and no copy of the old one is left, the image runs with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=complete`. Whatever only the old version used is removed; a renamed column takes its new name, a retyped one takes its place.

A version that is abandoned before complete — its start failed, it did not come up, or a newer push took its place — gets **rollback**, which removes what start added and restores what it loosened. Data written meanwhile stays.

A database's migrations are one machine's: a second machine that asks to run them is refused (`409 database_migrated_elsewhere`). Another machine may be given the same database without migrations; it binds to the schema version its own files describe, so it carries the same schema files and is released after the one that migrates.

## The app migrates itself

The migration is not the platform's code. It is Palgres — the same library that serves your queries — inside your own image. `PalbaseFactory.create` reads `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE`: set, it migrates the database to the `schemas` it was given and exits; unset, it serves.

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";
import schema from "./db/public";

// Serves on $PORT. Run with PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start|complete|rollback by a
// release, it migrates the database as its owner (PALBASE_DB_OWNER_URL) and exits.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { db: { schemas: [schema] } });
```

```ts
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";

// The app's modules, listed here as ever: a migration run builds none of them.
@Module({ imports: [] })
export class AppModule {}
```

The schema the engine plans from and the engine that applies it are always the same version, because they are in the same image, and a migration run sees nothing but its own image. The run connects as the database's **owner** (`PALBASE_DB_OWNER_URL`, given to migration runs alone); the version that serves connects as the app's login (`PALBASE_DB_URL`) and cannot alter a table.

How a run exits is all the platform reads of it:

| Exit | What it says | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `0` | done, or nothing to do | the release goes on: rollout after start, and so on |
| `1` | the migration's own verdict — it is refused, or the rows do not fit it (two rows where a new unique index wants one). Run again, it would end the same | the release stops. What start began is taken back, the version serving stays, and the build says why |
| anything else | it was cut off — the database restarting, a lock not had in the tries it has, the run's node drained, its memory out (`75` when the app says so) | the run is made again, and picks up where it stopped |

A run's lines are in the machine's logs, marked as a migration run's, and its last line is the reason the build shows — see [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds). A migration the process dies in picks up where it stopped: each step is recorded when it commits, and copying a large table records its place with every batch. A step has a day, its attempts together — not a measure of the work, only the end of a run that would never end.

Only one migration is open at a time. A push that comes while one is open waits for its complete — or, when the version it belongs to has not rolled out yet, takes its place: that one is rolled back first.

## What start does, so nothing waits

- New tables and columns are added; **indexes are built `CONCURRENTLY`**.
- `CHECK`s and foreign keys are added `NOT VALID`, then validated while writes go on.
- `NOT NULL` is set through a validated `CHECK`.
- A type change adds a second column of the new type that the two versions write through each other.
- Each step takes the locks its statements need, waits at most 500 ms for them, then gives way and tries again — so a request queued behind it never waits longer than that. A writer is never the one sacrificed to break a lock cycle.
- A table is filled in batches that take only rows no writer holds (`SKIP LOCKED`); a write never waits for a batch longer than its commit.

## Adding things

Adding a table, a nullable column, a column with a default, an index, a unique index, a `CHECK` or a foreign key is an ordinary release — declare it and push. Two things to know:

- **A new `NOT NULL` column needs `.default(…)` or `.fillWith(sql)`**: the version still serving inserts rows without it.
- **Constraints apply at start.** A `CHECK`, unique index or foreign key added by a migration holds for every write once start is done — the old version's writes included. A row the old version writes that a new constraint refuses is refused.

## Renaming a column

A diff shown two names for one column cannot tell a rename from a drop and an add — and the second loses every value. Say which it is:

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    title: text(),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
  policies: (p) => [policy("notes_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```

The next release renames `title` and adds `pinned`:

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { boolean, defineSchema, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    subject: text().renamedFrom("title"),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
    pinned: boolean().default(false),
  },
  policies: (p) => [policy("notes_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```

```ts
// src/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Database, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  // The new version writes `subject`; the old one, still serving, writes `title` — the same column.
  create(owner: string, subject: string) {
    return Database.public.notes.insert({ owner, subject });
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesService } from "./notes.service";

@Module({ providers: [NotesService] })
export class NotesModule {}
```

While both versions run, the table keeps its old names and the new version reads and writes through its version's views, which hold the new names; at complete the column takes its new name. The typed tables work this way already. In the new version's **raw SQL** during that window, name tables bare (`notes`, not `public.notes` — a qualified name reaches the table under its old names), and name an `ON CONFLICT` target by its columns rather than its constraint (a view has none). Tools outside the app — psql, a BI tool — see the table itself: the old names until complete.

Once complete has run, `renamedFrom` is inert — the old name is gone — so delete it whenever you next touch the file.

## Changing a column's type

A type change is planned as a second column of the new type, which both versions write through each other by Postgres' cast both ways (an enum renamed, by its labels); at complete it takes the old column's place. Each version's own writes are cast across, so neither version's values are lost. What both versions cannot run through is refused — see the table below — and for those the way is a new column. A later release's `src/db/public.ts`:

```ts
import { boolean, defineSchema, defineTable, enumType, ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    subject: text(),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
    // `pinned` becomes a three-way visibility. Postgres has no cast from a
    // boolean to an enum, so it is a new column filled from the old one, and
    // `pinned` is ignored until the next release removes it.
    pinned: boolean().default(false).ignored(),
    visibility: enumType("note_visibility", ["normal", "pinned", "hidden"])
      .fillWith("(CASE WHEN pinned THEN 'pinned' ELSE 'normal' END)::public.note_visibility"),
  },
  policies: (p) => [policy("notes_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```

## Making a column `NOT NULL`

A nullable column with rows cannot just become `NOT NULL`: some rows are `NULL`, and the version still serving goes on writing `NULL`. `.fillWith(sql)` says what such a row gets — the rows already there and every write of the old version while both run — and the column is made `NOT NULL` only after. In this release's `src/db/public.ts`, `summary` was `text().nullable()` until now:

```ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, ownedByUser, policy, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

const notes = defineTable("notes", {
  columns: {
    id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
    owner: ownedByUser(),
    subject: text(),
    summary: text().fillWith("left(subject, 80)"),
    created_at: timestamp().defaultNow(),
  },
  policies: (p) => [policy("notes_own").for("all").using(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid())).withCheck(p.col("owner").eq(p.auth.uid()))],
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [notes] });
```

The fill is for the rows the new code does not write: the ones already there, and the old version's. The new version's own inserts must give the column — in its `palbase-env.d.ts` it is required, like any `NOT NULL` column without a default — so the release that adds the fill also changes the code that inserts.

`fillWith` is one SQL scalar expression over the row's own columns. A table, function or type it names is schema-qualified (`public.accounts`): it runs with a pinned `search_path`. It reads past RLS, and what it writes is readable by anyone who can read the row. It goes only on a `NOT NULL` column with no default that is not ignored — a constant is a `.default()` — and the value stays after a rollback, so make it one the old version reads correctly.

## Removing a column or a table

The release that drops a column must not be the release that stops reading it: the version still serving reads it until complete. So a column or a table **with data** goes in two releases:

1. Mark it — `.ignored()` on a column, `{ ignored: true }` on a table — and push. Nothing changes in the database; this release's code no longer names it, and the typed tables leave it out of every row and every statement.
2. Remove it from the schema and push. Its data goes at that release's complete.

A dropped or ignored `NOT NULL` column with no default needs one in the release that ignores it — the new version inserts rows without it, and the old version reads that value in them. Palgres does not make such a column nullable for you: the old version would then read it empty, and after a rollback go on doing so.

## Changing data once

A value a column can be worked out from — the rows already there, and each write of the version still serving — is a fill: `.fillWith(sql)`, run in batches beside both versions with nothing held. Every other change of data that is made once — a catalog's rows, data moved into a new shape, a repair — is a [task](/docs/backend/tasks), not part of the migration: it runs on your machine once the release is out, in your own code, and its progress shows in Studio.

```ts
// src/modules/people/split-full-names.task.ts
import { Database, Task, z } from "palbase/backend";

// Picks up only what is still to do: run again, it does nothing twice.
@Task({ name: "split-full-names", payload: z.object({}) })
export class SplitFullNames {
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    await Database.$asService().$query(
      "update people set first_name = split_part(full_name, ' ', 1) where first_name is null and full_name is not null",
    );
  }
}
```

Put it once the release is out, under a key, so a second put is the first one answered:

```sh
palbase machines:tasks:enqueue split-full-names --key split-full-names-1
```

A key holds for a day after the task is over: write the task so a later run finds nothing left to do, as above, rather than counting on the key. A change that is too large for one statement does a share of the rows each run, and puts itself again (`Tasks.enqueue`, with the next key) until none is left.

There is no `backfill(name, sql)` here: a bare `UPDATE` run as part of a release would race the writes of the version still serving, and stay in the schema file for good.

## What is refused, and what to do instead

A refused migration changes nothing, and the version serving keeps serving. The build says what was refused and the way through:

| Change | Instead |
|---|---|
| A column or table with data is removed from the schema | Mark it `.ignored()` / `{ ignored: true }` and release; remove it in the next release |
| A nullable column becomes `NOT NULL` | Give `.fillWith(sql)` |
| A new `NOT NULL` column has no default | `.default(…)` or `.fillWith(sql)` |
| A dropped or ignored `NOT NULL` column has no default | Give it a default in that release |
| The type of a column a `CHECK`, a policy, an expression or partial index, the primary key or another table's foreign key uses | Add a column of the new type with `.fillWith("old::newtype")`, move what uses it, then ignore the old column |
| A type Postgres has no cast to, either way (boolean to an enum, a timestamp to a boolean), or an enum to one whose labels differ | Add a column of the new type with `.fillWith(sql)`, move to it, then ignore the old column — refused on an empty table too |
| The primary key changes | Add a unique constraint |
| An enum loses a value | Add a new enum type and move the column to it |
| An identity column is added to a table with rows | Add a `bigint` column with a default, and fill it |
| A column of a domain with a `CHECK` is added to a table with rows | Add it as the domain's base type with a `CHECK` |
| A column changes type and becomes `NOT NULL` in one release | Change its type in this release, make it `NOT NULL` in the next |
| A raw unit that is a trigger, a rule or a view has no `drop` | Give it one: `raw(name, up, { drop })` |
| A raw index, domain, type or sequence changes under its name | An index: give the new one its own name. A domain, type or sequence: say the change as an `ALTER …` in a unit of its own |
| A policy reads a column (or a table) the same release renames | Rename in this release, change the policy in the next |

## What to know while both versions run

- **Constraints and policies apply at start**, for both versions: Postgres keeps one set of policies per table, and a new constraint holds for every write.
- **A unique the new version drops holds until complete** — the old version's upserts need it — so while both run, the new version cannot write what it forbids. A unique or index changed under its name is built beside the old one, and takes its name at complete.
- **A type change keeps both versions' values.** A value one version wrote is not cast back over when the other updates another column.
- **A stored generated column made plain** is computed for the old version's writes until complete; a rollback leaves it plain.
- **An enum value start added stays after a rollback** — Postgres cannot drop one — and so does a fill.

## Taking over a database Palgres did not make

A database another tool left — Prisma, Drizzle, a team's hand-written SQL — comes over as it is. Palgres writes schema files from it, read only; the address is an environment variable, not an argument, because it holds a password:

```bash
PALGRES_DATABASE_URL='postgresql://…' bun node_modules/palgres/src/cli.ts pull src
# wrote src/db/public.ts
#   column public.orders.user_id may hold a user's id: mark it ownedByUser() or userRef() so user.deleted reaches it
```

What the DSL's builders say is written with them; a default, check or policy they cannot say is written as its SQL. An index the typed form cannot say, and what the database holds besides tables — domains, types, sequences, functions, views, triggers — are raw units in Postgres' own words. The command prints what to look at: columns that may hold a user's id, and what it leaves as it is (a partitioned table, a view over one).

The first release with those files takes the database over. The declared schema is made in a shadow database — the owner has `CREATEDB` for it — and the two are compared the way Postgres writes them. Held as declared, the database becomes version 1 and nothing in it changes; held otherwise, it becomes version 1 as it is, and the ordinary migration to the declared schema does exactly the difference, with the same refusals. A refused take-over writes nothing. Row-level security forced on the owner is turned off — Palgres migrates as the owner, and the app never connects as it — and a database whose own `auth.uid()`, `auth.jwt()` or `auth.role()` reads its caller another way is refused until you rename yours.

## Related

- [Schema](/docs/backend/schema) — the declarations a release migrates to
- [Database](/docs/backend/database) — the typed tables, and raw SQL while a rename is open
- [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security) — policies, which apply at start
- [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds) — what a push does, and the migration run's lines
- [Databases](/docs/machines/databases) — giving a machine its database, with migrations on
