# Storage

Every project has storage: **buckets** of files, read and written by your backend with the secret key. In a `palbase/backend` app the module is `Palbase.storage`; from any other server it is `createServer({ url, secretKey }).storage` — the same client, generated from the storage contract. A client app never holds the secret key, so it reaches files in two ways only: a **public** bucket's objects, which anyone may read, and **signed URLs** your backend hands out — one to read an object, or one to upload it ([Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads)). An AI chat message holds to the same: a client attaches only a public bucket's file, and a private one is attached by your server ([AI](/docs/backend/ai)).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/avatars.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class AvatarsService {
  /** Stores the picture as the user's: it goes when they are deleted. */
  async save(userId: string, png: Blob): Promise<string> {
    const path = `${userId}/avatar.png`;
    await Palbase.storage.putObject({
      path: { bucket: "avatars", path },
      query: { owner_id: userId },
      body: png,
      contentType: "image/png",
    });
    return path;
  }

  /** A link that reads the object for ten minutes, by anyone holding it. */
  async link(path: string): Promise<string> {
    const signed = await Palbase.storage.createSignedUrl({ path: { bucket: "avatars" }, body: { path, expires_in: 600 } });
    return signed.data.url;
  }
}
```

## Buckets

A bucket is declared, and declaring it again makes it so. `PUT /storage/buckets/{bucket}` creates the bucket or changes it to what the body says:

| Field | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `public` | `false` | Anyone may read its objects at `/storage/public/{bucket}/{path}`, with no credential. |
| `file_size_limit` | the platform's, 5 GiB | The largest object it takes, in bytes. |
| `allowed_mime_types` | any | The content types it takes; `image/*` names a family. 64 at most. |
| `variants` | none | The renditions made of every picture put in it (below); 16 at most. |

A bucket's name is a lowercase letter, then lowercase letters, digits and `-`, 2 to 63 characters.

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/buckets.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class BucketsService {
  // A provider's onStart() runs at boot, before the app serves: the bucket
  // is as this code says on every machine that runs it.
  async onStart(): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.storage.putBucket({
      path: { bucket: "avatars" },
      body: {
        public: true,
        file_size_limit: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
        allowed_mime_types: ["image/*"],
        variants: [
          { name: "thumb", width: 128, height: 128, fit: "cover", format: "webp", quality: 80 },
          { name: "large", width: 1024, height: 0, fit: "inside", format: "jpeg", quality: 0 },
        ],
      },
    });
  }
}
```

The write carries an `Idempotency-Key` the client makes, so its own retry never declares twice; a declaration a renderer cannot honour is refused here (`400`), not at the first upload. `GET /storage/buckets` lists the project's buckets, `GET /storage/buckets/{bucket}` reads one, and `DELETE /storage/buckets/{bucket}` deletes an **empty** bucket — one that still holds objects is refused with `409 bucket_not_empty`, so no file goes by surprise.

Studio's **Storage › Buckets** screen lists the buckets, deletes them, and uploads and deletes files in one.

## Writing an object

`putObject` stores its body at the path, replacing what is there.

```ts
// src/modules/reports/reports.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class ReportsService {
  async publish(month: string, csv: string) {
    const written = await Palbase.storage.putObject({
      path: { bucket: "reports", path: `monthly/${month}.csv` },
      headers: { "If-None-Match": "*" }, // create only: an object already there is 412
      body: csv,
      contentType: "text/csv",
    });
    return written.data; // the StorageObject: path, size, content_type, checksum_sha256 …
  }
}
```

- **Its type is sniffed from the bytes**, not taken from `contentType`, which is used only when the bytes cannot tell (HEIC, say). The bucket's ceiling and its types are enforced while the bytes stream in (`413 payload_too_large`, `415 unsupported_media_type`).
- **`owner_id`** makes the object a user's: it is deleted when they are.
- **`If-None-Match: *`** creates only (`412 object_exists`); **`X-Checksum-Sha256`** (hex) refuses bytes that do not match (`400 checksum_mismatch`), keeping nothing.
- **A picture** gets its `width`, `height`, a `thumbhash` placeholder and the bucket's renditions, made inside the upload — the object answered is complete.
- **It emits `file.uploaded`** to the project's webhook ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)).

A route of a `palbase/backend` app reads its body as JSON, a megabyte by default, so a client's file does not come through your backend to get here: the client PUTs it straight to storage at a URL your backend signed. See [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads).

### What an object looks like

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `bucket`, `path` | Where it is. |
| `size`, `content_type` | Its bytes and the type they were sniffed as. |
| `checksum_sha256` | The bytes' sha256, hex. |
| `owner_id` | The user it belongs to, if any. |
| `width`, `height`, `thumbhash` | A picture's dimensions and placeholder. |
| `variants` | Its renditions, by name: each with its `content_type` and `size`. |
| `created_at`, `updated_at` | When an object was first stored at the path, and when its bytes or path last changed. |

## Reading an object

`getObject` answers the bytes as the `Response` itself, so a large file is never read into memory unless you do so:

```ts
// src/modules/reports/download.service.ts
import { Injectable, NotFound, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class DownloadService {
  async text(path: string): Promise<string> {
    const reply = await Palbase.storage.getObject({ path: { bucket: "reports", path } });
    if (reply.status === 304 || !reply.data) throw new NotFound(`no report at ${path}`);
    return reply.data.text();
  }

  async thumbnail(path: string): Promise<ArrayBuffer> {
    const reply = await Palbase.storage.getObject({ path: { bucket: "avatars", path }, query: { variant: "thumb" } });
    if (reply.status === 304 || !reply.data) throw new NotFound(`no avatar at ${path}`);
    return reply.data.arrayBuffer();
  }
}
```

A missing object is a `404` refusal (a `PalbaseError`). `Range` (one byte range, answered `206`) and `If-None-Match` (answered `304`, with no body) are honoured, and `headObject` reads the headers without the bytes. A read with the secret key names the object's owner in `X-Owner-Id`; a public or signed URL never does. What is served is made inert — `nosniff`, a sandboxing CSP, and a download for any type a browser does not render safely — and every read that reaches storage counts toward the project's egress ([The CDN](#the-cdn)).

## Three ways a client reads a file

| URL | Who may read it | Made by |
|---|---|---|
| `https://<ref>.palbase.studio/storage/public/{bucket}/{path}` | Anyone, with no credential — an `<img src>`, a CDN. A private bucket's object is `403`. | Nothing to make: the bucket is `public`. |
| `https://cdn.palbase.studio/<ref>/signed/{bucket}/{path}?…&sig=…` | Anyone holding the URL, until it expires (7 days at most). | `createSignedUrl` |
| `GET /storage/buckets/{bucket}/objects/{path}` | Your backend, with the secret key. | — |

The `{path}` in a URL is **one** percent-encoded segment: `a/b.jpg` is `a%2Fb.jpg`. `?variant=thumb` reads a rendition on all three.

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/urls.ts
const PROJECT = "https://<ref>.palbase.studio";

/** A public bucket's object, as an <img src> takes it. */
export function publicUrl(bucket: string, path: string, variant?: string): string {
  // The path is ONE segment: a/b.jpg goes as a%2Fb.jpg.
  const [b, p] = [encodeURIComponent(bucket), encodeURIComponent(path)];
  const url = new URL(`/storage/public/${b}/${p}`, PROJECT);
  if (variant) url.searchParams.set("variant", variant);
  return url.toString();
}
```

A signed URL is absolute, at the CDN's address under the project's ref, and opens nothing of another project's. Every parameter of it is covered by its signature: a URL changed by one character, expired, or naming another object is `403`. The object must exist when the URL is signed, and the URL names its bytes as they were: one signed after the object changed is another URL. A public object is read the same way at `https://cdn.palbase.studio/<ref>/public/{bucket}/{path}`.

## The CDN

`cdn.palbase.studio` is served by Cloudflare: a file read there is kept near whoever reads it, and the next read of it near them is answered from that copy without reaching your project.

- **A minute at most.** A public object is kept 60 seconds (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`), browsers included; a signed URL's object 60 seconds or until the URL expires, whichever comes first. A file deleted or replaced is gone from every copy within a minute. A refusal — `403`, `404` — is never kept.
- **Pictures and files, not video.** A video, or a file larger than 25 MiB, is not kept: the CDN's address answers `302` with the same path and query at the project's own address (`https://<ref>.palbase.studio/storage/…`), and it is read there. A client following redirects, as browsers and every SDK do, sees nothing of it.
- **No credential.** The CDN's address reads public and signed files alone — `GET` and `HEAD` — and no key or token sent there is read: what is kept is what anyone holding the URL is given.
- **Counted when it reaches storage.** A read answered from the CDN's copy is not your project's traffic: it is not counted, nor slowed. One that reaches storage is, as at the project's own address.

The project's own address answers the same reads (`/storage/public/…`, `/storage/signed/…`), without the CDN in front.

## Image renditions

A bucket's `variants` are made from every picture put in it, inside the upload, and kept beside the original:

| Field | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | a lowercase letter, then lowercase letters, digits and `_` (32 at most) | — |
| `width`, `height` | pixels; `0` derives one from the other and the picture's aspect | — |
| `fit` | `cover` fills the box and crops; `contain` and `inside` keep the whole picture inside it (`inside` never enlarges) | `contain` |
| `format` | `jpeg`, `png`, `webp` | `jpeg` |
| `quality` | 1 to 100 for jpeg and webp; `0` is the format's default | `0` |

A rendition is read by its name (`?variant=`), and served whole — a byte range applies to the original only. A copy carries the original's renditions with it.

## Listing, copying, moving, deleting

```ts
// src/modules/reports/archive.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";
import { pages } from "palbase/server";

@Injectable()
export class ArchiveService {
  /** Every report of a year, newest first, a page at a time. */
  async year(year: string): Promise<string[]> {
    const paths: string[] = [];
    for await (const page of pages((cursor) =>
      Palbase.storage.listObjects({ path: { bucket: "reports" }, query: { prefix: `monthly/${year}-`, limit: 1000, cursor } }),
    )) {
      paths.push(...page.objects.map((o) => o.path));
    }
    return paths;
  }

  async retire(path: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.storage.moveObject({ path: { bucket: "reports" }, body: { from: path, to: `retired/${path}` } });
  }

  async duplicate(path: string, to: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.storage.copyObject({ path: { bucket: "reports" }, body: { from: path, to, overwrite: true } });
  }

  async remove(path: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.storage.deleteObject({ path: { bucket: "reports", path } });
  }
}
```

- **A move** gives the object a new path and copies no byte; **a copy** writes a new object with the original's bytes and renditions. Either refuses an object already at `to` (`409 object_exists`) unless `overwrite`.
- **A delete** removes the object and its renditions; the bytes are swept from the store after.
- They emit `file.moved`, `file.uploaded` and `file.deleted`.

## Reacting to storage events

Every write emits an event — `file.uploaded`, `file.deleted`, `file.moved` — with `{ bucket, path, size, content_type, owner_id }`. A `palbase/backend` app handles them with `@On("file.uploaded")` ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)); any other server verifies the delivery with `palbase/server` ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)).

## The `Storage` service

A backend reaches a bucket with `Storage`: `Storage.buckets.<name>` for a bucket the project holds (its renditions in the type), `Storage.bucket(name)` for a name made while it runs. Each call answers `{ data, error, status }` and never throws for the platform's sake: a refusal is its `error` (`{ code, message }`), and a platform that could not be reached is `status: 0`.

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `upload(path, file, { contentType?, upsert? })` | Writes the object. Without `upsert` it only creates: an object already there is `409 already_exists`. |
| `download(path)` | The object's bytes, as a `Blob` |
| `getPublicUrl(path, { variant? })` | Its URL at the project's address — a public bucket's objects are read there by anyone; no call is made |
| `createSignedUrl(path, { expiresIn })` | A URL that reads it until it expires: `"90s"`, `"15m"`, `"1h"`, `"7d"`, a week at most |
| `list(prefix?, { limit?, offset? })` | Its objects whose path starts with `prefix`, newest first (100 when no `limit`) |
| `remove(paths)` | Deletes each, in order; the first refusal ends it |
| `move(from, to)`, `copy(from, to)` | Within the bucket |

```ts
// palbase/palbase-env.d.ts
declare module "palbase/backend/stack" {
  interface Buckets {
    avatars: { variants: "thumb" | "card" };
  }
}

export {};
```

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/avatar-urls.service.ts
import { Injectable, Storage } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class AvatarUrls {
  async save(userId: string, png: Blob): Promise<{ full: string; thumb: string } | null> {
    const path = `${userId}/avatar.png`;
    const { error } = await Storage.buckets.avatars.upload(path, png, { contentType: "image/png", upsert: true });
    if (error) return null;
    return { full: Storage.buckets.avatars.getPublicUrl(path), thumb: Storage.buckets.avatars.getPublicUrl(path, { variant: "thumb" }) };
  }
}
```

## From the CLI

```sh
palbase storage:buckets:set avatars --public --max-size 5MB --types image/*
palbase storage:buckets:list
palbase storage:cp ./avatar.png avatars:users/42/avatar.png   # up; bucket:path names an object
palbase storage:cp avatars:users/42 ./backup -r                # down, every object under the prefix
palbase storage:ls avatars:users/
palbase storage:url documents:invoices/7.pdf --expires 600      # a signed download URL
palbase storage:rm avatars:tmp/ -r
```

What `storage:buckets:set` is not given stays as it was; a new bucket is private, takes any type and has no renditions until `--variants-file` gives them. `storage:buckets:delete` removes an empty bucket only. See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#storage).


- [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads) — signed upload URLs, and the client's `PUT`
- [Web Uploads](/docs/web/uploads) — the browser's side of an upload URL
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals, retries and paging
- [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks) — `@On("file.uploaded")` in your backend

# Direct Uploads

A file a user uploads goes from their device **straight to storage**, never through your backend. Your backend decides what may be uploaded — which bucket and path, how large, of which types, belonging to whom — in one of two ways:

- **A signed upload URL.** Your backend signs a URL that grants exactly that, and the client `PUT`s the bytes to it. The signature is the credential: the client needs no key, and the URL opens one object, once its conditions hold, until it expires. This page's quick example.
- **An upload route.** A route declared with `@Upload` takes the file in the client's call: storage asks the route where the file goes before it writes a byte, and runs the route's handler once the file is stored. See [Upload routes](#upload-routes).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/dto.ts
import { z } from "palbase/backend";

export const UploadRequest = z.object({ contentType: z.enum(["image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/webp"]) });
export type UploadRequest = z.infer<typeof UploadRequest>;

export interface UploadGrant {
  url: string;
  expiresAt: string;
  path: string;
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/avatars/avatars.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Palbase, Post, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { UploadRequest, type UploadGrant } from "./dto";

@Controller("/avatars")
export class AvatarsController {
  // The user asks; the backend decides the path, the ceiling and the owner.
  @Post("/upload-url", { rateLimit: { max: 10, window: 60 } })
  async uploadUrl(@Body(UploadRequest) body: UploadRequest, @User() user: UserT): Promise<UploadGrant> {
    const ext = body.contentType.split("/")[1];
    const path = `${user.id}/avatar-${Date.now()}.${ext}`;
    const signed = await Palbase.storage.createUploadUrl({
      path: { bucket: "avatars" },
      body: { path, expires_in: 300, max_bytes: 2 * 1024 * 1024, owner_id: user.id },
    });
    return { url: signed.data.url, expiresAt: signed.data.expires_at, path };
  }
}
```

The client then sends the file to that URL:

```ts
// upload.ts
export async function upload(grant: { url: string }, file: Blob): Promise<void> {
  const res = await fetch(grant.url, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "content-type": file.type, "if-none-match": "*" },
    body: file,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`the upload was refused: ${res.status}`);
}
```

## The flow

1. **The client asks your backend** for a grant — a route of your own, with whatever the upload needs to say (the kind of file, which record it belongs to).
2. **Your backend signs it** with `POST /storage/buckets/{bucket}/upload-urls` (`Palbase.storage.createUploadUrl`) and answers the URL.
3. **The client `PUT`s the bytes** to the URL — `PUT /storage/signed/{bucket}/{path}`, with the signature in its query.
4. **Storage checks the grant while the bytes stream**, stores the object, answers it (`200`, or `201` for a new one), and emits `file.uploaded`.

Your backend is not on the upload's path, so it learns of the upload from the event: an `@On("file.uploaded")` handler ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)), or a route the client calls once its `PUT` is answered.

## What the URL grants

`createUploadUrl` takes:

| Field | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `path` | The object's path, chosen by your backend, never by the client. |
| `expires_in` | Seconds the URL works: 1 to 604800 (7 days). |
| `max_bytes` | A ceiling below the bucket's own `file_size_limit`. |
| `owner_id` | The user the object will belong to; it is deleted with them. |

The bucket's `allowed_mime_types` are pinned too. It answers `{ url, expires_at }`: an absolute URL at the project's own address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio/storage/signed/{bucket}/{path}?…`. Every one of its query parameters — the bucket, the path, the expiry, the ceiling, the types, the owner — is covered by its signature, so a client that edits one holds a URL that opens nothing.

## The `PUT`

| Header | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | Used only when the bytes cannot say what they are (HEIC): the type is sniffed from the bytes. |
| `If-None-Match: *` | Create only: an object already at the path is refused with `412`. |
| `X-Checksum-Sha256` | The bytes' sha256, hex: bytes that do not match are refused, and nothing is kept. |

| Answer | Why |
|---|---|
| `200` / `201` | Stored — the object, as JSON: `path`, `size`, `content_type`, `width`, `height`, `thumbhash`, `variants`. |
| `400 checksum_mismatch` | The bytes do not have the sha256 `X-Checksum-Sha256` named. |
| `403` | The signature is wrong, expired, another project's, or a download signature. |
| `412 object_exists` | `If-None-Match: *` and an object is already there. |
| `413 payload_too_large` | Larger than the URL's ceiling or the bucket's. |
| `415 unsupported_media_type` | A type the bucket, or the URL, does not take. |
| `422 unreadable_picture` | A picture the bucket's renditions cannot be made from: truncated, or a format storage does not read. |
| `429 quota_exceeded` | The project's storage for the period is used up under its quota (with `Retry-After`). |

A picture's renditions are made inside the upload, so the object the `PUT` answers already carries them.

> **Note:** A browser page on any site can make this `PUT`: it is preflighted, and the project's address answers the preflight. See [Web Uploads](/docs/web/uploads) for the browser.

## Upload routes

An upload route is one method that both decides where a file goes and runs once it is there. The client sends the file with the route's input in one call to the project's storage; storage asks your machine whether this caller may upload and where to, writes the bytes under the bucket's rules, then hands the route's handler the stored object. What the handler answers is the client's answer. Nothing is signed, the client makes no second call to say it is done, and the bytes still never pass through your machine.

```ts
// src/modules/profile/profile.controller.ts
import { Controller, PalError, Upload, UploadedObject, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

interface Avatar {
  owner: string;
  path: string;
  size: number;
  contentType: string;
  thumbhash?: string;
}

@Controller("/profile")
export class ProfileController {
  // Into the avatars bucket, under a folder of the user's: the client never names the path.
  @Upload("/avatar", { bucket: "avatars", pathTemplate: "{userId}/{uploadId}-{filename}", rateLimit: { max: 10, window: 60 } })
  avatar(@UploadedObject() file: UploadedObject, @User() user: UserT): Avatar {
    // Runs once the file is stored. A refusal thrown here deletes it.
    if ((file.width ?? 0) < 128) throw new PalError(422, "picture_too_small", "An avatar is 128 pixels wide at least");
    return { owner: user.id, path: file.path, size: file.size, contentType: file.contentType, thumbhash: file.thumbhash };
  }
}
```

The client calls it through the module `palbase apps:sync` writes, the file after the route's input: `pb.backend.profile.avatar(file, { onProgress })` in a browser ([Web Uploads](/docs/web/uploads#an-upload-route)).

`@Upload(subpath, options)` is a `POST` route of its controller, and takes:

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| `bucket` | The bucket its files go to: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, 2 to 63 long. Its rules (the largest file, the types it takes, its renditions) hold every upload as storage writes it. |
| `pathTemplate` | The path each file is stored under, made for each upload from the tokens below. Segments separated by `/`, none empty, `.` or `..`, no control character, 1024 bytes at most. |
| `auth` | Who may upload, as any route's `auth`: a signed-in user unless `auth: false`. |
| `rateLimit` | How many uploads a caller may start per window, as any route's `rateLimit`. Spent as an upload is asked for, before a byte is written. |

| Token | What it becomes |
|---|---|
| `{userId}` | The signed-in user's id; `anonymous` for no one, on a route with `auth: false`. |
| `{uploadId}` | The upload's own id, made by storage: `file.uploadId` in the handler. |
| `{filename}` | The name the client gave its file, made one path segment: control and invisible characters dropped, `/` and `\` a dash, a run of dots one dot, no leading dot or space, 200 characters at most; `file` when it gave none. |

A template that names another token, or is no path storage keeps, stops the app as it starts. Storage writes an upload's object only where none is: put `{uploadId}` in the template, or a second upload to the same path is refused `412 object_exists`.

The handler takes the stored object with `@UploadedObject()`, and what any route takes: the input the client sent beside the file with `@Body(schema)`, the caller with `@User()` or `@OptionalUser()`, `@Param` and `@QueryParams`. It runs as the caller does, their row-level security included. The caller is the one storage names, their id and session, not their token: an upload route cannot ask for a verified email, and `@Headers()`, `@Req()` and `@Client()` stop the app as it starts, because storage forwards none of the client's headers. A method is an upload route or another route, never both.

| `@UploadedObject()` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `uploadId` | The upload's id, the same as in its path. |
| `bucket`, `path` | Where it was stored, as `pathTemplate` made it. |
| `size` | Bytes, as storage counted them. |
| `contentType` | The type storage found in the bytes, not the file's name or what the client claimed. |
| `checksum` | The stored bytes' SHA-256, hex. |
| `width`, `height`, `thumbhash` | A picture's size in pixels, and its placeholder (ThumbHash). Absent for anything else. |
| `variants` | The renditions the bucket declares, by name, each its address: a public bucket's. None for a private bucket. |

### What storage does

1. **The client's call.** `POST /storage/upload/<machine>/<route>` at the project's address, with the publishable key and the user's token when someone is signed in. `<route>` is the route's path as one percent-encoded segment (`profile%2Favatar`), and the request's query is the route's. The body is `multipart/form-data`: a JSON `body` part of 1 MiB at most (the route's input), then the `file`.
2. **The machine authorizes it**, within 30 seconds. The route's `auth` and `rateLimit` are held as a request of the caller's would meet them, its `@Resolve` parameters and guards run, its query and the `body` are checked against their schemas, and `pathTemplate` is made into the path. A refusal is the client's answer, as the app gave it, and no byte is written.
3. **Storage writes the bytes** to the bucket under its rules, and measures them: size, checksum, the type the bytes are, a picture's size, placeholder and renditions. The object belongs to the signed-in user, and is deleted with them.
4. **The handler runs** with the stored object, within two minutes. Its answer (`200` with JSON, `204`, a `Response` it built, a refusal) is relayed to the client as it gave it. A refusal, or no answer in two minutes, deletes the object. A kept one is told as `file.uploaded` ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)).

What the client can be answered besides the route's own:

| Status | Why |
|---|---|
| `400` | Not an upload: not multipart, no `file` part, a `body` that is not JSON or is over 1 MiB, a route or machine name that is none; or a file name that makes the path longer than storage keeps. |
| `401` | The route needs a signed-in user, and no one is. |
| `404` | No such machine, no upload route at that path, or the bucket the route names is none. |
| `412 object_exists` | An object is already at the path the template made. |
| `413` | Larger than the bucket takes. |
| `415` | A type the bucket does not take. |
| `429` | The route's `rateLimit` for this caller (`Retry-After`), the project's storage used up under its quota, or its machine calls all under way. |
| `502` | The app did not answer, or its authorize named no bucket and path an object can have. |
| `503` | The machine is waking or building. Sending again is safe. |

## Why the backend asks first

There is no client-side object API: the publishable key opens nothing in storage, so a client cannot write a file anywhere your code did not name. Putting the decision in your backend gives it the whole say:

- **The path is yours.** A user cannot overwrite another's file, because they never choose the path.
- **The size and type are yours,** per upload, below the bucket's.
- **The owner is yours.** `owner_id` ties the object to the user it is for, and deleting the user deletes it.
- **The rate is yours.** The grant is a route of your own: `rateLimit` on it holds how often a user may upload.

## Uploading from your backend

When the bytes are already on your server — a generated report, a file fetched from elsewhere — write them with `putObject` and skip the URL: see [Storage](/docs/backend/storage).

## Related

- [Storage](/docs/backend/storage) — buckets, objects, renditions and signed download URLs
- [Web Uploads](/docs/web/uploads) — the browser's side, for a signed URL and for an upload route
- [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks) — acting on `file.uploaded`
- [Controllers & Routing](/docs/backend/controllers) — the grant's route and its `rateLimit`

# Secrets

A project keeps its application secrets — a payment provider's key, a signing secret, the project's own secret key for its backend — in its **secrets**, sealed with the project's own key, versioned, and audited on every read and write. They are kept in two sets, `production` and `development`. A machine is started with one set: every secret in it is in the machine's environment by name, so your code reads `process.env.STRIPE_KEY` and nothing else. A program that wants a value while it runs — or one that is not a machine — reads it with the secret key through the secrets module, `Palbase.secrets`.

## Quick example

In Studio, open the environment's **Secrets** screen and add `STRIPE_KEY`. In the machine's settings (**Backend › Machines › the machine › Edit settings**), choose the set its **Secrets** start with. The machine rolls out with the value, and the code reads it:

```ts
// src/modules/billing/billing.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class BillingService {
  // Read once, at boot: a secret that changes rolls the machine out with the new value.
  private readonly stripeKey = required("STRIPE_KEY");

  authorization(): string {
    return `Bearer ${this.stripeKey}`;
  }
}

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is not set: add it to the project's secrets and start the machine with them`);
  return value;
}
```

## The two sets

| Set | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `production` | What the machines that serve your users start with. |
| `development` | A second set, for machines and programs that must not see production's values. |

A machine names the set it starts with (`secrets`: `production`, `development`, or none) — in Studio on the machine's settings, or through the machines module (`PATCH /machines/{name}`). Studio's **Secrets** screen manages the set the environment's machines start with: `production` when none names one yet, and it refuses to choose for you when machines start with different sets.

## How a machine reads them

- **By name, in its environment.** Each secret of the set is an environment variable of the machine. A name the machine's own `env` also sets wins over the secret — keep a value in one place.
- **A change rolls the machine out.** Writing, rolling back or deleting a secret of the set starts the machine's new version with the new values beside the version that serves; nothing restarts in place, and no request meets a gap.
- **A build can wait for them.** A machine's `.env.example` names what it needs: a build whose names the machine's env and secrets do not hold waits (`waiting_config`, with `missing_env`) and rolls out once they are there. See [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds).

A `palbase/backend` app on a machine needs none of its own keys here: the platform starts every machine with its own secret key (`PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, listed under **Settings › API keys** as `machine: <name>`) and its webhook secret (`PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), beside `PALBASE_URL` and `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID`. A secret of the same name set by hand gives way to them. A value missing or malformed stops the boot, naming it.

## Names and sizes

| Rule | Limit |
|---|---|
| Name | An environment-variable name: `A-Z`, `0-9` and `_`, starting with a letter, 128 characters at most. |
| Value | 64 KiB. |
| Secrets per set | 1000. |

## Reading a value while it runs

`Palbase.secrets` (or `createServer(…).secrets`) reads and writes the secrets with the project's secret key:

```ts
// src/modules/billing/rotation.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class RotationService {
  /** The current value, read now rather than at boot. */
  async current(name: string): Promise<string> {
    return (await Palbase.secrets.getSecret({ path: { environment: "production", name } })).data.value;
  }

  /** Every value of the set, in one call: what a program outside a machine reads at startup. */
  async all(): Promise<Record<string, string>> {
    return (await Palbase.secrets.getEnvironmentValues({ path: { environment: "production" } })).data.values;
  }
}
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `listSecrets({ path: { environment } })` | The set's secrets by name, with their version — never their values. |
| `getSecret({ path: { environment, name } })` | One secret's current value and version. |
| `getEnvironmentValues({ path: { environment } })` | Every value of the set, and every version, in one call. |
| `putSecret({ path: { environment, name }, body: { value } })` | Writes the value as the secret's next version, creating it if it is new. |
| `listSecretVersions({ path: { environment, name } })` | Its versions, newest first, with the key that wrote each — never their values. |
| `rollbackSecret({ path: { environment, name }, body: { version } })` | Makes an earlier version's value the next version; the history stays whole. |
| `deleteSecret({ path: { environment, name } })` | Forgets the secret and every version of it. |
| `listSecretAudit({ query: { environment?, name? } })` | Every read and write, newest first, with the key that made it and the request id. |

Every write is a new version, so a rotation that goes wrong is a rollback away. A write, a rollback and a delete each emit `secret.changed` — the set, the name, the version and the change, **never the value** — to the project's webhook, so a receiver learns what changed and reads it with its own key ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)).

## Who can read them

Only the secret key. A publishable key ships in apps and is refused by every secrets route; a user's token opens none of them. Every read — a list, one value, the whole set — is in the audit trail with the id of the key that made it, which is one more reason to give each server its own secret key: the audit then says which one read what, and revoking one shuts out only that server.

## The `Secrets` service

A backend reads a secret with `await Secrets.get("NAME")`: the value or `null`. It reads the machine's environment — the set the machine starts with — so a changed secret arrives with the machine rolled out again. A name the platform puts there itself (`PALBASE_URL`, `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, `PALBASE_DB_URL` …) is not the project's secret, and answers `null`.

The names it takes are the ones the project holds: the CLI's `types:pull` writes them into `palbase/palbase-env.d.ts`, and a name the project does not hold does not compile.

```ts
// palbase/palbase-env.d.ts
declare module "palbase/backend/stack" {
  interface Secrets {
    STRIPE_KEY: true;
  }
}

export {};
```

```ts
// src/modules/billing/stripe-key.service.ts
import { Injectable, Secrets } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class StripeKey {
  async get(): Promise<string> {
    const key = await Secrets.get("STRIPE_KEY");
    if (!key) throw new Error("STRIPE_KEY is not among the secrets this machine started with");
    return key;
  }
}
```

## From the CLI

```sh
printf %s "$STRIPE_KEY" | palbase secrets:set STRIPE_KEY   # production: the value is read from stdin
printf %s "sk_test_…" | palbase secrets:set STRIPE_KEY --dev
palbase secrets:list                                       # names and versions, never values
palbase secrets:versions STRIPE_KEY
palbase secrets:rollback STRIPE_KEY --version 3            # a new version with version 3's value
palbase secrets:audit --name STRIPE_KEY                    # who read and wrote it, and when
```

`--dev` acts on the development set — what a backend run on your computer with `palbase run` or `palbase env:pull` reads — and its absence on production. A value is never taken from the command line, where the shell's history would keep it. `palbase secrets:get <NAME>` prints one value, for an admin; `palbase secrets:unset <NAME>` takes a secret away. Every command is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#secrets).

## Related

- [Machines](/docs/machines/overview) — a machine's environment, and the secret set it starts with
- [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds) — `.env.example`, and a build that waits for its settings
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — the secret key and `createServer`
- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks) — `secret.changed`



<!-- ===== backend/flags ===== -->

# Flags

Every project has feature flags and remote configuration: typed values, targeted by conditions, given to single users, read by its apps and kept up to date in them as they change. Apps **read** flags with the publishable key ([Web Flags](/docs/web/flags)). Your backend **defines** them, gives users their own values, and reads what any user would see — with the secret key: `Palbase.flags` in a `palbase/backend` app, `createServer(…).flags` anywhere else.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/checkout/checkout.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class CheckoutService {
  /** Turns the new checkout on for one user — a beta tester, a support case. */
  async enableNewFlow(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.flags.putUserValue({ path: { user_id: userId, key: "checkout.new_flow" }, body: { value: true } });
  }

  /** What that user's app reads for the flag now. */
  async newFlowFor(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const { data } = await Palbase.flags.getUserValues({ path: { user_id: userId } });
    return data.values["checkout.new_flow"] === true;
  }
}
```

## How a value is resolved

For each flag, a reader gets, in order:

1. **its own value**, if the user has one (`source: "override"`);
2. else the value of the **first condition that matches**;
3. else the flag's **default**.

A reader with no signed-in user has no values of its own and no percentile, so only the conditions that need neither can match it.

## Defining a flag

`PUT /flags/system/{key}` (`putDefinition`) defines a flag, or changes one:

```ts
// src/modules/checkout/flags.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class FlagsService {
  async onStart(): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.flags.putDefinition({
      path: { key: "checkout.new_flow" },
      body: {
        value_type: "bool",
        value: false,
        description: "The one-page checkout",
        conditions: [
          { when: "client.platform == 'ios' && client.app_version >= '2.10.0'", value: true },
          { when: "percentile <= 10", value: true },
        ],
      },
    });
    await Palbase.flags.putDefinition({
      path: { key: "home.theme" },
      body: { value_type: "string", value: "light", variants: ["light", "dark", "contrast"] },
    });
  }
}
```

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `value_type` | `bool`, `number`, `string` or `object`. |
| `value` | The default (8 KB at most). |
| `variants` | A string flag's allowed choices: every value — the default, a condition's, a user's — is one of them. |
| `conditions` | Targeting, in order, first match wins; 8 at most, each `{ when, value }`. |
| `description` | What the flag is for. |

A key is dot-separated segments, each a letter then letters, digits and underscores, 128 characters at most. A project defines **200 flags** at most. A write that would change the type under users' values, or leave a user's value outside the choices, is refused; so is a direct write while publishing is on (below). `listDefinitions`, `getDefinition` and `deleteDefinition` read and remove them; deleting a flag removes every user's value of it. Every reader is told of a change at once.

Studio's **Feature flags** screens edit the same definitions and users' values.

### Conditions

A condition's `when` is a small expression language: comparisons over a fixed set of variables, combined with `&&`, `||` and parentheses — no functions, no arithmetic. 512 characters and 16 comparisons at most.

| Variable | Where it comes from | Compared as |
|---|---|---|
| `client.platform` | the `X-Platform` header the app sends | a string |
| `client.locale` | the first language of `Accept-Language` | a string |
| `client.app_version` | `X-Palbase-Client-Version` | a version (`'2.10.0'` is above `'2.9.0'`) |
| `client.os_version` | `X-OS-Version` | a version |
| `percentile` | the signed-in user, hashed with the flag's key: 1 to 100 | a number |
| `server.country` | the country of the address the edge saw | a string (`'TR'`) |
| `server.now` | the server's clock | a time (`'2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'`) |

Operators: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `in ['ios', 'android']`, and for strings `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `contains`.

- **A variable outside the table** (`client.foo`) is refused when the flag is written — it could never match.
- **A variable the client did not send** does not match, and the flag falls back to its default.
- **`client.*` is what the client says.** Anyone can send any header, so a `client.*` condition chooses an experience, never access.
- **`percentile` is per flag:** `percentile <= 10` is a different tenth of users for each flag, so one unlucky user is not outside every experiment. It needs a signed-in user.
- **An unresolved country matches nothing**, `!=` included: "not Turkey" is never true of a caller whose country is unknown.
- **`server.now`** cannot be moved by a client's clock, which is what makes a scheduled change real.

## Users' own values

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `putUserValue({ path: { user_id, key }, body: { value } })` | Gives one user their own value for one flag. |
| `putUserValues({ path: { user_id }, body: { values } })` | Many flags for one user (1000 at most). |
| `batchUserValues({ body: { operations: [{ user_id, values }] } })` | Many users at once, 1000 operations at most: all of them, or none. |
| `deleteUserValue({ path: { user_id, key } })` | Removes one; the answer is what resolves for them now. |
| `deleteUserValues({ path: { user_id } })` | Removes all of theirs; their flags resolve as anyone's again. |

Each value is checked against the flag's type and choices. The user's apps are told at once, on the user's own channel (`flags:<ref>:<user_id>`); everyone's are told of a definition change on `flags:<ref>`. The web SDK side of that is in [Web Flags](/docs/web/flags).

## Reading as a user

```ts
// src/modules/checkout/preview.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class PreviewService {
  /** What an iOS 2.10 user would read — the conditions see this request's headers as the client's. */
  async asIosUser(userId: string): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
    const { data } = await Palbase.flags.getUserValues({
      path: { user_id: userId },
      headers: { "X-Platform": "ios", "X-Palbase-Client-Version": "2.10.0" },
    });
    return data.values;
  }
}
```

`getUserValues` resolves every flag for one user, as their client would read it: their own values and their percentiles, with the client context taken from the call's headers. `getValues` with the secret key resolves for nobody in particular — the defaults and the conditions that need no user.

## Publishing

By default a definition changes the moment it is written. A project that wants changes reviewed turns **publishing** on, once and for good: the live flags become version 1, and from then on a definition changes only through a published draft — a direct `putDefinition` is refused with `409 publish_required`.

| Step | Call |
|---|---|
| Turn publishing on | `activateTemplates({ body: {} })` |
| Start the shared draft from the active version | `createTemplateDraft({ headers: { "If-Match": "flags-active-<version>" }, body: {} })` |
| Write or remove a parameter | `putTemplateParameter` / `removeTemplateParameter`, each with the draft's `If-Match` |
| See what publishing would do | `reviewTemplateDraft()` — each change, how many users' values it touches, and the issues that block it |
| Publish | `publishTemplate({ headers: { "If-Match": "<draft etag>", "Idempotency-Key": "<key>" }, body: { note } })` |
| Go back | `restoreTemplateVersion({ path: { version }, … })` starts a draft from an earlier version |

Every step names the revision it read (`If-Match`), so two people editing the one shared draft never overwrite each other. A draft with issues is refused with `409 template_validation_failed` and the issues. The same `Idempotency-Key` answers the first publication again, and `getPublishReceipt` reads a publication's answer back for a client that lost it.

## Palbase-managed flags

Flags under `palbase.` are the platform's: their type is fixed and they are not deleted.

## Which builds are in use

Apps' reads are counted by installation: `getCurrentInstallations()` answers the builds that read their flags in the last day, by platform and app version, and `getInstallationsDaily({ query: { days } })` the curve, kept 90 days.

## The `Flags` service

A backend reads flags with `Flags`, **for the request's user**: the signed-in caller a handler serves, or a gateway's member. Their own value comes first, then the flag's. `isEnabled` is a plain boolean — a flag that cannot be read is off, and why is logged — and the other reads answer `{ data, error, status }`. A context names another user (`{ userId }`), or nobody (`{ userId: null }`): the flag's own value.

| Call | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `isEnabled(key, context?)` | Whether its value is truthy |
| `get(key, default?, context?)` | Its value; the default stands in when it is absent or cannot be read |
| `getVariant(key, context?)` | `{ name }` of a string value |
| `getAll(context?)` | Every flag: `{ name, enabled, variant? }` |
| `setOverride(key, value)` | The request's user's own value (400 without one) |
| `$asService().setOverrideForUser(userId, key, value)` … | Any user's, by id: `setOverridesForUser`, `clearOverrideForUser`, `clearAllOverridesForUser`, `batchSetOverrides` |

```ts
// palbase/palbase-env.d.ts
declare module "palbase/backend/stack" {
  interface Flags {
    new_checkout: true;
  }
}

export {};
```

```ts
// src/modules/checkout/checkout-flow.controller.ts
import { Controller, Flags, Get } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/checkout")
export class CheckoutFlowController {
  @Get("/flow")
  async flow(): Promise<{ flow: "new" | "classic" }> {
    return { flow: (await Flags.isEnabled("new_checkout")) ? "new" : "classic" };
  }
}
```

## Related

- [Web Flags](/docs/web/flags) — reading flags in the browser, and their live updates
- [Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime) — the socket the updates travel on
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals and retries
