<!-- ===== backend/notifications ===== -->

# Notifications

Every project has notify: email, push, SMS and WhatsApp to its users, one-time codes by text, topics users follow, and each user's preferences about what they take. Your backend sends with the secret key — `Palbase.notify` in a `palbase/backend` app, `createServer(…).notify` anywhere else. Apps only register their own devices and set their own user's preferences and topics, with the publishable key and the user's token.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/orders/notify.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class OrderNotices {
  async shipped(userId: string, email: string, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    // Through the project's own email provider: a message composed whole.
    await Palbase.notify.sendEmail({
      body: { to: email, user_id: userId, subject: `Order ${orderId} has shipped`, text: "It is on its way." },
    });
    // To every device of the user's, through the project's own push account.
    await Palbase.notify.sendPush({
      body: { to: { user_ids: [userId] }, title: "Shipped", body: `Order ${orderId} is on its way`, deep_link: `myapp://orders/${orderId}` },
    });
  }
}
```

A send is **queued**, not delivered: it answers `202` with the message's id, and the message ends `sent` or `failed` later — each emits `notification.sent` or `notification.failed` to the project's webhook ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)).

**A sign-in code never waits for a campaign.** A topic's or an audience's push — a campaign — is sent in a lane of its own, and every other message in another: auth's codes and links first, then your other sends. However many pushes a campaign has queued, and however slowly its providers answer, a code — your project's own or another project's — is taken at once and sent in a slot no campaign holds. Two projects' campaigns at once go side by side, neither waiting for the other to end.

## Every channel but one needs a provider of yours

| Channel | Goes through |
|---|---|
| Email | The platform's **shared sender**, within the project's limits — for the platform's templates only (the auth emails: verify, reset, magic link, codes …, as the project overrode them). Anything else — a message composed whole, a template of your own — goes through **your own email provider**: Azure Communication Services, Amazon SES, SendGrid or SMTP. |
| Push | Your own FCM, APNs or Expo account — a browser's through its own push service, with the project's Web Push key (nothing to set up). |
| Inbox, in-app messages | Palbase itself: nothing to set up. |
| SMS | Your own SMS providers — Twilio, Vonage or Azure Communication Services — in failover order. |
| One-time codes | Your own verification service (Twilio Verify), or your SMS providers — and with neither, **Palbase's Twilio Verify**: nothing to set up, billed at Twilio's price and 10% past $4 a month (`notify.sms.shared`, [Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)). |
| WhatsApp | Your own WhatsApp Business account (Meta). |

An email the shared sender may not send is refused with `403 own_provider_required`; past the shared sender's limits a send is `429 send_limit_reached`. A project with an active email provider sends all its email through it.

Providers are set in Studio (**Notifications › Providers**) or with `putNotifyProvider({ path: { channel, provider }, body: { credentials, priority, active } })`: the credentials are sealed with the project's own key, checked as the sender will use them, and never answered back. `getDeliverability()` says, per channel, whether it can send now, through what, why not and what to do.

From the CLI, the credentials are piped in as JSON — never written on the command line, where the shell would keep them:

```sh
palbase notify:providers:set email sendgrid < sendgrid.json   # {"api_key": "…", "from_domain": "example.com"}
palbase notify:providers:set sms twilio --priority 1 < twilio.json
palbase notify:deliverability                                  # can each channel send now, and through what
palbase notify:send email ada@example.com --template welcome --var name=Ada
palbase notify:messages --limit 20                             # what was sent, and what became of it
```

**Apple (APNs).** The credential is a team-scoped APNs key — `{ "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----…", "team_id": "…", "key_id": "…" }`, the `.p8` from Apple's Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys with Apple Push Notifications service on — and one key serves every app of the team, in both of Apple's environments. As it is saved, notify asks Apple about it, with a token no device holds, for each iOS app registered in the environment: a key Apple refuses (another team's, a revoked one, one not allowed for the app) is refused with `400 invalid_credentials`, saying Apple's answer; Apple not answering is `502 apns_unreachable`, and nothing is saved.

```sh
palbase notify:providers:set push apns < apns.json   # {"private_key": "…", "team_id": "ABCDE12345", "key_id": "3PSQ7G27A3"}
```

With an [Apple ID signed in](/docs/distribution/app-store#keys-made-for-you), Palbase makes the APNs keys for you instead: one for production and one for the sandbox, each scoped to the environment's iOS apps, and notify takes them as its provider — `key_id` signs production's pushes, `sandbox_key_id` (with `sandbox_private_key`) the sandbox's, and `made_by` is `"palbase"`. A key you set yourself is never replaced so.

A push to an iOS device goes **to the bundle of the app it was registered from** — the app whose publishable key registered it ([Client Apps](/docs/apps/overview)) — and **through the APNs environment its token is for**, which the iOS SDK says: `sandbox` for an app run from Xcode or signed for development, `production` for TestFlight, the App Store and ad hoc. So one environment reaches the development build (`com.example.app.dev`, sandbox), its TestFlight build (`com.example.app.dev`, production) and the App Store app (`com.example.app`, production), each app registered in it with its own key. A device that did not say (an older SDK) is tried in production when the key says `is_production`, else sandbox, then — Apple calling the token bad — the other; a key made for one environment alone, asked in the other, is asked in its own. The environment that reached a device is kept. A device whose app is not known (registered before its app was) goes to the environment's one iOS app, or to the key's optional `bundle_id`. Each push's delivery says where it went: `route` — `production com.example.app`.

**A provider that stops working** — an APNs key revoked, one not allowed for an app — fails every push alike. notify keeps it failing (`GET /notify/providers`: `failing_since`, `last_error`), Studio's **Notifications › Providers** shows it, and the organization's owners get an email — at most one a day a provider — as `notification.push_failing` (`{ project_id, channel, provider, error, failing_since }`) goes to your webhook. A push to the app it failed for that goes through, or the provider saved anew, ends it: a key that reaches one of your apps and not another stays failing for the other.

Templates (`notify:templates:*`), topics (`notify:topics:*`) and the message settings (`notify:settings:*`) have their commands too; every one is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#notify).

## Email

```ts
// src/modules/accounts/welcome.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class WelcomeService {
  async send(userId: string, email: string, name: string, locale: string): Promise<string | undefined> {
    const queued = await Palbase.notify.sendEmail({
      body: {
        to: email,
        user_id: userId, // the user's preferences hold, and deleting them deletes the message
        template: "welcome", // a template of your own: your own provider
        variables: { name },
        locale,
        category: "news", // only users who did not turn "news" off get it
      },
    });
    return queued.data.skipped ? undefined : queued.data.message_id;
  }
}
```

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `to` | One address. |
| `template`, `variables` | A template and what fills it — or `subject` with `html` and/or `text` (own provider only). Without a text part, the html's text is sent as one. |
| `locale`, `locales` | The language to render in; `locales` are more it would take, most wanted first: each, then its language alone, then the project's default and English. |
| `category` | `transactional` (the default) reaches every user; any other — `marketing`, `news` — only users who did not turn it off on this channel. |
| `user_id` | The user the message is for. |
| `from`, `reply_to` | The send's own sender (own provider only). |
| `priority` | `high` is tried again sooner when it could not leave. |
| `metadata` | Your own data about the message (a JSON object, 4 KiB), kept with its report. |

A send that the user's preferences turn off answers `{ skipped: true }`: nothing was queued or counted.

### Templates

Templates are Handlebars — `{{name}}`, `{{#if}}`, `{{#each}}` …; in an HTML body `{{name}}` is escaped and `{{{name}}}` is not. `listEmailTemplates()` answers every template the project's email renders from — the platform's defaults and your overrides — with the variables each uses. `putEmailTemplate({ path: { slug, locale }, body: { subject, html_body, text_body } })` overrides one in a locale, and `deleteEmailTemplate` brings the default back. SMS templates work the same way (`putSmsTemplate`), and WhatsApp slugs map to templates approved on your Meta account (`putWhatsAppTemplate`). Studio's **Notifications › Templates** screen edits them.

## Push

```ts
// src/modules/chat/push.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class ChatPush {
  async newMessage(to: string[], from: string): Promise<void> {
    const queued = await Palbase.notify.sendPush({
      body: {
        to: { user_ids: to },
        // A text, or one per locale: each device gets the one in its language.
        title: { en: "New message", tr: "Yeni mesaj" },
        body: { en: "{{from}} wrote to you", tr: "{{from}} size yazdı" },
        variables: { from },
        category: "chat",
        data: { kind: "message" },
      },
    });
    console.log(`queued ${queued.data.message_ids.length}, skipped ${queued.data.skipped_user_ids.length}`);
  }
}
```

A push is one message per user, delivered to **every device of theirs** — an Expo token through Expo, a VoIP token through APNs, an iOS token through APNs if the project has it (else FCM), Android through FCM, a browser through its own push service (Web Push, below). `to: { topic }` sends one message to a topic's followers instead. Fields beyond the title and body: `data` (4 KiB for the app), `deep_link`, `image` (https), `badge`, `sound`, `silent`, `content_available`, `mutable_content`, `collapse_key`, `ttl`, `priority`, and `push_type: "voip"` for a call ring to `ios_voip` devices.

**Devices are the app's to register**, and the iOS and Android SDKs do it for you: `POST /notify/devices` with the token its push SDK gave it (`device_id`, `platform` — `android`, `ios`, `ios_voip` or `web` — `token`, the install's `installation_id`, and an iOS token's `apns_environment`: `sandbox` or `production`). With no one signed in, the publishable key alone registers it as the install's, proven with the install's secret (`X-Palbase-Installation-Secret`): a push that names the install — `to: { installation_ids }` — reaches it, so an app reaches people who never signed up. When someone signs in, their registration takes the device and it is theirs; signed out, the app registers it as the install's again. A user's device is the session's it was registered in: when the session ends — the user signed out or ended it from another device, its refresh token was revoked, an admin revoked it — the device is forgotten, and no push of theirs reaches it. A token another device held moves to this one. Your backend reads a user's devices (never their tokens) with `listUserDevices({ path: { user_id } })`. It forgets one with `deleteMyDevice({ path: { device_id } })` and the secret key — every registration of that device in the environment, whoever is signed in on it, no one included: a test device, a lost phone, an install no session will forget; from a terminal, `palbase notify:devices:list` finds it and `palbase notify:devices:delete <device_id>` forgets it.

**An app taken off a phone** shows when its next push goes: APNs answers `410`, FCM `UNREGISTERED`. The device is forgotten, and `notification.uninstalled` (`{ platform, provider, device_id, installation_id, user_id }`) goes into the person's timeline and to your webhook — the uninstall you can count and reach back for by other means.

**How a push went on each device** is the app's to say, and the SDKs say it: every push carries a sealed receipt (`pb_receipt` in its data), and the app reports with it, no sign-in needed (`POST /notify/receipts`): it reached the phone (`delivered` — on iOS from the app's Notification Service Extension, even with the app closed; on Android as the app draws the notification), it could not be shown (`not_shown`: the app's notifications or its channel are off), it was `opened`, `dismissed`, or a button tapped (`action`). A push no device reported on by the time it expired (its `ttl`, or the providers' four weeks) is `unconfirmed`: the phone may have been off, or its report lost — not "not delivered". Each stage reached for the first time is an event (`notification.delivered`, `notification.opened` …) in the person's timeline. On Android a push goes to FCM as data only (`pb_title`, `pb_body`, `pb_receipt` and your own keys), and the app's own messaging service draws it ([Android notifications](/docs/android/notifications)): a system-drawn notification runs no app code, and nothing of it could be told.

### Push templates

A push written once — a title and a body per language (Handlebars, as a push's own), a picture and a link — and sent by name: `PUT /notify/templates/push/{slug}/{locale}` (Studio: Notifications → Templates → Push), then `template` in place of a title and a body. Each device gets its person's language; one the template does not have gets the project's default language, else the template's first.

```ts
// src/modules/orders/shipped.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class OrderShipped {
  async tell(userId: string, order: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.notify.sendPush({
      body: { to: { user_ids: [userId] }, template: "order.shipped", variables: { order }, category: "transactional" },
    });
  }
}
```

A send that names a template names no title or body of its own (`400 invalid_push`), and one the project has not is refused (`404 template_not_found`).

## Web push

A browser takes the project's pushes through **its own push service** (Chrome's, Firefox's, Safari's), with the standard Web Push and a VAPID key of the project's own — made as the first browser asks for it, sealed, nothing for you to set up or pay for. The web app subscribes with `pb.notify.push.subscribe()` (from a tap: browsers allow the prompt only then) and serves the SDK's service worker, `palbase/web/push-sw.js`, which shows each push, opens its link when it is tapped, and reports how it went — `delivered`, `opened`, `dismissed` — as the native SDKs do. A browser is a device like any other (`platform: "web"`): it is the signed-in user's, or the install's while no one is, and a push to the user reaches it with their phones. A subscription that ended — the person blocked the site, cleared it — is forgotten as it is next pushed, and `notification.uninstalled` goes into the timeline. `GET /notify/webpush` (Studio: Notifications → Providers) says how many browsers are subscribed.

## Inbox

Each person has an inbox: the messages your backend puts there, and — when a push says so (`inbox: true`), or the project's `inbox.push_copy` setting does — a copy of a push as it is delivered (once, however many devices took it). It is **the same on every device of theirs**: read on one, it is read on each; deleted, it is gone from each. A message stays its days — the project's `inbox.days` (90 unless set), or `expires_in_days` (1 to 365) — and an inbox keeps its newest 250. When the user is deleted, their inbox goes with them.

```ts
// src/modules/orders/inbox.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class OrderInbox {
  async receipt(userId: string, order: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.notify.sendInbox({
      body: {
        to: { user_ids: [userId] },
        title: { en: "Your receipt", tr: "Fişiniz" },
        body: { en: "Order {{order}} is paid.", tr: "{{order}} numaralı sipariş ödendi." },
        variables: { order },
        deep_link: `myapp://orders/${order}`,
        expires_in_days: 30,
      },
    });
  }
}
```

A message is a title and a body (a text, or one per language: each reader gets theirs), with a picture, a link and `data` — or a designed card (`card`, a message definition as the in-app messages' below, `presentation: { type: "card" }`), drawn by the SDKs' renderer. The apps read the signed-in person's inbox (`GET /notify/inbox`, how many are unread with it), mark messages read (`POST /notify/inbox/read`, some or all) and delete one (`DELETE /notify/inbox/{id}`); the iOS, Android and web SDKs draw it ready (`InboxView`, `pb.notify.inbox.mount`). Your backend reads anyone's with `listInboxMessages({ query: { user_id } })` (Studio: Notifications → Log → Inbox).

## In-app messages

A message shown **in the app** — over it (a modal), across the whole screen, or as a banner at an edge — when something happens there. A campaign is what it shows, what shows it, whom it is for and how often:

```ts
// src/modules/growth/cart-reminder.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class CartReminder {
  async create(audienceId: string): Promise<string> {
    const { data } = await Palbase.notify.listInAppTemplates();
    const welcome = data.templates.find((t) => t.key === "welcome");
    if (!welcome) throw new Error("no welcome template");
    const { data: campaign } = await Palbase.notify.createInAppCampaign({
      body: {
        name: "Cart reminder",
        status: "active",
        definition: welcome.definition,
        // An event the app records — session_start as it opens — with properties it must have.
        trigger: { event: "cart_viewed", where: { plan: "pro" } },
        // None: everyone. An audience: its people who allowed personalization.
        audience_id: audienceId,
        // Beside the project's caps: at most this often for this campaign.
        limits: { per_day: 1, max_total: 3 },
        // The person's event within its hours of seeing it: counted as its conversion.
        conversion: { event: "purchase", hours: 24 },
      },
    });
    return campaign.id;
  }
}
```

- **What it shows** is a definition, the same kind as a paywall's: a theme and a free layout of components, in every language it has, drawn natively by the iOS, Android and web SDKs with their paywall renderer. Start from the module's designed messages (`listInAppTemplates`; Studio's editor shows each as the apps draw it). Its buttons go to a link, ask for push (the system's prompt, after the message's own ask; allowed, the device registers for pushes), show a paywall, or call the app's own code.
- **What shows it** is an event of the app's: one analytics records (`capture`, screens, page views) or the app names (`inApp.trigger`). Triggers are matched **on the device**: no event leaves it for them, whatever the person chose of analytics.
- **Whom it is for**: everyone, or an audience — and then only its people who **allowed personalization** (`personalization` consent). A message to everyone needs no consent to be shown.
- **How often**: the project's caps hold across every campaign — one a session, three a day, ten minutes apart unless its `in_app` settings say otherwise — and a campaign adds its own (`per_session`, `per_day`, `min_minutes`, `max_total`). The server counts each showing on every device of the person and refuses one past a cap (`409 frequency_capped`): two phones do not show it twice.
- **What it did**: each showing, button tapped and conversion is an event in the person's timeline (`notification.in_app_shown`, `notification.in_app_clicked`, `notification.in_app_converted`) and in the campaign's counts (`getInAppCampaignStats`: shown, people, clicked, dismissed, converted). A conversion is reported by the app while the person allows analytics.

The apps fetch the person's campaigns as each session starts (`GET /notify/in-app/messages`) and ask before showing one (`POST /notify/in-app/impressions`); the SDKs do both: `.palbaseInAppMessages(pb)` on iOS, `PalbaseInAppMessages(pb) { … }` on Android, `pb.notify.inApp.start()` on the web.

## Topics

```ts
// src/modules/teams/topics.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class TeamTopics {
  async create(teamId: string, members: string[]): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.notify.createTopic({ body: { name: `team.${teamId}`, self_subscribe: false } });
    await Palbase.notify.addTopicSubscribers({ path: { name: `team.${teamId}` }, body: { user_ids: members } });
  }

  async announce(teamId: string, text: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.notify.sendPush({ body: { to: { topic: `team.${teamId}` }, title: "Team", body: text } });
  }
}
```

A topic is **closed** unless `self_subscribe`: only your backend adds its followers, and a user asking is refused (`403 topic_closed`). An open topic is followed from the app — `POST /notify/topics/{name}/subscription` with the user's token — and any user may leave any topic. `changeTopic` opens or closes one, `removeTopicSubscriber` takes a user off, `deleteTopic` deletes it and who follows it.

## Preferences

A user's preferences are channel → category → whether they take it. `transactional` is always on and not theirs to turn off; a category they never set is on. The app reads and sets its own user's (`GET` and `PUT /notify/preferences`); your backend reads and sets anyone's with `getUserPreferences` and `setUserPreferences({ path: { user_id }, body: { email: { marketing: false } } })`. Every send with a `user_id` and a `category` honours them.

## When a message goes

A send may say when it goes, with `schedule`: `at`, a moment for everyone, or `local_time`, an hour on each recipient's own clock — a date and time with no zone. A recipient's clock is their newest device's time zone, which the iOS and Android SDKs register with the push token (`timezone` on `POST /notify/devices`); for one whose devices say none, it is the project's `default_timezone`. A local time already past on someone's clock goes to them at once.

```json
{
  "to": { "user_ids": ["usr_01a1…", "usr_01a2…"] },
  "title": { "en": "Good morning", "tr": "Günaydın" },
  "category": "marketing",
  "schedule": { "local_time": "2026-10-15T10:00" }
}
```

That push goes at 10:00 in New York to a user whose phone is in New York, and at 10:00 in Istanbul to one in Istanbul. Until then each message is `scheduled`, with `send_at` saying when.

A message that is not transactional also keeps to the project's **send rules**, set with `putNotifySettings` or in Studio (**Notifications › Settings › When marketing goes**). A settings write that names none of the three keeps them as they are, so a client written before them does not wipe them; one named `null` is taken off:

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `default_timezone` | The clock of a recipient whose devices say none, an IANA name (`Europe/Istanbul`); UTC when unset. |
| `quiet_hours` | `{ start, end }`, `HH:MM` on the recipient's clock (`22:00` to `08:00` spans midnight; on the night the clocks change they still end at `08:00`). A message that would arrive in them is `held` until they end, then sent. |
| `marketing_cap` | `{ count, hours }`: how many such messages one recipient gets at most in a window. One more is `skipped`, with `skip_reason: "frequency_cap"`. |

Transactional messages — codes, receipts, security notices — go at once, whatever the hour and however many. When a waiting message's time comes it is decided again: what the user chose meanwhile holds (a category turned off skips it, `preferences`), and it waits out quiet hours and keeps to the cap like a new send.

| Status | What it means |
|---|---|
| `scheduled` | Waiting for its time (`send_at`). |
| `held` | Waiting out its recipient's quiet hours (`send_at`: when they end). |
| `skipped` | Not sent, and never will be. `skip_reason` says why: `consent` (they refused this channel's marketing), `frequency_cap`, `preferences`, `iys` (İYS holds no consent for it). |
| `canceled` | Taken back while it waited. |

`POST /notify/messages/{id}/cancel` takes back a `scheduled` or `held` message; one already on its way answers `409 message_not_waiting`. Studio's **Notifications › Log** shows each waiting message with when it goes, and takes it back.

An email, text or WhatsApp message a rule skips answers `{ message_id, skipped: true, skip_reason }` — its message is in the log; one the user's preferences turned off answers `{ skipped: true }` alone, and nothing was queued. A skipped text does not count against its number's one text a minute and ten a day.

## To an audience

`to: { audience: "<id>" }` sends a push to each member of an analytics audience once ([Analytics › Audiences](/docs/web/analytics#audiences)): a member who signed in, as their user; one who never did, on each install of theirs. Each member's push keeps to their own clock, quiet hours, the cap and what they allowed, like a send to them alone. The audience's members are taken as the send is worked through, so a push to a large audience goes out over a little while rather than in one burst.

A push to an audience or a topic with `schedule.at` waits whole until that moment and is spread then; with `schedule.local_time` it is spread at once, each member's push waiting for their own hour. Either way, taking back the push (`POST /notify/messages/{id}/cancel`, its own id) takes it back whole: its spreading stops, and every member's push still waiting goes with it.

## Consent, İYS and texts that say stop

What a person allowed in the app ([consent](/docs/web/analytics#consent)) holds for messages too: a send that is not transactional to someone who refused this channel's marketing — `marketing_push`, `marketing_email`, `marketing_sms`, `marketing_whatsapp` — is skipped (`consent`).

**A text that says stop.** Point your Twilio number's "A message comes in" webhook at `https://<ref>.<domain>/notify/webhooks/sms/twilio/inbound`. A text that is `STOP`, `STOPALL`, `UNSUBSCRIBE`, `CANCEL`, `END` or `QUIT` alone, or `DUR`, `İPTAL`, `IPTAL` or `RET` alone or with one word after it (your brand: `RET ACME`), in any case, is the refusal — "Cancel my order" is a question, not a refusal — of marketing texts of the user whose verified phone number sent it: recorded as their choice (`marketing_sms`, source `sms_stop`), it reaches their apps and your backend as any choice does, and their next marketing text is skipped. Twilio signs each call with your auth token and an unsigned one is refused; nothing is replied to the sender.

**İYS.** A brand that sends commercial messages in Turkey must hold each recipient's consent in İYS (İleti Yönetim Sistemi). Give notify your brand's own İYS API user — `putNotifyProvider({ path: { channel: "iys", provider: "iys" }, body: { credentials, priority: 0, active: true } })`, with `credentials` `{ username, password, iys_code, brand_code, recipient_type }` (`recipient_type` is `BIREYSEL` unless your recipients are traders, `TACIR`) — and then:

- a text to a Turkish number (`+90…`) or an email that is not transactional goes only where İYS holds an `ONAY`; one it does not is skipped (`iys`), and so is one İYS refuses to answer about as it stands. İYS out of reach, the message waits and is tried again. A number abroad is not İYS's, and is not asked about.
- each choice a user makes of `marketing_sms` or `marketing_email` from then on — in the app, by a stop text, through your server — is written to İYS as `ONAY` or `RET`, with where it was made (`HS_MOBIL` in the app, `HS_MESAJ` by a text, `HS_EPOSTA` by an email's link, `HS_CAGRI_MERKEZI` through your support), for their verified Turkish number (`+90…`) or their verified address. The choice holds for your messages at once; İYS is told by a job of your project's, tried again for about three days while İYS is out of reach.

Palbase is not an İYS integrator: the account is yours, and İYS's records are your brand's.

## SMS, codes and WhatsApp

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sendSms({ body: { to, body } })` | A text to one number in E.164 form (`+14155551212`): a body, or a `template` with `variables`. A number gets one text a minute and ten a day. It answers the segments and encoding the text takes. |
| `startVerification({ body: { to } })` | Has your verification service — Palbase's when you have none — generate a one-time code and text it. A number Twilio cannot text is refused (`400 verification_refused`); past a free environment's $4 of Palbase's codes a month, `429 quota_exceeded`. |
| `checkVerification({ body: { to, code } })` | `{ approved }`: whether the code is the one it sent. |
| `sendWhatsApp({ body: { to, template_slug, variables } })` | A WhatsApp message: a text inside a conversation the user opened in the last 24 hours, a template approved on your Meta account, or one of your slugs. |

The project's message settings say where texts may go: `putNotifySettings` sets the default locale, the sender of email through your own provider, the countries texts may (`sms_countries`) and may not (`sms_blocked_countries`) reach, and the send rules ([When a message goes](#when-a-message-goes)).

## Reports

`listNotifyMessages({ query })` answers the project's messages, newest first — their delivery reports, never what they said — filtered by channel, status, user, category or a window. `getNotifyMessage({ path: { id } })` reads one: its status, attempts, provider, and what the provider reported after it left (delivered, bounced, opened …) when its credential lets it report — and, a push, how it went on each device and when it got to each stage. `getMetricsSummary()` counts them per channel, status and day. Studio's **Notifications** screens show the same reports, devices and metrics.

## The `Notifications` service

A backend sends with `Notifications`, and each send answers `{ data, error, status }`:

- `Notifications.email.send({ to, subject?, html?, text?, templateSlug?, locale?, variables?, from?, reply_to?, category? })` — `to` one address, or several: one message each, in order, the first refusal ending them.
- `Notifications.push.send({ to, title?, body?, data?, deep_link?, category?, priority?, … })` — `to` a user's id, several, or `{ topic }`.

```ts
// src/modules/invites/invite-mail.service.ts
import { Injectable, Log, Notifications } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class InviteMail {
  async send(to: string, link: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const { error } = await Notifications.email.send({ to, subject: "You're invited", html: `<a href="${link}">Join</a>`, category: "invite" });
    if (error) Log.warn("the invitation was not sent", { code: error.code });
    return error === null;
  }
}
```

## Journeys

A journey sends a person messages over time after something they did — a welcome over their first week, a win-back after they stopped buying — with waits, branches and A/B splits between them: [Journeys](/docs/backend/journeys).

## Related

- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks) — `notification.sent`, `notification.failed`, `notification.received`, `notification.uninstalled`, `notification.push_failing`
- [Analytics](/docs/web/analytics#audiences) — the audiences a push can go to, and each person's consent
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals, retries and `Idempotency-Key`
- [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets) — the values your own code reads (a provider's credentials are kept by notify, sealed)
- [Test Users](/docs/backend/test-users) — users to send to while you try a flow



<!-- ===== backend/journeys ===== -->

# Journeys

A journey takes each person who does something — signs up, stops opening the app, buys, joins an audience — through the steps you set: messages, waits, branches, A/B splits, coupons and grants. It is built in Studio's **Journeys** or kept as a JSON file and handled with the CLI, tried on a test user, published, and then reported on: who entered, what each step came to, how many reached its goal.

Journeys are the project's server's: their API takes the secret key (or a member's session in Studio), never the publishable key.

## Quick example

A journey that welcomes a new user, checks a day later whether they finished setting up, and A/B tests the reminder for those who did not:

```json
{
  "name": "Onboarding",
  "entry": { "event": { "name": "sign_up" } },
  "goal": { "event": { "name": "onboarding_completed" }, "within": "P7D" },
  "start": "welcome",
  "steps": {
    "welcome": { "inbox": { "title": { "en": "Welcome aboard" }, "body": { "en": "Here is how to get the most out of the app." } }, "next": "wait_1d" },
    "wait_1d": { "wait": { "for": "P1D" }, "next": "finished" },
    "finished": { "branch": { "if": { "event": { "name": "onboarding_completed" } }, "then": "end", "else": "tip" } },
    "tip": { "split": [{ "name": "push", "weight": 50, "next": "tip_push" }, { "name": "inbox", "weight": 50, "next": "tip_inbox" }] },
    "tip_push": { "push": { "title": { "en": "One step left" }, "body": { "en": "Finish setting up in under a minute." } }, "next": "end" },
    "tip_inbox": { "inbox": { "title": { "en": "One step left" }, "body": { "en": "It is all in one place." } }, "next": "end" }
  }
}
```

```bash
palbase journeys:validate onboarding.json            # every problem, at its path, with what to do about it
palbase journeys:push onboarding.json --publish      # save it as a draft (key: the file's name) and publish it
palbase journeys:stats onboarding                    # who entered, each step, the goal's conversions, each A/B way
```

## A journey

A definition has who enters (`entry`), the steps by id with the first one (`start`), what the journey is for (`goal`), what takes a person out early (`exit`) and whether a person enters again (`reentry`). Each step does one thing and names the step after it in `next`; `end`, or no `next`, ends the person's run. A person is in a journey once at a time.

| Who enters (`entry`, one of) | |
|---|---|
| `event: { name, where }` | A person who does the event — an app's own (`sign_up`), or a module's: `purchases.purchase.completed`, `purchases.coupon.redeemed`, `audience.entered` — with the properties `where` names, each equal. |
| `audience: "<id>"` | A person who comes to be in an analytics audience. |
| `inactive: { event, for }` | A person who has not done the event for a while (1 hour to 90 days): the moment it passes since their last one. `$session_start` is someone who has not opened the app. |
| `members_of: "<id>"` | An audience's members, once, as the journey is published. |

`goal: { event, within }` — a run that sees the event within `within` of entering (30 days unless it says, 90 at most) ends **converted**; a run that completed before it is counted converted too. `exit: { events, audience_left }` takes a person out when they do one of the events or leave the audience. `reentry.mode` is `once` (the default: never again), `always` (each time, once their run ended) or `after` (once `after` has passed since they last entered). Whatever it says, a person enters one journey 20 times a day at most, so a journey whose own steps cause its entry event does not loop.

Durations are ISO 8601: `PT30M`, `PT2H`, `P2D`, `P1W`.

## Steps

| Step | What it does |
|---|---|
| `push` | A push to the person's devices: `title` and `body` by locale (`en`, `tr`, `pt-BR`), or one of the project's push `template`s; `deep_link`, `image`, `data`, `category`; `inbox: true` keeps a copy in their inbox. |
| `inbox` | A message in the person's inbox: `title` and `body` by locale, `deep_link`, `image`, `expires_in_days`. |
| `email` | An email from one of the project's email templates, with its `variables`. |
| `in_app` | One of the project's in-app campaigns made for journeys, shown the next time it is triggered in their app (waiting up to `days`, 7 unless it says). |
| `coupon` | Gives the person their code of one of the project's coupons; `{{coupon}}` in the messages after it is that code. |
| `offer` | Gives the person one of the catalog's grant offers: an entitlement for a while. |
| `set` | Writes properties of the person's (analytics' people): 1 to 20. |
| `event` | Tells your backend: a `journey.event` with the step's `name` and `data` — a webhook, or an `@On`. |
| `wait` | Holds the person: `for` a while (1 minute to 90 days), `until` a time of day where they are (`"09:00"`, in their `$timezone`), or until they do an `event`, at most `timeout` — then `next`, or `timeout_next` when it timed out. |
| `branch` | Sends the person to `then` when `if` holds of them, else to `else`. A condition asks a `property` of theirs (`eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `contains`, `exists`, `missing`), whether they are in an `audience`, whether they did an `event` (since entering, or `within` a while), or `all`, `any` or `not` of others. |
| `split` | An A/B split: 2 to 5 ways whose `weight`s add up to 100. Each person takes one way by chance — the same one every time — and the report counts each way's conversions. |

A message step is sent by the project's send rules ([Notifications › When a message goes](/docs/backend/notifications#when-a-message-goes)): quiet hours, the marketing cap and what the person allowed. A message they did not allow is skipped and the run goes on. A journey has 100 steps at most, every one reachable from `start`, and no way back to a step already taken but through a wait.

## From your backend

A step your backend sees — a document approved, a first upload — moves a journey when your server tells it as the user's event: `POST /analytics/capture` with the secret key and `user_id`. It enters them into a journey of that event, takes them past a wait for it, counts toward a goal, and answers a branch that asks whether they did it, as an event their app sent would.

```bash
curl -s -X POST "https://<ref>.palbase.studio/analytics/capture" \
  -H "apikey: $PALBASE_SECRET_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"event": "crew_verified", "user_id": "usr_123", "properties": {"airline": "TK"}}'
```

## In Studio

**Journeys** lists the environment's journeys with their status and who enters. **New journey** starts one from a template — *Onboarding*, *Win back* (a customer who has not bought for 30 days) or *Didn't come back* (a user who has not opened the app for a week) — or from a blank page.

A journey's page draws it top to bottom: who enters at the top, each step under the one before, a branch's or a split's ways side by side until they meet, the goal at the bottom. A step opens its form in the side panel; the **+** between two steps adds one there. The module checks the draft a moment after each change, and each problem shows under the field it is about (`steps.welcome.inbox.title.en` under the welcome step's English title) and in the problems list, which takes you to it. **JSON** shows the definition the CLI pushes; a change there is the flow. **Preview** walks a made-up person through what is on screen — their properties, audiences, time zone and what they do after entering — and shows each step they would take and when; nothing is sent.

## Trying a journey on a test user

`POST /journeys/{key}/test` with `{ "user_id": "…" }` runs the saved journey — a draft too — for one of the project's [test users](/docs/backend/test-users) from its first step. Its messages really go to that user, each wait is a minute long, and the try is counted in no report and no month's people; its `journey.*` events carry `test: true`. Studio's **Try on a test user** does the same, and follows the run beside what landed in the person's inbox. A user who is not a test user is refused (`422 not_a_test_user`), and so is a stopped journey (`409 journey_stopped`). A new try of the same journey ends that user's try still running.

## Publishing, stopping and copying

`POST /journeys/{key}/publish` makes a draft live: people enter it from then on (a `members_of` journey enrolls the audience's members now). A live journey does not change (`409 journey_published`): copy it into a new draft (`POST /journeys/{key}/copy` with `{ "key": "…", "name": "…" }`), publish that, and stop the old one. `POST /journeys/{key}/stop` lets no one in any more and ends the runs in it; its report stays. `DELETE /journeys/{key}` deletes a journey with its runs and its report.

A project keeps 500 journeys and runs 50 at once. An environment without its paid rights — on Free, held for its payment account's charge unpaid, or at its monthly limit — runs 2 at once (`402 live_journeys_limit`); on Pay as you go, the people who enter its journeys are billed by the month ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)): the first 1,000 people a month are free, then $2 for each 1,000 more.

## The report

`GET /journeys/{key}/stats` answers who entered (`entered`), how many reached the goal (`converted`), who is in it now (`in_progress`: `active`, `waiting`, `held`), how the runs ended (`ended`: `completed`, `converted`, `exited`, `stopped`, `failed`, `erased`), each step's outcomes from the start (`steps[].outcomes`: `sent`, `skipped`, `waited`, `then`, `else`, a split's way …) and, for a split, each way's conversions (`steps[].converted`). `GET /journeys/{key}/runs` pages each person's run — its state, the step it is at, each step it took and what came of it — filtered by `user_id` or `state`; `GET /journeys/people/{user_id}` is one person's runs in every journey. Studio's **Report** shows the same.

People who enter while the organization's monthly people are used up are held (`held`) until it has them again.

## Events

Each run tells the project's backend as it goes — a [webhook](/docs/server/webhooks#the-events), or an `@On`:

| Type | Sent when |
|---|---|
| `journey.entered` | A person entered a journey. |
| `journey.step` | A person's run took a step. |
| `journey.event` | A journey's `event` step told the project's backend. |
| `journey.converted` | A person's run reached the journey's goal. |
| `journey.ended` | A person's run ended: completed, converted, exited, stopped. |

## The API

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /journeys` | The project's journeys, newest first: `status`, `limit`, `cursor`. |
| `POST /journeys` | A new draft: `{ key, definition }`. |
| `GET /journeys/{key}` | A journey whole, with its definition. |
| `PUT /journeys/{key}` | A draft's definition, written whole: `{ definition }`. |
| `DELETE /journeys/{key}` | Deletes it with its runs and its report. |
| `POST /journeys/validate` | Every problem of a definition, each at its path: `{ definition }` → `{ valid, problems }`. Nothing is kept. |
| `POST /journeys/simulate` | A made-up person's way through a journey — the project's (`key`) or one not saved (`definition`) — with each step and when. Nothing is sent. |
| `POST /journeys/{key}/test` | Tries the saved journey on a test user: `{ user_id }`. |
| `POST /journeys/{key}/publish` | Makes a draft live. |
| `POST /journeys/{key}/stop` | Stops a live journey. |
| `POST /journeys/{key}/copy` | Copies a journey into a new draft. |
| `GET /journeys/{key}/stats` | Its report. |
| `GET /journeys/{key}/runs` | Each person's run. |
| `GET /journeys/people/{user_id}` | One person's runs in every journey. |

```bash
curl -s -X POST "https://<ref>.palbase.studio/journeys/onboarding/test" \
  -H "apikey: $PALBASE_SECRET_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"user_id": "usr_test_1"}'
```

## From the CLI

A journey is kept as a file and handled with the CLI: saved as a draft, published, then followed.

```bash
palbase journeys:validate winback.json             # every problem, at its path, with what to do about it
palbase journeys:simulate winback.json --event purchases.purchase.completed@P1D   # walk a made-up person through it; nothing is sent
palbase journeys:push winback.json --publish       # save it as a draft (key: the file's name) and publish it
palbase journeys                                   # the environment's journeys: key, name, status, way in
palbase journeys:stats winback                     # who entered, how their runs ended, the goal's conversions
palbase journeys:runs winback                      # each person's run: its state, the step it is at
palbase journeys:stop winback                      # no one enters it any more, the runs in it end
```

`journeys:get` prints a journey's definition to edit and push again, `journeys:copy` copies one into a new draft, `journeys:publish` publishes a draft, and `journeys:delete` deletes one with its runs and its report. Every command is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#journeys).

## Related

- [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications) — the send rules a journey's messages keep to, push templates and inboxes

# Realtime

Every project has realtime: **channels** its clients join over one socket, a **broadcast** on a channel that reaches every subscriber, and a **shared state** per channel — keyed entries every subscriber with state access reads, a snapshot when it joins and the changes after. Clients join and listen ([Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime)). Your backend publishes as the project's server, with the secret key: `Palbase.realtime` in a `palbase/backend` app, `createServer(…).realtime` anywhere else. Who may join which channel is the project's [channel declaration](/docs/backend/channels).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/orders/live.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class OrderLive {
  /** Tells the order's owner, on their own channel, that its status changed. */
  async statusChanged(userId: string, orderId: string, status: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.realtime.broadcast({
      body: { messages: [{ topic: `orders:${userId}`, event: "status", payload: { orderId, status } }] },
    });
  }
}
```

With `orders:{uid}` declared as an `owner` channel ([Channels](/docs/backend/channels)), the signed-in user — and only they — joins `orders:<their id>` and hears it as a `broadcast`:

```ts
// watch.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function watch(userId: string, onStatus: (change: unknown) => void): Promise<() => void> {
  const channel = pb.socket.channel(`orders:${userId}`);
  const off = channel.on("broadcast", (frame) => {
    if (frame.event === "status") onStatus(frame.payload);
  });
  await channel.join(); // refused unless the declaration lets this user join
  return () => {
    off();
    channel.leave();
  };
}
```

## Broadcast

`POST /realtime/broadcast` publishes 1 to 100 events in one call, each `{ topic, event, payload }`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `topic` | The channel's name, such as `orders:usr_123` — without the `realtime:` prefix the socket carries. |
| `event` | The event's name, which the client reads as the frame's `event`. |
| `payload` | Any JSON. |

It answers `202` with how many were published. A broadcast reaches every subscriber on every replica of realtime, but the one that sent it — and the server is no subscriber, so a server broadcast reaches them all.

**A broadcast is delivered at most once.** A client that was not on the channel at that moment — offline, reconnecting, not joined yet — does not get it later, and nothing is kept. That makes a broadcast a *nudge*: "order 42 changed, look again". What a client must not miss belongs in your database, or in the channel's state.

## Revalidate

`POST /realtime/revalidate` asks every replica to decide again, now, who may be on channels whose decision may no longer hold, and drops the members who may not. It names one channel (`topic`), or every channel of a pattern whose named parameters have the values given (`pattern` and `params`), and optionally one user's memberships alone (`user`). With a `topic` and no `user`, `end: true` ends the channel instead: every member is dropped without being asked, and what a durable channel kept is forgotten. It answers `202`. A dropped member's client is told the channel closed, and its rejoin is decided on the merits. Without it, a decision holds until the user's token runs out, fifteen minutes at most.

## Shared state

Each channel has a keyed state that outlives any one connection. Your backend writes it with `POST /realtime/state`, 1 to 100 operations a call:

```ts
// src/modules/boards/board-state.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class BoardState {
  async setCard(boardId: string, cardId: string, card: { title: string; column: string }): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.realtime.writeState({ body: { ops: [{ topic: `board:${boardId}`, key: cardId, value: card }] } });
  }

  async removeCard(boardId: string, cardId: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.realtime.writeState({ body: { ops: [{ topic: `board:${boardId}`, key: cardId, delete: true }] } });
  }
}
```

- **Durable.** Entries the server writes stay until they are removed. A subscriber that joins gets the whole state (a `state_snapshot` frame), then what changed as it changes (`state_diff`); a client that lost the thread asks for it all again (`state_resync`).
- **Small.** A value is any JSON, 16 KiB at most, and each channel has a budget: a write past it is refused with `422`, and the operations before it in the call stay applied.
- **Read by subscribers with state access.** Who has it is the declaration's `state_read` (and who may write from the client, `state_write`) — see [Channels](/docs/backend/channels).

Clients may also write **ephemeral** entries — their own presence — which are gone when they leave.

## Limits

`getLimits()` reads the limits the project holds its clients to, and the platform's above them; `putLimits({ body })` sets them: connections open at once (`max_connections`), broadcasts and state writes per second (`max_events_per_second`), joins per second (`max_joins_per_second`), and channels on one connection (`max_channels_per_connection`). `null` is the platform's own, and a value above the platform's has no effect beyond it. Studio's **Realtime** screen shows and sets the same limits, and can send a test message.

## The socket, from the client's side

The socket is `GET /realtime/v1/websocket` at the project's address — Phoenix Channels v2 frames, one socket per client for every channel it is on. The publishable key opens it; a client says who it is with the access token each join carries, so the user's rights on a channel are decided per join and again when the declaration changes. The web SDK speaks it for you (`pb.socket`): it opens on the first join, sends a heartbeat every 25 s, reconnects with growing pauses, and joins its channels again after a drop.

Your backend never subscribes: `palbase/server` has no socket. What a client sends that the server must act on is a call to one of your backend's routes.

## Channel names

A channel is `:`-separated segments: `orders:<user_id>`, `board:7f3a`, `game:42:chat`, 255 bytes at most. The namespaces `roles:`, `flags:`, `messaging:`, `calls:` and `debug:` are the platform's — flags' live updates travel on `flags:<ref>` and `flags:<ref>:<user_id>`, a user's permission set on `roles:<ref>:<user_id>`. A channel the declaration does not match belongs to no one, and no client may join it.

## The `Realtime` service

A backend broadcasts with `Realtime`: `Realtime.broadcast(channel, event, payload?)`, and a channel's state with `Realtime.state.set(channel, key, value)` and `Realtime.state.clear(channel, key)`. Each answers `{ data, error, status }`: the platform taking it, not every subscriber receiving it; it never fails the handler.

```ts
// src/modules/projects/project-signal.service.ts
import { Injectable, Realtime } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class ProjectSignal {
  async changed(projectId: string, what: string): Promise<void> {
    await Realtime.broadcast(`project:${projectId}`, what, {});
  }
}
```

## Related

- [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways) — a `palbase/backend` app's own realtime channels
- [Channels](/docs/backend/channels) — who may join, publish and write state
- [Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime) — joining and listening in the browser
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals and retries
- [Flags](/docs/backend/flags) — the live updates that ride the same socket



<!-- ===== backend/gateways ===== -->

# Gateways

A gateway is a realtime channel of your app: a class marked `@Gateway(pattern, options)` and listed in a module's `providers`. Its pattern names the channels it is: `room:{roomId}` is the gateway of `room:42`, `room:43`, …, each a channel of its own. The class says who may join, the events it sends, the messages its members may send and the ack each one is answered with, and it is told when a channel fills and when it empties.

A gateway is the one way an app talks realtime to your backend. `palbase apps:sync` writes each app a typed client of the backend's gateways ([Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways)): the app joins `RoomGateway` with `{ roomId }`, and writes no channel name, event name or payload type of its own.

## Quick example

The rooms, and who is in each:

```ts
// src/modules/rooms/rooms.service.ts
import { Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

export interface RoomMessage {
  id: string;
  from: string;
  text: string;
}

// Kept in memory to keep the example small; a real app keeps its rooms in its database.
@Injectable()
export class RoomsService {
  private readonly members = new Map<string, Set<string>>();

  add(roomId: string, userId: string): void {
    this.members.set(roomId, (this.members.get(roomId) ?? new Set()).add(userId));
  }

  isMember(roomId: string, userId: string): boolean {
    return this.members.get(roomId)?.has(userId) === true;
  }

  post(from: string, text: string): RoomMessage {
    return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), from, text };
  }
}
```

The gateway:

```ts
// src/modules/rooms/room.gateway.ts
import { Authorize, Gateway, GatewayRefusal, OnConnect, Subscribe, z } from "palbase/backend";
import type { GatewayAuthorizeContext, GatewayContext, GatewayGrant, GatewayMessageContext } from "palbase/backend";
import { RoomsService } from "./rooms.service";

export const Say = z.object({ text: z.string().min(1).max(2000) });
export const Said = z.object({ id: z.string() });
export const Message = z.object({ id: z.string(), from: z.string(), text: z.string() });
export const Welcome = z.object({ members: z.number() });

// room:<id>, one channel per room. Its members hear `message`; they send `say`.
@Gateway("room:{roomId}")
export class RoomGateway {
  static readonly events = { message: Message, welcome: Welcome };

  constructor(private readonly rooms: RoomsService) {}

  // Who may join: the room's members, and no one else.
  @Authorize()
  enter(ctx: GatewayAuthorizeContext): GatewayGrant {
    return this.rooms.isMember(ctx.params.roomId, ctx.user.id);
  }

  // Said to the member who joined, alone.
  @OnConnect()
  joined(ctx: GatewayContext): void {
    ctx.emit("welcome", { members: ctx.count });
  }

  // A member's message, checked against Say before this runs. What it returns is the member's ack.
  @Subscribe("say", Say, { reply: Said })
  say(ctx: GatewayMessageContext<z.infer<typeof Say>>): z.infer<typeof Said> {
    if (ctx.payload.text.startsWith("/")) throw new GatewayRefusal("no_commands");
    const message = this.rooms.post(ctx.user.id, ctx.payload.text);
    ctx.emit("message", message);
    return { id: message.id };
  }
}
```

A route that makes the user a member, and one that posts to a room from outside it:

```ts
// src/modules/rooms/rooms.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Forbidden, Palbase, Param, Post, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { RoomGateway, Say } from "./room.gateway";
import { RoomsService } from "./rooms.service";

@Controller("/rooms")
export class RoomsController {
  constructor(private readonly rooms: RoomsService) {}

  // From now on the gateway lets this user into room:<roomId>.
  @Post("/{roomId}/members")
  join(@Param("roomId") roomId: string, @User() user: UserT): void {
    this.rooms.add(roomId, user.id);
  }

  // A message posted over HTTP reaches the room's members as one said in it.
  @Post("/{roomId}/messages")
  post(@Param("roomId") roomId: string, @Body(Say) body: { text: string }, @User() user: UserT): { id: string } {
    if (!this.rooms.isMember(roomId, user.id)) throw new Forbidden("not a member of this room");
    const message = this.rooms.post(user.id, body.text);
    Palbase.gateways.to(RoomGateway, { roomId }).emit("message", message);
    return { id: message.id };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/rooms/rooms.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { RoomGateway } from "./room.gateway";
import { RoomsController } from "./rooms.controller";
import { RoomsService } from "./rooms.service";

@Module({ controllers: [RoomsController], providers: [RoomsService, RoomGateway] })
export class RoomsModule {}
```

A gateway is a provider like any other: its module lists it in `providers`, it takes its dependencies by constructor, and it is built once, so what one method starts another can stop. A `@Gateway` that no module lists stops the boot by name, and so does a class that is both a controller and a gateway.

## Options

| Option | What it is | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `access` | Who may join, with no method of yours: `"owner"`, the signed-in user whose id the pattern's one `{param}` is; `"public"`, any signed-in user. Left out, an `@Authorize` method decides. | none |
| `durable` | Keeps what it sends: `true` for a day, or `{ keepSeconds }` from 1 to 604800 (a week). See [Durable gateways](#durable-gateways). | not kept |
| `graceMs` | How long the channel is held after its last member left before it is empty (`@OnEmpty`), in milliseconds. | 60000 |
| `publish` | Its members may broadcast to one another on the channel. A gateway with no method only: one with methods takes its members' messages itself (`@Subscribe`). | `false` |
| `chat` | It carries a chat of the project's agents: its event `chat` is the platform's, and every generated client holds the chat's state. Kept a day unless `durable` says how long. See [AI](/docs/backend/ai#a-chat-in-an-app). | `false` |

Who may join is said once: `access` or an `@Authorize` method, never both and never neither. The boot refuses either mistake by name.

## Patterns

A pattern is `:`-separated segments, as a channel's name is. A segment written `{name}` takes exactly one non-empty segment of the channel, and the method is given it in `ctx.params`. Any other segment matches itself.

| Pattern | Its channels | Not its channels |
|---|---|---|
| `lobby` | `lobby` | `lobby:2` |
| `room:{roomId}` | `room:42` | `room`, `room:42:chat` |
| `game:{gameId}:team:{team}` | `game:7:team:red` | `game:7:team` |

A pattern is 255 bytes at most, has no `/` and no control character, and names each `{param}` once. The namespaces `roles:`, `flags:`, `messaging:`, `calls:` and `debug:` are the platform's. A pattern that breaks one of these rules is refused when its class is declared.

When two of an app's patterns match one channel, the more specific one decides it: a named segment beats a `{param}`, from the left, so `lobby:staff` decides `lobby:staff` and `lobby:{id}` every other lobby. Two gateways of the same channels (`room:{roomId}` and `room:{id}`) are refused at boot. Two of the project's machines that declare the same channels have neither: the channel is refused until one of them gives it up.

The class's name is the gateway's name in every generated client (`RoomGateway`), so it is an identifier and one of a kind in the app.

## Who may join

Only a signed-in user joins a gateway. The access token the client's socket carries is who they are.

With `access: "owner"`, the pattern's one `{param}` must be the joining user's id: `inbox:{userId}` is joined by that user alone. With `access: "public"`, any signed-in user of the project joins. Either way no code of yours decides it.

Otherwise its `@Authorize` method decides, at each join. It is given the user and the channel's parameters, and it runs as that user, in a transaction of its own: `Database` is theirs, and [row-level security](/docs/backend/row-level-security) holds. It answers a grant:

| Answer | Means |
|---|---|
| `true` | In, to hear and to send. |
| `{ write: false }` | In, to hear. A message they send is refused (`forbidden`). |
| `{ read: false }`, `false`, `null`, `undefined` | Not in. |

Anything else lets no one in: `{}`, a row, a number, or `{ read: member?.canRead }` when there is no member (`undefined` is no answer). So does a method that throws. Each of these is in the app's log, without the value it answered. A refused join reaches the client as `unauthorized`; a join the app could not be asked about, as `unavailable`, which is worth trying again.

A grant holds until the user's token runs out, fifteen minutes at most — a minute for a gateway declared with `chat: true` — and then `@Authorize` is asked again. When a decision stops being true before that (a member taken off a team, a document unshared), say so: `POST /realtime/revalidate` with the secret key, naming the channel (`{ "topic": "board:42" }`) or a pattern's channels by some of their parameters (`{ "pattern": "board:{boardId}:user:{userId}", "params": { "userId": "usr_…" } }`), optionally one user's memberships alone (`"user"`). Every replica asks `@Authorize` again for those memberships at once, and a member it no longer lets in is told the channel closed; their rejoin is refused. A chat gateway needs none of this: the platform revalidates its channel itself when a member is taken out of the chat, and ends it when the chat is deleted.

## Events

What a gateway sends is declared on its class: `static readonly events = { name: schema }`, each a [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) of the payload. The generated clients type each event by it.

From a gateway's own methods, `ctx.emit(event, payload)` sends to every member of the channel. In `@OnConnect` it sends to the member who joined, and no one else. From anywhere else in the app (a route, a service, a [task](/docs/backend/tasks), an [`@On`](/docs/backend/hooks)) `Palbase.gateways.to(Gateway, params)` names one channel, and its `emit` is typed by the gateway's events:

```ts
// src/modules/rooms/room-notices.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";
import { RoomGateway } from "./room.gateway";

@Injectable()
export class RoomNotices {
  /** The room hears it as a message from no one in particular. */
  closingSoon(roomId: string, minutes: number): void {
    Palbase.gateways.to(RoomGateway, { roomId }).emit("message", { id: crypto.randomUUID(), from: "", text: `This room closes in ${minutes} minutes.` });
  }
}
```

- **In order.** Events to one channel are sent in the order they were emitted. Those emitted while one is on its way go together in the next send.
- **Never thrown.** `emit` returns at once and does not fail the method. An event the gateway does not declare, or a payload that is not JSON, is not sent, and the app's log says so. So is an event that could not be sent.
- **At most once,** unless the gateway is [durable](#durable-gateways): a member that was not on the channel when an event was sent does not get it later.

A member hears only what the gateway sends. Members' own messages go to the backend, never to one another: what the others should hear, the method emits.

## Messages and acks

`@Subscribe(name, schema, { reply })` marks the method that takes one message its members send. The payload is checked against `schema` before the method runs. One that does not fit never reaches it, and the member is told the schema's issues.

The method is given a `GatewayMessageContext`: the channel, its `params`, the member as `ctx.user`, and the payload as the schema made it (`ctx.payload`). It runs as the member, in a transaction of its own, committed when it returns and rolled back when it throws. What it returns is the member's **ack**, which their `send` resolves with. `reply` is the ack's schema, which the generated clients type it by and which the ack is checked against.

What a member's `send` is answered:

| The method | The member is told |
|---|---|
| Returns a value | The value, as JSON carries it. Past 64 KiB, `reply_too_large`. |
| Returns nothing | `ok`, with no ack. |
| Throws `new GatewayRefusal("muted")` | The refusal, with your reason: `muted`. What the method wrote is rolled back. |
| Throws anything else | `handler_failed`. The error is in the app's log, never in the member's answer. |
| Returns an ack its `reply` refuses | `handler_failed`, and the log says why. |

A `GatewayRefusal`'s reason is a word your app acts on: `not_your_turn`, `too_many_messages`, `muted`. It is 256 bytes at most. A message the gateway does not declare is refused with its name.

## Moments

A gateway with methods is told of its channels' moments:

| Decorator | When | Runs as |
|---|---|---|
| `@OnFirst()` | The channel has a member and is held by no one. Told once, however many members come at once, and before the first of them is answered. | The app |
| `@OnConnect()` | A member joined, after they were answered. What it emits goes to them alone. | The member |
| `@OnDisconnect()` | A member left. | The member |
| `@OnEmpty()` | Nobody has been on the channel for its `graceMs`. | The app |

"The app" is the service role, as a [cron](/docs/backend/cron)'s work is: every row in reach. Each moment's `GatewayContext` carries `channel`, `params`, `count` (its members now), `user` (`id` is `""` in `@OnFirst` and `@OnEmpty`, which no one in particular caused), `emit`, `pipe`, `signal` and `owner`.

`ctx.signal` is the channel's own. It aborts when the channel empties, before `@OnEmpty` runs, so what `@OnFirst` started stops on it without a method to remember it. `ctx.owner.hold(work)` runs `work` past the method, until that signal aborts. A failure of it is logged, never the app's crash. `ctx.owner.release()` gives the channel up at once: its signal aborts, and the next member to come finds it held by no one, so `@OnFirst` runs again.

```ts
// src/modules/prices/prices.gateway.ts
import { Gateway, Log, OnEmpty, OnFirst, z } from "palbase/backend";
import type { GatewayContext } from "palbase/backend";

export const Tick = z.object({ symbol: z.string(), price: z.number() });

// prices:<symbol>: a price read from the exchange only while someone watches it.
@Gateway("prices:{symbol}", { access: "public", graceMs: 30_000 })
export class PricesGateway {
  static readonly events = { tick: Tick };

  // The first watcher came: read the price every second until the channel empties.
  @OnFirst()
  open(ctx: GatewayContext): void {
    const symbol = ctx.params.symbol;
    ctx.owner.hold(async (signal) => {
      while (!signal.aborted) {
        const res = await fetch(`https://quotes.example.com/v1/${encodeURIComponent(symbol)}`, { signal });
        const { price } = (await res.json()) as { price: number };
        ctx.emit("tick", { symbol, price });
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
      }
    });
  }

  // Thirty seconds with nobody watching: the loop above has stopped already.
  @OnEmpty()
  closed(ctx: GatewayContext): void {
    Log.info("nobody watches", { symbol: ctx.params.symbol });
  }
}
```

A moment whose method throws is told again 1, 5 and 15 seconds later. A join or a leave told again is run once.

## Durable gateways

A durable gateway keeps what it sends: every event is kept and numbered as it is sent, for a day (`durable: true`) or for `{ keepSeconds }`, a week at most. A member that comes back, a phone that walked out of range or a socket that dropped, is sent everything after the last event it had, in order and once. A member that joins is sent what the gateway keeps first, unless it asks for only what comes next ([Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways#durable-gateways)).

```ts
// src/modules/orders/order-updates.gateway.ts
import { Gateway, z } from "palbase/backend";

export const Status = z.object({ orderId: z.string(), status: z.enum(["paid", "packed", "shipped", "delivered"]) });

// orders:<user id>: a user's own order updates, kept a week.
@Gateway("orders:{userId}", { access: "owner", durable: { keepSeconds: 604_800 } })
export class OrderUpdates {
  static readonly events = { status: Status };
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/orders/order-status.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";
import { OrderUpdates } from "./order-updates.gateway";

@Injectable()
export class OrderStatus {
  shipped(userId: string, orderId: string): void {
    Palbase.gateways.to(OrderUpdates, { userId }).emit("status", { orderId, status: "shipped" });
  }
}
```

Every event delivered to a member counts toward the project's realtime messages, the ones sent again to a member that came back included. What a project's durable gateways keep is bounded: an event past the bound is not kept or sent, and the app's log says so. Keep a durable gateway for what members must not miss while they are away. What must outlive the conversation belongs in your database.

## Pipes

`ctx.pipe(source)` has the platform write `source` into the gateway's channel from then on. `Palbase.gateways.to(Gateway, params).pipe(source)` does the same from anywhere in the app. The backend is not in the stream: after the call, what the source says reaches the channel's members without passing through the machine.

The source today is a chat of the project's agents, `Palbase.ai.chats.events(chatId)`, piped into a gateway declared with `chat: true`. See [AI](/docs/backend/ai#a-chat-in-an-app).

## A gateway with no method

A gateway that has no method, only its access, its events and perhaps `publish`, never wakes the machine. Realtime decides its joins from the app's contract alone, and `Palbase.gateways.to(…).emit` sends to it from wherever the app runs. `OrderUpdates` above is one: a user's app can hold `orders:<their id>` open all day while the machine sleeps.

A gateway with a method is the machine's. Its joins, its members' messages and its moments are signed calls the platform makes to the machine, waking it if it sleeps. A join or a message is answered within 8 seconds and a moment within 30, or realtime gives up on it: a join is then `unavailable`, and a moment is told again.

A release's gateways are what realtime goes by within 30 seconds of it serving.

## Limits

| | |
|---|---|
| A pattern, a channel, an event's or a message's name | 255 bytes |
| An ack | 64 KiB of JSON |
| A refusal's reason | 256 bytes |
| What a durable gateway keeps | a week |
| An `@Authorize` or a message, answered | within 8 seconds |
| A moment, answered | within 30 seconds |

What the project's clients may use (connections, joins and events per second, channels per connection) is set with `putLimits` ([Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime#limits)).

## On your computer

Off the platform (the app started on your computer, or in a test) nothing joins a gateway: realtime is what calls a machine about one. `Palbase.gateways.to(…).emit` sends as the app, to the project its `PALBASE_URL` names. Test a gateway's methods as plain methods of a class ([Testing](/docs/backend/testing)).

## Gateways and the channel declaration

A channel a gateway matches is the gateway's, whatever the project's [channel declaration](/docs/backend/channels) says. The declaration (`Palbase.realtime.putChannels`, Studio's **Realtime › Channels**) is the realtime module's own list, for a backend that is not a `palbase/backend` app: a server that broadcasts with the secret key ([Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime)) and channels its clients join by name. A `palbase/backend` app declares its channels as gateways.

## Related

- [Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways): joining a gateway from an app, its events, messages and acks
- [AI](/docs/backend/ai): a chat of the project's agents, carried by a gateway
- [Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime): the project's realtime from any server
- [Modules & Dependency Injection](/docs/backend/modules): providers, and what is refused at boot
