# Tasks

A task is work your backend puts on its machine's queue to be done once, now or later: a receipt mailed when an order is paid, a reminder a day after sign-up, a report built in the background. Mark a provider with `@Task({ name })` and give it a `run(payload, meta)` method; put a task with `Tasks.enqueue(TheClass, payload)`. The platform keeps the queue. When a task is due it wakes the machine and calls `run`; an attempt that fails is made again later, and a task with no attempt left is kept, to be tried again from Studio or the CLI.

Nothing polls: a machine with no task due sleeps. A [cron](/docs/backend/cron) that wakes every minute to look in a table for work keeps it awake for nothing, and takes up to a minute to notice.

## Quick example

The table the task works on:

```ts
// src/db/public.ts
import { defineSchema, defineTable, text, timestamp, uuid } from "palbase/backend";

// The app's own: no policy lets a user reach it, the service role does.
export const orders = defineTable("orders", {
  columns: { id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(), email: text(), receipt_sent_at: timestamp().nullable() },
});

export default defineSchema("public", { tables: [orders] });
```

```ts
// src/modules/orders/send-receipt.task.ts
import { Database, Log, Notifications, Task, TaskFailure, z, type TaskMeta } from "palbase/backend";
import { now } from "palgres";

const Receipt = z.object({ orderId: z.string().uuid() });

// Mail an order's receipt. A failed attempt is made again: up to five more, 10 s, 20 s, 40 s… apart.
@Task({ name: "send-receipt", payload: Receipt, retry: 5, concurrency: 10 })
export class SendReceipt {
  async run(payload: z.infer<typeof Receipt>, meta: TaskMeta): Promise<void> {
    const order = await Database.public.orders.findUnique({ where: { id: payload.orderId } });
    // The order is gone: no attempt will ever find it.
    if (!order) throw new TaskFailure(`order ${payload.orderId} is gone`);
    if (order.receipt_sent_at) return; // an attempt made again after one that finished
    await Notifications.email.send({ to: order.email, templateSlug: "receipt", variables: { order: order.id } });
    await Database.public.orders.update({ where: { id: order.id }, set: { receipt_sent_at: now() } });
    Log.info("receipt sent", { order: order.id, task: meta.id, attempt: meta.attempt });
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/orders/orders.controller.ts
import { Controller, Param, Post, Tasks } from "palbase/backend";
import { SendReceipt } from "./send-receipt.task";

@Controller("/orders")
export class OrdersController {
  @Post("/{id}/paid")
  async paid(@Param("id") id: string) {
    // Put once per order: the same key again answers the task already put.
    const task = await Tasks.enqueue(SendReceipt, { orderId: id }, { key: `receipt:${id}` });
    return { receipt: task.id };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/orders/orders.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { OrdersController } from "./orders.controller";
import { SendReceipt } from "./send-receipt.task";

@Module({ controllers: [OrdersController], providers: [SendReceipt] })
export class OrdersModule {}
```

A task type is a provider like any other: its module lists it in `providers`, and it takes its dependencies by constructor. A class is one task type.

## Putting a task

```ts
// src/modules/users/reminders.ts
import { Task, Tasks, type TaskMeta } from "palbase/backend";
import { SendReceipt } from "../orders/send-receipt.task";

@Task({ name: "remind" })
export class Remind {
  async run(payload: { userId: string }, meta: TaskMeta): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`remind ${payload.userId} (task ${meta.id})`);
  }
}

export async function put(orderId: string, userId: string, trialEnds: string): Promise<void> {
  await Tasks.enqueue(SendReceipt, { orderId });                       // due now
  await Tasks.enqueue(Remind, { userId }, { delay: 24 * 3600 });       // in a day
  await Tasks.enqueue(Remind, { userId }, { runAt: new Date(trialEnds) });
  await Tasks.enqueue(SendReceipt, { orderId }, { key: `receipt:${orderId}` });
}
```

What `Tasks.enqueue` takes is checked as it is written: the payload is what the class's `run` takes, and anything else does not compile. It answers the task as it was put — `id`, `state`, `runAt` — and `duplicate: true` when a task of the type was put already under the same key.

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| `delay` | Due this many seconds from now: 30 days at most |
| `runAt` | Due at this time: 30 days from now at most; a time past is now |
| `key` | Put once: another task of the type under the same key, until a day after the first is over, is not put — the first is answered |

A task carries 64 KiB of JSON at most, kept and handed to `run` as the bytes it was given: name what it works on — an id — and read it where it runs. A project's queues hold 100,000 tasks not yet done, or 256 MiB of what the tasks kept carry; past that, `Tasks.enqueue` is refused (`429`, `queue_full`) until some are done.

`Tasks.cancel(id)` takes a task that is waiting off the queue; `Tasks.get(id)` reads one as it is now. A task of another of the project's machines is put by its type's name: `Tasks.enqueue("rebuild-index", payload, { machine: "search" })`.

## Options

| Option | What it is | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | The task type: what its tasks are put under, kept under and called by. Letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, at most 64. | required |
| `payload` | A schema (zod, valibot, arktype — any Standard Schema) what a task carries is checked against before `run`; `run` is given what it gives | none |
| `timeout` | Seconds one attempt may take before it is a failed one: 1–900 | 60 |
| `retry` | Attempts after a failed one: 0–20 | 5 |
| `concurrency` | How many of its tasks the machine runs at once, however many copies it has: 1–50 | 5 |

A machine has at most 50 task types; two of one name are refused at boot.

## How a task goes

1. **Due.** When its time comes, the platform calls the machine for it — waking it if it sleeps — once the type has room under its `concurrency` (and the project under 50 at once). Tasks are taken type by type, oldest first: one type's backlog holds no other's back.
2. **Signed.** The call is `POST /_palbase/tasks/<name>`, signed with the machine's `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`, as the platform's other calls into a machine are. Nothing from the internet reaches it.
3. **Checked, then run in one transaction, as the service role.** What it carries is checked against `payload`, then `run` runs in a database transaction of its own, given its `TaskMeta`, with every row in reach as a [cron](/docs/backend/cron)'s is.
4. **Done, failed for good, or made again.**
   - `run` returned: the task succeeded.
   - What it carries is not what `payload` takes, or `run` threw a `TaskFailure`: the task **failed** at once and is not tried again — no attempt would do better.
   - `run` threw anything else, or ran past its `timeout`: the attempt failed and its transaction is rolled back. The next one is made after 10 s, then 20 s, 40 s, … an hour apart at most, until `retry` is spent; then the task **failed**.

A task that succeeded lets go of what it carried; only a task that may be tried again keeps it.

A task is delivered **at least once**: its `id` is the same through every attempt, and an attempt can run and still be counted as failed (the machine finished, its answer was lost). Key the work on the task's `id`, or on what it works on, as the receipt above does with `receipt_sent_at`.

A project whose machine time for the period is used up runs no task: a task due then fails ("its machine time for the period is used up"), and none is put meanwhile (`429`, `quota_exceeded`). Once the time comes back, the failed ones are tried again by hand — not run in a heap the moment it does.

## What a task is given

| Field of `TaskMeta` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `env` | The app's environment variables as it started, the platform's keys left out |
| `environmentId` | The project's id |
| `task` | The task type's name |
| `id` | The task's id: the same for every attempt of it |
| `attempt` | 1 for the first, then one more for each attempt made again |
| `createdAt` | When it was put on the queue |

## Failed tasks

A task that succeeded or was cancelled is kept a day; one that failed, 30 — with why its last attempt failed. On the machine's **Tasks** tab in Studio, or with the CLI:

| | Studio | CLI |
|---|---|---|
| The types, and what each one's queue holds | Task types | `palbase machines:tasks:types` |
| The tasks, of one state or type | Tasks, with Show | `palbase machines:tasks --state failed` |
| A task, with what it carries | | `palbase machines:tasks:get <id>` |
| Try a failed task again: due now, with as many attempts again as its type gives — its attempts counted on, not from zero | Retry | `palbase machines:tasks:retry <id>` |
| Take a waiting task off the queue: it is not run, nor tried again, and what it carried is let go | Cancel | `palbase machines:tasks:cancel <id>` |
| Put a task by hand | | `palbase machines:tasks:enqueue <type> --payload '<json>'` |

Trying again and cancelling are an admin's, as every change is; so is reading what a task carries — a member sees the queue, not what is in it.

## On your computer

Off the platform — the app started on your computer, or in a test — it runs its own tasks, in its own process, as the platform would: each when it is due, its type's `concurrency` kept, a failed attempt made again later, a key held a day. Nothing of that queue outlives the process. `Tasks.enqueue` of another machine's type is refused there.

## Without palbase/backend

Any program a machine runs takes tasks by answering two signed calls, as it takes [crons](/docs/machines/overview#crons-and-tasks); anything with the project's secret key puts them: `POST /machines/<machine>/tasks` with `{"task", "payload", "delay" | "run_at", "key"}`.

## Related

- [Cron](/docs/backend/cron): work on a schedule
- [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks): the platform's events, delivered as they happen
- [Database](/docs/backend/database): the transaction a task runs in



<!-- ===== backend/cache ===== -->

# Cache

Every project has a cache: short-lived entries, each a value a server worked out and wants again, kept by the platform rather than in your machine's memory. Every copy of a machine reads the same entries, a push does not empty them, and a machine that slept finds them when it wakes. In a `palbase/backend` app it is `Cache`; from any other server it is `createServer({ url, secretKey }).cache`, the cache module's calls as its contract states them. Only the secret key reaches it: an app never reads or writes the cache.

A cache is not a database. Every entry runs out, after thirty days at most, and an entry may be gone before its time, dropped to make room. What must not be lost belongs in a [database](/docs/backend/database).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/modules/products/products.service.ts
import { Cache, Database, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

type Product = { id: string; name: string; price_cents: number };

@Injectable()
export class ProductsService {
  /** The catalog, read from the database at most once every five minutes. */
  async catalog(): Promise<Product[]> {
    return Cache.getOrSet("catalog", 300, () => Database.$query<Product>("select id, name, price_cents from products order by name"));
  }

  /** After a change, the next read goes to the database again. */
  async changed(): Promise<void> {
    await Cache.del("catalog");
  }
}
```

## The `Cache` service

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `get<T>(key)` | The value, or `null` when there is none, or when the cache could not be reached |
| `set(key, value, ttl?)` | Writes the value for `ttl` seconds, replacing what was there and its time left. Without a `ttl` it lasts thirty days |
| `getOrSet(key, ttl, fn)` | Reads through: on a hit the value; on a miss `fn`'s, kept for `ttl` seconds |
| `incr(key)` | Adds one to the key's count and answers the new count |
| `del(key)` | Deletes the entry. Deleting what is not there is not an error |

- **A key** is UTF-8 text, 1 to 512 bytes. Every project has keys of its own: no key reaches another project's entries, so a key needs no prefix for that.
- **A value** is JSON, 512 KiB at most. What is kept is what `JSON.stringify` makes of it: a `Date` comes back as its ISO string, a class instance as its fields, `undefined` as `null`. A value written as `null` reads as `null` from `get`, the same as a miss; `getOrSet` counts it as a hit.
- **A `ttl`** is in seconds. A fraction is rounded up; none, `0` or less is thirty days, and more than thirty days is thirty days (`CACHE_MAX_TTL`, which `palbase/backend` exports).

### When the cache cannot be reached

The cache keeps three copies of the entries, one in each zone of the region. When the copy that takes the writes is lost, or stops answering, another takes over within a few seconds: a call made meanwhile waits for it, up to six seconds, and is answered then, instead of failing. An `incr` waited through a takeover is counted once. A copy that stops for maintenance hands over first, and an entry written before it is there after. A copy lost all at once has not handed over: the others receive each write a moment after it is answered, so a write answered in its last moment may be missing from the copy that takes over, an `incr`'s count among them. A count that must be exact belongs in a database.

The app is not stopped by a cache that is away either. A call that cannot reach it, or that is refused for now (`429`, `503`), is treated by what it is for:

| Call | When the cache is away |
|---|---|
| `get` | A miss: `null`, and a warning in the machine's log |
| `set` | The write is let go, with a warning |
| `getOrSet` | `fn` runs and its value is answered, not kept |
| `del` | Throws: the old value would come back after the delete said it was done |
| `incr` | Throws: there is no number to make up |

A read is sent again first, as every read of the server SDK is, waiting the `Retry-After` the cache asks for. Any other refusal, such as a key longer than 512 bytes or a value larger than 512 KiB, throws a `PalbaseError` from every call ([Server SDK](/docs/server/overview)).

### Reading through: `getOrSet`

On a miss, `fn` is called and its value kept for `ttl` seconds. Misses on the same key that arrive while `fn` runs, in the same process, wait for that one call: a hundred requests that miss at once work the value out once. The sharing is a process's own, so two copies of a machine that miss at the same moment each call `fn`. When `fn` throws, every caller waiting on it gets that error, and nothing is kept.

### Counting: `incr`

`incr` is atomic across every copy of the machine: two callers never get the same number.

```ts
// src/modules/exports/exports.service.ts
import { Cache, Injectable, TooManyRequests } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class ExportsService {
  /** A user's exports today, the fifth the last. */
  async allow(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    const day = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
    const n = await Cache.incr(`exports:${userId}:${day}`);
    if (n > 5) throw new TooManyRequests({ retryAfter: 3600 }, "five exports a day");
  }
}
```

- An entry that is not there, or holds something other than a whole number, counts from zero.
- A count keeps the time its entry had left; a new count lasts thirty days. A count started with `set(key, 0, ttl)` ends with that `ttl`.
- A count stops at fifteen digits: one more is refused (`409 count_too_large`) and nothing is counted.
- `incr` is never sent again by the client. When the cache was reached but did not answer, the count may have been taken: read the entry before counting again.

For a route's own limit on how often a caller may call it, use the route's `rateLimit` ([Controllers & Routing](/docs/backend/controllers)), not a count of your own.

## Room in the cache

An entry weighs what the cache keeps for it: its value plus three times its key, a quarter more, and 320 bytes. A project's entries together weigh at most its quota, 25 MiB.

A write past the quota does not fail. The project's own entries nearest their end are dropped to make room, and the write's answer says how many (`evicted`). When the cache as a whole is full, the project that weighs the most gives back first; a project under its share keeps its entries. One entry larger than the whole quota is refused (`413 entry_too_large`).

A project reads and writes so many bytes a second (8 MiB read, 2 MiB written; the second's first call is taken whatever its size), and makes at most its requests per second of calls to the cache. Past either, a call is `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After`.

The cache's calls are not counted as the project's API requests, and they are not lines of its request [log](/docs/getting-started/logs). What the project's entries weigh is metered as **Cache memory**, and the bytes its reads carry out as **Cache reads**, on the project's **Settings › Usage** in Studio ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)). A deleted environment's entries are deleted with it.

## From any server

`createServer(...).cache` is the cache module's calls, with the secret key:

```ts
// server/cache.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const written = await palbase.cache.putCacheEntry({ query: { key: "greeting" }, body: { value: { text: "hello" }, ttl: 600 } });
console.log(written.data.expires_in, written.data.evicted);

const read = await palbase.cache.getCacheEntry({ query: { key: "greeting" } });
if (read.data.found) console.log(read.data.value, read.data.expires_in);

const usage = await palbase.cache.getCacheUsage();
console.log(usage.data.bytes, usage.data.limit_bytes, usage.data.entries);
```

| Call | HTTP | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `getCacheEntry({ query: { key } })` | `GET /cache/entry?key=` | `{ found, value?, expires_in? }`: a key with no entry is `found: false`, not an error |
| `putCacheEntry({ query: { key }, body: { value, ttl? } })` | `PUT /cache/entry?key=` | `{ expires_in, evicted }`. A `ttl` is 1 to 2592000 seconds; outside it, `400` |
| `deleteCacheEntry({ query: { key } })` | `DELETE /cache/entry?key=` | `{ deleted }`: whether there was an entry |
| `incrementCacheEntry({ query: { key } })` | `POST /cache/entry/increment?key=` | `{ value }`: the new count |
| `getCacheUsage()` | `GET /cache/usage` | `{ bytes, limit_bytes, entries }`: what the live entries weigh, the quota, how many there are |

The key is a query parameter, which the request's log line does not keep. A publishable key is refused (`403 secret_key_required`), and so is the secret key sent with a user's token beside it. A cache that could not be reached is `503 cache_unavailable`, and one that takes no more at this moment `503 cache_busy`; both carry `Retry-After`.

## In tests

`withServices({ Cache: … })` gives the code a cache of the test's own ([Testing](/docs/backend/testing#the-services-the-code-reads-withservices)). A test that does not give one, and runs code that reads `Cache`, is refused by name: the real calls would reach a platform no test serves.

## Related

- [Database](/docs/backend/database) — what must be kept
- [Machines](/docs/machines/overview) — copies, sleep, and what a copy keeps in its own memory
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals, retries
- [Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits) — what is metered



<!-- ===== backend/translations ===== -->

# Translations

Write the sentences your backend says to people in one language, and `t()` answers each request in the language its caller reads: the first of their languages your app has a translation for, and the language you wrote it in otherwise.

```ts
import { Controller, Post, t } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/payments")
export class PaymentsController {
  @Post("/charge")
  charge() {
    // …
    return { message: t("Kartınız reddedildi ({{amount}} ₺)", { amount: 50 }) };
  }
}
```

The sentence itself is the key. `{{name}}` takes a value from the second argument; `{{{name}}}` is left as it is.

## How a request's language is chosen

Every request says its user's languages in `Accept-Language`, best first: a browser sends them, and the iOS and Android SDKs send the device's languages in its order. For each sentence, `t()` takes the first of them your app has a translation of, then the language the sentences are written in.

Each language is matched as a table names it, from the most specific down: `pt-BR` reads `pt-BR.json`, then `pt.json`; `zh-TW` reads `zh-TW.json`, then `zh-Hant.json`, then `zh.json`. A device's regional preferences (`fr-FR-u-mu-celsius`) are not part of the language.

The answer says which: `Content-Language: en` (a list when one answer mixes languages; unless your handler set it). An app with `palbase/strings/` answers every request with `Vary: Accept-Language`, so a cache never hands one user's language to another.

`t()` outside a request — a scheduled job, an event hook, a gateway, the app's start — has no caller to ask, and says the sentence as it is written.

## palbase/strings/

The translations live in your repository, next to the code, one file per language:

```text
palbase/strings/
  _meta.json   { "version": 3, "source": "tr" }
  en.json      { "Kartınız reddedildi ({{amount}} ₺)": "Your card was declined ({{amount}} ₺)" }
  de.json      { "Kartınız reddedildi ({{amount}} ₺)": "" }
```

- `_meta.json` names the language the sentences are written in (`source`). It has no file of its own: its text is the key.
- Each other language is `<language>.json`, named as the language is written (`en`, `de`, `pt-BR`): `"sentence": "translation"`.
- An empty translation is not one yet: that sentence is said in the source language.

Correct a translation in the file and deploy, as any change to your app: the machine reads the table when it starts. The build checks it too: a table that breaks a rule — a file named `EN.json`, a translation that is not a string, a file for the source language, a table still in the earlier format below — stops the build before it takes traffic, and the log names the file and the rule.

Dockerfiles made by `palbase init` 0.3.1 or later copy `palbase/` into the image; check yours, or one you wrote, for `COPY palbase ./palbase`. An app that started without a table says so, with where it looked, the first time `t()` is called.

## Keep the files with the code

Run it in your backend's directory (or below it: it works in the nearest directory up with a `package.json`):

```bash
npx palbase strings --source tr --add en   # start the table: the sentences are in Turkish; en.json is made, empty
npx palbase strings --translate            # fill what is empty
npx palbase strings                        # after a change to the code
npx palbase strings --add de               # one more language
```

`palbase strings` reads every `t("…")` your backend calls — `t` imported from `palbase/backend`, or from a module of your app that re-exports it — with the TypeScript compiler. A sentence new in the code is added to every language's file, empty; a translation is kept. A sentence the code no longer calls is kept too, with its translations, and listed: `--prune` takes it out of every file. Run it again and it changes nothing.

What it cannot read is pointed out, with its file and line: a `t()` whose sentence is not written out (`t(message)` — no file can hold its translation: write the sentence itself, its values as `{{name}}`), and a `t` imported from a module it does not follow (a path alias such as `@/lib/i18n`). If it reads no sentence at all while the table has some, it changes nothing.

A table in the format of the earlier Palbase (`"version": 2`, a `{"value", "state"}` object for each sentence) is written in this one the first time you run it, every translation kept; until then the app does not start with it.

## Translate with your AI module

```bash
npx palbase strings --translate
```

Each empty translation of a sentence the code calls is sent to your environment's AI module — the same models, usage and cost as any other call your project makes, under your own key on this computer — and written into the file as it comes back. On the production environment it asks first: its AI budget is the one your app's own calls use. A translation that does not keep every `{{placeholder}}` of its sentence, or comes back empty, is not taken: it is listed, and stays empty. The command ends with what it cost, from your environment's AI usage (or says when not every call is there yet).

A translation is used as it is written: read the files' diff before you commit it, and correct it there.



<!-- ===== backend/test-users ===== -->

# Test Users

A **test user** is a real user of the project — it signs in, gets tokens, owns rows and files — made with the project's secret key for testing, and marked as such everywhere it goes. Test users skip the breach check and the password's minimum length, are not counted as active users, and only test users can be deleted through the test-user route, so a cleanup that goes wrong cannot take a real account with it. Your backend sees the mark: `user.test` is `true` on a test user's requests.

Whatever sign-in your app uses, a test user can go through it: it is made of the kind the sign-in asks for (passwordless, unverified, with a second factor, with a phone), and **what the platform sends it is kept for it** — its sign-in link, its verification and second factor's codes, your project's own mail and texts — in its [test inbox](#its-mail-and-texts), where a test reads the code or the link.

## Quick example

```ts
// scripts/make-test-users.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

// Three users with generated credentials, and an access token each.
const made = await palbase.auth.adminCreateTestUsers({ body: { count: 3, with_tokens: true } });
for (const u of made.data.users) {
  // The password is shown once: keep what you need now.
  console.log(u.user_id, u.email, u.password, u.access_token?.slice(0, 16));
}
```

## Making them

`POST /admin/test-users` (`auth.adminCreateTestUsers`) creates up to 1000 at a time — **all of them, or none** — and answers their credentials once: a password is never retrievable afterwards.

| Body | What it makes |
|---|---|
| `{ count: n }` | `n` users with generated emails and passwords. |
| `{ users: [{ email, password }] }` | Users with exactly these credentials; `users` wins when both are sent. |
| `{ users: [{ email, password, phone, otp }] }` | Also a verified phone, and the fixed six-digit code that phone accepts at sign-in — so a phone sign-in can be tested without a text being sent. |
| `with_tokens: true` | Also an access token per user, for calls made as them. |

An entry of `users` says the kind of user; what it leaves out is made — an address (`test-…@test.invalid`, which receives no mail: its mail is kept in its test inbox), a password, a phone's fixed code:

| Field | The user it makes |
|---|---|
| `email` | Its own address. One of yours gets its mail too — and the copy is kept. |
| `password` / `passwordless: true` | A password of yours, or none: it signs in by a link, a code or a passkey. |
| `email_verified: false` | Unverified: your app's verification is tested on it. |
| `phone` (+ `otp`) | A verified phone, texted nothing: it accepts its fixed six-digit code (made when `otp` is left out) at a phone sign-in and as an SMS second factor. |
| `email_otp` | A fixed six-digit code its email accepts — its verification code and its email second factor — for a person with no inbox to read, such as an app store's reviewer. The mail is still sent, carrying it. |
| `mfa: "totp" \| "sms" \| "email"` | A second factor from the start. `totp` answers its key once (`totp_secret`, `totp_url`): a test makes its codes with it. `sms` is its phone. |

Each answered user carries `user_id`, `email`, `email_verified`, its `password` (none when passwordless), what else it was made with (`phone`, `otp`, `email_otp`, `mfa`, `totp_secret`) and, with `with_tokens`, `access_token` — shown this once.

```ts
// scripts/make-reviewer.ts — an account an app store's reviewer signs in with:
// a password, and an email second factor whose code they are given.
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });
const [reviewer] = (await palbase.auth.adminCreateTestUsers({
  body: { users: [{ email: "review@yourapp.com", password: "a-long-review-password", mfa: "email", email_otp: "246802" }] },
})).data.users;
console.log(reviewer.user_id, reviewer.email_otp); // what the reviewer is given
```

| Refusal | Why |
|---|---|
| `409 user_exists` | An email is already taken (nothing was made). |
| `409 test_user_cap_exceeded` | The batch would take the project past its test-user cap (its test users and its unused sign-up addresses). |
| `400 invalid_request` | Neither a positive `count` nor `users`; a kind no user can have — passwordless with a password, a fixed code that is not six digits, a phone's code with no phone, a second factor it cannot have (`sms` with no phone, `email` unverified). |

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header to make the creation safe to retry: the same key and the same request answer the first result again instead of creating twice. A fixture made with chosen emails is easy to make *if missing* — treat `409 user_exists` as "already there".

`PUT /admin/test-users/phone` (`adminSetTestUserPhone`) gives an existing test user, found by email, a verified phone and its fixed code; setting the same again succeeds, and an email that is not a test user's is `404 test_user_not_found`.

## Its mail and texts

Every email and text the project sends a test user is kept for it for 7 days — auth's sign-in links and codes, its resets and verifications, your project's own sends — and read with the secret key: `GET /notify/test-users/{user_id}/messages` (`notify.listTestUserMessages`, `palbase auth:test-users:messages <id>`, Studio's **Messages** of a test account). Each message answers what it said (`subject`, `text`, `html`), the `variables` its template had, and the `code` and `link` it carried, picked out.

A made address (`…@test.invalid`) is mailed nothing, and a test user's phone is texted nothing — the kept copy is the message; an address of yours is mailed as well (`delivered: true`). A user who is not a test user is refused, `403 not_a_test_user`: no one else's mail is kept.

```ts
// scripts/read-a-sign-in-link.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });
const [user] = (await palbase.auth.adminCreateTestUsers({ body: { users: [{ passwordless: true }] } })).data.users;
await fetch(`${process.env.PALBASE_URL}/auth/magic-link`, { method: "POST", headers: { apikey: process.env.PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY!, "content-type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ email: user.email }) });
const [mail] = (await palbase.notify.listTestUserMessages({ path: { user_id: user.user_id }, query: { channel: "email" } })).data.messages;
const token = new URL(mail.link!).searchParams.get("token"); // the link the user would tap
console.log(mail.code, token);
```

## Testing a sign-up

Your app's sign-up form opens a new account — a real one, counted, its mail sent. A **sign-up address** makes it a test user instead: `POST /admin/test-users/addresses` (`palbase auth:test-users:address`, Studio's **Sign-up address**) answers `signup-…@test.invalid`; typed into the form, the account it opens is a test user — its token says `test`, it is not counted as an active user, and its verification mail is kept in its test inbox, never sent.

Only the secret key makes one: each holds a place of the project's test-user cap until it is used — once — or lapses, a day after it was made. A sign-up with any other address opens an ordinary user.

## Sign-in with Google, Apple and others

A provider's sign-in goes through the provider's own screen, which a test user cannot pass: test it with the provider's own test accounts (Google's OAuth test users, an Apple sandbox account). What comes after the sign-in — your app as a signed-in user — is tested with a test user's token.

## In a route

A test user's token says `test: true`, and `palbase/backend` hands it to the route as `user.test`:

```ts
// src/modules/admin/reset.controller.ts
import { Controller, Forbidden, Post, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/admin")
export class ResetController {
  // A route only the suite may call: every other user is turned away.
  @Post("/reset-demo")
  reset(@User() user: UserT): { reset: true } {
    if (!user.test) throw new Forbidden("this route serves test users only");
    return { reset: true };
  }
}
```

The flag is the platform's, set when the user was made with the secret key: a user who signs up cannot give it to themselves.

## Calling your backend as one

With `with_tokens`, each user's `access_token` goes on a call to your machine as `Authorization: Bearer …`, exactly as a signed-in app's does:

```ts
// scripts/call-as-test-user.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });
const [user] = (await palbase.auth.adminCreateTestUsers({ body: { count: 1, with_tokens: true } })).data.users;

const res = await fetch("https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio/notes", {
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${user.access_token}` },
});
console.log(res.status, await res.json());

await palbase.auth.adminDeleteTestUser({ path: { uid: user.user_id } });
```

They sign in like anyone else, too — with `palbase/web`'s `pb.auth.signIn(email, password)`, or by phone with their fixed code.

## Listing and removing them

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `adminListTestUsers()` | Every test user of the project, newest first, whole: their number is capped, so the list is one answer. Each carries `is_test: true`. |
| `adminDeleteTestUser({ path: { uid } })` | Deletes a test user and everything that belongs to it. A user who is not a test user is refused, `403 not_a_test_user`. |

Deleting a test user is a user deletion like any other: it emits `user.deleted` (with `is_test: true`), so your backend forgets them as it forgets anyone ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)), and storage objects owned by them go with them — its kept mail too.

## Made for a test run

A test run makes the users its tests act as, and deletes them when it ends: `palbase test --users alice,bob` on your computer, a machine's `test_users` on the platform before each new build takes traffic. Each is a test user like these, at an address of the run's own, with its access token; a test acts as one with `api.signInAs("alice")` ([Testing](/docs/backend/testing#over-http-api-as-test-users)).

## From Studio

Studio's **Test accounts** tab under Authentication makes test logins of the kind a sign-in asks for, lists and searches them, shows each one's **Messages**, and makes a **Sign-up address**, for the environment you are in.

## Related

- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication) — `@User()`, `user.test`, and how a token is checked
- [Testing](/docs/backend/testing) — testing a backend, with and without a network
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — `createServer`, refusals and `Idempotency-Key`
- [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth) — signing in as one from an app



<!-- ===== backend/testing ===== -->

# Testing

A backend is tested where it runs, and the same tests run in three places: on your computer (`bun test`), against your app as test users made for the run (`palbase test`), and on the platform against **each new build before it takes traffic**. `palbase/backend/test` is the kit they are written with:

| Name | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `isolated()` | a service built with the dependencies the test chooses, nothing else |
| `withServices()` | the services the code reads (`Database`, `Cache`, `Storage`, …) given by the test |
| `fakeDatabase()` | a database in memory, for `withServices({ Database })` |
| `api`, `testRun` | the app over HTTP, as the run's test users (`api.signInAs("alice")`) |
| `createTestApi`, `TestApiError` | a client of your own; what a refusal throws |

The HTTP half is `palbase/server/testing` — the same names, for a backend written with any framework (NestJS, Express, …). The tests run with **Bun's test runner** (`bun:test`), as the platform runs them: Bun keeps the decorator metadata `isolated()` reads a constructor's dependencies from. `palbase init` starts a backend with its tests in `tests/` and `"test": "bun test ./tests"`.

## Unit tests: `isolated()`

A service takes its dependencies by constructor. `isolated()` builds the class the test asks for, with what `.with()` gives in place of a dependency — however deep it is — and every other one built as the app builds it:

```ts
// src/modules/mail/mailer.ts
import { Injectable, Log } from "palbase/backend";

export abstract class Mailer {
  abstract send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void>;
}

@Injectable()
export class LogMailer extends Mailer {
  async send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void> {
    Log.info("mail", { to, subject });
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/mail/welcome.service.ts
import { BadRequest, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";
import { Mailer } from "./mailer";

@Injectable()
export class WelcomeService {
  constructor(private readonly mailer: Mailer) {}

  async welcome(email: string): Promise<void> {
    if (!email.includes("@")) throw new BadRequest({ fields: [{ field: "email", message: "not an address" }] });
    await this.mailer.send(email, "Welcome");
  }
}
```

```ts
// tests/welcome.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { BadRequest } from "palbase/backend";
import { isolated } from "palbase/backend/test";
import { Mailer } from "../src/modules/mail/mailer";
import { WelcomeService } from "../src/modules/mail/welcome.service";

class RecordingMailer extends Mailer {
  readonly sent: string[] = [];
  async send(to: string): Promise<void> {
    this.sent.push(to);
  }
}

describe("WelcomeService", () => {
  it("mails the address it is given", async () => {
    const mailer = new RecordingMailer();
    await isolated().with(Mailer, mailer).get(WelcomeService).welcome("ada@example.com");
    expect(mailer.sent).toEqual(["ada@example.com"]);
  });

  it("refuses what is not an address, naming the field", async () => {
    const welcome = isolated().with(Mailer, new RecordingMailer()).get(WelcomeService);
    await expect(welcome.welcome("ada")).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(BadRequest);
  });
});
```

Each `isolated()` is a container of its own: one instance of each class within it, nothing shared with another test or with the app. Two classes that need each other to be built are refused, naming the circle; `.with()` one of them and there is none.

## The services the code reads: `withServices()`

`Database`, [`Cache`](/docs/backend/cache), `Secrets`, `Storage`, `Notifications`, `Flags`, `Realtime` and `Log` are read where the code needs them, not passed in. `withServices(given, fn)` runs `fn` as a request does, with the services given: `Database` is the client given (`fakeDatabase().raw`), each other service the object given. A service the code reads and the test did not give is refused **by name** — its real calls would reach a platform no test serves — and `Log` writes as it always does.

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.service.ts
import { Cache, Database, Injectable } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class NotesService {
  async count(owner: string): Promise<number> {
    const cached = await Cache.get<number>(`notes:${owner}`);
    if (cached !== null) return cached;
    const n = await Database.$count("notes", { owner });
    await Cache.set(`notes:${owner}`, n, 60);
    return n;
  }
}
```

```ts
// tests/notes.service.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { fakeDatabase, isolated, withServices, type RuntimeServices } from "palbase/backend/test";
import { NotesService } from "../src/modules/notes/notes.service";

describe("NotesService", () => {
  it("counts a user's notes, and keeps the count for a minute", async () => {
    const db = fakeDatabase();
    db.seed("notes", [
      { id: "n1", owner: "ada", title: "one" },
      { id: "n2", owner: "ada", title: "two" },
      { id: "n3", owner: "bob", title: "three" },
    ]);
    const kept = new Map<string, unknown>();
    const cache = {
      get: async (key: string) => kept.get(key) ?? null,
      set: async (key: string, value: unknown) => void kept.set(key, value),
    } as unknown as RuntimeServices["Cache"];

    const n = await withServices({ Database: db.raw, Cache: cache }, () => isolated().get(NotesService).count("ada"));
    expect(n).toBe(2);
    expect(kept.get("notes:ada")).toBe(2);
  });
});
```

`withServices` also carries a string table for `t()` ([Translations](/docs/backend/translations)): `withServices(given, fn, { strings, acceptLanguage: "en" })`, with `loadStringsTable(root)` reading the project's `palbase/strings`.

### A database in memory: `fakeDatabase()`

`fakeDatabase()` answers the engine's operations with the engine's filters and refusals: `seed(table, rows)` puts rows in, `inserted`, `updated` and `deleted` say what the code wrote, and raw SQL is recorded in `queries`, not run. What it cannot answer as Postgres would — a unique key, a relation, a cursor, search, an `$atomic`'s isolation — it refuses by name. It has no schema (no column's default, type or constraint is applied), it reads text of digits as the number it spells, it gives rows in the order they were written unless `orderBy` says otherwise, and there is no row-level security. What depends on those is tested against the app over HTTP, or against a Postgres of your own (below).

## Over HTTP: `api`, as test users

`api` calls the app under test where the run says it answers (`PALBASE_TEST_BASE_URL`), as the test users the run made for it (`PALBASE_TEST_IDENTITIES`, each with its access token). `testRun.stack` says whether an app answers: an HTTP test skips itself where none does, so `bun test` passes on a computer with no app started.

```ts
// tests/notes.http.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { api, TestApiError, testRun } from "palbase/backend/test";

describe.skipIf(!testRun.stack)("notes, over HTTP", () => {
  it("are each user's own", async () => {
    const title = `a test run's note ${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
    await api.signInAs("alice");
    const note = await api.post<{ id: string }>("/notes", { title });
    expect((await api.get<{ title: string }>(`/notes/${note.id}`)).title).toBe(title);

    await api.signInAs("bob");
    const refused = await api.get(`/notes/${note.id}`).catch((e: unknown) => e);
    expect(refused).toBeInstanceOf(TestApiError);
    expect((refused as TestApiError).status).toBe(404);
  });

  it("refuses a caller with no token", async () => {
    api.asAnonymous();
    const refused = await api.post("/notes", { title: "x" }).catch((e: unknown) => e);
    expect((refused as TestApiError).status).toBe(401);
  });
});
```

- `api.signInAs(name)` acts as the run's test user of that name; `api.asAnonymous()` as no one. `api.signIn({ email, password })` signs in at the project's auth (it needs a publishable key: `PALBASE_TEST_API_KEY`).
- A refusal throws `TestApiError`: its `status`, its code (`error`), its `data` and the whole `body`, the platform's envelope.
- `testRun.minted("alice")` says whether the run made that user. `createTestApi({ baseUrl, identities, … })` is a client of your own, for a test that calls two apps.

### A sign-in's link or code

What the project sends a test user — a magic link, a verification or second factor's code, a password reset — is kept for it, never sent to a made address: a test reads it with the secret key or an environment token (`GET /notify/test-users/{user_id}/messages`, `palbase auth:test-users:messages <id>`) and goes on with the `link` or `code` it picks out — see [Its mail and texts](/docs/backend/test-users#its-mail-and-texts). A test of your app's sign-up form types in a sign-up address (`palbase auth:test-users:address`): the account it opens is a test user, not a counted one — see [Testing a sign-up](/docs/backend/test-users#testing-a-sign-up).

## Running them

| Where | How | What runs |
|---|---|---|
| Your computer | `bun test` | the unit tests; the HTTP tests skip themselves |
| Your computer, against your app | `palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url http://localhost:8080 -- bun test ./tests` | all of them, as test users made for this run in the environment you use, deleted when the command ends — Ctrl-C too |
| As a machine runs them | `palbase test --machine backend --base-url http://localhost:8080` | the machine's own test command, as its test users (it shows the command and asks before running it; `-y` says yes) |
| An agent with an environment's token, against the deployed machine | `PALBASE_TOKEN=pbe_… palbase test --users alice,bob --base-url https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio -- bun test ./tests` | all of them, against the version that serves, as test users made with the token (scope `auth:test-users`) and deleted when the command ends. No key is made: the command gets no `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, so it starts no app of its own. In `main`, `-y` confirms the test users made there |
| The platform | `palbase machines:update backend --test-command "bun test ./tests" --test-users alice,bob` | every new build, against the new version itself, before it takes traffic |

On the platform the tests run against the new version **as it will run** — its env, its secrets, its database, after its migration has started: they pass and it takes traffic; one fails and the build fails, naming the test, while the machine keeps serving the version it runs (see [Builds](/docs/machines/builds#tests-before-it-takes-traffic)). The tests write where the app writes, so write them as a real user's session: a note of their own, not a table they expect empty. What a test user owns goes with them — the run deletes its users, and a deleted user's rows are erased (`ownedByUser()`, on `user.deleted`).

The image has to carry the tests: `palbase init`'s `Dockerfile` copies `tests/`, and Bun's types are a dev dependency the image does not install.

When a test fails with a `500`, its `TestApiError` names the request's id (`request_id`). What the app printed for it — its error, its stack, on a line with that id — is in the build's log after what the tests printed (`palbase machines:builds:log <build>`), and in the machine's log as `source: "test"`: `palbase machines:logs <name> --search <request_id>` finds it. An environment token with `machines:logs` reads both.

## Without the network

The kit tests the app as it is deployed. The app can also be tested inside the test's own process — its routes, auth, validation and refusals answering a `Request` through `handle()`, no port opened.

### The app in the process: `handle()`

`PalbaseFactory.create` answers a `Request` through the app's `handle()`, the same path a request from the network takes. A test builds the app with its own environment, on a free port, without exiting on a crash:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

export const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
export type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): { owner: string; title: string } {
    return { owner: user.id, title: body.title };
  }

  @Get("/health", { auth: false })
  health(): { ok: true } {
    return { ok: true };
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes.controller";

@Module({ controllers: [NotesController] })
export class NotesModule {}
```

```ts
// tests/notes.handle.test.ts
import { afterAll, beforeAll, describe, expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { PalbaseFactory, type PalbaseApplication } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesModule } from "../src/modules/notes/notes.module";

const env = {
  PALBASE_URL: "https://abcd1234.palbase.studio",
  PALBASE_PROJECT_ID: "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
  PALBASE_SECRET_KEY: "pb_abcd1234_s0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
};

let app: PalbaseApplication;
beforeAll(async () => {
  app = await PalbaseFactory.create(NotesModule, { env, port: 0, host: "127.0.0.1", exitOnFatal: false });
});
afterAll(() => app.close());

const call = (path: string, init?: RequestInit) => app.handle(new Request(`http://app.test${path}`, init));

describe("notes over HTTP", () => {
  it("serves a public route", async () => {
    const res = await call("/notes/health");
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(await res.json()).toEqual({ ok: true });
  });

  it("refuses a caller with no token, in the envelope", async () => {
    const res = await call("/notes", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ title: "x" }) });
    expect(res.status).toBe(401);
    expect(await res.json()).toMatchObject({ error: "unauthorized", status: 401 });
  });

  it("lists the routes it serves", () => {
    expect(app.routes).toEqual(["POST /notes", "GET /notes/health"]);
  });
});
```

- `env` stands in for what the platform and the project's Secrets give a machine. Nothing is called with these values until a route needs the project: a route with no token never asks for the project's keys.
- `port: 0` takes a free port, so tests can run side by side. `exitOnFatal: false` leaves a crash to the test runner instead of exiting the process.
- `app.close()` stops it and runs every `onShutdown()`.

### Signed-in requests, without the network

A signed-in route needs a token the app verifies against a key set. In a test the key set is the test's own: `createApp` (the engine `PalbaseFactory` serves) takes a `TokenVerifier` you build, and `createServer` takes a `fetch` that answers the project's module calls however the test says. A helper that makes all three:

```ts
// tests/project.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";
import { TokenVerifier } from "palbase/backend";

export const url = "https://abcd1234.palbase.studio";
export const projectId = "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555";

const b64 = (bytes: Uint8Array | string): string =>
  Buffer.from(typeof bytes === "string" ? new TextEncoder().encode(bytes) : bytes).toString("base64url");

/** A signing key of the test's own, the key set that publishes it, and tokens it signs. */
export async function testProject(answer: (url: URL, init: RequestInit) => Response = () => Response.json({})) {
  const pair = (await crypto.subtle.generateKey({ name: "ECDSA", namedCurve: "P-256" }, true, ["sign", "verify"])) as CryptoKeyPair;
  const jwk = { ...(await crypto.subtle.exportKey("jwk", pair.publicKey)), kid: "test", alg: "ES256", use: "sig" };

  const verifier = new TokenVerifier({
    issuer: url,
    projectId,
    fetch: async () => Response.json({ keys: [jwk] }),
    // Every session stands; a test of sign-out answers false for its session.
    standing: async () => true,
  });

  async function token(userId: string, claims: Record<string, unknown> = {}): Promise<string> {
    const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
    const body = {
      iss: url, aud: [url], sub: userId, exp: now + 900, iat: now, auth_time: now,
      email: `${userId}@example.com`, email_verified: true, role: "authenticated",
      session_id: `ses_${userId}`, project_id: projectId, ...claims,
    };
    const head = b64(JSON.stringify({ alg: "ES256", kid: "test", typ: "JWT" }));
    const payload = b64(JSON.stringify(body));
    const signature = await crypto.subtle.sign({ name: "ECDSA", hash: "SHA-256" }, pair.privateKey, new TextEncoder().encode(`${head}.${payload}`));
    return `${head}.${payload}.${b64(new Uint8Array(signature))}`;
  }

  // `Palbase.*` inside the app: each call answered by `answer`, sent once.
  const server = createServer({
    url,
    secretKey: "pb_abcd1234_s0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    fetch: async (input, init) => answer(new URL(String(input)), init ?? {}),
    retry: { attempts: 1, maxWaitSeconds: 0 },
  });

  return { verifier, token, server };
}
```

```ts
// tests/notes.signed-in.test.ts
import { describe, expect, it } from "bun:test";
import { createApp } from "palbase/backend";
import { testProject } from "./project";
import { NotesModule } from "../src/modules/notes/notes.module";

describe("notes for a signed-in user", () => {
  it("takes the user from the token", async () => {
    const project = await testProject();
    const app = createApp({ modules: [NotesModule], verifier: project.verifier, server: project.server });
    await app.start();

    const res = await app.handle(
      new Request("http://app.test/notes", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${await project.token("usr_ada")}` },
        body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Ship it" }),
      }),
    );
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(await res.json()).toEqual({ owner: "usr_ada", title: "Ship it" });

    // A refusal the schema makes, with the field it names.
    const bad = await app.handle(
      new Request("http://app.test/notes", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${await project.token("usr_ada")}` },
        body: JSON.stringify({ title: "" }),
      }),
    );
    expect(bad.status).toBe(400);
    expect(await bad.json()).toMatchObject({ error: "bad_request", data: { fields: [{ field: "title" }] } });
    await app.stop();
  });
});
```

`createApp` takes the same settings the bootstrap does (`auth`, `rateLimit`, `maxBodyBytes`, `cors`, `webhookSecret`) and builds the container at once, so a wiring mistake throws right there. `start()` runs every `onStart()`, and `stop()` runs every `onShutdown()`. It opens no port. To test an [`@On` handler](/docs/backend/hooks), give it a `webhookSecret` and hand it a signed delivery.

> **Note:** Classes are recorded process-wide when their files are imported. Build each test file's app from modules that own every `@Controller`, `@Injectable()` and `@On` class that file's imports bring in, or the build stops with `unowned class`.

### Against a Postgres of your own

`Database` is the request's transaction against a real Postgres, so a test that reaches it needs one: Postgres 18, with the roles the platform's databases have, and the app's schema migrated into it. The roles, made once:

```sql
CREATE ROLE anon NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE authenticated NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE service_role NOLOGIN BYPASSRLS;
CREATE ROLE app_owner LOGIN CREATEDB;
CREATE ROLE app_login LOGIN NOINHERIT;
GRANT anon, authenticated, service_role TO app_login;
```

Migrate it with the app itself, as a release does: run it once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start` and once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=complete`, each with `PALBASE_DB_OWNER_URL` naming the owner. Then build the app with `db: { schemas }` and `PALBASE_DB_URL` naming `app_login`. A migration run exits the process, so run it before the tests, not inside them. The default database driver is Bun's SQL: tests that run on Node give the app a driver of their own. See [Database](/docs/backend/database) and [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

# Overview

`palbase/web` is the Palbase client for web and JavaScript apps. One function, `createClient`, makes the client for one project, and the client holds every module an app uses: `auth` signs a person in and keeps them signed in, `flags` holds the flags' values for them, `analytics` records what they do, `consent` keeps what they allowed, `notify` takes the project's pushes, inbox and in-app messages, `purchases` holds what they bought, and `socket` is the project's one realtime connection. Your own backend's routes and gateways join it as `pb.<backend>` once `palbase apps:sync` has written the app its module. Every call goes through the client's one transport, which carries the publishable key, the signed-in user's access token, refreshes and retries.

The client is built with the **publishable** key, the one that ships in an app. It refuses a secret key outright, and the secret key belongs in [`palbase/server`](/docs/server/overview).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

// The project's address. The browser calls it directly, from a page on any site.
export const pb = createClient({
  url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
  // The environment's publishable key, from Studio's Settings › API keys.
  publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5",
});
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const result = await pb.auth.signIn("ada@example.com", "correct-horse-battery-staple");
if (result.mfaRequired) {
  console.log("a second factor is needed:", result.mfaRequired.factors);
} else {
  console.log("signed in as", result.user.id);
}

pb.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, session) => {
  console.log(event, session?.userId ?? "nobody");
});

// The flags' values for whoever is signed in now, kept current as they change.
if (pb.flags.bool("new_checkout", false)) console.log("the new checkout is on");
```

`signIn` puts the session in the client's store, and from then on every call that acts for the user carries the user's access token. The client refreshes that token before it lapses, once, however many calls ask at the same moment and however many tabs share the session.

## Install

The web SDK is `palbase/web`, a part of the npm package `palbase`: `npm install palbase` (or `bun add palbase`).

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "palbase": "^0.10.0"
  }
}
```

A caret on a `0.x` version stays within that minor version: `^0.10.0` takes `0.10.1`, never `0.11.0`.

It is compiled JavaScript with its type declarations: any bundler takes it as it is (Next.js, Vite, esbuild — no setting). A browser or React Native bundle that imports `palbase/server`, `palbase/ai` or `palbase/backend` gets a module that throws: those parts hold the project's secret key or run a server, and never go into an app.

The package's web entry points:

| Import | What it is |
|---|---|
| `palbase/web` | `createClient` and everything it returns. |
| `palbase/web/ssr` | The session in cookies, for an app whose server renders its pages: `createServerClient`, `createBrowserClient`, `keepSession`. See [Next.js](/docs/web/nextjs). |
| `palbase/web/vite` | The Vite plugin: builds each mode against the environment you name for it, from what `palbase apps:sync` wrote, and type-checks the app against that environment's backend first. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#building-for-an-environment). |
| `palbase/web/palbe` | What the module `palbase apps:sync` writes registers your backend with. Your own code does not import it. |
| `palbase/web/push-sw.js` | The service worker that shows the project's pushes. See [Notifications](/docs/web/notifications#the-service-worker). |
| `palbase/web/calls-ui` | The call screens, ready-made: `mountCallUI(pb.calls, options)`. See [Calls](/docs/web/calls#ready-made-screens). |
| `palbase/web/paywall` | A paywall's definition resolved and drawn in the page (`renderPaywall`), and its prices formatted: what `pb.purchases.paywall(placement)` draws with (its `render(container, options)`), for an app that draws one itself. |
| `palbase/web/message` | An in-app message's definition resolved and drawn: over the page (`presentMessage`) or as an inbox card (`renderMessage`). What `pb.notify` draws with, for an app that draws one itself. |

## `createClient(options)`

| Option | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | `string` | The project's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`: where the client sends its calls and opens its socket. It is an origin alone: `https`, or `http` for a loopback address, no path, query or fragment. |
| `publishableKey` | `string` | The project's publishable key, `pb_<ref>_c…`. A secret key (`pb_<ref>_s…`) throws `TypeError` before anything is sent, and so does anything that is not a publishable key. |
| `storage` | `SessionStore` | Where the session is kept. Default: `localStorage` under `palbase.session.<origin>` in a browser, memory anywhere else. |
| `refresh` | `"behind" \| "before" \| "never"` | When the access token is renewed. `behind` (the default): in the background while it still works, so no call waits. `before`: in front of the call that finds it about to lapse. `never`: not at all. `palbase/web/ssr` sets it for a server. |
| `fetch` | `typeof fetch` | The `fetch` the transport calls. Default: the global one. |
| `webSocket` | `typeof WebSocket` | The WebSocket constructor the socket uses. Default: the global one. |
| `xmlHttpRequest` | `typeof XMLHttpRequest` | What an upload that reports its progress is sent with, since `fetch` tells nothing of a body as it goes. Default: the page's own, unless you gave a `fetch`. |
| `webauthn` | `CredentialsLike` | What passkeys call. Default: `navigator.credentials`. |
| `retry` | `RetryPolicy` | `{ attempts, maxWaitSeconds }`. Default: 3 attempts, and a `Retry-After` longer than 30 s is not waited for. See [Error Handling](/docs/web/errors). |
| `analytics` | `boolean \| AnalyticsOptions` | Starts the browser's own measures: a page view per address (`pageViews`), web vitals (`webVitals`) and each `fetch` the page makes (`network`), all on once started; `appVersion` is kept with every event. Left out, none of them starts, and `pb.analytics.capture` still sends what you capture. See [Analytics](/docs/web/analytics). |
| `calls` | `CallsOptions` | How the person's calls go: the others' voices played by themselves (`playAudio`, the default) or left to the app. See [Calls](/docs/web/calls). |
| `consent` | `ConsentOptions` | What is collected before the person chooses (`start`), the version of the consent text the app shows (`textVersion`), and the app's own keys (`customKeys`). See [Consent](/docs/web/consent). |
| `appVersion` | `string` | The app's version as its users see it (`"2.4.1"`), sent with flag reads and paywall requests for the conditions that read it. Nothing is sent without one. |
| `appId` | `string` | The registered app's id, a UUID, as `palbase apps:sync` writes it into the app's settings: sent with paywall requests for placement rules that name an app. A slug throws `TypeError`. |
| `language` | `string \| string[]` | The language the app shows itself in (`"tr"`, `["pt-BR", "pt"]`), sent with every request as `Accept-Language`: what auth's emails, a flag's conditions, a paywall's rules and your backend's translations read. Default: the browser's own. |

What comes back:

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pb.auth` | Sign-up, sign-in, the session, second factors, passkeys, magic links, phone codes, password and email flows. Every client operation of the auth contract is also there, typed, as `pb.auth.api`. See [Auth](/docs/web/auth). |
| `pb.flags` | The project's flags and remote configuration, resolved for this app and whoever is signed in, kept current as they change. See [Flags](/docs/web/flags). |
| `pb.analytics` | Events the app captures, page views, the person's properties, and the browser's own measures once started. See [Analytics](/docs/web/analytics). |
| `pb.consent` | What the person allowed, key by key: their choices, kept in the browser and sent to the project. See [Consent](/docs/web/consent). |
| `pb.notify` | This browser's pushes (`push`), the signed-in person's inbox (`inbox`) and the project's in-app campaigns (`inApp`). See [Notifications](/docs/web/notifications). |
| `pb.calls` | The signed-in person's voice and video calls: made, rung, answered — one to one or in a group. See [Calls](/docs/web/calls). |
| `pb.purchases` | What the signed-in customer has, kept current; the catalog's offerings and paywalls; buying on the web with Stripe Checkout. See [Purchases on the web](/docs/purchases/web). |
| `pb.installation` | This browser's install of the app: `pb.installation.id`, the same until the site's storage is cleared. Analytics, flags, consent and pushes say it with what they send. |
| `pb.socket` | The project's realtime socket. It is opened the first time a channel is joined, never before. See [Realtime](/docs/web/realtime). |
| `pb.transport` | The transport every call above goes through. See [Calls the client has no method for](#calls-the-client-has-no-method-for). |
| `pb.setLanguage(language)` | Changes the language every request says from now on; `null` goes back to the browser's. |
| `pb.chatToolCall(chatId, callId)`, `pb.chatWorkspaceFile(chatId, path)` | A chat's whole tool answer, and a file of its workspace, read with the member's own session. See [Gateways](/docs/web/gateways#chat-gateways). |
| `pb.<backend>` | Your backend's routes and gateways, typed: `pb.backend.notes.create({ title })`, from the module `palbase apps:sync` writes the app. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls) and [Gateways](/docs/web/gateways). |

A client is one project. Make it once and import it where you need it: each client keeps its own socket and its own copy of the session. An app whose checkout runs `palbase apps:sync` has its client made for it: it imports `pb` from `palbase/<app>`, made with its environment's address and key, and gives it the options above with `connect(options)` ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#the-generated-module)).

## Calling the project from a browser

A page on any site calls the project's address directly, as a page calls Supabase or Firebase. Give `createClient` the project's address as `url`, and the client's calls and its socket go there from the browser.

What the address answers a browser:

- **A preflight** (`OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method`) is answered `204` and needs no key. It allows `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`, and the headers the browser asks for: `apikey`, `authorization`, `content-type`, `idempotency-key` and any other. The browser may keep the answer for a day (`Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400`).
- **Every answer** carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`: the module's own, and the platform's refusals too (`401`, `403`, `429`, `404 no_route`), so your code reads an error's status and body. These response headers are exposed to your code: `retry-after`, `x-request-id`, `etag`, `idempotent-replayed`, `www-authenticate`, `location`, `link`, `content-range`, `content-disposition`, `dpop-nonce`, `x-thumbhash`, `x-message-id`, `x-ratelimit-remaining` and `x-ratelimit-reset`.
- **No cookie** is read. A call carries the publishable key in the `apikey` header and the user's access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`. Leave `fetch`'s `credentials` at its default: a browser refuses `credentials: "include"` against an answer that allows any origin. A session kept in cookies (`palbase/web/ssr`) is still sent this way: the cookie is where the session is kept, for your own server to read, not how a call proves it.

**Call the project from the browser, not through your server.** The address the project counts is the caller's. Auth's limits are per address: so many sign-in attempts from one address in a few minutes, and a burst of failed sign-ins from one address blocks it for a while. Auth's proof-of-work is asked of an address that looks like a bot. Analytics and flags read the country from the address. A server that passes every user's calls on to the project makes all of its users one address: one person's failed sign-ins then lock everyone out, and every event is given the server's country.

Your own backend is different. A machine answers at its own address (`https://<name>-<ref>.app.palbase.studio`, or `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio` for the machine named `backend`), and the platform adds no CORS there: a `palbase/backend` app answers browsers itself, for the origins it names in `PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { cors: { origins: ["https://app.example.com"] } })`. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#cross-origin-calls).

## Calls the client has no method for

The client has a method for what an app does most. A few calls a browser may make have none: the signed-in user's notification preferences (`GET`/`PUT /notify/preferences`) and the topics they follow (`POST`/`DELETE /notify/topics/{name}/subscription`). Make them through `pb.transport`, the client's own transport: it sends the publishable key and the user's current access token, refreshes a token refused before its time and sends the call again, waits out a "not now" on a read, and throws a `PalbaseError` for a refusal, as the client's own calls do.

```ts
// src/settings.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

type Preferences = Record<string, Record<string, boolean>>;

// Which categories the signed-in user takes on which channel.
const reply = await pb.transport.send({
  op: "notify.getMyPreferences",
  method: "GET",
  path: "/notify/preferences",
  // The publishable key with the user's access token.
  auth: [["ApiKeyAuth", "userJWT"]],
  // The answers the call has; any other is thrown as a PalbaseError.
  answers: { 200: "json" },
});
const prefs = reply.data as Preferences;
console.log(prefs.email);
```

[Notifications](/docs/web/notifications#preferences-and-topics) shows both calls in full. Storage has no other client door: listing, writing and deleting objects is the secret key's, and so is everything that changes a module's settings. Those calls are made from a server, with [`palbase/server`](/docs/server/overview) or from your machine as `Palbase.<module>`. A browser uploads through your backend: to its upload route, or to a URL it signed. See [Uploads](/docs/web/uploads).

## Sessions and storage

The session is `{ accessToken, refreshToken, expiresAt, userId, user? }`, kept by a `SessionStore`:

- **`localStore(key)`** is the browser default, under `palbase.session.<origin of url>`. Tabs share it: a refresh takes a lock across them (`navigator.locks`), a tab that finds the session already refreshed by another takes that one instead of spending a used refresh token, and a sign-out in one tab signs the user out of every tab. Storage that cannot be written (full, blocked, a private window) keeps the session in this page's memory rather than losing it.
- **`memoryStore()`** is the default anywhere without `localStorage`: one process, one session.
- **Cookies**, for an app whose server renders its pages and needs to know who is signed in: `createBrowserClient` and `createServerClient` from `palbase/web/ssr` keep the session in a cookie the page and the server both read. See [Next.js](/docs/web/nextjs).
- Your own store implements `load`, `save` and `clear`, and, if tabs share it, `shared: true` and `watch(onChange)`.

The default key is built from the `url` you give, so each project's session is kept apart from another's in the same browser. An app that gave `createClient` its own origin as `url` finds its users' sessions under that origin's key. To keep them signed in when it moves to the project's address, give that key: `storage: localStore("palbase.session.https://app.example.com")`.

A session belongs to one user. When a tab finds another user's session in the shared store, it says `SIGNED_OUT` and then `SIGNED_IN` and never carries one user's work into the other's account. The socket closes on every sign-in and sign-out for the same reason, and the client's flags, consent choices and push registration follow the new user by themselves. See [Auth](/docs/web/auth#listening-for-changes).

## Outside the browser

`createClient` runs anywhere `fetch` does: a Node or Bun script, a test, a React Native app. With no `localStorage` the session lives in memory, and nothing keeps it between runs unless you give a `storage`. A script gives the project's address as `url`, as a page does.

A server is a different job. It acts for the project, not for one signed-in person, and it holds the secret key. That is [`palbase/server`](/docs/server/overview), and `createClient` will not take its key. A server that renders one signed-in person's pages uses `createServerClient` from `palbase/web/ssr`, with the publishable key and the request's cookies: see [Next.js](/docs/web/nextjs#on-the-server).

- [Flags](/docs/web/flags) — the flags' values for this reader, kept current
- [Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) and [Consent](/docs/web/consent) — events, and what the person allowed
