# Auth

`pb.auth` signs a person in and keeps them signed in. Every flow that ends in tokens puts them in the client's session and tells your app, and every call that acts for the user carries the access token from then on. The flows an app writes most are methods here: email and password, second factors, passkeys, magic links, phone codes, password and email changes, the user's sessions. Every other client operation of the auth module is reachable typed as `pb.auth.api`.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/signin.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// Create the account. When the project signs new users in at once, the session starts too.
const created = await pb.auth.signUp({ email: "ada@example.com", password: "correct-horse-battery-staple" });
console.log("account", created.user.id, created.access_token ? "signed in" : "confirm your email first");

// Sign in. A second factor, when the account has one, comes back as mfaRequired.
const result = await pb.auth.signIn("ada@example.com", "correct-horse-battery-staple");
if (result.mfaRequired) {
  const code = window.prompt("The code from your authenticator app") ?? "";
  await pb.auth.mfa.challenge(result.mfaRequired.mfaToken, "totp", code);
}

const me = await pb.auth.getUser();
console.log(me.id, me.email_verified, me.has_mfa);
```

The client is built with the project's address as `url`: the browser calls auth there directly, so auth's limits count each user's own address. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

## The session

```ts
// src/session.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const session = await pb.auth.currentSession();
if (session) {
  console.log(session.userId, new Date(session.expiresAt));
}
```

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `currentSession()` | The session, `{ accessToken, refreshToken, expiresAt, userId, user? }`, or `null` when no one is signed in. It waits for the store to load, so call it at boot. |
| `getUser()` | Reads the signed-in user's profile fresh (`GET /auth/me`): id, email, whether it is verified, whether they have a password and a second factor, their linked providers and language. |
| `refreshSession()` | Refreshes now, rather than when the token is about to lapse. |
| `setSession({ access_token, refresh_token, expires_in })` | Starts the session from a token pair your app has from a flow of its own (the social sign-in below, a ceremony you run step by step). The session held before is gone. |
| `onAuthStateChange(listener)` | Tells you every change. Returns the unsubscribe. |

The access token is refreshed a minute before it lapses, in the background while it still works, so no call waits for a refresh until the token is dead. A call refused with a 401 that is about the token (`invalid_token`, `token_expired`, `session_expired`, `session_revoked`, `missing_token`) is refreshed once and sent again, and only for the user whose session sent it. Every other 401, such as a wrong password or a wrong code, is the caller's answer and is never sent again. A refresh the server refuses ends the session (`SESSION_EXPIRED`).

## Email and password

`signUp(body)` creates the account (`POST /auth/signup`). The body is `{ email, password, locale?, redirect_to? }`. `redirect_to` is where the verification link lands, and it must be on the project's redirect allow-list (see [Where email links land](#where-email-links-land)). What comes back is `{ user, access_token?, refresh_token?, expires_in? }`: the tokens are there, and the session starts, only when the project lets a new account sign in before it confirms its address. With email confirmation required, the user confirms first and then signs in.

`signIn(email, password)` (`POST /auth/login`) answers one of two shapes:

```ts
// src/login.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

export async function login(email: string, password: string): Promise<string> {
  const result = await pb.auth.signIn(email, password);
  if (result.mfaRequired) {
    // { mfaToken, factors }: finish with pb.auth.mfa.challenge(...) or .recovery(...)
    return `second factor: one of ${result.mfaRequired.factors.join(", ")}`;
  }
  return `signed in as ${result.user.id}`;
}
```

The password rules (the shortest length, whether an email must be confirmed first) are the project's auth settings: Studio's Auth screens, or `PUT /admin/auth-settings` with the secret key from a server. A password the policy refuses, or one known from a breach, is a `PalbaseError` with status 400 and a code that says which.

### Confirming an email

The confirmation email carries a link, or a code when the project uses codes:

```ts
// src/verify.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const token = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get("token");
if (token) {
  await pb.auth.email.verify({ token }); // the link's token
} else {
  await pb.auth.email.verify({ email: "ada@example.com", code: "482913" }); // or the code with the address
}

// The email did not arrive:
await pb.auth.email.resendVerification("ada@example.com");
```

## Where email links land

A link in an auth email (confirm the address, choose a new password, a magic link) is built from the project's auth settings, in this order:

1. the request's `redirect_to`, with `?token=` added, when it is on the allow-list: the auth settings' `redirect_urls`, together with the redirects of the project's web apps (`palbase apps:env:set <app> --redirect <url>`). Any other `redirect_to` is refused with `invalid_redirect`;
2. the project's site URL (`site_url`) with the action's page: `https://app.example.com/auth/verify-email?token=…`, `https://app.example.com/auth/reset-password?token=…`, `https://app.example.com/auth/magic-link?token=…`;
3. with neither, the page auth serves itself at the project's address, for confirming an email and choosing a password. A magic link has no such page, because it ends in a session that only your app can take: a project that sends magic links needs a site URL.

Those three pages are yours to build at your site. Each reads `token` from its query and calls the method below.

## Second factors

A sign-in that needs a second factor answers `mfaRequired: { mfaToken, factors }`. Finish it with one of these:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mfa.challenge(mfaToken, "totp" \| "sms" \| "email", code)` | Completes the sign-in with a code. Returns the user. |
| `mfa.recovery(mfaToken, code)` | Completes it with a recovery code instead. |
| `mfa.sendSmsCode(mfaToken)` / `mfa.sendEmailCode(mfaToken)` | Sends the sign-in code; then `challenge(mfaToken, "sms" \| "email", code)`. |

Enrolling, for the signed-in user:

```ts
// src/mfa.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// TOTP: the secret for the authenticator app, a QR code, and the recovery codes, shown once.
const totp = await pb.auth.mfa.enrollTotp();
console.log(totp.otpUrl, totp.recoveryCodes);
await pb.auth.mfa.verifyTotp("123456"); // the first code the app shows confirms it

const factors = await pb.auth.mfa.factors();
console.log(factors);

// Removing a factor asks for the account's password.
await pb.auth.mfa.removeFactor("fac_01", "correct-horse-battery-staple");
```

`enrollSms(phone)` and `verifySms(code)` enroll a phone, `enrollEmail()` the account's address, and `regenerateRecoveryCodes()` replaces the recovery codes.

### Stepping up

A backend route that asks for a second factor (`auth: { aal: "aal2" }`), or for a recent one (`maxAge`), refuses a password sign-in with `kind: "stepUpRequired"` (`data.acr_values`, `data.max_age`). Step the signed-in user up and call again:

```ts
// src/approve.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

await pb.auth.mfa.stepUp("123456"); // the code the authenticator app shows
// or, with one of the user's passkeys: await pb.auth.passkey.stepUp();
// or by text: await pb.auth.mfa.sendStepUpSmsCode(); then
//   await pb.auth.mfa.stepUpWithSms(codeFromTheText);
// the route called again now gets the aal2 token
```

Each returns the session, which holds the token at the new level from here on; its refreshes stay at that level (`TOKEN_REFRESHED` is told). The step-up is the session's last authentication, so a route's `maxAge` counts from it. An email code is not a way up: it is not a second factor ([Second factors and their strength](/docs/backend/authentication#second-factors-and-their-strength)).

## Passkeys

```ts
// src/passkeys.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// Create an account with a passkey and no password, and sign in with it.
const user = await pb.auth.passkey.signUp("ada@example.com", "Ada");

// Add another passkey to the signed-in user.
await pb.auth.passkey.register("Work laptop");

// Sign in: any passkey of the site (discoverable), or one user's.
await pb.auth.signOut();
const again = await pb.auth.passkey.signIn();
console.log(user.id === again.id);

console.log(await pb.auth.passkey.list());
```

The ceremony runs through `navigator.credentials`, or the `webauthn` you give `createClient`. Outside a browser with neither, a passkey method throws once the ceremony's first call has answered.

The passkey's relying party is the project's own host, and a page on your origin uses it through WebAuthn's related origins: the project publishes its registered web apps' origins at `GET /.well-known/webauthn`, and the same list decides which origins a ceremony is accepted from. Register your site as a web app of the environment, with its origin (`https://app.example.com`): at most five registrable domains across the environment's web apps. A browser without related-origin support refuses a passkey from an origin that is not the project's host.

`passkey.remove(id)` removes one. Renaming is `pb.auth.api.webauthnRenameCredential(...)`.

## Magic links

```ts
// src/magic.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

await pb.auth.magicLink.send("ada@example.com");

// On the page the link opened (https://app.example.com/auth/magic-link?token=…):
const token = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get("token");
if (token) await pb.auth.magicLink.verify(token);
```

## Phone codes

```ts
// src/phone.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

await pb.auth.phone.sendCode("+905551234567");
const result = await pb.auth.phone.verifyCode("+905551234567", "482913");
if (result.mfaRequired) console.log("a second factor is needed");
else console.log("signed in", result.user.id);
```

Phone sign-in must be enabled for the project (`provider_not_enabled` otherwise). A code is texted through the project's own SMS provider, or its verification service when the phone settings say so (`PUT /admin/providers/phone/settings`) — with neither, through Palbase's Twilio Verify. The answer is the same whether or not the number has an account, and sending is limited per number and per address.

## Social sign-in

Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft sign-in in a browser is a transaction the auth module keeps (`/auth/oauth/transactions`). The client has no one-call method for it. The steps are four calls, all on `pb.auth.api`:

1. `socialConfig` (`GET /auth/oauth/config`) answers the browser clients one application may use. `application_key` and `variant` are the ones the provider's browser client was set up with in Studio's Auth providers, and its return URIs are where the provider sends the user back.
2. `socialBegin` (`POST /auth/oauth/transactions`) takes the client's key, the return URI and a challenge made from a secret only this tab holds, and answers the provider's `authorization_url`.
3. The provider sends the user to the project's callback, which sends them on to your return URI with `?transaction_id=…&result_code=…`.
4. `socialComplete` (`POST /auth/oauth/transactions/{id}/complete`) takes the result code and the secret, and answers the session.

```ts
// src/social.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

function base64url(bytes: ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array): string {
  const u = bytes instanceof Uint8Array ? bytes : new Uint8Array(bytes);
  return btoa(String.fromCharCode(...u)).replace(/\+/g, "-").replace(/\//g, "_").replace(/=+$/, "");
}

/** On the sign-in page: open the provider. */
export async function startGoogle(): Promise<void> {
  const config = await pb.auth.api.socialConfig({ query: { application_key: "web", platform: "web", variant: "production" } });
  const google = config.data.clients.find((c) => c.provider === "google" && "mode" in c && c.mode === "browser");
  if (!google) throw new Error("no Google browser client is set up for this application");

  const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
  const challenge = base64url(await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)));
  const begun = await pb.auth.api.socialBegin({
    body: {
      client_key: google.key,
      completion_challenge: challenge,
      completion_challenge_method: "S256",
      purpose: "sign_in",
      return_uri: "https://app.example.com/signin/callback",
    },
  });
  sessionStorage.setItem(`social:${begun.data.transaction_id}`, verifier);
  if (begun.data.authorization_url) window.location.assign(begun.data.authorization_url);
}

/** On the return URI's page: finish it. */
export async function finishSocial(): Promise<string> {
  const q = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
  const id = q.get("transaction_id") ?? "";
  const verifier = sessionStorage.getItem(`social:${id}`) ?? "";
  sessionStorage.removeItem(`social:${id}`);
  const done = await pb.auth.api.socialComplete({
    path: { id },
    body: { completion_verifier: verifier, result_code: q.get("result_code") ?? "" },
  });
  const result = done.data;
  if (result.status === "signed_in") {
    await pb.auth.setSession(result.session);
    return result.is_new_user ? "welcome" : "welcome back";
  }
  if (result.status === "mfa_required") {
    // Finish with pb.auth.mfa.challenge(result.mfa_token, …)
    return `second factor: ${result.factors.join(", ")}`;
  }
  return "linked";
}
```

What the provider reported, a refusal or a cancel included, comes back from `socialComplete` as a `PalbaseError`. The callback itself always sends the user back. A transaction expires (`auth_transaction_expired`, 410), and the result code is good for a minute after the provider sends the user back. Completing again with the same body answers the same result. `socialCancel` abandons one that has not completed.

## Passwords

```ts
// src/password.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// Forgot it: the email's link lands on https://app.example.com/auth/reset-password?token=…
await pb.auth.password.requestReset("ada@example.com");
const token = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get("token");
if (token) await pb.auth.password.confirmReset(token, "a-new-long-passphrase");

// Signed in: change it, or add one to an account that has none (passkey or social).
await pb.auth.password.change({ current_password: "a-new-long-passphrase", new_password: "another-long-passphrase" });
const me = await pb.auth.getUser();
if (!me.has_password) await pb.auth.password.set({ new_password: "a-first-long-passphrase" });
```

## The user's sessions

```ts
// src/devices.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

console.log(await pb.auth.sessions.list());
await pb.auth.sessions.revoke("ses_01"); // one of them
await pb.auth.sessions.revokeAll(); // signed out everywhere
```

## Listening for changes

```ts
// src/listen.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const stop = pb.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, session) => {
  if (event === "SIGNED_OUT" || event === "SESSION_EXPIRED") window.location.assign("/login");
  if (event === "SIGNED_IN") console.log("hello", session?.userId);
});
// later: stop();
void stop;
```

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `SIGNED_IN` | A flow started a session, or another tab signed someone in. |
| `TOKEN_REFRESHED` | The access token was refreshed, here or in another tab. |
| `USER_UPDATED` | `getUser()` read the profile, and it was stored with the session. |
| `SIGNED_OUT` | `signOut()`, or a sign-out in another tab. |
| `SESSION_EXPIRED` | The refresh token was refused (revoked, reused, expired). |

`pb.auth.sessionEndReason` says why a session ended without the app signing out, set before `SESSION_EXPIRED` is told so a listener reads it: `expired`, `revoked`, `userDeleted` (the account was deleted) or `userBanned` (it was suspended). It is `null` again once someone signs in or the app signs out.

A tab that finds a different user's session in the shared store says `SIGNED_OUT` and then `SIGNED_IN`, and a call it had in flight is not sent again as the new user.

## Signing out and deleting the account

`signOut()` ends the session on the server (`POST /auth/logout`) and here. A failed call still signs out locally.

`deleteAccount(password?)` deletes the account (`DELETE /auth/user`), everything tied to it and its sessions, and ends the session here. An account with a password gives it — `has_password` on `getUser()` says whether it has one — and auth asks for it again: a password missing or wrong is `401 reauth_required`, and the session is kept. An account without one (passkey, social, phone) is deleted on the strength of its session, and a password sent for it is ignored:

```ts
// src/delete-account.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

/** Whether the confirmation asks for the password: only an account that has one gives it. */
export async function asksForPassword(): Promise<boolean> {
  return (await pb.auth.getUser()).has_password;
}

/** A missing or wrong password is a PalbaseError, 401 reauth_required, and the user stays signed in. */
export async function deleteAccount(password?: string): Promise<void> {
  await pb.auth.deleteAccount(password);
}
```

## `pb.auth.api`

Every client operation of the auth contract, typed, through the session's transport. A few an app reaches for:

| Call | Path |
|---|---|
| `pb.auth.api.updateMe({ body: { locale: "tr" } })` | `PATCH /auth/me` |
| `pb.auth.api.listIdentities()` | `GET /auth/identities` |
| `pb.auth.api.unlinkIdentity({ path: { id } })` | `DELETE /auth/identities/{id}` |
| `pb.auth.api.webauthnRenameCredential({ path: { id }, body })` | `PUT /auth/webauthn/credentials/{id}` |

The `/admin/*` operations are in the same client, and every one of them needs the secret key. From an app they are refused before anything is sent (`missing_credential`). Make them from a server with [`palbase/server`](/docs/server/overview).

## Proof of work

The auth module may answer a sign-in, a sign-up or a code request with `403 pow_required` and a challenge when the address looks like a bot. The client solves it (a SHA-256 search, longer the harder the challenge) and sends the same request once more with the answer. You never see the challenge. One the client cannot solve comes back as `pow_unsolved`.

# Calling Your Backend

Your own backend runs on a machine, at an address of its own: `https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio` for the machine named `backend`, `https://<name>-<ref>.app.palbase.studio` for any other. The app calls it through its client. `palbase apps:sync` reads the contract the backend serves (a `palbase/backend` app writes one of its routes, their schemas and the errors they throw; another program serves its own OpenAPI document) and writes the app a module in which each route is a typed method: `pb.backend.notes.create({ title })`. The call goes from the browser to the machine's address with the signed-in user's access token. A machine asks for no API key, and the client never sends it one: your routes are the gate.

## Quick example

The backend: a route, and the origins its browsers come from.

```ts
// server/src/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

interface Note {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  private readonly notes: Note[] = [];

  @Get("")
  list(@User() user: UserT): Note[] {
    return this.notes.filter((n) => n.owner === user.id);
  }

  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    const note = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner: user.id, title: body.title };
    this.notes.push(note);
    return note;
  }
}
```

```ts
// server/src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { NotesController } from "./notes/notes.controller";

@Module({ controllers: [NotesController] })
export class AppModule {}
```

```ts
// server/src/main.ts
import { PalbaseFactory } from "palbase/backend";
import { AppModule } from "./app.module";

// Browsers on this origin may call the machine: preflights are answered, CORS headers are sent.
await PalbaseFactory.create(AppModule, { cors: { origins: ["https://app.example.com"] } });
```

Once the backend is deployed, write the app its module from the checkout's root:

```sh
palbase apps:sync shop-web
```

The app imports `pb` from it, and the backend is `pb.backend`:

```ts
// src/notes.ts
import { pb } from "../palbase/shop-web";

// The user signs in with the project's auth; the backend's calls carry their token.
await pb.auth.signIn("ada@example.com", "correct-horse-battery-staple");

const created = await pb.backend.notes.create({ title: "Ship the docs" });
const mine = await pb.backend.notes.list();
console.log(created.id, mine.length);
```

What `palbase apps:sync` wrote, cut to this page's routes and put in one file:

```ts
// palbase/shop-web.ts
// Code generated by palbase apps:sync — DO NOT EDIT. (Cut to this page's routes.)
import { createClient, type BackendBase, type CallOptions, type ClientOptions, type PalbaseClient } from "palbase/web";
import { __registerBackend } from "palbase/web/palbe";

export interface NotesCreateRequest {
  title: string;
}

export interface NotesCreateResponse {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

export interface NotesListResponseItem {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

export type NotesListResponse = NotesListResponseItem[];

// The routes, for the clients of this environment's project alone.
__registerBackend("https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", "backend", "backend", "https://k3xq81w4m.app.palbase.studio", {
  notes: {
    create: { method: "POST", path: "/notes" },
    list: { method: "GET", path: "/notes", input: "none" },
  },
});

export interface Backend extends BackendBase {
  notes: {
    create(input: NotesCreateRequest, options?: CallOptions): Promise<NotesCreateResponse>;
    list(options?: CallOptions): Promise<NotesListResponse>;
  };
}

export const settings = {
  url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
  publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5",
  environment: "staging",
  app: "shop-web",
  appId: "0b6f2c1e-8d4a-4f7b-9c3e-5a1d2e3f4b6c",
} as const;

/** The app's client: its project's modules (pb.auth, …) and its backends, pb.backend. */
export type Client = PalbaseClient & { backend: Backend };

let client: Client | undefined;

/** The app's client, made once with these settings — and with options, when connect(options) is called before anything uses the client (pb). */
export function connect(options: Omit<ClientOptions, "url" | "publishableKey"> = {}): Client {
  if (client) {
    if (Object.keys(options).length > 0) throw new Error("palbase: connect(options) comes before the client is first used — call it as the app starts");
    return client;
  }
  client = createClient({ ...options, url: settings.url, publishableKey: settings.publishableKey, appId: settings.appId }) as Client;
  return client;
}

/** The app's client, made when it is first used: pb.<backend>.<controller>.<method>(), pb.auth, … */
export const pb: Client = new Proxy({} as Client, {
  get(_, key) {
    const c = connect();
    const value: unknown = Reflect.get(c, key, c);
    return typeof value === "function" ? value.bind(c) : value;
  },
  has: (_, key) => Reflect.has(connect(), key),
});
```

## The generated module

`palbase apps:sync` writes under `palbase/`, from what the project serves now, and touches nothing else in the checkout. For a web app, `palbase/<app>.ts` is what the app imports: its `settings`, `connect()` and `pb`, typed with each backend of the environment, and with one backend that backend's types, typed errors and gateways too (with several, each one's are in `palbase/palbe/<machine>.ts`). Each environment's own files sit beside them, which a build for that environment imports instead ([Building for an environment](#building-for-an-environment)). Every file it writes, the editor's environment, CI's `--check` and its refusals are in [Syncing an App's Settings](/docs/apps/sync#what-it-writes); registering the app is [Client Apps](/docs/apps/overview).

Run it again when the backend's routes change: a call the backend no longer takes is then a compile error in the app. To try a route no machine serves yet, `--backend <machine>=<dir>` makes the client from the backend's checkout on this computer ([`palbase apps:sync`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appssync)).

**The backend's name.** `pb.<backend>` is the machine's name camelCased: `pb.backend` for the machine named `backend`, `pb.shopApi` for `shop-api`. `palbase apps:sync --as shop-api=shop` names it otherwise, the same in every environment. A name the client already has (`auth`, `flags`, `storage`, …) is refused.

**A route's method.** A `palbase/backend` route is its controller's name without `Controller`, then its method's: `NotesController.create` is `pb.backend.notes.create`. The arguments are, in order: each path parameter (`/notes/{id}` takes `id` first), the input (the body, or for a `GET` the query its schema declares), then the options:

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| `headers` | Headers of your own, sent with the call. |
| `signal` | An `AbortSignal` that cancels it. |

A route the generated types do not have yet is `pb.backend.call("notes/create", input, options?)`: it `POST`s the input as JSON and answers the route's JSON, untyped.

**Options of the client.** `pb` makes its client the first time it is used, with the settings of its environment. Give it options of [`createClient`](/docs/web/overview#createclientoptions) (`analytics`, `consent`, `language`, `appVersion`, …) with `connect(options)` as the app starts, before anything reads `pb`:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { connect } from "../palbase/shop-web";

connect({ analytics: true, appVersion: "2.4.1", consent: { start: { analytics: "denied", performance: "denied" } } });
```

A backend is its own project's: the module registers it for the clients of its environment's project alone. A client made for another project that reads `pb.backend` throws a `TypeError` before anything is sent, so one project's users never send their token to another project's machine.

## Building for an environment

Each environment's backend has its own routes and its own address, so an app is built against one environment. In a Vite app, `palbase/web/vite` picks it by the build's mode:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { palbase } from "palbase/web/vite";

export default {
  plugins: [
    // vite (development) is built against staging; vite build (production) against main.
    palbase({ app: "shop-web", environments: { development: "staging", production: "main" } }),
  ],
};
```

In each mode the app's imports of `palbase/<app>` and `palbase/palbe/<machine>` are that environment's files. A mode the plugin is given no environment for fails the build and says so. Before `vite build`, the plugin type-checks the app against its environment with the app's own TypeScript and tsconfig, so a route that environment's backend does not have, or a call that no longer fits its types, fails the build instead of the app.

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| `app` | The app's slug, as `palbase apps:list` shows it. |
| `environments` | Each mode the app is built in (`vite --mode`), and the environment it is built against. |
| `dir` | Where `palbase apps:sync` writes. Default: `palbase`. |
| `tsconfig` | The app's tsconfig, from its root. Default: `tsconfig.app.json` where there is one, else `tsconfig.json`. |
| `typecheck` | Type-check the app before a build. Default: `true`. |

With another bundler, `palbase/<app>.ts` is the `--types` environment's, and `palbase/<app>.<env>.ts` is each environment's to import for a build of that environment.

## The token

Every call carries the signed-in user's access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`, and nothing when no one is signed in: the route decides whom it answers. The token is the session's, the one `pb.auth` keeps and refreshes. A token the machine refuses before its time is refreshed once and the call is sent again.

A write (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) carries an `Idempotency-Key` the client makes, the same one on every attempt of that call. The client sends a call again on its own as it does the project's calls ([Error Handling](/docs/web/errors#what-the-client-retries)): a read, or a write whose route keeps the key, never another.

A `palbase/backend` app checks the token on every call that sends one: the signature against the project's keys, and that the session still stands. A route that needs a user answers:

| Answer | When |
|---|---|
| `401 unauthorized` | No token. |
| `401 invalid_token` | A token that is not valid, or an `Authorization` header that is not a Bearer token. `data.reason` says which. |
| `403 email_not_verified` | The route asks for a verified email (`auth: { verifiedEmail: true }`) and the user's is not. |
| `503 auth_unavailable` | The token could not be checked just now. `Retry-After: 1`, and sending again is safe. |

A route marked open (`{ auth: false }`) answers anyone. On such a route a bad token is no one, not a refusal. See [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication).

## What comes back

A route's answer is its JSON, typed by its contract, or `undefined` for a route that answers nothing (`204`). A refusal rejects the call with a `BackendError`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `validation` (a `400` with the fields that failed, or a call the client refused before sending it), `unauthorized` (`401`), `rateLimited` (`429`), `network` (no answer came), `decode` (an answer that is not JSON), `server` (every other refusal). |
| `code` | The envelope's `error`: `bad_request`, `not_found`, your own `note_locked`, … |
| `status` | The HTTP status; `0` when no answer came. |
| `message` | The envelope's `error_description`. |
| `fields` | A `400`'s fields: `{ field, message }` for each. |
| `retryAfter` | Seconds to wait, when the answer said. |
| `requestId` | The request's id. Quote it to find the call in the machine's logs. |
| `data` | The envelope's `data`, as the route sent it. |

An error the route throws that its contract names (palbase/backend reads them from the route's source as it writes the contract) comes as its own generated class instead, with its `code`, `status`, typed `data` and the `BackendError` as its `cause`. See [Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors).

```ts
// src/create-note.ts
import { isBackendError } from "palbase/web";
import { pb } from "../palbase/shop-web";

export async function createNote(title: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const note = await pb.backend.notes.create({ title });
    return `created ${note.id}`;
  } catch (e) {
    if (!isBackendError(e)) throw e;
    switch (e.kind) {
      case "validation":
        return e.fields?.map((f) => `${f.field}: ${f.message}`).join(", ") ?? e.message;
      case "unauthorized":
        return "sign in again";
      case "rateLimited":
        return `too many notes; try again in ${e.retryAfter ?? 1} s`;
      default:
        return `not created: ${e.code} (${e.requestId ?? "no request id"})`;
    }
  }
}
```

`isBackendError(e)` holds where `instanceof BackendError` would not: two copies of the package loaded side by side make two classes.

A call the client refuses before anything is sent is a `BackendError` of kind `validation` with status `0`: a path parameter that is missing, empty, `.` or `..` (`missing_path_param`, `invalid_path_parameter`), an input for a route that takes none (`unexpected_argument`), a body for a `GET` (`unsupported_get_input`), a query value that is an object or an array (`invalid_query_value`), an upload's file that is not a `Blob` (`invalid_file`).

Every refusal of a `palbase/backend` app is the platform's envelope, whatever the route:

```json
{
  "error": "bad_request",
  "error_description": "Request body failed validation",
  "status": 400,
  "request_id": "req_6f1c2b9e-…",
  "data": { "fields": [{ "field": "title", "message": "Invalid input: expected string, received undefined" }] }
}
```

| Status | `error` | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `bad_request` | A parameter failed its schema. `data.fields` names each, 20 at most, and `data.more` counts the rest. |
| 401, 403 | `permission_denied` | The database refused the caller: a row-level security policy, or a table their role has no grant on. 403 to a signed-in user, 401 to no one, for whom signing in may be what is missing. See [Row-Level Security](/docs/backend/row-level-security). |
| 404 | `not_found` | No route for the method and path, or the handler said so. |
| 413 | `payload_too_large` | A body over the app's limit (1 MiB unless the app says more). |
| 429 | `too_many_requests` | Over the route's limit for this caller. `Retry-After` and `data.retryAfter` say when to try again. |
| 503 | `service_unavailable`, `database_unavailable`, `auth_unavailable` | Something the route needs did not answer. `Retry-After` says when to come back. |
| 500 | `internal_error` | The handler threw something that is not a refusal. The details are in the machine's logs under the `request_id`. |

## Encrypted fields

A field your route marks `encrypted()` — or answers through `encrypt()` — the module seals before the call leaves the browser and opens when its answer arrives: the network panel shows `pbt1.…`, your code the value, and the calls are written as any other. The module holds the project's id and signing key for it, which `palbase apps:sync` writes. What can be marked, the keys and their rotation, and the errors are in [Encrypted Requests](/docs/backend/request-encryption).

## Cross-origin calls

A machine's address is not your app's origin, so the browser sends a preflight before each call that carries a token or a JSON body. A `palbase/backend` app answers it for the origins of the project's web apps by itself: those you give with `palbase apps:env:set <app> --origin`. Name any others in `PalbaseFactory.create(…, { cors })`:

| `cors` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `{ origins: ["https://app.example.com"] }` | Exact origins: `https://host[:port]`, `http` only for `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`. A preflight from another origin is answered 403. |
| `{ origins: "*" }` | Any origin. The credential is a bearer token, not a cookie, so `*` hands nothing to another site by itself. |
| `maxAge` | Seconds a browser keeps a preflight's answer (default 600). |
| left out | The project's web apps' origins alone. With no web app in the project, no CORS at all: a browser on another origin cannot call the machine. |

The machine is started with the web apps' origins in `PALBASE_WEB_ORIGINS` (comma-separated), so a backend without `palbase/backend` can read them too. A web app's origin added or taken away rolls the machine out again with no downtime, within about 15 seconds.

The answer exposes `retry-after` and `x-request-id` to your code. Requested headers are allowed as asked, so a header of your own needs no setting.

This is the backend's own CORS: the platform adds no header at a machine's address. The project's address is a separate matter: it answers a page on any site by itself. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

## A backend without a contract

`palbase apps:sync` makes a client from the contract the machine serves. A `palbase/backend` app writes its own; a program built another way that serves an OpenAPI document names where with [`palbase machines:update <machine> --openapi-path <path>`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-machinesupdate). A machine with no contract gets no client, and the app calls it with `fetch` and the user's token:

```ts
// src/lib/api.ts
import { pb } from "./palbase";

const BACKEND = "https://k3xq81w4m.app.palbase.studio";

/** One call to the machine, as the signed-in user. */
export async function api<T>(method: string, path: string, body?: unknown): Promise<T> {
  const token = (await pb.auth.currentSession())?.accessToken;
  const res = await fetch(`${BACKEND}${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: {
      ...(token ? { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {}),
      ...(body !== undefined ? { "content-type": "application/json" } : {}),
    },
    body: body !== undefined ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${method} ${path} answered ${res.status}`);
  return (res.status === 204 ? undefined : await res.json()) as T;
}
```

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

`currentSession()` answers the session the client holds, which it refreshes before it lapses. A token the backend refuses with `401` before its time (revoked, refreshed in another tab) is worth `pb.auth.refreshSession()` and one more try.

## A machine that sleeps

A machine of a shared size sleeps when it is idle, and the next request wakes it. That request waits while the machine starts, so the first call after a quiet spell is slower than the rest. A machine of a dedicated size never sleeps. See [Machines](/docs/machines/overview).

# Error Handling

Every call through the client returns its answer or throws. There is no `{ data, error }` pair to unpack. What it throws for a refusal is a `PalbaseError`, the one error class of the Palbase SDKs, exported from `palbase/web` and `palbase/server` alike. It carries the HTTP status, the module's machine-readable code, its words, the request's id and, when the server said so, how long to wait. Before it throws, the client has already done what can be done without your code: it refreshed a token that was refused before its time, solved auth's proof-of-work, and waited out a "not now" on a call that is safe to send twice.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/login.ts
import { PalbaseError } from "palbase/web";
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

export async function login(email: string, password: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const result = await pb.auth.signIn(email, password);
    return result.mfaRequired ? "enter your second factor" : "signed in";
  } catch (e) {
    if (!(e instanceof PalbaseError)) throw e;
    if (e.status === 401) return "wrong email or password";
    if (e.status === 429) return `too many tries; wait ${e.retryAfter ?? 60} seconds`;
    if (e.status === 0) return "you are offline";
    console.error(e.op, e.status, e.code, e.message, e.requestId);
    return "something went wrong";
  }
}
```

## `PalbaseError`

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `status` | The HTTP status. `0` for a call that never got an answer (see below). |
| `code` | The envelope's `error`: `invalid_token`, `rate_limited`, `pow_required`, … When the answer carried no envelope it is `http_<status>`. |
| `message` | The envelope's `error_description`, in words a person can read. |
| `requestId` | The request's id (`request_id`, or the `x-request-id` header). Quote it to find the call in logs. |
| `retryAfter` | Seconds the server asked to wait (`Retry-After`, or the envelope's `retry_after`), when it asked. |
| `body` | The refusal's body as sent, read up to 64 KiB. Useful for answers that are not the envelope (OAuth errors, a proof-of-work challenge). |
| `op` | The operation that was refused (`Login`, `RefreshToken`, `WebauthnLoginFinish`, …). |
| `cause` | The underlying error, for a call that failed before an answer. |

Check it with `instanceof PalbaseError`. The modules' typed calls (`pb.auth.api`, `pb.flags.api`) throw the same class. A call to your own backend through `pb.<backend>` refuses with a `BackendError` instead: the same envelope's `code`, `status`, `requestId` and `retryAfter`, with a `kind` to switch on and the fields that failed. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#what-comes-back).

## The envelope

Every module and every `palbase/backend` app refuses in one shape:

```json
{
  "error": "rate_limited",
  "error_description": "Too many attempts; try again later",
  "status": 429,
  "request_id": "req_4b1f0c7e-…",
  "retry_after": 60
}
```

`status` mirrors the response's status. `retry_after` is there on a refusal that ends with time, and the `Retry-After` header says the same. A `palbase/backend` app may add `data`, such as the fields that failed their schema. `PalbaseError` keeps the whole body in `body`.

## What the client retries

A call is sent again only when sending it again cannot do the work twice:

- **Which calls.** Reads (`GET`, `HEAD`), and writes whose contract takes an `Idempotency-Key`. For those the client makes one key per call and every attempt carries the same one, so the server answers a repeat with the first answer and changes nothing. A write without one, a sign-in for example, is never sent twice by the client.
- **Which answers.** `429`, `502`, `503`, `504`, and a call that never reached the server (`network_error`). Every other answer is yours.
- **How long.** Three attempts in all, the first included. When the server said how long to wait, the client waits exactly that, and a `Retry-After` over 30 seconds is not waited for: the error comes to you with `retryAfter` set. When it said nothing, the client waits 0.5 s, then 1 s, with a little jitter.

Change it per client:

```ts
// src/lib/patient.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

// Five attempts, and wait up to two minutes when the server asks.
export const pb = createClient({
  url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
  publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5",
  retry: { attempts: 5, maxWaitSeconds: 120 },
});
```

`{ attempts: 1 }` turns retries off. A call you abort is not retried.

## A refused token

A call that acts for the user and is refused `401` with a code that means "this token is not good any more" (`invalid_token`, `token_expired`, `session_expired`, `session_revoked`, `missing_token`) gets one refresh of the session, and is sent once more, only if the session is still the same user's. Every other 401, such as a wrong password, a wrong code or a wrong current password, is the answer and goes to you as it came.

When the refresh itself is refused, because the refresh token was used twice, revoked or expired, the session is over. The client clears it, tells your app `SESSION_EXPIRED` through `pb.auth.onAuthStateChange`, and the call's error reaches you. Send the user to sign in from the listener, not from every `catch`. See [Auth](/docs/web/auth#listening-for-changes).

A session that changed under a refresh (another tab signed out, or signed in as someone else) throws an error whose `code` is `session_changed`, and the call that asked is not sent again. Read it by `code`: it is not a `PalbaseError`.

## Proof of work

Auth may answer a sign-in, a sign-up or a code request `403 pow_required` with a challenge, when the address it comes from looks like a bot. The client solves it and sends the same request once more with the answer. You see nothing of it unless solving fails, which comes back as `403 pow_unsolved`. A request whose body cannot be read twice (a stream) is not sent again, and the `pow_required` error comes to you.

## Errors the client makes itself

These never came from a server:

| `status` | `code` | When |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `network_error` | The request did not reach the project: offline, DNS, a refused connection, or a cross-origin call the browser blocked. Retried like a 503. |
| 0 | `missing_credential` | The operation needs what the client does not hold: a signed-in user, or the secret key for an `/admin/*` call. Nothing was sent. |
| 0 | `invalid_path`, `invalid_path_parameter` | A path parameter that is empty, `.` or `..`, or a path that would leave the project's address. Nothing was sent. |
| 2xx | `undeclared_answer` | The server answered a success the contract does not declare. The request may have taken effect. |
| 3xx | `undeclared_redirect` | The server answered a redirect. The client never follows one, because a redirect would carry the key to whatever host it names. |
| any | `invalid_json` | An answer the contract says is JSON was not. |

`createClient` itself throws a `TypeError`, not a `PalbaseError`, for a secret key, for anything that is not a publishable key, and for a `url` that is not an `https` origin (`http` only for a loopback address).

`network_error` is also what a browser's CORS refusal looks like from code: the browser hides why. The project's address answers a page on any site, its refusals included, so a call the client makes is not refused this way (see [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser)). A machine's address answers only the origins its backend names: see [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#cross-origin-calls).

## Codes worth handling by name

| Where | `status` / `code` | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Sign-in | `401` | Wrong email or password. Say so without saying which. |
| Sign-in | `429` with `retryAfter` | The account is locked for a while after repeated failures, or the address is limited. Show the wait. |
| Sign-up, password | `400` | A password the policy refuses or one known from a breach; `message` says which. |
| A code (MFA, phone, email) | `401` | A wrong or used code. |
| Social sign-in | `410 auth_transaction_expired` | The transaction expired. Start again. |
| Any module | `429` | Over the project's request rate or a module's quota. Honour `retryAfter`. |
| Any module | `503` | The platform could not answer now. The client already retried a safe call. |

- [Overview](/docs/web/overview) — the client and its options
- [Auth](/docs/web/auth) — the flows and their answers
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls) — your backend's refusals as a `BackendError`

<!-- ===== web/uploads ===== -->

# Uploads

A browser sends a file to the project's storage, never through your machine, in one of two ways, and your backend decides in both. With a **signed upload URL**, your backend asks storage for a grant of one object (its path, a size ceiling, the content types the bucket takes, the user it will belong to) and the browser `PUT`s the bytes to it. With an **upload route** of your backend, the app's call sends the file and storage asks the machine first ([An upload route](#an-upload-route)). A publishable key alone cannot write, list or delete objects: the grant, or the route's yes, always comes from your backend.

## Quick example

The backend half, a route that grants the signed-in user one upload into the `avatars` bucket:

```ts
// server/src/uploads/uploads.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Palbase, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const UploadRequest = z.object({ name: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type UploadRequest = z.infer<typeof UploadRequest>;

@Controller("/uploads")
export class UploadsController {
  @Post("/avatar")
  async avatar(@Body(UploadRequest) body: UploadRequest, @User() user: UserT): Promise<{ url: string; path: string }> {
    const path = `${user.id}/${crypto.randomUUID()}-${body.name}`;
    const grant = await Palbase.storage.createUploadUrl({
      path: { bucket: "avatars" },
      // Ten minutes, 5 MB at most, and the object is the user's: it goes when they are deleted.
      body: { path, expires_in: 600, max_bytes: 5_000_000, owner_id: user.id },
    });
    return { url: grant.data.url, path };
  }
}
```

```ts
// server/src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { UploadsController } from "./uploads/uploads.controller";

@Module({ controllers: [UploadsController] })
export class AppModule {}
```

The browser half:

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/upload.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const BACKEND = "https://k3xq81w4m.app.palbase.studio";

interface StoredObject {
  bucket: string;
  path: string;
  size: number;
  content_type: string;
}

export async function uploadAvatar(file: File): Promise<StoredObject> {
  const token = (await pb.auth.currentSession())?.accessToken ?? "";
  const asked = await fetch(`${BACKEND}/uploads/avatar`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ name: file.name }),
  });
  if (!asked.ok) throw new Error(`the backend refused the upload: ${asked.status}`);
  const { url } = (await asked.json()) as { url: string };

  // The URL is at the project's address: send the bytes to it as it is.
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "content-type": file.type || "application/octet-stream" },
    body: file,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`storage refused the upload: ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()) as StoredObject;
}
```

## An upload route

A route your `palbase/backend` app declares with `@Upload`, naming its bucket and a path template (`{userId}/{uploadId}-{filename}`), takes the file itself. The app calls it as any route, the file after its input, and the call goes to the project's storage in one request (`POST /storage/upload/<machine>/<route>`), with the user's token when someone is signed in. Storage asks the machine whether this caller may upload, writes the file where the template says (held to the bucket's size and types), then runs the route's handler with the stored object. What the handler answers is the call's answer; a refusal deletes the object. The app asks for no grant first, and the path is never the browser's to choose. The backend's side, its options and storage's steps are in [Upload routes](/docs/backend/direct-uploads#upload-routes).

The backend half:

```ts
// server/src/profile/profile.controller.ts
import { Controller, Upload, UploadedObject, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

@Controller("/profile")
export class ProfileController {
  // Into the avatars bucket, under a folder of the user's.
  @Upload("/avatar", { bucket: "avatars", pathTemplate: "{userId}/{uploadId}-{filename}" })
  avatar(@UploadedObject() file: UploadedObject, @User() user: UserT): { path: string; size: number; contentType: string } {
    console.log(`${user.id} uploaded ${file.size} bytes`);
    return { path: file.path, size: file.size, contentType: file.contentType };
  }
}
```

The browser half, with what `palbase apps:sync` writes for that route:

```ts
// palbase/shop-web.ts
// Code generated by palbase apps:sync — DO NOT EDIT. (Cut to this page's route.)
import { createClient, type BackendBase, type PalbaseClient, type UploadOptions } from "palbase/web";
import { __registerBackend } from "palbase/web/palbe";

export interface ProfileAvatarResponse {
  path: string;
  size: number;
  contentType: string;
}

__registerBackend("https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", "backend", "backend", "https://k3xq81w4m.app.palbase.studio", {
  profile: {
    avatar: { method: "POST", path: "/profile/avatar", input: "none", upload: true },
  },
});

export interface Backend extends BackendBase {
  profile: {
    avatar(file: Blob, options?: UploadOptions): Promise<ProfileAvatarResponse>;
  };
}

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" }) as PalbaseClient & { backend: Backend };
```

```ts
// src/avatar.ts
import { isBackendError } from "palbase/web";
import { pb } from "../palbase/shop-web";

export async function changeAvatar(file: File, bar: HTMLProgressElement): Promise<string> {
  try {
    // Told as the bytes go out, and once more when the answer is in.
    const stored = await pb.backend.profile.avatar(file, { onProgress: ({ loaded, total }) => { bar.value = loaded / total; } });
    return `saved as ${stored.path}`;
  } catch (e) {
    if (isBackendError(e)) return `not saved: ${e.code}`;
    throw e;
  }
}
```

| Argument | What it is |
|---|---|
| path parameters, input | As the route takes them ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls#the-generated-module)). The input goes as JSON beside the file. |
| `file` | A `Blob`; a `File` is one, and its name is the template's `{filename}`. |
| `onProgress` | Told `{ loaded, total }` as the bytes go out, through `XMLHttpRequest` where the page has one. |
| `signal` | An `AbortSignal` that cancels the upload. |

An upload is never sent again on its own: a lost answer can follow a file that was kept and a handler that ran. Its refusals reject with a `BackendError`, the route's own and storage's alike (`413` past the bucket's size, `415` a type it does not take).

## The grant

`POST /storage/buckets/{bucket}/upload-urls` takes the secret key, so it is made by your backend (`Palbase.storage.createUploadUrl` on a machine, `createServer(…).storage.createUploadUrl` anywhere else):

| Field | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `path` | The object's path in the bucket. Your code chooses it: put the user's id in it, never a name the browser chose alone. |
| `expires_in` | Seconds the URL works, 1 to 604800 (7 days). |
| `max_bytes` | A ceiling below the bucket's own. |
| `owner_id` | The user the object belongs to. It is deleted with them. |

The content types are the bucket's. A bucket declared to take `image/*` refuses a PDF whatever the grant says. Declare buckets in Studio's Storage screens, or with `Palbase.storage.putBucket` from a server. See [Storage](/docs/backend/storage).

What comes back is `{ url, expires_at }`. The URL is `https://<ref>.palbase.studio/storage/signed/{bucket}/{path}?…`, and every parameter in its query is covered by its signature: change one and storage answers 403. The object's path is one percent-encoded segment (`a/b.jpg` is `a%2Fb.jpg`), so pass the URL on as it is.

## Sending the bytes

`PUT /storage/signed/{bucket}/{path}` needs no key: the signature is the credential. A `PUT` with a file's content type is preflighted by the browser, and the project's address answers the preflight from a page on any site, so the browser sends the bytes to the URL as it is. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

| Header | Effect |
|---|---|
| `content-type` | What the bytes are. Storage also sniffs the type from the bytes and keeps that one. |
| `if-none-match: *` | Create only: an object already at the path is refused with 412. |
| `x-checksum-sha256` | The bytes' SHA-256 in hex: bytes that do not match are refused and nothing is kept. |

The answer is the stored object: `201` when it was created, `200` when it replaced one. It is `{ bucket, path, size, content_type, checksum_sha256, owner_id?, width?, height?, thumbhash?, variants, created_at, updated_at }`, with a picture's size, its placeholder (ThumbHash) and the renditions the bucket made of it. An upload emits `file.uploaded` to the project's webhook, so your backend can [react to it](/docs/backend/hooks).

## Progress

`fetch` reports no upload progress. `XMLHttpRequest` does:

```ts
// src/progress.ts
export function putWithProgress(url: string, file: File, onProgress: (fraction: number) => void): Promise<unknown> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
    xhr.open("PUT", url);
    xhr.setRequestHeader("content-type", file.type || "application/octet-stream");
    xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => {
      if (e.lengthComputable) onProgress(e.loaded / e.total);
    };
    xhr.onload = () => (xhr.status === 200 || xhr.status === 201 ? resolve(JSON.parse(xhr.responseText)) : reject(new Error(`storage answered ${xhr.status}`)));
    xhr.onerror = () => reject(new Error("the upload did not reach storage"));
    xhr.send(file);
  });
}
```

Cancel with `xhr.abort()`, or with an `AbortController`'s signal on `fetch`. Nothing is kept of an upload that did not finish.

## What can go wrong

| Status | Why |
|---|---|
| 403 | The signature does not hold: expired, edited, another project's, or a download grant used for an upload. Ask the backend for a new one. |
| 412 | `if-none-match: *` and an object is already at the path. |
| 413 | Larger than the grant's `max_bytes` or the bucket's ceiling. |
| 415 | A content type the bucket does not take. |
| 400 `checksum_mismatch` | The bytes did not match `x-checksum-sha256`. Nothing was kept. |
| 422 `unreadable_picture` | A picture storage cannot decode: truncated, or a format it does not read. |
| 429 | The project's storage quota or request rate. Honour `Retry-After`. |

Check the size and type in the browser before you ask for a grant, so the user is told at once, but the grant and the bucket are what storage enforces.

## Showing what was uploaded

Reading needs no key either:

- **A public bucket**: `GET /storage/public/{bucket}/{path}`, with `?variant=<name>` for a rendition. Put it in an `<img src>` straight from the project's address: an image load is not preflighted.
- **A private bucket**: your backend signs a download URL, `Palbase.storage.createSignedUrl({ path: { bucket }, body: { path, expires_in } })`, which answers at `GET /storage/signed/{bucket}/{path}`. The same applies: an `<img src>` loads it, and a `fetch` from the page reads its bytes.

## Related

- [Storage](/docs/backend/storage) — buckets, objects, signed URLs and renditions from the server
- [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads) — the grant and upload routes, in full
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls) — the generated module, and the call that asks for the grant
- [Overview](/docs/web/overview) — what the project's address answers a browser



<!-- ===== web/flags ===== -->

# Flags

`pb.flags` holds the project's feature flags and remote configuration as this browser's reader sees them: every flag's value resolved by the project for this app and whoever is signed in, kept current as the flags change. A read takes no network: the client answers from the values it holds, which it keeps in the browser between visits, and brings them up to date behind your code. Flags are defined in Studio's flags screens or by a server, never from the browser (see [Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags)).

## Quick example

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({
  url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
  publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5",
  // What a flag's conditions on the app's version read.
  appVersion: "2.4.1",
});
```

```ts
// src/checkout.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// The values the client holds now: last visit's for this reader, or the fallback before the first read.
const newCheckout = pb.flags.bool("new_checkout", false);
const banner = pb.flags.string("banner_text", "");
const limit = pb.flags.number("cart_limit", 20);
const theme = pb.flags.json<{ accent: string }>("theme", { accent: "#2f6feb" });
console.log(newCheckout, banner, limit, theme.accent);

// Told the keys whose values changed: a change in Studio, a sign-in, a sign-out.
const stop = pb.flags.onChange((keys) => {
  if (keys.includes("new_checkout")) console.log("the checkout is now", pb.flags.bool("new_checkout", false));
});

// Wait for the values to be current before the first render, when that matters more than speed.
await pb.flags.refresh();
console.log(pb.flags.all());
stop();
```

The client starts on first use: the first read, listener or `refresh()` reads the values for whoever is signed in and joins the flags' change channels. The read goes from the browser straight to the project's address, which answers a page on any site. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

## Reading values

| Member | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `bool(key, fallback)` | A boolean flag's value, or `fallback` when there is none or it is not a boolean. |
| `string(key, fallback)` | A string flag's value, or `fallback`. |
| `number(key, fallback)` | A number flag's value (a finite one), or `fallback`. |
| `json<T>(key, fallback)` | An object flag's value as your type, or `fallback`. The shape is not checked. |
| `value(key)` | A flag's value, any JSON, or `undefined` when there is none yet. |
| `all()` | Every flag's value by key. |
| `source(key)` | Where a value came from: `system` (the flag's), `override` (the user's own), or `experiment` (an experiment's variant). |
| `version` | The version the values are current as of. |
| `onChange(listener)` | Calls `listener(keys)` with the keys whose values changed. Returns the unsubscribe. |
| `refresh()` | Brings the values up to date now. It resolves when they are. |

Every read answers at once, from what the client holds. Before the first read has come back, a reader the browser has seen before gets the values it had last time, and a new one gets the fallback. Give every read a fallback the app works with.

## A signed-in user's values

The values are one reader's: the signed-in user's, or, with no one signed in, this browser's. When someone signs in or out, the values held go (and a listener is told their keys), the new reader's are read, and the listener is told again. One reader's values are never read out to another, even for the moment the new ones take to arrive. A signed-in user's values follow the order below: their own values first, then their experiment's variant, then the flag's conditions.

## What a value is resolved from

Every read is resolved by the project for its reader, in this order:

1. **The user's own value**, when a signed-in user has one. A server gives users their values with the secret key (see [Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags#users-own-values)).
2. **The variant of an experiment** running on the flag, when the reader is one of its people.
3. **The flag's first condition that matches.** Conditions read what the client says about itself, the share of users a percentile picks (signed-in users only), the country of the address the request came from, the server's clock, and the analytics audiences the reader is in when they allowed personalization ([Consent](/docs/web/consent)).
4. **The flag's default.**

What the client says about itself, with every read:

| Header | Sent as | Read as |
|---|---|---|
| `X-Platform` | `web` | `client.platform` |
| `X-Palbase-Client-Version` | `createClient`'s `appVersion`, when given | `client.app_version` |
| `Accept-Language` | `createClient`'s `language`, or the browser's own | `client.locale`, its first language |
| `X-Palbase-Installation` | `pb.installation.id` | Counted toward which versions of your app are in use. |
| `X-Palbase-Installation-Secret` | The install's secret, kept in the browser, with no one signed in | Proves the install, so audiences and experiments can place a reader who is not signed in. |

The country is the one of the address the request came from: the user's own, because the browser calls the project directly.

A value is any JSON the flag's type allows: a boolean, a number, a string (one of the choices a string flag declares) or an object.

## Experiments

A value an experiment gave says so: `source(key)` is `experiment`. When the app reads such a flag by its key (`bool`, `string`, `number`, `json` or `value`), the client records the analytics event `$flag_exposure` with `{ flag, experiment, variant }`, once per analytics session for each flag and experiment, and only while the person allows analytics. That event is what an experiment's results count. `all()` records none, so read a flag in an experiment by its key where the person sees it.

## Keeping up to date

The client keeps the values current by itself. The project announces every change on two realtime channels, which the client joins on the project's socket:

| Channel | Who may join | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `flags:<ref>` | Anyone reading the project's flags, with no one signed in too | The project's flags changed. |
| `flags:<ref>:<user_id>` | That user only | That user's own values changed. |

Told of a newer version, the client asks for what changed since the one it holds (`GET /flags/delta`). When the delta can no longer bring its values up to date (the reader's context, country or audiences changed, a time condition turned, or the deletions it would need are older than the 30 days kept), the project answers `410`, and the client reads a whole snapshot instead (`GET /flags/snapshot`, sent with the `ETag` of what it holds, answered `304` when nothing changed). A channel the project refuses, with realtime off, still leaves the reads: `refresh()` brings the values up to date.

Every read a client makes — `GET /flags`, a snapshot or a delta, a `304` among them — is metered against the project's flag reads.

## The calls under it

Every client call of the flags module is also on `pb.flags.api`, typed, through the client's session:

| Call | Method | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /flags/snapshot` | `api.getSnapshot()` | `{ values, sources, experiments?, sync_version, context_hash, fetched_at }`, `304` with `If-None-Match` when unchanged. |
| `GET /flags/delta?since=<sync_version>` | `api.getDelta({ query: { since } })` | `{ ops: [{ op: "put" \| "delete", key, value?, source, experiment?, version }], sync_version }`, `304` when nothing changed, `410` when a snapshot is needed. |
| `GET /flags` | `api.getValues()` | Every flag's value for this reader, alone. |

An app that reads flags with `pb.flags` makes none of them itself.

## Errors

A read never throws: it answers the fallback. `refresh()` rejects with a `PalbaseError` when the read it waits for fails:

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| 401 | A key of another project, or a token that is not valid. |
| 429 | The project's request rate, or its flag reads for the period, are used up. `Retry-After` says when to try again. |
| 503 | The platform could not answer now. The read is made again with the next change, or the next `refresh()`. |

## Related

- [Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags) — defining flags and giving users their own values
- [Realtime](/docs/web/realtime) — the socket the change notices travel on
- [Consent](/docs/web/consent) — personalization, which audience conditions need
- [Overview](/docs/web/overview) — the client's options, `appVersion` and `language`



<!-- ===== web/realtime ===== -->

# Realtime

`pb.socket` is the project's one realtime connection, shared by every channel the page is on. It opens the first time a channel is joined and never before, so a page that only signs in or reads flags opens none. On it, a channel delivers what is published to it: broadcasts, and the channel's shared state when the channel has one. The client listens, and broadcasts on a channel declared to let it. The project's server broadcasts and writes state with the secret key.

> **Note:** Your own backend's realtime channels are its [gateways](/docs/web/gateways), joined through the module `palbase apps:sync` writes: typed events, and messages the backend answers with an ack. This page is the socket under them, and the channels a server declares by name.

## Quick example

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/room.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const room = pb.socket.channel("room:42");

const stop = room.on("broadcast", (frame) => {
  // { type: "broadcast", event, payload }
  console.log(frame.event, frame.payload);
});

try {
  await room.join();
} catch (e) {
  // The server's reason: not declared, not yours, too many channels, …
  console.error(e instanceof Error ? e.message : e, room.refusal);
}

// later:
stop();
room.leave();
```

And the backend that publishes to it:

```ts
// server/src/rooms/rooms.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class RoomsService {
  /** Every subscriber of room:<id> hears it. */
  async announce(roomId: string, text: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.realtime.broadcast({
      body: { messages: [{ topic: `room:${roomId}`, event: "message", payload: { text } }] },
    });
  }
}
```

## Channels

`pb.socket.channel(name)` returns the channel of that name, the same object each time it is asked for. A channel is joined once however many listeners it has.

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `join()` | Joins and resolves once the server took it. Rejects with the server's reason when it did not. |
| `leave()` | Leaves the channel and forgets it: a later `channel(name)` is a new one. |
| `on(event, listener)` | Listens to one event. Returns the unsubscribe. A listener that throws does not take the socket down. |
| `push(event, payload)` | Sends one event on the joined channel and resolves with what became of it, `{ status, response }`: `ok`, `error` with the server's `reason`, or `timeout` (`no reply`) when nothing answered in ten seconds. It never rejects. On a channel that is not joined it sends nothing and resolves `error`, `not joined`. |
| `onClosed(listener)` | Told when what was joined ends for good: a sign-out, or another user's sign-in. Not a drop, after which the channel is joined again. Returns the unsubscribe. |
| `state` | `closed`, `joining`, `joined` or `refused`. |
| `refusal` | Why the server refused the last join, when it did. |

The events a channel delivers:

| Event | Payload |
|---|---|
| `broadcast` | `{ type: "broadcast", event, payload }`: one published event. A broadcast reaches every subscriber but the one that sent it. |
| `state_snapshot` | `{ seq, entries }`: the channel's whole state, on join. Each entry is `{ v, life }`. |
| `state_diff` | `{ from_seq, seq, set, del }`: what changed since `from_seq`. A client holding exactly `from_seq` applies it. |

State is a keyed map per channel that outlives the connections reading it. A server writes it with `Palbase.realtime.writeState`, and a channel declared with `state_read` hands it to its subscribers. A `durable` entry stays until it is removed. An `ephemeral` one is its writer's presence, gone when the writer leaves.

Names are `:`-separated segments, 255 bytes at most. On the wire each carries a `realtime:` prefix, and the client adds it for you.

## Who may join

A channel name is a string a client chooses, so proving who you are says nothing about which channels are yours. The project's server **declares** its channels (`PUT /realtime/channels` with the secret key, or `Palbase.realtime.putChannels`), and a channel no declaration matches belongs to no one:

| Declared `kind` | Who joins |
|---|---|
| `owner` | The pattern's one `{name}` segment is the joining user: `user:{uid}` is joined by that user alone, who may do everything on it. |
| `public` | Any signed-in user of the project, with the rights the declaration gives: `publish`, `state_read`, `state_write`. |

Patterns match in their order, the first one deciding. A declared channel is joined only by a signed-in user, whose access token travels in each join. See [Channels](/docs/backend/channels).

Some namespaces are the platform's, and no declaration can claim them:

| Channel | Who joins | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| `flags:<ref>` | Anyone, signed in or not | The project's flags changed. See [Flags](/docs/web/flags). |
| `flags:<ref>:<user_id>` | That user | Their own flag values changed. |
| `roles:<ref>:<user_id>` | That user | Their permissions, as state. |

A refused join rejects with the server's reason: `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `invalid_topic`, `rate_limited`, `too_many_channels`, `state_budget` or `unavailable`. Only `unavailable` is worth trying again. A user who is turned away mid-connection, because a declaration changed or their session ended, gets the channel closed under them (`state` becomes `closed`). Ask again and the server answers on its merits.

A client broadcasts on a channel declared with `publish`:

```ts
// src/typing.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

export async function sayTyping(roomId: string): Promise<void> {
  const room = pb.socket.channel(`room:${roomId}`);
  await room.join();
  // Every other subscriber hears { type: "broadcast", event: "typing", payload }; the sender does not.
  const reply = await room.push("broadcast", { type: "broadcast", event: "typing", payload: { typing: true } });
  // A refusal is answered (not declared with publish, over the rate); a broadcast the server took is answered by no one.
  if (reply.status === "error") console.warn("not sent:", reply.response.reason);
}
```

A broadcast the server took is not answered, so its `push` resolves `timeout` after ten seconds: do not hold the page on it. The channel's state is the server's to write. What a client must not be able to say, publish from your backend, which decides what reaches a channel.

## One socket, one user

The socket opens at `wss://<url's host>/realtime/v1/websocket` with the publishable key in its `apikey` parameter, because a browser cannot set a header on a WebSocket. Who the client is, is the access token each join carries. When the session is refreshed, the new token goes to every joined channel without leaving it.

The socket is one person's. When someone signs in, signs out, or the session expires, the client closes it, and every channel with it. Join again for the user who is there now:

```ts
// src/rejoin.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

async function joinMine(): Promise<void> {
  const session = await pb.auth.currentSession();
  if (!session) return;
  const mine = pb.socket.channel(`user:${session.userId}`);
  mine.on("broadcast", (frame) => console.log("for me:", frame.event, frame.payload));
  await mine.join();
}

pb.auth.onAuthStateChange((event) => {
  if (event === "SIGNED_IN") void joinMine();
});
await joinMine();
```

## When the connection drops

The socket sends a heartbeat every 25 seconds. One that goes unanswered closes the socket, because a network that went away without a close leaves a socket half-open. A socket that drops is opened again after 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, then every 30 seconds, each pause jittered by ±20%, and every channel that was joined is joined again. A broadcast published while the socket was down is not delivered: broadcasts are delivered at most once. A channel's state comes back whole with the snapshot of the new join. `pb.socket.reconnects` counts the reopens, for your own diagnostics.

`pb.socket.disconnect()` closes it for good. The next `join()` opens a new one.

## Where the socket opens

The socket's address is built from the client's `url`: `wss://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio/realtime/v1/websocket`, at the project's address, with the publishable key in its query. A WebSocket is not preflighted, and the project's address takes a socket from a page on any site, so the browser opens it there directly. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

## Limits

The project holds its clients to limits the platform sets and the project may lower (`PUT /realtime/limits` from a server): connections open at once, broadcasts and state writes per second, joins per second, channels per connection. A frame over 1 MiB closes the socket. A project over its connection limit, or whose realtime quota is used up, is refused a new socket.

## Related

- [Gateways](/docs/web/gateways) — your backend's channels, typed, with messages and acks
- [Channels](/docs/backend/channels) — declaring who may join what
- [Realtime in your backend](/docs/backend/realtime) — broadcasting and writing state
- [Flags](/docs/web/flags) — the change notices on `flags:<ref>`
- [Auth](/docs/web/auth) — the session the socket belongs to
- [Overview](/docs/web/overview) — the client, and calling the project from a browser
