# Notifications

`pb.notify` is what a browser takes of the project's messages: its pushes (`pb.notify.push`, Web Push through the browser's own push service), the signed-in person's inbox (`pb.notify.inbox`), and the project's in-app campaigns shown in the page (`pb.notify.inApp`). The signed-in person's preferences and the topics they follow are two more calls. Sending is your backend's ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)); the browser subscribes, reads and shows.

## Web push

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/push-button.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

export async function turnOnPush(): Promise<string> {
  // From a tap: a browser shows its prompt only then.
  if (pb.notify.push.permission() === "unsupported") return "This browser takes no notifications";
  const on = await pb.notify.push.subscribe();
  return on ? "Notifications are on" : "Notifications were not allowed";
}
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

// As the app starts: the browser's subscription registered again, without a prompt, when it has one.
await pb.notify.push.refresh();
```

| Member of `pb.notify.push` | What it does |
|---|---|
| `supported()` | Whether the browser takes pushes at all: a service worker, the Push API and notifications. |
| `permission()` | `granted`, `denied`, `default` (not asked yet) or `unsupported`. |
| `subscribe(options?)` | Asks the person (call it from a tap), registers the service worker, subscribes the browser with the project's key through its own push service, and registers the subscription as a device. `true` when the browser takes pushes now, `false` when the person refused or the browser has none. `options`: `serviceWorker`, the worker's path (`/palbase-sw.js` unless given), and `scope`, its scope (its folder unless given). A scope another worker holds is refused: it would replace that one. |
| `unsubscribe()` | Ends the browser's subscription. The project forgets the device as it next pushes it. |
| `refresh()` | Registers the subscription again, without a prompt, when the person allowed it and there is one. |

The device is the signed-in user's, or this install's (`pb.installation.id`) while no one is signed in: a push that names the install reaches it then. It is registered again by itself as people sign in and out, one change at a time. When that registration cannot be sent — the browser offline, the server unreachable — Palbase's subscription ends and a new one takes its place, registered for whoever is signed in once the server answers (tried again after 1 s, 5 s, 30 s, 2 min and 10 min, and at the next change): one person's pushes are never shown to the next. The project's key for Web Push (VAPID) is its own, made as the first browser asks for it: no account of another provider is needed.

### The service worker

The pushes are shown by the SDK's service worker, served from your site's own origin. Copy `node_modules/palbase/dist/web/push-sw.js` (the package exports it as `palbase/web/push-sw.js`) into the folder your site serves as it is, as `palbase-sw.js`: `public/palbase-sw.js` in Next.js or Vite. Copy it again when you update `palbase`. To serve it elsewhere, name its path: `subscribe({ serviceWorker: "/sw/palbase.js" })`.

Palbase touches only its own worker and subscription. A scope holds one worker, so where your app's own worker (an offline cache, another service's pushes) holds the folder's scope, Palbase's registers at `palbase-push/` beside it: a push reaches its worker whatever pages that controls, and yours stays as it is. A worker is Palbase's for this project when its URL carries this project's key.

`subscribe()` registers it with the project's address and publishable key in its URL, which it reports with. The worker shows each push, opens its link when it is tapped (an `https` address, or one of your site's; a tab of your app at that address is focused rather than opened again), and tells the project how each went — delivered, opened, dismissed — with the push's own receipt as the credential. It tells your open pages too:

```ts
// src/push-events.ts
// What the service worker tells each open page of the app.
navigator.serviceWorker?.addEventListener("message", (e: MessageEvent) => {
  const m = e.data as { type?: string; event?: "received" | "opened"; url?: string; data?: Record<string, string> };
  if (m.type === "palbase.push" && m.event === "received") console.log("a push arrived", m.data);
});
```

## Inbox

```ts
// src/inbox.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

const badge = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#inbox-badge")!;
const view = pb.notify.inbox.mount(document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#inbox")!, {
  onUnread: (n) => { badge.textContent = n ? String(n) : ""; },
  onOpen: (_item, link) => { window.location.assign(link); },
  labels: { empty: "No messages yet" },
});

// Or its calls, for a list of your own:
const page = await pb.notify.inbox.list({ limit: 20 });
await pb.notify.inbox.markRead(page.items.filter((m) => !m.read_at).map((m) => m.id));
await pb.notify.inbox.markRead("all");
if (page.items[0]) await pb.notify.inbox.remove(page.items[0].id);
view.destroy();
```

The signed-in person's inbox is the same on every device of theirs: read here, it is read on their phone; deleted, it is gone there. `mount()` draws it ready — newest first, the unread marked, a designed card drawn by its definition — and asks for it again as the page comes back into view and as people sign in and out. A tap marks a message read and opens its link (an https address in a new tab, your app's in this page, unless `onOpen` takes it). No one signed in: an empty list.

| Member of `pb.notify.inbox` | What it does |
|---|---|
| `list({ limit?, cursor?, locale? })` | A page of the inbox, newest first, with how many of it all are unread; `next_cursor` reads the next page. |
| `unread()` | How many messages are unread. |
| `markRead(ids \| "all")` | Marks messages read on every device of the person's; answers how many became read. |
| `remove(id)` | Deletes a message from every device of the person's. |
| `mount(container, options?)` | Draws the inbox into an element and keeps it current. `options`: `locale`, `appearance`, `limit` (50), `onOpen`, `onCustom` (a designed card's own buttons), `onUnread`, `labels`. |

## In-app messages

```ts
// src/in-app.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

pb.notify.inApp.start({
  // A button's link of your app's: your router's, not a page load.
  onDeepLink: (link) => { window.history.pushState(null, "", new URL(link).pathname); },
  // A button that shows a placement's paywall: drawn here, bought through Stripe Checkout.
  onShowPaywall: async (placement) => {
    const paywall = await pb.purchases.paywall(placement);
    paywall?.render(document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#paywall")!, {
      successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks",
      cancelUrl: window.location.href,
    });
  },
});

// Events analytics records come by themselves; name one of your own:
pb.analytics.capture("cart_viewed", { plan: "pro" });
pb.notify.inApp.trigger("level_completed", { level: 3 });
```

Once started, the person's campaigns are asked for as each session starts — the first page of one, the page back in view after half an hour away, a sign-in or out — and an event shows the first campaign it triggers that the caps let: the project's (one a session, three a day, ten minutes apart unless its settings say otherwise) and the campaign's own. The server counts each showing on every device of the person, so two tabs or a tab and a phone do not show it twice. The message is drawn by the SDK's screen renderer, the one paywalls are drawn with (`palbase/web/message` for an app that draws one itself), as a modal (the browser's own modal dialog), the whole page, or a banner at an edge that goes by itself when it says so.

Triggers are matched **in the page**: no event leaves it for them, and a message is shown whatever the person chose of analytics. A campaign to an audience reaches only who allowed personalization ([Consent](/docs/web/consent)), which the server holds to. A button that asks for push shows the browser's prompt and subscribes it (`pb.notify.push.subscribe()`) unless `onRequestPush` does it. A button that takes an offer claims it, or opens Stripe Checkout with it, unless `onOffer` does it. A tap is reported as a click and a close as a dismissal; a conversion — the campaign's event after it was seen — only while the person allows analytics.

`stop()` stops showing campaigns, `refresh()` asks for them again, and `settled()` waits for the events given so far to be taken, which a test or a page about to navigate awaits.

## Preferences and topics

The signed-in person chooses which kinds of message they take on which channel, and follows the topics the project opened to them. The client has no method for these four calls: make them through the client's own transport, which sends the user's access token and refreshes it as the client's own calls do (see [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calls-the-client-has-no-method-for)).

```ts
// src/lib/as-user.ts
import { pb } from "./palbase";

/** A notify call as the signed-in user; a refusal is thrown as a PalbaseError. */
export async function asUser<T>(method: "GET" | "PUT" | "POST" | "DELETE", path: string, body?: unknown): Promise<T> {
  const reply = await pb.transport.send({
    op: `${method} ${path}`,
    method,
    path,
    auth: [["ApiKeyAuth", "userJWT"]],
    answers: { 200: "json", 204: "empty" },
    body: body === undefined ? undefined : { kind: "json", contentType: "application/json", value: body },
  });
  return reply.data as T;
}
```

```ts
// src/settings.ts
import { asUser } from "./lib/as-user";

/** channel (email, sms, whatsapp, push) → category → whether they take it. */
type Preferences = Record<string, Record<string, boolean>>;

const prefs = await asUser<Preferences>("GET", "/notify/preferences");
console.log(prefs.email?.marketing);

// Stop marketing email. The answer is all of their preferences.
await asUser<Preferences>("PUT", "/notify/preferences", { email: { marketing: false } });

// Follow a topic, and stop following it.
await asUser<void>("POST", "/notify/topics/product-updates/subscription");
await asUser<void>("DELETE", "/notify/topics/product-updates/subscription");
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /notify/preferences` | `{ channel: { category: on } }` for each channel (`email`, `sms`, `whatsapp`, `push`): `transactional` (always on), `marketing`, and every other category set for them. A category the user never set is on. |
| `PUT /notify/preferences` | Sets the ones it names, 100 at most in a write, and answers all of them. `transactional` is not theirs to turn off and is left as it is. A user keeps 50 categories. |
| `POST /notify/topics/{name}/subscription` | Follows a topic the project opened to its users (`self_subscribe`). `403` for any other. |
| `DELETE /notify/topics/{name}/subscription` | Stops following it. |

They are the signed-in user's: with no one signed in, the transport throws before anything is sent (`missing_credential`). What the person allowed in the app ([Consent](/docs/web/consent)) holds as well: a send that is not transactional is skipped for someone who refused that channel's marketing key (`marketing_push`, `marketing_email`, `marketing_sms`, `marketing_whatsapp`).

## Related

- [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications) — sending pushes, inbox messages and in-app campaigns from your backend.
- [Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) — the events that trigger in-app messages.
- [Consent](/docs/web/consent) — the marketing keys, and personalization for audiences.



<!-- ===== web/nextjs ===== -->

# Next.js

A Next.js app uses Palbase in two places. In the browser, `palbase/web` signs the user in and calls the project's address directly. On the server (the proxy, server components, server actions, route handlers), the same client reads who is signed in from the request's cookies, and `palbase/server` acts as the project with the secret key. `palbase/web/ssr` joins the two: it keeps the session in a cookie the page and your server both read, as `@supabase/ssr` does for Supabase.

## Quick example

The browser's client keeps its session in the page's cookies:

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
"use client";

import type { PalbaseClient } from "palbase/web";
import { createBrowserClient } from "palbase/web/ssr";

// The environment's address and publishable key, from Studio. Public: they go into the bundle.
export const PROJECT = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL ?? "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio";
export const PUBLISHABLE_KEY = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY ?? "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5";

let client: PalbaseClient | undefined;

/** The browser's client, made on first use: from an effect or an event handler, which run in the browser. */
export function palbase(): PalbaseClient {
  client ??= createBrowserClient({ url: PROJECT, publishableKey: PUBLISHABLE_KEY });
  return client;
}
```

```tsx
// src/app/signin/page.tsx
"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { useState } from "react";
import { palbase } from "../../lib/palbase";

export default function SignInPage() {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [problem, setProblem] = useState<string | null>(null);

  async function submit(form: FormData) {
    // From the browser: auth's limits count this person's own address.
    const result = await palbase().auth.signIn(String(form.get("email")), String(form.get("password")));
    if (result.mfaRequired) return setProblem("a second factor is needed");
    // The session is in the cookie now: the server's pages see it.
    router.push("/account");
    router.refresh();
  }

  return (
    <form action={(form) => void submit(form).catch(() => setProblem("those details were not accepted"))}>
      <input name="email" type="email" />
      <input name="password" type="password" />
      <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
      {problem && <p role="alert">{problem}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}
```

A server component reads who it is from the request:

```ts
// src/lib/palbase-server.ts
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import type { PalbaseClient } from "palbase/web";
import { createServerClient } from "palbase/web/ssr";

const PROJECT = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL ?? "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio";
const PUBLISHABLE_KEY = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY ?? "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5";

/** A server component's client: it reads the request's cookies and never writes them. */
export async function readingClient(): Promise<PalbaseClient> {
  const jar = await cookies();
  return createServerClient({ url: PROJECT, publishableKey: PUBLISHABLE_KEY, cookies: { getAll: () => jar.getAll() } });
}

/** A server action's or a route handler's client: it may renew the session and write it back. */
export async function writingClient(): Promise<PalbaseClient> {
  const jar = await cookies();
  return createServerClient({
    url: PROJECT,
    publishableKey: PUBLISHABLE_KEY,
    cookies: {
      getAll: () => jar.getAll(),
      setAll: (cs) => cs.forEach((c) => jar.set(c.name, c.value, c.options)),
    },
  });
}
```

```tsx
// src/app/account/page.tsx
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";
import { keepSession } from "palbase/web/ssr";
import { readingClient } from "../../lib/palbase-server";

export default async function AccountPage() {
  // Auth's answer for the token in the cookie: never the cookie's word alone.
  const user = await keepSession(await readingClient());
  if (!user) redirect("/signin");
  return <p>Signed in as {user.email ?? user.id}</p>;
}
```

## The browser calls the project directly

The browser calls `https://<ref>.palbase.studio` itself. The project's address answers a page on any site, preflights included, so the app needs no rewrite of the modules' paths, and should have none. Through a rewrite every user's call reaches the project from your Next.js server's address, and what the project decides from a caller's address is then decided from yours, for all your users at once: auth's limits on sign-in attempts, the proof-of-work it asks of a busy address, the country a flag's condition reads and an analytics event is given. See [Overview](/docs/web/overview#calling-the-project-from-a-browser).

For the same reason, sign the user in **in the browser**, as the example does, and not in a server action: a sign-in your server makes for every user comes from one address.

## The session cookie

`createBrowserClient` keeps the session in a cookie named `pb-<ref>-session`, split into `pb-<ref>-session.0`, `.1`, … when it is longer than a cookie holds. It is written for the whole site (`path=/`), `SameSite=Lax` so a link from elsewhere (a sign-in email) opens the page signed in, `Secure` (the browser's client leaves it off on a page served over http, such as `http://localhost:3000`, and the server's needs `cookieOptions: { secure: false }` there), and readable by the page's script, because the browser's client reads it there. The browser keeps it as long as it keeps any cookie (400 days); the session itself ends when its refresh token does. `cookieOptions` changes any of that, for the browser's client and the server's alike: `{ domain: ".example.com" }` shares the session with the site's other subdomains.

The cookie is where the session is kept, not how a call proves it. Every call still carries the access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`, and the project reads no cookie. What a cookie says is what the browser wrote, and a browser can write anything: `keepSession` asks auth whose the token is before your code acts on it.

## On the server

`createServerClient({ url, publishableKey, cookies })` is one request's client: its session is the request's cookies. Give it `getAll`, which reads them, and, where the server can write the response's cookies, `setAll`.

Who renews the session matters. A renewal hands out a new refresh token and the old one stops working, so a renewal whose new token cannot be written back ends the session at the next one. The client follows what you gave it:

| Where | `cookies` | What the client does |
|---|---|---|
| The proxy (`src/proxy.ts`) | `getAll` and `setAll` | Renews a session with five minutes or less left on the way in, before any page renders. |
| A server action, a route handler | `getAll` and `setAll` | Renews before a call that finds the token about to lapse, and writes the new session back. |
| A server component | `getAll` only | Never renews: Next.js lets a server component read cookies, not write them. Run the proxy before the pages that read the session, so none renders with a token that has lapsed. |

`keepSession(pb)` is who is signed in, as auth says: it renews first when the client can and the session has little left, then asks auth whose the access token is (`GET /auth/user`). It answers the user, or `null` when no one is signed in, the session is over, or auth does not take the token. When auth cannot be asked, it throws a `PalbaseError`: the network failed, or a server component's token lapsed with no proxy to renew it (`missing_credential`). It writes nothing but a renewal, so it never puts back an older session over one the browser renewed meanwhile.

The proxy keeps the session fresh for every page it runs before:

```ts
// src/proxy.ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { createServerClient, keepSession } from "palbase/web/ssr";

export async function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  let response = NextResponse.next({ request });
  const pb = createServerClient({
    url: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL ?? "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
    publishableKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY ?? "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5",
    cookies: {
      getAll: () => request.cookies.getAll(),
      setAll: (cookies, headers) => {
        // The pages rendered after this see the renewed session...
        for (const c of cookies) request.cookies.set(c.name, c.value);
        response = NextResponse.next({ request });
        // ...and so does the browser.
        for (const c of cookies) response.cookies.set(c.name, c.value, c.options);
        // An answer that writes one person's session is kept by no cache.
        for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(headers)) response.headers.set(name, value);
      },
    },
  });

  const user = await keepSession(pb);
  if (!user && request.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith("/account")) {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/signin", request.url));
  }
  return response;
}

export const config = {
  // Every page, not the build's static files.
  matcher: ["/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)"],
};
```

`setAll` is given the cookies and the headers to send with them: `Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, max-age=0`, `Expires: 0` and `Pragma: no-cache`. An answer that writes a session is one person's, and a cache between your server and the browser that kept it would hand it to the next person. Set them on the response with the cookies.

The redirect is a convenience for the reader, not the check: a page that shows one person's data asks `keepSession` itself, as the account page above does.

## Acting as the project

A route handler that does what only the project may, such as sending an email, checks who is asking with the request's client and then acts with the secret key:

```ts
// src/lib/server.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const PROJECT = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL ?? "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio";

/** The project, with its secret key: server code only. */
export const server = createServer({ url: PROJECT, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY ?? "" });
```

```ts
// src/app/api/invite/route.ts
import { keepSession } from "palbase/web/ssr";
import { writingClient } from "../../../lib/palbase-server";
import { server } from "../../../lib/server";

export async function POST(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const user = await keepSession(await writingClient());
  if (!user) return Response.json({ error: "unauthorized" }, { status: 401 });
  const { to } = (await request.json()) as { to: string };
  await server.notify.sendEmail({
    body: { to, subject: "You're invited", text: `${user.email ?? "A friend"} invited you.`, category: "transactional" },
  });
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}
```

```ts
// src/invite.ts
"use client";

export async function invite(to: string): Promise<void> {
  // Same origin: the browser sends the session cookie with it.
  const res = await fetch("/api/invite", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ to }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`the invite was refused: ${res.status}`);
}
```

A message composed whole like this one goes out through the project's own email provider. A template goes through the platform's shared sender too. See [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications).

`createServer` takes the same address as the browser's client. It refuses to run where there is a `document`, and its package resolves to an error in a browser bundle, so the secret key cannot ship to the client by accident.

A larger backend, with its own database and routes, is a machine of its own rather than route handlers, and the browser calls it with the user's token. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls).

## Without cookies

`createClient` from `palbase/web` keeps the session in the browser's `localStorage` instead. Then the server sees no session of its own, and an app renders what is the user's in client components and keeps server components for what is the same for everyone. A client made with `createClient` belongs in client components (`"use client"`), made on first use as `palbase()` above is: a module that called it at import would run on the server too while Next renders the client component's first HTML, where there is no `localStorage`.

Everything in [Auth](/docs/web/auth) and [Realtime](/docs/web/realtime) works with either client as written.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_URL` | Build, browser and server | The environment's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`. Read by the browser's client and by the server. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Build, browser and server | The publishable key, `pb_<ref>_c…`. Public by design. |
| `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` | Server only | A secret key, `pb_<ref>_s…`, from Studio's Settings › API keys. Never `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. |

A `NEXT_PUBLIC_` value is built into the bundle, so the address and the key are fixed at build time: build once per environment.

## Related

- [Overview](/docs/web/overview) — the client, and what the project's address answers a browser
- [Auth](/docs/web/auth) — the flows, and the pages auth's emails link to
- [Realtime](/docs/web/realtime) — channels over the project's socket
- [Uploads](/docs/web/uploads) — sending a file to a signed URL
- [Server SDK](/docs/server/overview) — `createServer` and the secret key



<!-- ===== ios/overview ===== -->

# iOS SDK

Palbase's iOS SDK is Swift. Its core product, `Palbase`, holds the project's address and publishable key, the transport every call goes through, the signed-in user's session, the realtime socket and the person's consent, with auth in it. Every other module is a product of its own that the app links or leaves out: an app that sends no push carries none of push's code.

The SDK is distributed compiled, as binary XCFrameworks, from [github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift](https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift). It needs **iOS 18** and **Xcode 16** or newer, and its API is Swift 6 concurrency throughout: `async` calls, `Sendable` types, and observable state for SwiftUI.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import SwiftUI

/// The app's one client: the environment its build configuration names.
let pb = PalbaseClient(.environment)

struct RootView: View {
    var body: some View {
        // Drawn again on every sign-in and sign-out.
        if let user = pb.auth.state.user {
            Text("Signed in as \(user.email ?? user.id)")
        } else {
            Button("Sign in") {
                Task { _ = try? await pb.auth.signIn(email: "ada@example.com", password: "correct-horse-battery-staple") }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`.environment` is not typed by you: `palbase apps:sync` writes it, and the build compiles in the one its configuration names (below).

## Install

In Xcode, **File › Add Package Dependencies…**, enter `https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift`, and add the products the app uses to its target. In a `Package.swift`:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift", from: "0.4.0")
```

| Product | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Palbase` | The core: configuration, transport, session, [auth](/docs/ios/auth), the realtime socket, [consent](/docs/ios/consent). Every app links it. |
| `PalbaseFlags` | [Feature flags](/docs/ios/flags), kept live. |
| `PalbaseAnalytics` | [Events, screens, the person's properties](/docs/ios/analytics), timings and reports, as the person allowed. |
| `PalbaseRealtime` | [Channels](/docs/ios/realtime): broadcasts and a state the members share. |
| `PalbaseNotify` | [Push](/docs/ios/notifications): this install's token, preferences, topics, the inbox, in-app messages. |
| `PalbaseNotificationService` | The app's notification service extension: each push reported delivered, its picture shown. |
| `PalbaseStorage` | [Files](/docs/ios/storage): uploads and downloads at URLs your backend signs. |
| `PalbasePurchases` | [Buying in the App Store](/docs/ios/purchases), and what the signed-in customer has bought in any store. |
| `PalbaseUI` | The renderer of the screens a project designs (paywalls, in-app messages, inbox cards), in SwiftUI. The two products below bring it. |
| `PalbasePurchasesUI` | The paywall the project publishes, drawn natively. |
| `PalbaseNotifyUI` | In-app messages shown over the app, and the person's inbox, drawn natively. |
| `PalbaseDebug` | The [in-app debug console](/docs/ios/debug-console)'s screens. |
| `Palbe` | What the [backend clients](/docs/ios/backend-calls) `palbase apps:sync` generates compile against. Link it when the project has a backend. |

A chat's live voice is a package of its own, [palbase-swift-voice](https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift-voice), because it brings WebRTC: see [Voice](/docs/ios/voice). So are voice and video calls, [palbase-swift-calls](https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift-calls) (`PalbaseCalls`, and `PalbaseCallsUI` for the ready screens): see [Calls](/docs/ios/calls).

## Connect the app to the project

The app never holds a URL or a key you type. The CLI writes each environment's settings into the app's repository, and the Xcode build compiles in the environment its configuration names. Debug can build against `staging` and Release against `main`, the project's first environment and its production one, from one source tree.

**1. Register the app**, once per project, with its Apple team, and give it its bundle in each environment it runs in:

```sh
palbase apps:create ios "Shop" --slug shop --team-id ABCDE12345
palbase apps:env:set shop --bundle com.example.shop -E staging
palbase apps:env:set shop --bundle com.example.shop -E main
```

The team is the 10 characters under **Apple Developer › Membership**. The app's widgets and extensions are not apps of their own: they share its sign-in. See [`apps:create`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appscreate) and [`apps:env:set`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appsenvset).

**2. Write its settings into the repository**, from the repository's root:

```sh
palbase apps:sync shop
```

It writes `palbase/` and nothing outside it:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `palbase/environments/<env>/shop.json` | The environment's client document: its address, the app's publishable key, the keychain group, auth's passkey domain, the backends' addresses. |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/contracts/<machine>.openapi.json` | Each backend's contract, as its machine serves it. |
| `palbase/shop.palbase` | Each environment's Swift: `PalbaseConfiguration.environment` and every backend's typed client (`pb.<name>`). |
| `palbase/project.json` | The checkout's project and its apps. |

Commit them. Run `palbase apps:sync` again when the project changes (a new environment, a backend's routes); `palbase apps:sync --check` exits 1 in CI when the committed files are not what the project gives now. `palbase apps:sdkconfig shop` prints the client document without writing anything. See [`apps:sync`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appssync).

**3. Set up the Xcode project.** Three steps, no plugin, and nothing reaches the network at build time:

1. Add `palbase/shop.palbase` to the **Compile Sources** of every target that uses Palbase: the app, and each widget or extension.
2. In each of those targets, **Build Rules › +**: *Source files with names matching* `*.palbase`, *Custom script* with the script below, and one output file, `$(DERIVED_FILE_DIR)/$(INPUT_FILE_BASE)-palbase.swift`. Leave *Run once per architecture* off. The script reads only its input, so it runs under Xcode's user script sandboxing.
3. Add a user-defined build setting, `PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT`, on every build configuration, its value the environment's slug: `staging` for Debug and `main` for Release, as the project names them.

```sh
[ -n "${PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT:-}" ] || { echo "error: Palbase: the build configuration $CONFIGURATION names no environment: set PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT"; exit 1; }
plutil -extract "environments.$PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT.swift" raw -o "$SCRIPT_OUTPUT_FILE_0" "$INPUT_FILE_PATH" || { echo "error: Palbase: no environment $PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT in $INPUT_FILE_NAME (run palbase apps:sync)"; exit 1; }
```

A configuration that names no environment, or one the app is not set in, stops the build with that message.

**4. Give the targets their capabilities**, from what the client document names:

| Capability | Value | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| **Keychain Sharing** | the document's `keychain_group` without its team prefix (`com.example.shop.palbase`; Xcode adds `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)`) | The app and every extension that uses Palbase: they share the session, the device's key, the install and the consent choices through it. |
| **Associated Domains** | each entry of `auth.associated_domains` (`webcredentials:<ref>.palbase.studio`) | An app that signs in with [passkeys](/docs/ios/auth#passkeys). |
| **Push Notifications** | — | An app that registers for [push](/docs/ios/notifications). |

## The client

```swift
import Palbase

let pb = PalbaseClient(.environment)
```

Make one client for the app and keep it: every module hangs off it (`pb.auth`, `pb.flags`, `pb.notify`, …), made once on first use and sharing its transport and its socket. A module's property exists once its product is imported: `pb.flags` needs `import PalbaseFlags`.

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pb.auth` | Sign-in, the session and the user: [Auth](/docs/ios/auth). |
| `pb.consent` | What the person allowed, key by key: [Consent](/docs/ios/consent). |
| `pb.socket` | The project's one realtime socket, opened the first time a channel is joined. `pb.socket.status.state` is observable: `idle`, `connecting`, `connected`, `reconnecting`, `disconnected`. |
| `pb.installation` | This install of the app: `id`, which push, consent and analytics name it by. |
| `pb.debug` | The [debug console](/docs/ios/debug-console)'s recording. |
| `pb.configuration` | The configuration it was made with: `url`, `publishableKey`, `environmentInfo` (`ref`, `slug`, `name`, `production`), `backends`. |
| `pb.currentSession()` | The session now, or `nil`. |
| `pb.setPreferredLanguages(_:)` | The languages every request says (`Accept-Language`), when the app has a language setting of its own; `nil` for the device's. Auth's emails, flag and paywall rules and a backend's translations read them. |

`PalbaseClient(_:sessionStorage:retry:)` takes two more settings. `sessionStorage: .memory` keeps the session in this process alone instead of the keychain. `retry:` is a `RetryPolicy` (below).

### What the app adds to the configuration

The generated `.environment` holds what the project says. What is the app's own is added with `with(consent:analytics:appGroup:)`:

```swift
import Palbase

let pb = PalbaseClient(try! .environment.with(
    consent: ConsentOptions(start: ["analytics": .granted, "performance": .granted], textVersion: "2026-10"),
    analytics: AnalyticsOptions(appBackground: false),
    appGroup: "group.com.example.shop"
))
```

- `consent`: what the app starts with until the person chooses, and the version of the text its consent screen shows ([Consent](/docs/ios/consent)).
- `analytics`: which of analytics' own events it makes ([Analytics](/docs/ios/analytics#the-apps-own-events)).
- `appGroup`: the app group the app shares with its notification service extension, where the extension leaves a report it could not send ([Notifications](/docs/ios/notifications#the-notification-service-extension)).

A configuration given in code, for a test or a tool, is `PalbaseConfiguration(url:publishableKey:keychainGroup:backends:passkeyRelyingParty:consent:analytics:appGroup:)`. The address must be `https` (plain `http` only for `localhost`) and the project's origin alone, and the key must be the publishable one (`pb_<ref>_c…`): a secret key is refused with a `ConfigurationError`, because it never goes in an app.

## The session

The session is kept in the keychain, readable after the device's first unlock and never moved to another device, in the group the app shares with its extensions: a widget or a notification service extension reads the same signed-in user. The access token is renewed ahead of its end while the app is in the foreground, and a call refused for a dead token is renewed once and sent again, only for the user whose session sent it.

A sign-in is sent with a proof made by a key that is created on the device and kept in its keychain. A session the project binds to that key (DPoP, RFC 9449) is sent with a fresh proof on every call that carries its token, to the project and to your backend alike, so a token copied off the device opens nothing on its own. Nothing in the app's code changes for it.

## Errors

A module's call that fails throws a `PalbaseError`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `status` | The HTTP status; `0` when no answer came, or the refusal was made on the device. |
| `code` | A stable code: the server's (`invalid_credentials`, `rate_limited`, …) or the client's (`network_error`, `timeout`, `passkey_cancelled`, …). |
| `message` | What happened, in English, for a log. |
| `op` | The operation that failed, as the contract names it (`Login`, `GetMe`). |
| `requestId` | The request's id, when the server answered: the line to find in Studio's Logs. |
| `retryAfter` | The seconds the server asked to wait, when it did. |
| `body` | The refusal's body as sent, as `JSONValue`. |
| `isNetworkError` | True when the request was never answered (no network, the host unreachable, no answer in time). Ask this rather than `status == 0`. |

```swift
import Palbase

func signIn(email: String, password: String) async -> String {
    do {
        _ = try await pb.auth.signIn(email: email, password: password)
        return "Welcome back"
    } catch let e as PalbaseError where e.isNetworkError {
        return "You are offline"
    } catch let e as PalbaseError where e.code == "invalid_credentials" {
        return "Wrong email or password"
    } catch {
        return "Something went wrong: \(error)"
    }
}
```

A call to your own backend throws its route's typed error instead: see [Calling Your Backend](/docs/ios/backend-calls#errors).

### Retries

A call is sent again only when that cannot do its work twice: a read (`GET`, `HEAD`, `QUERY`), or a write its contract takes an `Idempotency-Key` on, with one key made for the call and carried by every attempt. What is retried is an answer that says "not now" (`429`, `502`, `503`, `504`) and a request that never reached the server, waiting what the server's `Retry-After` asks, or 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s with jitter when it says nothing. Everything else is the caller's at once.

```swift
import Palbase

// Five attempts, and a Retry-After of up to a minute waited for.
let patient = PalbaseClient(.environment, retry: RetryPolicy(attempts: 5, maxWaitSeconds: 60))
```

The default is `RetryPolicy.default`: three attempts in all, and a `Retry-After` longer than 30 seconds is not waited for (the error goes to the caller). `RetryPolicy.once` sends each call once.

- [Auth](/docs/ios/auth): sign-in, passkeys, Sign in with Apple, the session

- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#apps): every `apps` command

# Auth

`pb.auth` signs a person in and keeps them signed in. It is in the core product, `Palbase`. Every flow that ends in tokens starts the session, and every call that acts for the user carries it from then on: to the project's modules, to your backend, and on the realtime socket. The flows an app writes most are methods here: email and password, guests, passkeys, Sign in with Apple, Google, second factors, magic links, phone codes, passwords, the user's sessions. Every other client operation of the auth module is reachable, typed, as `pb.auth.api`.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import SwiftUI

struct SignInView: View {
    @State private var email = ""
    @State private var password = ""
    @State private var problem = ""
    @State private var mfaToken: String?

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Email", text: $email).textContentType(.username).textInputAutocapitalization(.never)
            SecureField("Password", text: $password).textContentType(.password)
            Button("Sign in") { Task { await signIn() } }
            Button("Sign in with a passkey") { Task { await passkey() } }
            if let reason = pb.auth.state.sessionEndReason, reason == .userBanned {
                Text("This account is suspended.")
            }
            Text(problem)
        }
    }

    private func signIn() async {
        do {
            switch try await pb.auth.signIn(email: email, password: password) {
            case .signedIn: problem = ""
            case .mfaRequired(let token, _): mfaToken = token // finish with pb.auth.mfa.challenge(...)
            }
        } catch {
            problem = "\(error)"
        }
    }

    private func passkey() async {
        do {
            try await pb.auth.passkeys.signIn()
        } catch let error where pb.auth.wasCancelled(error) {
            // The sheet was dismissed: nothing to show.
        } catch {
            problem = "\(error)"
        }
    }
}
```

## Who is signed in

`pb.auth.state` is an `@Observable` object on the main actor. A SwiftUI view that reads it is drawn again when it changes, with no listener to write:

```swift
import Palbase
import SwiftUI

struct Root: View {
    var body: some View {
        if let user = pb.auth.state.user {
            Text("Hello \(user.email ?? user.id)")
        } else {
            SignInView()
        }
    }
}
```

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `isSignedIn` | Whether someone is signed in. It does not change when the token is refreshed. |
| `userId` | The signed-in user's id, or `nil`. |
| `user` | The user as auth last answered (`AuthAPI.User`: `id`, `email`, `emailVerified`, `isAnonymous`, `roles`, `metadata`, …), or `nil`. |
| `session` | The `Session` (`accessToken`, `refreshToken`, `expiresAt`, `userId`, `user`); it changes with every refresh. Printed or logged, it shows no token. |
| `sessionEndReason` | Why the last session ended without the app signing out: `.expired`, `.revoked`, `.userDeleted` or `.userBanned`; `nil` once someone signs in or the app signs out. |

It holds the session kept on the device from the first frame: the keychain is read when the client is made. It follows a sign-out in another process too, such as the app's widget, and a session that auth ended (the account deleted or suspended, signed out everywhere) is seen within one token's lifetime while the app is in the foreground, even when it makes no call.

Outside SwiftUI:

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `currentSession()` | The session now, or `nil`. |
| `currentUser()` | The user as auth last answered, without a call. |
| `getUser()` | Reads the profile fresh (`GET /auth/me`): `AuthAPI.MeProfile`, with `emailVerified`, `hasPassword`, `hasMfa`, `isAnonymous`, `providers` and `locale`. |
| `refreshSession()` | Renews the session now. |
| `changes` | An `AsyncStream<AuthEvent>` of every change: `.signedIn`, `.tokenRefreshed`, `.userUpdated`, `.signedOut`, `.sessionExpired`. |
| `sessionEndReason()` | The same reason as `state.sessionEndReason`, read from any thread. |

```swift
import Palbase

func followSession() async {
    for await event in pb.auth.changes where event == .sessionExpired {
        let why = await pb.auth.sessionEndReason()
        print("signed out by the project:", why.map { "\($0)" } ?? "unknown")
    }
}
```

When someone signs out, or someone else signs in, the realtime socket closes and every module forgets what it held for the last user: the next user's flags, inbox and purchases are read for them.

## Email and password

```swift
import Palbase

func createAccount() async throws {
    let created = try await pb.auth.signUp(email: "ada@example.com", password: "correct-horse-battery-staple")
    if created.accessToken == nil {
        // The project asks for the address to be confirmed before a sign-in.
        print("check your email")
    }
}
```

`signUp(email:password:locale:)` creates the account (`POST /auth/signup`), and starts the session when the project lets a new account sign in before it confirms its address. `locale` is the language auth writes this user's emails in; with none given, it is the language the app itself is shown in, so an English app on a Turkish phone gets English mail. `signUp(_:)` takes the whole `AuthAPI.SignupRequest`, with its `redirectTo`.

`signIn(email:password:)` (`POST /auth/login`) answers a `SignInResult`: `.signedIn(user)`, or `.mfaRequired(mfaToken:factors:)` when the account has a second factor.

The password rules, and whether an email must be confirmed first, are the project's auth settings: Studio's Auth screens, or [`palbase auth:settings:set`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authsettingsset).

### Confirming an email

```swift
import Palbase

func confirm(code: String) async throws {
    try await pb.auth.email.verify(.init(code: code, email: "ada@example.com"))
}

func resend() async throws {
    _ = try await pb.auth.email.resendVerification(email: "ada@example.com")
}
```

`email.verify(_:)` takes the link's `token`, or the `code` with the `email`, as the project sends them.

## Guests

```swift
import Palbase

func continueAsGuest() async throws {
    let guest = try await pb.auth.signInAnonymously()
    print(guest.id, guest.isAnonymous) // a real user id, true
}
```

`signInAnonymously(locale:)` (`POST /auth/anonymous`) makes an account with no email or password and signs it in on this device. Its session is held and renewed like any other, and what the guest buys or writes is theirs. The project turns guests on (the auth setting `anonymous_sign_ins`); off, the call is refused with `403 anonymous_sign_ins_disabled`.

A guest becomes an account, keeping its id, with an address and a password: `pb.auth.api.convertAnonymousUser(body: .init(email:password:))` mails a code to the address (`POST /auth/anonymous/convert`), and `pb.auth.api.verifyAnonymousConversion(body: .init(code:))` confirms it.

## Passkeys

A passkey signs in with Face ID or Touch ID, and nothing is typed. The app needs the **Associated Domains** capability with the `webcredentials:` entry its client document names (`auth.associated_domains` in `palbase/environments/<env>/<app>.json`, `webcredentials:<ref>.palbase.studio`). The project publishes the app at `/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` once its bundle is set in the environment ([`apps:env:set`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appsenvset)); Apple caches that file, so a device can take a day to see a change.

```swift
import Palbase

func passkeyAccount() async throws {
    // A new account whose only credential is a passkey, then a sign-in with it.
    switch try await pb.auth.passkeys.signUp(email: "ada@example.com", displayName: "Ada") {
    case .signedIn(let user): print("signed in", user.id)
    case .confirmationRequired(let userId): print("confirm the address first", userId)
    }
}

func addPasskey() async throws {
    // For the signed-in user: the next sign-in is one tap.
    let credential = try await pb.auth.passkeys.register(name: "iPhone")
    print(credential.id, credential.isPasskey)
}
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `passkeys.signIn()` | Signs in with any passkey this device, the user's iCloud Keychain or a phone nearby holds for the project: the sheet lists them. |
| `passkeys.signUp(email:displayName:)` | Opens an account with a passkey and no password, then signs in with that passkey. `email` is the account's identifier, an address or a phone number as the project's passkey settings ask, or `nil` when it asks for none (then `displayName` is required). Answers `.signedIn(user)`, or `.confirmationRequired(userId:)` when the project asks for the address to be confirmed before a sign-in. |
| `passkeys.register(name:userName:)` | Adds a passkey to the signed-in account. Auth asks for a recent sign-in (`reauthentication_required` otherwise). `userName` is what the sheet shows, needed only by an account with no address or phone. |

The user's passkeys are listed with `pb.auth.api.webauthnListCredentials()`, renamed with `webauthnRenameCredential(id:body:)` and removed with `webauthnDeleteCredential(id:)`. A sheet the user dismisses throws `passkey_cancelled`; a relying party that is not the one the client document names throws `passkey_relying_party_mismatch`, and running `palbase apps:sync` again fixes it.

## Sign in with Apple and Google

```swift
import Palbase

func apple() async {
    do {
        if case .mfaRequired(let token, let factors) = try await pb.auth.signInWithApple() {
            print("second factor needed", token, factors)
        }
    } catch let error where pb.auth.wasCancelled(error) {
        // The sheet was dismissed.
    } catch {
        print(error)
    }
}
```

`signInWithApple(variant:)` shows Apple's own sheet; `signInWithGoogle(variant:)` opens Google's page in the system's browser sheet and exchanges its code on the device, with no client secret in the app. Each starts the session, or answers `.mfaRequired`. The provider must be on for the project, with a **native client** for this app in Studio's **Auth › Providers**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Application key | The app's slug (`shop`), as `palbase apps:create` registered it. |
| Platform | `ios` |
| Variant | `release`, or a label of the build's own: the `variant:` the app passes (default `"release"`). |
| Flow | Native OAuth |
| Apple | **Bundle ID**: the app's bundle. The app also needs the **Sign in with Apple** capability. |
| Google | **Bundle ID**, the Google Cloud **iOS Client ID**, and the **Native redirect URI**: a URI whose scheme is that client's iOS URL scheme (`com.googleusercontent.apps.1234-abcd:/oauth2redirect`). |

The SDK signs in with the native client alone. With no native client for the app, platform and variant, or one set up for another bundle than the running app's, the call throws `auth_client_not_configured` or `auth_client_mismatch` before any sheet opens. A sheet the user dismisses throws `oauth_cancelled`; `wasCancelled(_:)` is true for it, for a dismissed passkey sheet and for a cancelled task.

Once the provider has answered, the SDK keeps the answer in the keychain until auth has taken it, and sends it again while the answer is "not now". A sign-in interrupted before then is never finished into a later one: the next sign-in with that provider cancels it.

## Second factors

A sign-in that needs a second factor answers `.mfaRequired(mfaToken:factors:)`, `factors` being among `totp`, `sms`, `email` and `webauthn`. Finish it:

```swift
import Palbase

func finish(mfaToken: String, code: String) async throws {
    try await pb.auth.mfa.challenge(mfaToken: mfaToken, type: .totp, code: code)
}
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mfa.challenge(mfaToken:type:code:)` | Completes the sign-in with a code: `type` is `.totp`, `.sms` or `.email`. |
| `mfa.recovery(mfaToken:code:)` | Completes it with a recovery code. |
| `mfa.sendSmsCode(mfaToken:)`, `mfa.sendEmailCode(mfaToken:)` | Sends the code first, for `.sms` and `.email`. |

For the signed-in user:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mfa.enrollTotp()` | Starts a TOTP factor: `secret`, `otpUrl`, a `qrCode` and the `recoveryCodes`, shown once. |
| `mfa.verifyTotp(code:)` | Confirms it with the first code the authenticator shows. |
| `mfa.enrollSms(phone:)`, `mfa.verifySms(code:)` | Adds a phone: auth texts it a code, which confirms it. |
| `mfa.enrollEmail()` | Adds the account's address. |
| `mfa.factors()` | The factors: each one's `id`, `type`, `verified`. |
| `mfa.removeFactor(id:currentPassword:)` | Removes one; it asks for the account's password. |
| `mfa.stepUp(code:)` | Steps the session up to aal2 with the authenticator's code: what a route that answers `stepUpRequired` asks. Returns the session. |
| `mfa.sendStepUpSmsCode()`, `mfa.stepUp(smsCode:)` | The same by text: the first sends the code to the user's SMS factor, the second steps up with it. |
| `passkeys.stepUp()` | The same with one of the account's passkeys: Face ID or Touch ID. |

A step-up keeps the session's refresh token; its refreshes stay at the new level, and a route's `maxAge` counts from the step-up. An email code is not a way up ([Second factors and their strength](/docs/backend/authentication#second-factors-and-their-strength)).

New recovery codes are `pb.auth.api.mfaRegenerateRecoveryCodes()`.

## Magic links and phone codes

```swift
import Palbase

func magicLink(token: String?) async throws {
    if let token {
        try await pb.auth.magicLink.verify(token: token) // the token the email's link carried
    } else {
        try await pb.auth.magicLink.send(email: "ada@example.com")
    }
}

func phone(code: String?) async throws {
    if let code {
        if case .mfaRequired = try await pb.auth.phone.verifyCode(phone: "+905551234567", code: code) {
            print("a second factor is needed")
        }
    } else {
        _ = try await pb.auth.phone.sendCode(phone: "+905551234567")
    }
}
```

A magic link lands where the project's links land ([Where email links land](/docs/web/auth#where-email-links-land)), with its `token` in the query: an app that sends them opens that address as a universal link and passes the token to `verify(token:)`. Phone sign-in must be on for the project (`provider_not_enabled` otherwise); `sendCode(phone:)` texts a code through the project's SMS provider and answers the same whether or not the number has an account.

## Passwords

```swift
import Palbase

func passwords() async throws {
    // Forgot it: the email's link carries a token for confirmReset.
    try await pb.auth.password.requestReset(email: "ada@example.com")

    // Signed in: change it, or add a first one to an account that has none (passkey, guest, social).
    let me = try await pb.auth.getUser()
    if me.hasPassword {
        try await pb.auth.password.change(.init(currentPassword: "old-long-passphrase", newPassword: "a-new-long-passphrase"))
    } else {
        try await pb.auth.password.set(.init(newPassword: "a-first-long-passphrase"))
    }
}
```

`password.confirmReset(token:newPassword:)` finishes a reset with the link's token.

## The user's sessions

```swift
import Palbase

func devices() async throws {
    let list = try await pb.auth.sessions.list()
    for s in list.sessions { print(s.id, s.current, s.userAgent ?? "", s.lastActivity) }
    try await pb.auth.sessions.revokeAll() // signed out everywhere
}
```

`sessions.revoke(id:)` ends one of them.

## Signing out and deleting the account

`signOut()` ends the session on the server (`POST /auth/logout`) and on the device; a failed call still signs out here. If another process of the app (its extension) signed someone else in meanwhile, theirs is the session that ends.

`deleteAccount(password:)` deletes the account (`DELETE /auth/user`) and ends the session. An account with a password gives it (`getUser().hasPassword` says whether it has one): missing or wrong, the call is refused with `401 reauth_required` and the user stays signed in. An account without one is deleted on the strength of its session.

## A session from tokens of your own

`setSession(accessToken:refreshToken:expiresIn:)` starts the session from a token pair the app has from a flow it runs itself, step by step, through `pb.auth.api`.

## `pb.auth.api`

Every client operation of the auth contract, typed, through the session's transport. A few an app reaches for:

| Call | Path |
|---|---|
| `pb.auth.api.updateMe(body: .init(locale: "tr"))` | `PATCH /auth/me` |
| `pb.auth.api.listIdentities()` | `GET /auth/identities` |
| `pb.auth.api.unlinkIdentity(id:)` | `DELETE /auth/identities/{id}` |
| `pb.auth.api.webauthnListCredentials()` | `GET /auth/webauthn/credentials` |

An operation of the contract that needs the secret key cannot be made from an app.

## Proof of work

Auth may answer a sign-up, a sign-in or a code request with a proof-of-work challenge when the address looks like a bot. The SDK solves it on the device and sends the request once more; the app never sees it.

# Calling Your Backend

Your own backend runs on a machine, and an iOS app calls it through a typed client that `palbase apps:sync` generates from the backend's contract: every route is a Swift method with its own request, response and error types, and every call carries the signed-in user's session. The client is compiled into the app with the environment's configuration (`palbase/<app>.palbase`, see [Overview](/docs/ios/overview#connect-the-app-to-the-project)), and it compiles against the `Palbe` product: link `Palbe` in each target that compiles the file.

## Quick example

The backend, a `palbase/backend` app on the machine named `backend`:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

interface Note {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  private readonly notes: Note[] = [];

  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    const note = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner: user.id, title: body.title };
    this.notes.push(note);
    return note;
  }

  @Get("/{id}")
  read(@Param("id") id: string, @User() user: UserT): Note | null {
    return this.notes.find((n) => n.id === id && n.owner === user.id) ?? null;
  }
}
```

The app, after `palbase apps:sync`:

```swift
import Palbase
import Palbe

func addNote(title: String) async {
    do {
        let note = try await pb.backend.notes.create(.init(title: title))
        print("saved", note.id)
    } catch .other(let failure) {
        print("refused:", failure.code, failure.errorDescription ?? "")
    } catch {
        print(error)
    }
}
```

`pb.backend` is the machine named `backend`; `notes.create` is `NotesController`'s `create`. The request is `NotesCreateRequest`, the answer `NotesCreateResponse`, and the call throws `NotesCreateError`, typed.

## The generated client

`palbase apps:sync` reads each backend's contract, the OpenAPI document its machine serves, and writes the client into `palbase/<app>.palbase` for every environment the app is set in. Run it again when the backend's routes change: a route the backend no longer has, or a field it no longer takes, is then a compile error in the app.

| What the backend has | What the app calls |
|---|---|
| The machine `backend` | `pb.backend`. A machine's name is camelCased (`shop-api` is `pb.shopApi`), unless `palbase apps:sync --as shop-api=shop` names it, the same in every environment. |
| `NotesController` | `pb.backend.notes`: the class's name without `Controller`, its first letter lowercased. |
| Its method `create` | `pb.backend.notes.create(…)` |
| A path parameter `{id}` | An argument: `read(id: "n_1")` |
| A `@Body` | The request type, first and unlabelled: `create(.init(title: "Milk"))` |
| `@QueryParams` | A `query:` argument of its own type |
| The method's return | The response type, decoded. A route that answers `204` returns nothing. |

The types are named by the route's operation: `NotesCreateRequest`, `NotesCreateResponse`, `NotesCreateError`, `NotesReadResponse`. Everything is `Codable` and `Sendable`. The names the client gives backends never collide with the client's own (`auth`, `flags`, `storage`, …): `apps:sync` refuses one that would.

A backend the environment does not name is not a build error: each of its calls throws `.transport`, saying which backends the environment has.

## What a call carries

| | |
|---|---|
| The user | The signed-in user's access token, when there is one; nothing when no one is signed in, and the route says whether it needs one ([Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication)). A session bound to the device's key is sent with its proof. The publishable key is not sent: a machine asks for none. |
| A dead token | Refreshed once and the call sent again, only for the user whose session sent it. |
| "Not now" | A read (`GET`, `QUERY`) answered `429`, `502`, `503` or `504`, or never answered, is sent again after the server's `Retry-After`. A write is sent again only when the backend keeps its idempotency key (its contract declares the header); otherwise a write that reached the backend before its answer was lost could be done twice. |
| Languages | `Accept-Language`: the device's, or what `pb.setPreferredLanguages(_:)` named. A backend's `t()` reads it ([Translations](/docs/backend/translations)). |
| Redirects | Never followed: the user's token stays with the backend's own address. |
| Encrypted fields | A field the route marks `encrypted()` is sealed before the call leaves the device, and one it answers through `encrypt()` is opened when the answer arrives: the client `palbase apps:sync` wrote holds the project's id and signing key for it ([Encrypted Requests](/docs/backend/request-encryption)). A call sent again is the same sealed request. |

A path parameter is sent as exactly one path segment, percent-encoded. A value that would not stay one however a server reads it (empty, `.` or `..`, or one that hides them between slashes, `a/../b`) is refused before anything is sent, as `.encode`.

## Errors

A generated method throws its own error type, so a `do`/`catch` switches on named outcomes:

```swift
import Palbase
import Palbe

func read(_ id: String) async -> String {
    do {
        let note = try await pb.backend.notes.read(id: id)
        return note.title
    } catch .other(let failure) {
        switch failure {
        case .unauthorized: return "Sign in again"
        case .validation(let v): return v.fields.map { "\($0.field): \($0.message)" }.joined(separator: "\n")
        case .rateLimited(let r): return "Try again in \(r.retryAfter ?? 1) s"
        case .network: return "You are offline"
        case .server(let s): return "\(s.code) (\(s.requestId ?? "no request id"))"
        default: return failure.errorDescription ?? "Something went wrong"
        }
    } catch {
        return "\(error)"
    }
}
```

A code the route's contract declares is a case of its own (`NotesCreateError.forbidden` for a route that declares `403 forbidden`); every other failure is `.other(BackendError)`. `BackendError` is the backend's error envelope, classified:

| Case | When |
|---|---|
| `.server(ServerFailure)` | The backend refused: `code`, `status`, `message`, `requestId`, `details` and `data`, the error's payload (`decodeData(_:)` reads it as a type of yours). |
| `.validation(ValidationFailure)` | `400`, the input failed the route's schema: `fields`, each a `field` and its `message`. |
| `.rateLimited(RateLimitInfo)` | `429`, the route's limit: `retryAfter` in seconds. |
| `.unauthorized(AuthFailure)` | `401`, after the client already refreshed the token once. |
| `.stepUpRequired(StepUpFailure)` | `401 insufficient_user_authentication`: the route asks for a stronger sign-in (`acrValues`, e.g. `["aal2"]`; `maxAge`). The session is fine and is not refreshed: step the user up with their second factor — `pb.auth.mfa.stepUp(code:)` with an authenticator code, `pb.auth.mfa.stepUp(smsCode:)` after `sendStepUpSmsCode()`, or `pb.auth.passkeys.stepUp()` with one of the account's passkeys — then call again (`maxAge` counts from the step-up); the session holds the aal2 token from then on, refreshes included. |
| `.appAttestRequired(AuthFailure)` | `401 app_attest_required` the device's proof could not settle: the SDK enrolled, proved and sent the call again, and the backend still refused ([Device attestation](#device-attestation)). |
| `.attestationUnavailable(AttestationFailure)` | The route asks for the device's proof and this device cannot give one now: `reason` says why (`unsupported_device`, a Simulator or hardware without App Attest; `enrolment_rate_limited` with `retryAfter`; `app_attest_not_configured`, no iOS app registered). Nothing more is sent. |
| `.network(TransportFailure)` | No answer: no network, the connection lost, a timeout. |
| `.transport(TransportFailure)` | Not sent: a backend the environment does not name. |
| `.decode(CodecFailure)`, `.encode(CodecFailure)` | The answer is not the type the contract declares; the input could not be encoded, or a path parameter is not one segment. |

`code`, `statusCode`, `requestId` and `failure` (the envelope, whichever case it is) are on every `BackendError`. The `requestId` is the line to look for in the machine's logs ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds)).

## Device attestation

A route the backend marks `attest: true` is called only by your app on a genuine iPhone or iPad ([Device attestation](/docs/backend/authentication#device-attestation)). The SDK proves each call by itself with Apple's App Attest:

- once per install it makes an App Attest key and enrols it: auth checks Apple's attestation of it for your registered app (team and bundle);
- each call to such a route then carries an assertion over the call's method, path, body and a short-lived challenge, with the key's counter, so a captured call cannot be sent again or changed;
- the route's generated method knows it attests (`palbase apps:sync` writes it from the contract), so its first call is proved: the SDK enrols before it if needed and asks your backend for a fresh challenge (`GET /.well-known/palbase/attest-challenge`, once for calls made together), with no `401` round trip first. A route not marked carries no proof;
- a `401 app_attest_required` from a route its client does not know as attested — a client generated before the route was marked — is answered by itself: enrol if needed, prove, send once more; the route is proved from then on while the app runs. `palbase apps:sync` again marks it.

What only you set: Xcode's **App Attest** capability on the app target. It writes `com.apple.developer.devicecheck.appattest-environment` = `development`, Apple's sandbox, for a build run from Xcode; a TestFlight or App Store build uses Apple's production environment whatever the value says, so one entitlements file serves Debug and Release. `palbase apps:sync` reminds you when an environment's backend has an attested route. A Simulator cannot attest: under enforce its calls end in `.attestationUnavailable`.

## Files

A route your backend declares as an upload (palbase/backend's `Upload`, with a bucket and a path template) is a generated method that takes the file: `file: PBFileSource`, the route's input, and an `onProgress` closure. The bytes go straight to storage at a URL the backend signs, never through the backend, and the method returns what the route's handler answered once the file is stored.

```swift
import Foundation
import Palbase
import Palbe

func setAvatar(_ png: Data) async throws {
    // posts.photo: an upload route of PostsController, with a path parameter.
    _ = try await pb.backend.posts.photo(postId: "p_1", file: .data(png, contentType: "image/png")) { progress in
        switch progress.phase {
        case .authorizing: print("starting")
        case .uploading: print("\(Int(progress.fraction * 100))%")
        case .processing: print("the backend is handling it")
        }
    }
}
```

`PBFileSource.url(_:filename:contentType:)` streams a file from disk; `.data(_:filename:contentType:)` sends bytes in memory, its type read from the bytes when none is given (a photo from `PhotosPicker` is HEIC, PNG or JPEG). The type matters: storage holds every upload to its bucket's types and size. `BackendUploadProgress` says the `phase` (`authorizing`, `uploading`, `processing`), `sentBytes`, `totalBytes` and `fraction`. The upload route's own name and arguments are your backend's; the example's are an illustration.

To store a file the app has without a route of its own for it, see [Storage](/docs/ios/storage).

## Gateways

A backend's gateways, its realtime channels, are in the same client: `pb.backend.join(RoomGateway(roomId: "42"))`. See [Gateways](/docs/ios/gateways).

## Calls the contract does not type

`call(_:_:as:method:headers:)` calls a route by its path with an `Encodable` input and a `Decodable` answer, and `call(_:as:method:headers:)` one with no input; the method is `POST` unless `method:` says otherwise. It throws `BackendError`.

```swift
import Palbase
import Palbe

struct Ping: Decodable, Sendable { let ok: Bool }

func ping() async throws -> Bool {
    let pong: Ping = try await pb.backend.call("health/ping", method: .get)
    return pong.ok
}
```

## A backend on your computer

`palbase apps:sync --backend ../server` generates the client from a backend checkout on this computer, before any machine serves its routes: its `palbase/backend` app writes its contract and exits, and nothing is connected to. `pb.palbe(url:)` is a client of a backend at an address of its own, such as `http://localhost:8080` in the simulator, for its untyped calls and its gateways; the address must be `https`, or `http` on `localhost`.
