# Gateways

Your backend's [gateways](/docs/backend/gateways) are its realtime channels, and an iOS app joins them through the client `palbase apps:sync` generates ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/ios/backend-calls)). `pb.backend.join(RoomGateway(roomId: "42"))` returns once the backend let the signed-in user in, with a handle: the gateway's events arrive on it as a Swift enum, and its messages go out through it, each answered with the backend's ack. The app writes no channel name, event name or payload type of its own, and a gateway that carries a chat holds the chat's state for SwiftUI.

## Quick example

The backend's `RoomGateway` ([Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways#quick-example)): its pattern `room:{roomId}`, the events `message` and `welcome`, and the message `say`, answered with the new message's id.

```swift
import Palbase
import Palbe

func enterRoom(_ roomId: String) async {
    do {
        // Throws PBGatewayError.unauthorized when the backend does not let this user in.
        let room = try await pb.backend.join(RoomGateway(roomId: roomId))

        let listener = await room.on { event in
            switch event {
            case .message(let m): print("\(m.from): \(m.text)")
            case .welcome(let w): print("\(w.members) in the room")
            }
        }

        // The ack the backend's @Subscribe returned, as the message's case.
        if case .say(let said) = try await room.send(.say(.init(text: "hello"))) {
            print("taken as", said.id)
        }

        // When the screen goes:
        await room.off(listener)
        await room.leave()
    } catch let e as PBGatewayError {
        print("not taken:", e.reason) // the backend's own word, or the platform's: forbidden, unavailable, …
    } catch {
        print(error)
    }
}
```

## The generated types

Each gateway of the backend is a struct named by its class, `RoomGateway`, made with a value for each `{param}` of its pattern: `RoomGateway(roomId: "42")` is the channel `room:42`. Inside it:

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Event` | The events it sends, one case each, with its payload type: `.message(RoomGatewayMessageEvent)`, `.welcome(RoomGatewayWelcomeEvent)`. |
| `Send` | The messages a member may send: `.say(RoomGatewaySayMessage)`. |
| `Reply` | The acks, one case per message: `.say(RoomGatewaySayReply)`. |
| `pattern`, `durable`, `topic` | Its pattern, whether it keeps what it sends, and the channel this value names. |

An event the generated code does not know, from a backend that moved ahead of the app, is not delivered. Run `palbase apps:sync` again when the backend changes a gateway: a payload it no longer takes is then a compile error.

## Joining

`join(_:history:)` takes the generated value, opens the project's socket if it is not open, and returns a `GatewayHandle` once the backend let the user in. A param that is empty or holds a `:` would name another channel, and is refused before anything is sent (`invalid params`).

| Member of the handle | What it does |
|---|---|
| `on(_:)` | Listens to every event the gateway declares, as its `Event` enum. Returns a token. |
| `off(_:)` | Stops the listener the token names. |
| `send(_:)` | Sends one message and waits for the backend to take it: returns its `Reply`, or throws `PBGatewayError`. |
| `leave()` | Drops the handle's listeners and lets go of the channel. |
| `topic` | The channel: `room:42`. |
| `seq` | A durable gateway's number of the last event the handle was sent; `nil` on one that keeps nothing. |
| `chat` | A chat gateway's chat: see [Chat gateways](#chat-gateways). |

`GatewayHandle` is an actor: its methods are awaited. Hold a handle for as long as its screen is on screen, and leave it when the screen goes (`.onDisappear`, or the end of a `.task`): a gateway with members is one its backend still runs for. Two handles of the same channel share one membership, and the channel is left with the last of them.

Only a signed-in user joins: the session the socket carries is who they are. The socket is one person's, and it closes when someone signs out or someone else signs in.

## Messages and acks

`send(_:)` returns what the backend's `@Subscribe` returned, as the message's `Reply` case. It throws `PBGatewayError`, whose `reason` says why the message was not taken:

| `reason` | What it means |
|---|---|
| The backend's own word | Its method threw `GatewayRefusal("…")`: `no_commands`, `not_your_turn`. Act on it. |
| `forbidden` (`.forbidden`) | The user may only listen on this channel, or the platform refused with no reason given. |
| `rate_limited` (`.rateLimited`) | Past the project's events per second. |
| `unavailable` (`.unavailable`) | The backend could not be asked just then. Worth trying again. |
| `no reply`, `socket closed` | No answer came. The message may have been taken. |
| `not joined` (`.notJoined`) | Nothing was sent: the handle was left, its socket closed for good, or the socket is being opened again. |
| `undecodable reply` | The backend took it, but its ack is not what the app's generated code reads: run `palbase apps:sync`. |

A join that is refused throws too: `unauthorized` when the backend did not let the user in, `unavailable` when it could not be asked (worth trying again). The values are static members of `PBGatewayError` to compare with: `catch let e as PBGatewayError where e == .unauthorized`.

A message goes to the backend alone, never to the other members. They hear what the backend emits.

## Durable gateways

A [durable gateway](/docs/backend/gateways#durable-gateways) keeps what it sends. A handle that joins one is sent what it keeps first, in order, then what comes after; `join(_:history: false)` asks for only what comes after the join. The channel's first handle decides: a second handle of the same channel gets the events from where it joins.

When the socket drops, it is opened again by itself and every gateway joined again; a durable one after its `seq`, so the handle is sent what it missed, in order, and nothing twice. Meanwhile `send` throws `not joined`. When the socket closes for good (a sign-out, another user's sign-in) every handle on it ends: its listeners are dropped, and `send` throws `not joined`. Join again as the user who is there now.

## Chat gateways

A gateway declared with `chat: true` carries a chat of the project's agents, which the platform writes into its channel ([AI](/docs/backend/ai#a-chat-in-an-app)). Its handle's `chat` is a `PBChat`, the chat's state folded from what the platform writes: from the chat's start, since the channel keeps it, and then each change as it comes. In SwiftUI, hold it as a `PBChatModel`, an `@Observable` on the main actor:

```swift
import Palbase
import Palbe
import SwiftUI

struct SupportChat: View {
    let chatId: String
    @State private var support: GatewayHandle<SupportGateway>?
    @State private var chat: PBChatModel?
    @State private var text = ""

    var body: some View {
        List {
            if let chat {
                ForEach(chat.state.items) { item in
                    switch item {
                    case .message(let m): Text(m.text).frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: m.mine ? .trailing : .leading)
                    case .response(let r): Text(r.text)
                    case .goal, .voice: EmptyView()
                    }
                }
                TextField("Message", text: $text)
                Button("Send") {
                    Task { _ = try? await support?.send(.say(.init(text: text))); text = "" }
                }
            }
        }
        .task {
            guard let joined = try? await pb.backend.join(SupportGateway(chatId: chatId)) else { return }
            support = joined
            chat = PBChatModel(joined.chat)
        }
        .onDisappear { Task { [support] in await support?.leave() } }
    }
}
```

`SupportGateway` and its `say` message are the backend's own, as [AI](/docs/backend/ai#a-chat-in-an-app) declares them. What the member does in the chat goes through the gateway's messages, and the backend does it as them: `say`, `decide` (an approval's yes or no), `answer` (a client tool's output) and `stop`.

| Member of `PBChat` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `state` | The chat now: the same value until something changes. |
| `onChange(_:)` | Told each time the state changes; a burst of parts is one change. Returns what stops it. |
| `updates` | An `AsyncStream` of the state now, then each change (the newest, for a reader that falls behind), until the gateway is left. |
| `hasOlder`, `loadOlder(_:chatId:limit:)` | The channel keeps a day of the chat. `loadOlder(pb, chatId:)` reads the page before what the state holds, with the member's own session (the project's AI settings let its users' sessions reach their chats: `clients`), and folds it in front; it returns whether there is more, `false` once a page reached the chat's start. `loadOlder(limit:load:)` reads the page through your backend instead: `load` is given a `PBChat.PartsQuery` and returns a `PBChat.PartsPage`. |

What `state` holds:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `items` | The conversation in order, an `Item` each: `.message(Message)`, `.response(Response)`, `.goal(GoalEvent)` and `.voice(VoiceEvent)`. Each has an `id` for `ForEach`. A subagent's answer is a part of its parent's. |
| `messages` | Each member's (or the server's) message: `clientId`, `id`, `text`, `author` (`nil`: the server), `authorName`, `status` (`.pending` until the agent has it, then `.delivered`, or `.failed` with its `error`), `kind` (`.text`, or `.voice` for a line said in the chat's voice), `attachments`, `metadata`, `createdAt`, and `mine`. |
| `responses` | Each answer, the subagents' too: `id`, `status` (`running`, `waiting`, `completed`, `failed`, `canceled`, `timed_out`, `budget_exceeded`), `end` and `error` once it ended, `text` so far, `parts`, `thinking`, `goal`, `startedBy`, and `mine`. |
| `turn` | The last turn's state: its `status`, and in `waiting.reason` what it waits for: `approval`, `tool_output`, `subagents` or `message`. |
| `waiting` | What waits for the signed-in user: `approvals`, the tool calls of their own turns waiting for their yes, and `outputs`, their client tool calls waiting for the app's answer. |
| `goal` | The chat's goal once one was set: `objective`, `status`, its stop code and reason, and its `events`. |
| `voice` | The chat's live voice, the last that began, live or ended: `status` (`started`, `closed`), `mine`, `seconds`, `closeReason`. See [Voice](/docs/ios/voice). |
| `forkedFrom` | A fork's: the `chatId` it was forked from and the message it was cut before. |

An answer's `parts` are its pieces in order: `.text(String)`, `.tool(Tool)` (a tool call: `callId`, `name`, `status`, `input`, `output`, and `approvalId` while it waits for a yes), `.agent(Agent)` (a subagent handed work) and `.thinking(Thinking)` (a step's reasoning, when the agent shows it). A tool call's `output` is its last 16 KiB, `omittedBytes` how much came before; `pb.chatToolCall(chatId:callId:)` reads the whole answer.

A picture or a file a message carries is read back with `pb.chatAttachment(chatId:message:_:)`, as `Data` of the attachment's `contentType`. A file is attached by your backend, which sends the message naming it. Both reads go with the member's own session, as `loadOlder(pb, chatId:)` does.

`PBChat(parts:me:)` makes a chat from parts you give it, through the same fold: what a SwiftUI preview or a test shows a chat with.

# Realtime

`pb.realtime` (the `PalbaseRealtime` product) is the project's channels on its one realtime socket: what members broadcast, and a state every member sees the same. The socket, `pb.socket`, is in the core: it opens the first time a channel is joined and never before, so an app that only signs in or captures analytics opens none. Flags' live updates, consent and your backend's [gateways](/docs/ios/gateways) ride the same socket.

> **Note:** Your own backend's realtime channels are its [gateways](/docs/ios/gateways), joined through the client `palbase apps:sync` generates: typed events, and messages the backend answers with an ack. This page is the channels the project declares by name.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseRealtime

func follow(roomId: String) async throws {
    let room = pb.realtime.channel("room:\(roomId)")

    let stopMessages = await room.onBroadcast("message") { payload in
        if case .string(let text)? = payload["text"] { print("message:", text) }
    }
    room.onState { entries in
        print("\(entries.count) here")
    }

    // Throws the server's reason when it does not let the user in.
    try await room.join()

    // Presence: an ephemeral entry lives as long as this connection.
    try await room.set("typing:me", .bool(true), life: .ephemeral)
    try await room.broadcast("message", ["text": .string("hello")])

    // When the screen goes:
    await stopMessages()
    await room.leave()
}
```

Payloads and values are `JSONValue`: `.string`, `.number`, `.bool`, `.object`, `.array`, `.null`, and `decode(_:)` reads one as a `Decodable` type of yours.

## Channels

`pb.realtime.channel(_:)` returns a `RealtimeChannel` for that name. A channel is joined once however many listeners it has.

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `join()` | Joins; returns once the server let the user in, throws its reason when it did not. |
| `leave()` | Leaves, and forgets the state it held. |
| `onBroadcast(_:_:)` | Listens to one event's broadcasts, a member's or the project's server's. Returns what stops it (an `async` closure). |
| `broadcast(_:_:)` | Sends an event to the channel's other members; the sender does not hear its own. The call does not wait for the server: one it refuses comes to `onRefused`. |
| `onRefused(_:)` | Listens to the server refusing a broadcast: `{event, reason}`, with `forbidden`, `rate_limited`, … Returns what stops it. |
| `entries` | The channel's state as the server last told it: `[String: Entry]`, each an `Entry` with its `value` and its `life`. |
| `onState(_:)` | Told the whole state each time it changes. Returns what stops it. |
| `set(_:_:life:)` | Writes one entry. The state changes when the server says so, for every member alike. |
| `deleteOwn(_:)` | Removes one entry this membership wrote: every other entry is its writer's. |
| `name` | The channel's name. |

An entry's `life` is `.durable` (the default), which stays until it is removed, or `.ephemeral`, which is its writer's presence and goes when the writer's connection does. A member that joins is handed the whole state, and each change after it; one that missed a change asks for the whole state again by itself.

Names are `:`-separated segments, 255 bytes at most.

## Who may join

A channel name is a string the app chooses, so being signed in says nothing about which channels are the user's. The project's server **declares** its channels ([Channels](/docs/backend/channels), `PUT /realtime/channels` with the secret key), and a channel no declaration matches belongs to no one:

| Declared `kind` | Who joins |
|---|---|
| `owner` | The pattern's one `{name}` segment is the joining user: `user:{uid}` is joined by that user alone, who may do everything on it. |
| `public` | Any signed-in user of the project, with the rights the declaration gives: `publish` (broadcast), `state_read`, `state_write`. |

A refused join throws the server's reason: `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `invalid_topic`, `rate_limited`, `too_many_channels`, `state_budget` or `unavailable`. Only `unavailable` is worth trying again. Some namespaces are the platform's, and no declaration can claim them: `flags:<ref>` and `flags:<ref>:<user>` carry [flag](/docs/ios/flags) changes, and the SDK joins them itself.

## The socket

`pb.socket.status` is an `@Observable` on the main actor. A view that reads `state` is drawn again when it changes:

```swift
import Palbase
import SwiftUI

struct ConnectionBadge: View {
    var body: some View {
        let state = pb.socket.status.state
        Label(state.rawValue, systemImage: state == .connected ? "bolt.fill" : "bolt.slash")
    }
}
```

| `state` | What it means |
|---|---|
| `idle` | Never opened: nothing has joined a channel yet. |
| `connecting` | Being opened. |
| `connected` | Open; the channels wanted are joined on it. |
| `reconnecting` | Dropped (the network went, a heartbeat went unanswered), and opened again after a pause. |
| `disconnected` | Closed by the client: someone signed out or in, or no channel is wanted. |

`status.since` is when it last changed, and `status.changes` is an `AsyncStream` of every change in order, where a view reading `state` is drawn with the newest only.

The socket sends a heartbeat every 25 seconds. One that goes unanswered closes the socket, and a socket that drops is opened again after 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, then every 30 seconds, each pause jittered, with every channel still wanted joined again. A broadcast sent while the socket was down is not delivered; a channel's state comes back whole with the new join. When the session is refreshed, the new token goes to every joined channel without leaving it.

The socket is one person's. When someone signs in, signs out, or the session ends, the client closes it, and every channel with it, and a channel forgets the state it held. Join again for the user who is there now, for example from `pb.auth.changes` or a SwiftUI `.task(id: pb.auth.state.userId)`.

## Limits

The project holds its clients to limits the platform sets and the project may lower (`PUT /realtime/limits` from a server): connections open at once, broadcasts and state writes per second, joins per second, channels per connection. A project over its connection limit, or whose realtime quota is used up, is refused a new socket.

## Related

- [Gateways](/docs/ios/gateways): your backend's channels, typed, with messages and acks
- [Channels](/docs/backend/channels): declaring who may join what
- [Realtime in your backend](/docs/backend/realtime): broadcasting and writing state from a server
- [Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime): the same channels in a browser

# Messaging

`pb.messaging` is the signed-in person's conversations on iOS: their list, each conversation's timeline and its threads, as `@Observable` objects SwiftUI draws, kept in the app's SQLite between launches and current over the project's socket. The app writes; it opens no socket, appends nothing and syncs nothing itself. With the notification service extension, a message that arrives while the app is closed is already on the phone when it opens. What the module is — history, encryption, timers, moderation, prices — is [Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview).

## Install

Add `https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift` with Swift Package Manager, at 0.10.0 or later:

- the app's target: `Palbase` and `PalbaseMessaging`;
- the notification service extension's target (below): `PalbaseMessagingNotificationService`.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseMessaging
import SwiftUI

struct Inbox: View {
    let pb: PalbaseClient
    // The person's conversations, the latest first: drawn from the phone at once, then kept current.
    @State private var list: ConversationList?

    var body: some View {
        List(list?.items ?? [], id: \.id) { conversation in
            NavigationLink(conversation.title ?? "Chat") { Chat(view: pb.messaging.conversation(conversation.id)) }
        }
        .navigationTitle("Chats (\(list?.unread ?? 0))")
        .task { list = pb.messaging.conversations() }
    }
}

struct Chat: View {
    let view: ConversationView
    @State private var text = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            List(view.entries) { entry in
                switch entry {
                case .message(let m): Text(m.text ?? "a file")
                case .pending(let item): Text(item.request.text ?? "a file").foregroundStyle(.secondary) // on its way
                }
            }
            TextField("Message", text: $text)
                .onSubmit {
                    let words = text
                    text = ""
                    // Drawn at once, sent now or when the network is back — once.
                    Task { _ = try? await view.send(words) }
                }
        }
        .onAppear { view.onScreen(true) }
        .onDisappear { view.onScreen(false) }
        .task { try? await view.markRead() }
    }
}
```

`pb.messaging.direct(with: userId)` is the direct conversation with someone (the one there is, or a new one, shown to them with its first message); `group(title:memberIds:)` makes a group. `ConversationView` has `entries`, `members`, `typing`, `hasEarlier` and `loadEarlier()`; `thread(_:)` is a message's thread, `scheduled()` the person's messages for later.

## Spaces and open groups

A conversation may belong to a place of your app's — an organization, a workspace — when it is made with a `space` your app names (`org:<id>`), for good: `direct(with: userId, space: org)` opens the pair's conversation there (the two have one in each space, and one with none), `group(title:space:visibility:)` makes a group there, `conversations(spaces: [org])` lists a space's — its `unread` that space's — and `search(_:space:)` searches one. Each conversation says its `space` (`nil`: none).

An open group (`visibility: .open`; `isOpen` on the conversation) is a channel: `openGroups(space:)` lists a space's, each with whether the person is in it (`joined`), and `join(_:)` lets the person in — the group then in their list at once. Making one, listing and joining ask the project's hook (`open_group`, `list_open`, `join`): refused, a `PalbaseError` with code `not_allowed`; an open group names its space (`space_required`). One an admin removed does not join again by themselves (`removed`).

```swift
// Sources/Workspace/Channels.swift
let org = "org:2f6c0c1e-8a3b-4c1d-9e5f-0a1b2c3d4e5f"
let sidebar = pb.messaging.conversations(spaces: [org])
let channels = try await pb.messaging.openGroups(space: org)
for c in channels.items where !c.joined { _ = try await pb.messaging.join(c.id) }
let dm = try await pb.messaging.direct(with: "usr_01a1684c796e7394aa8ec75d893a8fe2", space: org)
```

A message your server wrote as someone (an assistant sending their words) says what wrote it: `message.via` (`"pal"`) — show it beside the message.

## Writing

`send(_:_:)` takes text, or `SendOptions`: `replyTo`, `threadId` and `alsoInConversation`, `mentions`, `files` (encrypted on the phone before they are uploaded), `expiresIn` with `expiresFrom`, `viewOnce`, and `sendAt` for a message the server sends later. A message waits in the outbox while the phone is offline and goes once it can, once. `edit`, `remove`, `react`, `unreact`, `markRead`, `typing`, `cancelScheduled` and `editScheduled` change what was said; `open(_:attachment:)` downloads and decrypts a file, and a message seen once gives its files by `viewOnce(_:)` alone — held by the app, never by the phone's copy.

## Search

`search(_:)` finds the person's messages that say every word asked — a word's beginning finds it, "toplanti" finds "Toplantıda" — the newest first, across their conversations or in one (`in:`). Each `SearchHit` carries what a result row draws: the conversation's `title` and `photo` (a group's, or the other person's in a direct one), its `sender`, `peer`, and its `matches` — where its text or a file's name says what was asked, in UTF-16 code units. The first page also lists the person's conversations whose name says it (`conversations`), found on the phone. What the module finds and never finds: [Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#search).

```swift
let found = try await pb.messaging.search("toplanti")
for c in found.conversations { print(c.title ?? "Chat") }   // their names say it: draw them first
for hit in found.messages {
    let text = hit.message.text ?? ""
    var row = AttributedString(text)   // the text, what was asked in bold
    for m in hit.matches where m.field == .text {
        let from = text.utf16.index(text.startIndex, offsetBy: m.offset)
        let to = text.utf16.index(from, offsetBy: m.length)
        if let r = Range(from..<to, in: row) { row[r].inlinePresentationIntent = .stronglyEmphasized }
    }
}
let more = try await pb.messaging.search("toplanti", cursor: found.nextCursor)   // while nextCursor is not nil
```

A find opens where it was said: `conversation(_:at:)` is the conversation's page around it, `focus` naming the message to scroll to and mark. `loadEarlier()` reads back from there and `loadLater()` forward; once it reaches the newest, `hasLater` is false and it is kept current as any. An answer the conversation's timeline does not show has a `threadRootId`: open its thread at it.

```swift
if let root = hit.threadRootId {
    thread = pb.messaging.thread(hit.conversation.id, root: root, at: hit.message.id)
} else {
    chat = pb.messaging.conversation(hit.conversation.id, at: hit.message.id)   // chat.focus == hit.message.id
}
```

### By meaning

With the project's `search_by_meaning` on ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#by-meaning)), `search(_:by: .meaning)` finds the messages nearest what the question means, in none of its words: "uçuş saati kaçta" finds "Uçağımız sabah dokuzda Sabiha Gökçen'den kalkıyor". The nearest come first, one page (`nextCursor` is nil), each with `score` — how near, 0.3 to 1 — and no `matches`; `conversations` is empty. A hit opens as any does: `conversation(_:at:)`.

```swift
do {
    let found = try await pb.messaging.search("uçuş saati kaçta", by: .meaning)
    for hit in found.messages { print(hit.score ?? 0, hit.title ?? "", hit.message.text ?? "") }
} catch let e as PalbaseError {
    // search_by_meaning_off: the project searches by words alone. too_many_searches: a person asks
    // 30 at once, one more a minute. ai_payment_required: the project's AI use is spent.
    print(e.code)
}
```

## A message while the app is open

A message's push is not drawn as the system's banner while the app is in front: the message is synced, and `incoming()` gives it to the app to draw its own banner. Answer the system with what `Messaging.foregroundPresentation` says:

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseMessaging
import UIKit
import UserNotifications

final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate, UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate {
    let pb = PalbaseClient(try! PalbaseConfiguration.environment.with(appGroup: "group.com.example.chat"))

    func application(_ application: UIApplication, didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken deviceToken: Data) {
        Task { try? await pb.notify.register(apnsToken: deviceToken) }
    }

    func userNotificationCenter(_ center: UNUserNotificationCenter, willPresent notification: UNNotification,
                                withCompletionHandler completionHandler: @escaping (UNNotificationPresentationOptions) -> Void) {
        pb.notify.willPresent(notification)
        // A message's push: none (the app draws its own); any other push: as the app wants.
        completionHandler(Messaging.foregroundPresentation(for: notification, of: pb) ?? [.banner, .sound])
    }
}
```

`incoming()` gives each message someone else wrote that is new to the phone once, whether the socket or the push brought it first — never what a sync or a page read, the person's own messages, or a muted conversation's. `onScreen` is true for the conversation on the screen:

```swift
.task {
    for await m in pb.messaging.incoming() where !m.onScreen {
        banner = m // m.message, m.conversation: draw it; a tap opens pb.messaging.conversation(m.message.conversationId)
    }
}
```

## Messages that arrive while the app is closed

The `PalbaseMessagingNotificationService` extension shows a message's push and, while it does, brings that conversation's new messages into the phone's copy: open the app without a network and they are there.

1. **Add the extension.** *File › New › Target › Notification Service Extension*; give it `PalbaseMessagingNotificationService`, and replace its `NotificationService.swift`:

   ```swift
   import PalbaseMessagingNotificationService

   final class NotificationService: PalbaseMessagingNotificationService {}
   ```

2. **Share the copy and the session.** In *Signing & Capabilities*, give the app and the extension the same:
   - **App Groups**: one group, such as `group.<bundle id>` — where the conversations are kept;
   - **Keychain Sharing**: `<bundle id>.palbase`, the `keychain_group` `palbase apps:sync` writes to the environment's file — where the extension reads the session, and writes it back when it renews it.

   The app alone has **Push Notifications**.

3. **Give the app the group** (above): `PalbaseConfiguration.environment.with(appGroup: "group.<bundle id>")`, so it reads what the extension wrote. The extension reads the app's configuration from the shared keychain: the app must have been opened once.

The extension's `Info.plist` is Xcode's: `NSExtensionPointIdentifier` `com.apple.usernotifications.service`, `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` `$(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).NotificationService`. iOS gives an extension about 30 seconds, enough for a conversation's new messages. A muted conversation sends no push: its messages come when the app opens.

## Screenshots

iOS cannot stop a screenshot. A conversation's screen says it is shown (`onScreen(true)` as it appears, `onScreen(false)` as it goes): when a screenshot is taken while it shows a conversation in vanish mode or a message seen once, the others are told. A conversation in vanish mode drops what the person read when they leave it: call `close()` as its screen goes.

## A deleted group

When a group's owner or an admin deletes it — or its last member leaves — it goes from everyone's `conversations()` at once, and those who were in it can still report it for 14 days ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#moderation)). `pb.messaging.deletedGroups()` is `@Observable`: its `items` are the groups the person can still report, the latest to stop first, each with `id`, `title`, `deletedBy` and `reportableUntil`, and one goes at its `reportableUntil`. `report(_:)` names it by its id with no message; the last 30 messages the person saw in it go with the report. A group the project's server deleted is not among them.

```swift
let deleted = pb.messaging.deletedGroups()
for group in deleted.items {
    print(group.title ?? "a group", group.reportableUntil)
}
if let group = deleted.items.first {
    try await pb.messaging.report(.init(conversationId: group.id, reason: .harassment, userId: group.deletedBy))
}
```

The title is the one the device had; it is nil when the device no longer had the group as the word came — on the deleter's own device now and then.

## Signing out

When the person signs out, what the phone kept of their conversations is dropped, unless `pb.messaging.keepOnSignOut` is true — then it is theirs again when they sign back in. Kept or not, no one else who signs in on the phone reads it.



<!-- ===== ios/calls ===== -->

# Calls

`pb.calls` is the signed-in person's voice and video calls on iOS. A call rings the phone as any call does — the system's own call screen through CallKit, on the lock screen and with the app closed, woken by a VoIP push — and an `@Observable` `PBCall` is what the app draws: where the call is, its cameras, its controls. Every call's media — one to one or in a group — goes through the platform's media server (LiveKit): a third person or the project's agent comes into the same room, and where UDP is shut it goes over TCP to port 443. `PalbaseCallsUI` draws the screens for an app that wants them ready-made. What the module is — kinds of call, who may call whom, ringing, history, prices — is [Calls](/docs/calls/overview).

## Install

The calls are a Swift package of their own, so an app that makes no calls takes none of their weight. Add `https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift-calls` with Swift Package Manager, at the same version as `palbase-swift`:

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/palgroup/palbase-swift-calls", exact: "0.14.1")
```

Link `PalbaseCalls` (the calls, headless) and, for the ready screens, `PalbaseCallsUI`. They bring Palbase's core and `PalbaseNotify` of the same version, and LiveKit's WebRTC and client SDK, which the media server's calls go through. **Do not add LiveKit's own Swift package beside them**: its client SDK is already inside `PalbaseCalls`. It needs iOS 18 and Xcode 16.3 or newer.

The app:

- says why it asks for the microphone (`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`) and, for video calls, the camera (`NSCameraUsageDescription`) in its `Info.plist`;
- has the **Push Notifications** capability, and the **Background Modes** `voip` (Voice over IP) and `audio` (Audio, AirPlay, and Picture in Picture).

## A call rings the phone

A call that comes while the app is closed, in the background or the phone is locked rings by a **VoIP push** (PushKit), which wakes the app, and is handed to **CallKit** at once: iOS draws its own call screen — the caller's name, the app's name and icon, its ringtone — and the call is answered or declined there.

- **The APNs key.** VoIP pushes go through the project's APNs key, the same `.p8` its notifications use ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications#every-channel-but-one-needs-a-provider-of-yours)): the platform sends them to the app's bundle id with `.voip` after it. Nothing else is set up.
- **The token.** `PalbaseCalls` registers the app's PushKit token with the project's notifications as a device of its own (platform `ios_voip`), beside the app's notification token, for the person signed in. The app writes no PushKit code.
- **Configure at launch.** `pb.calls.configure(_:)` sets the system's call screen and the VoIP pushes up. Call it once, before `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)` returns — a VoIP push that launched the app must find it there: iOS stops sending VoIP pushes to an app that does not report each one to CallKit at once.

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseCalls
import UIKit

final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate {
    func application(_ application: UIApplication, didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
        // A 40-point template image of the app's assets, shown on the system's call screen.
        pb.calls.configure(.init(callKit: .inBackground, iconTemplateImageName: "CallIcon"))
        return true
    }
}
```

`Calls.Configuration`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `callKit` | Whether the system's call screen carries the calls: `.inBackground` (the default) — a call that comes while the app is in the background, locked or closed rings on the system's screen, and in the open app the app's own screen rings; `.always` — every call, in the app too; `.never` — none: calls ring in the app alone, while it runs, and no VoIP push is taken |
| `iconTemplateImageName` | A 40-point template image of the app's assets, on the system's call screen |
| `ringtoneSound` | A sound file of the app's bundle the system rings with — and the app's own ring; the system's ringtone when `nil` |
| `includesCallsInRecents` | The calls are listed in the Phone app's recents (`true` by default) |

## Making a call

```swift
import PalbaseCalls
import SwiftUI

struct CallButton: View {
    let userId: String

    var body: some View {
        Button("Video call") {
            Task {
                // Rings every device of theirs; the media goes through the media server.
                let call = try await pb.calls.call(userId, video: true)
                call.setMuted(true)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `call(_ userId:, video:, conversationId:, metadata:, name:, imageURL:)` | Rings one person: a direct call. `name` and `imageURL` are what they see of the caller (else the caller's messaging profile's) |
| `callGroup(_ userIds:, video:, ring:, conversationId:, metadata:, name:, imageURL:)` | A group call — several people, or one others may be asked to later. `ring: false` rings no one: the people asked join when they like (a huddle) |
| `join(_ callId:)` | Comes into a group call the person was asked to — rung, missed, declined, or in before |
| `history(missed:, limit:, cursor:)` | The person's calls, the newest first, with how each went for them; `missed: true` the ones they missed |
| `call(id:)` | The call by its id, while it is on the device |

Each that makes or joins a call answers its `PBCall` and throws the module's refusal as a `PalbaseError`: `not_allowed`, `in_another_call`, `too_many_calls`, `quota_exceeded` and the rest of [Calls over HTTP](/docs/calls/http#making-a-call); `not_signed_in` when no one is. A call to someone who is calling this person that very moment is their call, answered.

`pb.calls` is `@Observable` too: `live` (the calls on the device — ringing, being made, going on; one that ends stays a moment, for its screen to say so), `ringing` (a call ringing in the app, not on the system's screen) and `current` (the call the person is in on this device, or makes). `deviceId` is the install's device, as the server names it.

## The call

A `PBCall` is `@Observable`: a SwiftUI view that reads it is drawn again as it changes.

| Property | What it is |
|---|---|
| `phase` | `.ringing` (someone calls them), `.invited` (asked into a huddle: `join()` comes in), `.calling` (they call; the other side rings), `.connecting`, `.connected`, `.reconnecting` (the media dropped and is coming back), `.elsewhere` (in it on another of their devices), `.ended(CallEndReason)`; `phase.isHere` while they are in it on this device |
| `snapshot` | The call as the server last told it ([A call](/docs/calls/http#a-call)) |
| `isIncoming`, `isVideo`, `isGroup` | Someone called them; a video call; a group |
| `title`, `imageURL` | What a screen names the call by — the others' names — and the other person's picture in a direct call |
| `others`, `joinedOthers` | The other people (and agents) in the call; those in it now |
| `media` | `.idle`, `.connecting`, `.connected`, `.reconnecting`, `.failed` |
| `isMuted`, `isCameraOn`, `isSpeakerOn`, `isFrontCamera` | The controls' state |
| `localVideo`, `remoteVideos`, `video(of:)` | This phone's camera while it is on, the others' cameras each with whose it is (`CallVideoTrack.userId`), and one person's |
| `connectedAt` | When it was answered (a direct call) or the person came in (a group): what a duration counts from |
| `problem` | The last thing that went wrong here — a refusal, the media failing: what a screen may show |
| `onSystem` | The system's call screen carries it |

`CallEndReason` is the server's `end_reason` — `.hungUp`, `.canceled`, `.declined`, `.missed`, `.busy`, `.failed`, `.ended` — or the person's own in a group that goes on (`.left`), and `.answeredElsewhere` when another of their devices took it.

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| `accept()` | Answers on this device — through the system's screen when it rings there. Throws the server's refusal: `answered_elsewhere` when another of the person's devices took it first |
| `join()` | Comes into a group call the person was asked to: a huddle, or one they declined or missed |
| `decline()` | Turns a ringing call down: a direct call ends; a group goes on without them |
| `hangUp()` | Hangs up — or cancels the call they are making, or turns down one ringing |
| `setMuted(_:)`, `setSpeaker(_:)` | The microphone muted; the sound through the speaker |
| `setCamera(_:)`, `flipCamera()` | The camera on or off, and the other camera — a video call's |
| `invite(_ userIds:, ring:)` | Asks more people in: a direct call becomes a group in the same room, going on |

`CallVideoView(track, fill: true, mirrored: nil)` draws a camera in SwiftUI: filling its frame or fitted in it, this phone's own camera mirrored unless said otherwise.

## Ready-made screens

`PalbaseCallsUI` shows the calls over the app: an incoming call that rings in the app (who calls, voice or video, Decline and Accept), then the call the person is in — the others' cameras or their picture, this phone's camera in a corner, how long it has gone on, and mute, speaker, camera, flip and hang up.

```swift
import PalbaseCalls
import PalbaseCallsUI
import SwiftUI

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor(AppDelegate.self) var delegate

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            ContentView()
                .callScreens(pb.calls)
                .callTexts(turkish)
        }
    }

    private var turkish: CallTexts {
        var t = CallTexts()
        t.incomingVoice = "Sesli arama"
        t.incomingVideo = "Görüntülü arama"
        t.accept = "Aç"
        t.decline = "Reddet"
        t.hangUp = "Kapat"
        return t
    }
}
```

- `.callScreens(pb.calls)` — the ready screens, `IncomingCallView` and `InCallView`.
- `.callScreens(pb.calls, incoming: { call in … }, inCall: { call in … })` — the app's own screen for either or both, each given the `PBCall`.
- `.callTexts(_:)` — every word they say (`CallTexts`: `incomingVoice`, `incomingVideo`, `calling`, `connecting`, `reconnecting`, `elsewhere`, `ended`, `accept`, `decline`, `hangUp`, `mute`, `speaker`, `camera`, `flip`).
- The parts, for a screen of the app's own: `CallStatus(call:)` (where the call is, in words, and its duration), `CallControls(call:)`, `CallAvatar(call:size:)`.

A call on the system's screen is answered there; the app's screens show it once the app is in front.

## Permissions

The first time a call is made or answered, the SDK asks for the microphone — and the camera for a video call — with the reasons the `Info.plist` gives. It does not refuse a call the person said no to: ask before, and send someone who refused to the app's Settings, where they allow it.

<!-- ===== ios/flags ===== -->

# Flags

`pb.flags` (the `PalbaseFlags` product) holds the project's feature flags and remote configuration as this app's reader sees them: every flag's value resolved by the project for the app's platform, version and language and for whoever is signed in, kept current as the flags change. A read takes no network: it answers from the values held, which are kept on the device between launches, and brings them up to date behind your code. Flags are defined in Studio's flags screens or by a server, never from the app ([Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags)).

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseFlags
import SwiftUI

struct Checkout: View {
    var body: some View {
        // Drawn again when one of these flags changes: in Studio, the user's own value, another user signing in.
        let flags = pb.flags.state
        VStack {
            Text(flags.string("banner_text", default: "Welcome"))
            if flags.bool("new_checkout", default: false) {
                Text("Up to \(flags.int("cart_limit", default: 20)) items")
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The module starts on first use: the values held on the device are read at once, the latest are fetched for whoever is signed in, and the flags' change channels are joined on the project's socket.

## Reading values

The same reads are on `pb.flags.state`, an `@Observable` on the main actor for SwiftUI, and on `pb.flags` itself, from any thread:

| Member | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `bool(_:default:)` | A boolean flag's value, or the default when there is none or it is not a boolean. |
| `string(_:default:)` | A string flag's value, or the default. |
| `number(_:default:)` | A number flag's value as a `Double`, or the default. |
| `int(_:default:)` | A number flag's value when it is a whole number, or the default. |
| `decode(_:as:)` | An object flag's value as your `Decodable` type, or `nil`. |
| `value(_:)` | A flag's value as `JSONValue`, or `nil` when there is none. |
| `all` | Every flag's value by key. |

A view that reads one flag from `state` is drawn again when that flag's value changes, and only then; a view that reads `all` is drawn again on any change. Every read answers at once. Before the first fetch has answered, the app reads the values it held at its last launch, or the default on its first. Give every read a default the app works with.

On `pb.flags`:

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `source(_:)` | Where a value came from: `system` (the flag's), `override` (the user's own) or `experiment` (an experiment's variant). |
| `version` | The version the values are current as of. |
| `holds(reader:)` | Whether the values held are this user's (`nil`: no one signed in). |
| `onChange(_:)` | Calls the listener with the keys whose values changed. Returns what stops it. |
| `changes` | The same, as an `AsyncStream<Set<String>>`. |
| `refresh()` | Brings the values up to date now, and returns when they are. It throws a `PalbaseError` when the read fails. |

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseFlags

struct Theme: Decodable { let accent: String }

func applyFlags() async {
    // Wait for current values before a first screen that depends on them.
    try? await pb.flags.refresh()
    let theme = pb.flags.decode("theme", as: Theme.self)
    print(theme?.accent ?? "default accent", pb.flags.source("theme") ?? "none")

    for await keys in pb.flags.changes where keys.contains("maintenance") {
        print("maintenance is now", pb.flags.bool("maintenance", default: false))
    }
}
```

## A signed-in user's values

The values are one reader's: the signed-in user's, or with no one signed in, this install's, proven with its secret. When someone signs in or out, the values held go, and listeners are told their keys; the new reader's are read, and listeners are told again. One reader's values are never read out to another, even for the moment the new ones take to arrive: a gate on a flag closes for the next user rather than staying open with the last one's value.

## What a value is resolved from

Every read is resolved by the project for its reader, in this order:

1. **The user's own value**, when a signed-in user has one. A server gives users their values with the secret key ([Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags#users-own-values)), and so does [`palbase flags:users:set`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-flagsusersset).
2. **The variant of an experiment** running on the flag, when the reader is one of its people.
3. **The flag's first condition that matches.** Conditions read what the app says about itself, the share of users a percentile picks, the country of the address the request came from, the server's clock, and the analytics audiences the reader is in, when they allowed personalization ([Consent](/docs/ios/consent)).
4. **The flag's default.**

What the app says about itself, with every read:

| Header | Sent as | Read as |
|---|---|---|
| `X-Platform` | `ios` | `client.platform` |
| `X-Palbase-Client-Version` | The app's `CFBundleShortVersionString` | `client.app_version` |
| `X-OS-Version` | The system's version (`18.6.2`) | `client.os_version` |
| `Accept-Language` | The device's languages, or what `pb.setPreferredLanguages(_:)` named | `client.locale`, its first language |
| `X-Palbase-Installation` | `pb.installation.id` | Counted toward which versions of your app are in use. |
| `X-Palbase-Installation-Secret` | The install's secret, with no one signed in | Proves the install, so audiences and experiments can place a reader who is not signed in. |

## Experiments

A value an experiment gave says so: `source(_:)` is `experiment`. When the app reads such a flag by its key (`bool`, `string`, `number`, `int`, `decode` or `value`, on `pb.flags` or `state`), the SDK records the analytics event `$flag_exposure` with `{ flag, experiment, variant }`, once per analytics session for each flag and experiment, through `pb.analytics` while the person allows analytics. That event is what an experiment's results count, so the app links `PalbaseAnalytics` and has used `pb.analytics` once. `all` records none: read a flag in an experiment by its key where the person sees it.

## Keeping up to date

The SDK keeps the values current by itself. The project announces every change on two realtime channels, which it joins on the project's socket:

| Channel | Who may join | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `flags:<ref>` | Anyone reading the project's flags, with no one signed in too | The project's flags changed. |
| `flags:<ref>:<user_id>` | That user only | That user's own values changed. |

Told of a newer version, the SDK asks for what changed since the one it holds (`GET /flags/delta`). When the delta can no longer bring its values up to date (the reader's context or audiences changed, or the deletions it would need are older than the project keeps), the project answers `410`, and the SDK reads a whole snapshot instead (`GET /flags/snapshot`, sent with the `ETag` of what it holds). A channel the project refuses, with realtime off, still leaves the reads: `refresh()` brings the values up to date.

## The debug console

The flag `palbase.debug_console`, given to one user as their own value, opens the [debug console](/docs/ios/debug-console) for them.

## Related

- [Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags): defining flags and giving users their own values
- [Analytics](/docs/ios/analytics): `$flag_exposure`, and the audiences conditions read
- [Realtime](/docs/ios/realtime): the socket the change notices travel on
- [Web Flags](/docs/web/flags): the same flags in a browser



<!-- ===== ios/analytics ===== -->

# Analytics

`pb.analytics` (the `PalbaseAnalytics` product) records what the app's users do, how its screens and requests perform, and its log when something goes wrong, each behind its own consent key: `analytics` for events, screens and the person's properties, `performance` for timings and request traces, `diagnostics` for the log sent with a report. Nothing waits on it: what is collected is held, sent together a few seconds later, and a send that fails is let go. What the project makes of it (people, funnels, retention, audiences) is in Studio's Analytics screens.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseAnalytics
import UIKit

final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate {
    func application(_ application: UIApplication, didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
        // Touched at launch: from here it makes the app's own events ($install, $app_open, …).
        _ = pb.analytics
        return true
    }
}

func checkedOut(total: Double) {
    pb.analytics.capture("checkout_completed", properties: ["total": .number(total), "currency": .string("EUR")])
}
```

Nothing is collected for a key the person has not granted, and nothing for one with no choice and no starting value: give the app's starting values in [Consent](/docs/ios/consent), or ask first.

## Events and screens

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `capture(_:properties:)` | Records an event: a name (a letter or `$`, then letters, digits and `_.:-$`, 64 at most) and its properties. |
| `screen(_:properties:)` | Records a screen the user saw. |
| `identify(traits:)` | Ties this device's anonymous events to the signed-in user, with their traits. It is done by itself after each sign-in. |
| `flush()` | Sends what is held now. |

An event is held for up to 5 seconds, or until 20 are held, and they go together; what is held when the app goes to the background goes then, and what is held when it closes offline is kept on disk and sent at the next launch. With no one signed in, events are an anonymous id's, made the first time one is needed; after a sign-in they are the user's, and the anonymous id's are tied to them. A session is a run of events with no gap of 30 minutes.

## The person's properties

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseAnalytics

func onboarded(plan: String) async {
    await pb.analytics.people.set(["plan": .string(plan)])
    await pb.analytics.people.setOnce(["first_seen_plan": .string(plan)])
    await pb.analytics.people.add(["projects_created": 1])
}
```

`people` is the signed-in user, or with no one signed in this device's anonymous id, whose properties become the user's once they sign in. `set`, `setOnce` (only where none is set), `unset` and `add` (to a number) are sent at once, while `analytics` is granted.

## The app's own events

From the moment `pb.analytics` is first touched, it records these by itself, each while `analytics` is granted:

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `$install` | Once per install, timed at the first launch even when analytics is allowed later. `$reinstall: true` when the keychain kept the install from before the app was deleted; `$apple_ads_token`, Apple's attribution token, while `ads_measurement` is granted. |
| `$app_open` | Each time the app comes to the foreground; `$cold: true` on a launch. |
| `$app_background` | Each time it goes to the background. |
| `$session_start` | Each time a session begins, after 30 minutes without an event. |
| `$app_updated` | When the app's version is not the one it last ran as: `$previous_version`, `$version`. |
| `$timezone` | The person's time zone, a property, set when it is not the one last set. |

Each one can be turned off in the configuration: `PalbaseConfiguration.environment.with(analytics: AnalyticsOptions(appBackground: false))` ([Overview](/docs/ios/overview#what-the-app-adds-to-the-configuration)). An app extension (a widget, a notification service) makes none of them.

## Performance

While `performance` is granted, the SDK times on its own, with no code of the app's:

- **Each request the app's `URLSession` makes** — the project's, its backend's and every other service's; async, completion handler or delegate alike — as a `network` sample: its method, its address as its route (no query, an id in the path as `:id`), its status and how long it took. What analytics itself sends is not timed, nor a request the app cancelled, nor a web socket.
- **How long the launch took**, from the process's start to the app before the person, as an `app_start` sample named `cold`. A launch the system began ahead of the person (prewarming), or one begun in the background (a push, a fetch) and opened later, is not one.

Before `performance` is granted nothing of the app's networking is touched. Each is turned off in the configuration: `AnalyticsOptions(network: false, appStart: false)`.

The SDK's privacy manifest declares these timings as **Performance Data**, linked to the user, for analytics, so Xcode's Privacy Report lists it. An app whose users can grant `performance` adds Performance Data to its App Privacy answers in App Store Connect.

What the app measures itself:

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseAnalytics

func loadFeed() async {
    let trace = pb.analytics.startTrace("feed_load")
    // … load it …
    trace.stop(attributes: ["source": "network"])
    pb.analytics.measure("feed_items", value: 42)
}
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `startTrace(_:)` | Starts timing something; the trace's `stop(attributes:)` records how long it took, in milliseconds. |
| `measure(_:value:kind:attributes:)` | Records one measurement. `kind` is `.custom` (the default), `.screen`, `.appStart` or `.network`. |
| `recordRequest(method:endpoint:status:durationMs:requestId:error:)` | Records a request the app made and how it ended. |

They are collected while `performance` is granted. While `analytics` is not, a timing goes with the publishable key alone: no user's token, no person's id, no install's id.

## Diagnostics

`log(_:level:)` keeps a line of the app's log in memory (the last 200, levels `.debug`, `.info`, `.warning`, `.error`), and `report(_:)` sends what it kept as what led to an error: `.error` (the default), `.crash` or `.userReport`. Both work while `diagnostics` is granted, and nothing of it is written to disk.

## When consent changes

While a key is not granted, nothing of it is made: no event, no queue, no file, no request, and no anonymous id. When it is withdrawn, what was held of it is deleted, on disk too, and with `analytics` the anonymous ids. When someone signs out, the next person on the device is someone new: the anonymous ids go. See [Consent](/docs/ios/consent).

## App Tracking Transparency

`pb.tracking` reads App Tracking Transparency's answer and shows its prompt when the app asks:

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbaseAnalytics

func askToTrack() async {
    if pb.tracking.status == .notDetermined {
        let answer = await pb.tracking.requestAuthorization()
        print(answer) // .authorized, .denied, .restricted
    }
}
```

The prompt's words are the app's `NSUserTrackingUsageDescription`. Palbase never asks on its own and never reads the advertising identifier: what the app does with the answer is its own. Ad measurement is a consent key of its own (`ads_measurement`).

## Related

- [Consent](/docs/ios/consent): the keys analytics collects behind
- [Flags](/docs/ios/flags#experiments): `$flag_exposure`, what an experiment's results count
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics): the same events from a browser
- [Debug Console](/docs/ios/debug-console): what the SDK records on the device, apart from analytics



<!-- ===== ios/consent ===== -->

# Consent

`pb.consent` is what the person allowed the app to collect and use, key by key. It is in the core product, and every module that collects asks it first: analytics records nothing for a key that is not granted, and a marketing message goes only where its channel's key is. A choice is kept on the device and stands the moment it is made, and it goes to the project with when it was made. The app's starting values never leave the device, so they can never override a refusal the project holds.

## Quick example

```swift
import Palbase

// What the app starts with until the person chooses, and the version of the text its screen shows.
let pb = PalbaseClient(try! .environment.with(consent: ConsentOptions(
    start: ["analytics": .granted, "performance": .granted, "diagnostics": .granted],
    textVersion: "2026-10",
    customKeys: ["custom.newsletter"]
)))

func consentScreen() async throws {
    let region = try await pb.consent.region()     // .gdpr asks first; .us collects until refused
    let ask = try await pb.consent.needsAsking()   // never chosen, or chosen under another text
    if region.jurisdiction == .gdpr || !ask.isEmpty {
        // … show the screen, then:
        try pb.consent.setMany(["analytics": .granted, "marketing_push": .denied, "custom.newsletter": .granted])
    }
    print(pb.consent.state("analytics")?.rawValue ?? "no choice and no starting value")
}
```

## The keys

| Key | What it allows |
|---|---|
| `analytics` | Events, screens, identify and the person's properties ([Analytics](/docs/ios/analytics)). |
| `performance` | Timings and request traces. |
| `diagnostics` | The log sent with a report. |
| `personalization` | Placing the person in analytics audiences, which flag conditions and in-app campaigns read. |
| `marketing_push`, `marketing_email`, `marketing_sms`, `marketing_whatsapp` | Marketing messages on each channel ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)). |
| `ads_measurement` | Measuring ads: Apple's attribution token with `$install`. |
| `ads_personalization` | Personalized ads. |
| `custom.<name>` | The app's own (`a`–`z`, `0`–`9` and `_`, 48 at most), named in `customKeys`. |

`keys()` lists them in the order a consent screen shows them: the platform's with their words, in English and Turkish (`title` and `description` by language), then the app's own, which the app words itself. Each `ConsentKeyInfo` has its `key`, its `category` (`measurement`, `personalization`, `marketing`, `advertising`, or `custom`) and `ads`, true for what the US laws call selling or sharing.

## Reading and choosing

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `state(_:)` | The key's state: `.granted` or `.denied`, the person's choice, else the app's starting value; `nil` when there is neither, and a module collects nothing then. |
| `set(_:_:)` | Records one choice: it stands at once and is sent to the project. |
| `setMany(_:)` | Records the choices of one screen, made together. A key that is not one throws `invalid_consent_key`. |
| `onChange(_:)` | Told every key whose state changes: the person's choice, a refusal from the project, a sign-in or a sign-out. Returns what stops it. |
| `lastDeniedAt(_:)` | When the key was last refused: here, on another of the person's devices, or by the project on their word. |
| `region()` | Where the person is, as the project tells from their address: `country`, and `jurisdiction`, `.gdpr` (the EU, the EEA, the UK, Switzerland), `.us` or `.other`. |
| `needsAsking(_:)` | The keys the app is to ask about (all, unless given): those never chosen, and those chosen on the app's screen under another `textVersion`; in the US, not an ads key the person refused within twelve months. |

What the app starts with until the person chooses is the app's to say, through `ConsentOptions.start`: where the law asks first (`region()` is `.gdpr`), start the collecting keys denied or not at all, and ask. A key the SDK collects for with no starting value and no choice collects nothing.

A choice that cannot be sent now is sent later, still saying when it was made: after 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 2 minutes, then every 10 minutes, and when the app returns to the foreground or the network comes back. A choice the project refuses never stands: the key is read again, and until it can be, reads `.denied`, as it does while what the device kept cannot be read.

## Whose the choices are

- With no one signed in, the choices are the device's: this install's, which proves itself with a secret kept in the keychain.
- On sign-in, the device's newer choices become the account's, and the device takes the account's.
- Signed in, a refusal made elsewhere (an unsubscribe link, an SMS STOP, another of the person's devices) arrives on the person's own realtime channel and stands at once.
- On sign-out, the device goes back to the app's starting values.

The app's extensions read the same choices through the keychain group the app shares with them ([Overview](/docs/ios/overview#connect-the-app-to-the-project)).

## The install

`pb.installation.id` is the install's id: the first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of a secret made on the device (32 random bytes, kept in the keychain), base64url. The secret goes only with the device's own consent calls, its push registration and its flag reads with no one signed in. A keychain that outlived the app's deletion keeps the install, and analytics' `$install` says `$reinstall`.

## Related

- [Analytics](/docs/ios/analytics): what the measurement keys hold back
- [Notifications](/docs/ios/notifications): marketing push, and the person's preferences
- [Web Consent](/docs/web/consent): the same keys in a browser
