# Calling Your Backend

Your own backend runs on a machine at an address of its own. An Android app calls it through a client generated from the backend's contract: `palbase apps:sync` writes it into the app as `palbase/environments/<env>/palbe/<machine>.kt`, and the build compiles the variant's environment in ([The environment in the build](/docs/android/overview#the-environment-in-the-build)). Each route is a typed `suspend` function, each error the route can throw is a typed case, and every call carries the signed-in user's token.

The client needs `studio.palbase:palbase-palbe` and the kotlinx.serialization Gradle plugin, because its types are `@Serializable` classes:

```kotlin
// app/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization")
}

dependencies {
    implementation(platform("studio.palbase:palbase-bom:0.4.0"))
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase")
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-palbe")
}
```

## Quick example

The backend, a `palbase/backend` app on the machine named `backend`:

```ts
// src/modules/notes/notes.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, NotFound, Param, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const CreateNote = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) });
type CreateNote = z.infer<typeof CreateNote>;

interface Note {
  id: string;
  owner: string;
  title: string;
}

@Controller("/notes")
export class NotesController {
  private readonly notes = new Map<string, Note>();

  @Post("")
  create(@Body(CreateNote) body: CreateNote, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    const note = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), owner: user.id, title: body.title };
    this.notes.set(note.id, note);
    return note;
  }

  @Get("/{id}")
  read(@Param("id") id: string, @User() user: UserT): Note {
    const note = this.notes.get(id);
    if (!note || note.owner !== user.id) throw new NotFound("no such note");
    return note;
  }
}
```

The app, after `palbase apps:sync`:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.generated.*   // the backends' clients and their types

val note = pb.backend.notes.create(NotesCreateRequest(title = "Groceries"))

val again = try {
    pb.backend.notes.read(note.id)
} catch (e: NotesReadError) {
    when (e) {
        NotesReadError.NotFound -> null                 // the route's own error, typed
        is NotesReadError.Other -> throw e.backend      // anything else: a BackendError
    }
}
```

## The generated client

`apps:sync` writes one Kotlin file for each backend of each environment the app is set in, in the package `studio.palbase.generated`:

- **The backend** is a property of the client: `pb.<name>`. The name is the machine's, camelCased (`pb.shopApi` for the machine `shop-api`), unless `palbase apps:sync --as shop-api=shop` names it. It is the same in every environment.
- **A namespace per controller, a function per route.** `NotesController`'s `create` is `pb.backend.notes.create(…)`, as the backend's contract names it.
- **Its types** are named after the route: `NotesCreateRequest` (the body), `NotesCreateQuery` (the query string), `NotesCreateResponse` (the answer) and `NotesCreateError`. A path parameter is a `String` argument.
- **Its gateways** are classes the app joins: [Gateways](/docs/android/gateways).

A backend the environment does not name is not a build error: each of its calls fails with `BackendError.NotConfigured`, in the route's `Other`. Run `palbase apps:sync` again when the backend's routes change. `palbase apps:sync --backend <dir>` makes the client from a backend's checkout on this computer, to call an endpoint before any machine serves it ([`apps:sync`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appssync)).

## What a call carries

A call goes to the address the environment names for the machine, with:

- the signed-in user's access token, when someone is signed in. When the session is bound to the device ([Auth](/docs/android/auth#how-the-session-is-kept)), the request also carries a proof signed by the device's key. When no one is signed in, the call goes without a token, and the route decides whether it needs one;
- no API key: a machine asks for none;
- `Accept-Language`, the user's languages, which the backend's translations read;
- an `Idempotency-Key` on every write;
- a field the route marks `encrypted()` sealed, and one it answers through `encrypt()` opened when the answer arrives: the client `palbase apps:sync` wrote holds the project's id and signing key for it ([Encrypted Requests](/docs/backend/request-encryption)). A call sent again is the same sealed request.

A call refused with a `401` about the token is refreshed once and sent again, for the same user. A read is sent again when the answer says "not now" (`429`, `502`, `503`, `504`) or the request never got an answer, as the project's calls are ([Errors and retries](/docs/android/overview#errors-and-retries)). A write is sent again only when the backend's contract says the route keeps its idempotency key, and always with the same key. Any other write is sent once, because one that reached the backend before its answer was lost would be done twice. No redirect is followed.

## Errors

Each generated function throws its route's own error type: a sealed class with a case for every error the backend's contract says the route can throw, and `Other` for the rest.

```kotlin
// palbase/environments/staging/palbe/backend.kt, as apps:sync wrote it (shortened)
sealed class NotesReadError(message: String, cause: Throwable? = null) : Exception(message, cause) {
    data object NotFound : NotesReadError("not_found")   // 404 not_found: the route throws NotFound
    data class Other(val backend: BackendError) : NotesReadError("Backend error", backend)
}
```

The contract's errors are what the route throws, as the backend's build reads them from its code: the framework's error classes and your own. A case is matched on the answer's status and code.

`Other` carries a `BackendError` (package `studio.palbase.backend`):

| Case | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Http(status, code, description, requestId, details, data)` | An answer that is not 2xx, as the backend sent it in its error envelope. `decodeData(serializer)` reads `data` as a type of yours. |
| `Validation(fields, …)` | A `400` that names fields: each `FieldError(field, message)`. |
| `Unauthorized(…)` | A `401` after the refresh did not mend it. |
| `RateLimited(retryAfter, …)` | A `429`, with the seconds to wait. |
| `IntegrityRequired(code, …)` | A `401 app_attest_required` the device's proof could not settle: the SDK enrolled, proved and sent the call again, and the backend still refused ([Device attestation](#device-attestation)). |
| `AttestationUnavailable(reason, …)` | The route asks for the device's proof and this device cannot give one: an emulator or a key that is not in secure hardware (`hardware_key_unavailable`, `software_key`), an unlocked bootloader (`device_not_locked`), the keystore not answering now (`keystore_unavailable`, asked again later). Nothing more is sent. |
| `StepUpRequired(acrValues, maxAge, …)` | A `401 insufficient_user_authentication`: the route asks for a stronger sign-in (`acrValues`, e.g. `urn:nist:800-63:aal2`). The session is fine and is not refreshed: step the user up with their second factor — `pb.auth.mfa.stepUp(code)` with an authenticator code, `pb.auth.mfa.stepUpWithSms(code)` after `sendStepUpSmsCode()`, or `pb.auth.passkeys.stepUp(context)` with a passkey — then call again (`maxAge` counts from the step-up); the session holds the aal2 token from then on, refreshes included. |
| `Network(ioCause)` | No answer: no network, the host unreachable. |
| `Decoding(decodeCause)` | A 2xx whose body is not what the contract declares. |
| `Encoding(encodeCause)` | The request could not be written; it was not sent. |
| `NotConfigured` | The environment names no such backend: run `palbase apps:sync`. |

`Http`, `Validation`, `Unauthorized` and `RateLimited` have the answer behind them in `envelope`: the status, the code, the message and the request id, whatever they were classified as. A generated error matches its cases against it, so a route that declares a `401` or a `429` of its own still gets its typed case.

## Device attestation

A route the backend marks `attest: true` is called only by your app on a genuine phone ([Device attestation](/docs/backend/authentication#device-attestation)). The SDK proves each call by itself:

- once per install, it makes a key in the phone's secure hardware and enrols it: auth checks the key's attestation chain against Google's roots and revocation list, that the phone is locked with a verified boot, and that the app is your registered package signed with one of its registered certificates;
- each call to such a route then carries a signature with that key over the call's method, path, body and a short-lived challenge, and a counter, so a captured call cannot be sent again or changed;
- the route's generated method knows it attests (`palbase apps:sync` writes it from the contract), so its first call is proved: the SDK enrols before it if needed and asks your backend for a fresh challenge (`GET /.well-known/palbase/attest-challenge`, once for calls made together), with no `401` round trip first. A route not marked carries no proof;
- a `401 app_attest_required` from a route its client does not know as attested — a client generated before the route was marked — is answered by itself: enrol if needed, prove, send once more; the route is proved from then on while the app runs. `palbase apps:sync` again marks it.

What only you set: the SHA-256 of the certificates your releases are signed with, registered with the app (`palbase apps:env:set <app> --sha256 play_signing=AB:CD:…`; Play's app signing key and your upload key). Do not register a debug key where attestation is enforced: a debug build can be driven over adb to sign requests. An emulator cannot attest: under enforce its calls end in `AttestationUnavailable`.

## Uploads

A route the backend declares with `@Upload` takes the file in the app's call: the call goes to the project's storage, which writes the file where the route's template says and then runs the route's handler with it ([Upload routes](/docs/backend/direct-uploads#upload-routes)). Its generated function takes the bytes, a file name, an optional content type and a progress callback:

```kotlin
// ProfileController's @Upload("/avatar", …) avatar route, with no body of its own:
val avatar = pb.backend.profile.avatar(
    file = bytes,
    filename = "me.jpg",
    contentType = "image/jpeg",
    onProgress = { p -> progress = p.fraction },   // UploadProgress: phase, bytesSent, totalBytes
)
```

A route with path parameters, a body or a query string takes them first, in that order, as any generated call does, and then the file.

`UploadProgress.phase` is `UPLOADING` while the bytes go, then `PROCESSING` while the backend's handler runs, with `fraction` at 1. A content type left out is read from the bytes, then from the file name's extension. What the handler answers is the call's answer (`ProfileAvatarResponse` here), and a refusal it throws deletes the file. A file a backend signed an upload URL for goes through [Storage](/docs/android/storage) instead.

## Untyped calls

A route the generated client does not have yet can be called by its path, with types of yours: a `POST`, its body as JSON.

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.backend.call
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

@Serializable data class Todo(val id: String, val title: String)
@Serializable data class NewTodo(val title: String)

val todo = pb.backend.call<NewTodo, Todo>("todos/create", NewTodo("Milk"))   // POST /todos/create
```

A path built from a value is held to plain path segments, and anything else is refused before it is sent.

## A backend on your computer

`pb.palbe(URI("http://10.0.2.2:8080"))` (`import studio.palbase.backend.palbe`) is a client of a backend at an address of its own: in a debug build, one running on the computer the emulator runs on. It carries the user's token as the environment's backends do. The generated namespaces hang on the backend's own type, `PB<Name>Backend`, which the app's module can make around it:

```kotlin
val local = PBBackendBackend(pb.palbe(URI("http://10.0.2.2:8080")))
val note = local.notes.create(NotesCreateRequest(title = "Groceries"))
```

# Gateways

A [gateway](/docs/backend/gateways) is a realtime channel of your backend: a `@Gateway` class that says who may join, the events it sends, the messages its members may send and the ack each one is answered with. `palbase apps:sync` writes each of the backend's gateways into the app's generated client ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/android/backend-calls)) as a class of its own. The app joins it with the pattern's values, and writes no channel name, event name or payload type of its own.

## Quick example

For the backend's `RoomGateway` (`@Gateway("room:{roomId}")`, with the events `message` and `welcome` and the message `say`, in [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways#quick-example)), the generated client has `RoomGateway(roomId)`, its events as `RoomGatewayEvent`, and its messages as `RoomGatewaySend`:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.backend.join
import studio.palbase.generated.*

val room = pb.backend.join(RoomGateway(roomId = "42"))   // returns once the backend let the user in

val listening = room.on { event ->
    when (event) {
        is RoomGatewayEvent.Message -> show("${event.payload.from}: ${event.payload.text}")
        is RoomGatewayEvent.Welcome -> show("${event.payload.members} in the room")
    }
}

// The backend's ack, typed: what its @Subscribe("say") returned.
val said: RoomGatewaySayReply = room.send(RoomGatewaySend.Say(RoomGatewaySayMessage(text = "hello")))

room.off(listening)
room.leave()
```

In Compose, hold the handle while the screen is on screen and leave it when the screen goes:

```kotlin
@Composable
fun Room(roomId: String) {
    val lines = remember { mutableStateListOf<String>() }
    LaunchedEffect(roomId) {
        val room = pb.backend.join(RoomGateway(roomId = roomId))
        room.on { event -> if (event is RoomGatewayEvent.Message) lines += event.payload.text }
        try { awaitCancellation() } finally { room.leave() }
    }
    LazyColumn { items(lines) { Text(it) } }
}
```

## Joining

`pb.<name>.join(gateway, history = true)` opens the project's socket if it is not open, and returns once the backend let the signed-in user in. Each `{param}` of the pattern is a constructor argument: a value that is empty or holds a `:` would name another channel, and is refused with `invalid params` before anything is sent.

| Member of the handle | What it does |
|---|---|
| `on { event -> }` | Listens to every event the gateway declares, as its sealed type. Returns a `GatewayRegistration`. |
| `off(registration)` | Stops one listener. |
| `send(message)` | Sends one message and waits for the backend to take it. It returns the ack, typed as the message says, or throws `PBGatewayError`. |
| `leave()` | Drops the handle's listeners and lets go of the channel. |
| `topic` | The channel: `room:42`. |
| `seq` | A durable gateway's number of the last event its channel was sent; `null` on one that keeps nothing. |

Only a signed-in user joins: the access token the socket carries is who they are. Two handles of the same channel share one membership, and the channel is left with the last of them. A gateway with members is one its backend still runs for, so leave a handle when its screen goes.

An event the generated client does not know, from a backend that moved ahead of it, is not delivered, and a listener that throws does not take the socket down. A listener is called on the socket's thread, not the main thread: hand what it gets to state a composable reads, or to the main thread.

## Messages and acks

`send` returns what the backend's `@Subscribe` returned. A message goes to the backend alone, never to the other members, who hear what the backend emits. It throws `PBGatewayError`, whose `reason` says why the message was not taken:

| `reason` | What it means |
|---|---|
| The backend's own word | Its method threw `GatewayRefusal("…")`: `no_commands`, `not_your_turn`. Act on it. |
| `forbidden` | The user may only listen on this channel, or the platform refused with no reason given. |
| `rate_limited` | Past the project's events per second. |
| `unavailable` | The backend could not be asked just then. Worth trying again. |
| `no reply`, `socket closed` | No answer came. The message may have been taken. |
| `not joined` | Nothing was sent: the handle was left, or its socket closed for good. |
| `undecodable reply` | The backend took it, but its ack is not what this client reads: a backend that moved ahead of the app. |

A join that is refused throws `PBGatewayError` too: `unauthorized` when the backend did not let the user in, `unavailable` when it could not be asked, and `rate_limited` past the project's limits. `PBGatewayError` has the reasons the client names as constants: `PBGatewayError.UNAUTHORIZED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_JOINED`, and the others.

## Durable gateways

A [durable gateway](/docs/backend/gateways#durable-gateways) keeps what it sends. A handle that joins one is sent what it keeps first, in order, then what comes after. `join(gateway, history = false)` asks for only what comes after the join. The channel's first handle decides: a second handle of the same channel gets the events from where it joins.

When the socket drops, the channel is joined again after `seq`: the handle is sent what it missed, in order, and nothing twice.

## When the connection drops

The socket reconnects by itself ([Realtime](/docs/android/realtime#the-socket)), and every gateway that was joined is joined again with it. An event that a gateway that is not durable sent while the socket was down is not delivered.

When the socket closes for good, every handle on it ends: its listeners are dropped, and `send` throws `not joined`. That happens on a sign-out, or when another user signs in. Join again, as the user who is there now.

## Chat gateways

A gateway declared with `chat: true` carries a chat of the project's agents, which the platform writes into its channel ([AI](/docs/backend/ai#a-chat-in-an-app)). Its generated class is a `PBChatGateway`, and joining it returns a `ChatGatewayHandle`. That handle is the gateway's own (`on`, `send`, `leave`) and also has `chat`: the chat's state, folded from what the platform writes there, from the chat's start, then each change as it comes.

```kotlin
@Composable
fun Support(support: ChatGatewayHandle<SupportGatewayEvent, SupportGatewaySend>) {
    val chat by support.chat.state.collectAsState()
    LazyColumn {
        items(chat.items, key = { it.key }) { item ->
            when (item) {
                is PBChat.Item.Message -> Text(item.message.text)
                is PBChat.Item.Response -> Text(item.response.text)
                is PBChat.Item.Goal -> Text(item.event.kind.value)
                is PBChat.Item.Voice -> Text(item.event.status.value)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

What the user does in the chat (a message, a yes or a no, stop) is the gateway's own typed messages, which its backend acts on: `support.send(SupportGatewaySend.Say(SupportGatewaySayMessage(text = "Merhaba")))`. The chat's state says what is, and never sends.

`support.chat.state` is a `StateFlow<PBChat.State>`, and `support.chat.updates` the same states as a flow that ends when the gateway is left. A change is told after the parts that made it: a run of an answer's text is one change.

| Member of `PBChat.State` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `items` | The conversation in order: `PBChat.Item.Message`, `.Response`, `.Goal` (a word of the chat's goal) and `.Voice` (the chat's voice began or ended). Each has a stable `key`. |
| `messages` | Each member's (or the server's) message: `text`, `author` (`null`: the server), `authorName`, `status` (pending until the agent has it, then delivered or failed), `kind` (text, or voice for a line said in the chat's voice), `attachments`, and `mine`. |
| `responses` | Every answer, a subagent's too, as it began. An answer's `parts` split its text at its tools (`PBChat.Part.Tool`), its subagents (`.Agent`) and the model's reasoning (`.Thinking`). |
| `turn` | The last turn: its `status`, and its `error` or what it is `waiting` on. |
| `waiting` | What waits for the signed-in user: `approvals`, tool calls of their own turns waiting for their yes, and `outputs`, client tools waiting for the app's answer. |
| `goal` | The chat's goal, once one was set. |
| `voice` | The chat's voice, the last that began in it, live or ended. See [Voice](/docs/android/voice). |
| `forkedFrom` | A fork's: the chat it was forked from, and the message it was cut before. |

### The chat's past

The channel keeps a day of the chat. `chat.loadOlder(pb, chatId)` reads the page before what the state holds (`GET /ai/chats/{id}/parts`) and folds it in front, each part once. It reads with the member's own session, which the project allows its app's users with its AI settings' `clients` (`Palbase.ai.settings.put`, [AI](/docs/backend/ai#chats)). It returns whether there is more before it, and `chat.hasOlder` says the same without reading.

```kotlin
while (support.chat.loadOlder(pb, chatId)) {
    if (enoughShown()) break
}
```

When the project's app reaches no chat of its own, the app's backend can read the page for it: `support.chat.loadOlder { query -> … }` hands the lambda the page asked for (`PBChat.PartsQuery`: `before`, `cursor`, `limit`), and the lambda answers it as a `PBChat.PartsPage(parts, nextCursor)` read through a route of yours.

### Attachments, tool calls and workspace files

A message's pictures and files are read back with the member's session:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.realtime.chatAttachment

val picture = message.attachments.first { it.kind == PBChat.AttachmentKind.IMAGE }
val bytes = pb.chatAttachment(chatId, message, picture)
val bitmap = BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(bytes, 0, bytes.size)
```

`pb.chatToolCall(chatId, callId)` reads a tool call's whole answer, where the channel shows its last 16 KiB. `pb.chatWorkspaceFile(chatId, path)` reads a file of the chat's workspace. Both throw `PalbaseError` like any project call. Attaching a file is the backend's: the app uploads it, and the backend sends the message naming it.

## Related

- [Gateways](/docs/backend/gateways): declaring one in the backend
- [AI](/docs/backend/ai): chats, their agents and their voice
- [Realtime](/docs/android/realtime): the socket the gateways share
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/android/backend-calls): the generated client

# Realtime

`pb.realtime` (`studio.palbase:palbase-realtime`) is the project's channels: what members broadcast on them, and a state each channel's members share. The channels go over the project's one realtime socket, `pb.socket`, which every module that needs one shares. It opens the first time a channel is joined and never before, so an app that only signs in or captures analytics opens none.

> **Note:** Your own backend's realtime channels are its gateways, joined through the generated client: typed events, and messages the backend answers with an ack ([Gateways](/docs/android/gateways)). This page is the socket under them, and the channels the project declares by name.

## Quick example

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.realtime.realtime
import kotlinx.serialization.json.buildJsonObject
import kotlinx.serialization.json.put

val room = pb.realtime.channel("room:42")

val stop = room.onBroadcast("message") { payload ->
    println("${payload["from"]}: ${payload["text"]}")
}
room.onRefused { refusal -> println("refused: $refusal") }   // {event, reason}

room.join()   // throws the server's reason when it does not let the user in
room.broadcast("message", buildJsonObject { put("from", "ada"); put("text", "hello") })

// later:
stop()
room.leave()
```

## Channels

`pb.realtime.channel(name)` is the channel of that name. Names are `:`-separated segments.

| Member | What it does |
|---|---|
| `join()` | Joins, and returns once the server let the user in. Throws `PalbaseError` when it did not ([Who may join](#who-may-join)). |
| `leave()` | Leaves the channel. |
| `onBroadcast(event) { payload -> }` | Listens to one broadcast event, a member's or the platform's. Returns what stops it. |
| `broadcast(event, payload)` | Sends an event to the channel's other members; the sender does not hear its own. The server says nothing of one it takes. |
| `onRefused { refusal -> }` | Listens to the server refusing a broadcast: `{event, reason}`, with reasons such as `forbidden` and `rate_limited`. |
| `entries` | The channel's state as the server last told it: a `Map<String, RealtimeChannel.Entry>`, each a `value` and its `life`. |
| `onState { entries -> }` | Called with the whole state each time it changes. Returns what stops it. |
| `set(key, value, life)` | Writes one entry, and returns once the server took it; a refusal is thrown. The state changes when the server says so (its next change), for every member alike. |
| `deleteOwn(key)` | Removes an entry this membership wrote, as `set` does. Every other member's entry stays theirs. |

A channel's state is a keyed map that outlives the connections reading it. A `Life.DURABLE` entry (the default) stays until it is removed. A `Life.EPHEMERAL` one is its writer's presence, gone when the writer leaves:

```kotlin
import kotlinx.serialization.json.JsonPrimitive

room.onState { entries ->
    val here = entries.filterValues { it.life == RealtimeChannel.Life.EPHEMERAL }.keys
    println("in the room: $here")
}
room.join()
room.set("presence:${pb.auth.userId.value}", JsonPrimitive("online"), RealtimeChannel.Life.EPHEMERAL)
```

The state arrives whole as a snapshot when the channel is joined, then as changes. A change that does not follow from the state held means something was missed, and the client asks for the whole state again. While the channel is not joined, `entries` is empty. Listeners are called on the socket's thread.

## Who may join

A channel name is a string a client chooses, so proving who you are says nothing about which channels are yours. The project **declares** its channels, and a channel that no declaration matches belongs to no one. A server declares them with `PUT /realtime/channels` and the secret key, or from a terminal:

```sh
palbase realtime:channels:set --file channels.json
```

```json
{
  "channels": [
    { "pattern": "user:{uid}", "kind": "owner" },
    { "pattern": "room:{id}", "kind": "public", "publish": true, "state_read": true, "state_write": true }
  ]
}
```

| `kind` | Who joins |
|---|---|
| `owner` | The pattern's one `{name}` segment is the joining user: `user:{uid}` is joined by that user alone, who may do everything on it. |
| `public` | Any signed-in user of the project, with the rights the declaration gives: `publish` (broadcast), `state_read`, `state_write`. |

Patterns match in their order, and the first one decides. A declared channel is joined only by a signed-in user, whose access token goes with each join. See [Channels](/docs/backend/channels).

A refused join throws `PalbaseError` with the code `join_refused` and the server's reply in its `body`: `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `invalid_topic`, `rate_limited`, `too_many_channels`, `state_budget` or `unavailable`. Only `unavailable` is worth trying again. A join that got no answer at all is `join_failed`.

## The socket

`pb.socket.status` is the socket's connection as a `StateFlow`, and `pb.socket.statusChanges` every change in order:

| `RealtimeSocket.ConnectionState` | What it means |
|---|---|
| `IDLE` | Never opened: nothing has joined a channel yet. |
| `CONNECTING` | Being opened. |
| `CONNECTED` | Open, and the channels wanted are joined on it. |
| `RECONNECTING` | Dropped (the network went, a heartbeat was not answered), and opened again after a pause. |
| `DISCONNECTED` | Closed by the client: the user signed out, or no channel is wanted any more. |

```kotlin
@Composable
fun Connection() {
    val status by pb.socket.status.collectAsState()
    if (status == RealtimeSocket.ConnectionState.RECONNECTING) Text("Reconnecting…")
}
```

The socket sends a heartbeat every 25 seconds. A socket that drops is opened again after 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, then every 30 seconds, each pause jittered, and every channel still wanted is joined again. A broadcast sent while the socket was down is not delivered: broadcasts are delivered at most once. A channel's state comes back whole with the snapshot of the new join. `pb.socket.reconnects` counts the reopens.

### One socket, one user

The socket opens at `wss://<ref>.palbase.studio/realtime/v1/websocket`, the project's address. The publishable key goes in its `x-api-key` header, never in the address. When the session is bound to the device, the user's token and a proof signed by the device's key go there instead. Who the user is, is the access token each join carries, and a refreshed token is pushed to the joined channels without leaving them.

The socket is one person's. When the user signs out, someone else signs in, or the session ends, the client closes it, and every channel with it. Join again for the user who is there now:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.session.AuthEvent

suspend fun joinMine() {
    val user = pb.auth.userId.value ?: return
    val mine = pb.realtime.channel("user:$user")
    mine.onBroadcast("note") { payload -> println("for me: $payload") }
    mine.join()
}

// scope: a CoroutineScope of the app's own.
pb.auth.onChange { event, _ ->
    if (event == AuthEvent.SIGNED_IN) scope.launch { joinMine() }
}
```

`pb.socket.disconnect()` closes the socket. The next join opens a new one.

## Limits

The project holds its clients to limits the platform sets and the project may lower (`PUT /realtime/limits` from a server, or `palbase realtime:limits:set`): connections open at once, broadcasts and state writes per second, joins per second, channels per connection. A frame over 1 MiB closes the socket. A project over its connection limit, or whose realtime quota is used up, is refused a new socket.

## Related

- [Gateways](/docs/android/gateways): your backend's channels, typed, with messages and acks
- [Channels](/docs/backend/channels): declaring who may join what
- [Realtime in your backend](/docs/backend/realtime): broadcasting and writing state from a server
- [Flags](/docs/android/flags): kept current over the same socket



<!-- ===== android/messaging ===== -->

# Messaging

`pb.messaging` is the signed-in person's conversations on Android: their list, each conversation's timeline and its threads as `StateFlow`s Compose collects, kept in the app's own SQLite between launches and current over the project's socket. The app writes; it opens no socket, appends nothing and syncs nothing itself. A message's push brings its conversation onto the phone even while the app is closed. What the module is — history, encryption, timers, moderation, prices — is [Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview).

## Install

Palbase's packages come from its own repository; let the `studio.palbase` group come from there alone:

```kotlin
// settings.gradle.kts
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        google()
        mavenCentral()
        exclusiveContent {
            forRepository { maven("https://palgroup.github.io/palbase-android/") }
            filter { includeGroup("studio.palbase") }
        }
    }
}
```

```kotlin
// app/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("studio.palbase:palbase-bom:0.9.0"))
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase")
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-notify")     // pushes: the FCM token, and the service that draws them
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-messaging")  // pb.messaging
}
```

## Quick example

```kotlin
@Composable
fun Inbox(pb: PalbaseClient, open: (String) -> Unit) {
    // The person's conversations, the latest first: drawn from the phone at once, then kept current.
    val list by remember { pb.messaging.conversations() }.state.collectAsState()
    Text("${list.unread} unread")
    LazyColumn {
        items(list.items, key = { it.id }) { c -> Text(c.title ?: "Chat", Modifier.clickable { open(c.id) }) }
    }
}

@Composable
fun Chat(pb: PalbaseClient, id: String) {
    val chat = remember(id) { pb.messaging.conversation(id) }
    val state by chat.state.collectAsState() // entries: its messages and those on their way; members; typing
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    var text by remember { mutableStateOf("") }
    LazyColumn { items(state.entries) { e -> Text(e.toString()) } }
    TextField(text, { text = it })
    Button(onClick = {
        val words = text
        text = ""
        scope.launch { chat.send(words) } // drawn at once; with no network, sent once it is back
    }) { Text("Send") }
}
```

`pb.messaging.direct(userId)` is the direct conversation with someone (the one there is, or a new one, shown to them with its first message). A message waits in the outbox while the phone is offline and goes once it can, once. Files are encrypted on the phone (AES-256-GCM) before they are uploaded; `pb.messaging.open(message, attachment)` downloads and decrypts one, and a message seen once gives its files by `pb.messaging.viewOnce(message)` alone.

## Spaces and open groups

A conversation may belong to a place of your app's — an organization, a workspace — when it is made with a `space` your app names (`org:<id>`), for good: `direct(userId, space = org)` opens the pair's conversation there (the two have one in each space, and one with none), `group(title, space = org, visibility = …)` makes a group there, `conversations(spaces = listOf(org))` lists a space's — its `unread` that space's — and `search(query, space = org)` searches one. Each conversation says its `space` (`null`: none).

An open group (`visibility` open) is a channel: `openGroups(space)` lists a space's, each with whether the person is in it (`joined`), and `join(conversationId)` lets the person in — the group then in their list at once. Making one, listing and joining ask the project's hook (`open_group`, `list_open`, `join`): refused, a `PalbaseError` with code `not_allowed`; an open group names its space (`space_required`). One an admin removed does not join again by themselves (`removed`).

```kotlin
// app/src/main/java/com/example/workspace/Channels.kt
val org = "org:2f6c0c1e-8a3b-4c1d-9e5f-0a1b2c3d4e5f"
val sidebar = pb.messaging.conversations(spaces = listOf(org))
val channels = pb.messaging.openGroups(org)
for (c in channels.items) if (!c.joined) pb.messaging.join(c.id)
val dm = pb.messaging.direct("usr_01a1684c796e7394aa8ec75d893a8fe2", space = org)
```

A message your server wrote as someone (an assistant sending their words) says what wrote it: `message.via` (`"pal"`) — show it beside the message.

## Search

`pb.messaging.search(query)` finds the person's messages that say every word asked — a word's beginning finds it, "toplanti" finds "Toplantıda" — the newest first, across their conversations or in one (`conversationId`). Each `SearchHit` carries what a result row draws: the conversation's `title` and `photo` (a group's, or the other person's in a direct one), its `sender`, and its `matches` — where its text or a file's name says what was asked, in UTF-16 offsets, as a `String`'s. The first page also lists the person's conversations whose name says it (`conversations`), found on the phone. What the module finds and never finds: [Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#search).

```kotlin
val results = pb.messaging.search("toplanti")
results.conversations.forEach { c -> Text(c.title ?: "Chat") } // their names say it: draw them first
results.messages.forEach { hit ->
    Text(hit.title ?: "Chat")
    Text(buildAnnotatedString {
        append(hit.message.text ?: "")
        hit.matches.filter { it.field == SearchMatch.Field.TEXT }.forEach { m ->
            addStyle(SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), m.offset.toInt(), (m.offset + m.length).toInt())
        }
    })
}
// More: pb.messaging.search("toplanti", cursor = results.nextCursor) while nextCursor is not null —
// a page may hold fewer messages than asked, even none.
```

A find opens where it was said: `pb.messaging.conversation(hit.conversation.id, at = hit.message.id)` is the conversation's page around it, `focus` naming the message to scroll to and mark. `loadEarlier()` reads back from there and `loadLater()` forward; once it reaches the newest, `hasLater` is false and it reads on live. An answer the conversation's timeline does not show has a `threadRootId`: open its thread at it.

```kotlin
val view = hit.threadRootId?.let { root -> pb.messaging.thread(hit.conversation.id, root, at = hit.message.id) }
    ?: pb.messaging.conversation(hit.conversation.id, at = hit.message.id)
```

### By meaning

With the project's `search_by_meaning` on ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#by-meaning)), `search(query, by = SearchBy.MEANING)` finds the messages nearest what the question means, in none of its words: "uçuş saati kaçta" finds "Uçağımız sabah dokuzda Sabiha Gökçen'den kalkıyor". The nearest come first, one page (`nextCursor` is null), each with `score` — how near, 0.3 to 1 — and no `matches`; `conversations` is empty. A hit opens as any does: `conversation(id, at = hit.message.id)`.

```kotlin
try {
    val found = pb.messaging.search("uçuş saati kaçta", by = SearchBy.MEANING)
    found.messages.forEach { hit -> Text("${hit.title}: ${hit.message.text} (${"%.2f".format(hit.score)})") }
} catch (e: PalbaseError) {
    // search_by_meaning_off: the project searches by words alone. too_many_searches: a person asks
    // 30 at once, one more a minute (e.retryAfter). ai_payment_required: the project's AI use is spent.
}
```

## Pushes

The app uses its own Firebase project:

- put `app/google-services.json` in the app and apply the `com.google.gms.google-services` plugin;
- connect the same Firebase project to the Palbase project as its FCM push provider ([Notifications](/docs/android/notifications));
- touch `pb.notify` at launch: the installation's token is registered — the installation's while no one is signed in, the person's once someone is;
- on Android 13 and later, the app asks for `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` (the permission is in the module's manifest; asking is the app's).

`palbase-notify` brings its FCM service with its manifest: nothing more to declare. The project sends data messages, and the SDK draws them.

## Messages that arrive while the app is closed

Nothing to set up. While the app is closed or in the background, a message's push is drawn, and the same push reads its conversation into the phone's copy: open the app with no network and it is there.

## A message while the app is open

While the app is in front, a message's push is not drawn in the tray: its conversation is synced, and `pb.messaging.incoming` — a `SharedFlow<Message>` — gives the app each message someone else wrote that is new to the phone, once, whether the socket or the push brought it first. A sync, a page read, the person's own messages, system messages and removed ones never come through it. Skip the conversation on the screen:

```kotlin
var banner by remember { mutableStateOf<Message?>(null) }
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    pb.messaging.incoming.collect { m -> if (m.conversationId != openConversationId) banner = m }
}
banner?.let { m -> IncomingBanner(m) { banner = null; openConversationId = m.conversationId } }
```

## Screenshots

While a photo or a video seen once is shown, keep the window out of screenshots and recordings (`FLAG_SECURE`): they come out black.

```kotlin
DisposableEffect(Unit) {
    val release = pb.messaging.protectViewOnce(activity)
    onDispose { release() }
}
```

In vanish mode, a screenshot taken while the conversation is open is told to the others (Android 14 and later; `DETECT_SCREEN_CAPTURE` is in the module's manifest):

```kotlin
DisposableEffect(id) {
    val stop = pb.messaging.watchScreenshots(activity, id)
    onDispose { stop() }
}
```

## A deleted group

When a group's owner or an admin deletes it — or its last member leaves — it goes from everyone's `conversations()` at once, and those who were in it can still report it for 14 days ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#moderation)). `pb.messaging.deletedGroups` is a `StateFlow<List<DeletedGroup>>` of the groups the person can still report, the latest to stop first, each with `id`, `title`, `deletedBy` and `reportableUntil`; one goes at its `reportableUntil`. `report` names it by its id with no message; the last 30 messages the person saw in it go with the report. A group the project's server deleted is not among them.

```kotlin
val deleted by pb.messaging.deletedGroups.collectAsState()
deleted.forEach { group -> Text(group.title ?: "a group") }

deleted.firstOrNull()?.let { group ->
    pb.messaging.report(MessagingAPI.ReportRequest(conversationId = group.id, reason = MessagingAPI.ReportRequest.Reason.HARASSMENT, userId = group.deletedBy))
}
```

The title is the one the device had; it is null when the device no longer had the group as the word came — on the deleter's own device now and then.

## Signing out

The phone's copy is kept in the app's own SQLite, in files not backed up. When the person signs out it is dropped, unless `pb.messaging.keepOnSignOut = true` — then it is theirs again when they come back. Whoever signs in next never reads it; and unless copies are kept, the person who signs in drops any other's left there.



<!-- ===== android/calls ===== -->

# Calls

`pb.calls` (`studio.palbase:palbase-calls`) is the signed-in person's voice and video calls on Android. A call rings the phone as a phone call does — over the lock screen and with the app closed, woken by a high-priority FCM message — and lives in the system's call integration (Telecom): its audio route, Bluetooth, a watch or a car answering. A `PBCall` is what the app draws, its state as `StateFlow`s. Every call's media — one to one or in a group — goes through the platform's media server (LiveKit): a third person or the project's agent comes into the same room, and where UDP is shut it goes over TCP to port 443. `palbase-calls-ui` draws the screens in Compose. What the module is — kinds of call, who may call whom, ringing, history, prices — is [Calls](/docs/calls/overview).

## Install

```kotlin
// app/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(platform("studio.palbase:palbase-bom:0.14.1"))
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase")
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-notify")     // the FCM token, and the service a ring arrives through
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-calls")      // pb.calls, headless
    implementation("studio.palbase:palbase-calls-ui")   // the call screens and the activity a ring opens
}
```

Palbase's packages come from its own repository, as every module's do ([Android Overview](/docs/android/overview)).

- **Push.** A call rings through the project's FCM provider and the app's Firebase project, as every push does ([Notifications](/docs/android/notifications#setting-up-push)). palbase-notify's messaging service (`PalbaseMessagingService`, declared by its manifest) hands a call's push to the calls — no code. An app with a `FirebaseMessagingService` of its own subclasses `PalbaseMessagingService`, calling `super` first, or a ring never reaches the calls.
- **The client in the `Application`.** Make the client there and touch `pb.calls`: the person's calls channel is followed from then on, and a process FCM starts for a ring uses the app's own client.
- **What the manifests add.** palbase-calls declares its permissions (`RECORD_AUDIO`, `CAMERA`, `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, `USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT`, `MANAGE_OWN_CALLS`, the foreground service types `phoneCall`, `microphone` and `camera` …), the foreground service a call holds the app with, and the receiver a notification's Decline and Hang up go to; palbase-calls-ui the activity a ring opens. An app that makes voice calls alone may remove `CAMERA` and the camera service type (`tools:node="remove"`). The app declares the foreground service types in Google Play's declaration (phone call, microphone, camera).

## A call rings the phone

The project rings an Android phone with a **high-priority FCM data message**. The SDK posts at once a **CallStyle** notification on its own channel — the ringtone, looping until the call is answered, declined, answered on another device or missed — with a **full-screen intent** that opens the call's screen over the lock screen. The call is in Telecom, and a foreground service of type `phoneCall` holds the app while it rings and goes on (with `microphone`, and `camera` in a video call, once it is answered).

- **Ask for the permissions.** On Android 13 and newer the app asks for `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` at runtime, as for any push: a missed call's notification needs it. The microphone (`RECORD_AUDIO`) — and the camera for a video call (`CAMERA`) — are asked before a call is made or answered: without the microphone, a call is refused with `microphone_denied`. palbase-calls-ui's Accept asks for them itself.
- **Full screen over the lock screen.** From Android 14, Google Play grants `USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` to calling apps alone, and the person may turn it off. `pb.calls.canRingFullScreen` says whether it is granted — without it a ring is a heads-up notification with Answer and Decline — and `pb.calls.fullScreenSettings()` is the system's page where the person allows it.
- **A closed app rings; a force-stopped one does not.** A process the system ended — or `adb shell am kill` — still gets the ring: FCM starts it. An app the person force-stopped (Settings › Force stop, or `adb shell am force-stop`) gets no FCM message at all, Android's rule, until it is opened again.

```kotlin
// Before the first call: what the phone needs to ring.
if (!pb.calls.canRingFullScreen) {
    // Explain why, then:
    context.startActivity(pb.calls.fullScreenSettings())
}
```

## Making a call

```kotlin
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
Button(onClick = {
    scope.launch {
        // Rings every device of theirs; the media goes through the media server.
        val call = pb.calls.call(userId, video = true)
        call.setMicrophone(false)
    }
}) { Text("Video call") }
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `call(userId, video, conversationId, metadata, callerName, callerImageUrl)` | Rings one person: a direct call. `callerName` and `callerImageUrl` are what they see of the caller (else the caller's messaging profile's) |
| `callGroup(userIds, video, ring, conversationId, metadata, callerName, callerImageUrl)` | A group call — several people, or one others may be asked to later. `ring = false` rings no one: the people asked join when they like (a huddle) |
| `join(callId)` | Comes into a group call the person was asked to — rung, missed, declined, or in before |
| `open(callId)` | The call on this device: the one held, or read from the server — what a notification's tap opens in a process that holds none. `null` when it is not this person's, or over |
| `history(limit, cursor, missedOnly)` | The person's calls, the newest first, with how each went for them; `missedOnly` the ones they missed or were busy for |

Each that makes or joins a call answers its `PBCall` and throws the module's refusal as a `PalbaseError`: `not_allowed`, `in_another_call`, `too_many_calls`, `quota_exceeded` and the rest of [Calls over HTTP](/docs/calls/http#making-a-call). A call to someone who is calling this person that very moment is their call, answered; their being in another call ends it at once (`endReason` `busy`).

`pb.calls.current` is a `StateFlow` of the call on this device — ringing here, calling out, going on — or `null`; `pb.calls.rung` a `SharedFlow` of each call as it starts ringing here. `deviceId` is this install's device, as notify registered it.

## The call

| `StateFlow` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `status` | `RINGING`, `CALLING`, `CONNECTING`, `CONNECTED`, `RECONNECTING` (the media was lost and is coming back), `ENDED` |
| `endReason` | Why it ended: the server's `hung_up`, `canceled`, `declined`, `missed`, `busy`, `failed`, `ended` — or this device's `answered_elsewhere` and `declined_elsewhere` |
| `snapshot` | The call as the server last told it ([A call](/docs/calls/http#a-call)); `null` until read, for a call rung by push |
| `peers` | The other people (and agents): `userId`, `name`, `imageUrl`, `state`, `bot`, and their `video` while their camera is on |
| `localVideo` | This phone's camera, while it is on |
| `microphoneOn`, `cameraOn` | The controls' state |
| `group` | A group call: more than two people, or a call people join |
| `connectedAt` | When the media first flowed: the call's clock starts here |
| `audioRoute`, `audioRoutes` | Where the sound plays now, and where it may: `EARPIECE`, `SPEAKER`, `WIRED_HEADSET`, `BLUETOOTH` … each with its name |

And as plain values: `id`, `incoming` (this device was rung for it), `video`, `caller` (`userId`, `name`, `imageUrl`).

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| `accept()` | Answers on this device; the person's other devices stop ringing. Needs the microphone |
| `decline()` | Turns it down on every device of the person's: a direct call ends; a group goes on without them |
| `hangUp()` | Leaves it: a direct call ends for both (`canceled` while it rings); a group goes on while someone is in it |
| `invite(userIds, ring)` | Asks more people in: a direct call becomes a group, going on |
| `setMicrophone(on)` | The microphone heard, or muted |
| `setCamera(on)`, `flipCamera()` | The camera on or off in a video call, and the front or the back one |
| `setSpeaker(on)`, `setAudioRoute(route)` | The speaker or the earpiece (a headset when one is connected), or any route of `audioRoutes` |

A camera is drawn by `PBVideoView` (a `View`: set its `track`) or palbase-calls-ui's `CallVideo(track, mirror = …)`.

## Ready-made screens

palbase-calls-ui draws a call in Compose: `IncomingCallScreen` (who calls, Accept and Decline — Accept asks for the microphone, and the camera for video, then answers), `InCallScreen` (the other's video filling the screen and this phone's camera in a corner, or their picture in a voice call; a group in a grid; the call's state and clock; `CallControls`: mute, camera, flip, speaker, hang up) and `CallEndedScreen`. `CallScreen(call)` shows the right one; each takes its parts as slots (`avatar`, `controls`, a person's tile) and `CallColors`.

**Over the app**, while it is open:

```kotlin
setContent {
    CallHost(pb.calls) {
        MyApp()
    }
}
```

**The activity a call opens** — over the lock screen as it rings, Answer from the notification, a tap on the call going on — is palbase-calls-ui's `PalbaseCallActivity`, declared for `Calls.ACTION_CALL`. It draws `CallScreen`, and ends itself a moment after the call does. To draw your own screen in it, set its content in the `Application`, before a ring can come:

```kotlin
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        pb.calls // the calls channel followed from launch
        PalbaseCallActivity.content = { call -> CallScreen(call, incoming = { MyIncoming(it) }) }
    }
}
```

**An activity of your own** replaces it: declare it for the action, and the SDK opens it instead. It reads the call's id and whether the person tapped Answer from its intent:

```xml
<activity android:name=".CallActivity" android:exported="false" android:showWhenLocked="true" android:turnScreenOn="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="studio.palbase.calls.action.CALL" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>
```

```kotlin
val id = intent.getStringExtra(Calls.EXTRA_CALL_ID) ?: return finish()
val answer = intent.getBooleanExtra(Calls.EXTRA_ANSWER, false)
lifecycleScope.launch {
    val call = pb.calls.open(id) ?: return@launch finish()
    if (answer) call.accept()
}
```

**The words** the screens say are string resources: an app gives its own with strings of the same names (`values-tr/strings.xml`) — `palbase_calls_ui_accept`, `palbase_calls_ui_decline`, `palbase_calls_ui_incoming_voice`, `palbase_calls_ui_incoming_video`, `palbase_calls_ui_calling`, `palbase_calls_ui_connecting`, `palbase_calls_ui_reconnecting`, `palbase_calls_ui_ended`, `palbase_calls_ui_busy`, `palbase_calls_ui_declined`, `palbase_calls_ui_missed`, `palbase_calls_ui_elsewhere`, `palbase_calls_ui_failed`, `palbase_calls_ui_mute`, `palbase_calls_ui_camera`, `palbase_calls_ui_speaker`, `palbase_calls_ui_flip`, `palbase_calls_ui_hang_up`, `palbase_calls_ui_someone`.

## Related

- [Calls](/docs/calls/overview) — kinds of call, who may call whom, a call's life, prices
- [Ringing](/docs/calls/ringing) — how a call rings each platform, and what its push carries
- [Notifications](/docs/android/notifications) — FCM and the app's pushes



<!-- ===== android/flags ===== -->

# Flags

`pb.flags` (`studio.palbase:palbase-flags`) is the project's flags as this reader sees them: each value resolved by the project for the app's platform, version and language, the signed-in user and their own values. It is read without waiting, because the values the app last had are kept on the device and are what it starts with. It is kept current: a change made in Studio reaches the app over the project's socket within moments, with no call of yours.

## Quick example

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.flags.flags

// Read now, with a default for a flag the app does not have (yet).
if (pb.flags.bool("checkout.new_flow", default = false)) showNewCheckout()
val greeting = pb.flags.string("home.greeting", default = "Hello")
val limit = pb.flags.int("cart.max_items", default = 20)
```

In Compose, collect the values, and the screen is drawn again when one changes:

```kotlin
import kotlinx.serialization.json.JsonPrimitive

@Composable
fun Greeting() {
    val flags by pb.flags.values.collectAsState()
    val text = (flags["home.greeting"] as? JsonPrimitive)?.takeIf { it.isString }?.content ?: "Hello"
    Text(text)
}
```

## Reading values

| Member | What it returns |
|---|---|
| `bool(key, default)`, `string(key, default)`, `number(key, default)`, `long(key, default)`, `int(key, default)` | The flag's value as that type, or `default` when there is no such flag or its value is another type. |
| `decode<T>(key)` | An object flag as a `@Serializable` type of yours; `null` when it is missing or does not fit. `decode(key, deserializer)` takes the serializer. |
| `value(key)` | The value as JSON (`JsonElement`), or `null`. |
| `all` | Every flag's value by key. |
| `values` | The same, as a `StateFlow<Map<String, JsonElement>>`. |
| `source(key)` | Where the value came from, as the project says: `override` for the user's own value. |
| `version` | The version the values are current as of. |

```kotlin
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

@Serializable
data class Banner(val title: String, val color: String)

val banner = pb.flags.decode<Banner>("home.banner")
```

A value is any JSON the flag's type allows: a boolean, a number, a string or an object.

## A signed-in user's values

The values are one reader's: the signed-in user's, or, with no one signed in, this app's. The values kept on the device are read at launch only when they are the same reader's. When someone signs in or out, the values held go (`values` is empty, and a listener is told their keys), the new reader's are read, and the listener is told again. One reader's values are never shown to another, even for the moment the new ones take to arrive.

## What a value is resolved from

Every read is resolved by the project for its reader, in this order: the user's own value when a signed-in user has one ([Users' own values](/docs/backend/flags#users-own-values)), then the variant of an experiment running on the flag, then the flag's first condition that matches, then its default ([How a value is resolved](/docs/backend/flags#how-a-value-is-resolved)).

What the client says about itself, with every read:

| Header | Sent as |
|---|---|
| `X-Platform` | `android` |
| `X-OS-Version` | The device's Android version (`Build.VERSION.RELEASE`) |
| `X-Palbase-Client-Version` | The app's `versionName` |
| `Accept-Language` | The user's languages ([Languages](/docs/android/overview#languages)) |
| `X-Palbase-Installation` | `pb.installation.id`, with each snapshot: the install a percentage places, counted toward which versions of your app are in use |

The country a condition reads is that of the address the request came from: the device's own, because the app calls the project directly.

At this version the Android SDK records no `$flag_exposure` analytics event when it reads a value an experiment gave.

## Keeping up to date

The flags start being kept current the first time `pb.flags` is used: the latest values are read, and the client joins the project's two flags channels on its socket.

| Channel | Who joins | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `flags:<ref>` | Anyone reading the project's flags, with no one signed in too | The project's flags changed. |
| `flags:<ref>:<user_id>` | That user only | That user's own values changed. |

Told of a newer version, the client asks for what changed since the one it holds (`GET /flags/delta`). When the delta can no longer bring its values up to date, the project answers `410`, and the client reads a whole snapshot instead (`GET /flags/snapshot`, sent with the `ETag` of what it holds, answered `304` when nothing changed). A sign-in or a sign-out reads the values again for whoever is signed in now.

To hear which flags changed:

```kotlin
val stop = pb.flags.onChange { keys -> println("changed: $keys") }
// or, in a coroutine: pb.flags.changes.collect { keys -> … }
```

`pb.flags.refresh()` brings the values up to date now: what changed since the version held, or a snapshot. It throws `PalbaseError` when the project could not be read, and the values held stay as they are.

## Turning a flag on for one user

A user's own value wins over the flag's conditions: give one from a server ([Users' own values](/docs/backend/flags#users-own-values)) or from a terminal, and it reaches their device on their channel:

```sh
palbase flags:users:set <user-id> checkout.new_flow true
palbase flags:users:get <user-id>
```

The debug console is opened for one user the same way ([Debug Console](/docs/android/debug-console)).

## Related

- [Flags in your backend](/docs/backend/flags): defining flags, conditions and users' own values
- [Realtime](/docs/android/realtime): the socket the changes come over
- [Overview](/docs/android/overview): the client and its observable state



<!-- ===== android/analytics ===== -->

# Analytics

`pb.analytics(startingConsent)` (`studio.palbase:palbase-analytics`) is the app's analytics, performance samples and diagnostics, each behind its consent category: events the app captures and screens it shows (analytics), timings (performance), and its log and failed requests (diagnostics). Nothing waits on it. What is collected is held and sent together, and a send that fails is let go.

## Quick example

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.Consent
import studio.palbase.analytics.analytics
import kotlinx.serialization.json.JsonPrimitive

// Nothing is collected until the person says yes.
val analytics = pb.analytics(startingConsent = Consent.State.DENIED)

// The person's choice, from the app's consent screen:
pb.consent.set(Consent.Category.ANALYTICS, Consent.State.GRANTED)

analytics.screen("Checkout")
analytics.capture("checkout_started", mapOf("items" to JsonPrimitive(3), "plan" to JsonPrimitive("pro")))
```

`pb.analytics(…)` is made once. The first call's starting consent is the one kept, so make it at launch, with the starting consent the app's users need.

## Consent

`pb.consent` is the one gate every collecting module asks. While a category is not granted, nothing of it is made: no event, no queue, no file, no request, and no anonymous id.

| `Consent.Category` | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `ANALYTICS` | Events the app captures, and screens viewed |
| `PERFORMANCE` | Timings: launches, screens, requests |
| `DIAGNOSTICS` | The app's log, its reports and its failed requests |

There is no default. The app says what it starts with when it makes analytics (`startingConsent`), because whether its users must opt in is the app's to know. That applies to every category until the user's own choice is recorded, which then wins:

```kotlin
pb.consent.set(Consent.Category.PERFORMANCE, Consent.State.DENIED)
val chosen: Consent.State? = pb.consent.state(Consent.Category.ANALYTICS)   // null: not chosen yet
val stop = pb.consent.onChange { category, state -> println("$category is now $state") }
pb.consent.reset()   // forget the choices: the starting consent applies again
```

When a category is withdrawn, what was held of it is deleted, on the device too, and with analytics the anonymous id and the session go as well. A store that cannot be read counts as a refusal, never as the starting value. The choices are kept on the device: at this version the Android SDK does not send them to the project.

## Events and screens

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `capture(event, properties)` | Records an event. The name is a letter or `$`, then letters, digits and `_.:-$`, 64 at most. `properties` is a `Map<String, JsonElement>`. |
| `screen(name, properties)` | Records a screen the user saw. |
| `identify(traits)` | Ties this device's anonymous events to the signed-in user, with their traits. It is done by itself at sign-in, with the next send. |
| `flush()` | Sends what is held now, of the categories granted now. |

An event is sent as the signed-in user, or, with no one signed in, under an anonymous id the device keeps (`anon_…`). A session is the events with no more than 30 minutes between them. When the user signs out, the anonymous id goes, and the next person on the device is someone new.

What is held goes together: 5 seconds after the first of it, as soon as 20 events, screens and timings are held, and when the app's screens are hidden. What is held when the app closes is kept on the device and sent at the next launch.

## Timings

While `PERFORMANCE` is granted, the SDK times on its own how long the launch took, from the process's start to its first activity started, as an `app_start` sample named `cold` — a process begun for a push, a job or a widget and opened later is not one. In an app built with the Palbase Gradle plugin it also times each request the app makes — its own OkHttp clients and `HttpURLConnection`s and every library's, the SDK's among them — as a `network` sample: its method, its address as its route (no query, an id in the path as `:id`), its status and how long it took. What analytics itself sends is not timed.

```kotlin
// settings.gradle.kts
pluginManagement { repositories { gradlePluginPortal(); google(); mavenCentral(); maven("https://palgroup.github.io/palbase-android/") } }

// app/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
    id("studio.palbase") version "0.10.0"
}
```

The plugin rewrites, as the app is built, each `OkHttpClient()`, `OkHttpClient.Builder.build()`, `URL.openConnection()` and a connection's `getResponseCode()` and `getInputStream()` — in the app and in every library it takes — to the SDK, which does what was asked and times it. It reaches no network, and an app without `palbase-analytics` is built as it was. Each timing is turned off in `AnalyticsOptions(network = false, appStart = false)`.

An app whose users can grant `PERFORMANCE` declares these timings in Play Console's Data safety form as **App info and performance › Diagnostics**, collected, for analytics.

What the app measures itself:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.analytics.Analytics

val trace = analytics.startTrace("load_feed")
loadFeed()
trace.stop(mapOf("source" to "network"))

analytics.measure("image_decode", 12.5, Analytics.Measure.CUSTOM, mapOf("format" to "webp"))   // milliseconds
```

`Analytics.Measure` is the kind of a measurement: `CUSTOM`, `SCREEN`, `APP_START` or `NETWORK`. Each is collected only with `PERFORMANCE` granted.

## Diagnostics

```kotlin
analytics.log("cart is empty at checkout", Analytics.Level.WARNING)   // kept in memory, the last 200 lines
analytics.report()                                                     // sends the lines kept, as what led to an error

analytics.recordRequest(method = "GET", endpoint = "/v1/feed", status = 500, durationMs = 840, requestId = "req_01")
```

`log` keeps a line in memory and sends nothing, so the lines go only with a `report()`, which sends them as what led to an error (or, with another `trigger`, what the user reported). `recordRequest` records a request the app made and how it ended. Each is collected only with `DIAGNOSTICS` granted.

Studio's Analytics screens show what the app sent: its events, people, funnels and retention.

## Related

- [Overview](/docs/android/overview): the client, consent and the installation
- [Debug Console](/docs/android/debug-console): what the SDK records on the device for a bug report
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics): the same events from a browser, and what the project reads back



<!-- ===== android/notifications ===== -->

# Notifications

`pb.notify` (`studio.palbase:palbase-notify`) is what the app does for the project's messages: it records this device's push token for the signed-in user, and reads and writes the user's own preferences and topics. Sending is the project's server's, with the secret key ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)), never the app's.

A push reaches an Android device through Firebase Cloud Messaging, with the project's own FCM account.

## Setting up push

1. **The app's Firebase project.** Add the app to a Firebase project, put its `google-services.json` in the app module, and apply the `com.google.gms.google-services` plugin with `com.google.firebase:firebase-messaging`, as Firebase's setup says.
2. **The project sends with it.** Give the environment the Firebase project's service account, the JSON key of an account that may send with FCM:

   ```sh
   palbase notify:providers:set push fcm < service-account.json -E staging
   ```

   The credentials are read from stdin, checked as the sender will use them, and never shown again.
3. **Ask to notify.** On Android 13 and newer, the app asks for `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` at runtime and declares it in its manifest.
4. **Record the token** for the signed-in user, and **show what arrives**, both from the app's `FirebaseMessagingService` (below).

## Recording the token

```kotlin
// app/src/main/kotlin/com/example/shop/Push.kt
import com.google.firebase.messaging.FirebaseMessaging
import studio.palbase.notify.notify

// appScope: a CoroutineScope of the app's own, as long as the process.
fun startPush() {
    FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token.addOnSuccessListener { token ->
        appScope.launch { runCatching { pb.notify.register(fcmToken = token) } }
    }
}
```

`register(fcmToken, locale)` records the token for the signed-in user and returns the device as the project has it. The token is this install's, and the device row is the user's:

- **Signed out**, `register` throws `PalbaseError` `missing_credential`, and the token is kept: it is recorded for whoever signs in next, with no call of yours.
- **Signing out** forgets the device for that user while they can still be named. The call is left with the client for that moment, and made even by a later process that never loaded `pb.notify`. The next person on the phone does not get the last one's notifications.
- **Someone else signing in** gets the token the app last gave.

`pb.notify.deviceId` is how the project names this device: `android-` and the installation's id. `unregister()` forgets it for the signed-in user, and it receives nothing until it is registered again. `devices()` lists the user's devices.

## Showing a push

A push reaches an Android app as an FCM data message, never as a notification the system draws by itself. Its parts are in the message's data, beside the push's own `data`:

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pb_title`, `pb_body` | The push's title and body. |
| `pb_image`, `pb_sound` | Its image's https address and its sound, when it has them. |
| `deep_link` | Its deep link, when it has one. |
| `pb_receipt` | The push's sealed receipt for this device. |

A silent push (`silent: true`) carries none of the title, body, image and sound: it wakes the app with its data alone.

At this version the SDK draws nothing, so the app's own service shows it:

```kotlin
// app/src/main/kotlin/com/example/shop/PushService.kt
import android.app.NotificationChannel
import android.app.NotificationManager
import androidx.core.app.NotificationCompat
import com.google.firebase.messaging.FirebaseMessagingService
import com.google.firebase.messaging.RemoteMessage
import studio.palbase.notify.notify

class PushService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
    // A token FCM changed goes to the project for whoever is signed in.
    override fun onNewToken(token: String) {
        appScope.launch { runCatching { pb.notify.register(fcmToken = token) } }
    }

    override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
        val title = message.data["pb_title"] ?: return   // a silent push: data alone
        val manager = getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java)
        manager.createNotificationChannel(NotificationChannel("messages", "Messages", NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT))
        val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, "messages")
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_notification)
            .setContentTitle(title)
            .setContentText(message.data["pb_body"])
            .setAutoCancel(true)
            .build()
        manager.notify(message.messageId.hashCode(), notification)
    }
}
```

```xml
<!-- app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS" />
<application>
    <service android:name=".PushService" android:exported="false">
        <intent-filter>
            <action android:name="com.google.firebase.MESSAGING_EVENT" />
        </intent-filter>
    </service>
</application>
```

`onMessageReceived` runs in the background too, so a process the push woke makes the client as the app's `Application` does. A call it makes as the user, to your backend for example, renews the session only if the call needs it.

The project counts how each push went on each device from what the device reports with `pb_receipt` (`POST /notify/receipts`). The Android SDK at this version reports nothing, so a push sent to an Android device is `unconfirmed` unless the app reports it itself.

## Preferences and topics

```kotlin
// channel → category → whether they take it
val preferences: Map<String, Map<String, Boolean>> = pb.notify.preferences()
pb.notify.setPreferences(mapOf("push" to mapOf("marketing" to false)))

pb.notify.follow("release-notes")
pb.notify.unfollow("release-notes")
```

A write sets some of the user's preferences and answers all of them. A category the user never set is on, and `transactional` is always on: it is not theirs to turn off. A topic's followers get what the server sends to it with `to: { topic }`.

## The inbox

The signed-in person's inbox holds the messages your backend put there and the copies of pushes it chose to keep, the same on every device of theirs: read on one, it is read on each; deleted, it is gone from each. A message stays its days (90 unless the project said) and an inbox keeps its newest 250.

`InboxView` (`studio.palbase:palbase-notify-ui`) draws it ready, in Compose:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.notify.ui.InboxView

@Composable
fun InboxScreen() {
    var unread by remember { mutableLongStateOf(0L) }
    Scaffold(topBar = { TopAppBar(title = { Text(if (unread > 0) "Inbox ($unread)" else "Inbox") }) }) { pad ->
        InboxView(pb, Modifier.padding(pad).fillMaxSize(), onUnread = { unread = it }, empty = "No messages yet")
    }
}
```

`InboxView(client, modifier, locale, onOpen, onCustom, onUnread, empty, deleteLabel, onOffer, onOfferError)` takes the language to write it in (the person's chosen one unless given), what a tap on a message's link does (the system opens it unless given), a designed card's own buttons, the unread count as it changes, what an empty inbox says, and a designed card's offer button (the purchases module takes the offer unless given, once the app uses `pb.purchases`).

An app that draws its own uses `pb.notify.inbox`:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `list(limit, cursor, locale)` | A page, newest first: `items`, `nextCursor` and `unread`. Each `Inbox.Item` has its id, title, body, image, deep link, category, data, designed card, and when it was made, ends and was read. |
| `unread()` | How many are unread: what a badge shows. |
| `markRead(ids)`, `markAllRead()` | Marks messages read, on every device of the person's. |
| `remove(id)` | Deletes a message, from every device. |

## In-app messages

The project's in-app campaigns (a modal, a banner or a whole screen, designed in Studio) are shown over the app once started. `PalbaseInAppMessages` around the app's root starts them and draws them in Compose:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.notify.ui.InAppHandlers
import studio.palbase.notify.ui.PalbaseInAppMessages

setContent {
    PalbaseInAppMessages(pb, InAppHandlers(
        onDeepLink = { url -> startActivity(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse(url))) },
        onShowPaywall = { placement -> showPaywall(placement) },
    )) {
        AppNavigation()
    }
}
```

The person's campaigns are asked for as each session of theirs starts (the launch, a return after half an hour away, a sign-in or out). An event the app records with `pb.analytics` (its captures and screens), or names with `pb.notify.inApp.trigger(event, properties)`, shows the first campaign it triggers, the highest priority first, that its caps let: the project's (in a session, in a day, the least time between two) and the campaign's own. Triggers are matched on the device, so no event leaves it for them, and a message is shown whatever the person chose of analytics; a campaign to an audience reaches only people who allowed personalization. A [journey](/docs/backend/journeys)'s in-app step opens one of these campaigns for its person, shown the next time it is triggered.

`InAppHandlers` says what the app does with a message's buttons: `onDeepLink`, `onShowPaywall` (a placement's paywall), `onCustom` (the app's own code: a name and a value), `onRequestPush` (the push ask) and `onOffer` (one of the catalog's offers; the purchases module takes it unless given, once the app uses it). A button whose action the app does not take is not drawn.

An app that draws its own calls `pb.notify.inApp.start { presentation -> … }`, which hands it each `InAppPresentation` to show (its `definition`, its `variables`) and `null` when what is shown must go. The app tells back `clicked(action)`, `dismissed()` or `closed()`. `stop()` stops them, and `refresh()` asks for the person's campaigns again.

## Related

- [Notifications in your backend](/docs/backend/notifications): sending push, email, SMS and WhatsApp
- [Auth](/docs/android/auth): the sign-in the device row follows
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-notifyprovidersset): `notify:providers:set`



<!-- ===== android/storage ===== -->

# Storage

`pb.storage` (`studio.palbase:palbase-storage`) carries files between the app and the project's storage. The app writes and reads a file through a URL the project's backend signed, which says which object, for how long, how large and whose: the backend decides, and the app carries the bytes. A public bucket's objects are anyone's to read.

## Uploading

The backend signs an upload URL for one object (`Palbase.storage.createUploadUrl`, [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads)) and answers it from a route of its own. The app sends the bytes to it:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.storage.storage

// grantUrl: what your backend's route answered, an upload URL it signed.
val stored = pb.storage.upload(bytes, signedUrl = grantUrl, contentType = "image/jpeg")
println("${stored.bucket}/${stored.path}: ${stored.size} bytes, ${stored.contentType}")
```

`upload(data, signedUrl, contentType)` returns the object as storage stored it (`StorageAPI.StorageObject`: `bucket`, `path`, `size`, `contentType`, `checksumSha256`, `width` and `height` for an image, `ownerId`). The content type is used only when the bytes cannot say what they are, since storage reads the type from the bytes. Storage checks the grant while the bytes stream: a file past the URL's `max_bytes`, of a type the bucket does not take, or sent after the URL expired is refused with a `PalbaseError`.

The URL's conditions (the bucket, the path, the expiry, the ceiling, the types, the owner) are all covered by its signature, so a URL changed on the device opens nothing.

## Downloading

A private object is read with a download URL the backend signed (`Palbase.storage.createSignedUrl`, [Storage](/docs/backend/storage)):

```kotlin
val bytes: ByteArray = pb.storage.download(signedUrl)
val bitmap = BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray(bytes, 0, bytes.size)
```

## Public buckets

A public bucket's objects need no URL of the backend's:

```kotlin
val logo: ByteArray = pb.storage.publicObject("public-assets", "logo.png")

// The address itself, for an image loader or a share sheet:
val address: java.net.URI = pb.storage.publicUrl("public-assets", "logo.png")
```

`publicUrl` is `https://<ref>.palbase.studio/storage/public/{bucket}/{path}`, with each part encoded as one path segment.

## Signed URLs stay at the project's address

A signed URL is taken only at the project's own address, the configuration's `url`. A URL that names another host is refused before anything is sent (`foreign_signed_url`), so a URL from somewhere else never takes the user's request away from the project. A URL that is not a signed object URL is `invalid_signed_url`.

## Through your backend's upload routes

A backend route declared with `@Upload` takes the file in the same call as its body, and its generated function reports progress ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/android/backend-calls#uploads)). Use one when the backend's code must run with the file. Use a signed URL when the backend only grants the write.

## Related

- [Direct Uploads](/docs/backend/direct-uploads): signing an upload URL
- [Storage in your backend](/docs/backend/storage): buckets, objects, public reads and signed URLs
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/android/backend-calls): the route that answers the URL



<!-- ===== android/purchases ===== -->

# Purchases

`pb.purchases` (`studio.palbase:palbase-purchases`) is what the signed-in customer has, whatever store they bought in, and buying on Google Play. What they have is one answer, `CustomerInfo`, the same the web, the iOS app and the project's backend read: a Pro bought on the web is this app's Pro too. Buying goes through Google Play Billing 9, which the artifact brings with it.

Google Play is connected to the environment first: the service account Play Console invites, the Android app linked, and Play's notifications ([Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play)). The catalog's `android` plans are what the app sells ([Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog)).

## Quick example

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.purchases.PurchaseResult
import studio.palbase.purchases.StoreProduct
```
