```kotlin
import studio.palbase.purchases.isEntitled
import studio.palbase.purchases.purchases

class PaywallViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val products = MutableStateFlow<List<StoreProduct>>(emptyList())
    val isPro = MutableStateFlow(false)
    val message = MutableStateFlow("")

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val found = pb.purchases.products()
            products.value = found.products
            found.diagnosis?.let { Log.w("Paywall", it.toString()) }   // why Play returned fewer
        }
        viewModelScope.launch {
            // Kept current: a purchase on another device or in another store, a renewal, a refund.
            pb.purchases.customerInfoUpdates.collect { info -> isPro.value = info?.isEntitled("pro") ?: false }
        }
    }

    fun buy(activity: Activity, product: StoreProduct) = viewModelScope.launch {
        when (val result = pb.purchases.purchase(activity, product)) {
            is PurchaseResult.Purchased -> isPro.value = result.customerInfo.isEntitled("pro")
            is PurchaseResult.AlreadyEntitled -> message.value = "${result.entitlement} is already yours, from ${result.store.value}"
            PurchaseResult.Pending -> message.value = "Waiting for the payment"
            PurchaseResult.Cancelled -> Unit
        }
    }

    fun restore() = viewModelScope.launch {
        isPro.value = pb.purchases.restore().isEntitled("pro")
    }
}
```

Touch `pb.purchases` at launch, in the `Application`, even before a paywall is shown. What Play holds unreported (a report that failed, a pending purchase since paid, one made outside the app) is reported then, as whoever is signed in.

## What the customer has

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `customerInfo()` | Everything the signed-in customer has, read now. |
| `latest` | The newest known: what listeners were last told, or the app's own last read. `null` before any, and for anyone but who is signed in now. |
| `isEntitled(key)` | Whether the customer has the entitlement now, from `latest`. `false` when nothing is known. |
| `onCustomerInfo { info -> }` | Called once it is read, then each time it changes, and with `null` while no one is signed in. Returns what stops it. Called on a background thread. |
| `customerInfoUpdates` | The same, as a `Flow<CustomerInfo?>`; the newest when the collector falls behind. |
| `offerings(channel)` | The paywall's catalog: each product's text and price on a channel, this app's (`OfferingsChannel.ANDROID`) unless another is named. |

`CustomerInfo` holds `entitlements` (by key: `active`, `expiresAt`, `willRenew`, `billingIssue`, `store`, `isSandbox`, `manage`), `subscriptions`, one-time `purchases`, `credits` balances, `limits` and their use, and `guest` for a guest customer. `info.isEntitled("pro")` is the entitlement active and, unless it is for life, ending after now: the rule the backend's `isEntitled` reads.

What the customer has is kept current while it is listened to. The customer's own realtime channel says when it changed, and it is read again then. When another user signs in, their channel is followed, and listeners hear `null` until theirs is read: one user's is never shown as the next one's. A read that fails is asked again a few times, then on the next change or the app's return to the foreground. A listener is told what is, never an error.

## Buying on Google Play

`products()` returns the catalog's Android plans as Google Play has them for this user, in the catalog's order: a subscription once per base plan. A product Play does not return is left out, never silently: `diagnosis` names it, with Play's reason and the likely causes (also logged, tag `Palbase`). It throws `PurchasesException` when Play Billing fails, and `PalbaseError` when the catalog cannot be read.

| `StoreProduct` | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id`, `basePlanId`, `offerId` | Google Play's product id, a subscription's base plan, and the offer it is bought with (its introductory offer, when the catalog's plan has one and Play says the user may take it). |
| `name`, `title`, `description` | As Google Play has them, in the user's language. |
| `formattedPrice`, `priceAmountMicros`, `priceCurrencyCode` | The price for the user's country: a one-time product's, or the price a subscription renews at. |
| `billingPeriod` | A subscription's period, ISO 8601 (`P1M`, `P1Y`). |
| `entitlements` | What buying it gives. |
| `offering`, `plan` | The catalog's product and plan it was paired with. |
| `productDetails` | Play's own `ProductDetails`: its offers and every pricing phase. |

`purchase(activity, product, planChange)` opens Google Play's purchase sheet over `activity`. What the customer has is read first: an entitlement it gives that is already on from another store answers `AlreadyEntitled` without opening Play, so nothing is charged twice. Otherwise Play sells it with the customer's obfuscated account id, and the purchase is reported to the environment, which reads it from Play and acknowledges it (a consumable's is consumed). The SDK never acknowledges a purchase itself. A report that fails leaves the purchase unacknowledged, and it is reported again at the next start.

| `PurchaseResult` | What it means |
|---|---|
| `Purchased(customerInfo)` | Bought, and the environment has it. |
| `AlreadyEntitled(store, entitlement, manage)` | An entitlement it gives is already on, from another store or from this Google account on Play. `manage` is where it is managed: the web's is the Stripe portal. |
| `Cancelled` | The user closed the sheet. |
| `Pending` | Waiting for the payment, or a parent's approval. Once it is paid, Play hands the purchase over, it is reported, and listeners are told. |

Play's failures throw `PurchasesException`, whose `code` is one of `PurchasesException.Code`: `PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE`, `ALREADY_OWNED`, `BILLING_UNAVAILABLE`, `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` (try again in a moment), `NETWORK_ERROR`, `DEVELOPER_ERROR`, `PAYMENT_DECLINED`, `INELIGIBLE_FOR_OFFER`, `PURCHASE_IN_PROGRESS`, `PLAN_CHANGE_NOT_ALLOWED` and others. Its message is one sentence, and `responseCode` and `debugMessage` are Play's own, for a log. The environment's refusals throw `PalbaseError`, and so do `session_required` (no one signed in) and `session_changed` (the signed-in user changed meanwhile).

### Changing plans

A subscription bought while the customer has another plan of its group on Google Play replaces it. Play moves the customer over as `planChange` says, and the environment ends the old purchase. `PlanChange.DEFAULT` is Google's recommendation for the change:

| Between | An upgrade | A downgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Two subscriptions | Now: `CHARGE_PRORATED_PRICE` when the new plan costs more per day, `WITH_TIME_PRORATION` when it does not | At the old plan's renewal: `DEFERRED` |
| Two base plans of one subscription | Now, at the full price: `CHARGE_FULL_PRICE` | From the next billing date: `WITHOUT_PRORATION` |

To a prepaid plan the change is always `CHARGE_FULL_PRICE`. A mode Play does not take for the change throws `PLAN_CHANGE_NOT_ALLOWED`, naming the ones it does, before Play is opened. The plan the customer already has is not bought again: `AlreadyEntitled`.

### Restoring

`restore()` is "Restore purchases", the user's own action, never automatic. Everything this Google account owns on Play is reported as restored, so a purchase made while signed in as another of the app's accounts may move to this one. It answers what the customer has now. When a purchase stays where it was, the rest is still applied and it throws `PalbaseError`: `restore_account_owned` (403: a guest restoring an account's purchase must sign in to that account), `restore_other_account` (403: another account bought it — Play's obfuscated account id names that one), `restore_other_environment` (403: another environment of the project made it) or `restore_limit` (409: moved too often lately).

## Web purchases bought without an account

Someone who bought on the web without an account is sent a link that gives the purchase to whoever opens it in the app: `<package>://palbase/redeem?token=…`, or its page's `https://…/purchases/redeem?token=…`. The app redeems the link it was opened with, for the signed-in user (a guest too):

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.purchases.redemptionToken

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    val link = intent.dataString ?: return
    if (redemptionToken(link) != null) lifecycleScope.launch { pb.purchases.redeem(link) }
}
```

A link works once (`409 already_redeemed`). One past its hour (`410 redemption_expired`) sends a new one to the buyer's email. `redemptionToken(link)` says whether a link is one, without asking anything.

## Paywalls

The Android SDK at this version draws no paywall, and asks for no placement: the app shows its own screen, from `products()`, which carries Play's prices, and from `offerings()`, which carries the catalog's text. The paywalls the project publishes are drawn by the iOS and web SDKs ([Paywalls › In the app](/docs/purchases/paywalls#in-the-app)).

## On your server

Check the entitlement where the content is served, not only in the app: `Palbase.purchases.getCustomer` and `isEntitled` from `palbase/server`, and the `purchases.entitlement.changed` event ([Checking an entitlement](/docs/purchases/entitlements#checking-an-entitlement)). The app's answer decides what the app shows; what a purchase opens on your server is checked there.

## Related

- [Purchases](/docs/purchases/overview): the catalog, the stores and how a purchase becomes access
- [Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play): connecting the environment to Google Play
- [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog): the products and plans the app sells
- [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements): what `CustomerInfo` holds, and spending credits
- [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls): the paywalls the project publishes
- [Auth](/docs/android/auth#guests): guests, whose purchases stay theirs when they become an account



<!-- ===== android/voice ===== -->

# Voice

A chat of the project's agents can be talked to out loud ([AI › Voice](/docs/backend/ai#voice)). `PBVoice` (`studio.palbase:palbase-voice`) is that voice on the device: the microphone goes to the platform's voice provider and its voice comes back, over WebRTC. The app makes the WebRTC offer, the app's own backend starts the voice with it, and the provider's key never leaves the platform.

WebRTC comes with this artifact alone, so an app that takes no voice carries none of it. Its native library is about 12 MB for each ABI.

## Quick example

The backend starts the voice for the signed-in member, from a route of its own:

```ts
// src/modules/support/voice.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Palbase, Param, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";

const Offer = z.object({ sdp: z.string().min(1) });

@Controller("/voice")
export class VoiceController {
  // The app's WebRTC offer in; the voice's id and the provider's answer out.
  @Post("/{chatId}")
  async start(@Param("chatId") chatId: string, @Body(Offer) body: z.infer<typeof Offer>, @User() user: UserT): Promise<{ id: string; sdp: string }> {
    const voice = await Palbase.ai.chats.voice.start(chatId, { sdp: body.sdp, as: user.id });
    return { id: voice.id, sdp: voice.sdp };
  }

  @Post("/{chatId}/{voiceId}/close")
  async close(@Param("chatId") chatId: string, @Param("voiceId") voiceId: string, @User() user: UserT): Promise<{ seconds: number }> {
    const voice = await Palbase.ai.chats.voice.close(chatId, voiceId, { as: user.id });
    return { seconds: voice.seconds };
  }
}
```

The app connects, after `palbase apps:sync` wrote the backend's client:

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.generated.*
import studio.palbase.voice.PBStartedVoice
import studio.palbase.voice.PBVoice

// The person allowed RECORD_AUDIO first.
val voice = PBVoice.connect(context, start = { sdp ->
    val started = pb.backend.voice.start(chatId, VoiceStartRequest(sdp = sdp))
    PBStartedVoice(started.id, started.sdp)
})

voice.mute(true)
voice.mute(false)

// Done: here, then on the backend.
voice.close()
pb.backend.voice.close(chatId, voice.id)
```

## Connecting

`PBVoice.connect(context, start, audio, iceTimeoutMillis, onError, onState)` makes the offer, hands it to `start`, sets the answer it gets back and returns the voice. Its `state` then says when the connection is up:

| Argument | What it is |
|---|---|
| `start` | The round trip to the app's own backend: the offer (an SDP) in, the voice's id and the provider's answer out, as a `PBStartedVoice(id, sdp)`. |
| `audio` | Who holds the device's audio while the voice talks. `PBVoice.Audio.MANAGED` (the default): the voice sets it up (in communication, through the speaker unless a headset is connected, with the audio focus taken) and gives it back as it found it on close. `PBVoice.Audio.APP`: the app set it up already, and the voice leaves it as it is. |
| `iceTimeoutMillis` | How long the offer's network candidates are gathered at most before it is sent: 10 seconds by default, then `PalbaseError` `ice_timeout`. |
| `onError` | The provider's word that something went wrong in the voice, on WebRTC's thread. |
| `onState` | The connection's state each time it changes, on WebRTC's thread. |

The app asks the person for the microphone first: `RECORD_AUDIO` is a runtime permission, and without it `connect` throws `PalbaseError` `microphone_denied`. The artifact declares `RECORD_AUDIO` and `MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS` in its manifest. When the coroutine that connects is cancelled, or the backend refuses, whatever was opened is closed.

A member starts at most 5 voices an hour, and one voice talks in a chat at a time: the backend's `start` throws `429 too_many_voices` or `409 voice_active` ([AI › Voice](/docs/backend/ai#voice)).

## The voice

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The voice the backend started: what it reads, tells and closes it by. |
| `state` | The connection's state as a `StateFlow<PBVoice.State>`: `NEW`, `CONNECTING`, `CONNECTED`, `DISCONNECTED`, `FAILED`, `CLOSED`. |
| `muted`, `mute(on)` | Whether the microphone is heard. |
| `close()` | Ends it here: the connection, the microphone, and the audio it set up. Callable from any thread. |

Call `close()` when the voice is done, in a screen's `onDispose` or a ViewModel's `onCleared`. Ending it is the app's, and its backend's (`Palbase.ai.chats.voice.close`). A voice the app lets go of without closing it is closed once the garbage collector takes it, but not at once: the microphone stays open until then.

## What was said

Nothing of the conversation is read on the device. What is said either way is the chat's: on a [chat gateway](/docs/android/gateways#chat-gateways), the chat's state has the voice (`PBChat.State.voice`: when it began and ended), and each line said in it is among the messages, of kind voice, the person's and the voice's own.

## Related

- [AI › Voice](/docs/backend/ai#voice): starting, telling and closing a voice from the backend
- [Gateways](/docs/android/gateways#chat-gateways): the chat the voice talks in
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/android/backend-calls): the generated client the offer goes through



<!-- ===== android/debug-console ===== -->

# Debug Console

Every app records what happened on the device from launch: the SDK's own requests and realtime frames, its modules' lines, and whatever the app adds. `studio.palbase:palbase-debug` shows that record, in Compose, and only while the project has turned the console on for the signed-in user. So a build that already shipped can open it for the one person reporting a bug, and what it shows includes everything recorded before it was turned on.

## Quick example

```kotlin
import studio.palbase.debug.PBLogLevel
import studio.palbase.debug.ui.PalbaseConsole
import studio.palbase.debug.ui.enabled

@Composable
fun Settings() {
    var showing by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    val on by pb.debug.enabled.collectAsState()          // followed as the flag flips

    if (showing && on) {
        // A whole screen: its round × and system back close it.
        PalbaseConsole(pb.debug, Modifier.fillMaxSize(), onClose = { showing = false })
        return
    }
    if (on) Button({ showing = true }) { Text("Debug console") }
    Button({ pb.debug.log("cart is empty", PBLogLevel.WARNING, label = "checkout") }) { Text("Log a line") }
}
```

Turn it on for one user:

```sh
palbase flags:users:set <user-id> palbase.debug_console true
```

## What is recorded

Recording runs from launch whether or not the console is on, and stays on the device: in the app's no-backup files, up to 32 MB, the last 20 launches. Credentials are masked before anything is written. When someone else signs in, the last user's records are wiped.

| What | How it gets there |
|---|---|
| The SDK's requests to the project and to your backends | By itself, measured in full: the phases (DNS, connect, TLS, waiting), the connection, the bytes. |
| The realtime socket | By itself: the connection, the channels and the last frames, on the console's Realtime tab. |
| The modules' own lines | By itself, under `palbase.<module>`: a sign-in, a flag change, a purchase reported. |
| The app's log | `pb.debug.log(message, level, label, metadata)` and `pb.debug.error(throwable, label)`. The `label` is the line's category, any word the app likes, and the console filters by it. |
| The app's own OkHttp traffic | `pb.debug.client(appClient, label)` returns a client that records and measures each request like the SDK's own, keeping `appClient`'s settings and connection pool. `pb.debug.interceptor(label)` goes in a client built by hand, and records without the phases. |
| Anything else | `pb.debug.record(method, url, requestHeaders, requestBody, statusCode, responseHeaders, responseBody, error, durationMs, label)`: an exchange the SDK did not make, masked on the way in like a captured one. |

A backend call's [encrypted field](/docs/backend/request-encryption) is recorded as it went, sealed (`pbt1.…`); **Reveal** beside it in the body shows its value. The values are kept in memory alone, only while the console is on for the user and recording, and are gone when the console is cleared, another user signs in or the console is turned off.

`PBLogLevel` is `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `NOTICE`, `WARNING`, `ERROR` or `CRITICAL`.

```kotlin
import okhttp3.OkHttpClient
import okhttp3.Request

// One client for the app's own requests: recorded beside the SDK's, under the label "app".
val http: OkHttpClient = pb.debug.client(OkHttpClient(), label = "app")
// Off the main thread, as any OkHttp call:
http.newCall(Request.Builder().url("https://api.example.com/v1/feed").build()).execute().use { println(it.code) }
```

| Member of `pb.debug` | What it does |
|---|---|
| `isRecording`, `start()`, `stop()` | Whether it records. Recording is on from launch, and `stop()` keeps what was recorded. |
| `clear()` | Discards every record, on the device and in the console's screens. |
| `export()` | This launch's records as JSON lines, already masked: what to attach to a bug report. |
| `sessions()` | Every launch on the device, newest first. |
| `realtime` | The socket, inspected, as a `StateFlow`: the connection, the channels and the last frames. |

## Who sees it

`PalbaseConsole(pb.debug)` draws nothing unless the project has turned the console on for the signed-in user: the flag `palbase.debug_console`, given to that user as their own value. It is decided by the project, never by the build. `pb.debug.isEnabled` is the same answer (`import studio.palbase.debug.ui.isEnabled`), and `pb.debug.enabled` follows it as it changes. Gate your own way in on it: a row in a settings screen, a long press. It is `false` until it is shown to be true: before the flags load, when they cannot be read, and when nobody turned it on.

Turning it off again is `palbase flags:users:unset <user-id> palbase.debug_console`. The flag reaches the device on the user's own flags channel, so the console opens or shuts without a relaunch ([Flags](/docs/android/flags#keeping-up-to-date)).

## The screens

The console has two tabs, Console and Realtime, under a floating tab bar, each with its own back stack: the list of records, a network inspector, a body viewer, filters, the launches, and the realtime inspector. It draws edge to edge and keeps its own bars clear of the system's, so give it the whole screen. With `onClose`, each tab's root shows a round ×, and system back (predictive on Android 14 and newer) walks a tab's pages before it closes the console. Without `onClose`, there is no close button, and back at a root is the host's.

`palbase-debug` brings Compose and `palbase-flags` with it. Compose is in no other artifact of the SDK, so an app that never shows the console does not take it, and its recording is the core's either way.

## Related

- [Flags](/docs/android/flags): the per-user value that opens the console
- [Analytics](/docs/android/analytics#diagnostics): the diagnostics a project collects, with consent
- [Logs](/docs/getting-started/logs): the environment's own record of every request



<!-- ===== server/overview ===== -->

# Overview

`palbase/server` is Palbase for servers: one client, made with the project's **secret key**, that reaches every module's server calls — auth's user management, storage, notify, secrets, flags, analytics, realtime's broadcast and channel declaration, and machines. Use it from anything that runs on a server you control: a Next.js route handler, a worker, a script, a backend that is not a Palbase machine. A `palbase/backend` app does not construct one: its `Palbase` is this same client, built from the machine's environment (see [Backend SDK Overview](/docs/backend/overview)).

## Quick example

```ts
// server.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({
  url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, // https://<ref>.palbase.studio
  secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY!, // pb_<ref>_s…
});

// Every call takes { path, query, headers, body } as its operation needs them,
// and answers { status, data, headers }.
const { data } = await palbase.storage.listBuckets();
console.log(data.buckets.map((b) => b.name));

// Give one user their own value of a flag; their apps are told at once.
await palbase.flags.putUserValue({ path: { user_id: "usr_123", key: "checkout.new_flow" }, body: { value: true } });
```

## The secret key

An environment has publishable keys (`pb_<ref>_c…`, for apps — each [registered app](/docs/apps/overview) has its own) and any number of named secret keys (`pb_<ref>_s…`, for servers). Make a secret key in Studio under **Settings › API keys › Create secret key**: it is shown **once**, and each one can be revoked on its own without touching the others — one per server is the habit that makes a leak cheap to shut out.

A secret key opens the whole project: every user, every file, every secret. `createServer` refuses to run where one could reach a browser:

| Where | What happens |
|---|---|
| A bundle built for a browser or React Native | The package's export conditions resolve `palbase/server` to a module that **throws when the bundle loads** — before a key can ship in it. |
| A page (`document` exists), a browser worker (`navigator.userAgent` starts `Mozilla/`), or React Native | `createServer` throws a `TypeError` naming `palbase/web` as what apps use. |
| A publishable key passed as `secretKey` | `createServer` throws: a publishable key belongs in `palbase/web`. |

Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers and edge runtimes resolve the real client.

## `createServer(options)`

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | — | The project's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`. https only (http only for a loopback address); the origin alone, with no path. |
| `secretKey` | — | The project's secret key, from the server's environment. |
| `retry` | `{ attempts: 3, maxWaitSeconds: 30 }` | How a call that was answered "not now" is sent again (below). |
| `fetch` | `globalThis.fetch` | The fetch the calls go through. |
| `solveProofOfWork` | `false` | Solve auth's proof-of-work challenge here and send the call again. Left off, a sign-in a server makes for a user answers `403 pow_required` with the challenge, for the user's own device to solve. |

It answers a `PalbaseServer`:

| Member | Module | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | users, sessions, test users, auth settings (`/admin/…`) | auth |
| `storage` | buckets, objects, signed URLs | storage |
| `notify` | email, push, SMS, WhatsApp, templates, topics | notify |
| `secrets` | the project's secrets, by environment | secrets |
| `flags` | definitions, users' values, publishing | flags |
| `analytics` | captures, and reading events back | analytics |
| `realtime` | broadcast, state, the channel declaration, limits | realtime |
| `calls` | the calls settings and hook, the project's calls read and ended, an agent's ticket ([Calls](/docs/calls/server)) | calls |
| `machines` | machines, builds, logs, databases | machines |
| `transport` | the one transport every call goes through | — |

Each module's methods are generated from its contract, one per operation, named by its operation id in camelCase: `PUT /storage/buckets/{bucket}` is `storage.putBucket`, `GET /admin/users` is `auth.adminListUsers`. The module pages say what each module does: [Storage](/docs/backend/storage), [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets), [Flags](/docs/backend/flags), [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications), [Realtime](/docs/backend/realtime), [Channels](/docs/backend/channels), [Test Users](/docs/backend/test-users), and [Machines](/docs/machines/overview) for machines and databases.

## The shape of a call

A call takes one object with the parts its operation has — `path` for the path's parameters, `query`, `headers`, `body` — and answers a `Reply`: the `status` the module answered, its `data` (the JSON body, parsed), and its `headers`.

```ts
// users.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const created = await palbase.auth.adminCreateUser({
  body: { email: "grace@example.com", password: "a long passphrase of her own", email_verified: true },
});
console.log(created.status, created.data.id); // 201 usr_…

const user = await palbase.auth.adminGetUser({ path: { uid: created.data.id } });
await palbase.auth.adminUpdateUser({ path: { uid: user.data.id }, body: { metadata: { plan: "pro" } } });
```

A path parameter is always **one** URL segment: the client percent-encodes it, so a storage path `avatars/ada.png` travels as `avatars%2Fada.png`, and an empty value, `.` or `..` is refused before anything is sent (`invalid_path_parameter`). An answer the module sends as bytes — an object's contents — arrives as the `Response` itself, for you to read as you need (`await reply.data.arrayBuffer()`).

The types of every request and answer are exported, by module, as `types`:

```ts
// report.ts
import type { types } from "palbase/server";

export function describe(object: types.storage.StorageObject): string {
  return `${object.path}: ${object.size} bytes of ${object.content_type}`;
}
```

## Refusals are `PalbaseError`

Every answer the contract calls a refusal throws a `PalbaseError` carrying the module's envelope:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `status` | The HTTP status; `0` when the request never got an answer. |
| `code` | The envelope's `error` (`user_exists`, `bucket_not_empty`, `own_provider_required` …). |
| `message` | The envelope's `error_description`. |
| `requestId` | The request's id, for the module's logs. |
| `retryAfter` | Seconds the module asked to wait (`Retry-After`, or the envelope's `retry_after`). |
| `body` | The body as sent, for the answers that are not the envelope. |
| `op` | The operation, such as `PutBucket`. |

```ts
// make-user.ts
import { createServer, PalbaseError } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

export async function ensureUser(email: string, password: string): Promise<string | null> {
  try {
    return (await palbase.auth.adminCreateUser({ body: { email, password } })).data.id;
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof PalbaseError && e.code === "user_exists") return null;
    throw e;
  }
}
```

A few codes are the client's own, with `status: 0`: `network_error` (the request did not reach the project), `missing_credential`, `invalid_path` and `invalid_path_parameter`. Two more are about answers the contract does not have: `undeclared_answer` (a 2xx the operation does not declare — the request **may have taken effect**) and `undeclared_redirect`.

The client never follows a redirect. The key goes to the project's origin and nowhere else: a request URL that would leave it is refused, and a 3xx is a refusal rather than a hop that would carry the key to whatever host it names.

## Retries

A call is sent again only when doing so cannot do the work twice:

- **What is retried:** `429`, `502`, `503` and `504`, and a request that never reached the server (`network_error`).
- **Which calls:** reads (`GET`, `HEAD`), and the writes whose contract takes an `Idempotency-Key`. For those the client makes one key per call and every attempt carries it, so the module answers a retry with the first answer (`Idempotent-Replayed: true`) instead of doing the work again. Pass your own `Idempotency-Key` header to make a write safe across your own retries too — a job that runs again after a crash, say.
- **How long:** what the module's `Retry-After` asks, never more than `maxWaitSeconds`; with no word from the module, 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s … with a little jitter. A wait longer than `maxWaitSeconds` is not waited for: the error reaches you.

Everything else is yours: a `400`, a `409`, a `404` is the module's answer, and sending it again would only get it again. A body that can be read only once (a stream) is not sent twice.

```ts
// strict.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

// One attempt, no waiting: the caller decides.
export const strict = createServer({
  url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!,
  secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY!,
  retry: { attempts: 1, maxWaitSeconds: 0 },
});
```

## Listings, a page at a time

Listings answer a page and a `next_cursor`; the next page is the same call with that cursor, until a page carries none. `pages(call)` walks them for you:

```ts
// sweep.ts
import { createServer, pages } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

let banned = 0;
for await (const page of pages((cursor) => palbase.auth.adminListUsers({ query: { limit: 200, cursor, banned: true } }))) {
  banned += page.users.length;
}
console.log(`${banned} banned users`);
```

A listing that answers a cursor it has answered before is a loop, and `pages` throws rather than page forever.

## From a Palbase machine

A `palbase/backend` app reaches the same client as `Palbase`, imported, never constructed: it is built at boot from `PALBASE_URL` (which the platform sets on every machine) and `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` (a project secret you add — see [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets)). Everything on this page holds for it: `Palbase.storage.putBucket(…)` is `createServer(…).storage.putBucket(…)`.

## Related

- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks) — the project's events delivered to your server, and `verifyWebhook`
- [Backend SDK Overview](/docs/backend/overview) — `Palbase`, `Database` and `Log` inside a machine
- [Storage](/docs/backend/storage) · [Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications) · [Flags](/docs/backend/flags) · [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets) — the modules, from a server
- [Web SDK Overview](/docs/web/overview) — the publishable-key client for apps
