# Webhooks

When something happens in a project — a user is deleted, a file is uploaded, a secret changes, an email bounces — the platform POSTs an **event** to each of the project's webhook endpoints that takes its type, signed with that endpoint's secret. `palbase/server` checks the signature: `verifyWebhookRequest(request, secret)` answers the event, or throws. A `palbase/backend` app does not call it at all — its `@On` handlers receive the events already checked (see [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)).

## Quick example

```ts
// server.ts
import { verifyWebhookRequest, WebhookSignatureError } from "palbase/server";

const secret = process.env.PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET!; // whsec_…, shown once when the endpoint was made
const handled = new Set<string>();

export async function handle(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  let event;
  try {
    event = await verifyWebhookRequest<{ user_id?: string }>(request, secret);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof WebhookSignatureError) return new Response(e.code, { status: 401 });
    throw e;
  }
  // A delivery may come twice: the event's id says it is the same one.
  if (handled.has(event.id)) return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
  if (event.type === "user.deleted") {
    console.log(`forget everything about ${event.data.user_id}`);
  }
  handled.add(event.id);
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}
```

Any `2xx` is delivery. Anything else — another status, a timeout, a refused connection — and the platform sends the event again.

## Endpoints

An endpoint is an `https` URL on the public internet and the event types it takes — up to 50 of them, each dotted lowercase words such as `user.deleted`; an endpoint that names none takes every type, but `messaging.message.created` and `messaging.conversation.read` — one a message, one a read — which go only to an endpoint that names them. A project has **5 endpoints at most**, besides the ones the platform keeps for its machines. When an endpoint is made, its secret (`whsec_` and 64 hex characters) is answered **once**; keep it in the receiving server's secrets.

Manage a project's endpoints in Studio, under an environment's **Settings › Webhooks**: add an endpoint (its secret is shown once, with a copy button), change its address or events, or delete it. Reading the list is open to the organization's members; adding, changing and deleting are an admin's — a person, or an admin [access token](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens). Each endpoint shows who made it: a person, an access token or an environment token, by the name it had then. An endpoint stays when the token that made it is deleted. Palbase's own environment is shown read-only. A `palbase/backend` app on a machine needs none of this: the platform gives the machine its `PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` and keeps an endpoint for exactly the events its app takes, listed as the machine's — not changed or deleted from here, and gone with the machine ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)).

The CLI does the same:

```sh
palbase webhooks:create https://api.example.com/palbase --events user.deleted,file.uploaded --secret-to RECEIVER_WEBHOOK_SECRET
palbase webhooks:list
palbase webhooks:update <id> --events user.deleted
palbase webhooks:delete <id>
```

`--secret-to` keeps the new endpoint's secret in the environment's secrets (production, or development with `--dev`) instead of printing it, so a receiver that is itself a machine of the environment reads it by name. See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#webhooks).

### Failed deliveries

A delivery is tried 12 times, the wait growing up to five minutes between tries. When the endpoint still has not taken it, Palbase gives up and keeps the delivery for **30 days** under **Settings › Webhooks › Failed deliveries**: the event, the endpoint, how many times it was tried and why the last try failed. **Redeliver** sends the same event, with the same `Palbase-Event-Id` and body, to that endpoint again within seconds, signed afresh, as Stripe's *Resend* does. Your receiver already handles an event more than once by its id, so a redelivery is safe. Members read the list; an admin redelivers, and the redelivery is written to the organization's audit log. Studio's API does the same: `GET /v1/environments/{ref}/webhooks/deliveries?failed=true` and `POST /v1/environments/{ref}/webhooks/deliveries/{id}/redeliver`. A delivery whose endpoint was deleted is sent nowhere (`409 endpoint_gone`).

## What a delivery is

A delivery is a `POST` with a JSON body — the event — and three headers:

| Header | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `Palbase-Signature` | `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<t>.<body>")>` |
| `Palbase-Event-Id` | The event's id (also in the body): the same id twice is the same event delivered again. |
| `Palbase-Event-Type` | The event's type (also in the body). |

```json
{
  "id": "6f2c1c9e-…",
  "type": "file.uploaded",
  "project_id": "2b7d…",
  "created_at": "2026-10-08T09:41:22Z",
  "data": { "bucket": "avatars", "path": "usr_123/face.png", "size": 48211, "content_type": "image/png", "owner_id": "usr_123" }
}
```

The platform waits **10 seconds** for an answer, follows no redirect, and tries an event up to **12 times**, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … up to five minutes between attempts. One project's slow or silent receiver holds back only that project's events.

**Delivery is at least once.** An event that reached your endpoint may be sent again — a retry after a timeout your server answered too late, or the platform's sender starting again — so key the work on the event's `id`, not on its arrival. An event is never dropped because an endpoint was down for a while: it is retried until it is taken or its attempts run out.

## The events

| Type | Sent when | `data` |
|---|---|---|
| `user.deleted` | A user is deleted — by themselves, or with the secret key. | `{ user_id, is_test, deleted_at }` |
| `session.ended` | A user's session ends — they signed out, ended it from another device, it was revoked (by an admin, a ban, a password reset, its refresh token used twice), it ran out with no one back to renew it (`ended_at` is then the moment its time was up), or the user was deleted. | `{ user_id, session_id, ended_at }` |
| `file.uploaded` | An object is written: a `PUT`, a copy, an upload through a signed URL. | `{ bucket, path, size, content_type, owner_id }` |
| `file.deleted` | An object is deleted. | the same fields |
| `file.moved` | An object is given another path. | the same fields |
| `secret.changed` | A secret is written, rolled back or deleted. The value is never in the event. | `{ environment, name, version, change }` |
| `notification.sent` / `notification.failed` | A message ended sent, or failed. | `{ message_id, channel, rail, template, … }` |
| `notification.received` | A user sent a WhatsApp message to the project's number. | the message |
| `notification.uninstalled` | A push service said no app holds a device's token any more: the app was taken off the phone. The device is forgotten. | `{ platform, provider, device_id, installation_id, user_id }` |
| `notification.push_failing` | A push provider started failing for its own fault — its APNs key refused, a topic the key may not send to: every push through it fails until its setting is fixed ([Apple (APNs)](/docs/backend/notifications#every-channel-but-one-needs-a-provider-of-yours)). At most once a day a provider. | `{ project_id, channel, provider, error, failing_since }` |
| `journey.entered` / `journey.converted` | A person entered a journey, or their run reached its goal. A try on a test user's events carry `test: true` ([Journeys](/docs/backend/journeys#events)). | `{ journey, journey_id, run_id, user_id, test }` |
| `journey.step` | A person's run took a step. | `{ journey, journey_id, run_id, user_id, step, kind, outcome, test }` |
| `journey.event` | A journey's `event` step told the project's backend. | `{ journey, journey_id, run_id, user_id, step, name, data, test }` |
| `journey.ended` | A person's run ended: `completed`, `converted`, `exited`, `stopped`. | `{ journey, journey_id, run_id, user_id, reason, test }` |
| `messaging.report.created` | A person reported a conversation, someone in it or messages of it. Read what it carries with the secret key (`GET /messaging/admin/reports/{report_id}`); an organization that runs its customers' apps passes it on to them from here ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#moderation)). | `{ report_id, conversation_id, reporter_id, reported_user_id, reason, message_count }` |
| `messaging.conversation.created` / `messaging.conversation.deleted` | A conversation was made — by a person, or the project's server — or deleted for everyone. | `{ conversation_id, kind, created_by, member_ids, space }` / `{ conversation_id, deleted_by }` |
| `messaging.message.created` | A message reached a conversation — a person's, or the project's server's (`via`) — with whom it is for and whom it names; its text only with the setting `event_text`. Sent only to an endpoint that names it, never to one of every event ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview#your-server)). | `{ conversation_id, conversation_kind, space, message_id, seq, kind, sender_id, via, thread_id, mention_ids, recipient_ids, has_attachments, text?, created_at }` |
| `messaging.conversation.read` | A person read a conversation, or a thread of it, further. Sent only to an endpoint that names it. | `{ conversation_id, space, user_id, read_seq, thread_id }` |
| `calls.call.started` / `calls.call.ended` | A call was made — ringing, or a group going on — or ended (`end_reason` says why) ([Calls](/docs/calls/server#webhooks)). | `{ call_id, kind, video, mode, state, caller_id, conversation_id, room }`, and `end_reason` when it ended |
| `calls.participant.joined` / `calls.participant.left` | A person answered or joined a call, or left it; or the project's agent came into it, or left ([Agents](/docs/calls/agents)). | the same fields, and `user_id`, `participant_kind` (`user` or `bot`) |
| `audience.entered` / `audience.exited` | A person came to be in an analytics audience, or left it. | `{ audience_id, audience_name, person_id, user_id }` |
| `machine.created` / `machine.updated` / `machine.deleted` | A machine was opened, changed, or taken away. | `{ name, source, size, replicas, port, version }` |
| `stores.apple.changed` | The Apple account was connected, checked (and Apple's answer changed) or disconnected. The key is never in the event. | `{ change, issuer_id, key_id, status, capabilities }` |
| `stores.app.changed` | An app was linked to its store. | `{ change, app_id, bundle_id, asc_app_id }` |
| `stores.package.changed` | A package was made, or its build arrived. | `{ change, package_id, app_id, build_number, version }` |
| `stores.delivery.requested` | A delivery to TestFlight was sent, or sent again. | `{ package_id, channel }` |
| `stores.delivery.changed` | A delivery moved: `queued`, `signing`, `uploading`, `processing`, `compliance`, `ready` or `failed`. | `{ package_id, channel, status, asc_build_id, error_code, error }` |
| `stores.group.changed` | A tester group was made, renamed, deleted, its testers set, or a build given to it. | `{ change, group_id, app_id, name, testers, package_id }` |
| `stores.action.changed` | A planned action (Beta App Review, export compliance, expiring a build, an App Store page or version step) was done, declined or failed. | `{ action_id, kind, package_id, app_id, status, summary }` |
| `stores.version.changed` | An app's App Store version came to a new state: sent to App Review, in review, approved, rejected, withdrawn or released. `result` is App Review's answer, `approved` or `rejected`, or `null`; `source` who told it: `apple_webhook`, `poll` or `action`. | `{ app_id, bundle_id, name, version, asc_version_id, previous_state, state, result, source }` |
| `stores.google.changed` | The Play connection was made, checked (and Play's answer changed) or disconnected. | `{ change, service_account, status, capabilities }` |
| `stores.webhook.changed` / `stores.build.changed` / `stores.beta_review.changed` / `stores.feedback.received` / `stores.product.changed` / `stores.play_release.changed` / `stores.vitals.changed` | An app's App Store Connect webhook, its build uploads, Beta App Review, testers' feedback, its in-app purchases' review, its Play releases and its crash data — each one is in [App Health](/docs/distribution/health#the-events). | the event's own |
| `database.created` / `database.updated` / `database.deleted` / `database.undeleted` / `database.purged` / `database.password_changed` / `database.restoring` | A database's life. | `{ name, size }` |
| `purchases.*` | A purchase, a renewal, a refund, an entitlement or credits changing — each one is in [Purchases › Entitlements](/docs/purchases/entitlements#events). | the event's own |
| `ai.response.started` | A chat's turn began: a member's message, the server's, the chat's goal, or the late messages of the turn before opened it. | `{ response_id, status: "running", model, metadata, chat_id, user_id, message_metadata, goal_id, goal_turn }` |
| `ai.response.completed` / `ai.response.failed` | A response started with `background: true` ended, or a chat's turn did. A turn's `status` is `completed`, `failed`, `stopped` or `budget_exceeded`, its `metadata` the chat's labels, and one that failed says why in `error`. | `{ response_id, status, model, metadata, cost_nano_usd, error?: { code, message, retryable } }`, a turn's with `chat_id, user_id, message_metadata, goal_id, goal_turn` |
| `ai.goal.updated` | A chat's goal was set, its status changed, or it was cleared. | `{ chat_id, goal_id, status, previous_status, stop_code, stop_reason, set_by, metadata }` |
| `ai.voice.started` / `ai.voice.closed` | A chat's voice began, or ended (closed, replaced, its member taken out, its chat deleted, lost). | `{ chat_id, voice_id, user_id, delegation, status, seconds, close_reason, metadata }` |
| `ai.voice.delegated` | A person asked a voice of `delegation: "events"` for something out loud: have it done, and answer with the voice's `speak`, naming the delegation. | `{ chat_id, voice_id, delegation_id, text, earlier, user_id, metadata }` |
| `ai.workspace.published` | A chat's workspace published a tree (mid-turn, as a build writes its product, and once more as its machine lets it go): what changed against the tree it replaced. Read a file of it with `GET /ai/chats/{id}/workspace/files?path=&manifest=`. | `{ chat_id, manifest_id, previous_manifest_id?, changed: [{ path, change, size_bytes }], changed_count, changed_truncated, metadata }` |
| `ai.workspace.pushed` | A chat's agent pushed its work to the chat's branch. | `{ chat_id, repo, repository, branch, head_sha, commits: [{ sha, subject, author_name, author_email }], commits_truncated, response_id, user_id, metadata }` |

The modules' contracts say which of their operations emit which event; each is noted on the operation (for example, `PUT /storage/buckets/{bucket}/objects/{path}` "Emits file.uploaded").

## Checking a delivery

The signature is an HMAC of the body **exactly as it arrived** — the bytes, before any JSON parsing. A parsed and re-serialised body is a different string and never verifies, so read the raw body first.

| Function | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `verifyWebhookRequest(request, secret, { toleranceSeconds?, now?, maxBytes? })` | A fetch `Request` (Node, Bun, Deno, Workers, a Next.js route handler): reads its body — 1 MiB at most unless `maxBytes` says — and its header. |
| `verifyWebhook({ secret, signature, body, toleranceSeconds?, now? })` | A body you already hold, as a string or bytes, and the header's value. |
| `verifySignature({ secret, signature, body, … })` | The check alone, for a signed call whose body is not an event (see below). |

Each throws a `WebhookSignatureError` whose `code` says why:

| `code` | Why |
|---|---|
| `missing_signature` | No `Palbase-Signature` header. |
| `malformed_signature` | The header is not `t=…,v1=…`. |
| `stale_timestamp` | `t` is more than `toleranceSeconds` (300 by default) from now: an old delivery sent again is not taken. |
| `signature_mismatch` | No `v1` is this body signed with this secret — a changed body, or another endpoint's secret. |
| `invalid_body` | The signed body is not JSON, or not an event (`id`, `type`, `project_id`, `created_at`, `data`). |
| `body_too_large` | The body is larger than `maxBytes`. |

`verifyWebhook` takes only an endpoint secret (`whsec_…`): an API key passed by mistake is a `TypeError`, not a check that quietly fails.

```ts
// app/api/palbase/route.ts
import { verifyWebhook, WebhookSignatureError } from "palbase/server";

export async function POST(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const body = await request.text(); // the raw body, before anything parses it
  try {
    const event = await verifyWebhook({
      secret: process.env.PALBASE_WEBHOOK_SECRET!,
      signature: request.headers.get("palbase-signature"),
      body,
    });
    console.log(event.type, event.id);
    return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof WebhookSignatureError) return new Response(e.code, { status: 401 });
    throw e;
  }
}
```

## The platform's own calls to a machine

The platform signs what it asks of a machine the same way, with the key it starts every machine with in `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`: the crons' and tasks' lists and calls (`GET /_palbase/crons`, `POST /_palbase/crons/<name>`, `GET /_palbase/tasks`, `POST /_palbase/tasks/<name>`). Those paths are reached only by the platform: a request from outside whose path names them never gets to the machine. A program that serves them checks the call with `verifySignature`, whose body is the request's (empty for a `GET`). See [Machines](/docs/machines/overview).

## Related

- [Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks) — `@On` handlers in a `palbase/backend` app
- [Backend Webhooks](/docs/backend/webhooks) — a third party's deliveries (Stripe, GitHub, …) to a `palbase/backend` app, with `@Webhook`
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — `createServer`, refusals and retries
- [Storage](/docs/backend/storage) — what emits `file.uploaded`, `file.deleted` and `file.moved`
- [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets) — where a receiving server keeps its endpoint secret



<!-- ===== cloud/overview ===== -->

# Overview

`palbase/cloud` is Palbase run from your own server: one client, made with your **organization's access token**, that does everything Studio and the CLI do through the API — open organizations, projects and environments, put them on Pay as you go and have your payment account pay for them, read their usage and invoices, build machines and databases — and reaches every project's modules at its own address: its users, files, analytics, purchases and their charts, AI, messaging and the rest. It is for a product that opens a Palbase project for each of its own customers and keeps Palbase out of their sight: your customers sign in to your product, and your server does the rest with one token.

Use it from a server you control. It refuses to run in a browser — the token can open, change and pay for every project of your organization, so it never belongs in an app or a web page. An app keeps using `palbase/web`, the iOS or Android SDK, with its project's publishable key.

## The token

Make an access token in Studio (**Organization → Access tokens**) with the **admin** role, or **member** for a server that only reads. Making one is a person's to do — a token never makes another — as are accepting the terms and saving the organization's card. Keep it in your server's secrets, as `PALBASE_TOKEN`:

- It starts with `pbo_` and ends in a checksum: `palbase/cloud` refuses one that is cut short, mistyped or of another kind before anything is sent (`tokenIsWellFormed(token)` asks the same). Tokens made before 2026-10-25 carry no checksum: make a new one.
- It does what its role does, in your organization alone. Another organization's project answers `404`, the same as a project that does not exist.
- It ends on its date, when it is removed, and when the person who made it leaves the organization or is made less than its role.

## An organization for each customer: account tokens

An **account token** (`pbu_…`) is yours, not one organization's: with it your server opens an organization for each of your customers, and their projects in it. Make one in Studio (**Account → Tokens**) or with the CLI — it is shown once — and keep it in your server's secrets:

```bash
palbase account:tokens:create my-product --days 365
palbase account:tokens:list      # each by its hint (pbu_…a1b2), with the organizations it opened
palbase account:tokens:revoke <id>
```

- It reaches the organizations it opened, and only those: you are their owner, the token an admin of each. Every other organization answers `404`.
- In them it does what an admin does — projects, environments, their modules, billing — and renames an organization or deletes an empty one; never more than your own role there now. Members, invitations, tokens and project keys stay yours, in person.
- It stops at once, everywhere, when you delete it, when you leave one of its organizations (there, for good), or when your account is deleted. The keys of the environments it opened go with it.

One payment account pays for every organization you link to it: you are charged once a month for all of them, and its report is each organization's month, item by item — what you bill your own customers by.

```ts
// customers.ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN! });

// An organization for a new customer, paid for by your own organization's payment account.
const { data: customer } = await cloud.orgs.create({ body: { name: "Customer 1042" } });
await cloud.billing.payer({ path: { id: customer.id }, body: { account: process.env.PALBASE_PAYER_ORG_ID! } });
const { data: made } = await cloud.projects.create({ path: { id: customer.id }, body: { name: "shop" } });
await cloud.projects.addEnvironment({ path: { id: made.project.id }, body: { name: "main", slug: "main" } });

// At the month's end: what each customer's organization owed, environment by environment.
const { data: month } = await cloud.billing.report({ path: { id: process.env.PALBASE_PAYER_ORG_ID! }, query: { period: "2026-11" } });
for (const org of month.organizations) console.log(org.name, org.owed_micros / 1_000_000);
```

## Quick example

```ts
// server.ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN! });

// One project for one of your customers, and its environment — Free until you move it to Pay as you go.
// A project opened by the API has no environment yet; its keys are shown once, as the environment is added.
const org = process.env.PALBASE_ORG_ID!;
const { data: made } = await cloud.projects.create({ path: { id: org }, body: { name: "customer-1042" } });
const { data: added } = await cloud.projects.addEnvironment({ path: { id: made.project.id }, body: { name: "main", slug: "main" } });
const ref = added.environment.ref;

// On Pay as you go: what it uses past its free quota is charged to the payment account that pays for the organization,
// at the month's end — at most $200 a month.
await cloud.billing.steer({ path: { id: org, ref }, body: { plan: "pay_as_you_go", monthly_limit_micros: 200_000_000 } });

// What it used, and its users — at the project's own address.
const usage = await cloud.projects.usage({ path: { ref } });
const users = await cloud.project(ref).auth.adminListUsers({ query: { limit: 50 } });
console.log(usage.data, users.data.users.length);
```

Every call takes `{ path, query, headers, body }` as its operation needs them and answers `{ status, data, headers }`; a refusal is thrown as a `PalbaseError` with its `status` and `code`, as in [palbase/server](/docs/server/overview). Writes take an `Idempotency-Key` header and are safe to send again with the same one.

## What is in it

The client's own namespaces are Studio's API — the same calls Studio's screens make:

| Namespace | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `orgs`, `projects` | the organization, its members and audit log; projects and their environments, usage, keys' hints, GitHub installations shared to a new environment |
| `billing` | the bill, cards, invoices and charges; an environment's plan and monthly limit; the payment account that pays for the organization |
| `webhooks`, `orgWebhooks` | an environment's webhook endpoints and deliveries; the organization's own endpoints for its projects' billing events |
| `environmentTokens` | tokens for one environment: an agent's, or one of your users' (below) |
| `apps`, `snippets`, `chartViews`, `accessRequests`, `docs` | client apps, saved database snippets and chart views, access requests, the docs' search |

`cloud.project(ref)` is one environment's modules: `auth`, `storage`, `analytics`, `purchases`, `ai`, `messaging`, `notify`, `flags`, `journeys`, `secrets`, `stores`, `realtime` and `machines` (its machines and databases) — every call of theirs a server makes, by the names their API reference gives them. What only an app's user calls — signing in, signing up, a password reset — is not there: that is the apps' SDKs'.

## Your users: a token each

Your customers' people never get a Palbase account. When one of them works in your product — your dashboard, an AI agent acting for them — mint them a token for their project alone, in their role, for the time they need it:

```ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN! });
const ref = "abcd1234efgh"; // the customer's environment

const { data: minted } = await cloud.environmentTokens.mint({
  path: { ref },
  body: { name: "dashboard", role: "member", on_behalf_of: "ada@customer-1042.com", expires_in_minutes: 60 },
});
// minted.token (pbe_…) reads that environment alone: another answers 404, a member's write 403.
```

The token is shown once. It does at most what its role does and never more than what minted it; it makes no token and does no organization's work; `on_behalf_of` is recorded beside its every call in the environment's audit. It ends after `expires_in_minutes` (5 to 240), when it is revoked, and when what minted it ends.

## Confirming for your users

A few steps are a person's to confirm — sending an app to App Review, releasing it, expiring a build ([Actions](/docs/distribution/overview#actions)). Your users have no Palbase account, so your server confirms for them with your organization's token, once an owner or an admin turns on **Confirms for people** for it in Studio (**Organization › Access tokens**). Each confirmation names the person, and the action keeps them as its decider:

```ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const ref = "abcd1234efgh"; // the customer's environment
const forAda = new PalbaseCloud({
  token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN!,
  fetch: (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit) => {
    const request = new Request(input, init);
    request.headers.set("Palbase-For", "yourplatform:user_42"); // who clicked, in your product
    return fetch(request);
  },
});
const stores = forAda.project(ref).stores;
const { data: action } = await stores.getAction({ path: { action_id: "the planned action's id" } });
// Shown to your user first: action.summary. Then, on their yes:
await stores.confirmAction({ path: { action_id: action.id }, body: { hash: action.hash } });
```

Ask your user before you confirm, with the plan's own summary: the hash makes sure what runs is what they read. A token without **Confirms for people** that names anyone is refused (`403 token_does_not_confirm`).

## Billing events to your server

Register your organization's endpoint once, and each of your projects' billing events reaches it as it happens — with its `ref`, its name and the amounts:

```ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN! });
const org = process.env.PALBASE_ORG_ID!;

const { data: endpoint } = await cloud.orgWebhooks.add({
  path: { id: org },
  body: { url: "https://api.example.com/palbase/billing", events: ["org.billing.limit_reached"] },
});
// endpoint.secret is shown once: verify each delivery's Palbase-Signature with it.
```

They are signed as a project's events are ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)). An environment's own endpoints get its `billing.*` events with its `ref` and never an amount: the amounts are the organization's.



<!-- ===== auth/overview ===== -->

# Auth

Every environment has its own auth: its users, their sessions, the ways they may sign in, and the rules for all three. Nothing of it is shared with another environment, and nothing in it needs code of yours. This section is about setting it up and running it. Signing a person in from an app is [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth), and checking their token in a backend is [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication).

## Where it is configured

Three places change the same configuration, and each sees what the others did:

- **Studio**, under the environment's **Auth** section: **Overview** (sign-ups and sign-ins over time), **Users**, **Providers**, **Sessions**, **Audit**, **Test accounts**, **Templates** and **Settings**.
- **The CLI**: its `auth:*` commands act on the environment chosen with `palbase use`, or the one `-E` names. A change to a production environment asks for confirmation first ([CLI](/docs/cli/overview#choosing-an-environment)).
- **The auth module's admin calls**, `/admin/*` at the project's address, with a secret key: `createServer({ url, secretKey }).auth` on any server, `Palbase.auth` in a `palbase/backend` app. An app's publishable key reaches none of them.

| What | Studio | CLI | Admin call |
|---|---|---|---|
| The settings | **Auth › Settings** (passwords, email confirmation, passkeys, email links, token lifetimes, security emails) | [`auth:settings:get`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authsettingsget), [`auth:settings:set`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authsettingsset) | `GET`/`PUT /admin/auth-settings` |
| Sign-in providers | **Auth › Providers** | `auth:providers:*` | `/admin/providers`, `/admin/social-auth` |
| Users | **Auth › Users** | `auth:users:*`, `auth:import` | `/admin/users` |
| Sessions | **Auth › Sessions** | `auth:users:sign-out` | `/admin/sessions` |
| Roles | — | `auth:roles:*` | `/admin/roles` |
| Blocking hooks | — | `auth:hooks:*` | `/admin/hooks` |
| OAuth clients | — | `auth:oauth-clients:*` | `/admin/oauth-clients` |
| Signing keys | — | `auth:signing-keys`, `auth:signing-keys:rotate` | `/admin/signing-keys` |
| The audit trail | **Auth › Audit** | `auth:audit`, `auth:audit:export`, `auth:audit:verify` | `/admin/audit` |
| Test users | **Auth › Test accounts** | `auth:test-users:*` | `/admin/test-users` |
| Auth's emails | **Auth › Templates** | `notify:templates:*` | `/notify/templates/email/{slug}/{locale}` |

The pages of this section:

- [Sign-in Providers](/docs/auth/providers): email, phone, Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft, and guest accounts.
- [Users & Roles](/docs/auth/users): the users list, banning, signing out, deleting and exporting a user, roles, and bringing users over from another project.
- [Blocking Hooks](/docs/auth/hooks): an endpoint of yours that auth asks, and waits for, before a sign-up, a sign-in or a token.
- [Audit Trail](/docs/auth/audit): who did what, chained so a change to the record shows.
- [OpenID Provider](/docs/auth/openid-provider): other apps signing in with your users' accounts, service accounts, and sign-in tokens your server makes.

## The settings

```sh
palbase auth:settings:get
palbase auth:settings:set password_min_length=12 confirm_email_required=true
palbase auth:settings:set redirect_urls='["https://app.example.com/**","myapp://callback"]'
```

`auth:settings:set` takes `key=value` pairs. A value that reads as JSON is taken as JSON (`12`, `true`, a list); any other is text, so `site_url=https://app.example.com` needs no quotes. Only the keys given change.

A change is made against the revision it was read at. `GET /admin/auth-settings` answers the revision in its `ETag` header, and `PUT /admin/auth-settings` needs it back in `If-Match`: without it the answer is `428 settings_revision_required`, and with a revision that is no longer current, `412 settings_revision_conflict`. A change someone made in the meantime, in Studio or another terminal, is never overwritten; the CLI and Studio do this for you. From a server:

```ts
// scripts/auth-settings.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const current = await palbase.auth.adminGetAuthSettings();
const saved = await palbase.auth.adminUpdateAuthSettings({
  headers: { "If-Match": current.headers.get("etag") ?? "" },
  // Only the fields sent change; an unknown field is refused.
  body: { password_min_length: 12, confirm_email_required: true },
});
console.log(saved.data.password_min_length, saved.headers.get("etag"));
```

Every field is checked against the values that will be in force together, so a maximum password length below the minimum, or a refresh token shorter-lived than the access token, is refused (`400`).

### New users

`signups_enabled` (default `true`) lets your apps create accounts. Off, every way a client opens one answers `403 signups_closed`: a sign-up with a password, a passkey sign-up, a guest, a phone's first code and a provider's first sign-in. People who have an account sign in as before, and your server still creates users with the secret key (`POST /admin/users`, imports, test users): it is how a closed app lets someone in.

```sh
palbase auth:settings:set signups_enabled=false
```

### Passwords and email

| Key | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `password_min_length` | `8` | The shortest password accepted, 6 to 64. |
| `password_max_length` | `64` | The longest, never below the shortest. |
| `confirm_email_required` | `false` | A new email account confirms its address before it signs in. With it on, a sign-up answers no session, and a sign-in before the confirmation is `403 email_not_confirmed`. |
| `email_verification_method` | `code` | How an address is confirmed: a one-time `code` in the email, or a `link`. |

A password found in a known breach is refused at sign-up and on every change (`400 password_breached`). Users created with the secret key can skip that check (`skip_password_hibp`).

### Links in auth emails

| Key | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `site_url` | none | The base of the links in auth emails: `https://app.example.com/auth/verify-email?token=…`, and the same for `reset-password` and `magic-link`. Empty: the pages auth serves itself. |
| `redirect_urls` | `[]` | Where a request's `redirect_to` may send a link instead: up to 100 URLs, wildcards and app schemes (`myapp://callback`) allowed. |

The order in which they are used, and the pages your site needs, are in [Where email links land](/docs/web/auth#where-email-links-land). A web app registered with `palbase apps:env:set <app> --redirect <url>` adds its redirects to the allow-list too.

### Sessions and tokens

| Key | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `access_token_ttl_seconds` | 1800 (30 minutes) | The access token's lifetime, 60 to 86400. |
| `refresh_token_ttl_seconds` | 2592000 (30 days) | The refresh token's, 3600 to 7776000: how long a user stays signed in without using the app. |
| `max_concurrent_sessions` | `0` | The most live sessions one user may hold; `0` is no limit. |
| `concurrent_session_strategy` | `revoke_oldest` | Past the limit: end the user's oldest sessions (`revoke_oldest`), or refuse the new sign-in with `409 max_sessions_reached` (`deny_new`). |
| `session_device_binding` | `false` | A session belongs to the device it was opened on: a refresh from another device, browser or operating system ends it. A change of network is only recorded in the audit trail. |
| `inactive_user_days` | `0` | Ban accounts with no sign-in, refresh or session activity for this many days, with the reason `inactive`: `0` is never, otherwise 30 to 3650. Test users are left alone; unbanning lets them back in. |

A refresh token is used once: each refresh answers a new pair. The same refresh token presented again, past a 30-second allowance for a retry, ends the session: someone else holds a copy of it.

### Passkeys

| Key | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `passkey_require_identifier` | `true` | A passkey sign-up carries an identifier. With it off, an account can be only its passkey. |
| `passkey_identifier_kind` | `email` | Which identifier that is: `email` or `phone`. |

The origins a passkey is accepted from are the environment's web apps; see [Passkeys](/docs/web/auth#passkeys).

### Guests

`anonymous_sign_ins` (default `false`) lets a visitor have an account and a session without signing up. See [Guests](/docs/auth/providers#guests).

### Risk

| Key | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `risk_engine_enabled` | `false` | Score every sign-up and sign-in for risk, from 0 to 1. |
| `risk_step_up` | `0.3` | At this score a sign-in asks for a second factor: an email code when the account has none (it proves the inbox; the session it opens is `aal1`, as an email code is not a second factor). |
| `risk_strict_step_up` | `0.6` | At this score it asks for a strong one, an authenticator app or a passkey, when the account has one. |
| `risk_block` | `0.8` | At this score the sign-up or sign-in is refused, answered as a wrong password or a failed sign-up would be, so the refusal does not tell anyone the account exists. |

The three scores are set together, in that order (step up < strict step up < block). The score is made from the device's attestation, the account's own sign-in history, and, when the environment connects its own account with them, [Fingerprint](https://fingerprint.com) and [MaxMind](https://www.maxmind.com). A risk engine that cannot answer refuses a sign-up with `503` rather than letting it through.

Those two, and [Have I Been Pwned](https://haveibeenpwned.com), are connected with the environment's own credentials, from a server:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `PUT /admin/integrations/fingerprint` | `{ api_key, region? }`: a Server API key, and `us`, `eu` or `ap`. The app sends the agent's visitor id as `fingerprint_visitor_id` with a sign-in. |
| `PUT /admin/integrations/maxmind` | `{ account_id, license_key }` |
| `PUT /admin/integrations/hibp` | `{ api_key, requests_per_minute? }`: turns on the breached-account watch. Each user's address is checked every 30 days, and an account found in a breach must reset its password at its next sign-in (`403 password_reset_required`). `GET /admin/breach-watch` says how many it checked and found. |

`GET /admin/integrations` says which are connected; the credentials are never answered. `DELETE /admin/integrations/{name}` disconnects one.

### Security emails

`security_notifications` lists the changes a user is emailed about: `password_changed`, `email_changed` (told to the old address), `identity_linked`, `identity_unlinked`, `mfa_factor_enrolled`, `mfa_factor_removed`, `mfa_recovery_code_used` (with how many codes are left), `passkey_added`, `passkey_removed`. A second factor or a passkey added or removed, and a recovery code used (`mfa_factor_enrolled`, `mfa_factor_removed`, `mfa_recovery_code_used`, `passkey_added`, `passkey_removed`), are mailed by default, in every project: a change to what a user signs in with that they did not make is how a stolen password shows. A recovery code opens that one sign-in: the account's second factors stay, and the next sign-in asks for one again. The others are off until the project turns them on. Each is sent only to a confirmed address, in the user's language, with its own template (`auth.security_<kind>`). **Auth › Settings › Security notifications** turns each on and off.

### The OpenID provider

`oauth_login_url` and `fapi_enabled` are the environment's [OpenID Provider](/docs/auth/openid-provider#its-sign-in-page)'s.

### App Attest

`app_attest_mode` is `off` (the default), `monitor` or `enforce`: the switch of the backend routes marked `attest: true` ([Device attestation](/docs/backend/authentication#device-attestation)), read by the environment's machines every 30 seconds. `monitor` and `enforce` need an iOS or Android app registered with the environment (`palbase apps:env:set`).

Auth enrols a device when the app proves it: an iOS device's App Attest key (`POST /auth/devices/attest/ios`), or an Android device's Keystore key, whose attestation chain must end in one of Google's hardware attestation roots with no certificate on Google's revocation list, the key in the phone's secure hardware, the phone locked with a verified boot, and the app the registered package signed with a registered certificate (`POST /auth/devices/attest/android`). Both take the challenge of `POST /auth/devices/challenge` and need no session. The three are limited to 10 calls in 15 minutes per installation (or signed-in user) at an address, and 600 per address over every installation behind it: one install retrying does not stop the next phone behind the same carrier's address. Past either: `429 rate_limit_exceeded` with `Retry-After`, which the SDKs report as `enrolment_rate_limited`. Auth verifies a request's proof when a server asks it to (`POST /admin/attest/devices/assert`, with the secret key; a passing verdict names the device, its `device_id` and `platform`), and answers the mode at `GET /admin/attest/devices/attest-policy` and the last hours' counts at `GET /admin/attest/devices/observations`. Palbase's iOS and Android SDKs do the enrolment and the proofs by themselves.

## Signing keys

The environment's tokens are signed with its own keys, `ES256`, and its key set is public at `https://<ref>.palbase.studio/.well-known/jwks.json`. That is how a backend checks a token without asking auth ([How the token is verified](/docs/backend/authentication#how-the-token-is-verified)).

```sh
palbase auth:signing-keys
palbase auth:signing-keys:rotate
```

Keys rotate on their own every 90 days. A key is published in the key set a day before it starts signing, so a verifier that reads the key set once a day already holds it. A key that stops signing goes on verifying the tokens it signed until the longest of them has expired, and is then retired. Its status says where it is: `next` (published, not signing), `active` (signs), `grace` and `verification_only` (verify only), `retired` (gone from the key set).

`auth:signing-keys:rotate` (`POST /admin/signing-keys/rotate`) makes the change now: the published next key, or a new one, signs from then on. Tokens already issued keep working. Rotate when you think a key may have been exposed; a verifier that sees the new `kid` reads the key set again.

## Auth's emails and texts

Auth sends its emails through the project's notifications, from templates that belong to the environment: `auth.email_verify` and `auth.email_verify_code` (confirming an address), `auth.password_reset`, `auth.magic_link`, `auth.mfa_otp` (a sign-in code by email), and the security emails above. A phone code is the SMS template `auth.sms_otp`.

**Auth › Templates** edits them in each language and sends a test. Until the environment has its own email provider, auth's mail goes through the platform's shared sender with the default text; your edits are used once your own provider is connected ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications#every-channel-but-one-needs-a-provider-of-yours)). The same templates are reachable as any others: `palbase notify:templates:set`, or `PUT /notify/templates/email/{slug}/{locale}` ([Templates](/docs/backend/notifications#templates)).

## Between environments

```sh
palbase config:diff --from staging --to main
palbase config:copy --from staging --to main
```

The auth part of `config:copy` makes the target's settings, phone sign-in, social providers, roles, blocking hooks and OAuth clients equal to the source's. Secrets are not copied: a provider secret the target lacks is named, with the command that sets it, and a hook or confidential OAuth client made in the target gets a secret of its own, printed once.

## Related

- [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth): the sign-in flows in an app
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication): the token in a backend
- [Test Users](/docs/backend/test-users): accounts for tests
- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks): `user.deleted`, `session.ended` and the other events auth sends
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#auth): every `auth:*` command



<!-- ===== auth/providers ===== -->

# Sign-in Providers

An environment's users sign in with email, a phone number, or an account at Google, Apple, GitHub or Microsoft, and visitors can have a guest account before they sign up. Email is always on. Every other way is off until you turn it on, in Studio's **Auth › Providers** or with `palbase auth:providers:set`.

```sh
palbase auth:providers:list
```

`auth:providers:list` prints each provider, whether it is on, its clients, and the secrets it keeps (by name; a secret is never printed).

## Email

Email sign-in cannot be turned off, and has no switch of its own: an account with an address signs in with its password, a magic link or a passkey, as the app offers. Its rules are the environment's [auth settings](/docs/auth/overview#passwords-and-email): password lengths, whether an address is confirmed before the first sign-in, whether the confirmation is a code or a link, and where the links in its emails land.

The emails are sent through the environment's notifications ([Auth's emails and texts](/docs/auth/overview#auths-emails-and-texts)).

## Phone

A phone number signs in with a code texted to it (`POST /auth/otp`, then `POST /auth/otp/verify`), and a text can be a second factor. Its codes go through the environment's own SMS provider or verification service, set up in the notifications module ([SMS, codes and WhatsApp](/docs/backend/notifications#sms-codes-and-whatsapp)) — and, with neither, through Palbase's Twilio Verify, with nothing to set up, at Twilio's price and 10% past $4 a month ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)).

```sh
palbase auth:providers:set phone --enable
palbase auth:providers:set phone otp_ttl_seconds=120 otp_max_attempts=5 allow_signups=false
palbase auth:providers:disable phone
```

| Setting | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `allow_signups` | `true` | A code sent to a number no account has makes an account. With it off, only existing accounts sign in by phone. |
| `otp_ttl_seconds` | `300` | How long a code is good for, 1 to 300 seconds. |
| `otp_max_attempts` | `5` | Wrong codes allowed before the code is spent, 3 to 10. |
| `sender` | `sms` | Who makes the code: `sms` (auth makes it, and texts it through your SMS provider with the template `auth.sms_otp`) or `verify` (your verification service makes and checks it). |
| `sms_second_factor` | `true` | Whether a text may be a user's second factor. Turn it off if you hold texts too weak for one. |

Studio sets them under **Auth › Providers**, the phone row's settings. Which countries a text may reach is the notifications settings' (`sms_countries`, `sms_blocked_countries`). A phone sign-in that is off answers `provider_not_enabled`.

## Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft

Social sign-in has three parts, set up per provider:

- **The switch.** A provider that is off signs no one in, whatever its clients say.
- **Clients.** A client is one app's way in: its `key`, the `application_key`, `platform` (`web`, `ios`, `macos`, `android`) and `variant` (a build: `release`, `debug` …) it serves, and the provider's own identifiers for it. An app asks for the clients of its application, platform and variant (`GET /auth/oauth/config`) and gets what a sign-in button needs, with nothing secret in it. A **browser client** sends the person to the provider's page and back; a **native client** signs in with the platform's own sheet (Sign in with Apple, Google's and Microsoft's SDKs) and hands auth the provider's ID token.
- **Secrets.** A browser client names the stored secret it uses (`credential_ref`). Secrets are kept by a name you choose, encrypted, and never answered. A native client needs none.

### What each provider needs

Register this callback with the provider, for every browser client:

```text
https://<ref>.palbase.studio/auth/oauth/callback/<provider>
```

`<provider>` is `google`, `apple`, `github` or `microsoft`. Studio shows it, ready to copy, as **Backend callback URL** in the provider's settings. After the provider sends the person back there, auth sends them on to your app's **return URI**: one of the client's `return_uris`, exactly as listed, or the sign-in is refused (`invalid_return_uri`).

| Provider | Browser client | Its secret | Native clients |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google | `web_client_id`: the OAuth client id of a **Web application** client in Google Cloud | That client's secret | iOS and macOS: `bundle_id`, `ios_client_id`, `redirect_uri`. Android: `package_name`, `android_client_id`, `server_client_id` (the Web application client's id), `signing_certificate_sha1` |
| Apple | `services_id`: a **Services ID** with Sign in with Apple turned on | A Sign in with Apple **key** (the `.p8` file), with your Team ID and the key's Key ID | iOS and macOS: `bundle_id` |
| GitHub | `oauth_client_id`: an **OAuth App**'s client id | The OAuth App's client secret | — (browser only) |
| Microsoft | `application_id`: an app registration's **Application (client) ID**, and the `directory` it takes accounts from | A client secret of that registration | iOS, macOS and Android: `application_id`, `bundle_id` or `package_name`, `redirect_uri`, `directory` |

A Microsoft `directory` is `common` (work, school and personal accounts), `organizations` (work and school), `consumers` (personal), or the id of one organization's directory, for its accounts alone. Apple on Android signs in through the browser.

### From the CLI

```sh
# Google: a browser client named web, its return URI, and its secret from stdin.
palbase auth:providers:set google --client-id 1234567890-abc.apps.googleusercontent.com \
  --return-uri https://app.example.com/signin/callback --secret-stdin < google-secret.txt
palbase auth:providers:set google --enable

# Apple: the Services ID, and the .p8 key with its team and key ids.
palbase auth:providers:set apple --client-id com.example.web --return-uri https://app.example.com/signin/callback \
  --secret-stdin --team-id ABCDE12345 --key-id XYZ987WVU6 < AuthKey_XYZ987WVU6.p8
palbase auth:providers:set apple --enable

# Microsoft, for work and school accounts only.
palbase auth:providers:set microsoft --client-id 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 --directory organizations \
  --return-uri https://app.example.com/signin/callback --secret-stdin < microsoft-secret.txt
```

- `--client-id` sets the browser client that `--client` names (`web` by default), making it when the provider has none of that name. `--application` and `--variant` say what it serves (`app` and `release` by default); `--return-uri`, repeated, replaces its return URIs.
- `--secret-stdin` reads the secret from standard input, never from the command line, and keeps it under `--credential` (the provider's name by default).
- `--clients-file clients.json` replaces the provider's clients with a file's `{ "browser_clients": […], "native_clients": […] }`: the way to set native clients, and several at once.
- `palbase auth:providers:disable <provider>` turns a provider off and keeps its clients and secrets. `palbase auth:providers:secret:delete <name>` deletes a stored secret; one a client still uses is refused.

### In Studio

**Auth › Providers** lists every provider with its switch. A social provider's settings hold its clients (**Add client**: the client key, application key, platform, variant, browser or native, and the fields the table above names) and its **Browser credentials**: a secret saved under a credential key, which a browser client then selects. A Google client JSON or an Apple `.p8` file can be imported instead of pasting.

A change is made against the configuration read when the form opened: one saved elsewhere in the meantime is refused, and the form asks you to reopen it. The admin calls are the same: `GET /admin/social-auth` answers an `ETag`, and `PATCH /admin/social-auth/providers/{provider}` and `PUT /admin/social-auth/credentials/{key}` take it in `If-Match`.

### When the address is an existing account's

A provider account that is already linked signs in to its user. One that is not:

- **links to the account that holds its email address**, and signs in to it, when the provider hosts that address (Google for Gmail and Workspace addresses, Apple for iCloud addresses) and the account's address was confirmed and it has no second factor;
- **is refused** with `409 identity_link_required` when another account holds the address on any other terms: the person signs in to that account and links the provider from there;
- **makes a new account** when no account holds the address.

A signed-in user links another provider to their own account with the same flow (`purpose: "link"`). The app's side of the browser flow is in [Social sign-in](/docs/web/auth#social-sign-in).

## Guests

A guest is an account with no address, password or credential: only its session. A visitor can use your app as a guest and sign up later, and the account keeps its id, so what they did as a guest stays theirs. Turn guests on in the settings:

```sh
palbase auth:settings:set anonymous_sign_ins=true
```

Off, a guest sign-in answers `403 anonymous_sign_ins_disabled`. A guest is held to what holds a sign-up: the environment's user limit, proof of work, the risk engine and your `before.user.create` [hook](/docs/auth/hooks) (told `is_anonymous: true`), and 30 guests an hour from one address. Its access token says `is_anonymous: true`.

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/guest.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

/** A visitor's first visit: a guest account and its session. */
export async function startAsGuest(): Promise<string> {
  const current = await pb.auth.currentSession();
  if (current) return current.userId;
  const { data } = await pb.auth.api.signInAnonymously({ body: { locale: navigator.language } });
  if (!data.access_token || !data.refresh_token || !data.expires_in) throw new Error("the guest has no session");
  await pb.auth.setSession({ access_token: data.access_token, refresh_token: data.refresh_token, expires_in: data.expires_in });
  return data.user.id;
}

/** Later: the guest becomes an account with an address and a password, under the same id. */
export async function keepAccount(email: string, password: string): Promise<void> {
  await pb.auth.api.convertAnonymousUser({ body: { email, password } });
}

/** With the code the email carried. */
export async function confirmAccount(code: string): Promise<void> {
  await pb.auth.api.verifyAnonymousConversion({ body: { code } });
  await pb.auth.refreshSession(); // the new tokens no longer say is_anonymous
}
```

The address is the account's only once its owner confirms it: with the emailed code (`POST /auth/anonymous/convert/verify`, in the guest's own session) or, when the environment confirms by link, the link's token (`POST /auth/verify-email`). Until then the account is still a guest. An address another account holds is `409 email_exists`, and the guest stays signed in. A guest also becomes an account by adding a passkey, or by linking a social provider with its session; either way it keeps its id. Your backends hear `user.converted`.

<!-- ===== auth/users ===== -->

# Users & Roles

An environment's users are its auth module's: each has an id (`usr_…`), and any of an email address, a phone number, a password, linked provider accounts, passkeys and second factors. People make their own accounts from your app ([Web Auth](/docs/web/auth)). This page is about the other side: finding them, helping them, stopping them, and the roles your app gives them.

## Finding a user

Studio's **Auth › Users** lists the environment's users, newest first: their address or phone, whether they are active or banned, a test user, or have a second factor, which addresses are confirmed, when they signed up and last signed in. **Account status** shows the banned alone. A user's page has their contact details, how they sign in, their second factors, their sessions and their metadata, and the actions below.

```sh
palbase auth:users:list --limit 500
palbase auth:users:list --banned
palbase auth:users:get usr_01J…
```

`auth:users:get` adds how they sign in and the roles they hold. From a server, `GET /admin/users` pages through them (`limit`, `cursor`, `banned`) and `GET /admin/users/{uid}` reads one, with the email and phone in clear.

## Making one

```sh
palbase auth:users:create ada@example.com --verified < password.txt
```

The password is read from standard input, never from the command line. The account is made at once, with no email sent: share the password through a channel you trust. **Auth › Users › Create user** does the same. `POST /admin/users` takes `{ email, password, email_verified?, metadata?, skip_password_hibp? }`; it skips the self-service sign-up's rate limits and bot checks, but still holds the password to the environment's policy and, unless told not to, to the known-breaches check.

`PATCH /admin/users/{uid}` changes a user's `email`, `email_verified` and `metadata`. A new address is unconfirmed unless `email_verified` is sent with it, and one another user has is `409 user_exists`. `metadata` is merged into what the user has: a key set to `null` is removed.

## Helping someone back in

| Studio (the user's page) | CLI | Admin call | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Create reset token** | — | `POST /admin/users/{uid}/reset-password` | A one-hour password reset token, answered to you, with no email sent. The person sets a new password with it (`pb.auth.password.confirmReset(token, …)`). |
| **Reset MFA** | — | `DELETE /admin/users/{uid}/mfa` | Removes every second factor and recovery code, for someone who lost their authenticator: they sign in with their first factor and enroll again. |
| **Revoke all sessions** | `auth:users:sign-out` | `POST /admin/users/{uid}/sessions/revoke-all` | Ends every session: each device signs in again. |
| — | — | `POST /admin/users/{uid}/credentials/revoke-all` | Ends every session and refresh token, and revokes the user's attested and trusted devices and pending transactions, at once. The account stays. |

## Banning

```sh
palbase auth:users:ban usr_01J… --reason "chargeback fraud"
palbase auth:users:unban usr_01J…
```

A banned user's sessions end, and their sign-ins are refused with `403 user_banned` until they are unbanned. The reason is kept as `ban_reason`, and Studio shows it. **Ban user** and **Unban user** on the user's page do the same; the admin calls are `POST /admin/users/{uid}/ban` (`{ reason? }`) and `POST /admin/users/{uid}/unban`.

The environment can ban idle accounts by itself: `inactive_user_days` in the [auth settings](/docs/auth/overview#sessions-and-tokens).

## Sessions

Studio's **Auth › Sessions** lists the environment's live sessions: whose, the device and browser, the address, the authentication level, when each started and was last used. One can be revoked there. From a server, `GET /admin/sessions` (with `user_id` for one user's) and `DELETE /admin/sessions/{id}`.

Revoking a session deletes its refresh tokens, so it is never renewed. An access token it already issued is valid until it expires, but a `palbase/backend` app stops taking it within 15 seconds ([How the token is verified](/docs/backend/authentication#how-the-token-is-verified)). Backends hear `session.ended`.

## Deleting a user

```sh
palbase auth:users:delete usr_01J…
```

The user and everything auth holds for them go in one step: sessions, tokens, second factors, passkeys, linked providers, consents, roles. It cannot be undone. The project's other modules delete what is the user's too (a file stored with their `owner_id`, their flag values, their devices and messages), and your backends hear `user.deleted` to delete what is theirs in your own tables ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks)). **Delete user** on the user's page, and `DELETE /admin/users/{uid}`, do the same. A person deletes their own account from your app with `deleteAccount` ([Web Auth](/docs/web/auth#signing-out-and-deleting-the-account)).

## A user's own data

```sh
palbase auth:users:export usr_01J… --out ada.json
```

Everything auth holds about one person, as they may ask for it under the GDPR (articles 15 and 20), as JSON: their profile with the email and phone in clear, linked providers, sessions, consents, second factors, passkeys, devices, and their part of the audit trail. It holds no secrets: no password hash, no factor secret, no token. The export is itself recorded in the [audit trail](/docs/auth/audit). The file `--out` writes is readable by you alone. **Export user data** on the user's page, and `GET /admin/users/{uid}/export`, answer the same.

## Roles

A role is a name your app gives users, with the permissions it stands for. Roles are defined in the environment and given to users with the secret key; your code decides what they allow.

```sh
palbase auth:roles:set editor --permissions posts.publish,posts.delete_any --description "Edits everyone's posts"
palbase auth:roles:set member --permissions posts.write --default yes
palbase auth:roles:list
palbase auth:roles:delete editor --force
```

- A role's name is lowercase letters, digits and `_`, 64 at most. `anon`, `authenticated`, `service_role` and names starting `backend_` are the platform's.
- A permission is `resource.action`: lowercase, one dot, no wildcard (`posts.delete_any`). `--permissions` replaces the role's list; `""` empties it. Users who hold the role have the new list at once.
- `--default yes` gives the role to every new user. One role at most is the default.
- A role users hold is deleted only with `--force`, which takes it from them; without it the answer is `409`.

There is no CLI command that gives a user a role: that is your app's decision, made from your server.

| Admin call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `PUT /admin/users/{uid}/roles/{role}` | Gives the user the role. A role that is not defined is `400 role_not_defined`. |
| `DELETE /admin/users/{uid}/roles/{role}` | Takes it from them. |
| `GET /admin/users/{uid}/roles` | The roles they hold. |
| `PUT /admin/roles/{name}`, `DELETE /admin/roles/{name}` | What `auth:roles:set` and `auth:roles:delete` call. |

The roles a user holds are in the `user` of every sign-in answer, as `roles`, not in their access token. A backend asks for them where it decides (the [Roles](/docs/backend/authentication#roles) section of Authentication shows how), and hears `user.permissions_changed`, with the user's whole permission list, each time a role is given, taken or changed. `palbase types:pull` writes the environment's role names into `palbase/palbase-env.d.ts`.

## Bringing users over

`auth:import` brings users from another Palbase project, or from any source written as import bodies, with what they sign in with, so they notice nothing:

```sh
palbase auth:import users.ndjson --pepper-stdin < pepper.txt
palbase auth:import ./export/        # users-0001.json, users-0002.json … in order
```

A file is one import body (`{ "hash": { … }, "users": [ … ] }`, with no pepper in it), JSON lines with a user a line, or one JSON array of users. Each user keeps:

| Field | What is kept |
|---|---|
| `id` | Their id, `usr_` and a lowercase UUID. |
| `email`, `phone`, `email_verified`, `phone_verified`, `email_confirmed_by` | Their addresses, and who confirmed the email (`email`, `admin`, `google`, `apple`). |
| `password_hash`, `recovery_code_hashes` | Their password and recovery codes, as the source hashed them: `palbase-argon2id` only. Verified with the source's pepper until the user's next sign-in hashes the password again with this environment's. |
| `identities` | Their linked provider accounts: `provider` and the provider's `subject`. |
| `mfa_factors` | Second factors, at most one of each type: an authenticator app's secret, a phone, an email. |
| `passkeys` | Their WebAuthn credentials. A passkey signs in here when the environment's passkey host is the one it was registered for. |
| `sessions` | Their open sessions: the refresh token their app holds goes on working, here. An ended session, or a banned user's, is left behind. |
| `metadata`, `locale`, `banned`, `ban_reason`, `created_at`, `last_login_at` | As they were. |

The source's pepper, which the hashes were made with, is read from standard input (`--pepper-stdin`), never from a file or the command line. Auth keeps it sealed and uses it only to verify.

Users go 1000 to a call, and each is written whole or not at all. One user refused does not stop the others: the command lists each by id and why. A user whose id, address, phone, provider account, passkey or session the environment already has is refused (`user_exists`, `email_exists` …), never overwritten, so running the same import again writes only what the first run did not. The admin call is `POST /admin/users/import`, 1000 users and 1 MiB a call.

## Test users

Accounts made for tests, marked `test: true` in their tokens and left out of the counts, are [Test Users](/docs/backend/test-users): `palbase auth:test-users:create`, and Studio's **Auth › Test accounts**.
