- [Overview](/docs/auth/overview): the environment's auth settings
- [Audit Trail](/docs/auth/audit): what was done to each user, and by whom
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication): the user in a backend route
- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks): `user.deleted`, `session.ended` and the other events
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authuserslist): the `auth:users:*` commands



<!-- ===== auth/hooks ===== -->

# Blocking Hooks

A blocking hook is an endpoint of yours that auth calls, and waits for, before it does something: creating an account, signing someone in, issuing a token. The endpoint answers `allow` or `deny`, and auth goes on or refuses. An allow before a token can also put claims of yours in it. The call and the answer are both signed with the hook's own secret, so auth knows the answer is yours and you know the call is auth's.

What happens *after* an operation is not a hook: it is an event, delivered to the project's webhooks (`user.deleted`, `session.ended`, `user.converted` …), and it cannot change what happened ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)).

## Quick example

Register the hook. Its signing secret is printed this once:

```sh
palbase auth:hooks:create --event before.user.create --url https://hooks.example.com/auth
```

```text
Registered hook_01J…: before.user.create → https://hooks.example.com/auth.
signing secret (shown this once): whsec_…
```

Keep it where the endpoint reads it, here `AUTH_HOOK_SECRET`. Then the endpoint: any server that answers HTTPS at a public address. This one is Node with nothing installed:

```ts
// hooks/server.ts
import { createHmac, randomUUID, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { createServer } from "node:http";

// whsec_ and the key in base64, as auth:hooks:create printed it.
const key = Buffer.from(process.env.AUTH_HOOK_SECRET!.replace(/^whsec_/, ""), "base64");

function sign(id: string, timestamp: string, body: string): string {
  return createHmac("sha256", key).update(`${id}.${timestamp}.${body}`).digest("base64");
}

interface HookCall {
  event: string;
  user?: { id?: string; email?: string; email_verified?: boolean; is_anonymous?: boolean };
  context?: { ip?: string; user_agent?: string; risk_score?: number };
}

interface HookAnswer {
  verdict: "allow" | "deny";
  reason?: string;
  custom_claims?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

function decide(call: HookCall): HookAnswer {
  if (call.event === "before.user.create" && call.user?.email && !call.user.email.endsWith("@example.com")) {
    return { verdict: "deny", reason: "Sign-ups are open to example.com addresses only." };
  }
  if (call.event === "before.token.issue") {
    // Your own data about the user goes into the token they are about to get.
    return { verdict: "allow", custom_claims: { plan: "pro" } };
  }
  return { verdict: "allow" };
}

createServer((req, res) => {
  const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
  req.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => chunks.push(chunk));
  req.on("end", () => {
    // The signature is over the bytes as they arrived: read them before parsing anything.
    const body = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8");
    const id = String(req.headers["webhook-id"] ?? "");
    const timestamp = String(req.headers["webhook-timestamp"] ?? "");
    const expected = Buffer.from(`v1,${sign(id, timestamp, body)}`);
    const given = String(req.headers["webhook-signature"] ?? "").split(" ").map((s) => Buffer.from(s));
    const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(timestamp)) < 300;
    if (!fresh || !given.some((s) => s.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(s, expected))) {
      res.writeHead(401).end();
      return;
    }

    // The answer is signed the same way, with an id and a time of its own.
    const answer = JSON.stringify(decide(JSON.parse(body) as HookCall));
    const answerId = `msg_${randomUUID()}`;
    const answerTimestamp = String(Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000));
    res.writeHead(200, {
      "content-type": "application/json",
      "webhook-id": answerId,
      "webhook-timestamp": answerTimestamp,
      "webhook-signature": `v1,${sign(answerId, answerTimestamp, answer)}`,
    });
    res.end(answer);
  });
}).listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8080));
```

A sign-up with any other address is now refused with `403 hook_denied`, and its message is your `reason`.

## The events

| Event | Auth calls it before | It is sent |
|---|---|---|
| `before.user.create` | An account is made: an email sign-up, a passkey sign-up, a social sign-up, a guest, a guest becoming an account | `user.email`, `user.email_verified`, `user.is_anonymous` (no id yet) |
| `before.login` | A password, magic-link, passkey or social sign-in | `user.id`, `context.ip`, `context.user_agent`, `context.risk_score` |
| `before.password.reset` | A password reset email is sent | `user.id` |
| `before.mfa.verify` | An authenticator-app or text code is checked as a second factor | `user.id` |
| `before.social.link` | A provider account is linked to a user | `user.id` |
| `before.token.issue` | A user's access token: at every sign-in, whatever its way, and at every refresh | `user.id` |
| `before.token.refresh` | A session is refreshed | `user.id`, `context.ip`, `context.user_agent` |
| `before.transaction.approve` | A user approves a transaction | `user.id` |
| `before.device_grant.initiate` | A device asks for a code ([OpenID Provider](/docs/auth/openid-provider#signing-in-a-device)) | — |
| `before.device_grant.authorize` | A user approves a device's code | `user.id` |

The body is `{ event, user?, context?, client_metadata? }`; a social sign-in or sign-up also sends `client_metadata.transaction_id`. A phone-code sign-in, or a phone sign-up, calls `before.token.issue` alone.

## The call and the answer

Auth POSTs the JSON body to the hook's URL with three headers, as [Standard Webhooks](https://www.standardwebhooks.com) has them:

| Header | What it is |
|---|---|
| `webhook-id` | The call's id, `msg_…`. |
| `webhook-timestamp` | When it was sent, in Unix seconds. |
| `webhook-signature` | `v1,` and the base64 HMAC-SHA256, under the secret's key, of `<webhook-id>.<webhook-timestamp>.<body>`. |

The key is the secret's part after `whsec_`, decoded from base64. An endpoint checks the signature against the body's bytes before it reads them, and refuses a timestamp more than a few minutes away.

The answer is `2xx` with a JSON body, **signed the same way**: its own `webhook-id`, a `webhook-timestamp` within five minutes of auth's clock, and a `webhook-signature` over that id, that time and the answer's body, with the same key.

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `verdict` | `allow` or `deny`. |
| `reason` | Why, for a deny. A sign-up, a guest and a guest's conversion pass it to the person refused, as the message of their `403 hook_denied`; other operations answer `hook_denied` in their own words. |
| `custom_claims` | On an allow of `before.token.issue`: claims put in the access token under its `custom_claims` claim. A `palbase/backend` route reads them as the user's `metadata` ([The `UserT` shape](/docs/backend/authentication#the-usert-shape)). |

A token's claims are asked for again at each refresh, so they are never older than the token. A `before.password.reset` that denies sends no email, and the request answers as it always does, so no one learns from it whether the address has an account.

Several hooks on one event are called one after another, oldest first. The first deny refuses; the `custom_claims` of the allows are merged, a later hook's key winning.

## Timeouts and failures

`--timeout` is how long auth waits for an answer, 100 to 5000 ms (5000 by default). A hook **fails** when it does not answer in that time, or answers with a status other than `2xx`, without a valid signature, or with a body that is not JSON. What auth does then is the hook's `--failure-mode`:

| `failure_mode` | When the hook fails |
|---|---|
| `deny` (the default) | The operation fails, as an error rather than as `hook_denied`: a sign-up or a password sign-in answers `500 internal_error`. |
| `allow` | The operation goes on as if the hook had allowed it, with no claims added. |

The two device-grant events go on when their hook fails, whatever its failure mode.

Choose `deny` for a hook that is a rule (who may sign up, who may sign in), and `allow` for one that only adds something. Every sign-in waits for its hooks, so put the endpoint where it answers at once: a [machine](/docs/machines/overview) of a size that sleeps makes the first sign-in after it fell asleep wait for it to wake.

The URL is `https`, and it must not resolve to a private address.

## Managing hooks

```sh
palbase auth:hooks:list
palbase auth:hooks:update hook_01J… --timeout 2000 --failure-mode allow
palbase auth:hooks:update hook_01J… --disable
palbase auth:hooks:delete hook_01J…
```

`auth:hooks:update` changes the event, the URL, the timeout, the failure mode or the switch; the secret stays. A hook registered with `--disable`, or turned off, is not called. Deleting one stops the calls at once. The admin calls are `GET`/`POST /admin/hooks` and `PUT`/`DELETE /admin/hooks/{id}`; `PUT` replaces the hook whole, and an optional field it leaves out takes its default, not its current value.

`GET /admin/hooks/{id}/executions` lists a hook's calls, newest first, for thirty days: what it was sent (without the email address), what it answered, how long it took, and the verdict auth took (`allow`, `deny`, `timeout` or `error`). Deleting the hook deletes them.

## Related

- [Overview](/docs/auth/overview): the rest of an environment's auth
- [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks): the events auth sends after an operation
- [Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication): the token, and its claims, in a backend
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authhookscreate): `auth:hooks:create` and its flags



<!-- ===== auth/audit ===== -->

# Audit Trail

Auth records what happens in it as events: sign-ins that worked and ones that did not, sign-ups, password and email changes, second factors, sessions and tokens, and every change made with the secret key, to a user or to the settings. Each event names who acted, from which address, what it was done to, and whether it worked. Events are chained: each carries a hash of itself and of the one before it, so an event changed, removed or put out of order breaks the chain where it happened, and verifying the trail finds it.

## Reading it

Studio's **Auth › Audit** shows the latest 100 events with a chart of failed sign-ins per day (the last 7, 30 or 90 days), filtered by result and searched by event, actor, target or metadata. An event's details hold its code, actor, target and metadata. A change made with a secret key is shown as **Admin (secret key)**.

```sh
palbase auth:audit
palbase auth:audit --event auth.login.failure --limit 200
```

`auth:audit` prints the events newest first: when, the event, the result, who, from where, and on what. From a server, `GET /admin/audit` pages through them (`limit` up to 100, `cursor`, `event_type`).

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `event_type` | What happened, as a dotted name (below). |
| `result` | `success` or `failure`. |
| `actor` | `{ user_id, email?, ip? }`: the user who acted, or `service_role` for a call made with a secret key. |
| `target_type`, `target_id` | What it was done to: a user, a session, a setting. |
| `auth_method` | How the user signed in, for a sign-in. |
| `risk_score` | The score the [risk engine](/docs/auth/overview#risk) gave, when it scored. |
| `metadata` | What else the event says: a failure's reason, the setting that changed. |
| `event_hash`, `prev_hash` | Its place in the chain. |

The actor and the metadata are kept encrypted. When a user is deleted, their part of the record stays in the chain, and its actor and metadata can no longer be read.

### Event types

| Kind | Types |
|---|---|
| Signing up and in | `auth.signup`, `auth.login.success`, `auth.login.failure`, `auth.social.login`, `auth.magic_link.request`, `auth.magic_link.verify`, `auth.phone.signup`, `auth.phone.login`, `sms.otp.send`, `webauthn.login`, `auth.step_up.success`, `auth.step_up.failure` |
| Passwords and addresses | `auth.password.change`, `auth.password.reset.request`, `auth.password.reset.complete`, `auth.email.verify` |
| Second factors and passkeys | `mfa.enroll`, `mfa.remove`, `mfa.verify.success`, `mfa.verify.failure`, `mfa.recovery.used`, `webauthn.register`, `webauthn.remove`, `webauthn.clone_detected` |
| Linked providers | `social.link`, `social.unlink` |
| Sessions and tokens | `session.create`, `session.revoke`, `session.device_change`, `token.issue`, `token.refresh`, `token.revoke`, `trusted_device.register`, `trusted_device.used`, `trusted_device.revoke` |
| With the secret key | `admin.user.create`, `admin.user.update`, `admin.user.delete`, `admin.user.import`, `admin.user.deactivate_inactive`, `admin.mfa.reset`, `admin.config.change`, `admin.key.rotate`, `admin.audit.export` |
| Abuse and breaches | `bot.pow.challenge`, `bot.stuffing.detected`, `bot.ip.blocked`, `breach.detected`, `breach.forced_reset` |
| Personal data | `gdpr.export`, `gdpr.erasure`, `gdpr.consent.revoke` |
| Service accounts | `serviceaccount.create`, `serviceaccount.rotate`, `serviceaccount.revoke` |

`--event` and `event_type` take one type exactly.

## Exporting it

```sh
palbase auth:audit:export --out audit.ndjson
palbase auth:audit:export --format csv --from 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z --to 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z --out october.csv
palbase auth:audit:export --event admin.config.change --out config-changes.ndjson
```

The export is the whole trail, or the span `--from` (inclusive) to `--to` (exclusive), oldest first: JSON lines, an event a line in the shape above, or CSV. Its size is not limited. The file `--out` writes is readable by you alone. An export that fails halfway breaks off rather than ending as if it were whole, and the export is itself recorded (`admin.audit.export`). The admin call is `GET /admin/audit/export`, with `format`, `from`, `to` and `event_type`.

## Verifying it

```sh
palbase auth:audit:verify
```

```text
The audit trail is whole: 18342 events, each chained to the one before.
```

`auth:audit:verify` (`GET /admin/audit/verify`) computes every event's hash again and checks each link to the event before it, oldest first. A trail that is not whole is an error naming the first event where the chain breaks, and the command exits with `audit_trail_broken`: there, an event was changed or taken out. The answer of the admin call is `{ valid, total, broken_at? }`.

## Related

- [Users & Roles](/docs/auth/users): the changes a user's record shows
- [Overview](/docs/auth/overview): the settings `admin.config.change` records
- [Logs](/docs/getting-started/logs): every request to the environment, and auth's events among them
- [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-authaudit): `auth:audit`, `auth:audit:export`, `auth:audit:verify`

# OpenID Provider

Every environment is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server and OpenID Connect provider for its own users. Another app (a partner's site, a CLI, a TV app, a tool of your own) signs a person in with their account in your app, the way apps offer "Sign in with Google", and gets an access token and an ID token for them. You register each such app as an **OAuth client** of the environment. This is not how your own app signs its users in: that is [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth).

The provider's issuer is the project's address, and everything about it is in its discovery document:

```text
https://<ref>.palbase.studio/.well-known/openid-configuration
```

| Endpoint | What it is |
|---|---|
| `GET /oauth/authorize` | The authorization endpoint: the browser leg of the authorization code flow, with PKCE (`S256`). |
| `POST /oauth/token` | Tokens for the grants `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, `client_credentials` and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. |
| `POST /oauth/par` | Pushed authorization requests (RFC 9126). |
| `POST /oauth/device` | Device authorization (RFC 8628). |
| `GET /oauth/userinfo` | The claims of the token's scopes: `sub`, `email`, `email_verified`, `name`, `preferred_username`. |
| `POST /oauth/introspect` | Introspection (RFC 7662), for the secret key or a confidential client. |
| `POST /oauth/revoke` | Revocation (RFC 7009). |
| `GET /oauth/logout` | RP-initiated logout, with `id_token_hint` and a registered `post_logout_redirect_uri`. |
| `GET /.well-known/jwks.json` | The keys tokens are signed with ([Signing keys](/docs/auth/overview#signing-keys)). |

A client talks to these with its own credentials, never with a Palbase key. The scopes are `openid`, `profile`, `email` and `offline_access`.

## Registering a client

```sh
# A web app with a server: a confidential client, its secret printed once.
palbase auth:oauth-clients:create "Partner Portal" --redirect-uri https://partner.example.com/callback --grant authorization_code --grant refresh_token

# A CLI or a mobile app: a public client, with no secret, signing in with PKCE.
palbase auth:oauth-clients:create "Acme CLI" --public --redirect-uri http://127.0.0.1:8976/callback

palbase auth:oauth-clients:list
palbase auth:oauth-clients:delete oidc_7f3a…
```

| Flag | What it says |
|---|---|
| `--public` | A public client (a CLI, a mobile app, a single-page app) has no secret. Without it the client is confidential, and its secret is printed this once. |
| `--redirect-uri` | Where the browser may be sent back with the code; repeat it for several. `https`, or, for a public client, its own scheme or `http` on the loopback address. |
| `--grant` | `authorization_code` (the default), `refresh_token`, `client_credentials`, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. |
| `--scope` | What it may ask for; `openid`, `profile` and `email` by default. |
| `--client-id` | A `client_id` of your choosing, kept as it is; a random `oidc_…` one by default. |

The admin calls hold more: `POST /admin/oauth-clients` takes `token_endpoint_auth_method` (`client_secret_basic`, the default for a confidential client, `client_secret_post`, `private_key_jwt` with the client's `jwks`, or `none` for a public one), `post_logout_redirect_uris`, `id_token_lifetime_secs` (3600 by default) and `dpop_bound_access_tokens` (every token request proves a key, RFC 9449). `PATCH /admin/oauth-clients/{id}` changes any of them but whether the client is public. A secret client can move to `private_key_jwt`, giving up its secret, and never back.

## Its sign-in page

The provider has no sign-in page of its own: the person signs in on a page of yours, which you name in the auth settings.

```sh
palbase auth:settings:set oauth_login_url=https://app.example.com/oauth/login
```

Without it, `/oauth/authorize` refuses: there is nowhere to sign the person in. With it, the flow is:

1. The client sends the browser to `GET /oauth/authorize` with its `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state` and PKCE challenge.
2. The provider sends the browser to your page with `?auth_request_id=…`.
3. Your page signs the person in with `POST /auth/login`, sending the `auth_request_id` with the email and password. The answer's `oidc_callback_url` is where the browser goes next.
4. From there, the provider sends the browser back to the client's `redirect_uri` with the `code`, the `state` and the issuer (`iss`). The client exchanges the code at `POST /oauth/token`.

```ts
// src/lib/palbase.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

export const pb = createClient({ url: "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_k3xq81w4m_cZ8yX7wV6uT5" });
```

```ts
// src/oauth-login.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

/** The form on https://app.example.com/oauth/login?auth_request_id=… */
export async function signInForClient(email: string, password: string): Promise<string> {
  const authRequestId = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get("auth_request_id") ?? "";
  const { data } = await pb.auth.api.login({ body: { email, password, auth_request_id: authRequestId } });
  if ("mfa_required" in data) return "This account signs in with a second factor, which this page does not complete.";
  if (data.oidc_callback_url) window.location.assign(data.oidc_callback_url);
  return "Signed in";
}
```

The request is completed by a password sign-in: a sign-in that answers `mfa_required` does not complete it.

## Signing in a device

A device with no keyboard, a TV or a terminal, signs in with the device flow, when its client has the `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` grant:

1. The device calls `POST /oauth/device` with its `client_id`, and shows the person the `user_code` it is answered.
2. The person opens a page of your app on their phone or computer, signed in, and enters the code. The page shows what asked (`GET /auth/device/requests/{user_code}`: the client's name, the address and user agent it asked from) and approves or denies it (`POST /auth/device/verify`).
3. The device polls `POST /oauth/token` with its `device_code` every `interval` seconds; until the person decides, the answer is `authorization_pending`.

Auth has no approval page to show: the `verification_uri` it answers is its own, and answers JSON. Show the person your page's address.

```ts
// src/device.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

/** What the approval page shows before the person decides: a code someone else sent names a device they do not know. */
export async function describeDevice(userCode: string): Promise<string> {
  const { data } = await pb.auth.api.devicePendingRequest({ path: { user_code: userCode } });
  return `${data.client_name}, from ${data.ip ?? "an unknown address"} (${data.user_agent ?? "unknown device"})`;
}

export async function decideDevice(userCode: string, approve: boolean): Promise<void> {
  await pb.auth.api.deviceVerifySubmit({ body: { user_code: userCode, action: approve ? "approve" : "deny" } });
}
```

The [blocking hooks](/docs/auth/hooks) `before.device_grant.initiate` and `before.device_grant.authorize` can refuse either step.

## FAPI 2.0

```sh
palbase auth:settings:set fapi_enabled=true
```

`fapi_enabled` holds the provider to the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile, for clients that need it (open banking, payments): an authorization request is taken only as a push (`POST /oauth/par`) and names its `redirect_uri`, PKCE is `S256`, clients are confidential and authenticate with `private_key_jwt`, every token is DPoP-bound, access tokens live five minutes at most, refresh tokens are not rotated, and the device flow is off.

## Service accounts

A service account is a machine's identity in the environment: a `client_id` and a secret, for `grant_type=client_credentials` at `POST /oauth/token`. Its token has no user and no session behind it: a `palbase/backend` route refuses it, since its routes take users. It is for services of your own that verify it against the key set or with `POST /oauth/introspect`.

| Admin call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /admin/service-accounts` | `{ name, scopes?, credential_ttl_days? }`: makes one, and answers its `client_secret` once. |
| `GET /admin/service-accounts`, `GET /admin/service-accounts/{id}` | Lists them, reads one; never the secret. |
| `POST /admin/service-accounts/{id}/rotate` | A new secret, answered once. The old one keeps working for 30 seconds, so a deployment can switch. |
| `DELETE /admin/service-accounts/{id}` | Revokes it at once: its secrets stop working and no token is issued to it again. |

`credential_ttl_days` (1 to 3650) is how long a secret lives before the account must be rotated; without it a secret does not expire.

## Signing in with your own server

When your server decides who a person is in a way of its own (an employee directory, a game console's account, a sign-in your company already has), it can sign them in to the environment as one of its users. The user must exist: make them first with `POST /admin/users`, or [import](/docs/auth/users#bringing-users-over) them.

1. Your server mints a custom token for the user: `POST /admin/token/custom` with the secret key, `{ user_id, expires_in? }` (at most an hour, the default).
2. It hands the token to the app, which exchanges it for a session at `POST /auth/token/exchange` (`{ custom_token }`).

The token is good once (`401 token_used` a second time); a banned user's is refused (`403 user_banned`).

```ts
// server/sign-in-as.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

/** After your own check of who they are: a token the app trades for their session. */
export async function customTokenFor(userId: string): Promise<string> {
  const { data } = await palbase.auth.adminCreateCustomToken({ body: { user_id: userId, expires_in: 300 } });
  return data.custom_token;
}
```

```ts
// src/exchange.ts
import { pb } from "./lib/palbase";

export async function signInWith(customToken: string): Promise<string> {
  const { data } = await pb.auth.api.exchangeCustomToken({ body: { custom_token: customToken } });
  await pb.auth.setSession({ access_token: data.access_token, refresh_token: data.refresh_token, expires_in: data.expires_in });
  return data.user.id;
}
```

- [Overview](/docs/auth/overview): the auth settings and signing keys
- [Blocking Hooks](/docs/auth/hooks): approving a sign-in, a token or a device from your own code
- [Audit Trail](/docs/auth/audit): `token.issue`, `serviceaccount.*` and the rest

<!-- ===== purchases/overview ===== -->

# Purchases

Every project has a purchases module. It holds **one catalog** of what the app sells — subscriptions, one-time products, packs of credits — sold in the **App Store**, on **Google Play** and on the **web** through the environment's own Stripe account. And it gives **one answer** to "what does this customer have", whatever store they bought in: a Pro bought on the web is Pro in the iOS app.

Apps buy with each store's own machinery — StoreKit on iOS, Play Billing on Android, Stripe Checkout on the web — through Palbase's SDKs. Palbase verifies every purchase with the store, keeps it in the project's **ledger**, and keeps each customer's entitlements, credits and quotas current: in the apps, live, and on your server, by a read or an event.

## Quick example

The app hears what the signed-in customer has, and sends them to buy on the web:

```ts
// app/pro.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

// Told now, and again whenever it changes: a purchase in any store, a renewal, a refund.
pb.purchases.onCustomerInfo((info) => {
  const pro = info?.entitlements["pro"]?.active === true;
  document.body.classList.toggle("pro", pro);
});

export async function buyYearly(): Promise<void> {
  const url = await pb.purchases.checkout({
    product: "pro",
    plan: "yearly",
    successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks",
    cancelUrl: "https://app.example.com/pricing",
  });
  location.assign(url); // Stripe Checkout
}
```

The server checks the entitlement where the content is served, with the secret key:

```ts
// server/pro.ts
import { createServer, isEntitled } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

export async function isPro(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
  // A user who has bought nothing reads as a customer with nothing.
  const { data } = await palbase.purchases.getCustomer({ path: { customer_id: userId } });
  return isEntitled(data, "pro");
}
```

## The parts

| | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Catalog** | The project's one definition of what it sells, saved in revisions: each product once, with its kind, its plans and prices, its name in each language, the channels it is sold on (`ios`, `android`, `web`) and what it gives. See [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog). |
| **Product** | One thing sold: a `subscription` (renews until canceled), a `non_consumable` (bought once, kept), a `consumable` (bought again and again, for credits) or a `non_renewing` period. |
| **Plan** | How a product is paid for: a subscription's period and price (`monthly`, `yearly`), or the one price of anything else. The stores know a plan as `<product>.<plan>`. |
| **Entitlement** | Something a customer has or not: `pro`. Products give entitlements, and apps and servers check entitlements — never products — so a plan can change without the checks changing. |
| **Credits** | A balance the customer spends: `tokens`. A consumable gives them per purchase, a subscription per period. |
| **Limit** | A quota counted in a window: `ai_requests` a month, with a free tier, and what each product gives on top. |
| **Offerings** | The catalog as a paywall shows it: each channel's text and price, and the id each store sells a plan by. Any of the project's keys reads it. |
| **Customer** | A user of the project, a guest included: the customer's id is the user's id. What they have is **`CustomerInfo`**: each entitlement (on or off, until when, whether it renews, which store gives it), their subscriptions and one-time purchases, credit balances and quota use. |
| **Paywall**, **placement** | What an app draws to sell the catalog, designed in Studio and published without an app update; a placement is the place in the app that shows one. See [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls). |
| **Offer**, **coupon** | A discount, a longer free trial or a grant, for an audience or everyone, once a customer; a coupon is a code that opens one. See [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers). |

## The stores

| Channel | Store | The app buys with | The environment needs | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ios` | The App Store | StoreKit 2, through `PalbasePurchases` | An In-App Purchase key; an App Store Connect API key to write the catalog | [App Store](/docs/purchases/app-store) |
| `android` | Google Play | Play Billing, through `palbase-purchases` | A service account your Play Console invites, and the app's notifications topic in Play Console | [Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play) |
| `web` | Stripe | Stripe Checkout, through `pb.purchases.checkout()` | The environment's own Stripe account | [Connect Stripe](/docs/purchases/connect-stripe), [Web](/docs/purchases/web) |

Each environment connects its own stores: `staging` can sell through Stripe's test mode while `production` takes live payments.

## How a purchase becomes access

1. **The app buys**, naming the customer to the store: StoreKit with the customer's `appAccountToken`, Play Billing with their obfuscated account id, Checkout with the customer's session. The SDKs do this; nothing personal goes to Apple or Google.
2. **The purchase reaches Palbase.** The iOS and Android apps report what the store gave them; Stripe reports its own. Nothing is taken on the device's word: an App Store transaction is checked against Apple's signature and the subscription read from Apple with the environment's key, a Play purchase is read from Play by its token, a Stripe object is read again from Stripe.
3. **The ledger applies it**, and the customer's entitlements, credits and quotas follow. A Google Play purchase is acknowledged once the ledger has it — the SDK never does.
4. **Everyone hears it.** The customer's apps are told at once (each customer has a realtime channel of their own, `purchases:<ref>:<user id>`, read-only), and your backend receives `purchases.*` events.
5. **The stores keep it current.** Apple's App Store Server Notifications, Google Play's real-time developer notifications and Stripe's events bring renewals, cancellations, billing issues and refunds into the ledger, with the app closed.

An entitlement already on from one store is not sold again in another: the iOS and Android SDKs answer `alreadyEntitled` without opening the store, and a web checkout is refused (`409 already_entitled`), naming the store it is managed in. A free trial is given once per customer, across every channel.

## Who calls what

| Caller | Key | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| A customer's app | The publishable key and the user's session (a guest's too) | Reads the offerings and a placement's paywall; reads what the customer has (`GET /purchases/me`); buys, reports, restores; redeems web purchases and coupons; takes offers; opens the Stripe portal; moves a guest's purchases to an account. |
| Your server | A secret key | Everything else: the catalog and its plans, the stores' connections, every customer, grants, credits and limits, paywalls, placements and experiments, offers' figures and coupons, charts, settings. |
| The stores | None: each signs its own | Their notifications, at the environment's own address. |

In a `palbase/backend` app the module is `Palbase.purchases`; from any other server it is `createServer({ url, secretKey }).purchases` — the same client, generated from the purchases contract, one method per operation (`GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}` is `getCustomer`).

## Test purchases

Purchases nobody pays for are **test purchases**: the App Store's sandbox (where TestFlight and App Review buy), Xcode's StoreKit Testing, Google Play's license testers and Stripe's test mode. Each is marked `is_sandbox` — in what the customer has and in the purchase events — and the environment's settings say whether they open entitlements: for **everyone** (the default), only for customers on an allowlist, or for **nobody**. App Review buys in the sandbox: on the environment a build in review uses, a test purchase that opens nothing gets the app rejected. See [Customers](/docs/purchases/customers#settings).

Test the iOS side end to end with [Test Apple Purchases](/docs/purchases/testing-apple).

## Setting up, in order

1. **Write the catalog** — in Studio, **Purchases › Catalog**, or as a file with `palbase purchases:catalog:put`. [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog)
2. **Connect the stores you sell in** — the [App Store](/docs/purchases/app-store), [Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play), [Stripe](/docs/purchases/connect-stripe).
3. **Bring the stores to the catalog** — plan it, read what each store will get, and confirm: `palbase purchases:catalog:plan`, then `palbase purchases:catalog:confirm`. Palbase creates the products and prices in each store.
4. **Buy from the apps** — [iOS](/docs/ios/purchases), [Android](/docs/android/purchases), [the web](/docs/purchases/web).
5. **Check access where the content is served** — [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements).
6. When the app needs them: [paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls) designed in Studio, [offers and coupons](/docs/purchases/offers), and [charts](/docs/purchases/charts) of what sold.

## In Studio

Each environment's **Purchases** has these screens:

| Screen | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Catalog** | The products, each with its plans, text, channels and what it gives. |
| **Stores** | The Stripe account, Google Play purchases, and the plans that bring the stores to the catalog, each store's part shown before you confirm it. |
| **App Store** | The In-App Purchase key, what selling in the App Store still needs, Xcode's test purchases and the team's sandbox testers. |
| **Paywalls** | The paywalls, their drafts and versions, and the placements that show them, with their targeting rules. |
| **Experiments** | Paywalls tried against each other on a placement, and which sells best. |
| **Offers**, **Coupons** | The catalog's discounts, trials and grants, and the codes that open them. |
| **Charts** | Revenue, subscriptions, conversion and retention, from the ledger. |
| **Customers** | What a customer has, from every store; an entitlement or credits given, saying why. |
| **Settings** | What test purchases open, a deleted user's web subscriptions, the quotas' time zone, and how charts count money. |

## The CLI

The `purchases` commands cover the catalog, the stores' connections, paywalls, placements, experiments, charts and customers; the `stores` commands connect the App Store Connect and Google Play accounts the catalog is written with. Every one is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#purchases).

- [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls) · [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers)

# Catalog

The catalog is the project's one definition of what it sells. Each product is written **once** — its kind, its plans and prices, its name in each language, the channels it is sold on and what it gives — and each channel adds only what is its own there: the App Store's shorter name, a web price without the stores' commission.

It is one JSON document, saved in **revisions**. Edit it in Studio (**Purchases › Catalog**) or keep it as a file in your repository and save it with the CLI. Saving a revision writes nothing to a store: a **plan** brings the App Store, Google Play and Stripe to it, store by store, after you have read what each will get and confirmed it.

Each environment has its own catalog.

## Quick example

A subscription sold on all three channels, and a pack of credits sold in the App Store and on the web:

```json
{
  "base_locale": "en",
  "entitlements": [{ "key": "pro", "name": "Pro" }],
  "credits": [{ "key": "tokens", "name": "Tokens", "low_at": 10 }],
  "limits": [{ "key": "ai_requests", "name": "AI requests", "window": "calendar_month", "free": 10 }],
  "products": [
    {
      "key": "pro",
      "type": "subscription",
      "group": "membership",
      "tier": 1,
      "locales": {
        "en": { "name": "Pro", "description": "Everything, every month" },
        "tr": { "name": "Pro", "description": "Her şey, her ay" }
      },
      "plans": [
        { "key": "monthly", "period": "P1M", "price": { "currency": "USD", "amount": 999 }, "intro": { "mode": "free_trial", "duration": "P1W" } },
        { "key": "yearly", "period": "P1Y", "price": { "currency": "USD", "amount": 7999 } }
      ],
      "channels": {
        "ios": { "family_shareable": true },
        "android": { "locales": { "en": { "benefits": ["No ads", "Every feature"] } } },
        "web": { "prices": { "monthly": { "currency": "USD", "amount": 799 } } }
      },
      "entitlements": ["pro"],
      "credits": { "currency": "tokens", "amount": 100, "rollover": "none" },
      "quota": [{ "limit": "ai_requests", "max": 500 }]
    },
    {
      "key": "tokens_100",
      "type": "consumable",
      "locales": { "en": { "name": "100 tokens", "description": "A pack of tokens" } },
      "plans": [{ "key": "once", "price": { "currency": "USD", "amount": 499 } }],
      "channels": { "ios": {}, "web": {} },
      "credits": { "currency": "tokens", "amount": 100 }
    }
  ]
}
```

`pro` gives the `pro` entitlement, 100 tokens each period and 500 AI requests a month; on the web its monthly plan costs 7.99 instead of 9.99. `tokens_100` gives 100 tokens each time it is bought.

## The catalog as a file

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:get --out catalog.json -E staging
```

It writes the newest revision and prints its number. Edit the file, then check it and save it on the revision it was edited from:

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:validate --file catalog.json -E staging
palbase purchases:catalog:put --file catalog.json --revision 3 -E staging
```

`validate` lists every problem with its path in the file (`products[0].channels.ios.locales.en.name`) and the store whose rule it breaks; it saves nothing. `put` checks the same way and saves nothing when a problem is left (`422 invalid_catalog`, every problem listed); a **warning** — something a store goes without — does not stop it. Of two people editing at once, the second is told the catalog moved past the revision they edited (`412 catalog_changed`) and nothing is saved over the first: read it again, make the edit on it, save that. The first save is on revision `0`.

Each environment's catalog is its own. To give `production` what `staging` has, get it from one and put it on the other's revision:

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:get --out catalog.json -E staging
palbase purchases:catalog:get -E production   # prints production's revision
palbase purchases:catalog:put --file catalog.json --revision 7 -E production
```

## Revisions, and putting one back

Every revision is kept. **Purchases › Catalog › Revisions** lists them, the newest first — who saved each, when, what it defines, and when a confirmed plan of it was written to the stores — and opens any of them. **Put this revision back** saves an older revision's catalog as the next revision, the way an edit is saved: on the revision on screen (`If-Match`; `412 catalog_changed` when someone saved since), checked against the catalog's rules today (an older revision may break one added since: `422 invalid_catalog`, every problem listed), and keeping what customers bought. Nothing is written to a store until a plan of the new revision is made and confirmed, as for any edit.

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:revisions -E production
palbase purchases:catalog:revision 4 --out catalog-4.json -E production
palbase purchases:catalog:restore 4 -E production   # saved as the next revision
palbase purchases:catalog:plan -E production        # then the stores
```

From a server: `GET /purchases/catalog/revisions` (`next_cursor`, sent back as `cursor`, is the next page), `GET /purchases/catalog/revisions/{revision}` and `POST /purchases/catalog/revisions/{revision}/restore` with `If-Match`.

A saved revision emits `purchases.catalog.changed`; one put back says which it came from (`restored_from`). See [`purchases:catalog:get`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescatalogget), [`purchases:catalog:put`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescatalogput) and [`purchases:catalog:validate`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescatalogvalidate).

## Bringing the stores to the catalog

A plan is what writing the newest revision to each store takes, worked out before anything is written:

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:plan -E staging
```

It prints each store's part, step by step, and the plan's **hash**. Read it, then write it by naming that hash:

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:confirm <plan id> --hash <hash> -E staging
```

The CLI shows what will be written and asks first, in every environment (`-y` confirms without asking); `palbase purchases:catalog:decline <plan id>` drops a plan unwritten. In Studio, **Purchases › Stores › Apply the catalog** plans it, shows each store's part, and writes it when you confirm.

| Store | What its part writes | What to know |
|---|---|---|
| Stripe | A product for each web product, a price for each plan, on the environment's [Stripe account](/docs/purchases/connect-stripe) — written as you confirm. | A Stripe price never changes: a new amount is a new price, which takes over the plan's lookup key, while customers on the old one keep paying it. |
| The App Store | A subscription group for each group, a subscription or an in-app purchase for each plan, with its text, price and introductory offer — written to App Store Connect with the environment's [App Store Connect API key](/docs/purchases/app-store#connect-the-app-store). | The price is the App Store's price point nearest to it in the currency's storefront; Apple prices the other storefronts. A product id, once made, is never free again. |
| Google Play | A subscription for each subscription product, with a base plan for each plan, and a one-time product for each other product — written for the app [Google Play purchases](/docs/purchases/google-play) are connected for. | Google converts the price to every region. A product id, once made, stays Google's. |

The plan's hash is its Stripe part's; with no Stripe account connected, its App Store part's; with neither, its Google Play part's. A plan is written only as it was shown: once the catalog is saved again, an older plan goes **stale** and is refused, and you plan again.

A plan writes only what changed since a store last took the catalog: a product it already has gets an update step with its new text, price or review details, and a product that did not change has no step. The App Store gives a subscription its new price from the day after tomorrow (UTC) on, in every storefront — App Store Connect schedules a price change a day or two ahead — and its subscribers keep the price they pay; an in-app purchase gets its new price at once; Google Play gives a base plan its new price for new subscribers. A language a store has that the catalog does not is left there. When a store did not answer a confirmed plan written — it stopped part way, or has not answered yet — what it holds of that plan's products is not known: the next plan writes each of them again, all of it, whatever changed.

The Stripe part is written as you confirm: the plan is **applied**, with what the account holds now, or **failed**, with what Stripe said — a new plan picks up where it stopped. The App Store and Google Play parts are written after the answer: the plan in Studio, and `palbase purchases:catalog:plan <plan id>`, show what App Store Connect and Google Play hold once they have answered — each product's state, its price, and a subscription's new price with the day it starts — and `palbase purchases:doctor` says when App Store Connect took its part. From the confirmation on, a purchase of what the plan sells maps to the catalog's product and plan. Each store's answer emits `purchases.catalog.applied`.

| Status | Means |
|---|---|
| `planned` | Shown, waiting to be confirmed or declined. |
| `applying` | Confirmed; a store's part is being written. |
| `applied` | Written. |
| `failed` | A store refused a step; plan again. |
| `stale` | The catalog was saved since: plan again. |
| `declined` | Never written. |

### What the stores know a plan by

| Store | Id |
|---|---|
| The App Store | `<product>.<plan>` (`pro.monthly`), each plan a product of its own; the group's reference name is the group's key. |
| Google Play | The product's key (`pro`) and, for a subscription, the plan's key as its base plan, `_` written `-` (`pro` / `monthly`). |
| Stripe | The price's lookup key `palbase:<ref>:<product>.<plan>`. The ref keeps two environments that share a Stripe account apart. |

`<product>.<plan>` is 40 characters at most.

### Products a store already sells

A product you made in App Store Connect or the Play Console, by hand or with another tool, joins the catalog by its id: give its plan the store's id under `store_ids`, and the plan **links** it — nothing is made or changed at the store.

```json
"channels": {
  "ios": { "store_ids": { "monthly": { "product": "com.acme.app.pro.monthly" } } },
  "android": { "store_ids": { "monthly": { "product": "pro_sub", "base_plan": "monthly-1" } } }
}
```

In Studio, a product's **iOS** and **Android** tabs hold these ids under **Sold at App Store Connect already** and **Sold at the Play Console already**. On Google Play a subscription's plans are base plans of one product: map every plan of it, to the same product. Once the plan is confirmed, the purchases made before the catalog knew the product open what the catalog gives, and their buyers hear `purchases.entitlement.changed`. A store id stays once a plan linked it: a catalog that leaves it out is refused (`store_id_kept`), because the next plan would make a second product at the store.

### What a customer bought stays

A product, a plan, an entitlement or a credit that someone holds cannot leave the catalog, and changing a key is leaving it: the save is refused (`product_has_buyers`, `plan_has_buyers`, `entitlement_has_holders`, `credit_has_holders`, `limit_has_holders`). A product a confirmed plan wrote to a store stays too (`product_at_store`): the store keeps selling it, to an older build of your app or from its own resubscribe button. To stop selling one, retire it: `"retired": true` on the product or on a plan — in Studio, the product's **On sale** switch, or a plan's **Off sale** box. A retired product is not offered, not sold on the web, not given an offer, and no plan writes it to a store, while everyone who bought it keeps what it gives. Renaming it keeps their access; it is the key that counts.

What a store never changes of a product it sells stays as it was made: its type, its subscription group and a plan's period (`store_terms_fixed`). Retire it and make a new one instead.

## The document

Unknown fields are refused: the catalog is read strictly.

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `base_locale` | The language every product names itself in (`en`, `pt-BR`); the others are translations. Stripe keeps one name: this one's. |
| `entitlements` | What a customer has or not: each a `key` and a `name`. |
| `credits` | The kinds of credit the project counts: each a `key`, a `name`, and `low_at`, the balance under which your backend hears `purchases.credits.low`. |
| `limits` | The metered quotas: each a `key`, a `name`, a `window` and `free`, what a customer gets with nothing that gives more. `overflow` (`{ "currency": "tokens", "per_unit": 2 }`) spends credits past the limit instead of refusing. |
| `products` | The products (below). |
| `offers` | Discounts, trials and grants for a while: see [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers). |

A key is lowercase letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, 40 at most.

A limit's `window` is `calendar_month` or `calendar_day` — from midnight in the project's time zone ([settings](/docs/purchases/customers#settings)) — or `billing_period`: the period of the subscription that gives it, a calendar month without one.

### A product

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `key` | Its key. |
| `type` | `subscription` (renews until canceled), `non_consumable` (bought once, kept), `consumable` (bought again and again: it gives credits) or `non_renewing` (a period bought once). |
| `locales` | Its `name` and `description` by language: the base locale's at least. |
| `plans` | How it is paid for (below): a subscription's plans, one plan for anything else. |
| `channels` | Where it is sold — `ios`, `android`, `web` — each with what is its own there; `{}` when it is sold there as it is. At least one. |
| `entitlements` | The entitlements it gives. A consumable gives none. |
| `credits` | The credits it gives: per purchase for a consumable, per period for a subscription — `{ "currency", "amount" }`, and for a subscription `rollover`: `none` (a period's credits end with it) or `all` (they stay). Credits bought never end. |
| `quota` | How much of each limit it gives in each window: `[{ "limit", "max" }]`. A customer holding several products gets the largest. |
| `group`, `tier` | A subscription's group — the subscriptions a customer moves between — and its level in it, 1 or more, higher is more. The App Store sells every subscription in a group. |
| `retired` | Off sale: [what a customer bought stays](#what-a-customer-bought-stays). A plan can be retired on its own. |

### A plan

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `key` | Its key. |
| `price` | `{ "currency": "USD", "amount": 999 }`: the amount in the currency's minor units (999 is 9.99). Each store prices the other currencies its own way; `overrides` (`{ "EUR": 999 }`) sets amounts by hand. |
| `period` | A subscription's billing period, ISO 8601: `P1W`, `P1M`, `P2M`, `P3M`, `P6M`, `P1Y` in every store; Google Play also sells `P4W`, `P4M`, `P8M`; Stripe bills at most once a year. |
| `duration` | A non-renewing product's: how long it lasts (`P1M`). |
| `intro` | A subscription plan's introductory offer, once per customer across every channel: `mode` `free_trial`, `pay_as_you_go` (a `price` for a number of `periods`) or `pay_up_front` (one `price` for the whole `duration`; the web sells the plan without it). The App Store's free trials last `P3D`, `P1W`, `P2W`, `P1M`, `P2M`, `P3M`, `P6M` or `P1Y`. |

### A channel

| Field | Channel | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `locales` | any | Its own text, field by field, where a store's limits call for it: `name`, `description`, and Google Play's `benefits`. |
| `prices` | any | Its own price for a plan, by the plan's key: a web price without the stores' commission. |
| `family_shareable` | `ios` | Family Sharing for the purchase. |
| `review` | `ios` | What App Review sees: a `note` and the `screenshot` of the product in the app. |
| `store_ids` | `ios`, `android` | The store's own ids of the plans, by plan key: [products a store already sells](#products-a-store-already-sells). |
| `tax_code` | `web` | Stripe's tax code for the product. |

### Review screenshots

The App Store reviews every product with a screenshot and a note: without them the catalog warns (`review_missing`). Upload the screenshot, a PNG or JPEG at one of the App Store's screenshot sizes (1290x2796 for a 6.9-inch iPhone, 2064x2752 for a 13-inch iPad, or turned) — Apple fails any other size — and name it by the SHA-256 the command prints:

```sh
palbase stores:review-screenshot <app id> pro-paywall.png -E main
```

```json
"ios": { "review": { "screenshot": "sha256:9f86d081…", "note": "Settings → Pro" } }
```

In Studio, the product's **iOS** tab uploads it (**Review screenshot › Upload**) and names it for you. The next plan gives both to App Store Connect, and the product is then `READY_TO_SUBMIT`: it goes to App Review [with a version](/docs/distribution/app-store#send-it-to-app-review). A changed screenshot replaces Apple's.

## The stores' rules

`validate` checks each channel against its store, and a rule one store has is a problem on that channel alone — never a silent cut:

| Store | Its rules |
|---|---|
| The App Store | A name of 2 to 30 characters, a description of 45 at most; no emoji or symbols in a subscription's name; the six periods above; every subscription in a group. |
| Google Play | A name of 55 characters at most, a description of 200, 4 benefits of 40 characters each. |
| Stripe | A period of a year at most; a pay-up-front introductory offer is left out on the web (a warning). |

When the shared text is too long for one store, give that channel its own (`"ios": { "locales": { "en": { "name": "Pro Family" } } }`): the other channels keep the full text.

# App Store

The catalog's `ios` products are sold in the App Store with StoreKit 2: the app buys through `PalbasePurchases`, Apple takes the payment, and the environment verifies each transaction with Apple and keeps it in the ledger. Apple's App Store Server Notifications bring renewals, cancellations, billing issues and refunds to the environment, with the app closed.

An environment that sells in the App Store holds two of Apple's keys:

| Key | Made in App Store Connect | What the environment does with it |
|---|---|---|
| **App Store Connect API key** | **Users and Access › Integrations › App Store Connect API**, role App Manager | Writes the catalog to App Store Connect, points the app's server notifications at the environment, and runs the readiness checks. It is the same key Studio's **App Distribution** connects, for TestFlight and releases. |
| **In-App Purchase key** | **Users and Access › Integrations › In-App Purchase** | Verifies the app's purchases, reads its subscriptions from Apple, and signs promotional offers. |

Each goes from your computer (or a page of the environment's) straight to the environment, never through Studio.

## Connect the App Store

**1. Register the iOS app** with its bundle in the environment, if it is not yet — [iOS SDK › Connect the app to the project](/docs/ios/overview#connect-the-app-to-the-project):

```sh
palbase apps:create ios "Shop" --slug shop --team-id ABCDE12345
palbase apps:env:set shop --bundle com.example.shop -E staging
```

**2. Connect the App Store Connect API key:**

```sh
palbase stores:apple:connect --key-file AuthKey_ABC123DEF4.p8 --issuer-id 57246542-96fe-1a63-e053-0824d011072a -E staging
```

**3. Connect the In-App Purchase key**, for the app:

```sh
palbase purchases:apple:connect --key-file SubscriptionKey_XYZ987WVU6.p8 --app shop -E staging
```

Apple is asked, with a call that changes nothing, whether it takes the key for the app; then the environment keeps it, and has App Store Connect send the app's notifications — sandbox and production — to the environment's address. The key's id is read from the file's name, and the issuer is the one step 2 connected. In Studio, **Purchases › App Store** connects it. `--print-link` prints a link that takes the key in a browser instead, once, for 30 minutes. A key connected again replaces the one before.

**4. Bring App Store Connect to the catalog:** plan the catalog and confirm it ([Catalog › Bringing the stores to the catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog#bringing-the-stores-to-the-catalog)). Your subscription groups, subscriptions and in-app purchases are created in App Store Connect, with their text, prices and introductory offers.

**5. Check what selling still needs:**

```sh
palbase purchases:doctor -E staging
```

Apple is asked now. Each line is one check — ✓ holds, ✗ does not, `i` only informs — with the command or the place in App Store Connect that fixes it, and the command exits 1 until every check that is not informational holds. Studio's **Purchases › App Store** shows the same list.

| Check | Holds when |
|---|---|
| The In-App Purchase key | Apple takes it for the app. |
| Where the App Store reports | App Store Connect sends the app's notifications to this environment. |
| The TEST notification | Apple's TEST notification arrived: the address works. |
| The catalog confirmed | The newest revision of the catalog was confirmed for the stores. |
| The catalog in App Store Connect | App Store Connect holds that revision's products, each step's error said when it does not. |
| Test purchases | Informs: what test purchases open here ([settings](/docs/purchases/customers#settings)). |
| Xcode's purchases | Informs: whether Xcode's StoreKit Testing purchases are taken ([Test Apple Purchases](/docs/purchases/testing-apple)). |

When the app's notifications already go to another server, the environment does not take them over: the check says so. Clear both addresses in App Store Connect (**Apps › the app › App Information › App Store Server Notifications**), then run `palbase purchases:apple:connect` again.

`palbase purchases:apple` shows the connection as it is: the app, the key's id, the app's Apple ID once known, and where the App Store reports — never the key.

## Buying in the app

The app links `PalbasePurchases`, and `PalbasePurchasesUI` for paywalls drawn natively. `pb.purchases.products()` returns the catalog's iOS plans as the App Store has them for this user; `purchase(_:)` buys one; `restore()` is the user's own "Restore purchases". The SDK names the customer to StoreKit with their `appAccountToken`, reports each transaction to the environment and finishes it only once the environment has it, and listens to StoreKit's updates for whoever is signed in — so a renewal, an approved Ask to Buy or an interrupted purchase is reported too. See [iOS › Purchases](/docs/ios/purchases), and [Test Apple Purchases](/docs/purchases/testing-apple) for the whole flow in Xcode and the sandbox.

When `products()` returns fewer products than the catalog sells on iOS, its `diagnosis` says which and the likely causes: a product not ready in App Store Connect, the Paid Apps agreement not active, a bundle id that is not the project's, a StoreKit configuration file that lacks them. `palbase purchases:doctor` checks each.

## What the environment does with a transaction

**It verifies it.** A transaction counts only as the App Store signed it, for the connected app, in the sandbox or production. A subscription's state is never taken from the device: it is read from Apple with the environment's key. One sent again applies nothing twice.

**It gives it to a customer.** A purchase nobody has is the customer's its `appAccountToken` names, or the reporting customer's; one another customer has stays theirs, unless one of two things moves it:

- **A new purchase on it** — a switch of plan, a resubscription, an offer bought — whose `appAccountToken` names another customer moves it to them, whoever reports it, the app or Apple's notification. On an Apple ID shared among the app's accounts (a family's iPhone), the subscription follows who paid, and so does the offer it was bought with. A purchase with no token, a renewal, and a transaction reported again or late move nothing.
- **A restore** moves a purchase to the restoring customer only from the device StoreKit signed it for, and never from an account to a guest.

A purchase moves at most 3 times in 30 days, restores and new purchases counted together. A restore, or a customer's own new purchase, that leaves a purchase where it was is refused with `403 restore_not_this_device`, `403 restore_account_owned` or `409 restore_limit`, after the rest of it is applied. A move emits `purchases.ownership.transferred`, whose `via` is `purchase` or `restore`.

**It follows Apple.** A notification about a purchase applies what Apple signed — the transaction, the renewal info, the subscription's status — and the newest by Apple's time is the state. A refund, a revoked Family Sharing purchase or a chargeback turns the entitlement off and takes back the credits it gave (`purchases.refund.changed`). A subscription the App Store could not renew keeps its access through Apple's grace period, with `billing_issue` on the entitlement.

**Production waits for the app's Apple ID.** Production purchases and notifications are taken once the app's Apple ID is known; the environment reads it when it sets the notification address.

## Offers and offer codes

A catalog offer on an iOS subscription is written to App Store Connect as a **promotional offer**, and the app buys with it — `purchase(_:offer:)` — under a signature the environment makes with the In-App Purchase key: no key is ever in the app. An **App Store offer code** is a coupon of Apple's, redeemed in the App Store's own sheet. See [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers).

## Buying on the web from the iOS app

In the App Store's United States storefront, an app may link out to buy on the web beside In-App Purchase (App Review Guideline 3.1.1(a)). The SDK opens Stripe Checkout there for the signed-in customer and records the link with the checkout. See [Web › From a native app](/docs/purchases/web#from-a-native-app).

## Disconnecting

```sh
palbase purchases:apple:disconnect -E staging
```

The environment forgets the In-App Purchase key: the App Store's notifications and the app's reports are refused from then on, and purchases already made stay in the ledger. It emits `purchases.store.changed`, as connecting does.

# Test Apple Purchases

There are two ways to buy your app's products before anyone pays for them. Both use the catalog you already have, and Palbase writes nothing into your Xcode project.

| | A. In Xcode | B. In the App Store sandbox |
|---|---|---|
| What sells the product | Xcode, from a file made from your catalog | The App Store, with your products in App Store Connect |
| What you need from Apple | Nothing | A developer account, its agreements, two keys, a sandbox tester |
| Where it runs | Simulator or a device, run from Xcode | A device (or TestFlight) |
| Steps | **5**, about two minutes | **7**, the first time |
| Use it for | Building the paywall, every purchase flow, renewals in seconds | The last check before release: real App Store products, real server notifications |

Start with A. Move to B once your products are in App Store Connect.

Both run against a **test environment** of your project (`staging`, say), never the production one: production takes only purchases the App Store itself signed.

In Studio, **Purchases › App Store** shows the environment's In-App Purchase key, the readiness list, Xcode's certificate and the team's sandbox testers: each step below that has a command can be done there too.

## A. In Xcode, with no App Store (5 steps)

**1. Make the StoreKit file from your catalog.**

```sh
palbase purchases:storekit -E staging
```

It reads the environment's iOS offerings and writes one file, `palbase/environments/staging/<app>.storekit`: every iOS plan as the App Store product its store id names, with its text in each language the catalog has, its price, its subscription group and level, and its introductory offer. Nothing outside `palbase/` is written.

**2. Point the scheme at it.** In Xcode, **Product › Scheme › Edit Scheme… › Run › Options › StoreKit Configuration**, choose the file. If it is not listed, add it from that same menu.

**3. Save Xcode's certificate.** Select the `.storekit` file in the Project navigator, then **Editor › Save Public Certificate**. Purchases in this mode are signed by Xcode, not by Apple, with this certificate.

**4. Let the environment take Xcode's purchases.**

```sh
palbase purchases:apple:xcode-certificate ~/Desktop/StoreKitTestCertificate.cer -E staging
```

The environment now takes purchases signed with that certificate and records them as test purchases. Studio does the same under **Purchases › App Store › Xcode StoreKit Testing**. On the production environment both refuse.

**5. Run the app and buy.** Xcode shows its own payment sheet; no Apple account is asked for. The customer has the entitlement as soon as the app reports the purchase:

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:get <user id> -E staging
```

### When the catalog changes

Run `palbase purchases:storekit -E staging` again. The same catalog makes the same file. What you set from Xcode's **Editor** menu while the file is open (the storefront, the subscription renewal rate, Ask to Buy, an error to force) is kept.

The prices are in one storefront's currency: the price you entered, or the amount you set by hand for that currency. `--storefront DEU` makes the file for another storefront; a plan with no price in its currency keeps its own amount, and the command says which.

### Renewals, refunds and errors

- **Renewals in seconds:** open the `.storekit` file and choose **Editor › Subscription Renewal Rate**.
- **Refund, expire, cancel a purchase:** while the app runs, **Debug › StoreKit › Manage Transactions…**, select the transaction, then **Refund Purchase**. StoreKit hands the refunded transaction to the app, the app reports it, and the entitlement turns off as it would after an App Store refund.
- **Ask to Buy, failed payments, StoreKit errors:** the **Editor** menu of the open `.storekit` file.

## B. In the App Store sandbox (7 steps)

**1. Connect App Store Connect.** In App Store Connect, **Users and Access › Integrations › App Store Connect API**, make a key with the App Manager role and download it once.

```sh
palbase stores:apple:connect --key-file AuthKey_ABC123DEF4.p8 --issuer-id 57246542-96fe-1a63-e053-0824d011072a -E staging
```

Studio connects it under **App Distribution**.

**2. Connect the In-App Purchase key.** In the same place, the **In-App Purchase** tab, make a key. The environment verifies purchases and reads subscriptions with it.

```sh
palbase purchases:apple:connect --key-file SubscriptionKey_XYZ987WVU6.p8 -E staging
```

The issuer is the one step 1 connected; the key's id is read from the file's name. Studio connects it under **Purchases › App Store**. Both keys go from your computer straight to the environment, never through Studio.

**3. Put the catalog in App Store Connect.** In Studio, **Purchases › Stores**, plan the stores and confirm the plan; or from a terminal:

```sh
palbase purchases:catalog:plan -E staging
palbase purchases:catalog:confirm <plan id> --hash <hash> -E staging
```

Your products, subscription groups, prices and introductory offers are created in App Store Connect, and what Apple holds of each is shown under the plan. Apple can take up to an hour to show a new product in the sandbox.

**4. Check everything is ready.**

```sh
palbase purchases:doctor -E staging
```

Each line is one check: ✓ holds, ✗ does not, and `i` only says how things are. Under each ✗ is the command or the place in App Store Connect that fixes it. Run it again until every ✗ is gone. Studio's **Purchases › App Store** shows the same list.

**5. Make a sandbox tester.** In App Store Connect, **Users and Access › Sandbox**, click **+**, and give a name, an email address that is not an Apple Account yet, a password and a country or region.

**6. Sign in on the device.** Run the app from Xcode with the scheme's **StoreKit Configuration** set to **None**, and start a purchase. When the App Store asks you to sign in, use the tester. From then on the tester is under **Settings › Developer › Sandbox Apple Account**; your own Apple Account stays signed in.

**7. Buy.** The App Store's sheet says **[Environment: Sandbox]**. Nothing is charged. Apple's server notification about the purchase reaches the environment too; it is still one purchase.

### Renewals, history and interruptions

A sandbox subscription renews on a short clock and stops after 12 renewals. Make it faster:

```sh
palbase stores:apple:sandbox-testers -E staging
palbase stores:apple:sandbox-testers:set tester@example.com --renewal 3m -E staging
```

To buy the same products again, or to be eligible for an introductory offer again, clear the tester's history:

```sh
palbase stores:apple:sandbox-testers:clear tester@example.com -E staging
```

Then sign out of the sandbox account on the device and in again. `--interrupt on` makes the tester's next purchases stop halfway, as when a bank asks for a confirmation. Studio's **Purchases › App Store › Sandbox testers** changes the same settings and clears the same history.

The device has the same settings under **Settings › Developer › Sandbox Apple Account › Manage**.

### Refunds

Ask for one from the app, with StoreKit's refund sheet (`refundRequestSheet(for:isPresented:)` in SwiftUI). In the sandbox, any reason approves the refund. For a declined one, choose **Other** and type `DECLINE`; for a partial one, `GRANT_PRORATED`. The entitlement turns off and the refund's event reaches your backend.

## The app's code

The same code runs in both ways; StoreKit decides where the purchase goes. `pb` is the app's `PalbaseClient`.

```swift
import Palbase
import PalbasePurchases
import SwiftUI

struct Paywall: View {
    @State private var products: [Purchases.StoreProduct] = []
    @State private var isPro = false
    @State private var message = ""

    var body: some View {
        List {
            ForEach(products) { p in
                Button("\(p.product.displayName) — \(p.product.displayPrice)") {
                    Task { await buy(p) }
                }
            }
            Button("Restore purchases") {
                Task { isPro = (try? await pb.purchases.restore())?.isEntitled("pro") ?? isPro }
            }
            Text(isPro ? "Pro is on" : message)
        }
        .task { products = (try? await pb.purchases.products())?.products ?? [] }
        .task {
            // Kept current: a purchase on another device, a renewal, a refund.
            for await info in pb.purchases.customerInfoUpdates {
                isPro = info?.isEntitled("pro") ?? false
            }
        }
    }

    private func buy(_ product: Purchases.StoreProduct) async {
        do {
            switch try await pb.purchases.purchase(product) {
            case .purchased(let info): isPro = info.isEntitled("pro")
            case .alreadyEntitled(_, let entitlement, _): message = "\(entitlement) is already yours, bought elsewhere"
            case .pending: message = "Waiting for approval"
            case .cancelled: break
            }
        } catch {
            message = "\(error)"
        }
    }
}
```

`products()` returns only what the App Store (or Xcode) has. When some of the catalog's iOS products are missing, `products()` says why in `diagnosis`: a product id Xcode's file or App Store Connect does not have, or a bundle id that is not the app's.

## On your server

Check the entitlement where the content is served, not only in the app:

```ts
// src/modules/premium/premium.controller.ts
import { Controller, Forbidden, Get, Palbase, User, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { isEntitled } from "palbase/server";

@Controller("/premium")
export class PremiumController {
  @Get("")
  async premium(@User() user: UserT): Promise<{ pro: true }> {
    // A user who has bought nothing is read as a customer with nothing.
    const { data } = await Palbase.purchases.getCustomer({ path: { customer_id: user.id } });
    if (!isEntitled(data, "pro")) throw new Forbidden("Pro is needed", "entitlement_required");
    return { pro: true };
  }
}
```

And act when something changes, with a typed event:

```ts
// src/modules/premium/purchase-events.ts
import { Log, On, type PlatformEvent } from "palbase/backend";

export class PurchaseEvents {
  @On("purchases.entitlement.changed")
  changed(event: PlatformEvent<"purchases.entitlement.changed">): void {
    const { customer_id, entitlement, active, is_sandbox } = event.data;
    Log.info("entitlement changed", { customer_id, entitlement, active, test: is_sandbox });
  }

  @On("purchases.refund.changed")
  refunded(event: PlatformEvent<"purchases.refund.changed">): void {
    Log.info("payment taken back", { customer_id: event.data.customer_id, share: event.data.share_milli / 1000 });
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/modules/premium/premium.module.ts
import { Module } from "palbase/backend";
import { PremiumController } from "./premium.controller";
import { PurchaseEvents } from "./purchase-events";

@Module({ controllers: [PremiumController], providers: [PurchaseEvents] })
export class PremiumModule {}
```

A test purchase is marked: `is_sandbox` is `true` in its events and in what the customer has.

## When something is missing

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `products()` is empty in Xcode | The scheme has no StoreKit Configuration, or the file is older than the catalog: run `palbase purchases:storekit` again. |
| The purchase works in Xcode but the customer has nothing | The environment does not take Xcode's certificate yet: step A4. |
| `products()` is empty on a device | `palbase purchases:doctor` names it: the catalog is not in App Store Connect yet, an agreement is not signed, or the product is less than an hour old. |
| No **[Environment: Sandbox]** on the sheet | The scheme still points at the `.storekit` file: set it to **None** (B6). |
| The tester cannot buy again | Clear its history (`palbase stores:apple:sandbox-testers:clear`), then sign out and in on the device. |
