<!-- ===== purchases/google-play ===== -->

# Google Play

The catalog's `android` products are sold on Google Play with Play Billing: the app buys through `palbase-purchases`, Google takes the payment, and the environment reads each purchase from Play, keeps it in the ledger and acknowledges it. Play's real-time developer notifications tell the environment when a purchase changes — a renewal, a cancellation, a refund — with the app closed.

No key changes hands. Palbase makes a service account for the environment, your Play Console invites it, and the environment reads and acknowledges the app's purchases as that account.

## Connect Google Play

**1. Register the Android app** with its package and signing certificates in the environment, if it is not yet — [Android SDK › Registering the app](/docs/android/overview#registering-the-app):

```sh
palbase apps:create android "Shop" --slug shop-android
palbase apps:env:set shop-android --package com.example.shop --sha256 play_signing=AB:CD:… -E staging
```

**2. Connect the environment to Google Play:**

```sh
palbase stores:google:connect -E staging
```

It prints the service account Palbase made. In Play Console, **Users and permissions**, invite it with the app and, for purchases, **View financial data** and **Manage orders and subscriptions**. Link the Android app to Google Play (`palbase stores:apps:link <app id>`), then check what the account reaches:

```sh
palbase stores:google:check -E staging
```

Studio's **App Distribution** does the same.

**3. Sell on Google Play in the app:**

```sh
palbase purchases:google:connect --app shop-android -E staging
```

Palbase makes the app's notifications topic, which Play's own account may publish to, and has it pushed to this environment's address. It prints the topic. In Studio, **Purchases › Stores › Google Play purchases** connects it and shows the topic.

**4. Name the topic in Play Console:** **Monetize with Play › Monetization setup › Real-time developer notifications**, paste the topic, **Save**, then **Send test notification**.

```sh
palbase purchases:google -E staging
```

It says when the test notification arrived — the topic is set — and what is left to do. Every environment of the project that sells in the app reads the same topic.

**5. Bring Google Play to the catalog:** plan the catalog and confirm it ([Catalog › Bringing the stores to the catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog#bringing-the-stores-to-the-catalog)). Each subscription product is created on Play with a base plan per plan, each other product as a one-time product, for the app connected in step 3.

## Buying in the app

The app takes `studio.palbase:palbase-purchases`, which brings Play Billing with it. `pb.purchases.products()` returns the catalog's Android plans as Play has them for this user — a subscription once per base plan — with a `diagnosis` when Play returned fewer than the catalog sells; `purchase(activity, product)` opens Play's purchase sheet; `restore()` is the user's own "Restore purchases". Touch `pb.purchases` at launch: what Play holds unreported — a report that failed, a pending purchase since paid, one made outside the app — is reported then. See [Android › Purchases](/docs/android/purchases).

Buying a subscription while the customer has another plan of its group on Play replaces it, as `PlanChange` says: by default an upgrade now and a downgrade at the renewal, as Google recommends.

## What the environment does with a purchase

**It reads it from Play.** Nothing of the device's word is taken: each purchase is read from Play by its token, as the environment's service account, and applied to the ledger. One reported again applies nothing twice.

**It gives it to a customer.** A purchase nobody has is the customer's its obfuscated account id names — the SDK buys with it, and nothing personal goes to Google — or the reporting customer's. Play makes each new purchase a purchase token of its own, so what each of the app's accounts buys on a Google account they share is theirs from the start. One another customer has stays theirs, unless restored: a restore moves it to the restoring customer, never from an account to a guest, and at most 3 times in 30 days. A purchase that stays where it was is answered, after the rest is applied, with `403 restore_account_owned` (a guest restoring an account's), `403 restore_other_account` (another account's obfuscated id names it: sign in to that account), `403 restore_other_environment` (another environment of the project made it) or `409 restore_limit`.

**It acknowledges it** once the ledger has it, and consumes a consumable: the SDK never does. Play refunds a purchase not acknowledged in three days. A purchase the catalog does not map gives nothing and is not acknowledged.

**It follows Play.** A notification only says something changed: the purchase is read again from Play, and a voided one from the app's voided purchases. A refund turns the entitlement off and takes back the credits it gave (`purchases.refund.changed`).

**Test purchases** are Google Play's license testers': `is_sandbox`, opening entitlements as the [settings](/docs/purchases/customers#settings) say.

## Offers

A catalog offer on an Android subscription is written to Play as a developer-determined offer of the subscription's base plans, tagged `palbase`. The Android SDK buys a plan with its introductory offer when the catalog's plan has one and Play says the user may take it. See [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers).

## Disconnecting

```sh
palbase purchases:google:disconnect -E staging
```

Play's notifications stop reaching the environment and the app's reports are refused; purchases already made stay in the ledger. The app's topic stays, for the other environments that read it. `palbase stores:google:disconnect` deletes the environment's service account at Google: Play Console's invite of it then reaches nothing.

Connecting, a test notification arriving and disconnecting each emit `purchases.store.changed`.

## Related

- [Android › Purchases](/docs/android/purchases): `pb.purchases` in a Kotlin app
- [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog) · [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers)
- [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements): checking access on your server
- CLI: [`stores:google:connect`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-storesgoogleconnect), [`purchases:google:connect`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasesgoogleconnect), [`purchases:google`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasesgoogle)

# Connect Stripe

Your project sells its catalog on the web through your own Stripe account: Checkout, the customer portal, renewals and refunds all happen on it, and Palbase keeps each user's access in your app in step with them. Connect the account once per environment.

There are two ways. Use the first.

| | A. With one click | B. With a restricted key |
|---|---|---|
| What you do | Pick the account at Stripe and accept | Make a restricted key in the Stripe Dashboard and paste it |
| What Palbase holds | The access of Palbase's Stripe App, *Subscriptions by Palbase* | The key |
| Where Stripe's events go | Palbase's own endpoint, for every account that installed the App | An endpoint Palbase makes on your account |
| How to stop | Disconnect in Studio; uninstall the App in the Stripe Dashboard | Disconnect in Studio |

## A. With one click (Palbase's Stripe App)

**1. Open the environment's Stripe account.** In Studio, open the project and the environment, then **Purchases › Stores** and its Stripe account panel, and choose **Connect with one click**. From the command line:

```sh
palbase purchases:stripe:install -E staging
```

**2. Choose the mode.** Test mode sells in Stripe's sandbox, live mode takes real payments (`--live` on the command line). Connect a test environment in test mode first.

**3. Open Palbase's install page.** It names the Palbase project and environment the account will be connected to, then sends you to Stripe. The link works once, for 30 minutes.

**4. Pick the Stripe account and accept.** Stripe lists the accounts you can install apps on and shows what the App may do: write products, prices, customers, Checkout Sessions, subscriptions, customer portal sessions, coupons and promotion codes; read invoices, payment intents, charges, refunds, disputes and events. Coupons carry your offers' discounts to the web, and promotion codes your coupon codes. Accept, and Stripe sends you back to Palbase, which connects the account and says so.

**5. Check it.** Studio shows the account as active, connected through Palbase's Stripe App:

```sh
palbase purchases:stripe -E staging
```

Then bring the account to your catalog (Studio's catalog page, or `palbase purchases:catalog:plan` and `palbase purchases:catalog:confirm`): Palbase creates the catalog's products and prices on the account.

Nothing is made on your account for Stripe's events: they come to Palbase through the App.

## B. With a restricted key

In Studio, **Purchases › Stores** and its Stripe account panel, choose **Use a restricted key instead**, or run `palbase purchases:stripe:grant`. Make a restricted key in the Stripe Dashboard (**Developers › API keys › Create restricted key**) with **Write** on Products, Prices, Customers, Checkout Sessions, Customer portal, Subscriptions, Coupons, Promotion Codes and Webhook Endpoints, and **Read** on Invoices, Payment Intents, Charges, Disputes, Events and Account; open the page Palbase gives you and paste it there. Without Coupons and Promotion Codes the key still connects, but your offers' web discounts and your coupon codes cannot reach the account. A key that cannot read its account is refused with `422 stripe_permission_missing`, and so is one missing a permission Palbase checks for — the answer names it. The key goes from that page straight to Palbase, never through Studio. A secret key that can do anything is refused.

## Disconnecting

**Disconnect** in Studio stops selling through the account; purchases already made stay. With the App, uninstall it from the account too in the Stripe Dashboard (**Settings › Installed apps**); uninstalling it alone disconnects every environment connected through it.

## Related

- [Web](/docs/purchases/web): selling on the web with `pb.purchases` — Checkout, the customer portal, redemption links
- [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog): the products and prices a plan writes to the account
- [Purchases](/docs/purchases/overview): how the catalog, the stores and the customers fit together



<!-- ===== purchases/web ===== -->

# Web

The catalog's `web` products are sold through the environment's own Stripe account: Stripe Checkout takes the payment, Stripe's customer portal manages what was bought, and Stripe's events keep the ledger current — renewals, cancellations, refunds, disputes. Connect the account first: [Connect Stripe](/docs/purchases/connect-stripe).

In a browser, `pb.purchases` — the `palbase/web` client's purchases module — reads the offerings, opens Checkout and the portal, and keeps what the signed-in customer has current. Every call here takes the publishable key; what is the customer's takes their session too.

## Quick example

A pricing page: the web's plans with their prices, a button that buys one, and the page kept in step with what the customer has.

```ts
// app/pricing.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";
import { formatPrice } from "palbase/web/paywall";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

/** Every plan the web sells, priced in the catalog's currency. */
export async function plans(locale: string): Promise<{ product: string; plan: string; label: string }[]> {
  const { products } = await pb.purchases.offerings("web");
  return products.flatMap((p) =>
    (p.channels.web?.plans ?? []).map((plan) => ({
      product: p.key,
      plan: plan.key,
      label: `${p.channels.web?.locales[locale]?.name ?? p.key} — ${formatPrice(plan.price.amount, plan.price.currency, locale)}`,
    })),
  );
}

export async function buy(product: string, plan: string): Promise<void> {
  const url = await pb.purchases.checkout({
    product,
    plan,
    successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks",
    cancelUrl: "https://app.example.com/pricing",
  });
  location.assign(url);
}

// Told what the customer has once it is read, then whenever it changes; null while no one is signed in.
export const stop = pb.purchases.onCustomerInfo((info) => {
  document.body.dataset.pro = String(info?.entitlements["pro"]?.active === true);
});
```

## The offerings

`pb.purchases.offerings(channel)` is the catalog as a paywall shows it — each product's text in every language, its plans and their prices on a channel (the web's unless another is named), and the id each store sells a plan by. Nobody's purchases are in it: the publishable key reads it with no one signed in. Amounts are in the currency's minor units (`999` is 9.99); `formatPrice(amount, currency, locale)` from `palbase/web/paywall` writes one as the language writes it.

## Buying

`pb.purchases.checkout({ product, plan, successUrl, cancelUrl })` opens a Stripe Checkout session for one of the catalog's web plans, at its price on the environment's Stripe account, and answers its URL: send the buyer there. Stripe sends them back to `successUrl` once they paid, or to `cancelUrl`.

Both addresses go back to one of the project's registered apps — a web app's origin (`palbase apps:env:set <app> --origin https://app.example.com`), or a native app's own scheme — and nowhere else.

With a customer signed in — a guest too — the purchase is theirs once Stripe reports it, and `onCustomerInfo` hears it then: the success page shows the change when it arrives, not before.

| Refusal | Why |
|---|---|
| `409 already_entitled` | The customer already has the product, or a subscription of its group, from any store. Nothing is charged twice; the error's body names the `store` it is managed in. Credits can always be bought again. |
| `429 too_many_checkouts` | Checkouts are limited per address and per project with the publishable key alone, per customer and per address with a session. |

A free trial is given once per customer, across every channel — and on the web not to a guest, nor to a buyer with no account.

### A buyer with no account

With no one signed in, the buyer is no one yet: Checkout asks their email, and what they buy waits for the app user who redeems it. Put `{CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}` in `successUrl` — Stripe writes the session's id there — and the success page asks for the purchase's **redemption link**:

```ts
// app/thanks.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

// successUrl was "https://app.example.com/thanks?session={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}".
const session = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("session");
if (session) {
  // Stripe may not have told of the payment yet: it is asked again for up to 20 seconds.
  const link = await pb.purchases.redemptionLink(session);
  document.querySelector("#redeem")!.setAttribute("href", link.url);
}
```

The link works once, within an hour; the buyer is emailed one too. Opened on a phone, its page hands it to the app (`<scheme>://palbase/redeem?token=…`); opened on a computer, it shows a QR code to scan with the phone. The app — signed in, or a guest — redeems it, and the purchase is that customer's:

```ts
// app/redeem.ts
import { createClient, PalbaseError } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function redeem(link: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const info = await pb.purchases.redeem(link);
    return info.entitlements["pro"]?.active ? "Pro is yours" : "Redeemed";
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof PalbaseError && e.code === "redemption_expired") {
      // Past its hour: a new link goes to the buyer's email, once.
      const resent = (e.body as { resent?: boolean } | undefined)?.resent === true;
      return resent ? "That link expired: a new one is on its way to your email" : "That link expired";
    }
    if (e instanceof PalbaseError && e.code === "already_redeemed") return "That link was used already";
    throw e;
  }
}
```

`redemptionLink` keeps the key it needs in the tab's `sessionStorage` from the checkout on; the redirect to Stripe and back keeps it. Each call makes a new link, ten at most within an hour of the payment; past it, the email's is the one. Your server can make one for a buyer whose email went astray, with the secret key (`createCheckoutRedemption`, any time).

## What the customer has

`pb.purchases.me()` reads everything the signed-in customer has now — entitlements, subscriptions, one-time purchases, credits, quota use — whatever store they bought in. The first read makes the user a customer.

`pb.purchases.onCustomerInfo(listener)` tells the listener once it is read, then each time it changes — a purchase in any store, a renewal or its end, a refund, credits spent — and `null` while no one is signed in; it answers the function that stops it. The first listener joins the customer's own realtime channel, the last one's stop leaves it. A new user signing in is read anew.

What a page shows from it is for the page. The content a purchase opens is served by your server, which checks the entitlement itself: [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements).

## Managing what was bought

```ts
// app/account.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function manage(): Promise<void> {
  const info = await pb.purchases.me();
  const pro = info.entitlements["pro"];
  if (pro?.manage?.store === "stripe") {
    location.assign(await pb.purchases.portal("https://app.example.com/account"));
  } else if (pro?.manage?.url) {
    location.assign(pro.manage.url); // the App Store's or Google Play's own page
  }
}
```

`portal(returnUrl)` opens Stripe's customer portal for the signed-in customer, where they change, cancel or renew what they bought on the web and how they pay. A subscription bought in the App Store or on Google Play is managed there: its `manage.url` is the store's page.

## A paywall on the web

`pb.purchases.paywall(placement)` is the paywall the project published at a placement — designed in Studio, drawn by the SDK — and `render()` puts it in the page:

```ts
// app/upgrade.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function showPaywall(container: HTMLElement): Promise<void> {
  const paywall = await pb.purchases.paywall("settings", { attributes: { plan: "free" } });
  if (!paywall) return; // the web sells nothing
  const view = paywall.render(container, {
    successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks",
    cancelUrl: "https://app.example.com/settings",
    links: { terms: "https://example.com/terms", privacy: "https://example.com/privacy" },
    onClose: () => view.destroy(),
  });
}
```

Its purchase button opens Checkout for the package selected. The web has no restore button: a web purchase is the account's, wherever it signs in. See [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls).

## Offers and coupons

`pb.purchases.offers()` lists the catalog's offers the signed-in customer may take now. A discount or a free trial is bought with `checkout({ …, offer: key })`; a grant is taken with `claimOffer(key)`; a code the customer typed is `redeemCoupon(code)`; `offerShown(key)` counts an offer seen. See [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers).

## Guests

A guest — a user signed in with no account yet — buys like anyone else, and what it buys goes with it:

- A guest that **becomes** an account keeps its id, and its purchases with it: nothing to do.
- A guest that **signs in to an existing account** hands its purchases over. Before signing in, ask for the proof (`pb.purchases.mergeGrant()`, good for 5 minutes); once signed in, spend it (`pb.purchases.merge(grant)`): everything the guest bought goes to the account, for good.

See [Customers › Guests](/docs/purchases/customers#guests).

## From a native app

**On iOS**, an app may link out to buy on the web beside In-App Purchase in the App Store's United States storefront (App Review Guideline 3.1.1(a)). `PalbasePurchases` checks the storefront and opens Checkout in the system browser for the signed-in customer; back in the app, what they have is read again:

```swift
import PalbasePurchases

// Show the web button only where Apple lets the app link out.
if await pb.purchases.canOpenWebCheckout() {
    try await pb.purchases.openWebCheckout(product: "pro", plan: "yearly")
}
```

Elsewhere `openWebCheckout` throws `web_checkout_not_allowed` and asks nothing. Stripe sends the customer back to the app's own scheme, its bundle id. The checkout records where it was opened — iOS and the storefront — so the [charts](/docs/purchases/charts) can take off what the App Store may charge on such a purchase (nothing today).

**A redemption link** opens the app with `<scheme>://palbase/redeem?token=…`: hand it to `pb.purchases.redeem(_:)` on iOS, `pb.purchases.redeem(link)` on Android, and the web purchase is the app user's.

## Related

- [Connect Stripe](/docs/purchases/connect-stripe): the environment's Stripe account
- [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls) · [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers)
- [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements): checking access on your server
- [Web SDK](/docs/web/overview): `createClient` and its options

# Paywalls

A **paywall** is what an app shows to sell the catalog. It is designed once, as one JSON definition, and drawn natively from it — in SwiftUI on iOS (`PalbasePurchasesUI`), in the page on the web (`palbase/web`) — with each store's own prices filled in on the device.

A **placement** is a place in the app that shows a paywall: `onboarding`, `settings`, `out_of_credits`. The app asks for the placement, never for a paywall, so what it shows is decided in Studio or with the CLI — a new design, targeting rules, an experiment — and reaches the apps with no app update.

## Quick example

From a template to a placement the app asks for:

```sh
palbase purchases:paywalls:templates -E staging
palbase purchases:paywalls:new spring --template <key> -E staging
palbase purchases:paywalls:validate --file palbase/paywalls/spring.json -E staging
palbase purchases:paywalls:preview --file palbase/paywalls/spring.json --all -E staging
palbase purchases:paywalls:put spring --file palbase/paywalls/spring.json --revision 0 --publish -E staging
palbase purchases:placements:set settings --paywall spring -E staging
```

The web app draws it:

```ts
// app/settings.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function upgrade(container: HTMLElement): Promise<void> {
  const paywall = await pb.purchases.paywall("settings");
  paywall?.render(container, { successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks", cancelUrl: "https://app.example.com/settings" });
}
```

And the iOS app:

```swift
import PalbasePurchasesUI
import SwiftUI

struct SettingsView: View {
    @State private var showPaywall = false

    var body: some View {
        Button("Go Pro") { showPaywall = true }
            .paywall(placement: "settings", isPresented: $showPaywall)
    }
}

// Once, at the root of the app:
// RootView().palbasePurchases(pb.purchases).paywallLinks(terms: termsURL, privacy: privacyURL)
```

In Studio, **Purchases › Paywalls** does all of it: start from a template, edit its components, texts and colors with a live preview, publish, and give a placement its paywall.

## The definition

A paywall is a design system and a free layout of components that name it:

- **`theme`** — colors by name for light and dark (at least `background`, `surface`, `text`, `muted`, `accent` and `on_accent`), a type scale, radii and spacing.
- **`root`** — the part that scrolls, between a fixed **`header`** and **`footer`**; **`sheets`** it opens.
- **Components** — stacks, texts, icons, images, videos, dividers, spacers, buttons, packages, the purchase button, tabs, a switch, carousels, a countdown, a timeline, a features list, an HTML block — each with a style, a condition to be shown, a style for when it is selected, and an entrance animation.
- **Texts** — in each language the paywall has (`locales`), falling back to `default_locale`. A text holds variables the app fills from its store: `{{price}}`, `{{price_per_month}}`, `{{period}}`, `{{trial}}`, `{{savings}}`, `{{product_name}}`, `{{offer_price}}`. Prices are never in the definition. A text naming a variable its package has no value for — no trial, no savings — is not drawn.
- **Packages** — the catalog's plans it sells, as `product` and `plan`.

The least a paywall is — a title, a package that says its own price, the button that buys it, and the links App Review expects:

```json
{
  "schema": 2,
  "name": "Simple",
  "default_locale": "en",
  "theme": {
    "colors": {
      "light": { "background": "#FFFFFF", "surface": "#F2F2F7", "text": "#111114", "muted": "#6B6B70", "accent": "#5B5BD6", "on_accent": "#FFFFFF" },
      "dark": { "background": "#000000", "surface": "#1C1C1E", "text": "#F5F5F7", "muted": "#9A9AA0", "accent": "#8E8EF5", "on_accent": "#000000" }
    }
  },
  "root": {
    "type": "stack",
    "spacing": 16,
    "align": "stretch",
    "style": { "padding": 24, "background": "background" },
    "children": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Go Pro", "size": 28, "weight": 700 },
      { "type": "spacer" },
      {
        "type": "package",
        "product": "pro",
        "plan": "monthly",
        "selected": true,
        "style": { "padding": 16, "corners": 14, "background": "surface" },
        "children": [{ "type": "text", "text": "{{product_name}} — {{price}} / {{period}}", "weight": 600 }]
      },
      {
        "type": "purchase_button",
        "style": { "height": 52, "corners": 14, "background": "accent" },
        "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Continue", "color": "on_accent", "weight": 600 }
      },
      {
        "type": "stack",
        "axis": "horizontal",
        "spacing": 24,
        "distribution": "center",
        "children": [
          { "type": "button", "action": { "type": "restore" }, "visible": { "platform": ["ios", "android"] }, "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Restore", "size": 13, "color": "muted" } },
          { "type": "button", "action": { "type": "terms" }, "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Terms", "size": 13, "color": "muted" } },
          { "type": "button", "action": { "type": "privacy" }, "content": { "type": "text", "text": "Privacy", "size": 13, "color": "muted" } }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Every component and field, their bounds and two more examples to start from are in the CLI's guide — `palbase purchases:paywalls:guide`, made from the definition's JSON Schema, which `palbase purchases:paywalls:schema` writes for an editor to check a file against. A definition is held to bounds: 128 KiB of JSON, 400 components, 16 deep, 500 characters a text, 40 languages.

## Drafts and versions

A paywall has a **draft** and its **published versions**. The apps see only what is published.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `palbase purchases:paywalls` | The paywalls: each one's draft revision, the version published, and the placements that show it. |
| `palbase purchases:paywalls:get <name>` | Writes the draft — or `--version <n>` — to `palbase/paywalls/<name>.json`, with its revision. The file's first line names its JSON Schema, written beside it. |
| `palbase purchases:paywalls:validate --file <file>` | Checks it as publishing would, saving nothing: every rule of the schema, and every package against the catalog. |
| `palbase purchases:paywalls:put <name> --file <file> --revision <n>` | Saves it as the draft, on the revision it was edited from; `--revision 0` makes a new paywall. `--publish` publishes it too. |
| `palbase purchases:paywalls:publish <name>` | Publishes the draft as the next version. |
| `palbase purchases:paywalls:delete <name>` | Deletes the paywall and its versions — not one a placement or a running experiment shows. |

A problem's path is where it is in the file (`root.children[2].content.text`). A **warning** — what App Review expects of a subscription's paywall: a restore button, the legal links — does not stop a save or a publish; a broken rule does (`422 invalid_paywall`, every problem listed). Of two people editing at once, the second is told (`412 paywall_changed`), never overwritten. Publishing checks the paywall as the apps will get it: every package must be one the catalog sells, every asset still the bytes registered. A draft the same as the newest version publishes nothing new.

The newest 50 versions are kept. Each publish emits `purchases.paywall.published`; the apps asking for a placement that shows the paywall get the new version at once.

**Look before saving.** `palbase purchases:paywalls:preview` draws the file with the SDK's own renderer in a headless browser — Chrome, Chromium, Edge or Brave — as a PNG of the platform's screen; `--all` draws every platform in both appearances at both text sizes. `palbase purchases:paywalls:check` measures what is drawn on every screen and lists what is wrong — text cut off, a purchase button not on the first screen, contrast under WCAG's, targets too small — and exits 1 while anything is.

## Assets

A definition names the project's images, videos, fonts and HTML blocks as `asset:<id>`:

```sh
palbase purchases:paywalls:assets:upload hero.webp --kind image -E staging
```

The file goes to the project's public bucket `paywall-assets` — made when there is none — and is registered: the environment reads it there, says what it is by its bytes, and keeps their SHA-256. An app draws an asset only when what it downloaded is those bytes, and a paywall naming an asset whose file was since changed or removed is refused when published.

| Kind | Formats | At most |
|---|---|---|
| `image` | PNG, JPEG, WebP | 2 MiB |
| `video` | MP4, MOV | 50 MiB |
| `font` | TTF, OTF, WOFF2 | 5 MiB |
| `html` | A zip with `index.html` at its root | 5 MiB |

`palbase purchases:paywalls:assets` lists them; `:assets:delete` forgets one no paywall names. A project has at most 500 assets and 100 paywalls.

## Placements

```sh
palbase purchases:placements:set onboarding --paywall spring -E staging
```

gives a placement its **default paywall** — what it shows whoever none of its rules holds for — and makes the placement when it is new. A placement's key is lowercase letters, digits, `_` and `-`, 64 at most; a project has at most 200.

When an app asks for a placement, what it gets is decided in this order:

1. An **experiment** running for everyone at the placement: the viewer's variant.
2. The placement's **rules**, in order: the first in effect whose conditions all hold shows its paywall, or the variant of the experiment it sends to.
3. The placement's **default** paywall.

Each app gets the newest version it can draw: it says the newest paywall schema its SDK draws, and an app on an older SDK keeps getting the last version written in one it knows. With nothing published there — or no such placement — the SDK draws its own paywall from the catalog: every plan the store sells (the first six) with its price and period, the purchase button, the legal links and — in an app — restore, in the system's colors.

`palbase purchases:placements` lists them; `palbase purchases:placements:delete <placement>` forgets one, and the apps asking for it draw their own.

### Targeting rules

A placement's rules are one file, every rule in the order they are read:

```sh
palbase purchases:placements:rules:get onboarding --out palbase/onboarding-rules.json -E staging
```

```json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "Turkey, not yet Pro",
      "state": "live",
      "conditions": [
        { "field": "country", "op": "in", "values": ["TR"] },
        { "field": "entitlement", "op": "lacks", "values": ["pro"] }
      ],
      "target": { "paywall_id": "<a published paywall's id>" }
    },
    {
      "name": "Black Friday",
      "state": "scheduled",
      "starts_at": "2026-11-27T00:00:00Z",
      "ends_at": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z",
      "conditions": [{ "field": "app_version", "op": "gte", "value": "2.4.0" }],
      "target": { "paywall_id": "<a published paywall's id>" }
    }
  ]
}
```

```sh
palbase purchases:placements:rules:put onboarding --file palbase/onboarding-rules.json --revision 4 -E staging
```

A rule is `live`, `scheduled` (in effect from `starts_at`, until `ends_at`) or `inactive`. Its target is a published paywall (`paywall_id`) or the experiment running on the placement for the rules (`experiment_id`). At most 50 rules of at most 10 conditions; a rule with none holds for everyone.

| `field` | `op` | What it reads |
|---|---|---|
| `country` | `in`, `not_in` | The store's country the app sends, else the country of the request's address. ISO 3166-1 codes. |
| `platform` | `in`, `not_in` | `ios`, `android`, `web`. |
| `app` | `in`, `not_in` | The registered app's id. |
| `app_version` | `eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte` | The app's version, ordered as Semantic Versioning orders them. |
| `sdk_version` | the same, with `sdk` | The version of the SDK named (`palbase-swift`): a viewer on another SDK does not meet it. |
| `locale` | `in`, `not_in` | The first language the request asks for: `tr` covers `tr-TR`, `en-GB` covers `en-GB` alone. |
| `entitlement` | `has` (any of `values`), `lacks` (none of them) | The signed-in user's active entitlements, as the server knows them. |
| `first_seen_days` | `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte` | Whole days since the user was first seen, as the server knows it. |
| `attribute` | `in`, `not_in`, `exists`, `not_exists`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, with `key` | What the app says of the viewer: `pb.purchases.paywall("onboarding", { attributes: { plan: "free", sessions: 12 } })`. |

A value the request does not carry meets no condition on it, `not_in` included (`not_exists` aside). An app sends at most 20 attributes — texts, numbers or yes/no — of 2 KiB together.

**Targeting picks what to show; it is not access control.** The country, the attributes and the versions are what the app says of itself: no price or entitlement may hang on them.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `palbase purchases:placements:preview <placement>` | What the placement shows a viewer and why — the experiment, the rule that decided with every rule condition by condition, or the default — for `--platform`, `--country`, `--app-version`, `--locale`, `--attr`, `--user`, at `--at`; `--rules <file>` tries rules not yet saved. Nothing is counted. |
| `palbase purchases:placements:results <placement>` | What each rule, each variant and the default showed, and what its viewers did: exposures, viewers, purchases, conversion, revenue. |
| `palbase purchases:placements:attributes` | The attribute keys the apps sent, the most used first: suggestions for conditions. The keys are kept, never the values. |

## Experiments

An experiment splits a placement between 2 to 4 published paywalls, by weight. Each viewer — the signed-in user, a guest included, else the installation — sees the same variant every time, and the results say which sells best.

```sh
palbase purchases:experiments:start onboarding --variants spring=50,classic=50 -E staging
palbase purchases:experiments:results <experiment> -E staging
palbase purchases:experiments:winner <experiment> --variant a -E staging
```

| Audience | Who is in it |
|---|---|
| `placement` (the default) | Everyone at the placement, decided before its rules. The placement keeps its default for when the experiment ends. |
| `rules` | Only the viewers the placement's rules send to it: a rule's target names the experiment. |

One experiment runs on a placement at a time. Variants are keyed `a`, `b`, `c`, `d` unless `--variants` names them (`control:classic=50`); the **first** is what a stop keeps.

**The results** count, for each variant, its exposures and viewers, and the purchases its viewers made within the window after first seeing it (7 days unless `--window-days` says): the purchases the stores confirmed, never what an app reports — each counted once, for the first variant its buyer saw. Revenue is what was paid to date, renewals in, refunds out. Each variant's chance to convert best is Bayesian; the leader is called **confident** once every variant has been seen enough and its chance is high enough, and until then the results say why not. Test purchases count with `--sandbox`.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `palbase purchases:experiments:stop <experiment>` | Stops it at once: what it showed becomes its first variant's paywall. |
| `palbase purchases:experiments:winner <experiment> --variant <key>` | Ends it with a winner: for everyone at the placement, the winner becomes the placement's default — or, `--as-rule`, a live rule at the top of its rules shows it to everyone, to narrow later. For the rules, the rules that sent to it show the winner. |

Results stay after an experiment ends. In Studio, **Purchases › Experiments** starts one, shows its results and gives the winner to everyone in one step.

## In the app

The SDK asks for the placement in the newest schema it draws, with the app's version, its platform, its language and the attributes it is given; keeps the answer on the device, to ask again with its ETag and to show offline; downloads the assets and checks each; and counts the paywall shown, for the results. Purchases are never reported with it: the results read the ledger.

| Platform | How |
|---|---|
| Web | `pb.purchases.paywall(placement, { attributes })`, then `render(container, { successUrl, cancelUrl, links, onClose })`. The purchase button opens Stripe Checkout; the web has no restore button. See [Web › A paywall on the web](/docs/purchases/web#a-paywall-on-the-web). |
| iOS | `PaywallView(placement:)`, `.paywall(placement:isPresented:)`, or `.presentPaywallIfNeeded(entitlement:placement:)`, under `.palbasePurchases(pb.purchases)`. Its purchase button buys with StoreKit, its restore button restores, and it closes after a purchase. `.paywallComponent(id)` draws the app's own view in place of a component Studio named. See [iOS › Purchases](/docs/ios/purchases). |
| Android | The Android SDK does not draw paywalls: an Android app shows the products from `pb.purchases.products()` in its own screen. |

Any other client reads the placement with the publishable key: `GET /purchases/placements/{placement}/paywall` answers the definition and what it sells, or `204` when the app is to draw its own.

- [Offers & Coupons](/docs/purchases/offers): a package sold with an offer shows `{{offer_price}}`
- [Charts](/docs/purchases/charts): revenue and subscriptions by paywall and experiment

# Offers & Coupons

An **offer** is a price for a while, given to whom the project chooses — the members of an analytics audience, or everyone — and once to each customer. It gives one of three things:

| Kind | What the customer gets | Where it is sold |
|---|---|---|
| `discount` | A percentage off a subscription's plans, for a number of billing periods | Each store, as its own offer |
| `trial` | A free trial of a subscription's plans | Each store, as its own offer |
| `grant` | An entitlement for a time, with no store and no payment | Nowhere: the customer claims it |

A **coupon** is a code that opens an offer to whoever types it: a code many share, or a batch of one-time codes to give out.

## Offers are part of the catalog

An offer is written in the catalog's `offers`, and goes to the stores with the rest of it when a plan is confirmed ([Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog#bringing-the-stores-to-the-catalog)): a discount or a trial becomes the App Store's **promotional offer**, Google Play's **developer-determined offer** (tagged `palbase`) and a **Stripe coupon**, each by the offer's key. In Studio, **Purchases › Offers** adds and edits them, and shows how many customers were shown each and took it, by store.

```json
{
  "offers": [
    {
      "key": "winback_50",
      "name": "Win-back: half off for 3 months",
      "product": "pro",
      "plans": ["monthly"],
      "discount": { "percent": 50, "periods": 3 },
      "audience": "<an analytics audience's id>",
      "starts_at": "2026-11-01T00:00:00Z",
      "ends_at": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"
    },
    { "key": "long_trial", "name": "One month free", "product": "pro", "trial": "P1M" },
    { "key": "pro_week", "name": "A week of Pro", "grant": { "entitlement": "pro", "duration": "P7D" } }
  ]
}
```

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `key` | Its key, and its id at every store (hyphenated at Google Play). |
| `name` | Its name, 1 to 64 characters: the App Store's reference name. |
| `product`, `plans` | The subscription a discount or a trial is on, and its plans; no `plans`, every plan. A grant names no product. |
| `discount` | `{ "percent": 1–99, "periods": 1–12 }`. |
| `trial` | A free trial's length, ISO 8601: in the App Store `P3D`, `P1W`, `P2W`, `P1M`, `P2M`, `P3M`, `P6M` or `P1Y`. |
| `grant` | `{ "entitlement", "duration" }`: the catalog's entitlement, for `P7D`, `P1M` … from the moment it is claimed. |
| `audience` | The id of the analytics audience whose members are given it — those who allowed personalization; none, everyone. |
| `starts_at`, `ends_at` | When it is first given, and when it no longer is. |

On a product sold on the web, a discount of more than one period is one Stripe coupon, which lasts whole months: every plan it is on must bill by whole months, and by the same number of them — make one offer per plan length.

## Taking an offer in the app

The apps list the offers the signed-in customer may take now — live, not taken before, for everyone or for an audience they are in, or opened to them by a coupon they redeemed — each with what every store sells it as:

```ts
// app/offers.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function takeBestOffer(): Promise<string | null> {
  const offers = await pb.purchases.offers();
  const offer = offers[0];
  if (!offer) return null;
  await pb.purchases.offerShown(offer.key); // counted the first time

  if (offer.kind === "grant") {
    const grant = await pb.purchases.claimOffer(offer.key);
    return `${grant.entitlement} until ${grant.expires_at}`;
  }
  // A discount or a trial is bought with the offer, on one of its web plans.
  const plan = offer.web?.plans[0];
  if (!offer.product || !plan) return null;
  return pb.purchases.checkout({
    product: offer.product,
    plan,
    offer: offer.key,
    successUrl: "https://app.example.com/thanks",
    cancelUrl: "https://app.example.com/pricing",
  });
}
```

| | Web | iOS |
|---|---|---|
| The offers | `pb.purchases.offers()` | `pb.purchases.offers()` |
| Counted as shown | `offerShown(key)` | `offerShown(_:)` |
| Buy with a discount or a trial | `checkout({ …, offer })` | `purchase(_:offer:)` |
| Claim a grant | `claimOffer(key)` | `claim(_:)` |
| Take one by its key, whatever it is | — | `take(offer:)` |

A paywall's package sold with an offer the customer may take shows the offer's price as `{{offer_price}}`, and its purchase button buys with it.

**In the App Store**, a promotional offer is bought under Apple's signature for this customer, which the environment makes with the In-App Purchase key when the app asks — the app holds no key. The signature names an App Store transaction of the Apple account the app runs on, so it buys the offer for that Apple account alone: passed to someone else, it buys nothing. The iOS SDK sends the newest transaction of the group StoreKit holds on the device; without one, the customer's own newest subscription the environment knows is named. Apple gives a promotional offer only to a customer who subscribes, or subscribed, in the group: anyone else's purchase fails as `ineligibleForOffer`, and a customer with neither is signed none (`no_app_store_purchase`). On an Apple ID shared among the app's accounts, the second account is signed on the first's subscription, and what it buys with the offer is its own ([Customers](/docs/purchases/customers#restores-and-moved-purchases)). In Xcode, the StoreKit configuration's own Subscription Offers Key signs it ([Test Apple Purchases](/docs/purchases/testing-apple)). **On Google Play**, the Android SDK buys a plan with its introductory offer when Play says the user may take it. **On the web**, the checkout carries the offer's coupon.

A grant is claimed with an account: a guest is refused (`403 account_required`) unless a coupon opened the offer to it. An offer taken once is not taken again (`409 offer_taken`); one that is not the customer's to take now is `403 offer_not_open`. Taking one emits `purchases.offer.redeemed`.

## Coupons

A coupon opens one of the catalog's offers to whoever redeems its code, once a customer. Make one in Studio (**Purchases › Coupons › New coupon**) or from your server:

```ts
// server/coupons.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

// One code anyone may type, 500 times at most.
await palbase.purchases.createCoupon({
  body: { key: "launch", name: "Launch week", kind: "palbase", offer: "long_trial", code: "LAUNCH26", max_redemptions: 500 },
});

// 1,000 codes of one use each, to give out.
await palbase.purchases.createCoupon({
  body: { key: "partners", name: "Partner codes", kind: "palbase", offer: "pro_week", one_time_codes: 1000, signed_in_only: true },
});
```

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `palbase`: Palbase takes the code. `apple`: an App Store offer code, made in App Store Connect on one `plan` of the offer's product and redeemed in the App Store's own sheet. |
| `code`, `max_redemptions` | A code many share, 3 to 32 letters and digits, and how many times it is taken. On the web, a shared code of a discount is the Stripe promotion code of the offer's coupon too. |
| `one_time_codes` | Instead of `code`: how many codes of one use each to make, 1 to 25,000. |
| `signed_in_only` | A guest cannot redeem it. |
| `expires_at` | When it ends. An App Store batch's codes must end. |

`listCouponCodes` (`GET /purchases/coupons/{coupon_key}/codes`) lists a batch's codes — whom each was given to, who redeemed it — and answers a CSV file to hand out when asked for `text/csv`. `revokeCoupon` ends one: no code of it is redeemed from then on, and what was redeemed stays. An App Store coupon's `apple.state` says how App Store Connect took it: `pending`, `applied` or `failed`.

### Redeeming a code

The customer types the code in the app, in any case:

```ts
// app/redeem-code.ts
import { createClient, PalbaseError } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function redeemCode(code: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    const { offer, grant } = await pb.purchases.redeemCoupon(code);
    return grant ? `${grant.entitlement} is yours` : `${offer.name} is yours to take`;
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof PalbaseError && e.code === "redeem_at_app_store") return "Redeem this code in the App Store";
    if (e instanceof PalbaseError) return e.message;
    throw e;
  }
}
```

A grant is given at once; a discount or a trial is the customer's to buy from then on — `offers()` lists it, with the coupon. On iOS, `redeem(code:)` does the same and throws `CouponError`; an App Store offer code is redeemed in the App Store's sheet, `presentOfferCodeRedemption()`, and what it gives arrives as any App Store transaction does.

| Refusal | Why |
|---|---|
| `404 coupon_not_found` | No coupon has this code. |
| `409 coupon_redeemed`, `409 code_used` | The customer redeemed it or took its offer already; the one-time code was used. |
| `410 coupon_ended`, `410 coupon_exhausted`, `410 offer_ended` | The coupon ended or was taken as many times as it may be; its offer ended. |
| `403 sign_in_required` | A coupon for signed-in customers, and a guest typed it. |
| `422 redeem_at_app_store` | An App Store offer code: redeemed in the App Store. |
| `429 too_many_attempts` | Too many codes tried by this customer or from this network: try again after `retryAfter`. |

Redeeming emits `purchases.coupon.redeemed`, and `purchases.offer.redeemed` for a grant.

## Related

- [Catalog](/docs/purchases/catalog): where offers are written
- [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls): packages sold with an offer
- [Web](/docs/purchases/web) · [App Store](/docs/purchases/app-store) · [Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play)
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics): the audiences an offer is for

# Entitlements, Credits & Limits

What a customer has is one answer, `CustomerInfo`, whatever store they bought in: their **entitlements** (`pro`), their **credits** (`tokens`) and their use of each **limit** (`ai_requests` a month). The apps read it to decide what to show; your server reads it to decide what to serve — and spends credits and quota, which only a server does.

## Quick example

A route only Pro customers reach, and one that is paid for in tokens:

```ts
// src/modules/summaries/summaries.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Forbidden, Get, Headers, PalError, Palbase, Post, User, z, type UserT } from "palbase/backend";
import { PalbaseError, isEntitled, withReservation } from "palbase/server";

const Summarize = z.object({ text: z.string().min(1).max(20000) });
type Summarize = z.infer<typeof Summarize>;
const Retried = z.object({ "idempotency-key": z.string().min(1).max(255) });
type Retried = z.infer<typeof Retried>;

@Controller("/summaries")
export class SummariesController {
  @Get("/archive")
  async archive(@User() user: UserT): Promise<{ pro: true }> {
    const { data } = await Palbase.purchases.getCustomer({ path: { customer_id: user.id } });
    if (!isEntitled(data, "pro")) throw new Forbidden("Pro is needed", "entitlement_required");
    return { pro: true };
  }

  @Post("")
  async create(@Body(Summarize) body: Summarize, @Headers(Retried) headers: Retried, @User() user: UserT): Promise<{ summary: string }> {
    try {
      // 10 tokens are held while the job runs and taken once it returns; if it throws, they are released.
      // The same Idempotency-Key again (a retried request) is the same hold, never a second charge.
      return await withReservation(Palbase, user.id, { credits: "tokens", amount: 10, idempotencyKey: headers["idempotency-key"] }, async () => {
        const summary = await Palbase.ai.ask(`Summarize in three sentences:\n\n${body.text}`);
        return { summary };
      });
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof PalbaseError && e.code === "credits_insufficient") throw new PalError(402, "credits_insufficient", "Not enough tokens");
      throw e;
    }
  }
}
```

A customer without 10 tokens available is refused before the job runs: the purchases module answers `409 credits_insufficient`, and the route answers `402`. A module's refusal the handler does not catch answers `500` ([Responses & Errors](/docs/backend/errors#errors-from-the-projects-modules)).

## What a customer has

`CustomerInfo` is what `GET /purchases/me` answers the customer's app and `GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}` answers your server — the same document:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `customer_id` | The user's id. A guest merged into an account reads as the account. |
| `entitlements` | Every entitlement the customer has or had, by key (below). |
| `subscriptions` | Their subscriptions and non-renewing periods, oldest first: `product`, `plan`, `store`, `state`, `active`, `expires_at`, `will_renew`, `is_sandbox`, `manage`. |
| `purchases` | Their one-time purchases, oldest first: `product`, `store`, `state`, `purchased_at`, `is_sandbox`. |
| `credits` | Their balance in each credit (below). |
| `limits` | Their use of each limit in its current window (below). |
| `guest` | Whether the user is a guest. |
| `revision` | Rises with every change of what they have; `0` while they have nothing. |
| `requested_at` | When it was computed: what was active is as of then. |

An entitlement:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `active` | Whether the customer has it now. |
| `expires_at` | When it ends; `null` for life. |
| `will_renew` | Whether what gives it renews. |
| `store` | Where it comes from: `app_store`, `play_store`, `stripe`, or `promotional` (a grant). |
| `product`, `plan` | The catalog's product and plan that give it. |
| `period_type` | `normal`, `trial` (a free trial) or `promotional` (a grant). |
| `billing_issue` | The store could not charge the renewal: the customer keeps access through its grace period. |
| `is_sandbox` | A test purchase gives it. |
| `manage` | Where it is managed: the store, and its page (`url`) — none for Stripe, whose portal is opened on request. |
| `sources` | Everything that gives it, active ones first. |

An entitlement is read from the source that gives it longest: one for life wins, a real purchase wins over a test one.

A subscription's `state` is `trial`, `active` or `grace` while it gives access, and `pending`, `billing_retry`, `paused`, `expired`, `revoked` (refunded) or `replaced` (another purchase took it over) when it does not.

## Checking an entitlement

**On your server**, read the customer and ask `isEntitled(info, key)` from `palbase/server`: the entitlement is active and, unless it is for life, ends after now. It reads the `CustomerInfo` alone, so one kept a while still ends when its entitlement does. In a `palbase/backend` app the module is `Palbase.purchases`; from any server, `createServer({ url, secretKey }).purchases`. Reading a customer writes nothing: a user who has bought nothing reads as a customer with nothing — and with every limit's free tier.

**In the app**, what the customer has is kept current on its own:

| Platform | |
|---|---|
| Web | `pb.purchases.onCustomerInfo((info) => …)`; `info.entitlements["pro"]?.active`. |
| iOS | `pb.purchases.isEntitled("pro")`; in SwiftUI, `pb.purchases.state.isEntitled("pro")` draws the view again when it changes. |
| Android | `pb.purchases.isEntitled("pro")`; `pb.purchases.customerInfoUpdates`, a `Flow`. |

The app's answer decides what the app shows. What a purchase opens on your server — content, an API, a download — is checked on the server: the app's word is the app's.

## Credits

A customer's credits come from the catalog's products — a consumable per purchase, a subscription per period — and from grants your support gives. Each lot keeps its own end: a subscription period's credits end with the period unless the product rolls them over (`rollover: "all"`), credits bought never end, and a grant's may.

| Field of a balance | What it is |
|---|---|
| `currency` | The credit. |
| `balance` | What the live lots hold, less what the customer owes. |
| `available` | What a spend can take now: the balance less what open holds keep. |
| `reserved` | What open holds keep. |
| `debt` | What the customer owes: a refund took back credits already spent. The next credits pay it first. |
| `next_expiry` | When credits next expire; `null` when none do. |

### Spending

Credits are spent by your server, with the secret key, in one of two ways.

**In one step**, for work that is done or cannot fail:

```ts
// src/modules/exports/exports.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class ExportsService {
  /** Takes 5 tokens for the export: the same exportId again is the same spend, never a second. */
  async charge(userId: string, exportId: string): Promise<number> {
    const { data } = await Palbase.purchases.spend({
      path: { customer_id: userId },
      headers: { "Idempotency-Key": `export-${exportId}` },
      body: { credits: "tokens", amount: 5, metadata: { export: exportId } },
    });
    return data.balance_after ?? 0;
  }
}
```

**Held for a job, then committed.** A hold keeps the credits — still the customer's, but no other spend can take them — until it is committed (the job ran: `commitSpend`, all of it or `amount` of it), released (it did not: `releaseSpend`) or runs out (`ttl_seconds`, 10 minutes unless said, 24 hours at most; `extendHold` gives it more). `withReservation(server, customerId, reservation, fn)` from `palbase/server` does the three: it holds, runs `fn`, commits when `fn` returns and releases when it throws. Asked again with an `idempotencyKey` whose hold is already over, it throws `ReservationSettled`, and the job does not run again.

`reverseSpend` hands back what a committed spend took — the job failed afterwards — to the lots it came from.

Credits are taken from the lots that expire first, bought ones last. The **Idempotency-Key** names a spend for good: sent again, a minute or a month later, it answers the same spend (`200`, `Idempotent-Replayed`), never a second. Every movement — given, spent, expired, taken back by a refund, forgiven — is listed by `listCreditEntries`, newest first: support's answer to "where did my credits go".

| Refusal | Why |
|---|---|
| `409 credits_insufficient` | Not that many available. |
| `409 hold_expired` | The hold ran out before it was committed: what it kept is free again. |

### Giving credits

```ts
// src/modules/support/support.service.ts
import { Injectable, Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

@Injectable()
export class SupportService {
  async apologize(userId: string, ticket: string): Promise<void> {
    await Palbase.purchases.grantCredits({
      path: { customer_id: userId },
      headers: { "Idempotency-Key": `ticket-${ticket}` },
      body: { credits: "tokens", amount: 50, source: "support", reason: `Ticket ${ticket}: export failed twice`, expires_at: "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" },
    });
  }
}
```

A grant pays what the customer owes first. `source` is `promotion` or `support`, and `reason` is the record. `forgiveCredits` takes a debt off — all of it, or `amount` of it — when support lets a refunded spend go. Studio's **Purchases › Customers** gives credits too.

A balance that falls under its credit's `low_at` emits `purchases.credits.low`, once until it is back above; one that comes to nothing, `purchases.credits.depleted`.

## Limits

A limit is a quota counted in a window — `calendar_month`, `calendar_day` (from midnight in the project's time zone) or `billing_period` — with a free tier for everyone, and what each product gives on top: a customer gets the largest of their products'.

| Field of a limit's use | What it is |
|---|---|
| `limit` | The limit. |
| `max` | What this window allows them: the largest of their products, or the free tier — their own limit instead when one is set — plus what was granted them in the window. |
| `used`, `remaining`, `reserved` | What they used, what is left, what open holds keep. |
| `resets_at` | When the window ends. |

A limit is spent as credits are — `spend`, `holdSpend`, `withReservation` — naming `limit` instead of `credits`:

```ts
// src/modules/ai/quota.ts
import { Palbase } from "palbase/backend";

export async function countRequest(userId: string, requestId: string): Promise<void> {
  await Palbase.purchases.spend({
    path: { customer_id: userId },
    headers: { "Idempotency-Key": requestId },
    body: { limit: "ai_requests", amount: 1 },
  });
}
```

Past the window's `max`, a limit with `overflow` takes credits instead (`per_unit` of them a unit), and one without is refused: `409 limit_reached`. A hold counts in the window it was made in, even when it is committed after the window ends.

The refusal says what would give the customer more, for the app to offer: `upgrades` lists the entitlements whose products give more of the limit than the customer has now, the smallest step up first — empty when no product gives more.

```json
{
  "error": "limit_reached",
  "error_description": "the customer used this window's limit",
  "status": 409,
  "request_id": "req_…",
  "limit": "ai_requests",
  "upgrades": [{ "entitlement": "pro", "name": "Pro", "product": "pro", "max": 500 }]
}
```

`setCustomerLimit` gives one customer their own `max` — more for a customer support looks after, less for one who abuses it — until `expires_at` or `clearCustomerLimit`; `grantLimit` gives more units in the window it is in now. Each says why (`reason`).

A window used to 80% emits `purchases.quota.threshold`, and used to the end `purchases.quota.exhausted`, each once a window.

## Events

Each change of what a customer has emits an event to the project's webhooks and to a `palbase/backend` app's `@On` handlers ([Event Hooks](/docs/backend/hooks), [Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)):

```ts
// src/modules/premium/purchase-events.ts
import { Log, On, type PlatformEvent } from "palbase/backend";

export class PurchaseEvents {
  @On("purchases.subscription.changed")
  changed(event: PlatformEvent<"purchases.subscription.changed">): void {
    const { customer_id, product, change, store, expires_at } = event.data;
    if (change === "billing_issue") Log.warn("renewal not charged", { customer_id, product, store, expires_at });
  }
}
```

| Type | Sent when | `data` |
|---|---|---|
| `purchases.customer.changed` | Anything a customer has changed, and their revision rose. | `{ customer_id, revision }` |
| `purchases.entitlement.changed` | An entitlement turned on or off. | `{ customer_id, entitlement, active, expires_at, store, product, is_sandbox }` |
| `purchases.purchase.completed` | A purchase new to the ledger: a subscription's start or a one-time product, in any store. | `{ customer_id, chain_id, product, plan, store, is_sandbox }` |
| `purchases.subscription.changed` | A subscription `started`, `renewed`, was `canceled` or `uncanceled`, had a `billing_issue` or `recovered`, `expired`, or moved to another product (`product_changed`). | `{ customer_id, chain_id, change, product, plan, store, state, expires_at, will_renew, is_sandbox }` |
| `purchases.refund.changed` | A store took a payment back — a `refund`, a `chargeback`, Family Sharing ended (`family`) — or reversed that; its credits are taken back, or given back. | `{ customer_id, chain_id, transaction_id, kind, share_milli, reversed }` |
| `purchases.ownership.transferred` | A purchase moved to another customer: a restore, or another customer's new purchase on a store account they share (`via`). | `{ chain_id, from_customer_id, to_customer_id, product, store, via }` |
| `purchases.credits.low`, `purchases.credits.depleted` | A balance fell under its low mark, or to nothing. | `{ customer_id, currency, balance, available, debt, low_at }` |
| `purchases.quota.threshold`, `purchases.quota.exhausted` | A window was used to 80%, or to the end. | `{ customer_id, limit, used, max, percent, resets_at, window_id }` |
| `purchases.offer.redeemed` | A customer took an offer. | `{ customer_id, offer, kind, store, product, plan, chain_id, coupon, entitlement }` |
| `purchases.coupon.redeemed` | A customer redeemed a coupon. | `{ customer_id, coupon, offer, store, one_time }` |
| `purchases.customer.merged` | A guest's purchases went to the account it signed in to. | `{ from, into }` |
| `purchases.customer.erased` | A deleted user's purchases record was erased. | `{ customer_id }` |
| `purchases.catalog.changed` | A revision of the catalog was saved. | `{ revision }` |
| `purchases.catalog.applied` | A store's part of a plan was written, or failed. | `{ plan_id, revision, store, status }` |
| `purchases.paywall.published` | A paywall's draft was published. | `{ paywall_id, name, version, schema }` |
| `purchases.store.changed` | A store's connection was made, verified, checked or removed — never its key. | `{ store, change, … }` |

The customer's own apps hear of their changes on their realtime channel and read what they have again; the SDKs do it for you.

## Related
