# Customers

A **customer** is a user of the project — a guest included — and the customer's id is the user's id. There is nothing to create: a user becomes a customer when something is theirs, a purchase, a grant or credits, or when their app first reads what they have. What they have is the same answer in every app and on your server, whatever store they bought in ([Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements#what-a-customer-has)).

## Finding a customer

A person writing in rarely has their user id. In Studio, **Purchases › Customers**, find them by what they do have:

- their user id;
- an id their store gave a purchase: Apple's original transaction id or any transaction id from their receipt, a Google Play order id (`GPA.…`, a renewal's `..0` or not), a Stripe subscription, payment intent, invoice or customer id;
- the email a buyer with no account gave at checkout on the web, written whole (case and spaces around it do not matter). The address itself is not kept: an HMAC of it under the project's key is, so it is found by the whole address and by nothing less. A purchase whose link no one has redeemed yet is found too, as no one's.

One customer found opens them; several are listed. From a terminal:

```sh
palbase purchases:customers 2000000873521946 -E production
palbase purchases:customers buyer@example.com -E production
```

From your server, `GET /purchases/customers?q=…` answers the same list (`customer_id`, `matched_by`, the store and product of the purchase found).

## Looking a customer up

Their record shows their entitlements and where each is managed, their subscriptions, one-time purchases, credits and quota, test purchases marked. From a terminal:

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:get 3f6c2a1e-8d4b-4c1a-9b7e-2a5d8c0f1b3e -E production
```

From your server, `getCustomer`:

```ts
// server/support.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

export async function describe(userId: string): Promise<string[]> {
  const { data } = await palbase.purchases.getCustomer({ path: { customer_id: userId } });
  return Object.entries(data.entitlements).map(
    ([key, e]) => `${key}: ${e.active ? "on" : "off"} (${e.store}${e.is_sandbox ? ", test" : ""}) until ${e.expires_at ?? "for life"}`,
  );
}
```

A guest merged into an account reads as the account. A user never seen here reads as a customer with nothing, and the read writes nothing.

## What happened to them

Their **History**, the newest first, a page at a time: each payment and renewal, a refund (and its kind: refund, chargeback, family sharing), the subscription's renewal turned off or back on, a failed charge, its end, the grants given and taken back, the credits given, taken back, expired and forgiven, the purchases that moved to or from them, what support did at a store (`extension`, `refund_issued`, `cancel_requested`, with its days, the expiry it left, the refund's kind and support's note), and a refund they asked the App Store for (`refund_requested`, with what Apple was told: `answer`) — each with when, who did it (`store`, `customer`, the developer whose Studio or CLI call it was as `developer:…`, or the key as `key:…`) and why. Credits spent are the credits' own entries (**Credits** on the record, or `GET …/credits/entries`).

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:history <user id> -E production
```

`GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}/history` answers it to your server; `next_cursor`, sent back as `cursor`, is the next page.

## Giving an entitlement

Support gives one of the catalog's entitlements — for a promotion, a support case, a tester — for a while or for life, saying why:

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:grant <user id> pro --reason "Ticket 4821: billing mix-up" --for 30d -E production
```

The reason is the record (500 characters at most). Without `--for` or `--until` the grant is for life. Nothing is charged in any store, and a customer not seen before is made. Every grant a customer was given — active, ended and revoked, with who gave it, why, and who revoked it — is listed with its id, which ends it:

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:grants <user id> -E production
palbase purchases:customer:revoke <user id> <grant id> -E production
```

What the customer bought is not touched: the entitlement stays on while a purchase still gives it. Studio's **Purchases › Customers** lists, gives and revokes grants too — **Revoke** on a grant of the list; from a server they are `GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}/grants`, `grantEntitlement` and `revokeGrant`.

In Studio every member of the project reads a customer, their history and their grants; giving or revoking a grant and giving credits is an admin's or the owner's. A grant shows as `store: "promotional"`, `period_type: "promotional"`; turning the entitlement on or off emits `purchases.entitlement.changed`.

Credits and quota are given the same way, saying why — [Entitlements, Credits & Limits › Giving credits](/docs/purchases/entitlements#giving-credits).

## A subscription, at its store

Support moves a subscription's renewal later, refunds it or turns its renewal off from the customer's page (the buttons on a row of **Subscriptions**), from a terminal, or from your server with the secret key. The subscription's id is the one the record lists (`subscriptions[].id`). The store is asked to do it, then read again: the answer is the subscription as its store holds it after, and the history keeps what was done, by whom, and the note.

| | App Store | Google Play | Web (Stripe) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Extend** (1–90 days, for free) | Apple's renewal-date extension: a paid, active subscription, at most twice a year | The next renewal deferred | The next charge moved later |
| **Refund** (the latest payment, in full or what is left of its period) | Apple decides: `409 store_decides_refunds` | Revoked, refunded | Refunded, the subscription cancelled |
| **Turn the renewal off** | The customer's, in their Apple account: `409 customer_cancels` | Cancelled at the period's end | Cancelled at the period's end |

A refund ends the subscription and the customer's access as it answers; turning the renewal off leaves them the period they paid for.

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:get <user id> -E production            # the subscription's id
palbase purchases:customer:extend <user id> <subscription id> --days 7 --reason service_issue --note "Outage of the 21st" -E production
palbase purchases:customer:refund <user id> <subscription id> --mode prorated -E production
palbase purchases:customer:cancel <user id> <subscription id> -E production
```

`--reason` is `customer_satisfaction`, `service_issue` or `other`, as Apple asks it. From your server they are `extendSubscription`, `refundSubscription` and `cancelSubscription` (`POST /purchases/customers/{customer_id}/subscriptions/{subscription_id}/extend|refund|cancel`), each under an `Idempotency-Key`: sent again with it, it is done once. A store that refuses answers `409 store_refused` with what it said; one that cannot be reached, `502 store_unreachable` — sending again with the same key is safe.

## A refund the customer asks the App Store for

In the App Store the customer asks Apple for a refund (in the app with `Transaction.beginRefundRequest`, or at reportaproblem.apple.com). Apple then asks the app, within 12 hours, what they had of the purchase, and weighs the answer. The environment answers it for you — whether it gave what was bought, whether a free trial came first, how much of a pack of credits was spent — and says nothing of its own wish: the decision is Apple's.

It answers only for a customer who allowed it in the app; Apple takes no answer without that. Ask them once, where your app speaks of refunds or privacy, and record what they said:

```ts
// app/settings.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function rememberRefundChoice(allowed: boolean): Promise<void> {
  await pb.purchases.setRefundDataConsent(allowed); // PUT /purchases/me/refund-data-consent
}
```

On iOS it is `pb.purchases.setRefundDataConsent(true)`, on Android `pb.purchases.setRefundDataConsent(true)`; the latest word counts, for every app of the project. Never asked, or `false`: Apple is told nothing. The customer's page shows what they said and when (`refund_data_consent` on the record), and the history every question Apple asked, with its `answer`: `sent`, `pending`, `not_consented`, or `expired` when Apple could not be reached in its 12 hours.

## Credit entries, debts and limits

The customer's page lists every move of their credits — given, spent, taken back by a refund, expired, forgiven — with who did each and why (`GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}/credits/entries`). A refund of credits already spent leaves a debt, paid first from what they get next; support forgives it, all of it or an amount, saying why. A limit's maximum is set for one customer — above or below the catalog's, for a while or until cleared — and more of it given for its current period:

```sh
palbase purchases:customer:credits <user id> -E production
palbase purchases:customer:credits:give <user id> tokens 50 --reason "Ticket 4821" -E production
palbase purchases:customer:credits:forgive <user id> tokens --reason "Goodwill" -E production
palbase purchases:customer:limit:set <user id> ai_requests 500 --reason "Pilot" --for 30d -E production
palbase purchases:customer:limit:give <user id> ai_requests 20 --reason "A failed job" -E production
palbase purchases:customer:limit:clear <user id> ai_requests -E production
```

In Studio every member reads these; extending, refunding or cancelling a subscription, giving or forgiving credits and setting or giving a limit is an admin's or the owner's.

## Guests

A guest — a user signed in with no account, on one device — buys like anyone else: in the App Store, on Google Play, on the web, with a coupon. What a guest buys is theirs, and goes with them:

- **The guest becomes an account** (it signs up, adds a passkey, links a provider): it keeps its id, and everything it bought with it. Nothing to do.
- **The guest signs in to an account that already exists:** its purchases are handed over in two calls. With the guest's session, before signing in, the app asks for a proof (`POST /purchases/me/merge-grant`, good for 5 minutes); with the account's session, after, it spends it (`POST /purchases/me/merge`).

```ts
// app/sign-in.ts
import { createClient } from "palbase/web";

const pb = createClient({ url: "https://<ref>.palbase.studio", publishableKey: "pb_<ref>_c…" });

export async function signInKeepingPurchases(email: string, password: string): Promise<void> {
  const info = await pb.purchases.me();
  const grant = info.guest ? await pb.purchases.mergeGrant() : null;
  await pb.auth.signIn(email, password);
  if (grant) await pb.purchases.merge(grant); // the guest's subscriptions, purchases, grants, credits and quota use
}
```

The merge is one step and cannot be undone; asked again with the same proof, it is the same merge. From then on the guest's id points to the account: its session reads `409 customer_merged`. It emits `purchases.customer.merged`. The store ids the guest bought with — its `appAccountToken`, its obfuscated account id — go with it, so the stores' later notifications reach the account.

A guest may restore purchases, but never takes an account's (`403 restore_account_owned`): it signs in to that account instead. A grant offer is an account's unless a coupon opened it, and a coupon may be for signed-in customers alone.

## Restores and moved purchases

A store purchase stays the customer's it was bought by. Two things move it:

- **A new purchase on it by another customer.** When the app's accounts share one store account (a family's iPhone), a subscription follows who paid: in the App Store, a new purchase on it (a switch of plan, a resubscription, an offer bought) made with another customer's account token moves it to that customer, with the offer it was bought with. On Google Play every new purchase is a purchase of its own, so it is its buyer's from the start.
- **Restore purchases**, the customer's own action in the app, moves the store account's purchases to whoever restores, so a purchase made while signed in to another of the app's accounts follows the person. In the App Store this works only from the device StoreKit signed the purchase for, and never moves a purchase from an account to a guest.

One purchase moves at most 3 times in 30 days, the two counted together. Each move emits `purchases.ownership.transferred`. The project's backend reads a customer's moves, newest first, with what they have (`GET /purchases/customers/{customer_id}`, its `transfers`: who had the purchase, who has it since, how and when), and Studio shows them on the customer's page under **Purchases › Customers**. The customer's own apps never read them: `GET /purchases/me` names no other customer. See [App Store](/docs/purchases/app-store#what-the-environment-does-with-a-transaction) and [Google Play](/docs/purchases/google-play#what-the-environment-does-with-a-purchase).

## When a user is deleted

The user's purchases record is erased — and the guests merged into them — and their id is never a customer again (`purchases.customer.erased`). Their renewing web subscriptions stop renewing, keeping the period they paid, unless the settings say otherwise. A subscription bought in the App Store or on Google Play is the customer's to cancel there: no one else can.

## Settings

The project's choices for its customers' purchases, in Studio under **Purchases › Settings**, or with the secret key:

```ts
// server/settings.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

// Only the team's testers get anything from test purchases here; quotas' days begin in Istanbul.
await palbase.purchases.updateSettings({
  body: { sandbox_access: "allowlist", sandbox_allowlist: ["3f6c2a1e-8d4b-4c1a-9b7e-2a5d8c0f1b3e"], time_zone: "Europe/Istanbul" },
});
```

| Setting | Default | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| `sandbox_access` | `everyone` | Whether test purchases — the App Store's sandbox (where TestFlight and App Review buy), Xcode's, Google Play's license testers', Stripe's test mode — open entitlements and credits: for `everyone`, only the customers on `sandbox_allowlist` (`allowlist`, 1,000 at most), or `nobody`. App Review buys in the sandbox: limit them only while no build of the app is in review against this environment. |
| `cancel_on_delete` | `true` | Whether a deleted user's renewing web subscriptions stop renewing. |
| `time_zone` | `UTC` | Where the quotas' calendar days and months begin: an IANA name such as `Europe/Istanbul`. |
| `reporting_currency`, `store_commission`, `stripe_fee_bps`, `stripe_fee_fixed_micros`, `stripe_fee_fixed_currency`, `app_store_link_fee_bps`, `app_store_link_attribution_days` | `USD`, `standard`, 2.9% + 0.30 USD, 0%, 7 days | How the charts count money: see [Charts › Settings](/docs/purchases/charts#settings). |

`getSettings` reads them; a change touches only the fields it gives.

## Related

- [Entitlements, Credits & Limits](/docs/purchases/entitlements): what a customer has, and spending it
- [Charts](/docs/purchases/charts): what customers bought, over time
- CLI: [`purchases:customer:get`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomerget), [`purchases:customer:grant`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomergrant), [`purchases:customer:revoke`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomerrevoke), [`purchases:customer:extend`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomerextend), [`purchases:customer:refund`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomerrefund), [`purchases:customer:cancel`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchasescustomercancel)



<!-- ===== purchases/charts ===== -->

# Charts

The purchases module draws the project's revenue and subscription charts from its ledger — every purchase from every store, as the stores confirmed it. Each chart is computed when it is read, so a refund that arrives late, a renewal, a product change, a guest merged into an account or a change of the settings is in the next answer. Money is in one reporting currency.

In Studio, **Purchases › Charts** shows them, each with its definition, and the views of them the organization saved.

## Quick example

```sh
palbase purchases:charts:overview -E production
palbase purchases:charts:get mrr --resolution month --segment store -E production
palbase purchases:charts:get revenue --from 2026-09-01 --to 2026-09-30 --filter country:TR --revenue-type proceeds --csv --out palbase/revenue-tr.csv -E production
```

The overview is the project's figures at a glance: MRR, active subscriptions and active trials now; revenue, new customers and active customers over the last 28 days. From a server:

```ts
// server/report.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const { data } = await palbase.purchases.getChart({
  path: { chart: "mrr" },
  query: { resolution: "month", segment: "store" },
});
console.log(data);
```

## The charts

`palbase purchases:charts` lists every chart with its definition — what it counts, over which period, and how refunds, product changes, resubscriptions and test purchases count — and the dimensions it is split by.

| | Charts |
|---|---|
| Revenue | `revenue`, `mrr`, `mrr_movement`, `arr`, `non_subscription_purchases`, `refunds`, `refund_rate` |
| Subscriptions | `active_subscriptions`, `active_subscriptions_movement`, `active_trials`, `active_trials_movement`, `new_trials`, `paid_subscriptions`, `churn`, `subscription_status`, `subscription_retention` |
| Customers | `new_customers`, `active_customers`, `initial_conversion`, `conversion_to_paying`, `trial_conversion`, `realized_ltv_per_customer`, `realized_ltv_per_paying_customer`, `cohort_explorer` |

A **flow** counts what happened in a period; a **snapshot** is the state at its end (now, for the period now is in); a **ratio** divides its measures; a **cohort** follows what began in a period over its ages. A period marked `*` in the CLI is not over: its value may still change.

## Reading a chart

| Flag | Parameter | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--from`, `--to` | `from`, `to` | The first and last day, `YYYY-MM-DD`, both included, at most two years apart. By default the last 30 days, 12 weeks or 12 months. |
| `--resolution` | `resolution` | `day` (the default), `week` (ISO weeks, Monday to Sunday) or `month`. Days are UTC. |
| `--segment` | `segment` | Splits the chart by `store`, `platform`, `country`, `product`, `plan`, `duration`, `sandbox`, `paywall` or `experiment`: the 20 largest values each a segment, the rest together as `(other)`. |
| `--filter` | `filter` | Keeps what has one of the values given, one `dimension:value` each: `--filter store:app_store --filter country:TR`. |
| `--revenue-type` | `revenue_type` | `gross` (what customers paid, the default), `net_of_taxes`, or `proceeds` (net of taxes and of the store's commission or Stripe's fee). |
| `--currency` | `currency` | Money in another currency, for this answer. |
| `--window-days` | `window_days` | The conversion charts' timeframe and the lifetime charts' customer lifetime, in days from a customer's first day. |
| `--cohort` | `cohort` | The cohort explorer's cohorts: `new_customers` (by their first day) or `new_paying_customers` (by their first payment). |
| `--sandbox` | `sandbox` | Counts test purchases too; segment or filter by `sandbox` to tell them apart. |
| `--csv` | `Accept: text/csv` | The chart as CSV, a row a segment and period; `--out` writes it under `palbase/`. A value that would start a spreadsheet formula (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`) begins with a quote. |

**Money** is converted to the reporting currency at the European Central Bank's reference rate of the day it was paid; an amount in a currency the Bank does not publish is left out, and named. The ledger keeps what was paid as it was paid. The stores' commission and Stripe's fee are not in the ledger: proceeds are estimated with the [settings](#settings), and so are taxes a store did not state — the answer says what was estimated.

**Paywalls and experiments.** The `paywall` and `experiment` dimensions credit each subscription once, when its first purchase is recorded: to the paywall — and the experiment's variant — its owner saw first within the 7 days before buying. One that followed none is `none`, its renewals included.

A cohort chart follows at most 120 cohorts. A customer holding more than 20,000 transactions makes a chart refuse (`422 chart_too_large`).

### How often

The same request within a minute is answered from a cache, which a change of the settings clears. A project's charts are computed 20 in a row, then one every 2 seconds; past that a chart is refused with `429 too_many_charts` and `Retry-After` — an answer from the cache is not counted. A chart that takes longer than 15 seconds to compute is refused with `503 charts_busy` and `Retry-After`.

## Settings

How the charts count money:

```sh
palbase purchases:charts:settings --currency EUR --commission small_business -E production
```

| Flag | Setting | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--currency` | `reporting_currency` | `USD` | The currency the charts report money in: one the European Central Bank published a rate for in the last ten days. Changing it redraws every chart from its first day. |
| `--commission` | `store_commission` | `standard` | What proceeds take off App Store and Google Play payments: `standard` (30%; 15% of a subscription's renewals after its first paid year in the App Store, and of every Google Play subscription) or `small_business` (15%: the App Store Small Business Program, Google Play's first million). |
| `--stripe-percent`, `--stripe-fixed`, `--stripe-fixed-currency` | `stripe_fee_bps`, `stripe_fee_fixed_micros`, `stripe_fee_fixed_currency` | 2.9% + 0.30 USD | Stripe's fee of a web payment, its share and its fixed part. |
| `--app-store-link-percent`, `--app-store-link-days` | `app_store_link_fee_bps`, `app_store_link_attribution_days` | 0%, 7 days | What the App Store takes of a web purchase bought through a link out of an iOS app in its United States storefront, and for how many days after the link a purchase owes it. Nothing today; set it once Apple charges one. |

Without flags, the command prints the settings. They are the purchases module's settings, also read and changed in Studio (**Purchases › Settings**) and with `updateSettings` ([Customers › Settings](/docs/purchases/customers#settings)).

## Related

- [Customers](/docs/purchases/customers): one customer's purchases
- [Paywalls](/docs/purchases/paywalls): a placement's and an experiment's own results
- CLI: [`purchases:charts:get`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchaseschartsget), [`purchases:charts:settings`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-purchaseschartssettings)



<!-- ===== messaging/overview ===== -->

# Messaging

Messaging is chat between a project's people: direct conversations and groups, with answers, threads, reactions, mentions, files, messages for later, messages that go after a while, photos seen once and vanish mode. It is a module every project has, like auth: there is no server to run. The web, iOS and Android clients keep each person's conversations on the device, current over the project's socket, so an app draws them and writes — sending, syncing and catching up are the client's.

- **Web**: `pb.messaging` ([Web Messaging](/docs/web/messaging))
- **iOS**: the `PalbaseMessaging` product ([iOS Messaging](/docs/ios/messaging))
- **Android**: `studio.palbase:palbase-messaging` ([Android Messaging](/docs/android/messaging))

## A person's history is their account's

What a person said and read is kept by the project, not by a phone. Signing out, deleting the app or opening it on a new phone loses nothing: when they sign in again, every conversation comes back from the server.

- **On the device.** Each client keeps a copy of the signed-in person's conversations so the app opens on them at once, without the network. When the person signs out, the copy is dropped, unless the app asks to keep it (`keepOnSignOut`). Kept or not, it is that person's alone: whoever signs in next on the same device never reads it — and, unless copies are kept, a person who signs in drops any another left there.
- **Written offline.** A message written without the network is drawn at once and waits in the device's outbox; it goes once the network is back — once, however often the app retries (each message carries its own `client_message_id`).
- **The socket drops.** What came meanwhile is read from the server's record of what changed for the person (`GET /messaging/sync`) as the socket comes back: nothing is missed.

## Kept encrypted

Every conversation has a key of its own, kept wrapped by the project's key: its messages' words, its title and its files' keys are stored sealed, and a copy of the database or a backup holds none of them in the clear. A file is encrypted on the device, with a key of its own, before it is uploaded: storage holds only what it cannot read. This is not end-to-end encryption: Palbase opens a conversation's messages to deliver them, your server reads them with the secret key, and your organization's owners and admins read them in Studio — each read recorded, with who read it ([Your server](#your-server)). Your team's members see the conversations and the reports, not what was said.

## What people do

- **Direct conversations and groups.** The direct conversation of two people is one, whoever opens it (`POST /messaging/conversations/direct`); a group has up to 1,000 members, an owner, admins, and policies for who writes, who adds people and who changes it.
- **Spaces.** A conversation made with a `space` your app names (`org:<id>`, `project:<id>`) belongs to that place of the app's, for good: the same two people have one direct conversation in each space, and one with none. A person's list, your server's list and search are narrowed to spaces (`?space=`). Your hook is told the space, so it says who may reach whom there.
- **Open groups.** A group is open (`visibility: "open"`, in a space) — found in its space's open groups (`GET /messaging/groups/open?space=`) and joined by the person themselves (`POST /messaging/conversations/{conversation_id}/join`), as a channel — or closed (the default): joined when someone adds you. Your hook says who may make or open one in a space, and who may find and join its groups. One an admin removed does not join again by themselves. An open group stays when its last person leaves, to be found and joined — with no owner or admin left, your server moderates it (`PATCH /messaging/admin/conversations/{conversation_id}`, its members, its messages). Opening a closed group lets whoever joins read what its history shows newcomers.
- **Answers and threads.** A message answers another inline, or in its thread: one level deep, with its count of answers, its last one and who answered, each thread's unread count, and the threads a person follows (`GET /messaging/threads`). A thread's answer may be shown in the conversation too.
- **Changing what was said.** A message is edited within 15 minutes, and removed for everyone by its writer within 48 hours (by a group's admin at any time), or for oneself.
- **Reactions**, several a person to a message; **mentions**; **read receipts** and **typing**; **presence** (online, last seen).
- **Files**: pictures, videos, voice notes and any file, encrypted on the device.
- **For later.** A message scheduled for a time is sent then by the server, the writer's phone off or not; until then only its writer sees it, and may change or take it back. A scheduled message carries text alone.
- **Messages that go.** A conversation's timer (a day, a week, 90 days or any number of days) makes each new message go after it; a message of its own goes after its seconds, counted from when it was sent or from when everyone it was for read it. When a message's time is up it goes from the server and from every device.
- **Seen once.** A photo or a video sent to be seen once (or twice) opens for its seconds and is gone: its file's key is dropped on the server, and the app holds the opened bytes, never the device's copy.
- **Vanish mode** (a direct conversation's): a message read goes once its reader leaves the conversation.
- **Muting** a conversation, or its mentions alone: a muted one sends no push.
- **Blocking** a person: what they send does not reach whoever blocked them (to their writer it looks sent). **Reporting** a conversation, a person or messages: the report is the project's ([Moderation](#moderation)).

**Kept for a report.** What goes from people's screens without their choosing is kept on the server for 14 days, sealed as it was, for a report alone — Messenger reviews a deleted message reported within 14 days, Instagram keeps a vanish-mode message as long:

- a message seen once, its time up, in vanish mode, or taken back by its writer or a group's admin: one who saw it can still report it, and what it said, its files too, goes with the report. Only someone who was in the conversation when it went — and, for a photo or video seen once, who opened it — reports what it said;
- what an edited message said before each change: a report of the message shows its earlier versions, those changed while the reporter was in the conversation. The people in it see the last version alone;
- a group a person deleted — its owner or an admin, or the last to leave: it goes from everyone's list at once, and stays sealed 14 days; those who were in it, when it went or before, report it (the app has it as deleted until then), and the last 30 messages each saw go with their report. Then it is gone.

Nothing else reads what is kept, and after 14 days it is gone — even when the project's retention or a deleted account takes the message sooner: with `deleted_user_messages: delete`, a person deleting their account does not wipe what they took back before. Say so in your app's privacy policy. What the project itself removes — its server, its retention — is kept for nothing: a conversation the project's server deletes goes at once, a group still sealed too.

A person may hide their read receipts (`PATCH /messaging/me`, `read_receipts: false`): in direct conversations they then show no one what they read and see no one's; in groups receipts are always shown.

## Search

A person finds their messages by their words — in one conversation, or across all of theirs — the newest first (`GET /messaging/search`). A word's beginning finds it: "toplanti" finds "Toplantıda", as capitals, accents and the Turkish i's are one. Every word asked must be there, in what was said or in a file's name. Each message found comes with the conversation it is in, the people it shows (who wrote it, and the other person of a direct conversation) and where it says what was asked, to highlight. The app opens the conversation at that message (`around`) and pages back and forward from there. The clients also list, first, the conversations whose name matches.

- **Only what the person sees.** Nothing from before they joined a group that keeps its history from new members, nor after they left; nothing they cleared or removed for themselves, nor an answer in the thread of one; nothing a person they block sent them since, in their direct conversation; nothing removed.
- **Never found.** Messages seen once, and those of vanish mode. A message changed is found by what it says now.
- **Kept encrypted.** The words are kept as marks the conversation's key makes of their beginnings: never readable in the database, and one word said in two conversations leaves unrelated marks. Within one conversation the marks do show which of its messages share a word's beginning, and how often — not what the word is: the price of searching encrypted words on the server. A word's middle ("plantı") finds nothing, and a single letter finds only a word of one letter.

The 2,000 conversations a person spoke in last are searched. Search costs nothing extra: its marks are not counted in what the messages weigh.

### By meaning

With the project's `search_by_meaning` on, a person also finds their messages by what they mean, in none of the words asked: "uçuş saati" finds "THY 14:30'da kalkıyor" (`GET /messaging/search?by=meaning`). What is found is what is near the question, the nearest first, each with how near (`score`, 0.3 to 1) — one page; a message about something else may still come, further down. The same people see the same messages as by words, and a message changed is found by what it means now.

- **Your choice, off until you turn it on.** Each message's text — not a system message's, nor one seen once, nor one of vanish mode — goes to OpenAI to be embedded (`text-embedding-3-large`), billed to the project as its AI use ([AI](/docs/backend/ai#what-it-costs)): about $2.90 a million short messages (about twenty tokens each), and each question a person asks. OpenAI keeps what it is sent up to 30 days for abuse monitoring and never trains on it; say so in your app's privacy policy. Turned on, the messages written before are embedded too, in the background; turned off, nothing more goes to OpenAI and the vectors are removed.
- **Kept encrypted.** A message's vector says nearly what its text said, so it is kept sealed with the conversation's key, as the message is: a copy of the database holds none readable. A search opens the vectors of the person's conversations in the server's memory alone.
- **Within reason.** A person asks 30 questions by meaning at once and one more a minute (`429 too_many_searches`, with `Retry-After`); a question asked again within ten minutes is not asked of OpenAI again. Of each conversation, its newest 100,000 messages are searched by meaning. When the project's AI allowance or budget is spent (`402 ai_payment_required`), messages are sent as ever and found by their words; those written meanwhile are embedded once it is renewed.
- **Short messages.** A message of one word ("tamam") is found by its word, not embedded.

## Screenshots

A browser does not say when someone takes a screenshot, and a phone cannot always stop one:

| | A photo or video seen once | Vanish mode |
|---|---|---|
| **Android** | The screen is kept out of screenshots and recordings (`FLAG_SECURE`): they come out black | Taken, and the others are told |
| **iOS** | Taken (iOS cannot stop one), and the others are told | Taken, and the others are told |
| **Web** | Not known | Not known |

"Told" is a line in the conversation, as WhatsApp's and Instagram's (`POST /messaging/conversations/{conversation_id}/screenshot`). No app can stop a second phone's camera.

## Pushes and the app in front

A message to someone who is not in the app reaches them as a push, through the project's notifications ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)): set up an APNs key and Firebase for the apps first. The push says who wrote and what (`push_preview: false` for "a new message" alone), the app's badge is the person's unread count, and a conversation's messages group together.

While the app is in front, a message's push is not drawn as the system's banner: the client tells the app instead (web `onIncoming`, iOS `incoming()`, Android `incoming`), and the app draws its own banner — none for the conversation already on the screen.

On iOS and Android, the push also brings the message into the device's copy while the app is closed: open it with no network and it is there. On iOS this is the `PalbaseMessagingNotificationService` extension and an App Group ([iOS Messaging](/docs/ios/messaging#messages-that-arrive-while-the-app-is-closed)); on Android, the push itself ([Android Messaging](/docs/android/messaging#messages-that-arrive-while-the-app-is-closed)).

## Your server

With the secret key, your server makes conversations for people, adds and removes them, says something in a conversation (a booking's confirmation, a support agent), removes a message, and reads what was said — for moderation, support or an export (`GET /messaging/admin/conversations/{conversation_id}/messages`; a file's link: `GET …/messages/{message_id}/attachments/{attachment_id}`, the file opened with the key in its message).

Your organization's owners and admins read the same in Studio (**Messaging › Conversations**, a person's conversations by their user ID) and with the CLI (`palbase messaging:conversations:list --user <id>`, `palbase messaging:messages:list <conversation_id>`). A member of your team sees the conversations, not what was said: the platform refuses them. Every read of people's messages — a file opened too — is recorded with who read it: a developer by name, a key or a token by its id. Studio's **Access log** and `GET /messaging/admin/access-log` (`palbase messaging:access-log`) list them, 400 days.

**Who may write to whom** is everyone, unless the project's hook says otherwise: set `hook` in the settings and the project's endpoint is asked, signed as a webhook is, before a direct conversation is opened, someone is added to a group, a space's open groups are listed or one is joined — `messaging.can_message`, answering whether they may. When it does not answer, `on_error` says what happens: deny (the default; the app tries again) or allow — for a direct conversation and people added to a group alone: a space's open groups (making one, listing, joining) are refused while the hook is silent, whatever `on_error` says, as the hook is all that keeps one organization's groups from another's people. The hook is not asked for each message: a conversation already open stays open until your server closes it.

The hook is POSTed `{ event: "messaging.can_message", action, from_user_id, to_user_ids, conversation_id, space }` and answers `200 { allowed_user_ids: [...] }`: whom of `to_user_ids` the person may reach — `direct` (a direct conversation), `group_add` (people added to a group); or, `to_user_ids` being the person alone, whether they may have an open group in a space (`open_group`: making one, or opening theirs), find a space's open groups (`list_open`) or join one (`join`) — naming them lets them in. `space` is the conversation's (absent: none). A workspace app answers "only people of the same organization".

**Writing as someone.** An assistant your server runs (no session of the person's) sends their words when they ask: `POST /messaging/admin/conversations/{conversation_id}/messages` with `as_user_id` and `via` (`"pal"`; required with `as_user_id`, so the others always know it was not their own hand). The message is theirs as if they sent it — what they may send there, the others' unread counts and pushes from them ("Ayşe (via pal): …", the push's `data.via`) — though not their reading: what they had not read stays unread. Every app shows `via` with it. `thread_id` answers in a thread. Not one of the conversation's people: `403 not_a_member`. Each is in the access log, the person named. From `palbase/server`: `palbase.messaging.adminSendMessage(…)`.

**Events.** Your backend hears of each message and each read, to keep an activity feed — "Ayşe wrote to you", "you were mentioned in #general" — and clear it once the person read the conversation:

- `messaging.message.created`: `{ conversation_id, conversation_kind, space, message_id, seq, kind, sender_id, via, thread_id, mention_ids, recipient_ids, has_attachments, created_at }` — `recipient_ids` are the conversation's people but its writer. With the setting `event_text` on, `text` too: never a message meant to go (vanish mode, seen once, living a while), and the words then stay on the event stream 7 days, outside the sealed store; off (the default), your server reads the message with the secret key.
- `messaging.conversation.read`: `{ conversation_id, space, user_id, read_seq, thread_id }` — a person read a conversation, or a thread of it, further. Their own message is read by them: `sender_id` says it.

One a message, one a read: they go only to what names them — an `@On("messaging.message.created")` handler of `palbase/backend`, a webhook endpoint listing them ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)) — never to an endpoint that takes every event, and are written only while one does (an endpoint made now hears them within 15 seconds).

**Closing a conversation.** When what let two people write ends — one unfollows the other, a booking is over, an event ended — your server makes their conversation read-only: its people still read what was said in it, and nobody writes in it — no message, reaction, edit, file or screenshot notice, no change to its title, picture, timer or vanish mode, nobody added to it or given a role, and a message scheduled in it fails (`read_only`) — while your server still may say and change anything in it, and a group's admins still remove people from it. It is told in the conversation, and undone the same way:

- the direct conversation of two people: `GET /messaging/admin/conversations?user_id=<one>&with=<the other>`;
- read-only, or writable again: `PATCH /messaging/admin/conversations/{conversation_id}` with `{"read_only": true}` (or `false`); the app sees `settings.read_only`, and a write answers `403 read_only`;
- the same call changes what a group's admins may: its title, description, picture and timer, and who writes in it, edits it and adds people (`send_policy`, `edit_policy`, `add_policy`) — a group your server made, too.

## Moderation

A person reports a message, someone or a conversation from your app. What the reported messages say when reported — their files too, and a message already gone from the screen while it is kept for a report — is copied into the report, sealed, and kept with it whatever becomes of the message.

- **You hear of it**: the `messaging.report.created` event reaches your webhook, and your organization's owners and admins are mailed — at most once an hour for the whole organization, one mail with each environment's reports of the hour. The mail says how many and why, never what was reported; an organization that runs its customers' apps passes each report on to them from the event.
- **Studio**: **Messaging › Reports** lists them. An owner or admin opens one — its reporter's words, the messages and their files — removes the messages for everyone, and marks it resolved in their own words; a member sees the list alone. App stores expect reports to be looked at in good time.
- **The CLI**: `palbase messaging:reports:list`, `palbase messaging:reports:get <id>`, `palbase messaging:reports:resolve <id> --resolution removed`.
- **Your server**: `GET /messaging/admin/reports`, `GET /messaging/admin/reports/{report_id}` (a file's link: `…/attachments/{attachment_id}`), `POST /messaging/admin/reports/{report_id}/resolve`.

A report is kept 190 days once resolved — the EU's Digital Services Act keeps a decision open to complaint at least six months, and six calendar months reach 184 days — and two years when never resolved; its copies and files go with it.

## A deleted account

When a person's account is deleted, messaging forgets them at once: their profile, their blocks, their reactions, their scheduled messages and what they hid for themselves go, and they leave every conversation. Their id goes from everything that is kept: where it stood — their messages, what others' messages say of them (a mention, "added", "left"), what a report copied of their messages, the access log's reads — a deleted user stands, `deleted_…`, the same one everywhere, with nothing personal kept. What is kept, for your privacy policy:

| What | Kept | How long |
|---|---|---|
| Their messages | as `deleted_user_messages` says: kept with no one's name on them, or removed | `keep`: as long as the project keeps messages; `delete`: gone at once |
| What went from screens before | what it said, for a report alone | 14 days |
| Reports of their messages | what the messages said, the writer a deleted user | 190 days once resolved, two years when never resolved |
| The access log | reads of their messages, naming a deleted user | 400 days |
| The answer to a request an app sent again (its retry) | as it was given, sealed | 2 days |
| That the account was deleted | its id, so nothing brings them back: a profile, a conversation, a group, a block or a mention for them is refused (`409 user_deleted`, or `user_deleted` among those a group did not take) — a backend syncing as the deletion runs too | 7 days |

## The project's settings

In Studio (**Messaging**), with the CLI (`palbase messaging:settings:set`, `palbase messaging:hook:set`; `palbase config:diff` and `palbase config:copy` compare and copy them between environments), or with the secret key (`GET` and `PUT /messaging/settings`):

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `retention_days` | Messages older are removed; none (the default): kept for good |
| `push_preview` | Pushes say what a message says (the default), or only that one came |
| `deleted_user_messages` | A deleted user's messages: `keep` (the default), their writer shown as a deleted user with nothing personal kept, or `delete` — save what went from screens before, kept its 14 days for a report |
| `hook` | Who may write to whom (above); none: anyone to anyone |
| `search_by_meaning` | Messages are found by what they mean too ([Search](#by-meaning)); off (the default): by their words alone, and no message goes to a model |
| `event_text` | `messaging.message.created` says what the message says ([Events](#your-server)); off (the default): who wrote to whom, not what |

## What it costs

| | Free each month | Past it |
|---|---|---|
| Messages sent | 1 million | $5.25 a million |
| What the messages weigh where they are kept | 1 GiB | $1.05 a GiB-month |

A message weighs its sealed text and 768 bytes for its row and indexes: a GiB holds over a million short messages. Its files are the project's storage, its deliveries to people's sockets realtime messages, and its pushes push notifications — each on the bill as they are ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)). A message sent again with the same `client_message_id` is one.

A free project past either is slowed, never stopped: its messages go at about one a second, all its people together. A send waits its turn, 10 seconds at the most; one that would wait longer is `429 slowed` with `Retry-After`, and the clients keep it in their outbox and send it again. Reading, syncing and everything else go on at full speed.

# Calls

Calls are voice and video calls between a project's people: one to one, or a group of up to 100. It is a module every project has, like messaging: there is no server to run. A person's phone rings on the lock screen as any call does, and they answer on whichever of their devices they pick up. Your server, with the secret key, sets the module up, reads and ends calls, and lets its own agent into one.

The web, iOS and Android SDKs run a call for the app — ringing, answering, the media, the heartbeat — through the HTTP API this section describes ([Calls over HTTP](/docs/calls/http)):

- **Web**: `pb.calls`, and `palbase/web/calls-ui` for ready-made screens ([Web Calls](/docs/web/calls))
- **iOS**: the `PalbaseCalls` product, and `PalbaseCallsUI` for ready-made screens ([iOS Calls](/docs/ios/calls))
- **Android**: `studio.palbase:palbase-calls`, and `palbase-calls-ui` for ready-made screens ([Android Calls](/docs/android/calls))

## Kinds of call

- **A direct call** rings one person (`POST /calls` with one user id).
- **A group call** asks several people in (`POST /calls` with up to 99 user ids, or `group: true` with one). A person who missed or declined it may still join while it lasts.
- **A huddle** is a group call that rings no one (`ring: false`): the people asked see it and join when they like.
- **A direct call grows.** Asking a third person in — or letting the project's agent in — makes it a group, going on in the same room.

Every call's sound and picture go through Palbase's media server (LiveKit, open source), one to one too: each device sends its own once, however many listen, and gets the others' from the server. A device's address reaches no one else in the call. Where a network lets no UDP out, the media goes over TCP on port 443 (straight to the media server: a network that lets the web out only through an HTTPS proxy does not pass it). The server sees the media as it passes it on; nothing of it is kept.

A call is voice or video (`video`) from its start; a person may still turn their camera on or off in it. What a call costs is the data the media server sent its people ([What it costs](#what-it-costs)).

## Who may call whom

Anyone in the project may call anyone, except:

- **Blocks.** No one who blocked the caller, nor whom the caller blocked — the same blocks as messaging's ([Messaging](/docs/messaging/overview)).
- **Deleted accounts.** A deleted person cannot be called.
- **A conversation's members.** A call made from a conversation (`conversation_id`) reaches its members alone, and is kept in it as a `call` message: who called, voice or video, how it ended and how long it lasted.
- **Your hook.** With the project's hook set, your endpoint is asked before a call rings and before someone is asked into one (`calls.can_call`), and narrows who may be reached ([Your Server](/docs/calls/server#who-may-call-whom)).

A call to no one the caller may reach is `403 not_allowed`. A person starts 10 calls a minute at most, and the project's `calls_per_hour` an hour (60 unless it says otherwise): past either, `429 too_many_calls`.

## A call's life

1. **It rings.** The people called are rung on every device of theirs: a call screen on iOS and Android, even locked; a notification and a ring in a browser ([Ringing](/docs/calls/ringing)). The caller's app shows it ringing.
2. **Someone answers.** The first of a person's devices to answer has the call; their other devices stop ringing. A person in a call on one device cannot answer another call on a second device (`409 in_another_call`); an app that lost its call — killed, crashed — answers the next one on the same device, and the lost call ends.
3. **It goes on.** Each device in the call says so every 15 seconds (its heartbeat). A device silent for 45 seconds — its app gone, its network lost for good — is taken for gone: a direct call ends (`failed`), and a person leaves a group.
4. **It ends.** Every device in it is told how (`end_reason`), and the call is in each person's history.

| How a call ends | `end_reason` |
|---|---|
| Someone in an answered direct call hung up | `hung_up` |
| The caller gave up before an answer (the person called missed it) | `canceled` |
| The person called turned it down | `declined` |
| No one answered in 45 seconds | `missed` |
| The person called was in another call, or being rung by one | `busy` |
| A device in a direct call went silent | `failed` |
| Your server ended it, or everyone left a group | `ended` |

`ended_by` names who hung up, canceled or declined, or whose device went silent.

- **Busy.** A call to someone in another call ends at once (`busy`), and they are told they missed it. In a group, a busy person is not rung, and may join later.
- **Missed.** A person rung for 45 seconds without answering missed the call, and gets a missed-call notification; so do the people a caller stopped calling before they answered. A direct call ends; a group goes on without them.
- **Declined.** A direct call ends. In a group, the person is not rung any more, and may still join.
- **Calling each other at once.** When two people call each other in the same moment, the second call is the first one, answered: they are in one call, not two that refuse each other.
- **A group ends** when no person is in it or being rung: an agent alone does not keep it going.

## History

A person's calls are theirs to list, the newest first, each with how it went for them — `missed`, `declined`, `left` … (`GET /calls`; `missed=true` for the calls they missed). Studio lists the project's calls (**Calls › Calls**), any person's by their user id; your server reads them with the secret key (`GET /calls/admin/calls`).

A call's record is who called whom, when, how long each was in it and how it ended. Its sound and picture never pass through the API and are never kept. Ended calls are kept 400 days.

When a person's account is deleted, the direct calls they were in go from the history, their place in a group's record goes, and a group they started names `deleted-user` as its caller. What the media server sent them stays counted, under `deleted-user`.

## The project's settings

In Studio (**Calls**), or with the secret key (`GET` and `PUT /calls/settings`; [Your Server](/docs/calls/server#settings)):

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `max_participants` | How many people a call holds, agents included: 2 to 100 (the default) |
| `calls_per_hour` | How many calls one person may start in an hour: 1 to 1,000 (60 by default); 10 a minute whatever it says |
| `hook` | Who may call whom ([Your Server](/docs/calls/server#who-may-call-whom)); none: blocks alone decide |

## Webhooks

Your backend hears of the project's calls ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks#the-events)):

| Event | Sent when |
|---|---|
| `calls.call.started` | A call was made — ringing, or a group going on |
| `calls.call.ended` | A call ended (`end_reason` says why) |
| `calls.participant.joined` | A person answered or joined, or an agent came into the call |
| `calls.participant.left` | A person or an agent left the call |

`calls.call.started` and `calls.participant.joined` are when to send your agent in ([Agents](/docs/calls/agents)).

## What it costs

A call is billed by the data the media server sent its people: each person's, and each agent's, sound, picture and data from the others, and the server's own word to their app — as the server counts its packets, without the network's own headers. Voice and video, one to one and in a group, cost the same per GB; a voice call sends far less than a video one, and a picture sends less when it is small on the screen.

| | Free each month | Past it |
|---|---|---|
| Call data | 25 GB | $0.12 a GB |

A GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes. A caller alone in a call that rings is sent little: the server's word to their app, no one's sound or picture. What each person was sent is in the call's record (`bytes`, a minute behind at most), and the month's total in the project's usage. Past a free project's 25 GB, until the month ends, no new call starts (`429 quota_exceeded`): calls going on go on to their end. A project on Pay as you go goes on, paying for what is past them ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)).
