# Calls over HTTP

The SDKs make these calls for an app, on each of a person's devices. This page is what they do, for an app of your own making or to read what an SDK sends. Every call here is a person's: it carries the publishable key in the `apikey` header and the signed-in user's access token as `Authorization: Bearer …`, at the project's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`. What your server does with the secret key is on [Your Server](/docs/calls/server).

## A device

A person may have the app on several devices, and a call is in one of them. Every call that acts on a device names it: `device_id`, the app's own id for its install — 1 to 128 characters, no space — kept across launches. The device that answers has the call; its heartbeat, its media and its signals are that device's.

## Making a call

`POST /calls` from the caller's device:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `user_ids` | Who to call: one person (a direct call), or up to 99 (a group) |
| `device_id` | The device the call is made on |
| `video` | A video call; else voice |
| `ring` | Ring them (the default); `false`: a group call they join when they like (a huddle) |
| `group` | A group call even with one person asked, on the media server: others may be asked later |
| `conversation_id` | The conversation it is made from: its members alone may be called, and it keeps the call |
| `metadata` | Your app's own words about the call, shown to the people rung: 32 strings, 2 KiB at most |
| `caller_name`, `caller_image_url` | What those rung see of the caller; else the caller's messaging profile's name and picture |

```bash
curl -s "https://<ref>.palbase.studio/calls" \
  -H "apikey: $PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"user_ids": ["usr_bob"], "video": true, "device_id": "ios-6f1c"}'
```

It answers the call ([A call](#a-call)):

- `201`: the call, ringing — or a direct call already over, `busy`, when the person called is in another call.
- `200`: the person called was calling the caller that very moment: the answer is their call, answered on this device.

| Refusal | Why |
|---|---|
| `400 invalid_user_ids` | Not 1 to 99 other people |
| `400 call_full` | More people than the project lets a call hold (`max_participants`) |
| `400 invalid_device_id`, `invalid_conversation_id`, `invalid_metadata`, `invalid_caller` | That field is not one |
| `403 not_allowed` | The caller may reach none of them: blocks, deleted accounts, a conversation's members, your hook |
| `404 conversation_not_found` | The caller is not in the conversation named |
| `409 in_another_call` | The caller is in another call on another device |
| `429 too_many_calls` | 10 calls this minute, or the project's `calls_per_hour` this hour |
| `429 quota_exceeded` | A free project's call data is used up this month: calls going on go on, no new one starts |

## Answering, declining, joining, leaving

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `POST /calls/{call_id}/accept` with `{ "device_id" }` | Answers on this device. The first of the person's devices to answer has the call; the others stop ringing. Sent again from the same device, it is the same answer |
| `POST /calls/{call_id}/decline` | Turns the call down on every device of the person's: a direct call ends (`declined`); in a group, they are not rung any more and may still join |
| `POST /calls/{call_id}/join` with `{ "device_id" }` | Comes into a group call the person was asked to — rung, missed, declined, busy, or in it before. A direct call is answered, not joined (`409 not_joinable`) |
| `POST /calls/{call_id}/leave` | Takes the person out. A direct call ends for both: `canceled` while it rings (the person called missed it), `hung_up` once answered. A group goes on while a person is in it or being rung. Leaving a call that is over is done |
| `POST /calls/{call_id}/participants` with `{ "user_ids", "ring" }` | Asks more people into a call the person is in, ringing them unless `ring` is `false`. A direct call becomes a group on the media server, going on. A call not answered yet does not grow (`409 not_in_call`) |

Each answers the call as it is now. When the call is not what the request needs, the refusal is `409` and carries the call too (`{ "error", "error_description", "call" }`), so the app draws what is true: `call_ended`, `answered_elsewhere` (in on another of the person's devices), `not_ringing`, `call_full`. Asking more people in may also be `403 not_allowed` and `400 invalid_user_ids` (no one new to ask), as making a call is.

## Staying in the call

A device in a call says so every 15 seconds: `POST /calls/{call_id}/heartbeat` with `{ "device_id" }`. A device silent for 45 seconds is taken for gone: a direct call ends (`failed`, or `canceled` when the caller's device went silent while it rang), and a person leaves a group.

The heartbeat answers the call's `state`, its `version`, its `end_reason`, and whether this device is still in it (`in_call`). An app whose snapshot's `version` is lower than the heartbeat's missed a word on its channel: it reads the call again (`GET /calls/{call_id}`).

## The media

Every call's media goes through the media server, one to one too. `POST /calls/{call_id}/media` with `{ "device_id" }`, once the device is in the call, is its ticket into the call's room:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `url` | The media server's address (`wss://`) |
| `token` | The device's ticket into the call's room: 6 hours, and back in after a lost connection |
| `room` | The call's room |

The media server is LiveKit (open source): a device connects to `url` with `token` through LiveKit's client SDK, which the Palbase SDKs use. The caller is in a call from its start, so the caller's device joins the room as the call rings — it is sent no one's sound or picture until someone answers; a person called joins once they answered (or joined a group). A direct call that grows — someone asked in, an agent let in — goes on in the same room. Where a network lets no UDP out, LiveKit's client reaches the server over TCP on port 443 (straight, not through an HTTPS proxy).

Refused: `409 not_in_call` or `answered_elsewhere` (this device is not the one in the call), `409 call_ended`.

## The channel

Each person hears their calls on their own realtime channel, `calls:<ref>:<user_id>`, joined on the project's socket by their apps ([Web Realtime](/docs/web/realtime)). One event comes on it, `call`: a call of theirs as it is now — the same object `GET /calls/{call_id}` answers — each time it changes: rung, answered, declined, joined, left, grown into a group, ended.

Each `call` carries the call's `version`, which grows with every change: keep the highest seen, and drop an older snapshot that arrives late. What the channel tells is told once, as it happens: an app that was not listening reads the call (`GET /calls/{call_id}`), and the heartbeat's `version` says when it missed something.

## History

`GET /calls` lists the person's calls, the newest first, each with how it went for them (their participant's `state`): `limit` (1 to 100, 20 by default) and `cursor` (the previous page's `next_cursor`) page through them, `missed=true` keeps the ones they missed or were busy for, `state` the ones ringing, going on or ended. `GET /calls/{call_id}` reads one of theirs — what an app reads when it missed a word on its channel.

## A call

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The call's id |
| `kind` | `direct` (two people) or `group` |
| `video` | A video call; else voice |
| `ring` | Whether it rings the people asked; `false`: a huddle |
| `state` | `ringing` (a direct call not answered yet), `active`, `ended` |
| `caller_id` | Who called |
| `conversation_id` | The conversation it was made from, or null |
| `metadata` | The caller's app's own words about it |
| `max_participants` | How many it holds |
| `created_at`, `answered_at`, `ended_at` | When it was made, answered (a direct call) and ended |
| `end_reason`, `ended_by` | How it ended ([A call's life](/docs/calls/overview#a-calls-life)), and who ended it |
| `ring_until` | When a direct call's ring ends, unanswered |
| `version` | Grows with every change |
| `participants` | Its people and agents (below) |

A participant: `user_id` (an agent's is `bot:<identity>`), `kind` (`user` or `bot`), `role` (`caller`, `callee` — the one called in a direct call — or `member`), `state` (`ringing`, `invited` — asked to a huddle —, `joined`, `left`, `declined`, `missed`, `busy`), `device_id` (the device they are in it on), `name` and `image_url` as their profile shows them, `invited_at`, `joined_at` (when their present stretch in it began), `left_at`, `seconds` (how long they were in it before the present stretch), and `bytes` (what the media server sent them in it — what the call is billed by — a minute behind at most).



<!-- ===== calls/ringing ===== -->

# Ringing

A call rings every device of the people called — the app open, in the background or closed, the phone locked — through the project's notifications. Set up an APNs key for iOS, and Firebase for Android and the web, first ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)); with neither, a call rings only the apps that are open and listening on their channel. The SDKs register each device for its pushes and draw the call on it: this page is what they rely on.

## iOS

A call rings an iPhone with a **VoIP push** (PushKit). The app registers its PushKit token as an `ios_voip` device (`POST /notify/devices`), beside its notification token, and the push wakes it even when it was closed.

The app hands the call to **CallKit** the moment the push arrives, and iOS draws it: on the lock screen it is Apple's own call screen, with the caller's name, the app's name and icon, and its ringtone. Apple stops sending VoIP pushes to an app that does not report each one to CallKit at once, so the app does so even for a call it then ends — one already answered elsewhere, or over.

Answering or declining from CallKit is `POST /calls/{call_id}/accept` or `/decline` from that iPhone. How the app sets it up — the background modes, `configure`, the APNs key — is [iOS Calls](/docs/ios/calls#a-call-rings-the-phone). When the call is answered on another of the person's devices, or the caller gives up, the app hears it on its channel and ends the CallKit call: the phone stops ringing.

## Android

A call rings an Android phone with a **high-priority data message** (FCM). It carries no notification of its own: the app's messaging service wakes, and the SDK draws a **CallStyle** notification with a **full-screen intent** — the incoming-call screen over the lock screen — and its answer and decline buttons. From Android 14, the full-screen intent needs its own permission, which Google Play gives apps whose core function is calling and the person may take back; without it, Android shows the call as a heads-up notification.

When the call is answered on another of the person's devices, or the caller gives up, a second data message tells the phone to stop ringing. The permissions it needs, and the full-screen intent's, are [Android Calls](/docs/android/calls#a-call-rings-the-phone).

## The web

A call rings a browser with a **notification** — the caller's name, and "Incoming voice call" or "Incoming video call" in the person's language — through the browser's push service, as the project's web pushes go ([Notifications](/docs/backend/notifications)). While a tab of the app is in front, no notification is shown: the page hears the call itself (`pb.calls.onIncoming`) and rings — `palbase/web/calls-ui` draws the call and plays a soft ring ([Web Calls](/docs/web/calls#ringing-while-the-page-is-away)). A tap on the notification brings a tab of the app forward, where the person answers.

## A missed call

A person rung for 45 seconds without answering — or whose caller gave up before they answered, or who was busy in another call — is sent a missed-call notification on every device: the caller's name, and "Missed voice call" or "Missed video call". The call is in their history as one they missed — their participant's `state` is `missed`, or `busy` (`GET /calls?missed=true`).

## What a push carries

An app that draws calls itself reads them from the push's data:

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `pb_call` | `incoming` (ring), `silence` (stop ringing: answered elsewhere, or over) or `missed` |
| `call_id` | The call |
| `caller_id`, `caller_name`, `caller_image_url` | Who is calling, as those rung see them |
| `video` | `true` or `false` |
| `kind` | `direct` or `group` |
| `conversation_id` | The conversation it was made from, when it was |
| `ring_until` | When the ring ends, unanswered (RFC 3339) |

A ring push is worth delivering only until the ring ends: a phone that comes online later is not rung for a call that is over. A call's ring and the push that silences it replace each other on the device.

An app woken by a push reads the call (`GET /calls/{call_id}`) before it draws it: it may have been answered elsewhere, or ended, meanwhile. Once it is up, it hears the call change on its channel ([The channel](/docs/calls/http#the-channel)).



<!-- ===== calls/server ===== -->

# Your Server

With the project's secret key in the `apikey` header ([Server SDK](/docs/server/overview#the-secret-key)), your server sets the calls module up, decides who may call whom, reads and ends calls, and lets its agent into one ([Agents](/docs/calls/agents)). A publishable key is refused here (`403 secret_key_required`). From TypeScript, `palbase/server`'s `palbase.calls` makes each call below, typed ([Server SDK](/docs/server/overview)). Your organization's owners and admins do the same in Studio, under **Calls**, and with the CLI's `calls:*` commands; a member of your team reads the settings and the calls there, and changes nothing.

## Settings

`GET /calls/settings` reads them; `PUT /calls/settings` changes what it names, and answers them all:

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `max_participants` | How many people a call holds, agents included: 2 to 100 (the default). A call that would hold more is refused (`call_full`) |
| `calls_per_hour` | How many calls one person may start in an hour: 1 to 1,000 (60 by default). 10 a minute, whatever it says |
| `hook` | The endpoint asked who may call whom (below): `{ url, timeout_ms, on_error }`; `null` removes it |

```bash
curl -s -X PUT "https://<ref>.palbase.studio/calls/settings" \
  -H "apikey: $PALBASE_SECRET_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_participants": 8}'
```

From a terminal, as one of your organization's owners or admins — `palbase config:diff` and `palbase config:copy` compare and copy the settings between environments:

```bash
palbase calls:settings:get
palbase calls:settings:set --max-participants 8 --calls-per-hour 30
```

## Who may call whom

Anyone in the project may call anyone who has not blocked them and whom they have not blocked, and a call from a conversation reaches its members alone ([Calls](/docs/calls/overview#who-may-call-whom)). Your hook narrows it further: a follower calls only whom they follow, a booking's customer only its host, a patient only their doctor during the appointment.

Set it with `PUT /calls/settings`:

```json
{ "hook": { "url": "https://api.example.com/palbase/can-call", "timeout_ms": 2000, "on_error": "deny" } }
```

The first time a hook is set, the answer carries its signing secret, `hook_secret` (`whsec_…`): **here once**, never read back. Keep it where your endpoint checks the signature. `POST /calls/settings/hook-secret` makes a new one, given once the same way, and the old one signs nothing more (`409 no_hook` when there is no hook). Changing the hook's address keeps its secret; removing the hook (`"hook": null`) drops it.

The CLI sets it the same way, and keeps the secret in the environment's secrets instead of printing it with `--secret-to` — where a machine of yours reads it:

```bash
palbase calls:hook:set --url https://api.example.com/palbase/can-call --on-error deny --secret-to CALLS_HOOK_SECRET
palbase calls:hook:get
palbase calls:hook:secret:rotate --secret-to CALLS_HOOK_SECRET
palbase calls:hook:remove
```

Before a call rings — and before someone is asked into a call going on — your endpoint is sent a `POST`, after blocks, deleted accounts and a conversation's members are taken out:

```json
{
  "event": "calls.can_call",
  "action": "start",
  "from_user_id": "usr_ada",
  "to_user_ids": ["usr_bob", "usr_cem"],
  "video": true,
  "conversation_id": "5f0e…"
}
```

`action` is `start` (making a call) or `invite` (asking people into one, its `call_id` then given); `conversation_id` is there when the call is made from one. It is signed as the [Standard Webhooks](https://www.standardwebhooks.com) spec signs: `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` (Unix seconds) and `webhook-signature`, `v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256>` of `<webhook-id>.<webhook-timestamp>.<body>` with the secret's bytes (the base64 after `whsec_`). The libraries of Standard Webhooks check it as they are.

It answers `200` with the people the caller may reach:

```json
{ "allowed_user_ids": ["usr_bob"] }
```

Those it leaves out are not rung; when it leaves out everyone, the call is `403 not_allowed`. Anything but a `200` with that body — another status, a body it cannot read, no answer within `timeout_ms` (100 to 5,000; 2,000 by default) — is no answer, and `on_error` says what happens: `deny` (the default) refuses the call, `allow` lets it ring everyone blocks allow. The hook is asked again for each call: what it allowed once is not remembered. Redirects are not followed.

## Reading and ending calls

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /calls/admin/calls` | The project's calls, the newest first: `user_id` a person's (with `missed=true`, the ones they missed or were busy for), `state` those `ringing`, `active` or `ended`, `limit` (1 to 100, 20 by default) and `cursor` to page |
| `GET /calls/admin/calls/{call_id}` | A call as it is now |
| `POST /calls/admin/calls/{call_id}/end` | Ends the call for everyone in it (`ended`): their apps are told, and its room on the media server closes |

Each answers calls as a person's apps read them ([A call](/docs/calls/http#a-call)); a call that is not the project's is `404 call_not_found`. Studio's **Calls › Calls** is the same list: a person's calls by their user id, and **End call** on one going on. With the CLI:

```bash
palbase calls:list --user usr_ada --missed
palbase calls:list --state active
palbase calls:get 8a1e2f40-5c7d-4b8e-9a61-3f2d7c0b9e15
palbase calls:end 8a1e2f40-5c7d-4b8e-9a61-3f2d7c0b9e15
```

## Webhooks

Your backend's webhook endpoints hear of the project's calls ([Webhooks](/docs/server/webhooks)):

| Event | Sent when |
|---|---|
| `calls.call.started` | A call was made — ringing, or a group going on |
| `calls.call.ended` | A call ended |
| `calls.participant.joined` | A person answered or joined, or an agent came into the call |
| `calls.participant.left` | A person or an agent left the call |

Each one's `data` says of the call: `call_id`, `kind`, `video`, `mode`, `state`, `caller_id`, `conversation_id`, and `room` — its room on the media server, once it is there; a participant's event adds `user_id` and `participant_kind` (`user` or `bot`), and `calls.call.ended` its `end_reason`.

```json
{
  "id": "0b7c…",
  "type": "calls.participant.joined",
  "project_id": "2b7d…",
  "created_at": "2026-10-29T09:41:22Z",
  "data": { "call_id": "8a1e…", "kind": "group", "video": false, "mode": "sfu", "state": "active", "caller_id": "usr_ada", "conversation_id": null, "room": "2b7d…_8a1e…", "user_id": "usr_bob", "participant_kind": "user" }
}
```



<!-- ===== calls/agents ===== -->

# Agents

Your project's own agent can be in a call: a bot that transcribes it, takes notes, answers in a support line, translates. Your server lets it in with a ticket, and it joins as a participant everyone in the call hears (and sees), listed as an agent. Palbase runs no agent of its own: what the agent does with what it hears — and which model or service it uses — is yours.

## A ticket

`POST /calls/admin/calls/{call_id}/tickets`, with the secret key:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `identity` | The agent's identity in the call: 1 to 64 letters, digits, `_`, `.` or `-`, starting with a letter or a digit. It is in the call as `bot:<identity>` |
| `name` | Its name, as the call lists it |
| `can_publish` | It speaks (and shows) too — the default; `false`: it only listens |
| `metadata` | Its own words: 32 strings, 2 KiB at most |

```bash
curl -s "https://<ref>.palbase.studio/calls/admin/calls/$CALL_ID/tickets" \
  -H "apikey: $PALBASE_SECRET_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"identity": "notes", "name": "Notes", "can_publish": false}'
```

From TypeScript, `palbase/server`:

```ts
// src/agent-ticket.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

/** Lets the note taker into a call: the media server's address and a token it connects with. */
export async function letNotesIn(callId: string): Promise<{ url: string; token: string }> {
  const { data } = await palbase.calls.createCallTicket({
    path: { call_id: callId },
    body: { identity: "notes", name: "Notes", can_publish: false },
  });
  return { url: data.url, token: data.token };
}
```

It answers `201`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `url` | The media server's address (`wss://`) |
| `token` | The access token the agent connects with |
| `room` | The call's room |
| `identity` | `bot:<identity>` |
| `expires_at` | When the token ends: 6 hours on, or sooner when the credential that asked for it ends sooner. Until then it lets the agent back in after a lost connection |
| `call` | The call, with the agent among its participants ([A call](/docs/calls/http#a-call)) |

- **A direct call stays one.** The agent joins the call's room beside its two people; the call goes on as it was.
- **It counts as a person** against the project's `max_participants` (`409 call_full`), and what the media server sends it is billed as a person's ([What it costs](/docs/calls/overview#what-it-costs)).
- **The same identity again** is the same agent: a new ticket for it is its way back in.
- Refused: `409 call_ended`; `409 invalid_identity` when the identity is a person's in the call; `400` for a field that is not one; `404 call_not_found`.

## In the call

The media server is LiveKit (open source), and the ticket is what its own client and agent libraries connect with, as they are: [LiveKit Agents](https://docs.livekit.io/agents/) for a voice agent, or its real-time SDKs (Python, Node.js, Go, Rust …) for anything else.

- **Each person's audio is a track of its own**, published by a participant whose identity is their user id: the agent knows who said what, and transcribes each speaker apart.
- **The agent publishes its own**: a voice that answers, a video, as `can_publish` allows.
- **It is in the call** from when it connects, and the call lists it so (`kind: "bot"`, `state: "joined"`); it has left when it disconnects. `calls.participant.joined` and `calls.participant.left` tell your backend, with `participant_kind: "bot"`.
- **It does not keep a call going.** A group ends when no person is in it or being rung, an agent still connected or not; your server may end a call itself (`POST /calls/admin/calls/{call_id}/end`).

```python
import asyncio
from livekit import rtc

async def listen(url: str, token: str) -> None:
    room = rtc.Room()

    @room.on("track_subscribed")
    def on_track(track: rtc.Track, publication: rtc.RemoteTrackPublication, participant: rtc.RemoteParticipant):
        if track.kind == rtc.TrackKind.KIND_AUDIO:
            # participant.identity is the speaker's user id.
            asyncio.ensure_future(transcribe(participant.identity, rtc.AudioStream(track)))

    await room.connect(url, token)

async def transcribe(user_id: str, stream: rtc.AudioStream) -> None:
    async for event in stream:
        ...  # event.frame: this person's audio, to your speech-to-text
```

## When to send it

Your webhooks say when ([Your Server](/docs/calls/server#webhooks)):

- `calls.call.started` — a call was made: an agent that should hear it from the first word is sent in now.
- `calls.participant.joined` — someone answered or joined: send the agent in once a call has the people it is for — a support line's customer, a meeting's host.

A ticket is asked for a call that is not over; one asked for an ended call is `409 call_ended`.



<!-- ===== analytics/overview ===== -->

# Analytics

Every project has analytics: what people do in its apps, kept as events, and read back as counts, breakdowns, funnels, retention tables and each person's timeline. An app sends with the publishable key, through its SDK; a server sends and reads with the secret key; and Studio's **Analytics** screens show what was kept. Beside the events, analytics keeps how the apps run: timings measured on the devices, the requests they made, and a device's recent console history when something went wrong ([Performance](/docs/analytics/performance)).

Nothing needs to be turned on. The project's address takes events from its first request, and what an app may collect follows what its person allowed ([Consent](/docs/web/consent)).

## What is kept

| Kind | What it is | Sent by | Counted on the usage page as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Events | A capture (a name and its properties), a page view (`$pageview`), a screen view (`$screen`), an identify (`$identify`), an alias (`$alias`), and a person's properties set | An app's SDK; a server with the secret key | Analytics events (`analytics.events`) — all but setting a person's properties, which is not counted |
| Performance samples | App starts, screens, network calls, web vitals and custom measures, each a number | An app's SDK | `analytics.perf` |
| Request traces | One request as the app or a backend saw it: path, method, status, duration, error | An app's SDK; a `palbase/backend` app, one for each request it answers | `analytics.traces` |
| Console history | A device's recent log lines and network exchanges, sent when something went wrong: an error, a crash, a person's report | An app's SDK | `analytics.console` |

The platform adds events of its own to a person's timeline: a purchase, a push that reached their phone, a consent they changed, an audience they entered or left. `GET /analytics/catalog` lists every event a timeline can hold, the platform's with their fields and the app's own as they arrived.

Each event is given the place of the address it came from: its `country`, `region` and `city`. Places come from DB-IP's IP to City Lite database: IP geolocation by [DB-IP](https://db-ip.com), CC BY 4.0. An address says where its network is, not where the device is.

## Who did it

Every event is someone's, by a **distinct id**:

- **A signed-in user.** With the user's token beside the publishable key, the distinct id is the user's id, whatever the body says: a signed-in user's events are theirs however the app wrote them.
- **An anonymous visitor.** With no one signed in, the SDK makes an anonymous id for the browser or the install, and sends under it.
- **What a server names.** With the secret key, the distinct id is what the body says.

An **identify** ties the anonymous id a person had to the user they signed in as: their events before and after are one person's in funnels, retention and their timeline. The web SDK identifies on its own when someone signs in, and forgets the anonymous id when they sign out ([Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics#pbanalytics)). An **alias** says two ids are one user (`POST /analytics/alias`, `{ from, to }`, the event kept under `to`).

A **person** is a user, with the anonymous ids identified as them, or an anonymous id no one has identified. `GET /analytics/people?query=…` finds one by any id they went by or their email, and `GET /analytics/people/{person_id}` is what is known of them: the ids, the installs their events came from, their properties, when they were first and last seen, and where their newest event came from. See [People](/docs/web/analytics#people) and [Audiences](/docs/web/analytics#audiences).

A **session** is the SDK's: half an hour without an event ends one, and each event carries its `session_id`.

## Sending from a server

A server sends with the secret key, naming whose the event is:

```ts
// server/orders.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

/** Kept in the person's timeline beside what their apps sent. */
export async function orderShipped(userId: string, orderId: string, items: number): Promise<void> {
  await palbase.analytics.capture({ body: { event: "order_shipped", distinct_id: userId, properties: { order_id: orderId, items } } });
}
```

In a `palbase/backend` app the same calls are `Palbase.analytics`. An event's name is a letter or `$`, then letters, digits and `_.:-$`, 64 characters at most; its properties are 100 at most, 8 KiB each as JSON and 32 KiB in all. The calls an app's SDK makes, their headers and their answers are on [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics#what-an-app-sends).

A `palbase/backend` app sends a request trace for every request it answers, in batches behind the answers, with the signed-in caller as its distinct id. Nothing is to be written for it: Studio's **Analytics › Network** shows them beside the apps' own ([Performance](/docs/analytics/performance#requests)).

## Consent

What an app's SDK collects follows the person's choices, key by key: events, page views, identifies and person properties go only with `analytics` granted; performance samples and request timings with `performance`, and without the person's id unless `analytics` is granted too. A key with neither the person's choice nor a starting value collects nothing. See [Consent](/docs/web/consent).

The choices are kept by the SDK, which holds back what was not allowed before it is sent; the analytics module keeps what it is sent. A server that sends about a person with the secret key sends what they agreed to.

## How long it is kept

| Setting | What it says | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `retention_days` | How long events, performance samples and request traces are kept | 90 | 1 to 365 |
| `console_retention_days` | How long console history is kept | 14 | 1 to 30 |
| `perf_sample_pct` | The share of performance samples kept: the SDK samples at it before it sends, and the server again | 100 | 0 to 100 |
| `console_bodies` | Whether console history keeps request and response bodies; without it they are removed before anything is kept | `false` | |

A shorter retention removes what is older within minutes; a longer one keeps what is still there for longer. Every read is bounded by it: a window that reaches past the retention reads what is kept.

```sh
palbase analytics:settings:get
palbase analytics:settings:set retention_days=30 perf_sample_pct=10
```

A server reads them with `GET /analytics/settings` and changes them with `PUT /analytics/settings`, which takes all four ([CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#analytics)).

**A deleted user's analytics go with them**: everything under any id they went by — their own, the anonymous ids identified as them, the ids aliased to those — and the events of their installs from while no one was signed in. They leave every audience and come back to none.

## Limits

- A project takes 1,000 events, samples, traces and console records a second, all kinds together. Past it, a send is `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After`. What an app sends is counted against this, not against the project's requests per second.
- A batch of events is 100 at most and 3 MiB; of performance samples, 100 and 512 KiB; of console history, 500 records, 64 KiB each and 2 MiB in all.
- A send is answered once what it sent is kept: a `202` means the event will be there within seconds. A `503` kept nothing, and is sent again with the same `Idempotency-Key`, which keeps it once.
- When an environment has a limit set on one of the four kinds and the month's are used up, sending that kind is `429 quota_exceeded`, with `Retry-After` until the month ends ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)).

## Related

- [Reading Analytics](/docs/analytics/reading) — Studio's screens, summaries, breakdowns, funnels and retention
- [Performance](/docs/analytics/performance) — web vitals, app starts, requests and debug history
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) — sending from the browser, people and audiences
- [Consent](/docs/web/consent) — the keys analytics follows



<!-- ===== analytics/reading ===== -->

# Reading Analytics

What a project's analytics kept is read in two places: Studio's **Analytics** screens, for the people of the organization, and the analytics module's read calls, with the project's secret key, for a server, a report or an agent. Both read the same rows, and neither reads past the project's retention ([How long it is kept](/docs/analytics/overview#how-long-it-is-kept)).

## In Studio

Each screen reads the environment it is opened in, over the period chosen at its top: the last 24 hours, 7, 30 or 90 days.

| Screen | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Analytics** | The period's events, people, page views and events per person, its activity over time, then its most viewed pages and where their views came from, its most recorded events, its events by platform, OS version and app version, and by country |
| **Events** | How often the events you choose were recorded, hour by hour or day by day, and the latest events as they arrive, each with its person, session, time and properties |
| **People** | A person found by any id they went by or their email: every id, what they allowed, their properties and their whole timeline |
| **Audiences** | The people a rule picks, built a condition at a time, previewed before it is kept ([Audiences](/docs/web/analytics#audiences)) |
| **Event catalog** | Every event a timeline can hold: the platform's with their fields, and those your apps and backend sent in the last 30 days, each with a description your team writes |
| **Funnels** | Events in order, and how many people get from the first to the last within the time to convert, and where they leave |
| **Retention** | People by when they first did one event, and how many came back to do another, period by period |
| **Network** | Every request your apps and backend reported ([Performance](/docs/analytics/performance#requests)) |
| **Debug history** | What a device logged and sent before something went wrong ([Performance](/docs/analytics/performance#debug-history)) |

A member of the organization reads every screen; changing an audience or the catalog's descriptions is an admin's ([Organizations](/docs/getting-started/organizations#roles)).

## From a server

```ts
// server/weekly-report.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });
const WEEK = 7 * 24 * 3600;

const summary = await palbase.analytics.getSummary({ query: { window_seconds: WEEK } });
console.log(`${summary.data.total} events by ${summary.data.unique_users} people`);
for (const e of summary.data.events.slice(0, 5)) console.log(e.name, e.count);

const countries = await palbase.analytics.getEventBreakdown({ query: { by: "country", event: "purchase", window_seconds: WEEK, limit: 5 } });
for (const row of countries.data.rows) console.log(row.value || "unknown", row.events, row.users);

const funnel = await palbase.analytics.runFunnel({
  body: { steps: ["signup_started", "signup_completed", "checkout_started"], window_seconds: WEEK, conversion_window_seconds: 24 * 3600 },
});
for (const step of funnel.data.steps) console.log(step.step, step.name, step.users, step.conversion_rate);

const retention = await palbase.analytics.runRetention({
  body: { first_event: "signup_completed", return_event: "app_opened", period: "week", periods: 8, window_seconds: 8 * WEEK },
});
for (const row of retention.data.rows) console.log(row.cohort_start, row.cohort_size, row.returns);
```

In a `palbase/backend` app the same calls are `Palbase.analytics`. A publishable key is refused every read (`403`): an app sends, and only the project's server reads.

Every read takes `window_seconds`, how far back to look: an hour unless said, 400 days at most, and never past the project's retention. The answers that page say `next_cursor`, which the next call passes as `cursor`; the last page has none.

### Summary

`GET /analytics/summary` (`getSummary`): the window's events — `total`, by how many distinct ids (`unique_users`) — and its 50 most frequent names with their `count`. `window_seconds` in the answer is the window read, after the retention bounded it.

### Events

| Call | HTTP | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listEvents` | `GET /analytics/events` | A page of the window's events, newest first, each with its `event_id`, `name`, `distinct_id`, `session_id`, `timestamp` (corrected for the device's clock) and `properties`. `name`, `distinct_id` and `session_id` narrow it; `limit` is 100 unless said, 500 at most |
| `getEventTimeline` | `GET /analytics/events/timeline` | The window's events bucket by bucket, oldest first: `events` and `users` in each, `bucket_ms` its start (unix milliseconds, UTC). `bucket` is `hour` or `day`: hours for two days or less, days beyond, unless said; `name` narrows it to one event. A bucket with no event is not a row |
| `listEventNames` | `GET /analytics/event-names` | Every name the window's events had, 1,000 at most |

### Breakdown

`GET /analytics/breakdown` (`getEventBreakdown`) splits the window's events by one dimension, the most frequent value first: for each `value`, how many `events` had it and by how many distinct ids (`users`).

| `by` | Splits by |
|---|---|
| `platform`, `app_version`, `os_version` | What the app said of itself |
| `country`, `region`, `city` | Where the event came from: an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country, a province or state, a city or district |
| `event` | The event's name |
| `property:<key>` | One of the events' properties: letters, digits and `_ . $ -`, 64 at most |

An absent or empty value is `""`; a property that is not a string is its JSON (a number, `true`, an array). `event` narrows it to one event; `limit` is 10 unless said, 100 at most.

### Funnels

`POST /analytics/funnel` (`runFunnel`) counts how many people took each step, in order, each within `conversion_window_seconds` of their first step.

| Field | What it says | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `steps` | 2 to 10 event names, in order | — |
| `window_seconds` | How far back the first step may be | an hour |
| `conversion_window_seconds` | How long after the first step the last may be | an hour |
| `strict_order` | Any other of the funnel's events between two steps breaks the chain | `false` |

Each step answers its place (`step`, from 1), its `name`, the `users` who reached it and its `conversion_rate`: its share of the first step's. A person's anonymous events count with their signed-in ones once an identify joined them.

### Retention

`POST /analytics/retention` (`runRetention`) puts people in a cohort by the period in which they first did `first_event`, and counts how many of them did `return_event` in each period after.

| Field | What it says | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `first_event` | The event that puts a person in a cohort | — |
| `return_event` | The event that counts as coming back | — |
| `period` | `day`, `week` or `month` | `week` |
| `periods` | Periods followed after the cohort, 1 to 31 | 8 |
| `window_seconds` | How far back the cohorts start | 30 days |

The answer's `rows` are the cohorts, newest first: `cohort_start`, `cohort_size`, and `returns`, where `returns[0]` is the cohort's size and `returns[k]` the people back `k` periods later. `observable` says how many of the periods after have fully passed: a period still under way is not counted, so a young cohort's later columns are not zeros but not yet.

### People, the catalog and audiences

`GET /analytics/people`, `GET /analytics/people/{person_id}` and `GET /analytics/people/{person_id}/events` find a person, read what is known of them and their timeline; `GET /analytics/catalog` lists the events a timeline can hold; the audience calls make and read audiences. See [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics#people).

## From the CLI

```sh
palbase analytics:summary --window 7d
palbase analytics:events --name purchase --window 24h --limit 20
palbase analytics:events --user 3f2c9a1e-…    # one person's, newest first
```

`--window` takes `30m`, `24h`, `7d`; both commands read the environment chosen with `palbase use` or `-E` ([CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#analytics)).

## Errors

| Status | When |
|---|---|
| `400` | A field breaks its rule: a funnel of one step, a `by` that is not one of the dimensions, a `periods` past 31 |
| `403` | Not the project's secret key |
| `429` | Over the project's requests per second; `Retry-After` says when |
| `503` | The read could not be answered now; asking again is safe |

## Related

- [Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview) — what is kept, whose it is, and for how long
- [Performance](/docs/analytics/performance) — timings, requests and debug history
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) — sending, people and audiences
- [Server SDK Overview](/docs/server/overview) — calls, refusals, retries and paging

# Performance

Beside its events, a project's analytics keeps how its apps run on real devices and browsers: **performance samples** (how long an app took to start, a page's web vitals, a request's time), **request traces** (each request as the app or your backend saw it), and **console history** (what a device logged and sent just before something went wrong). Studio shows them on three screens: **Performance**, **Analytics › Network** and **Analytics › Debug history**. They are kept, read and limited as events are ([Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview)), with console history kept for a time of its own.

## Performance samples

A sample is one number: a duration in milliseconds, or a web vital's own unit.

| Type | What it measures | Sent by |
|---|---|---|
| `web_vital` | A page's LCP, INP, CLS, FCP and TTFB | The web SDK, on its own ([Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics)) |
| `network` | One request the app made: its method and route, its status, its time | The web SDK (each `fetch`) and the iOS SDK (each `URLSession` request) on their own; the Android SDK in an app built with the Palbase Gradle plugin (each OkHttp and `HttpURLConnection` request) |
| `app_start` | How long a mobile app took to open (`cold`): from the process's start to the app before the person | The iOS and Android SDKs, on their own |
| `screen` | How long a screen took | Your code (`measure` with the screen kind) |
| `custom` | Anything your code measures | Your code (`startTrace`, `measure`) |

**Nothing is measured until the app's user allows performance** — the consent key `performance`. An app with no consent screen says what it starts with ([iOS](/docs/ios/consent), [Android](/docs/android/analytics), [Web](/docs/web/consent)); a key with no starting value and no choice collects nothing, and the Performance screen stays empty:

```swift
// iOS: analytics and performance collected until the person chooses otherwise
let pb = PalbaseClient(try .environment.with(consent: ConsentOptions(start: ["analytics": .granted, "performance": .granted])))
```

The SDKs time every request the app makes — the project's, your backend's and every other service's — but not what analytics itself sends, nor a request the app cancelled, nor a web socket. A launch the person did not wait for (started by the system ahead of them, or for a push or a job and opened later) is not an `app_start`. Each is turned off in the app's analytics options (`network`, `appStart`).

A network sample's address is kept as its route: no query, and an id in the path is `:id`. Samples go without the person's id unless `analytics` is allowed too.

`perf_sample_pct` keeps a share of the samples, 100 unless changed. The SDKs read it (`GET /analytics/perf/config`, answered `304` while it has not changed) and sample at it before they send, and the module samples again, so a share of 10 sends and keeps about one sample in ten. A send answers how many samples were kept and how many dropped (`{ accepted, dropped }`): a bad shape, a time more than 7 days off, or one not sampled in is dropped, and that is not an error.

### In Studio

**Performance** has a tab for each type: **Network**, **App start**, **Web vitals** and **Custom**. Each lists the type's samples by name with their median (p50), p95, p99 and how many there were; a name chosen draws its percentiles over the period. A web vital is banded as Google bands it — LCP is good at 2.5 s or less and poor past 4 s, INP at 200 ms and 500 ms, CLS at 0.1 and 0.25, FCP at 1.8 s and 3 s, TTFB at 800 ms and 1.8 s — and the screen breaks the slowest 5% down by OS and by app version, and compares the same sample with another environment of the project.

### From a server

| Call | HTTP | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listPerfGroups` | `GET /analytics/perf/client` | The window's samples grouped by type and name and one more dimension (`group_by`: `name`, `app_version`, `platform` or `os_version`): `p50`, `p75`, `p95`, `p99` and `sample_count`, the most sampled first. `trace_type` and `name` narrow it |
| `getPerfTimeline` | `GET /analytics/perf/timeline` | One type's samples (`trace_type`, required) bucket by bucket, oldest first: `p50`, `p75`, `p95` and `sample_count`. A percentile is always of one type: an app start's milliseconds and a CLS score are never added together |

```ts
// server/vitals.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const lcp = await palbase.analytics.listPerfGroups({ query: { trace_type: "web_vital", name: "LCP", group_by: "app_version", window_seconds: 7 * 86400 } });
for (const row of lcp.data.rows) console.log(row.key, Math.round(row.p75), "ms at p75 over", row.sample_count, "samples");
```

## Requests

A request trace is one request as one side saw it: its `endpoint`, `method`, `status`, `duration_ms`, its error when it failed, and the request id the platform gave it. `source` says whose report it is:

- **`client`**: the app's. The SDKs' network samples (each request an app made, as its SDK timed it) are read here, in the same shape.
- **`backend`**: your backend's. A `palbase/backend` app reports every request it answers, with its route as declared (`/orders/{id}`) and the signed-in caller, in batches behind the answers ([Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview#sending-from-a-server)).

The app's report and the backend's of one request share its request id, so the two sides of a request are read together, and the difference between them is often where the time went.

**Analytics › Network** lists the requests newest first, filtered by status, method, endpoint, latency, source and user (**Errors only**, **Server errors** and **Slow >100ms** are ready-made), with the period's requests, its share of server and client errors, its median and its slowest 5%, and the requests by status and latency over time. A request opens with its hops, every report of it from either side; a session opens as a waterfall of its requests in order. **Live on** follows new requests as they arrive.

| Call | HTTP | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listTraces` | `GET /analytics/traces` | A page of the window's requests, newest first. `endpoint`, `source`, `method`, `status`, `status_class` (`2xx` … `5xx`), `duration_min_ms`, `duration_max_ms`, `distinct_id` and `request_id` narrow it |
| `getTraceSummary` | `GET /analytics/traces/summary` | The whole window's requests with the same filters, not a page's: counts by status class, `error_rate`, and the median, p95 and p99 durations |
| `getTraceTimeline` | `GET /analytics/traces/timeline` | The summary bucket by bucket, an hour's or a day's, oldest first |
| `getTraceHops` | `GET /analytics/traces/by-trace` | Every report of one request, by its trace id or its request id, in order; 500 at most |
| `listSessionTraces` | `GET /analytics/traces/session` | A page of one session's requests, in the order they happened |

These are what your apps and backend reported. Every request to the project's address, as the platform answered it, is in [Logs](/docs/getting-started/logs), and a machine's requests over time are on its page ([Machines](/docs/machines/overview)).

## Debug history

When something goes wrong on a device — an error, a crash, or the person reporting a problem — the mobile SDKs send what the app logged and the network exchanges it made just before: up to 500 records, 64 KiB each, 2 MiB in all, kept whole or not at all. Nothing is sampled away. **Analytics › Debug history** shows the records newest first, logs and requests in one stream, filtered by person and session; each says what made the device send it (`error`, `crash` or `user_report`).

Request and response **bodies** are kept only when the project says so (`console_bodies`, off unless changed): otherwise they are removed before anything is kept, and the record says they were. Console history is kept 14 days unless changed (`console_retention_days`, 1 to 30).

```sh
palbase analytics:settings:set console_bodies=true console_retention_days=7
```

Keep bodies only when you need them: a request's body can carry what a person typed, a token, a card's last digits.

| Call | HTTP | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listConsoleRecords` | `GET /analytics/console-records` | A page of the window's records, newest first, each as the SDK wrote it (JSON), and `retention_days`. `user` and `session` narrow it |
| `getConsoleConfig` | `GET /analytics/console-breadcrumbs/config` | Whether bodies are kept now (`bodies_enabled`) and why (`enabled`, `disabled`, or `unavailable`: the setting could not be read, and bodies are not kept), and an upload's limits |

## Related

- [Analytics](/docs/analytics/overview) — what is kept, for how long, and the settings
- [Reading Analytics](/docs/analytics/reading) — events, funnels and retention
- [Web Analytics](/docs/web/analytics) — the browser's own measures
- [Logs](/docs/getting-started/logs) — every request to the project's address



<!-- ===== apps/overview ===== -->

# Client Apps

An app is one product on one platform that calls the project: an iOS app, an Android app or a web app. You register it once in the project, then say what it is in each environment: its bundle on iOS, its package and signing certificates on Android, its origins on the web. From that, each environment gives the app a publishable key of its own, publishes the files Apple and Google read before an app may use the environment's passkeys, and learns which sites may call it and where a sign-in may return to.

Apps are registered with the CLI, or with Studio's API as the CLI does. Studio lists each app's key, by its last characters, under **Settings › API keys**, but has no screen to register an app.

## Quick example

```sh
# Once per project.
palbase apps:create ios "Shop" --team-id ABCDE12345
palbase apps:create android "Shop Android" --slug shop-android
palbase apps:create web "Shop Web"

# In each environment the app runs against.
palbase apps:env:set shop --bundle com.acme.shop -E main
palbase apps:env:set shop --bundle com.acme.shop.staging -E staging
palbase apps:env:set shop-android --package com.acme.shop --sha256 play_signing=AB:CD:EF:… --sha256 debug=12:34:56:… -E main
palbase apps:env:set shop-web --origin https://shop.example.com --redirect https://shop.example.com/auth/callback -E main

# Write the settings into the app's repository, from its root.
palbase apps:sync shop
```

The first `apps:env:set` in an environment prints the app's publishable key there. `palbase apps:sync` writes the app's settings and its backends' clients under `palbase/` in its repository: [Syncing an App's Settings](/docs/apps/sync).

## Registering an app

```sh
palbase apps:create ios|android|web <name> [--slug <slug>] [--team-id <id>] [--app-id-prefix <prefix>]
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | What it is called, 1 to 100 characters. `palbase apps:update <app> --name <name>` renames it. |
| Slug | Its name in a checkout and on the command line: `palbase/environments/<env>/<slug>.json`. Lower-case letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, 2 to 40 characters; made from the name unless `--slug` gives it. One per project. |
| Platform | `ios`, `android` or `web`, for good. The same product on another platform is another app. |
| Apple team | An iOS app's: `--team-id`, the 10 characters under **Apple Developer › Membership**. Required. `--app-id-prefix` only when the app's App ID prefix is not the team's: an app made before 2011, or one moved from another team. |

An app's widgets, notification service and other extensions are not apps of their own. Apple gives them bundles under the app's, and they share its sign-in.

A registered app is in no environment yet. `palbase apps:list` lists the project's apps with what each is in every environment; `palbase apps:get <app>` shows one, with its publishable key in each. The `apps:` commands name an app by its slug or its id. The id is a UUID, printed with `--json` and kept in the app's settings; the [App Distribution](/docs/distribution/overview) commands take it.

## What an app is in an environment

```sh
palbase apps:env:set <app> [--bundle <id> [--app-clip <id>] [--watch <id>]] [--package <id> --sha256 <label>=<fingerprint>…] [--origin <url>… --redirect <url>…] -E <env>
```

| Platform | Flags | What is checked |
|---|---|---|
| iOS | `--bundle`; `--app-clip`, `--watch` | A bundle identifier (`com.acme.shop`). An App Clip's and a watch app's bundle is the app's followed by one more part (`com.acme.shop.Clip`): Apple installs them under no other. |
| Android | `--package`; `--sha256 <label>=<fingerprint>`, once per certificate | The application ID, and the SHA-256 of every certificate the app is signed with, as Play Console and `keytool` print it (hex, with or without colons). A label is a short lower-case name: `play_signing`, `upload`, `debug`. At most 20 certificates. |
| Web | `--origin`, `--redirect`, each given again for more (or comma-separated) | 1 to 20 origins and at most 20 redirects. |

On Android, the certificate that matters on a device is the one the installed build is signed with: Google's app signing key for a build from Play (**Play Console › App signing**, not the upload key), and your debug key for a build from your computer (`./gradlew signingReport`). Give each.

A web origin is `https://` and a domain name a passkey can be used from: a registrable one, written in ASCII (punycode for an international name), with a port when it is not 443 and no path. `http://` is taken only for `localhost` or a loopback address. A redirect is an `https` address (`http` only on this computer) without a fragment; a wildcard in its host names part of one site's names, `https://*-preview.example.com/**`, never a whole site.

Setting an app again replaces what it is in that environment; its key stays. A value that is not one of these is refused with the field and why (`400 invalid_app`). The environment also refuses:

- a bundle, package or origin another app of the same platform has in the environment (`409 identity_taken`): Apple, Google and the browser could not tell the two apart;
- web origins across the environment's web apps on more than five registrable domains (`409 too_many_web_domains`): a browser takes related origins from five at most and skips the rest without a word;
- a 51st app in the environment (`409 too_many_apps`).

The same bundle, package or origin in two environments is said, not refused. Two builds can then not be installed side by side, and a device with both mixes their sign-ins: Apple and Google suggest a bundle of its own per environment.

`palbase apps:env:unset <app> -E <env>` takes the app out of one environment: its key there is revoked, and the environment's files stop naming it.

## Its publishable key

Each app has its own publishable key in each environment it is set in, `pb_<ref>_c…`, made the first time it is set there. It is a publishable key like any other: it ships in the app, its role is `anon`, and the signed-in user's token decides whose data a request reaches ([The keys](/docs/getting-started/introduction#the-keys)).

- **It is kept, not shown once.** Every copy of the app carries it, so `palbase apps:get <app>` prints it, `palbase apps:sdkconfig <app> -E <env>` prints the environment's settings with it, and `palbase apps:sync` writes it into the checkout.
- **An app has one live key.** `palbase keys:list` names it `app: <name>`. Revoking it (`palbase keys:revoke <key id>`) refuses the old key from then on and gives the app a new one in the same step, which `apps:sync` and `apps:sdkconfig` hand out. A build that carries the old key stops reaching the environment until it is rebuilt.
- One app's key is replaced, or taken out of an environment, without touching another app's.

The environment also has the publishable key it was made with, and any made under **Settings › API keys › Create publishable key** (`palbase keys:create --kind publishable`). Those are shown once, when they are made.

## What the environment publishes

Every environment serves three files at its address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio`, with no key, the way Apple, Google and browsers fetch them:

| Path | What it holds | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /.well-known/apple-app-site-association` | `webcredentials.apps`: `<App ID prefix>.<bundle>` for each iOS app, its App Clip and its watch app | iOS, before the app may use the environment's passkeys |
| `GET /.well-known/assetlinks.json` | One statement per Android app with a certificate: `delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds` for its package and the SHA-256 of each certificate | Android's Credential Manager, before the app may use the environment's passkeys and saved passwords |
| `GET /.well-known/webauthn` | `origins`: the web apps' `https` origins, sorted | A browser on one of those sites, before it uses a passkey whose relying party is the environment's address |

Each answers `200` with `application/json` and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`, and an empty list when the environment has no such app, so a device that is not associated says "not associated" rather than failing to fetch. Universal Links and App Links are not claimed: links on the environment's address are not an app's to open.

Apple's CDN caches its file: an iOS device sees a change in a day or so. Android 15 checks again within a week. The app's own half on iOS is the **Associated Domains** entitlement `webcredentials:<ref>.palbase.studio`, which its settings name in `auth.associated_domains` ([iOS SDK](/docs/ios/overview#connect-the-app-to-the-project)).

## What else an app decides

| Platform | What the environment does with it |
|---|---|
| iOS | Accepts App Attest keys from the app and its watch app (an App Clip attests as its app). Matches an App Store purchase, and a purchase made in Xcode with its StoreKit file, to the registered bundle. The app's settings name the keychain group its sign-in is kept in: `<App ID prefix>.<bundle>.palbase`. |
| Android | Accepts a passkey ceremony from the app as signed with one of its certificates, and a device's attested key from the app as signed with one of them ([Device attestation](/docs/backend/authentication#device-attestation)). Reads a Google Play purchase the app reports from Play under its package. |
| Web | Accepts a passkey ceremony from its `https` origins. Starts every [machine](/docs/machines/overview) of the environment with its origins, and a `palbase/backend` app answers their browsers' cross-origin requests by itself ([Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls)); a change rolls the machines out again with the new list. Adds its redirects to the addresses an auth email's link may return to ([Web Auth](/docs/web/auth#where-email-links-land)). |
| Every platform | A web checkout's `success_url` and `cancel_url` return to a web app's origin, or to an iOS or Android app's own scheme: its bundle or its package. |

While App Attest is in `monitor` or `enforce` in an environment, its last iOS or Android app cannot leave it, by `apps:env:unset` or `apps:delete`: a gate with no app would refuse every client. Turn App Attest off there first (`palbase auth:settings:set app_attest_mode=off -E <env>`).

## Deleting and restoring an app

```sh
palbase apps:delete shop
palbase apps:restore shop
```

A deleted app is suspended in every environment for 30 days: its keys are refused and the environments stop publishing it, so every build of it stops reaching the project at once. `apps:delete` asks first; `-y` confirms without asking. `palbase apps:restore` brings it back as it was, with the same keys, until the 30 days are out. Then it is removed for good, its keys revoked. `apps:list` shows a deleted app with the day it is removed, and `apps:sync` refuses to write a checkout that builds it meanwhile.

`palbase apps:update <app> --team-id <id>` moves an iOS app to another Apple team, and `--app-id-prefix ""` sets its prefix back to the team's; every environment it is in is told.

## Who can do what

| | Registers, changes, deletes apps | Reads apps and their settings |
|---|---|---|
| A member of the organization | — | Yes |
| An admin, signed in or with an admin [access token](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) | Yes | Yes |
| An environment token | — | Its own environment's alone, with the `apps:sync` scope or none |

An admin access token registers a product's apps with no one signed in, as a Firebase service account adds an app. Studio's API, which the CLI calls:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/projects/{id}/apps` | The project's apps, each with what it is and its key in every environment |
| `POST /v1/projects/{id}/apps` | Registers one: `{ "platform", "name", "slug"?, "team_id"?, "app_id_prefix"? }` |
| `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE /v1/projects/{id}/apps/{app}` | Reads, changes (`name`, `team_id`, `app_id_prefix`) or deletes one |
| `POST /v1/projects/{id}/apps/{app}/restore` | Restores a deleted one |
| `PUT /v1/environments/{ref}/apps/{app}` | What it is in the environment: `{ "ios": { "bundle", "app_clip"?, "watch"? } }`, `{ "android": { "package", "fingerprints": [{ "label", "sha256" }] } }` or `{ "web": { "origins": [], "redirects"? } }`; the answer has its key and any `warnings` |
| `DELETE /v1/environments/{ref}/apps/{app}` | Takes it out of the environment |
| `GET /v1/environments/{ref}/apps/{app}/config` | Its settings in the environment, as `apps:sdkconfig` prints them |

`{id}` is the project's id, `{ref}` the environment's, `{app}` the app's id.

## Related

- [Syncing an App's Settings](/docs/apps/sync): what `palbase apps:sync` writes into the app's repository
- [App Distribution](/docs/distribution/overview): an app's builds to TestFlight and Google Play
- [Web Auth](/docs/web/auth#passkeys): passkeys from a web app
- [CLI reference: `apps`](/docs/cli/reference#apps)



<!-- ===== apps/sync ===== -->

# Syncing an App's Settings

`palbase apps:sync` writes into an app's repository what the app is built with in each environment it is set in: the environment's address, the app's [publishable key](/docs/apps/overview#its-publishable-key), what the modules tell a client, and a typed client of each backend the environment runs. It writes under `palbase/` and touches nothing outside it. The build reads those files, so nothing reaches the network when the app is built, and a URL or key is never typed into the app.

## Running it

From the repository's root, name the apps it builds:

```sh
palbase apps:sync shop-web
```

The apps named join the checkout's, which `palbase/project.json` records. After that, `palbase apps:sync` with no name syncs them all. One checkout may build several apps: a web app and its admin site, or an iOS and an Android app side by side.

Run it again whenever the project changes: the app set in a new environment, its key replaced, a machine added, a backend's routes or gateways changed. Each file is made whole from what the project gives now and compared with the one on disk; only a file that differs is written. A file it made that the project no longer gives, such as an environment the app left or a machine removed, is deleted. Commit what it writes.

Each run prints what it added, changed and removed, and notes what needs you: an app in no environment yet, a machine with no contract to make a client from, the keychain entitlement an iOS app needs.

## What it writes

```text
palbase/
├── project.json
├── shop-web.ts                     web: the editor's environment
├── shop-web.main.ts                web: one per environment
├── shop-web.staging.ts
├── shop.palbase                    iOS: every environment, as Swift
├── palbe/
│   ├── backend.ts                  web: the editor's environment
│   ├── backend.main.ts
│   └── backend.staging.ts
└── environments/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── shop-web.json
    │   ├── shop-web.ts
    │   ├── shop.json
    │   ├── contracts/backend.openapi.json
    │   └── palbe/backend.ts
    └── staging/
        └── …
```

| File | For | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `palbase/project.json` | every checkout | The project's id and name; the checkout's apps (id, slug, name, platform); the editor's environment (`types_environment`); the backends' names in the apps (`clients`) |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/<app>.json` | every app | [The app's settings](#the-apps-settings) in that environment |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/contracts/<machine>.openapi.json` | an environment with a backend | The contract the machine's serving build answers |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/palbe/<machine>.ts` | a web app | The backend's typed client, in TypeScript |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/palbe/<machine>.kt` | an Android app | The backend's typed client, in Kotlin |
| `palbase/<app>.palbase` | an iOS app | Each environment's configuration and its backends' clients, in Swift: one file, which the Xcode build rule reads for the build's environment |
| `palbase/environments/<env>/<app>.ts` | a web app | The app's settings module: `settings`, `connect()` and `pb`, the client typed with the environment's backends |
| `palbase/<app>.ts`, `palbase/palbe/<machine>.ts` | a web app | The editor's environment, re-exported |
| `palbase/<app>.<env>.ts`, `palbase/palbe/<machine>.<env>.ts` | a web app | Each environment's, which a build made for it is type-checked against |

`palbase/environments/` and `palbase/palbe/` are the sync's own: a file there that it would not write is removed, except a `.storekit` file, which [`palbase purchases:storekit`](/docs/purchases/testing-apple) makes. At the top of `palbase/` it touches only `project.json`, `.palbase` files and files that start with its header, `// Code generated by palbase apps:sync`. When `palbase/`, or a folder or file in it, is a symbolic link, it writes nothing.

## The app's settings

`palbase/environments/<env>/<app>.json` is the document `palbase apps:sdkconfig <app> -E <env>` prints:

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "project": { "id": "0b9c4e7a-…", "name": "Shop" },
  "environment": { "ref": "k3xq81w4m", "slug": "staging", "name": "Staging", "production": false },
  "app": { "id": "4f6c2d10-…", "name": "Shop Web", "slug": "shop-web", "platform": "web", "web": { "origins": ["https://staging.shop.example.com"] } },
  "url": "https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio",
  "publishable_key": "pb_k3xq81w4m_c…",
  "auth": { "rp_id": "k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio", "associated_domains": ["webcredentials:k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio"] },
  "realtime": { "url": "wss://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio/realtime/v1" },
  "backends": [{ "machine": "backend", "url": "https://k3xq81w4m.app.palbase.studio", "contract_digest": "9e1f…" }],
  "digest": "sha256:5b2a…"
}
```

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `environment.production` | `true` for the project's first environment, `main` |
| `app` | The app, with what it is in this environment (`ios`, `android` or `web`) |
| `url`, `publishable_key` | What the app's client is made with: the environment's address and the app's own key |
| `keychain_group` | An iOS app's: `<App ID prefix>.<bundle>.palbase`, the keychain access group the app and its extensions keep the sign-in in |
| `auth` | The passkeys' relying party, and the iOS app's Associated Domains entry |
| `backends` | The environment's machines: each one's address, and the digest of the contract its serving build answers (none while it is unread) |
| `digest` | The SHA-256 of the document without this field: a build made with another digest is not current |

An iOS app needs the **Keychain Sharing** capability with the group `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)$(PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER).palbase` in every target that uses Palbase: without it the SDK keeps no session, and sign-in fails with `keychain_unavailable`. The sync reminds you each run.

`--format env` prints the address and key alone, for a build that does not read `palbase/` (another framework, a game engine):

```sh
palbase apps:sdkconfig shop-web --format env -E staging
```

```text
PALBASE_URL=https://k3xq81w4m.palbase.studio
PALBASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pb_k3xq81w4m_c…
```

The publishable key is public: it ships in the app. A secret key never does, and no file the sync writes holds one.

## A build and its environment

The settings of every environment are in the checkout; the build picks one.

- **Web.** An app imports `pb` from `palbase/<app>.ts`. For the editor, that is one environment's: `--types <env>` names it, `palbase/project.json` remembers it, and without one it is the first environment the app is in that is not `main`. A build imports its own environment's instead: the Vite plugin from `palbase/web/vite`, `palbase({ app: "shop-web", environments: { development: "staging", production: "main" } })`, maps each `vite --mode` to an environment and type-checks the app against that environment's backends first. See [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls).
- **iOS.** The Xcode build rule extracts the Swift of the environment its configuration's `PALBASE_ENVIRONMENT` names from `palbase/<app>.palbase`; a configuration that names none, or one the app is not set in, stops the build. See [iOS SDK](/docs/ios/overview#connect-the-app-to-the-project).
- **Android.** The app's `build.gradle.kts` maps each build variant to an environment and compiles that environment's `<app>.json` and Kotlin clients into the variant's sources; a variant that names no environment, or one the app is not set in, stops the build. See [Android SDK](/docs/android/overview#the-environment-in-the-build).

## Backends

Each machine of the environment becomes `pb.<name>` in its apps, typed from the contract its serving build answers: its routes, their models and typed errors, and its [gateways](/docs/web/gateways). The name is the machine's camelCased, `pb.shopApi` for the machine `shop-api`, unless `--as shop-api=shop` names it otherwise. A name is the checkout's, the same in every environment, kept in `palbase/project.json`, and never one of the client's own (`auth`, `flags`, `storage`, …).

- A machine whose contract has not been read yet gets no client, and the run says so. A contract is read once the build's version alone serves: a `palbase/backend` app writes its own; for another program, [`palbase machines:update <machine> --openapi-path <path>`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-machinesupdate) names where it serves one.
- When a push's version did not roll out (its contract was refused, its tests failed), the client is made from the build that serves, and the run says so.
- Two backends of one environment that declare the same type, both with a `HealthController` say, cannot share one Swift or Kotlin target: the run stops (`backends_collide`) and names it.

`--backend [<machine>=]<dir>` makes a backend's client from its checkout on this computer instead, to call a route before any machine serves it. The CLI runs `bun --no-env-file run src/main.ts` there with `PALBASE_CONTRACT_OUT` set: the `palbase/backend` app writes its contract and exits, connecting to nothing and reading no `.env` file. Sync again without `--backend` once the backend is deployed.

## In CI

```sh
palbase apps:sync --check
```

`--check` writes nothing. It exits 1 when the committed files are not what the project gives now, and lists each file as missing, differing or no longer given.

An environment token sees its own environment alone, so a sync made with one writes that environment's files and counts every other environment's as no longer given. For a checkout of several environments, run the check with an organization's [access token](/docs/getting-started/access-tokens) of the member role.

## When it refuses

| Code | Why |
|---|---|
| `another_project` | The checkout's `palbase/` is another project's. Run it for that project (`-P`), or in this project's own checkout. |
| `app_deleted` | The app is [deleted](/docs/apps/overview#deleting-and-restoring-an-app); `palbase apps:restore` brings it back. |
| `no_such_app` | The project has no app by that slug or id; the answer lists its apps. |
| `environments_collide` | Two environments' slugs differ only in letter case: their folders would be one on macOS and Windows. |
| `linked_path` | `palbase/` or a folder in it is a symbolic link. |
| `unusable_contract` | A backend's contract makes no client in the app's language: fix the backend, deploy it, and sync again. |
| `invalid_backend_name` | An `--as` name is a word the client or the language keeps. |

## Related

- [Client Apps](/docs/apps/overview): registering an app and setting it in an environment
- [Calling Your Backend](/docs/web/backend-calls) and [Web Gateways](/docs/web/gateways): `pb.<backend>` in a web app
- [CLI reference: `apps:sync`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appssync) and [`apps:sdkconfig`](/docs/cli/reference#palbase-appssdkconfig)
