<!-- ===== machines/overview ===== -->

# Machines

A **machine** is your own code running on Palbase: a small sandboxed computer that runs one image of your project's, built from a branch of a GitHub repository, and answers HTTPS at an address of its own. A [`palbase/backend`](/docs/backend/overview) app is the usual thing to run on one, but a machine runs whatever its build makes — a Next.js site, a Go service, a worker that only serves a health check.

You never deploy a machine by hand. You [connect GitHub](/docs/machines/github), open the machine on a repository, a branch and a directory, and from then on **a push to that branch is the deploy**: it is built, rolled out beside the version that serves, and only then takes traffic. See [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds).

In Studio, machines live under **Backend › Machines**. Everything Studio does there is the machines module's API, which takes the project's secret key — every step on these pages names the call beside the click.

## What a machine is

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, 32 characters at most. `backend` when left out. Not `github`, `network` or `sizes`, which are the API's own paths. |
| Source | A repository, a branch and a directory of it ([Connecting GitHub](/docs/machines/github)) |
| Size | How much CPU and memory it has, and whether it sleeps (below) |
| Port | The TCP port it listens on, `8080` unless you say otherwise. It also finds it in `PORT`. |
| Copies | How many copies run while it is awake, 1 to 5 |
| Health check | A path that answers 2xx while it serves |
| Environment | Variables of your own, and the project secret set it starts with |
| Database | One of the project's [databases](/docs/machines/databases), or none |

A project has **5 machines at most**, and a machine's name is that machine's alone. Deleting a machine frees its name at once.

## Its address

The machine named `backend` is the project's backend and answers at the project's own name under the app domain; any other machine answers at its name and the project's ref:

```text
https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio          the machine named backend
https://<name>-<ref>.app.palbase.studio   any other machine
```

The `url` field of the machine (Studio shows it as **Address**, with an **Open** button) is the address to use. A request there is your customers' own: no API key is asked for and none is added. Who may call a route is the app's to decide — a `palbase/backend` app checks the caller's access token on every route that needs one ([Authentication](/docs/backend/authentication)).

What the platform answers itself, before your program sees anything:

| Answer | When | Safe to send again |
|---|---|---|
| `404 no_such_machine` | The host names no machine (deleted, or never made) | — |
| `429 quota_exceeded` | The project has used its machine time for the period; `Retry-After` says until when | at that time |
| `429 rate_limited` | The project's machines are over its requests-per-second limit; `Retry-After: 1` | yes |
| `503 machine_waking` | The machine was asleep and is still coming up; the request did not reach it; `Retry-After: 5` | yes |
| `503 machine_unavailable` | The machine could not be woken or reached; `Retry-After: 2` | yes |

Every request to the address is counted where it arrives, whatever program answers it: Studio's machine page draws the machine's **Requests** by status class and its **Response time** (median and p95) over the period chosen — the platform's answers above among them, as your customers saw them. Thirty days are kept; of a request, only its time, status and duration — nothing of who sent it or what it asked.

A path whose first segment is `_palbase` — `/_palbase/health`, `/_palbase/crons` — is never sent to a machine from outside. It is the platform's own way in (its health checks, its [crons and tasks](#crons-and-tasks)), and a request for it from the internet is answered `404`. A backend's contract is not asked of it: its build writes it, and the platform keeps it with the build.

## Sizes

| Size | CPU | Memory | Sleeps |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shared-256` | 0.2 vCPU | 256 MiB | yes |
| `shared-512` | 0.5 vCPU | 512 MiB | yes |
| `shared-1024` | 1 vCPU | 1024 MiB | yes |
| `dedicated-1x` | 1 vCPU of its own | 2048 MiB | never |
| `dedicated-2x` | 2 vCPU of its own | 4096 MiB | never |

A **shared** size has a fraction of a CPU as its ceiling and is **put to sleep when it is idle** — after 15 minutes without a request — and woken by the next request, which waits for it. A request that waits longer than the wake allows is answered `503 machine_waking` with `Retry-After`, and asking again is what brings the answer. A **dedicated** size has whole CPUs of its own and never sleeps.

Sleeping has consequences for code: a machine that sleeps runs nothing while it sleeps. A timer, an in-memory cache or a background loop stops with it, and a request that wakes it pays the start-up. Work that must happen on a schedule is a [cron](#crons-and-tasks), and work to be done once, now or later, a [task](#crons-and-tasks): the platform wakes the machine for either.

`shared-256` is the size every project may open. The others are sizes that are paid for: open to an environment on Pay as you go with credit ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)); for another, opening a machine at one, or moving one to it, is refused with `403 size_not_available`; `palbase machines:sizes` lists the sizes the environment may open now ([Usage & Limits](/docs/getting-started/usage-and-limits)).

What a project's machines and databases reserve between them is held to the project's limit: a size or a number of copies that does not fit is refused with `409 machines_over_limit`.

## Copies

A machine runs **one copy** unless you give it more (`replicas`, **Copies** in Studio, 1 to 5). Each copy runs on a node of its own, a request goes to one of them, and a copy or a node that goes leaves the others serving. A node taken for maintenance or given back is emptied one copy at a time, and a machine of one copy is moved, not stopped: its copy starts on another node and takes requests before the old one stops. Every copy is of the machine's size and counts as one against the project's limits and its machine time.

What a copy keeps in its own memory or on its own disk, the others do not see — a session, a counter, a cache, a rate-limit window. A machine with more than one copy keeps those where every copy reaches them: its database, or the project's [cache](/docs/backend/cache). A long-lived connection (a WebSocket) stays with the copy that took it. The machine finds its number of copies in `PALBASE_REPLICAS`.

## The health check

A machine says it is well at a **health path**: a path on its port that answers 2xx while it serves. While it starts it has 90 seconds to answer there; once it serves, one that stops answering for about 6 seconds is started again.

Leave the path empty and the build says it: a directory whose `package.json` depends on `palbase/backend` is asked at `/_palbase/health`, which the framework answers `200` while it serves and `503` while it stops. A machine that says nowhere is asked only whether it listens on its port.

## Its environment

The platform starts every machine with these, whatever else it is given:

| Variable | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `PORT` | The port it listens on |
| `PALBASE_URL` | The project's address, `https://<ref>.palbase.studio` |
| `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID` | The project's id |
| `PALBASE_REPLICAS` | How many copies of it run |
| `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET` | The key the platform signs its own calls to this machine with ([crons and tasks](#crons-and-tasks), a backend's contract) |
| `PALBASE_MACHINE` | The machine's own name: what its program puts its tasks on the queue of |
| `PALBASE_DB_URL` | Given a database: where it answers, as the application's login |
| `PALBASE_DB_CONNECTIONS` | Given a database: how many connections to it one copy may hold |

Besides those, a machine has two sources of its own:

- **Environment variables** — settings, not secrets: one `NAME=value` a line in Studio's **Edit settings**, `env` in the API. 100 variables and 64 KiB at most. `PORT` is refused there, and a name the platform sets gives way to the platform's.
- **Secrets** — the project keeps its secrets in two sets, `production` and `development`, and a machine names the set it starts with (**Secrets** in **Edit settings**: *No secrets*, *Production secrets* or *Development secrets*). Every secret of the set is in the machine's environment by its name; a name in `env` wins over the same secret. When a secret of the set changes, the machine rolls out with the new value beside the version that serves. Studio's **Environment › Variables** screen holds the set the environment's machines start with — see [Secrets](/docs/backend/secrets).

A `palbase/backend` app also needs `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY` — the project's secret key, which nothing puts there for you. Make a secret key in **Settings › API keys** (it is shown once), add it as the secret `PALBASE_SECRET_KEY`, and start the machine with that set. Name it in the app's `.env.example` and a build waits for it instead of rolling out an app that cannot start ([Builds](/docs/machines/builds)).

A change of size, port, copies, environment, secrets or health path rolls out beside the version that serves; a change of source is built first and rolls out once its build is up.

## Opening one

In Studio: **Backend › Machines › New machine**. The sheet asks for the repository (only those the connected accounts can push to), the branch, the directory, the name, the size, the port and, optionally, a database and whether this machine runs its migrations. The branch's head is built at once; the machine answers at its address once that build is up.

From a server, with the secret key, it is one call — the same module Studio calls:

```ts
// scripts/open-machine.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const { data: machine } = await palbase.machines.createMachine({
  body: {
    name: "backend",
    size: "shared-512",
    port: 8080,
    source: { repository: "acme/notes", branch: "main", path: "server" },
    secrets: "production",
  },
});

console.log(machine.state, machine.url); // building https://<ref>.app.palbase.studio
```

Inside a `palbase/backend` app the same client is `Palbase.machines`. The calls:

| Call | HTTP | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `createMachine` | `POST /machines` | Opens a machine; its state is `building` |
| `listMachines` | `GET /machines` | The project's machines, by name |
| `getMachine` | `GET /machines/{name}` | What was asked for, and what runs |
| `updateMachine` | `PATCH /machines/{name}` | Changes its source, size, port, copies, env, secrets, health path or database |
| `deleteMachine` | `DELETE /machines/{name}` | Takes it away; its address stops answering |

A machine's `state` is `building` (no build of it runs yet), `starting`, `awake`, `asleep` or `failed` — `state_reason` says why it failed, or why a new version is not up. `version` counts the changes asked for and `running_version` the one that runs: they are equal once a change has rolled out.

## Crons and tasks

A machine that sleeps cannot keep a timer, and a timer in a machine with three copies fires three times. So the schedule — and the queue of work to be done once — are the platform's: the program **says** what crons and task types it has, and the platform **calls** it when a cron is due or a task's time comes — waking the machine for it, and calling one copy.

> **Note:** A backend on `palbase/backend` answers these calls itself: mark a provider with `@Cron` — see [Cron](/docs/backend/cron) — or `@Task` — see [Tasks](/docs/backend/tasks). Any other program answers the calls below.

The calls, all on the machine's own port, all signed with the key in `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`:

| Call | The program answers |
|---|---|
| `GET /_palbase/crons` | `{"crons": [{"name", "schedule", "time_zone", "timeout", "retry"}]}` — asked once each version comes up; `404` means it has none |
| `POST /_palbase/crons/<name>` | Runs the cron. The body is `{"cron", "run_id", "scheduled_at", "attempt"}`; the call is held open until it is done |
| `GET /_palbase/tasks` | `{"tasks": [{"name", "timeout", "retry", "concurrency"}]}` — asked with the crons; `404` means it has none |
| `POST /_palbase/tasks/<name>` | Does one attempt of a task. The body is `{"task", "id", "attempt", "payload", "created_at"}`; the call is held open until it is done |

A cron's `schedule` is five cron fields — minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week — on the clocks of `time_zone` (an IANA name; UTC when left out). `timeout` is the seconds an attempt has (30 when left out, 900 at most) and `retry` the attempts a run has after its first fails (5 when left out, 10 at most). A task type's `timeout` is 60 when left out (900 at most), its `retry` 5 (20 at most) and its `concurrency` — how many of its tasks are with the machine at once — 5 (50 at most). A name is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, 64 characters at most; a machine has 50 crons and 50 task types at most. What the platform cannot run (a bad schedule or zone, a value out of range) is left out of the list.

A `2xx` answer is done. For a cron, `404` is "no such cron in this version", and the run is skipped; anything else — or no answer within the timeout — is a failed attempt, made again after 10 s, 20 s, … up to five minutes apart. One run of a cron runs at a time: a cron due again while its last run is still going is **skipped**, not queued. For a task, `422` is "this task can never be done" — it fails at once — and anything else that is not `2xx` is a failed attempt, made again after 10 s, 20 s, … up to an hour apart.

Every call carries `Palbase-Signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256(key, "<t>.<body>")>` — a webhook's signature, with the machine's key. `verifySignature` from `palbase/server` checks it:

```ts
// crons/server.ts
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { verifySignature, WebhookSignatureError } from "palbase/server";

const key = process.env.PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET ?? "";

const crons = [{ name: "nightly-digest", schedule: "0 3 * * *", time_zone: "Europe/Istanbul", timeout: 120, retry: 3 }];

async function nightlyDigest(runId: string): Promise<void> {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: "digest", run_id: runId }));
}

createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(chunk as Buffer);
  const body = Buffer.concat(chunks);
  const path = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://machine").pathname;

  if (path !== "/_palbase/crons" && !path.startsWith("/_palbase/crons/")) {
    res.writeHead(200).end("ok");
    return;
  }
  try {
    // A GET is signed over "<t>." and an empty body; a POST over its bytes as they arrived.
    const signature = req.headers["palbase-signature"];
    await verifySignature({ secret: key, signature: Array.isArray(signature) ? signature[0] : signature, body });
  } catch (e) {
    res.writeHead(e instanceof WebhookSignatureError ? 401 : 500).end();
    return;
  }

  if (req.method === "GET" && path === "/_palbase/crons") {
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" }).end(JSON.stringify({ crons }));
    return;
  }
  if (req.method === "POST" && path === "/_palbase/crons/nightly-digest") {
    const run = JSON.parse(body.toString("utf8")) as { run_id: string; attempt: number };
    await nightlyDigest(run.run_id);
    res.writeHead(204).end();
    return;
  }
  res.writeHead(404).end();
}).listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 8080));
```

The same `run_id` comes with every attempt of one run, and the same `id` with every attempt of one task: key the work on it, and an attempt made again after a lost answer does not do it twice.

What the platform keeps of them, with the secret key:

| Call | HTTP | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listCrons` | `GET /machines/{name}/crons` | The crons the running version said, each with its zone, when it is next due, whether it is paused, and its latest run |
| `listCronRuns` | `GET /machines/{name}/crons/{cron}/runs` | A cron's latest 50 runs, newest first: `running`, `waiting`, `succeeded`, `failed` or `skipped`, with the attempts each took, why one failed, and whether it was asked to run now. Runs are kept 7 days. |
| `runCron` | `POST /machines/{name}/crons/{cron}/run` | Runs it now, apart from its schedule (`409` while a run of it is not over) |
| `pauseCron` / `resumeCron` | `POST /machines/{name}/crons/{cron}/pause`, `…/resume` | Paused, it is not run until resumed, whatever version comes up; resumed, it is due at its next time |
| `enqueueTask` | `POST /machines/{name}/tasks` | Puts a task — `{"task", "payload", "delay" \| "run_at", "key"}` — of a type the running version declares |
| `listTasks` | `GET /machines/{name}/tasks` | Its tasks, newest first, of one `state` and `task` type or all; a task that succeeded or was cancelled is kept a day, one that failed 30 |
| `getTask` | `GET /machines/{name}/tasks/{task}` | One task, with its payload |
| `retryTask` / `cancelTask` | `POST /machines/{name}/tasks/{task}/retry`, `…/cancel` | A failed task back on the queue, its attempts counted on; a waiting one taken off it |
| `listTaskTypes` | `GET /machines/{name}/task-types` | The task types the running version declared, with what each one's queue holds |

## Reaching the internet

A machine reaches the internet as any server does — a payment provider's API, a webhook of yours, a package registry — on any port but 25: send mail through a provider's API or its submission port (587). It reaches nothing of the platform's own network: not another project's machine and not the platform's services, except at the platform's public address, as any client of it does.

What a project's machines send to the internet is counted, in bytes, as **Machine internet traffic** on the project's usage page (`machines.egress`). What they send to the platform at its public address, what goes to their databases, and what they take from the internet is not. What the project's answers send its clients — its machines' answers, its modules' (files storage hands out among them) — is counted as **Response traffic** (`edge.egress`), in bytes on the wire.

A free project sends 5 GB a month at full speed: its machines' internet traffic and its response traffic together. Past it, until the month ends (UTC), it is slowed, never stopped — every byte still goes:
- its machines send to the internet at about 256 kbit/s between them — each copy of a machine its share; requests still go out, connections open at once and downloads keep going; what they send takes longer;
- its machines' answers to their clients go at about 256 kbit/s between them, as do the files its storage hands out (about 256 kbit/s for the project); its other answers — the API's JSON, realtime — are counted but not slowed.

Each machine's log says so when the slowing begins (`palbase: this project has sent 5 GB …`). What its machines send the project's databases and the platform at its public address is never slowed, DNS questions to the machine's resolvers keep a pace of their own, and a project that may use paid sizes is not slowed at all.

### Its outbound range

Every machine reaches the internet from one small range of addresses, the platform's, written as a CIDR (such as `203.0.113.8/29`). Studio shows it on the **Machines** page, under **Outbound address**. Add the whole range to a provider's allowlist when the provider — a bank, a payment or an SMS provider — lets in only the addresses it knows: a connection may leave from any address in it.

**The range is shared by every Palbase machine**, of every project. An allowlist of it lets in all of Palbase, not your project alone, so a provider must still know you by your own credentials, such as an API key. The range stays the same as the platform changes; a change of it is announced before it is made.

| Call | HTTP | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `getMachineNetwork` | `GET /machines/network` | `outbound_ips`: where machines reach the internet from, as ranges (CIDR); `shared`: `true`, every project's machines leave from them |

## Limits

| | |
|---|---|
| Machines per project | 5 |
| Copies per machine | 1 to 5 |
| What machines and databases reserve between them | 2 vCPU and 4096 MiB a project (a shared size reserves a quarter of its CPU ceiling, a dedicated one all of it; memory is reserved whole) |
| Builds | 50 a day (UTC) per project; one build at a time; 20 minutes at most each |
| Idle before a shared size sleeps | 15 minutes |
| Environment variables | 100, 64 KiB in all |
| Logs kept | 7 days, up to 1,200 lines a minute per machine |
| Traffic, free project | 5 GB a month at full speed, machine internet traffic and response traffic together; then machines' traffic and answers, and storage's files, at about 256 kbit/s until the month ends (UTC); see [Reaching the internet](#reaching-the-internet) |
| Connections to the internet open at once | Per copy of a machine, by its memory: 4,096 for 256 MiB, twice that for each doubling — 8,192 (`shared-512`), 16,384 (`shared-1024`), 32,768 (`dedicated-1x` and larger). One more is refused at once (`connection refused` / a reset). Connections to the platform, to your databases and DNS questions to the machine's resolvers are not counted. The cap keeps one machine from taking a server's whole connection table from the machines beside it: close connections you no longer use, and pool those you reuse |

# Connecting GitHub

A machine is built from GitHub: a **repository**, a **branch** of it and a **directory** in it. The platform reaches your repositories through its GitHub App, **Palbase Cloud**, installed on the GitHub account that owns them. Once an installation is connected to the project, every push to a machine's branch that changes what the machine is built from is built and rolled out — there is no other deploy step, and no command to run.

## Connect the App

In Studio: **Backend › Machines › New machine › Connect GitHub**. Studio opens GitHub in a new tab:

1. GitHub asks who you are, and where to install **Palbase Cloud** — on your own account or an organization's, on every repository or the ones you choose.
2. GitHub brings you back to Palbase, which shows the accounts Palbase Cloud is installed on that you can push to, and where to install it on another.
3. You connect the one you choose by writing the project's ref. That is the confirmation that this installation is for this project.
4. Back in Studio, **Refresh**: the sheet lists the repositories you can push to.

The link Studio opens holds for 15 minutes. Studio is not on GitHub's way back — it hears nothing of it — which is why the sheet asks you to refresh rather than waiting for a reply.

With the secret key, the same steps are calls of the machines module (`createServer(...).machines` from [`palbase/server`](/docs/server/overview), or `Palbase.machines` inside a backend):

| Call | HTTP | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `connectGitHub` | `POST /machines/github/connect` | Answers the address where the project's owner installs and connects Palbase Cloud (`url`, and `expires_at` 15 minutes on) |
| `listInstallations` | `GET /machines/github/installations` | The project's installations: the account each is on, and who connected it |
| `linkInstallation` | `POST /machines/github/installations` | Connects an installation with the user's own GitHub token for the App — a device flow's way, for a tool that is not a browser |
| `unlinkInstallation` | `DELETE /machines/github/installations/{installation}` | Disconnects one; refused while a machine is built from it |
| `listRepositories` | `GET /machines/github/repositories` | Every repository the installations reach: what a machine may be built from |

The CLI connects it the same way, and from a computer with no browser too:

```sh
palbase github:connect            # opens GitHub; back from it, you link the account by writing the environment's ref
palbase github:connect --device   # GitHub's device flow: a code you enter at github.com/login/device on any device
palbase github:list               # the accounts linked to the environment, and who linked each
palbase github:repos              # the repositories its machines may be built from
```

`--all-envs` links every environment of the project at once, and `--from <env>` links the installation another environment of the organization linked, with no GitHub sign-in. See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#github).

## Whose repositories

An installation reaches the repositories **the user who connected it can push to** — read when they connected it. A repository they could only read is not offered; connecting again picks up what they can push to now. Two consequences:

- A repository that does not appear in the sheet is either outside the installation (add it on GitHub, under the App's configuration) or one the connector cannot push to. Connect again as someone who can.
- A user who takes their authorization of the App back on GitHub disconnects what they connected.

Installations are a project's own, and in Studio every environment is a project of its own: connect GitHub in each environment whose machines are built from it. The machines of two environments may be built from one repository — a `staging` environment from the `staging` branch, `main` from `main`.

## Repository, branch, directory

A machine's `source`:

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `repository` | The repository's full name, `owner/name` — one `listRepositories` answers |
| `branch` | The branch whose pushes are built and rolled out. Studio fills in the repository's default branch. |
| `path` | The directory the machine is built from, relative to the repository's root — the root when left out. Its `Dockerfile`, `package.json` and `.env.example` are read here. |
| `context` | What the build is given, when that is not `path` itself: a directory above `path`, or `.` for the root |

In Studio's **New machine** sheet these are **Repository**, **Branch** and **Directory**; the branch can be changed later in **Edit settings**, and a new branch is built before it rolls out.

### One repository, several machines

A monorepo holds several apps, and each can be its own machine — a `backend` built from `server/`, a `web` machine built from `web/`:

```text
acme/notes
├── server/          ← machine "backend": path "server"
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   ├── package.json
│   └── src/
├── web/             ← machine "web": path "web"
│   └── …
└── packages/shared/ ← read by both
```

An app that needs a sibling package — `server/` importing `packages/shared/` — is built with the repository's root as its context: `path: "server"`, `context: "."`. Its `Dockerfile`, which stays in `server/`, then copies from the root (`COPY packages/shared ./packages/shared`); without a Dockerfile, the build plans the whole context.

## Which pushes build which machines

A push to the branch is built for a machine **when it changes a file in what that machine's build is given**: its `context`, else its `path`, matched by whole directory names, case-sensitively. With the layout above:

| The push changes | `backend` (`server`) | `web` (`web`) | a machine with `context: "."` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `server/src/notes.ts` | built | — | built |
| `web/app/page.tsx` | — | built | built |
| `packages/shared/x.ts` | — | — | built |
| `README.md` | — | — | built |
| `serverless/x.ts` | — (not `server/`) | — | built |

A push that changes nothing a machine is built from leaves it as it runs, and does not count against the project's builds for the day. A machine built from the repository's root is built by every push.

Where GitHub's account of a push may not be everything it changed, every machine built from the branch is built: a forced push, a branch's first push, a push of 2,048 commits or more, and a commit that names no files (an empty commit among them) or 3,000 or more.

## For platforms: building with a token

A platform whose own users give their repositories to **its** GitHub App — not to Palbase Cloud — builds their machines without asking them to install another app: it makes a token for each build and gives it with the deploy (`source.access: "token"`). Its users see only the platform; nothing of Palbase is installed on their accounts.

The token is the platform's GitHub App's **installation token, for the machine's repository alone, read-only** — GitHub's `POST /app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens` with `repositories: ["<name>"]` and `permissions: { contents: "read" }`. Palbase checks it with GitHub at once: it must be an installation's (`ghs_…`; a person's token is refused), reach the machine's repository and nothing else. What a token may do is not something GitHub tells whoever holds it, so read-only is yours to ask for: Palbase only ever reads with it. The build reads its source with it once and forgets it — no answer, log or build keeps it. One lasts an hour, so make one for each deploy.

```ts
// platform-server.ts
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN! });
const ref = process.env.CUSTOMER_ENV_REF!;
// Your GitHub App's installation token for this repository alone, read-only.
const token = process.env.REPOSITORY_TOKEN!;

// Opened with a token: its first build is the branch's head (or `commit`).
await cloud.project(ref).machines.createMachine({ body: {
  name: "backend", size: "shared-256",
  source: { repository: "customer/shop", branch: "main", access: "token" },
  git_access_token: token,
} });

// Each push your app hears of: a new token, and the commit to build.
await cloud.project(ref).machines.deployMachine({ path: { name: "backend" }, body: {
  commit: "4f6e1c2a9b0d7e3f5a8c1b2d4e6f7a9c0b1d2e3f",
  git_access_token: token,
} });
```

A machine read with tokens is deployed by its platform: no push GitHub delivers to Palbase builds it (your app hears the push — its `push` webhook — and deploys the commit), no check is put on its commits, and it does not wait for checks (`deploy_after_checks` is refused). Everything else is a machine's like any other: its builds, their logs, its own logs, rollbacks and its settings ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds)). A change of its branch is built at its next deploy. How it is read is chosen when it is made.

### Pull request previews, for platforms

No pull request of a machine read with tokens is heard by Palbase, so its platform previews them itself: as your app hears a pull request opened or pushed to (its `pull_request` webhook), it puts the preview at the head of the pull request's branch, with a new token; as the pull request closes, it closes it. The preview is any machine's preview ([Pull request previews](/docs/machines/hosting#pull-request-previews)): a machine of its own, `<name>-pr<number>`, a database of its own when the machine runs its database's migrations, the environment's settings and secrets, 3 days without a put before it is taken down — a put opens it again. Turn previews on in an environment kept for them, never production's (refused there: `previews_in_production`):

```ts
// platform-server.ts — the pull request webhook your app hears
import { PalbaseCloud } from "palbase/cloud";

const cloud = new PalbaseCloud({ token: process.env.PALBASE_TOKEN! });
const ref = process.env.CUSTOMER_ENV_REF!;
// Your GitHub App's installation token for this repository alone, read-only.
const token = process.env.REPOSITORY_TOKEN!;

await cloud.project(ref).machines.updateMachine({ path: { name: "backend" }, body: { previews: true } });

// Opened, or pushed to: the head of its branch, read with a new token.
await cloud.project(ref).machines.putMachinePreview({
  path: { name: "backend", pull_request: 12 },
  body: { branch: "feature/log-workouts", commit: "9c1b2d4e6f7a9c0b1d2e3f4f6e1c2a9b0d7e3f5a", git_access_token: token },
});

// Its address and state — building, ready, idle, refused (with why), closed:
const { data } = await cloud.project(ref).machines.listMachinePreviews({ path: { name: "backend" } });

// Closed:
await cloud.project(ref).machines.deleteMachinePreview({ path: { name: "backend", pull_request: 12 } });
```

The branch must be one of the repository's own: a fork's pull request is not built with the environment's secrets (`branch_not_found`) — who may open one is yours to decide before you put it. A commit named must be the branch's head: a put heard after a newer push answers `commit_not_head`, and a commit already built is not built again. Your app writes on its pull request itself; Palbase writes nothing there. A put takes an admin's full credential: no narrowed environment token puts one. `palbase machines:previews:open` reopens no preview of a machine read with tokens (`preview_needs_token`): put it again.

## What GitHub shows

Each build puts a check on its commit, named **Palbase Cloud · `<ref>`** for the `backend` machine and **Palbase Cloud · `<name>-<ref>`** for another: *Queued*, *Building*, *Waiting for configuration*, then *Rolled out*, *Build failed* or *Did not come up* — or *Left behind* when a newer commit of the branch is built first. The commit's checks are the quickest way to see what a push did; Studio's machine page has the same builds with their logs ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds)).

## Disconnecting

Disconnect an installation (`unlinkInstallation`, `DELETE /machines/github/installations/{installation}`) once no machine is built from it — it is refused while one is. Delete or move the machines built from it first.

## Related

- [Machines](/docs/machines/overview) — sizes, addresses, environment and jobs
- [Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds) — what a push does once it is built
- [Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure) — what a backend's directory holds
- [Quickstart](/docs/getting-started/quickstart) — connect GitHub and push a backend, end to end

# Builds, Logs & Rollback

Code reaches a machine one way: **a push to its branch**. The push is built into an image, the image is rolled out **beside the version that serves**, and traffic moves to it once it is up — so a request never meets a gap, and a version that does not come up never takes one. There is no deploy command, and nothing to run on your machine but `git push`.

This page follows one push from GitHub to traffic, then covers what you read on the way — the build's log, the machine's own lines — and how to go back.

## What a push does

```text
git push origin main
  └─ a build per machine whose directory the push changed   (Connecting GitHub)
       queued → building
         ├─ failed              the build's log says why
         ├─ waiting_config      .env.example names a variable the machine lacks
         └─ the image is ready
              └─ (a database's migrations, when this machine runs them: start)
                   ├─ testing           its tests run against the new version (test_command)
                   │    └─ failed       a test failed: the reason names it; it never takes traffic,
                   │                    the old one keeps serving, the migration is taken back
                   └─ the new version starts beside the old one
                        ├─ it answers its health check → traffic moves; the old one stops
                        │    └─ (migrations: complete, once nothing of the old version is left)
                        └─ it does not come up → the old one keeps serving
```

Each commit of the branch is built once for a machine, however often it is pushed. A project builds one thing at a time; a newer commit that arrives while an older one waits takes its place, and the older build ends `cancelled` (*Left behind* on its GitHub check).

A machine that deploys only after its commit's checks pass (`deploy_after_checks`, as Render's *After CI Checks Pass*) lets every push wait for its own checks, side by side. The first whose checks pass is built and leaves the older ones behind, so the machine only ever moves to a newer commit: an older push whose checks pass later is not built. A push whose checks fail ends `skipped`; the others keep waiting.

### Tests before it takes traffic

A machine that names a **test command** (`test_command`, as Render's pre-deploy command or a CI's test step) has every new build tested before it takes traffic — the build is `testing` meanwhile. Once its database's migration has started, the new version comes up beside the one that serves, **as it will run**: its env, its secrets, its database. The build's own image then runs the command in a shell (`bun test`, `npm test`) against it:

- `PALBASE_TEST_BASE_URL` is where the new version answers; `PALBASE_TEST_AUTH_URL` the project's auth;
- **test users** the run makes for its tests (`test_users`), each with its access token, are in `PALBASE_TEST_IDENTITIES` — `api.signInAs("alice")` from `palbase/backend/test` (or `palbase/server/testing`, whatever the backend is written with) acts as one; they are deleted when the run ends, however it ends.

The tests reach what the machine reaches — its database, the project's storage, mail and the rest — so they write as the machine does: write tests that leave the data as a real user's session would, and that do not depend on an empty database.

They pass, and the version takes traffic. One fails, and the build fails: its `reason` names the tests that failed, its GitHub check shows the end of what they printed (what the run was given that is secret written over), the version never takes traffic, the machine keeps the version it runs, and the migration is taken back. The build's log (`palbase machines:builds:log <build>`) keeps the end of what the tests printed and, under its own heading after it, the end of what **the new version itself** printed while they ran — where a `500` it answered a test with is, with its error, its stack and the request's id (`request_id`, the one the test's `TestApiError` names), secrets written over the same way. Those lines are in the machine's log too, as `source: "test"` (below). A run has 20 minutes. A build is tested as the machine named its tests when the build was released to it. `palbase test --machine <name>` runs the same command, as the same test users, on your computer.

### How the image is made

The build reads the machine's directory (its `path`):

- **With a `Dockerfile`** there, the build uses it, with the build context the machine names (its `context`, else its `path`).
- **Without one**, [Railpack](https://railpack.com) detects what the directory is — Node, Bun, Go, Python, … — and plans the image from it.

A `palbase/backend` app ships a `Dockerfile` (see [Project Structure](/docs/getting-started/project-structure)): its decorators need the TypeScript compiler options that Bun reads from `tsconfig.json`, and a Dockerfile says exactly how it is run. A build has 20 minutes, and a repository is built from at most 1 GiB and 100,000 files.

### `.env.example`: what the program must be given

A `.env.example` in the machine's directory is read as **the list of variables the program needs**: every `NAME=` line is a name (comments, blank lines and `PORT` are skipped; a value after `=` is ignored).

```text
# .env.example — the names this backend reads; their values live in Palbase.
PALBASE_URL=
PALBASE_PROJECT_ID=
PALBASE_SECRET_KEY=
```

When the build is done, every name is looked for among what the machine will start with: its own environment variables, its secret set, and what the platform gives it (`PALBASE_URL`, `PALBASE_PROJECT_ID`, `PALBASE_REPLICAS`, `PALBASE_PLATFORM_SECRET`, and with a database `PALBASE_DB_URL` and `PALBASE_DB_CONNECTIONS`). A name found nowhere stops the rollout: the build waits as **`waiting_config`** (*Waiting for variables* in Studio, *Waiting for configuration* on GitHub), its `missing_env` lists the names, and it **rolls out by itself once the machine has them** — add the secret, or the variable, and nothing has to be pushed again.

Without this file nothing is checked, and an app missing a setting is rolled out to fail at start. The version before it keeps serving either way, but the waiting build says what is wrong by name; the failed start says it in its logs.

## The rollout

The new version starts beside the one that serves, and is held to its [health check](/docs/machines/overview#the-health-check): 90 seconds to answer `2xx` at its health path. Up, it takes the traffic and the old version is stopped — a `palbase/backend` app finishes the requests in flight first (20 seconds at most), then runs its `onShutdown()`. Not up, it never takes a request: the old version keeps serving, the build's check on GitHub says *Did not come up*, and the machine's `state_reason` says why.

A change that is not a push rolls out the same way: a new size, port, number of copies, environment, secret set or health path, a changed secret of the machine's set, and a rollback.

**`SIGTERM` can come more than once.** A machine runs in a sandbox of its own (a small VM), and a version being stopped is sent `SIGTERM` twice, a few milliseconds apart. A `palbase/backend` app handles that. An app of your own should stop on the first and keep its handler for the rest: in Node and Bun `process.on("SIGTERM", …)`, not `process.once`. A process listening once dies of the second signal (exit 143), and its requests still in flight are cut (`503 machine_interrupted`).

### When a release migrates its database

A machine given a database with **Run migrations** on (`database.migrations: true`) migrates it as part of every release, with no step of yours:

1. **start** — before the new version starts, its image runs once with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start` and the owner's address: what the new version needs is added beside what the running version uses. The version rolls out only once start succeeded.
2. **rollout** — both versions run against the same tables.
3. **complete** — once the new version has served and nothing of the old one is left, the image runs once more with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=complete`, and what only the old version used is removed.

A start the app itself refuses — a change the schema cannot make while both versions run, or rows that do not fit it — ends the release: the machine stays on the build that serves, and what start began is taken back (`rollback`). A start that was only cut off (the database restarting, a lock not had in time) is run again and picks up where it stopped. What these runs write is in the machine's logs, marked `migration`. The schema side of all this is [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations); the database side is [Databases](/docs/machines/databases).

One migration is open at a time, and a database's migrations are one machine's: a second machine asking to run them is refused (`409 database_migrated_elsewhere`).

## Builds

Studio's machine page (**Backend › Machines › `<name>`**) lists its **Builds**, newest first — every commit of the branch built for it, its state, and a **Running** badge on the one that serves. **Log** opens a build's log; **Roll back** is on every build that succeeded and does not run.

| State | What it means |
|---|---|
| `waiting_checks` | Waiting for its commit's checks on GitHub (`deploy_after_checks`); `reason` names what it waits for |
| `queued` | Waiting its turn: one build at a time per project |
| `building` | Being built |
| `testing` | Released to its machine; its tests (`test_command`) run against it before it takes traffic — they fail and it fails, `reason` naming them, and the machine runs what it ran |
| `waiting_config` | Built, waiting for what `.env.example` names (`missing_env`); rolls out once the machine has it |
| `succeeded` | Built and rolled out — or a newer build already had |
| `failed` | Not built, or not up; `reason` says which |
| `cancelled` | A newer commit was built first, the head of the branch was asked for (a deploy, or a change of source), or the machine was deleted |
| `skipped` | Its commit's checks did not pass, or did not end in time; nothing of it was built (`reason`) |

| Call | HTTP | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `listBuilds` | `GET /machines/{name}/builds` | A page of builds, newest first (20 by default, `next_cursor` for the next) |
| `getBuild` | `GET /machines/{name}/builds/{build}` | One build: its commit and message, state, reason, `missing_env`, whether it runs |
| `getBuildLog` | `GET /machines/{name}/builds/{build}/log` | The build's log, its last MiB — where a failure is. `404 log_not_ready` before the build has started; `404 no_log` for one that ended before it ran (its `reason` says why) |

## Logs

What the machine writes to stdout and stderr is kept — every copy, every version (one that never came up too), its migration runs, and each new version while its tests ran against it — for **7 days**, up to 1,200 lines a minute per machine for each of those sources (its serving copies, its migration runs, a build's test run); past that, the rest of that minute is not kept — a test run that prints much takes nothing from the version that serves. Write one JSON object a line and each is one line to read back: `Log` from `palbase/backend` does exactly that, with the request's id on every line ([Backend SDK](/docs/backend/overview)).

Studio's machine page shows the last hour, the last 100, 500 or 2,000 lines of it. From a server, `readMachineLogs` (`GET /machines/{name}/logs`) answers NDJSON, one line object a line, oldest first:

| Query | |
|---|---|
| `since` | From when, inclusive (RFC 3339); an hour ago when left out, a week ago at most |
| `until` | Until when, exclusive; now when left out. Not with `follow`. |
| `lines` | How many lines at most, 1 to 5,000 (500 by default) — for a followed read, before it follows |
| `follow` | `true` holds the answer open and sends what the machine writes next |

Each line carries `ts` (to the nanosecond), `id` (ids sort as lines do, and the same line read twice has the same id), `stream` (`stdout` or `stderr`), `generation` (the machine's version that wrote it), `source` (`machine`, `migration` for a migration run, or `test` for what a new version printed while its tests ran against it), `line` (what was written) and which copy wrote it.

```ts
// scripts/tail.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

type LogLine = { ts: string; id: string; stream: "stdout" | "stderr"; generation: number; source: "machine" | "migration"; line: string };

const since = new Date(Date.now() - 10 * 60_000).toISOString();
const { data } = await palbase.machines.readMachineLogs({ path: { name: "backend" }, query: { since, lines: 200 } });

for (const raw of (await data.text()).split("\n")) {
  if (!raw) continue;
  const l = JSON.parse(raw) as LogLine;
  console.log(l.ts, `v${l.generation}`, l.source, l.stream, l.line);
}
```

A followed read is held open for 5 minutes at most (and ends when the machine is deleted). A project holds 5 followed reads open at once; a sixth is `429 too_many_follows`. A reader whose connection ends goes on with `since=` the time of the last line it had — a line may then come twice, and its `id` says so.

## Rollback

**Roll back** returns the machine to one of its builds that succeeded: a **new version** of the machine, running that build's image, rolled out beside the one that serves like any other. It is the only change of what a machine runs that is not made by a push. The images of a machine's last 10 successful builds are kept; an older build is refused (`409 build_not_deployable`).

```ts
// scripts/rollback.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

// The build that ran before the one that serves.
const { data: page } = await palbase.machines.listBuilds({ path: { name: "backend" } });
const previous = page.builds.find((b) => b.state === "succeeded" && !b.running);
if (previous) {
  const { data: machine } = await palbase.machines.rollbackMachine({ path: { name: "backend" }, body: { build: previous.id } });
  console.log(`rolling out version ${machine.version}: ${previous.commit}`);
}
```

The next push to the branch is built and rolled out as usual, so a rollback holds until then. To keep a machine off a bad commit, revert it on the branch — or point the machine at another branch in **Edit settings**.

> **Note:** A rollback changes code, never data. Once a release's migration has completed, the build you return to reads the tables as that migration left them — a column it dropped is gone. A migration still open when its version is abandoned is taken back instead. Make a change an older build cannot read in two releases, so the one before keeps working: [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations).

# Databases

A project's **database** is Postgres 18 of its own, with pgvector and PostGIS, reached from anywhere over TLS with a password. Give one to a [machine](/docs/machines/overview) and the machine starts with its address; connect to it from anything else — `psql`, a migration tool, a BI tool, a server of your own — with the credentials Studio shows once.

A database is the project's, not a machine's. One may be given to several machines, and one machine — the one that runs its migrations — owns its schema. A [`palbase/backend`](/docs/backend/database) app declares that schema in TypeScript and migrates it on every release; anything else that connects is an ordinary Postgres client.

In Studio, databases live under **Database › Databases**. Each step below names the machines module's call beside the click, for a script that holds the secret key.

## Opening one

**Database › Databases › New database** asks for:

| Field | API | |
|---|---|---|
| **Name** | `name` | Lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter, 32 at most; `main` when left out. It answers at `<name>-<ref>.db.palbase.studio`. |
| **Size** | `size` | One of the sizes below; `free` when left out. It can be changed later ([below](#changing-and-removing-one)) |
| **Allowed addresses** | `allow` | Who may connect, as addresses or CIDRs (`203.0.113.7`, `203.0.113.0/24`), 50 at most. Empty: anyone with the password. |
| **Backups kept** | `backup_days` | 1 to 35 days: how far back a [restore](/docs/machines/backups) reaches |

The database's volume is made and it starts; it answers once its state is `awake`. **The answer that opens it holds both of its passwords — the owner's and the application's — and no answer holds them again.** Studio shows them on the database's page once; copy them then. A password you did not keep is made new, not read back ([below](#passwords)).

```ts
// scripts/open-database.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

const { data: db } = await palbase.machines.createDatabase({
  body: { name: "main", size: "free", backup_days: 7 },
});
console.log(db.host, db.state); // main-<ref>.db.palbase.studio starting
```

A project has **3 databases** at most — a deleted one counts until it is purged — and **one of a free size** at a time.

## Sizes

| Size | CPU | Memory | Storage | Sleeps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `free` | 0.25 vCPU | 512 MiB | 1 GB | yes — and awake 400 hours a month at most |
| `hobby` | 0.25 vCPU | 512 MiB | 5 GB | yes |
| `shared-1g` | up to 1 vCPU | 1 GiB | 10 GB | never |
| `shared-2g` | up to 2 vCPU | 2 GiB | 25 GB | never |
| `shared-4g` | up to 2 vCPU | 4 GiB | 50 GB | never |
| `dedicated-1x` | 1 vCPU of its own | 4 GiB | 25 GB | never |
| `dedicated-2x` | 2 vCPU of its own | 8 GiB | 50 GB | never |

`free` is the size every project may open. The others are sizes that are paid for: open to an environment on Pay as you go whose payment account is not held ([Billing](/docs/getting-started/billing)); another is refused one with `403 size_not_available`.

A size that sleeps is put to sleep when it is idle and **woken by the next connection**, in about 10 seconds; the client's connection waits for it. A `free` database awake for its 400 hours sleeps until the month ends, and a client is told so; one asleep for a week is **archived**, and its next connection brings it back from its backup. The other sizes never sleep and live on a disk of their own.

The size is chosen when the database is opened and can be changed later ([below](#changing-and-removing-one)). What a project's machines and databases reserve between them is held to its limit, and a size that does not fit is refused with `409 machines_over_limit`.

### When it is full

A database holding its size's storage turns **read-only**: a transaction takes no writes unless it asks to, and reads go on. `read_only`, `used_bytes` and `quota_bytes` on the database say where it stands. To make room, write in a transaction that asks for it — `BEGIN READ WRITE`, then `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, or `DELETE` followed by `VACUUM FULL` (a `DELETE` alone frees no room). Once it holds less than 95% of its quota it takes writes again, within a minute.

## Connecting

Every database has two logins:

| Login | Who it is | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **Owner** | Owns the database and its tables | Migrations, `psql`, a tool that changes the schema (Prisma, …) |
| **App** | What a machine given the database connects as | Your app's queries. It cannot bypass row-level security; it may `SET ROLE anon`, `authenticated` or `service_role`. |

and two ways in:

| Port | Through | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `5432` | Postgres itself | Anything; the only choice for migrations, `LISTEN`, advisory locks and session settings |
| `6543` | PgBouncer, transaction pooling | Clients that open a connection per request (serverless functions). A session's `SET`, `LISTEN` and advisory locks do not hold here. |

TLS is required, and the URLs Studio gives check the server's name (`sslmode=verify-full`). A client that sends no TLS server name — libpq before 14, some drivers — connects as the user shown as **User for clients without SNI**, which carries the database's name in it.

**How to connect** (`getDatabaseCredentials`, `GET /databases/{name}/credentials`) answers everything but the passwords, ready to paste, for each login: a direct URL, a pooled URL, a `psql` command, a JDBC URL and the two lines of a Prisma schema's env (`DATABASE_URL` pooled for queries, `DIRECT_URL` for migrations). `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` stands where the password goes.

```text
postgresql://<owner-user>:[YOUR-PASSWORD]@main-<ref>.db.palbase.studio:5432/<database>?sslmode=verify-full
```

## Giving it to a machine

In the machine's **New machine** sheet or **Edit settings**, choose the **Database**, and whether this machine **runs its migrations**. Through the API it is the machine's `database`:

```ts
// scripts/give-database.ts
import { createServer } from "palbase/server";

const palbase = createServer({ url: process.env.PALBASE_URL!, secretKey: process.env.PALBASE_SECRET_KEY! });

await palbase.machines.updateMachine({
  path: { name: "backend" },
  body: { database: { name: "main", migrations: true } },
});
```

The machine is rolled out with two more variables:

- **`PALBASE_DB_URL`** — the database's address, as the **app** login. A `palbase/backend` app reads it by itself; any other program connects with it.
- **`PALBASE_DB_CONNECTIONS`** — how many connections to it **one copy** may hold. The database's connections are shared out among the copies of every machine given it, counted twice (a new version comes up beside the one that serves) and with a migration run's share apart. A `palbase/backend` app holds itself to it; a program of your own should size its pool by it. Copies the database could not serve are refused (`409 database_connections_short`), and the other machines given it roll out to their new share.

A machine's connection is a client like any other: it wakes a database that sleeps and keeps it awake while it holds one.

**Run migrations** (`migrations: true`) makes every release of the machine migrate the database before it serves — as the **owner**, with `PALBASE_DB_MIGRATE=start` before the rollout and `=complete` after ([Builds, Logs & Rollback](/docs/machines/builds#when-a-release-migrates-its-database)). A database's migrations are one machine's: a second machine asking for them is refused with `409 database_migrated_elsewhere`. The other machines given the database read and write it as the app login, and must read the schema the migrating machine declares.

A change of `database` gives it whole: `migrations` left out is `false`. `{ name: "" }` gives the machine none. A database that is not the project's is refused (`400 database_not_found`).

## A pull request preview's own

A machine that runs its database's migrations and previews its pull requests ([Pull request previews](/docs/machines/hosting#pull-request-previews)) has each preview given a database of its own, `<database>-pr<number>`, of the `preview` size: 0.25 vCPU, 512 MiB and 500 MB, asleep when idle, with **no backup to bring it back from**: no base backup is taken of it, and no moment of it can be restored. It is opened empty with its preview, migrated by the preview's releases, and deleted — at once, with no restore window — when its preview goes: its pull request closed, three days without a push, or the machine deleted. It is listed with the environment's databases, counts against none of them, and is not billed. No database is opened at the `preview` size, moved to it or from it, or named `<name>-pr<number>` by hand.

## Passwords

A password is shown once — when the database is opened, and when it is made new. **Make a new password** on the database's page (**New owner password**, **New app password**), or `changeDatabasePassword` (`POST /databases/{name}/password` with `role: "owner"` or `"app"`), answers the credentials with the new one; the other login carries `[YOUR-PASSWORD]`. The new password works once the database has taken it, a few seconds later.

- **Owner**: its current password stops working. Migrations, `psql` and anything else that connects as the owner need the new one — the machine that runs migrations is given it by the platform.
- **App**: the new password is set on a second app login, and the machines given the database move to it with **none of their connections refused**. The old login keeps working until the next change — so to shut out a leaked app password, make it new **twice**.

A change waits for the one before it to reach the database: `409 password_change_pending` with `Retry-After`, and the same while a database first starts.

## The SQL console

**Database › SQL** runs read-only SQL against a database — `SELECT`, `EXPLAIN`, `SHOW` — with autocomplete from its tables, a history and saved queries. It is `queryDatabase` (`POST /databases/{name}/sql`), and its rules are the module's:

- One statement, 64 KiB at most; two are refused (SQLSTATE `42601`).
- It runs as the **owner**, in a transaction that takes no writes and is always rolled back: a write is refused by Postgres (`25006`).
- It has 15 seconds (`57014`) and 5 seconds for a lock (`55P03`).
- It answers the columns and the first rows (1 to 1,000, `limit`), `truncated` when there were more, and how long it took. Values come as JSON: a timestamp in RFC 3339, `numeric` as a string, `bytea` as `\x` and its hex, `json` and `jsonb` as the JSON they hold.
- A statement Postgres refuses is `400 query_failed` with its message and its `sqlstate`.

`GET /databases/{name}/schema` answers what the console's autocomplete reads: every table outside Postgres' own schemas and Palgres', its columns in order — type as Postgres writes it, nullable, part of the primary key, the column a foreign key points at — and whether row-level security is on.

A sleeping database is woken for the console, the call held a few seconds (`503 database_waking` with `Retry-After` past that). A database being restored, or one that cannot start, is refused with `409`. A database runs a few console calls at once; past that, `429 too_many_queries`.

## Changing and removing one

`updateDatabase` (`PATCH /databases/{name}`, **Edit access and backups** in Studio) changes who may connect (`allow`), how many days of backups are kept (`backup_days`) and the database's size (`size`). Deleting one, taking it back and purging it are on [Backups & Restore](/docs/machines/backups#deleting-a-database).

A new size is answered at once with `202`: the database moves to it while it serves. Its sessions on the direct port end once, when it moves, and new logins wait a few seconds then. A change of size is refused with `409` when the database is already moving to another size (`database_resizing`), being brought back to a moment (`database_restoring`) or failed (`database_failed`), or when it holds more than the new size's storage (`database_too_large`); a smaller size waits until what the database holds has been measured, within minutes of its start (`database_not_measured`). A size that is paid for is refused with `403 size_not_available` while those sizes are not open.

| Call | HTTP | |
|---|---|---|
| `listDatabases` | `GET /databases` | The project's databases by name — deleted ones that may still be taken back among them |
| `getDatabase` | `GET /databases/{name}` | Its host and ports, size, `allow`, `backup_days`, state, how much it holds and how long it has been awake this month |
| `createDatabase` | `POST /databases` | Opens one; the answer holds both passwords, once |
| `updateDatabase` | `PATCH /databases/{name}` | Who may connect, and its backup days |
| `getDatabaseCredentials` | `GET /databases/{name}/credentials` | How to connect, without the passwords |
| `changeDatabasePassword` | `POST /databases/{name}/password` | A new owner or app password, shown once |

A database's `state` is `starting`, `awake`, `asleep`, `archived`, `restoring` or `failed` (`state_reason` says why).

## From the CLI

```sh
palbase databases:create main --size free --backup-days 7   # its passwords are kept on this computer
palbase databases:list
palbase db:url main --pooled                                 # a connection address for any tool
palbase db:shell main                                        # psql on it (it wakes if asleep)
palbase db:dump main --file main.dump                        # pg_dump's custom format, as its owner
palbase databases:update main --allow 203.0.113.0/24        # who may connect; --size moves it to another size
palbase db:copy --from main --to staging                     # one environment's data into another's
```

`palbase databases:sizes` lists the sizes, `palbase databases:password:reset <name> --role owner|app` makes a login's password new, and `palbase databases:restore <name> --to <time>` brings a database back to a moment ([Backups & Restore](/docs/machines/backups)). The schema commands — `db:plan`, `db:push`, `db:migrate`, `db:pull`, `db:seed`, `db:types` — work on the schema of a `palbase/backend` app ([Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations)). Every command is in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/reference#databases).

## Related

- [Backups & Restore](/docs/machines/backups) — point-in-time restore, and deleting, taking back and purging a database
- [Database](/docs/backend/database) — the queries a `palbase/backend` app runs against it
- [Schema](/docs/backend/schema) · [Schema changes](/docs/backend/migrations) — the schema a release migrates
